Decade by decade his world self-selects into the fooled and the complicit; he has then engineered out of his life precisely the people by whom he might have been corrected. "They deceive none but themselves" is thus not a pious slogan: it is a precise forecast of deception's terminal balance-sheet. The deception's intended victims lose, at worst, goods, trust, or time — all replaceable. Its author loses *himself* — the only irreplaceable item in the transaction.

**"Though They Are Unaware": The Loss of the Warning System**

The verse's finale — *wa mā yashʿurūn*, "though they are unaware/perceive not" — names the capstone tragedy: the self-deceiver is *unaware of his unawareness*. Arabic *shaʿara* names the most delicate, hair-trigger of the senses — the root is literally "hair," and the verb evokes what registers even the lightest touch. The phrase therefore denotes the numbing of the alarm-system itself. A bodily analogy maps it exactly: there are diseases of the nerves — leprosy is the historic textbook case — whose lethality is not that they destroy tissue directly but that they destroy *pain*, the body's alarm, so that grievous injury is suffered unfelt and untended. The *shaʿar* here is the soul's pain-point: the sharp register by which a person *notices* his own discrepancy — flinches at his own lie, cannot sleep over his own double-dealing. The serial hypocrite destroys that register. He reaches the stage the Qur'an maps in its spiritual pathology of the next verse as *disease in the heart* (2:10) and in its hardest profile as a *seal* (2:7): the discrepancy no longer registers; the alarm is silent; and the victim of the silencing, insulated from the sensation of his own state, is the last person who can be told.

**Double-Mindedness as a Modern Pathology**

An age of image-management gives this verse fresh purchase, because contemporary life has industrialized the production of double selves: the curated profile versus the private habit, the corporate value-statement versus the quarterly behavior, the public faith versus the private contempt. The hypocrite of the verse is the patron of all these productions: the one who manages, phrase by phrase, an image whose maintenance he mistakes for his identity — until the image is what he is, and the director of the performance has himself become an audience member convinced by the show. Two protections the tradition erected against this drift are worth carrying out of the verse. One is the devotional prayer inherited in the Prophet's own supplications for deliverance from hypocrisy and from of *riyāʾ* — showing off, hypocrisy's religious form:

> *"O God, I seek refuge in You from associating anything with You knowingly, and I seek Your forgiveness for what I do unknowingly... I fear for you the lesser shirk — showing off."* (Aḥmad; al-Ṭabarānī, from Abū Mūsā, graded fair, acting upon its sense being consensus)

The other is the structural remedy the sūrah itself goes on to display across 2:10–20: every attribute of the hypocrite is answered by an attribute of the sincere — awareness against unawareness, transparency against two-facedness, one story told to all against a story per audience. The believer leaves the verse not with new data about a 7th-century faction but with an uncomfortable diagnostic — *in which of my dealings do I maintain two mouths to the burrow?* — and the option of closing one of them before habit closes it from the inside.


**The Formula of the Boomerang in Two Books**

The scene of the deceiver undone by his own device is one of the Qur'an's recurring verdicts, and Sūrah Āl ʿImrān restates it with the same closing clause: "Some of the People of the Book wish to mislead you ˹believers˺. They mislead none but themselves, yet they fail to perceive it" (3:69). The structure is stable across chapters — a scheme aimed outward, a wound delivered inward, and the schemer's perception failing at the decisive point. Deception in the Book's moral physics is not a transfer of loss but a mirror: the lie leaves the liar carrying what he tried to hand over, and his blindness is part of the sentence, not an accident beside it.

That is why the verse can say the hypocrites deceive "only themselves" while their theatre is aimed at heaven and at the believers. The audience watches the show and pays nothing; the performer pays everything. A reader tempted to manage his own image — to appear praying, to appear generous, to appear loyal — should sit with the verse's arithmetic: appearance-management is the one project that consumes the manager first, since the self is the only property the deceiver actually controls, and it is the property he is spending.

**Deceit Struck from the Community's Methods**

The Prophet ﷺ drew the practical boundary with one sentence, in the marketplace of Madinah, over a heap of grain a seller had moistened to look its best: “He who cheats us is not one of us” (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 102, from Abū Hurayrah). The case was a handful of wet grain, the verdict was excommunication from the moral community of Islam — not a fine, not a rebuke, a declaration that the deceiver has left the fellowship by his own act. If wet grain puts a man outside "us", the verse's target — the management of one's whole standing before God and the believers by staged appearances — places him outside by every measure the Book recognises.

The two texts together give the believer a working test for his own dealings. A scheme can succeed for a season against every audience except two: the One who sees the interior, and the community that has been told what to watch for. The hadith arms the second audience — the believer who spots the moistened grain is not being cynical, he is being obedient — while the verse settles the account with the first. Between them, deception is the vice that fails in this world and the next at once.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:10

> **There is sickness in their hearts, and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase. They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Medical Verse for a Moral Condition**

The sūrah now names the diagnosis inside the hypocrite: *fī qulūbihim maraḍ* — "in their hearts is a disease." The metaphor is chosen with medical precision. A disease (*maraḍ*) is not an event and not an act: it is an internal *condition* that weakens function, distorts appetite, and — untreated — progresses. By calling the hypocrite's state a disease rather than a crime, the verse hands every generation of readers a clinical model for understanding certain sinners: persons whose moral perception itself is impaired, whose tastes have inverted so that what should be bitter tastes sweet, who labor not under an acute misdeed but under a *chronic disorder of the inner organ*. The Qur'an elsewhere identifies the symptom-cluster the term covers — doubt and hesitation (*shakk*, as in *"those in whose hearts is a disease"* wavering at 24:50), and evil desire's impulses (33:32) — but above all here it names the root illness of *nifāq*: the heart divided against itself, compelled to carry and conceal a contradiction it dare not resolve.

The clinical register also explains the verse's gentle capacity to frighten. Diseases, unlike accusations, can *spread without announcing themselves*. You can look well while sick — indeed early hypocrisy's entire premise is the maintenance of a healthy exterior upon an ailing interior. And disease is progressive by nature: a condition not opposed tends to *advance*. These implications are not dragged into the text; they are what the word *maraḍ*, honestly heard, already contains.

**"God Increased Them in Disease": The Law of Aggravated Condition**

The second segment is the verse's severe half: *fa-zādahumu Allāhu maraḍan* — "and God increased them in disease." The addition is stated as God's act, and it has between the schools the same disputed surface as the "sealing" of verse 7, with the same deep consensus underneath: God's "increase" of the disease is His judicial confirmation of a self-inflicted trajectory, His abandonment of the refusing heart to its own chosen dynamics, and His embedding of the sinner's choices into consequences. The Muʿtazilī commentators expressed the consensus most sharply: God does not inject the disease; He *lets grow* what is planted, compounds interest upon the principal the sinner himself deposited, and names the compounding His own act because every event unfolds only by His leave. The Ashʿarī formulations point in the same direction with their doctrine of *khadhlān* — withholding of aid from the one who expedites his own ruin.

Notice the awful exactness of the image. The disease *progresses*, as disease does; and the progression can remain *invisible from inside* — one does not feel more diseased day by day; one adjusts, normalizes, re-baselines. The modern world has a word for the social version of this — *radicalization*, the gradual slide by which ordinary persons acclimate to positions their former selves would have found monstrous — and another for its personal version: *habituation*, the dulling by which the first lie is grueling, the hundredth is conversational. The verse is fourteen centuries older than both words and more precise than either: the increase is both a natural process of the habituated heart *and* a divine sentence upon it — the two faces of a single event, visible or invisible according to the observer's frame.

**The Punishment Named Twice**

The verse closes: *wa lahum ʿadhābun alīmun bi-mā kānū yakdhibūn* — "and theirs is a painful punishment for having lied." Two observations settle the verse's balance. First, the punishment is expressly tied to *their own verb*: *kānū yakdhibūn*, "they used to lie" — a continuous tense of habitual practice, not a single lapse. The heart-disease is traced to a *practice*, a committed way of operating; the clinical condition is the crystallization of a biography. Second, the punishment is called *alīm* — *painful*. The master commentators note the word's appropriateness to the disease-image itself: illness joined to pain is the body's warning that something structurally wrong has been allowed to go too far. Earthly experience confirms the pairing: the hypocrite's ordinary life already carries the disease's pains — the chronic anxiety of exposure, the vigilance demanded by inconsistent stories, the hollowness of applause one knows to be purchased under false pretenses, the impossibility of rest in any company because every company threatens discovery of what was said to the last company. The afterlife punishment is thus not capricious invention: it is the disease *completed*, pain that can no longer be deadened because the anesthesia of distraction has run out.

**The Believer's Prescription from the Same Pharmacy**

For the reader who takes the verse in its intended clinical use — self-diagnosis — the tradition prescribes against the disease with two compounds. The first is honesty's strong daily dose, sized small: the Prophet ﷺ taught:

> *"Adhere to truthfulness, for truthfulness guides to righteousness, and righteousness guides to Paradise; and a man keeps telling the truth until he is recorded with God as truthful. And beware of lying, for lying guides to iniquity, and iniquity guides to the Fire; and a man keeps lying until he is recorded with God as a liar."* (al-Bukhārī 6094; Muslim 2607)

The parallel structure of the ḥadīth is the verse's own logic in reverse gear: as lying compounds to liarhood (a recorded condition, a *seal*), so truthfulness compounds to truth-of-heart. The second compound is the regular invitation for exposure to fresh air — bringing the interior into contact with what disinfects it: remembrance (*dhikr*), recitation, the company of the truthful (*"be with the truthful,"* 9:119), and above all the daily five-fold standing in a row whose whole choreography is the re-alignment of inner and outer into one direction. Disease of the heart is not cured by denial nor by despair, the verse implies by its reversibility everywhere else in the Book, but by the only therapy a contradiction ever answers: *resolve it* — choose one of the burrow's two mouths, and brick the other up.


**The Heart the Prophet Located**

The verse diagnoses a sickness of the heart, and the Prophet ﷺ fixed the organ's authority in the body in a hadith the community memorised: “Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is upright, the whole body is upright; and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart” (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 52, from an-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1599). The hadith and the verse share an anatomy: conduct is downstream of the heart's condition, which is why the Book can speak of a moral disease whose symptoms appear in speech, trade, loyalty and prayer. The sickness of verse 10 is not a metaphor for weakness but a claim about the control-room of the person.

The claim also reverses the modern instinct to treat belief as a skin. The Qur'an's map has no neutral self beneath: the heart is either healed by remembrance and obedience, or accruing the plaque of denial. 

**The Sickness Named by Its Symptoms Elsewhere**

The Book's later verses make the disease visible in behaviour. Sūrah al-Māʾidah shows its carriers racing to whichever power looks like winning: "We fear a turn of fortune will strike us." (5:52) — fear of losing position, not love of truth, steering their allegiance. Sūrah an-Nūr poses the diagnostic question directly: "Is there a sickness in their hearts? Or are they in doubt?" (24:50). And the sūrah of the confederacy counts the disease among the enemies of the community's life: "If the hypocrites, and those with sickness in their hearts, and rumourmongers in Medina do not desist, We will certainly incite you ˹O Prophet˺ against them" (33:60). The symptoms are consistent across fourteen centuries of the text: opportunism, doubt dressed as caution, and agitation against the believers.

Reading the symptom list is itself an examination. The believer who finds opportunism or chronic suspicion in himself has found the verse's address, and the Qur'an's prescriptions are not hidden: the company of the sincere, the recitation that increases faith (8:2), the prayer that forbids what is shameful (29:45). Diseases of the heart are treated in the Book the way diseases of the body are treated in medicine — by regimen, not by opinion.

**Why the Increase, and Why It Is Just**

The verse does not say God gave them the sickness; it says He "lets their sickness increase" — ratifies a chosen course by letting it run. The distinction carries the sūrah's whole doctrine of responsibility: freedom is real, choices are real, and the Judge's action begins where the creature's choice ends. A man who feeds a fever cannot blame the fever for growing; a community that nourishes its denial with lies cannot blame the Lord for the harvest. The punishment named at the verse's close — "for their lies" — ties the increase to what they earned, the lie being the sickness's daily bread.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:11

> **When they are told, “Do not spread corruption in the land,” they reply, “We are only peace-makers!”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Scene and Its Timeless Script**

The verse stages the hypocrite's first recorded confrontation with rebuke, and the scene has replayed in every century since: someone says to the disruptive man, in whatever vocabulary the age provides, "Stop — what you are doing is breaking things," and his answer is not denial of the acts but a re-branding of them: *innamā naḥnu muṣliḥūn* — "we are only setting things right." The commentators leave open who issues the rebuke — perhaps the Prophet ﷺ, perhaps sincere believers, perhaps even a victim of the disruption (al-Rāzī canvasses all three) — and the openness is itself instructive: the pattern matters more than the personnel. Corruption confronted, corruption re-labeled as reform. Scripture has caught in one sentence the eternal reflex of the agent of harm: he does not defend his fruits; he re-titles them.

**Fasād and Iṣlāḥ: The Book's Master-Pair**

To weigh the verse one must weigh its two technical terms, which together form one of the Qur'an's great governing oppositions. *Fasād* — corruption — is the undoing of a thing's proper order: the rot of fruit, the spoiling of grain, the breakdown of a marriage, the decay of a trust, the poisoning of relations between persons or nations. Its opposite, *iṣlāḥ* (whose agent-noun *muṣliḥ* appears here), is the restoration of things to their sound and due state. The Book assigns the two consistently: God hates fasād (*"God does not love the workers of corruption"* — 5:64; 2:205), forbids it *"in the earth after its being set right"* (7:56), and warns that it can spread from the human heart into the very elements: *"Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what men's hands have earned"* (30:41). And God repeatedly styles Himself and His prophets agents of iṣlāḥ — the messengers Shuʿayb, Moses, and Jesus each frame their mission with the vocabulary of setting right, never of rupturing.

Within Madinah's specific situation, "corruption upon the earth" as the hypocrites practiced it had concrete referents, and the early commentators — reporting from Ibn ʿAbbās — summarize it as open disobedience of God interlaced with the sabotage of communal bonds: feeding intelligence to the community's enemies, muttering rumor and slander between factions, praising each camp to its face and inflaming it behind its back, hedging every commitment the covenant of the city required. This is corruption at the *social* level: the corrosion of the trust-machinery by which any city, congregation, company, or marriage functions. Later Islam's generalization of the principle was natural and continuous: any vandalism of the order God loves, from the breakdown of kinship (*"Would you then, if you were given authority, work corruption in the land and sever your ties of kinship?"* — 47:22) to the degradation of the earth itself, falls within the verse's jurisdiction.

**The Reformer's Mask and the Test of the Claim**

The hypocrite's answer — *"We are only working righteousness"* — can be uttered in two very different inner states, and the commentators distinguish them. In the first, the speaker is cynically packaging: he knows his work of undermining and calls it peace-making, investor smoothing, strategic moderation, because a market exists for such euphemisms and no one may cross-examine his intent. In the second, more dangerous state, he *believes himself*: he has so thoroughly re-baptized his appetite as principle that rebuke genuinely strikes him as an attack on good. Al-Rāzī leans toward reading the Madinan hypocrites' answer in both registers at once — a claim sincerely half-believed and cynically half-deployed, which is of course the most common cocktail of self-presentation everywhere. The man who undermines two parties while claiming to reconcile them; the employer who renames exploitation as opportunity; the parent who calls sabotage of a child's adulthood "protection"; the writer who calls the poisoning of public discourse "just asking questions" — all of them speak this verse's line.

The verse thereby legislates a hermeneutical principle, permanent across time: claims of iṣlāḥ are not settled by the claimant's vocabulary but by God's definition of soundness and by observable fruits. The Prophet ﷺ fixed this test in an encapsulated general rule that juristic Islam never forgot: *"There is no obedience to a created being in disobedience to the Creator"* — and, complementarily, no reform of earth that is defiance of earth's Maker. The sincerity of one's self-description earns nothing when the description is wrong; the honest man who calls poison cure is still dispensing poison.

**Why the Answer Is Given at All**

A small feature of the verse rewards notice: the corrupters *answer* — they are not silent under rebuke. They feel compelled to justify, to re-label, to claim the moral high ground. Therein lies a veiled tribute to conscience: even the diseased heart (v. 10) cannot simply say "yes, we corrupt." The impulse to claim righteousness is involuntary — the devil's party must keep mumbling the vocabulary of good, because no congregation can be openly gathered in the name of rot. The tyrant frames his purges as law; the rumor-monger frames his slander as transparency; the hypocrite frames his sabotage as peacemaking. The universal instinct testified to in this verse is that evil must always wear the uniform of good to walk in daylight — and therefore that an open-eyed generation should learn to inspect the uniform's stitching rather than salute it.

**A Word to Every Reformer**

If the verse's first use is diagnostic, its second is cautionary for the sincere reformer himself. Salmān al-Fārsī is reported by al-Ṭabarī to have said that the people described by this passage *"have not yet come"* — an expansion the commentators preserve as a warning to every later generation, including ours: the category is not sealed with seventh-century names. The believer who reads the verse as only an unmasking of others has missed half its mercy. Every claim of *iṣlāḥ* — in the mosque's committee, the family dispute, the office, the national debate, the online cause — must pass the two questions the verse silently poses: Is the thing I am repairing actually broken by God's measure, or only out of step with my preference? And does the fruit of my labor show repair — reconciled hearts, restored security, lightened burdens — or scorched earth and heavier chains, traversed by slogans of improvement? The next verse renders heaven's verdict on the dialogue — and it reverses the labels.


**The Vocabulary of Building and Ruin**

The exchange stages the Book's master-pair: ṣ-l-ḥ, the root of setting right, against f-s-d, the root of rotting. The hypocrites claim the first — "We are only peace-makers!" — and heaven assigns them the second. The same two roots organise the sūrah's later teaching: the command not to "spread corruption in the land" after it has been set in order (7:56), the instruction that improving the condition of orphans is best (2:220), the verdict that corrupters "fail to perceive" (2:12). Arabic's root system makes the moral polarity audible: the claim and the verdict differ by one radical, and the whole dispute lives in that single letter.

The pairing also defines what real reform would look like, by contrast. The Book's reformers — the prophets — are named as mufliḥūn in their works, not mufsidūn: they build prayer, justice, honesty in weights, care for orphans. Any movement that calls itself reform can be audited against the roots: does it increase ṣalāh-phenomena (truth kept, trust honoured, the vulnerable protected) or f sād-phenomena (blood, banishment, devouring wealth)? Verse 11's scene gives the audit its origin story: the corruptor's first tool is always the vocabulary of the reformer.

**Why Heaven Answers the Claim**

A question the scene invites: why does God bother answering the pretence at all? The answer is in the audience. The exchange is reported for the believers, who must live alongside people claiming the language of repair while practising ruin; without the verdict, they would face a permanent fog in which every corruptor calls himself a peacemaker. Verse 11 hands the community the interpretive key — judge the work, not the slogan — and the sūrah will apply it within days of this scene in its own history, when Madinah's charter-talk of peace must be weighed against blood shed and wealth devoured.

The answer also protects the sincere reformer from despair. Because the Book distinguishes the roots so sharply, a genuine reformer is not lost in the fog the hypocrites create: his work is recognisable by the same tests that expose theirs. It corrupts only the counterfeit's ability to hide behind the word. 

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:12

> **Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verdict That Reverses the Labels**

Verse 11 ended with the self-description: *"We are only working righteousness."* Verse 12 returns the divine finding, phrased in Arabic's most exclusive grammatical register: *alā innahum humu al-mufsidūn* — "Nay — indeed *they*, precisely *they*, are the corrupters." The particles pile up to close every loophole: *alā* is the particle of abrupt correction (plainly: "but no"), *inna* fixes certainty, and the doubled pronoun *hum... hum* restricts the title exclusively to them. Where the human courtroom heard only the accused's self-description, the divine verdict arrives in the courtroom's final voice: the title *muṣliḥ* (reformer) is stripped, and *mufsid* (corrupter) is conferred — not upon their opponents, not upon the outspoken critics of their work, but upon *themselves*. In two short sentences the sūrah has enacted the entire juridical shape of moral judgment: self-nomination, cross-examination by reality, and a final naming that no re-branding campaign can appeal.

**"Though They Are Unaware": The Deepest Layer of the Disease**

The verse's coda repeats the word already met in verse 9 — *wa lākin lā yashʿurūn*, "yet they do not perceive." The repetition is thematic, not accidental: the defining tragic feature of the hypocritical condition, as the sūrah draws it, is *the corrosion of the alarm system*. The corrupter unaware of his corruption has passed beyond mere vice into vice that can no longer diagnose itself, and this is what made the first commentators treat nifāq as more dangerous than open disbelief. An open enemy of an order can be confronted, legislated against, or converted; an agent of decay *inside* the order, sincerely persuaded that he is its healer, meets every corrective as a threat to the patient. Al-Qurṭubī ties the closing phrase back to the clinical image of verse 10: a sickness whose pathology includes the deadening of the very nerves that would report sickness. The believer reads the formula and shudders, as the Prophet ﷺ intended his community to shudder — since the first protective reaction the verse ought to trigger is not finger-pointing at others but the prayer that one's own faculty of *shuʿūr* (moral sensation) never be numbed.

**The Logical Structure of Self-Fulfilling Corruption**

Why is the circularity — "we are reformers," "you are corruptors" — not a mere standoff of adjectives? Because the sūrah is teaching a criterion, not trading insults. The criterion, made explicit across the Book, is the *fruit-test*: corruption is identifiable by what the claimed reform leaves behind — severed trust, multiplied factions, the silencing of honest speech, the weakening of the worship-witness of a community, and the impoverishment of the vulnerable. God's verdict in verse 12 arrives *after* evidence has accumulated, not before. The procedure is the opposite of the scapegoating every crowd loves, in which labels are assigned first and evidence is gathered afterwards, if at all. The reader is thus taught an operational sequence: never accept self-description at face value (v. 11), but also never issue counter-labels on suspicion; weigh the trail left on the earth, then name. The sūrah elsewhere deploys the identical two-step against another seductive self-description: *"And when he turns away he strives in the earth to work corruption in it and destroy crops and progeny... And if he is told 'Fear God,' arrogance seizes him in sin"* (2:205–206) — a scene the commentators paired with ours as the portrait-gallery of the self-absolved corruptor.

**For the Twenty-First Century: The Industrial Re-Brander**

The machinery described here has been perfected into industries in our age, and the verse is the believer's field manual for reading them. The public relations firm retained to re-frame pollution as stewardship; the demagogue who names his demolition of institutions "draining" and "restoring"; the corporation whose algorithmic extraction of attention is called "connecting people"; the bully in the family whose every cruelty is prefaced "for your own good" — each is an exhibitor of the exact reflex the verse catches: the auto-confession through re-labeling. The verse gives the modern reader two disciplines. The first is semantic honesty: refuse to let words float free of their referents; ask of every grandiose claim of "fixing" the plain question, *what, measurably, has this enterprise set right?* The second is epistemic humility toward one's own record: *"Say: shall We inform you of the greatest losers in their works? Those whose effort is wasted in the life of this world, while they think they are doing good work"* (18:103–104) — the Qur'an itself echoes the tragedy of verse 12 in its most terrifying register: the *sincere* wasted effort, the life spent in good opinion of oneself upon works that count for nothing. The reverent reader therefore trains the opposite reflex from the hypocrite's: suspect your own labeling, invite cross-examination, and let the fruit be judge.

**The Mercy Inside the Severity**

Even this most damning of verses carries the sūrah's characteristic open door. Because it is the *unawareness* that seals the condition, anything that restores awareness re-opens it — and the Qur'an presents its own recitation as exactly such a restorer: *"the reminder benefits the believers"* (51:55). The hypocrite who one night, alone with the words *alā innahum humu al-mufsidūn*, hears them as addressed to himself, and flinches, and turns, has in that instant left the profile the verse describes. The verse is not a life sentence but a final summons inside a court still in session — Madinah itself witnessed hypocrites who repented and became the community's sincere sons, and the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to accept their outer allegiance for the duration while God handled their interior (9:101–106). Verdicts of this order belong to God; the believer's share in verse 12 is the trembling of self-audit and the honest work of naming where his own hands leave the earth worse than they found it.


**The Verdict That Closes the Dialogue**

The exchange now completes itself in three moves: the command "Do not spread corruption in the land" (2:11), the claim of peace-making, and heaven's rebuttal — "Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it." The grammar carries the weight: the emphatic pronouncement names them by the very word they denied, and the verse's brevity is its severity. There is no argument to answer because the claim was not an argument; it was a performance, and performances are answered by exposure. Sūrah al-Munāfiqūn will supply the anatomy of the exposure: "This is because they believed and then abandoned faith. Therefore, their hearts have been sealed, so they do not comprehend" (63:3).

Placed beside verse 11, this verse also teaches the reader how to hear the whole portrait's dialogue. The hypocrites speak once in each scene — the claim of faith, the claim of peace, the sneer at the fools, the confession to their own company — and heaven speaks once, and heaven's sentence is the one that stands. The believer reading these pages is being trained in a grammar of judgement: weigh the sentence that will be repeated in the Hereafter, not the one that wins the room tonight.

**Corruption They Cannot Smell**

The clause "but they fail to perceive it" is the verse's most frightening feature. Perjury against one's own eyes is detectable; corruption without perception is a man walking through a house of his own gas, immune by habit to the stench that would drive any stranger out. The Book explains the anaesthesia: the sealed heart of 2:7 does not merely block guidance, it blocks self-knowledge, so the last faculty a corruptor retains — the ability to smell his own work — is the first he loses. The Qur'an's mercy is that the diagnosis is published: the man who reads verse 12 and feels the chill has retained the sense the verse says the corruptors lose.

For the community, the clause is a standing caution against presumption in self-assessment. The people in this verse are not strangers; they are members of the congregational prayer, speakers of the creed, participants in the city's life. The distance between their self-image and the truth was not crossed in a day, and the warning is that the crossing is silent. The Book's counter-practice is the audit of deeds — prayer kept, wealth opened, truth spoken when it costs — because deeds, unlike intentions, leave evidence the self-deceiver cannot rewrite.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:13

> **And when they are told, “Believe as others believe,” they reply, “Will we believe as the fools believe?” Indeed, it is they who are fools, but they do not know.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Demand to Join the Common Company**

The rebuke of verse 13 is a remarkable request, and its form deserves attention before content: the hypocrites are not first asked to believe something *new* — only to believe *as the people believe* (*kamā āmana al-nās*). The entitled intelligence of the self-styled elite is being invited to a simple act of joining: step down from the observation deck and enter the common crowd of the convinced. The resistance that flares in the answer — *"Shall we believe as fools (al-sufahāʾ) believe?"* — is precisely the resistance the verse was revealed to expose. The commentators say the sneer "fools" was aimed at the Prophet's Companions — that rough, earnest company of freedmen, shepherds, shopkeepers, and farmers whose Islam was neither hedged nor sophisticated. And indeed Islam's earliest congregation was ever an offense to the refinement of the powerful: the master complained of the meekness of the assembled, the tribal aristocrat of the social class of the faithful, as the parallel account from Makkah had already recorded of the notable who demanded that the lowborn be expelled from the Prophet's company before he himself would deign to listen (6:52).

**The Sneer as Identity Work**

The linguistic counter-stroke — *alā innahum humu al-sufahāʾ*, "Nay, it is they who are the fools" — is the verse's famous inversion, structurally identical to verse 12's reversal of "reformers" into "corrupters." *Safah* in Arabic denotes not low intelligence but moral lightweightness: rash shallowness, the impulse-ruled mind, the man who cannot hold a weighty thing steadily. The Book does not here answer *contempt* with counter-contempt out of tit-for-tat; it returns the word with a redefined referent. Foolishness by God's lexicon is not what the illiterate shepherd carried; it is what the educated saboteur of his own salvation carries. And the coda — *wa lākin lā yaʿlamūn*, "though they know not" — shifts this verse's closing verb from *yashʿurūn* (perceive, v. 12) to *yaʿlamūn* (know): the hypocrite's impairment now extends even to his epistemic self-assessment; he is unintelligent *about his own unintelligence*. The early commentators note some of these very men *knew* the believers were the intelligent party in others' eyes, and sneered precisely to create distance — the sneer functioning as social technology, establishing the sneerer as above. Every age recognizes the move: mockery as the cheapest available proof of sophistication, requiring no actual accomplishment in understanding.

**Why Simplicity Is Called Believing "as the People Believe"**

The phrase enshrines a theological principle of lasting importance: saving faith, in its decisive content, is not a privilege of intelligence. It was offered first to the ordinary — to the *nās*, the people — and its acceptance by the unlearned was, to the Qur'an, evidence not of their naivety but of their fitrah, the unprogrammed moral original of the human creature, still operative in hearts uncluttered by the apparatus of status. The Book hails as much elsewhere:

> *"So set your face toward the religion, upright — the fitrah of God upon which He formed mankind."* (Qur'an 30:30)

The Prophet ﷺ described the same human constant in his celebrated narrative: *"Every child is born upon the fitrah"*, whose environment then writes upon it (al-Bukhārī 1385; Muslim 2658). History bears the further witness: Christianity's own scriptures record the same complaint lodged at fishermen-followers ("this crowd that does not know the Law is accursed," said its establishment), and revolutions of every century begin among the unfashionable. The believer learns from verse 13 to prize the religious instincts of the plain — the grandmother's unshakeable yaqīn, the laborer's exact honesty before God, the villager's spontaneous dhikr — not because ignorance is a virtue but because *the truth does not need a degree to be held*.

**The Real Intelligence and the Real Foolishness**

The verse draws an operational definition of intelligence that the tradition made standard: the actuallyintelligent man (*al-kayyis*) is the one who masters himself and works for what follows death; the fool is the one who serves his appetites and loiters in hopes. The Prophet ﷺ used exactly the word *al-kayyis* for it in the report on self-reckoning:

> *"The intelligent one is he who calls his soul to account and works for what comes after death; and the incapable one is he who lets his soul follow its desires and places hopes upon God."* (al-Tirmidhī 2459 from Shaddād ibn Aws; some weakness in its chain is noted, its meaning universally accepted and reinforced by stronger parallels)

Under this standard the tables of the verse turn completely: the elite of Madinah — clever men, measured by worldly yardsticks — were spending their cleverness on a trade guaranteed to destroy them (v. 16 will call it exactly that: an unprofitable commerce), while the "fools" of their sneer were compounding an eternal capital. There is no folly like a brilliant mind placed in the service of its own ruin; and no wisdom like a plain mind faithfully steered toward its Lord. The Book will repeat the definition many forms over: *"And the worldly life is but play and diversion; and the home of the Hereafter — that is the true life, if they but knew"* (29:64), closing with the same phrase our verse closes with: the true state of the case, and men *knowing not*.

**Reading the Verse Without Sneering Back**

The final discipline of the verse belongs to its sincere readers. It is possible to read "it is they who are the fools" as a license to reverse the sneer — for the religious to sneer at the secular, the pious at the worldly, in a perfect inversion of the original sin. The sūrah itself forecloses that abuse: the rebuke is God's verdict upon exposed hypocrisy, not a speech-style placed at the disposal of believers (2:14 will show the hypocrites *themselves* as the sneering party in private; the believers' way is *"invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and beautiful exhortation"* — 16:125). The believer's takeaway is instead contempt's antidote: refuse to be shamed out of your faith by cultural sneering, and refuse to make a ministry of sneering back. Hold the plain truth plainly, as the people believe, and let the weight of what you hold be its own sophistication — for as the age-long commentary on this verse has observed, there is no greater mark of folly than a man who could see the truth and finds it more urgent to be seen seeing through it.


**The Word That Cuts Both Ways**

The hypocrites' sneer uses the plural of the fool — "as the fools believe" — and the verse reverses the insult in a single clause: "Indeed, it is they who are fools, but they do not know." The reversal is the sūrah's signature device: the mockers are mocked, the corruptors corrupted, the blind are the ones who can see. The word sufahāʾ carries the sense of light-mindedness — the man whose judgement has no ballast, tossed by appetite — and the Qur'an accepts the category but redistributes its membership. Faith, the sneer assumes, is for the credulous; betting one's eternal interest on the visible world is the light-minded act.

The reversal also anticipates the sūrah's own echo at "The foolish among the people will ask" (2:142), where the same word returns for those who cannot see why prayer's direction would change. The Qur'an's picture of the fool is thus not the ignorant man — ignorance can be taught — but the man whose scale is broken: he weighs the seen against the unseen and always tips the same way. That is a disease of valuation, and it is precisely what the five-act portrait of verses 2–5 cures, by making the unseen the fixed weight on the scale's deep pan.

**Faith as the Community's Common Sense**

The sneer assumes belief is herd behaviour — "as others believe" — and the verse's rebuttal quietly re-describes what the herd actually is. The believing company described in verses 2–5 prays at stated hours, gives from real wealth, and holds certainty of the return; their common life is a discipline, not a contagion. The Qur'an never asks a man to believe because others do; it asks him to examine the signs, the revelation, the ends of things, and then to join the company whose members have already done the examining. The fools, on this reading, are the ones who have never once checked the herd they actually belong to — the crowd of the merely fashionable, whose creed is whatever this season admires.

There is practical counsel in the arrangement. A believer choosing his company is choosing his default settings: the community that prays normalises prayer, the community that mocks normalises mockery, and no one remains neutral under the influence of a room. Verse 13 tells the reader to count as "the people" those whose practices survive death — and the sneer's own logic, once applied honestly, drives the believer toward the company he was taught to despise.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:14

> **When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But when alone with their evil associates they say, “We are definitely with you; we were only mocking.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Audiences, Two Speeches**

The verse gives the hypocrite a stage-direction that captures his essence more vividly than any label: he is a man with *two performances*, each tailored to its audience. With the believers: *"We believe."* Alone with his *satans* — and the verse identifies his private companions with that loaded plural — the mask comes off: *"We are with you; we were only mocking."* Ibn Kathīr transmits the concrete occasion of the revelation with the economy of a courtroom deposition: a leading hypocrite of Madinah, after flattering certain Companions to their faces, returned to his own circle, boasted *"Watch how I divert these fools away from you"* — and instructed them to imitate his performance. The Companions reported it; the verse came down. What the general reader receives, however, is not gossip about one man's duplicity but the whole logic of audience-dependent identity laid bare.

**"Their Satans": The Company That Mirrors the Self**

The plural *shayāṭīn* receives from the commentators two complementary referents, both true. Outwardly, the word points to the leaders and fellow-travelers of disbelief — the inner circle to which the hypocrite swears his private allegiance. The Qur'an itself licenses the transition of *shayṭān* from the otherworldly rebel to human counterparts:

> *"Thus have We made for every prophet an enemy — satans (shayāṭīn) from among mankind and the jinn."* (Qur'an 6:112)

Inwardly, the word names what the spiritual commentators call the satan of the divided self: the whispering accomplice inside who approves the second performance and assures the performer that the first was only strategy. Both referents converge on one phenomenon: the hypocrite's private company is an *echo-chamber*, the social apparatus by which the second, truer audience confirms the primary allegiance. Every double life requires such an inner circle — the drinking companions who confirm your cynicism, the group chat that validates the prejudice you hide at work, the old friends who keep alive the version of you that the new life is trying to put to death. The verse directs attention precisely there: audit not the public self, which is managed, but *the satans* — the private witness-company in which your fled mask is put back on.

**Mockery as Belonging**

The content of the private speech is as diagnostic as its duplicity: *"We were only mocking"* (*innamā naḥnu mustahziʾūn*). Mockery (*istihzāʾ*) deployed *before the right audience* is here revealed as the hypocrite's actual sacrament — the act by which he renews his belonging among his own. With the believers he pretends a creed; with his satans he enacts one: a communion of contempt, in which the shared laugh at the "fools" functions exactly as a shared confession. The social psychology is universally observable: derisive laughter is the cheapest cement of in-group identity, requiring neither argument nor achievement — only a common target. The Islamic tradition measured the health of any gathering by this marker with unusual precision: the Prophet ﷺ said,

> *"It is sufficient sin for a man that he despises his brother Muslim."* (Muslim 2564)

And the Book names laughter-at-piety as itself a stage-line of nifāq (*"If you ask them, they will surely say: we were only jesting and playing. Say: Is it God, His verses, and His Messenger that you were mocking? Make no excuse — you have disbelieved after your faith,"* 9:65–66).

**The Spiritual Cost of Two Speeches**

The sūrah's long exposure of the hypocrites — thirteen verses — keeps returning to one fundamental damage: the impossibility of inner unity. A person with two court-suits of speech must maintain continuous internal surveillance — remembering which speech was given to whom, matching the moods demanded by each room, allocating loyalties so neither audience collides with the other. This is double-entry bookkeeping applied to the self, and it is exhausting in the distinctive way of unstable structures: they persist only by constant energy-input. The believer's contrary currency — *one* speech before all audiences — is not only morally cleaner; it is psychologically sustainable, the only identity-architecture that can be inhabited without maintenance-costs. The tradition's maxim interiorized by every spiritual master since: your public self and your private self are either one self moving toward integrity or two selves moving toward separation — and the verse teaches that the separation will always be cheaper to start and costlier to finish than it looks.

**The Modern Democracy of the Double Room**

Contemporary life multiplies the occasions for exactly the verse's performance: the employee progressive in the office and cynical in his private group, the religious man orthodox before the congregation and secular before his colleagues, the activist morally absolute online and compromising in the boardroom. Technologically the two rooms are now systematized: the public feed and the private channel, the broadcast account and the anonymous alias, the platform that encourages each user to build a distinct performance per audience and whispers to each that the "real" self is whichever mask feels most comfortable. Against this architecture the verse maintains an older measurement: *character is the speech you give when you are "alone with your satans."* The Reformers of every century have drawn the operational rule from this verse: tell one story; if a remark would embarrass you in another company, let it embarrass you *first* in its own. The believer who runs his private conversations through this filter will watch his satans dwindle — since the private circle that must be protected from the truth of the public self is, in the vocabulary of this verse, no longer a friendship but an employer.


**The Two Rooms and Their Scripts**

The verse is a doorway scene: the same man, two entrances, two scripts. In the believers' room he says, *We believe*; in the private room he reports to their evil associates and laughs at what he has said. Sūrah al-Munāfiqūn describes the finished product of such men: "When you see them, their appearance impresses you. And when they speak, you listen to their ˹impressive˺ speech. But they are ˹just˺ like ˹worthless˺ planks of wood leaned ˹against a wall˺" (63:4) — impressive surfaces with nothing structural behind them. The doorway scene of verse 14 is where the surface is manufactured, and the Qur'an's insistence on reporting the private room is its method of showing the reader the manufacture.

The scene also explains why the Qur'an audited speech so exactly. Words are the only part of the hypocrite that the community ever receives, and the Book insists that the rest of him — the second script — is known to God and, by revelation, now to the reader. No community can see both rooms; every community can, after this verse, understand that both rooms exist and that joining the believers' room carries no guarantee about the heart behind the greeting.

**The Company That Receives the Confession**

The private audience is named precisely: "their evil associates" — the translation's word for shayāṭīnihim, the satans attached to each of them. The confession "We are definitely with you; we were only mocking" is loyalty-speech, the sentence by which a double agent proves his membership to the other side. The Book treats such company as a spiritual fact, not a metaphor: association forms allegiance, and allegiance to the enemies of revelation is itself a standing in the unseen, whatever the mosque register says. The sūrah's next verse will show heaven's response to the confession, and the response treats the private words as fully binding — the mockers' own account is settled by what they said when they thought no one was listening.

For the reader, the verse asks one question: with whom do you laugh, and about what? Company is the visible half of allegiance, and the Qur'an's rule elsewhere is explicit — "who have made your faith a mockery and amusement" (5:57) marks the company the believer must not seek as guardians. The private room of verse 14 is wherever that rule is broken, and its door opens from inside the mosque.

**Mocking as the Price of Belonging**

The confession's last clause — "we were only mocking" (2:14) — deserves its own hearing. Mockery here is not amusement but tribute: the hypocrite pays the company he prefers in the currency of shared contempt, the cheapest proof of loyalty there is. The Qur'an returns to this payment repeatedly — the ridiculed messengers of "˹Other˺ messengers had already been ridiculed before you ˹O Prophet˺" (6:10) met the same tax — and the Book's consistent finding is that the payment is never affordable. The mocker's laughter is a signature on the other party's contract, and the sūrah's next verse will read that signature aloud in the only court that counts.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:15

> **Allah will throw their mockery back at them, leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Mockery Returned**

Verse 14 closed with the hypocrites' private boast: *"We were only mocking."* Verse 15 opens with the divine verb *in echo*: *Allāhu yastahziʾu bihim* — "God mocks them." The early commentators confronted the obvious difficulty with their characteristic care: can mockery — a gesture of derision, so often petty in human mouths — be ascribed to the All-Majestic? Their resolutions clarify both the language and the theology. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī explain that the ascription is *recompense in kind*: the "mocking" of God is not a mood but the *fitting return* of their own act upon themselves — the way Arabic idiom permits naming an action by its consequence, or answering a verb with its twin. The sentence means in full: their mockery will complete its circuit and land precisely upon its authors, arriving from a direction they never anticipated — from God Himself. Al-Rāzī adds the experiential reading: the "mockery" is the sustained situation in which the mocker is made to prosper in his false security, congratulating himself on a performance succeeding beautifully — while every door of actual felicity is quietly closing behind him, until the day the invoice arrives from the very hand he thought had been fooled.

That the Qur'an elsewhere employs the same rhetorical form in severe justice — *"they plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of planners"* (3:54; 8:30), *"they have forgotten God, so He has forgotten them"* (9:67) — confirms the idiom: the divine reply is named by the creature's own word, so that the crime itself carries the description of its punishment. Islamic theology has been unanimous on the boundary: nothing is predicated of God that implies deficiency; every such expression folds into the justice of full recompense.

**Rope: The Long Extension of Ṭughyān**

The verse's second clause carries its most exact image: *wa yamudduhum fī ṭughyānihim yaʿmahūn* — "and He extends them in their transgression, wandering blind." *Yamudduhum* derives from *madda*, to extend, to stretch, to give more length — the verb of giving rope. The tradition caught the image with precision: God does not trip the running hypocrite at his first stride against the rope; He pays out more line. The hypocrite interprets the slack as freedom; it is in fact the lengthening of the run before the rope's end. The Qur'anic name for the vice that has such rope is *ṭughyān* — from a root denoting a flood overspilling its banks, the trespass of a thing beyond its limit — the term the Book applies par excellence to Pharaoh (*"Go on to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed (ṭaghā),"* 20:24), the archetypal long-roped man, whose very throne was his engine of ruin.

The image explains one of the spiritually perplexing phenomena of life: the prosperity of the insolent. A believer watching hypocrisy advance — winning elections, cornering markets, crowding pulpits — can read the wins as the universe's verdict: perhaps bold shamelessness does pay. The verse re-reads the same data through the rope: the extension is not endorsement; it is *extension*, and its meter-ing serves only the completeness of the case against them at the appointed jerk.

**Wandering Confused: The Self-Portrait of the Directionless**

The final verb, *yaʿmahūn*, completes the picture — wandering blind, staggering in bewilderment, eyes working and path erased. The commentators pair it with the condition the Book attributes elsewhere to hardened unbelief (*"We shall confound their hearts and their eyes"* — 6:110). It is the state of movement without navigation: the hypocrite continues to *advance* — politically, financially, socially — and yet his every advance subtracts from his orientation. Modern life knows the type at scale: the high-functioning man perpetually accelerating whose inner map was falsified long ago, whose every win moves him faster toward he-knows-no-longer-what. The tradition's word for that condition names its deepest root: the *intention* lost its object, and with the object went all bearings. Where the believer has a qiblah — a fixed direction that orders every step regardless of geography — the wanderer has only the next quarter, the next audience, the next subterfuge: movement composed entirely of reaction to circumstances, eternally improvising toward the mirage.

**Justice Deferred and the Believer's Equanimity**

The operational lesson of the verse, for its readers across time, is a discipline regarding the apparent victory of shamelessness: *do not grade the rope by its slack*. A community that watches the cynical prosper is watching, by this verse, exactly the predicted sign of divine engagement with them — the extension, not the exemption. The Prophet's ﷺ own biography is the case-file: for twenty years Madinah watched hypocrisy occupy the front rows of its own assembly and profit from inside; and the same twenty years saw the slow, surgical exposure of every node of the network — through its own self-betraying moves, most of all its flinching from every costly call. The believer in any age thus inherits from the verse two securities at once: patience in seeing wrong paid its rope (the extension has a term), and sobriety in watching his own small ropes (his capacity to ignore conscience's tug is the same machinery, worn by another name). The final clause of the sūrah's paragraph-series embedded in this one verse is the most quietly terrifying of all: it is the picture of a man *still moving* — vital, energetic, ambitious — already lost, his motion itself the measure of his wandering. The sūrah's next verse will assign a price to that motion: the most unprofitable trade ever made.


**The Mockery Read Back to Its Authors**

The verse is pure reversal: "Allah will throw their mockery back at them, leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance" (2:15). The device is the Book's settled law of ridicule — Sūrah al-Anʿām states it as history: "˹Other˺ messengers had already been ridiculed before you ˹O Prophet˺, but those who mocked them were overtaken by what they used to ridicule" (6:10). The mockery is not confiscated; it is delivered, like a returned letter, to the address on its envelope. Justice in the Qur'an frequently takes the form of the sinner's own instrument turned around in his hands.

For the mocked believer, the verse is a standing consolation: no word of contempt spoken against faith escapes the ledger. The believer is not required to answer every sneer; he is required to remain among the truth-tellers and leave the response to the One who returns letters. That division of labour — the believer speaks, heaven answers — preserves the community from the bitterness that mockery is designed to produce.

**The Rope Held Out: Ṭughyān and the Long Fall**

The clause "leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance" translates an Arabic image of terrible physicality: yamudduhum fī ṭughyānihim yaʿmahūn — He extends them, draws them out as a rope is drawn, in their flood-rush. Ṭughyān is the word for water that has burst its bounds, the image is of a man carried along on his own overflow, beyond every limit he was built for. The Book pairs the image with its verdict elsewhere: "Whoever Allah allows to stray, none can guide, leaving them to wander blindly in their defiance" (7:186). 

The doctrine embedded here answers a question the scene raises: why do the doubled-hearted prosper? Because prosperity is not the issue; direction is. The extension gives the wanderer more road, not a destination, and the Qur'an counts the road itself as part of the punishment for those who chose mockery over guidance. The believer reading his own comfortable seasons should read the clause as its mirror image: comfort without direction is not the reward of faith, and hardship with direction is not its loss.

**The Justice That Mimics the Choice**

The verse's punishment is shaped exactly like the crime. The mockers chose theatre over truth; the sentence lets them keep the theatre and lose the truth. They refused guidance while claiming to have it; the sentence is "wandering blindly" — movement without map. Nothing is imposed from outside that they did not first select from inside, which is the Qur'an's consistent account of divine justice: the seal of 2:7, the increase of 2:10, the returned mockery of this verse are all verdicts that merely stop resisting a direction the sinner had already set. This is why the Book can be both utterly determined about the end of defiance and utterly serious about human choice — the determination follows the choice as the harvest follows the seed.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:16

> **They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance. But this trade is profitless, and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Marketplace of the Soul**

Verse 16 renders the verdict on the entire hypocritical enterprise in the vocabulary of trade: *ulāʾika alladhīna ishtaraw al-ḍalālata bi'l-hudā* — "it is they who bought error, paying guidance as the price." The Arabic is exact, and the exactness is the argument. *Ishtarā X bi-Y* names a complete commercial transaction: the buyer hands over Y as *thaman* (price) and takes delivery of X as his acquired commodity. In this case the acquired commodity is *ḍalāl* — wandering lostness — and the price surrendered is *hudā* — guidance. The item paid and the item received stand as economics' purest antithesis-value pair; nothing else in the entire Book names a worse swap-ration, and the verse insists it is actually occurring: men are executing this transaction daily, at full cost, and calling it negotiation skill.

The commercial metaphor for moral choice was native to the Qur'an's first audience — the merchant society of Quraysh, whose lifeblood was the caravan and the deal — and the Book deploys it with a completeness that amounts almost to a spiritual economics. The God of this sūrah has just been He who provided all wealth (v. 3's *razaqnāhum*); the sūrah will later legislate the purification of commerce (2:275–282) and will describe faith itself as a bargain (*"God has purchased from the believers their selves and their wealth in exchange for Paradise,"* 9:111). The hypocrite is here shown inside the same universal market, making the counter-trade: what God calls purchasing Paradise, he accomplishes as liquidating guidance for wandering.

**The Arithmetic of the Bad Bargain**

The verse's closing clauses audit the deal with the dryness of a ledger: *fa-mā rabihat tijāratuhum* — "and their trade did not profit." The chosen word *tijārah*, commerce, commerce-as-vocation, underlines that this was not an accidental swap on an off day: it was their *business model* — the systematic management of life for exactly these returns. And the fruit failed; there is no reported profit. The Qur'anic parallel verses make the audit explicit with two famous balance-sheets. First, 3:177:

> *"Indeed, those who have purchased disbelief for faith will not harm God at all, and theirs is a painful punishment."*

Second, the still starker 2:86:

> *"Those are the ones who purchased the worldly life for the Hereafter; so the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be helped."*

The tradition saw in the *rabihat* (profited) a deliberate inversion of expectation: commerce exists only for profit; trade that does not profit is not trade but waste. Hence the closing metanoia: *wa mā kānū muhtadīn* — "and they were not guided." Their journey produced no arrival; the market's most basic standard — did the trade benefit? — is failed on their own terms, by the very accounting they themselves profess to live by.

**Preference as Transaction: Al-Ṭabarī's Reading**

Al-Ṭabarī, joined by al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī, glosses *ishtaraw* with a philological refinement that deepens the analysis: the verb of buying here denotes *preferring*, as in the Book's account of Thamūd — *"they preferred blindness to guidance"* (41:17). The gloss matters because it shifts the scene from the exotic merchant hall to the ordinary motion of the will. Every moral choice is a preference exercised over alternatives: an act of "buying" in which the soul pays with whatever it surrenders (time, attention, integrity, possibility) and takes delivery of whatever it selects. Read that way, the verse is not describing only the dramatic hypocrites of Madinah; it is revealing the entrails of *every* choice in which the soul knowingly forsakes the better for the available. The deal is done not in a marketplace but in the heart's counter — a smaller shop, opened each morning, whose receipt printer never misses a line.

**The Two Safeguards Against Bad Trades**

The tradition distilled from this verse — read with its siblings — two safeguards that traverse the centuries. The first is the obligation of *pre-trade valuation*: inspect what you are about to pay as price, and what is actually being delivered, before the swap. The Prophet ﷺ advised this valuation-habit in the moral form of a general education:

> *"Whoever deceives us is not of us."* (Muslim 101)

and, even more pointedly for the buyer-side of the bargain, the persistent warning against trading the enduring for the transient:

> *"The world is a cursed thing; all that is in it is cursed, except the remembrance of God and what belongs to it, and the one who learns and the one who studies."* (al-Tirmidhī 2322 from Abū Hurayrah; graded with some discussion by the collectors, its meaning supported)

The second safeguard is *post-trade audit*: the merciful Islamic practice by which the believer regularly re-examines his account against the only currencies that compound — *muḥāsabah* again, ʿUmar's audit before the audit. The verse's own logic declares what such an audit must ask: not "did my commerce appear to prosper?" but "show me the profit." The hypocrite's capital steadily dwindles even as his activity increases; the believer's ledger must produce visible, truthful gain, or the honest confession that the deal being struck is of the losing kind.

**A Warning Written for Every Buyer**

The contemporary relevance is effortless — not because the modern world uniquely corrupted but because it is the most marketized human order ever formed, in which literally everything (attention, loyalty, reputation, privacy, the body) is re-described as asset and price. The verse delivers its ancient challenge in the grammar the age speaks natively: every day you are buying something with something; tell the truth about the exchange-rate. Guidance is the one commodity whose price rises the longer it is held unspent and whose liquidating yields nothing deliverable. The sūrah's verdict on those who close such a trade is merchant-clinic precisely: *mā rabihat tijāratuhum*. Their commerce did not profit — and against that verdict, in the divine market, there is no appeal, no liquidation window, and no buyer of last resort. The very next verses will take the same hypocrites out of the marketplace altogether and stand them in the dark beside a fire that has just gone out — to show what the unprofitable trade finally delivers.


**The Verb of Commerce: Ishtarā**

The verse moves the portrait from the courtroom to the marketplace: "They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance" (2:16). The verb ishtaraā is the ordinary word for buying — and the sūrah builds an entire commerce lexicon around it: "These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world" (2:86), and the mournful audit of the sorcery-buyers, "Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls, if only they knew!" (2:102). 

The marketplace framing also dignifies the reader's agency. A trade requires a trader: the verse does not describe the hypocrites as victims of a current but as principals of a transaction, and the same grammar applies to everyone. The question the verse puts to every holder of guidance is the merchant's question — what am I being offered, and what does the seller actually intend to deliver?

**Ribaḥ: The Trade That Denies Its Own Economy**

"But this trade is profitless" — the Arabic ribāḥ is the merchant's own word for gain, and the verse uses it to declare the transaction a loss at the moment of sale. The audit is deliberately double: the buyer gives the one commodity whose value never falls — guidance, the map to the only outcome that matters — and receives misguidance, which pays nothing anywhere. Elsewhere the Book prices the same trade in its real currency: whoever closes the trade of "the Hereafter for the life of this world" (2:86) has bought a term of days with his eternity. The verse's irony is precise: the hypocrites fancy themselves the shrewd party, the ones who keep both the community's respectability and the market's advantages, and the verse reports them as the only losers in a market where everyone else profits.

The word "profitless" also closes the loop opened by verse 9's self-deception. The deceiver cannot perceive his loss because the loss is denominated in the currency he has stopped believing in; the trade is profitless precisely from the vantage the trader has abandoned. No fraud is more complete than one in which the victim has burned the standard by which the fraud would be measured.

**The Trade Every Reader Conducts**

The verse universalises by its grammar, not its subject: every reader is somewhere in a transaction between guidance and its counterfeit, because every significant decision trades one good against another. The believer's protection is not retirement from the market — life is the market — but the prayer the sūrah itself will teach its pilgrims: "Our Lord! Grant us the good of this world and the Hereafter, and protect us from the torment of the Fire" (2:201). The Qur'an does not ask the believer to despise this world's goods; it asks him to refuse trades in which the Hereafter is the currency. The merchant who keeps both ledgers honest can take the world's lawful profit and still hold his shares in the next.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:17

> **Their example is that of someone who kindles a fire, but when it lights up all around them, Allah takes away their light, leaving them in complete darkness—unable to see.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Parable of the Extinguished Fire**

Having analyzed the hypocrite with eleven verses of theological precision, the sūrah now switches instruments — from diagnosis to depiction — and offers a *mathal*, a parable or likeness. The Arabic word for parable is itself suggestive: *mathal* means a similitude that puts an abstract truth into a visible scene, so that the mind can handle what pure statement would leave as fog. This first parable is brief and devastating. A man in the darkness of a wilderness kindles (*istaqada*, struck up, set alight) a fire. The verb itself notes labor: the fire was not given, it was *procured* — effort was expended, tinder prepared, spark coaxed. For one moment the flame performs everything a fire promises: *adhāʾat mā ḥawlahu* — "it lit up what was around him." He can now see his camp, his companions, the road's edge; warmth and safety seem to have arrived. Then: *dhahaba Allāhu bi-nūrihim* — "God took away their light" — and the man is *fī ẓulumāt*, plunged not into darkness but into the Arabic plural, *darknesses*, darkness layered upon darkness, *lā yubṣirūn*, seeing nothing.

**Mapping the Parable onto the Portrait**

The classical commentators read the parable's correspondences with unusual agreement, because the passage has already told us whose likeness this is. The darkness of the wilderness is the pre-Islamic condition — moral night, the *jāhiliyyah*. The laborious kindling is the hypocrites' outward entry into Islam: they "procured" the fire by pronouncing the shahādah, offering the prayers, marrying within the community, keeping its company. And the flame did, in fact, produce real light around them: within the Muslim polity they were protected, their property sacred, their legal position dignified — al-Ṭabarī records the gloss that the *light* was precisely what the declaration of faith brought of safety of blood and property and intermarriage. The fire was not counterfeit; the *kindling* was. Then comes the taking-away: upon death, or whenever the truth was demanded at cost — in the battles, in the boycotts, in the exact moments when a confession had to be signed in sacrifice — the purchased light failed. The loaned fire, never truly owned, was repossessed. They are left in *darknesses*, not merely at their starting night but worse: a darkness now advanced by the memory of light — the blindness of one who saw and lost sight being deeper than the blindness of one who never saw at all.

**The Theology of Borrowed Light**

The parable's severest implication is also its most clarifying: *nūr* — light — is not a commodity that can be held without its source. The hypocrites' light was always *borrowed* — borrowed from the community's observance, from the Prophet's presence, from the sheer reflected illumination of being near the fire of revelation. So long as they langer in the camp, they shared the glow; removed from it, they possessed nothing combustible of their own. This is the sūrah's whole doctrine of *nifāq* in one figure: the hypocrite does not forge light; he camps beside it. The Book will elsewhere give the positive counterpart of the same physics — the believer as a lamp whose oil is nearly self-luminous even untouched by flame (24:35) — and it will teach the daily recourse by which alone light is actually obtained: *"O God, place light in my heart, and light in my hearing, and light in my sight"* — the Prophet's own supplication transmitted in al-Bukhārī (6316) and Muslim (763) from Ibn ʿAbbās. One asks the Owner of light for light; one does not squat beside a neighbor's lamp and call it one's own.

**Why God "Takes Away"**

As with the sealing of verse 7 and the increased disease of verse 10, the taking-away of light is here God's deed — and the same theological resolution applies: the One who confirms a man's autonomy in choosing darkness consummates the choice. The manner matters: the fire is not *confiscated*, as though grace were snatched by force from a possessor; it *goes out*, as a fire goes out which its kindler never fed — for the hypocrite brought tinder but no fuel; he would have the warmth without the tending, the light without the purchase-price of belief. Ibn al-Qayyim and the spiritual masters generalize the principle beyond Madinah: every genuine religious experience carries this peril — the first brightness of a conversion, a Ramadan, a great retreat, a moment of decisive repentance, all of which *light the immediate surroundings* — and then must be *fed* by the fuel of continued practice and increase in knowledge, or be watched wither exactly as the parable depicts: *when it lit what was around it* — and no further sentence of tending follows — *God took away their light*. The verse is thus a manual of religious maintenance disguised as a parable of exposure: the light you are enjoying was fed by something, and the account of what feeds it must be settled daily.

**The Plural Darknesses and the Modern Reader**

The image requires no translation into contemporary terms, but one correspondence is unavoidable. The verse is the oldest extant map of a now-familiar modern figure: the person who passes through even a genuine religious season — a year of sincerity, a month of transformation — and then drifts back, and finds that the drift is not a return to the original pre-faith darkness but a descent into darknesses: cynicism about the very thing once held, embarrassment at his former earnestness, the hardening that comes from having *known better*. The parable warns that light once kindled raises the stakes: abandoned fire does not leave the camper where he was; it leaves him worse sighted. The believer who has experienced light in any measure is therefore urged by the verse to tend the fire in the plainest ways — prayer actually prayed, remembrances actually said, the Book actually read with response — since the darkness most to be feared is not the darkness of never seeing but the compounded darkness of *having seen*, and lost, and learned to live with the loss.


**The Parable's Twin in Sūrah an-Nūr**

The fire whose light is taken has a twin in the Light Verse's own chapter: "As for the disbelievers, their deeds are like a mirage in a desert, which the thirsty perceive as water, but when they approach it, they find it to be nothing" (24:39), and beside it the deeper darkness — "Or ˹their deeds are˺ like the darkness in a deep sea, covered by waves upon waves, topped by ˹dark˺ clouds. Darkness upon darkness! If one stretches out their hand, they can hardly see it." (24:40). The two parable-families divide the fate of appearances: the fire of 2:17 at least lights the ground before it is withdrawn; the mirage never held water at all. The hypocrite moves from the first parable toward the second — the borrowed light he lived by, examined on the day of reckoning, turns out never to have been his.

The pairing identifies what the light was. The fire was their own kindling — enthusiasm, the momentum of the crowd, the utility of religion for respectability — and the Book grants that such fires glow. The mirage is the same thing seen from the end of life: effort that had nothing beneath it. The believer's safeguard is to test his light's source before the darkness tests it.

**Light as a Gift, Darkness as a Wage**

Watch the parable's verbs: they kindle the fire, Allah takes away their light. The Book thus splits agency exactly where theology requires it: the creature produces the flame, and illumination — the ability to see by it — is granted or withdrawn by God alone. "And whoever Allah does not bless with light will have no light!" (24:40). This is why the hypocrite's loss is described as taking-away rather than as the fire's failure: the fire still burns; what departs is the profit. The same doctrine stands behind the seals of 2:7 — faculties present, benefit withheld — and behind the blindness that is not of the eyes: "Indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts in the chests that grow blind" (22:46).

The doctrine guards the sincere against arrogance about their clarity. Whatever light a believer walks by is on loan; gratitude, not pride, is the correct posture of one who can see the road. The Qur'an attaches gratitude to guidance and fright to its withdrawal; the parable trains both reflexes in a single image.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:18

> **They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Three Impairments in Five Words**

The description of the lightless ones tightens into a formula whose Arabic is famously percussive: *ṣummun, bukmun, ʿumyun; fa-hum lā yarjiʿūn*. Recited aloud, the very phonetics — the closed-lip *m*'s and the swallowed gutturals — mime the condition named: *ṣumm* (deaf), *bukm* (dumb), *ʿumy* (blind), and then *no return*. The commentators remark on the verse's sound-symbolism: the words themselves feel like a sealed room. Deafness cuts off the faculty by which revelation chiefly arrives — hearing, in the Qur'an's pedagogy, is the great gate of instruction (*"indeed they will not hear,"* paired throughout with refusal of the signs). Dumbness seals the faculty by which truth would be confessed and asked about — the tongue that could have said "teach me" has no speech. Blindness removes the faculty by which evidence in the world of the senses might still penetrate where revelation had not reached — creation's signs (*āyāt*) display nothing to a dead retina. The triad is thus total in its coverage of access: not hearing the message, not asking, not reading the world. It is the parable of verse 17 pressed into physiology.

**Spiritual Disability Is Not Physical Disability**

The tradition has always been scrupulous to separate this vocabulary from the human beings actually so impaired: the Book's own community — and the Prophet's own mosque — included the blind (the mu'adhdhin ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm, at whom Sūrah ʿAbasa descended, being the most honored exemplar), and the Qur'an's word for such a man was never *aʿmā* as a taunt. The verse speaks of faculties whose orifices are open while their function is dead; precisely the able-bodied in sense who are disabled in meaning.
