The Prophet ﷺ supplied the condition's daily antidote in ordinary devotion: the phrase every Muslim prays in opening the night prayer is a prayer about instruments — that light be made *in* the eye, the ear, the tongue — since the alternative to asking is exactly the verse's condition. Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on the triad summarized the school consensus: the affliction is not the absence of the organ but of the organ's *use* — and use was lost by disuse, by refusal, by choosing not to hear, not to ask, not to see, until the choice ossified into inability.

**"They Return Not": The Tersest Verdict of the Passage**

The phrase *fa-hum lā yarjiʿūn* — "so they do not return" — carries the whole weight of the verse. Return (*rujūʿ*) in the Book's vocabulary is the vocabulary of repentance: the Prodigal motion, the re-pathing toward the abandoned way. Its negation defines the verse's subjects as beyond the motion back — not because return's gate is shut (the Book elsewhere shuttles it wide: *"Say: O My servants who have transgressed, despair not,"* 39:53), but because the triply-impaired no longer hear the invitation, see the road, or say the word that would set their feet upon it. The door is open; the apparatus for passing through it is dead. The commentators note the past-tense-free nominal construction: it names a settled state, a condition that has hardened into character. And the two other senses the early authorities gave *yarjiʿūn* intensify the meaning rather than softening it: they do not return *to guidance* — the "commerce" of verse 16 completed with no route back through the market; and they do not return *from error* in repentance. The sentence is elliptical of necessity — each return necessitating the missing returnee.

**A Note on the Order of the Verbs**

The sequence — deaf, dumb, blind — is not arbitrary in the commentators' ear. Hearing is lost first because it was the organ first volunteered to truth's absence (*"when Our verses are recited to him, he turns away arrogantly as though he heard them not"* — 31:7); the verse traces the very disability to its vocational origin. Speech loss follows, since speech is the ordinary outlet of hearing: a man cannot long say what he has ceased to hear; the tongue's authenticity starves on a deaf ear. Blindness is the final faculty to go, because eye-evidence is the most obstinate — the world keeps insisting — and its closing marks the completion of the interior shutdown. The order thus has the shape of a *progression*: it is the natural history of a deliberately unbelieving life, mapped backwards from its end-state. The believer reading the verse is invited to scan for the earliest sign — the ear that no longer *moves* at the reminder, a hearing already hardened — while the rest of the faculties still function.

**The Practical Antidote Written into Worship Itself**

The sūrah having pronounced this triple impairment, Islam's ordinary worship prescribes the daily exercises that prevent it: the hearing kept alive by commanded recitation and its *samʿan wa ṭāʿatan* ("we hear and we obey" — 2:285); the tongue kept alive by dhikr and by duʿāʾ — for the dumb heart in the verse cannot *ask*, and the praying heart asks five times daily; the eye kept alive by the Qur'an's perpetual instruction to *look*: *"do they not look at the camels, how they are created, and at the sky, how it is raised?"* (88:17–18). The verse thus works on the believer not as observation of others' ruin but as a syllabus of spiritual physiotherapy: whatever faculties he still has, he must *use* — since use is the only maintenance religious faculties have ever had. They return not: the phrase read in fear is one of the most effective ever uttered against the complacency of a living believer, for whom return is still possible, and for whom the whole of the sūrah that follows is, in effect, a returning.


**The Deaf-Dumb-Blind Trope Across the Book**

The portrait's closing verse turns the impairments into a standing verdict, and the Qur'an repeats that verdict wherever refusal becomes settled. In this same sūrah, the flock-parable delivers it in pastoral terms: "˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb and blind so they have no understanding." (2:171). Sūrah al-Aʿrāf pronounces it over those with hearts that do not understand (7:179). Sūrah al-Isrāʾ fixes it as the posture of the gathered deniers: "And We will drag them on their faces on the Day of Judgment—deaf, dumb, and blind" (17:97). The recurrence is doctrine, not rhetoric: the impairments describe a state the sinner has purchased, and the Day of Judgment simply issues it in its final form.

The wilfully of the translation is doing precise work. The verses do not mock disability; they describe the abdication of faculties one has. Every impairment named is acquired in the scene of the parables — the man who stopped walking when the lightning left, the man who plugged his ears at the thunder — and the final verse refuses him even the excuse of never having had the means.

**Why They Return Not: The Locked Direction**

The verse's last clause — they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺ — is the direction's lock, and the parables explain the mechanism. A returning man needs memory of the road and the ability to hear the call back; the parables dismantled both: the darkness took the road from the eyes, the fingers took the call from the ears, and the tongue that would ask the way was already pledged to another company. "Have they not travelled throughout the land so their hearts may reason, and their ears may listen? Indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts in the chests that grow blind" (22:46) — the Book's standing invitation to the very journey this portrait refuses. Returning is therefore not barred by force; it is starved by neglect, which is a sentence severer than any chain, and one the sinner forges link by link.

For the reader who still trembles, the clause carries hope by contrast: everything it locks is lockable only from inside. The faculties of return — hearing the warning, speaking repentance, seeing the road — are described elsewhere as functioning in the communities this portrait's neighbours become. The verse describes what refusal becomes, not what the living are yet condemned to be.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:19

> **Or ˹those caught in˺ a rainstorm from the sky with darkness, thunder, and lightning. They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap for fear of death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Second Sky for the Same Soul**

Verse 19 opens with *aw* — "or" — the connector Arabic uses to offer an alternative likeness for the same reality. The hypocrite was first pictured by a fire in a night camp (v. 17); now he is shown under a storm-cloud from heaven: *ka-ṣayyibin mina al-samāʾ*, "like a downpour from the sky." A *ṣayyib* is no gentle rain but a torrential, audibly violent cloudburst — the kind desert travelers both pray for and dread: it can fill the wells and drown the wadi in a single hour. Inside this downpour the verse packs three phenomena: *ẓulumāt* (darknesses — again the plural, dark upon dark), *raʿd* (thunder), and *barq* (lightning). The scene has total geography: above the wanderer is no tranquil night-sky but the very roof of the world in convulsion.

The commentators, reading the parable onto the hypocrites' biography with unusual unanimity, map the storm's elements onto Islam's own arrival: the downpour is the Qur'an itself — rain from the heaven of revelation, potentially life-bearing — but to hearts unprepared or unwilling, the same rain that revives fields (30:48–50; 41:39) arrives as storm. Its *darknesses* are the obscurities of its demands upon pride, wealth, and ancestral custom; its *thunder* is the Qur'an's warnings — the heavy, dread-inducing announcements of fire and judgment; its *lightning* the dazzling, intermittent flashes of its proofs — brief, brilliant illuminations of truth too brilliant to stare at steadily. What the believing heart receives as the mercy of rain — *"and We send down from the sky blessed water, and bring forth thereby crops"* (50:9) — the double-hearted receive as a tempest threatening their whole encampment of interests.

**Fingers in Ears: The Absurdity of Self-Defense Against Heaven**

The parable's central figure is grotesque and comic simultaneously: men caught in the storm *put their fingers in their ears against the thunderclaps, fearing death* (*fī ādhānihim min al-ṣawāʿiqi ḥadhara al-mawt*). The commentators unpack the absurdity along two axes. First, the disproportion: a finger in an ear as a defense against *ṣayāʿiq* — thunderbolts, peals of thunder with lightning in them — is the parable of ineffectual self-protection, the defense-mechanism of a creature vastly outmatched by what confronts it. Second, the futility: thunder is not an attack; it is the *sound* of the attack's vicinity, the warning peal — and to stop the ears against the warning is not to escape the bolt but to remove one's only chance of moving. Ibn Kathīr reads in the detail the exact policy of the hypocrite confronted by the Qur'an's warnings: he does not refute them; he *protects his ears* from them — an early instance of what every age knows as avoidance: the changing of the channel, the boycotting of the mosque's reminder, the deletion of the unwelcome message, the learned deafness towards anything that asks.

The added phrase — *ḥadhara al-mawt*, "in fear of death" — names the lever that moves their fingers: not truth's discomfort but *existential dread*. This is the hypocrite's psychology at its deepest — and the sūrah's paradox at its sharpest: the man most terrorized by death is the one who has double-invested in this world, because for him death is total loss; and the verse wryly observes that this terror expresses itself not in preparation but in *finger-plugging*.

**"God Encompasses the Disbelievers": The Futility of Withdrawal**

The verse's closing clause is its thunderstroke: *wa Allāhu muḥīṭun bi'l-kāfirīn* — "and God is All-Encompassing of the disbelievers." *Muḥīṭ* — from the same root geometrical sense as a *circumference*, a total surrounding — means here: nothing falls outside His reach; the field of escape is *null*. Fingers in ears do not remove the storm; they only deafen the warned while the danger proceeds. The commentators parallel the clause to the Book's other "encompassing" verses (e.g., *"their Lord encompasses them from behind"* — 85:20) and note its direct address to the flight-instinct of flight found failing: you cannot *withdraw* from the weather when the weather is the sky itself. For the believer reading, the verse invites the exact mirror-operation: surrendering the ear-plugs — exposing the hearing deliberately to the Qur'an's thunder, even the fearful parts — since the same storm that strikes terror into the unwilling is, to the heart that has made peace with the sky, the very *rain of mercy*.

**The Storm as Mercy Redescribed**

The parable's final lesson — drawn by the spiritual commentators from its rain-imagery — is the unity of the revelation's mercy and the storms of its warnings: the thunder *is part of the rain*. The same downpour that the fingers-in-ears man receives as aggression is received by the prepared heart as irrigating abundance. The Book's own description of its purpose confirms the parable: *"And We send down of the Qur'an that which is healing and mercy for the believers — but it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss"* (17:82). The storm does not change; the hearer does. The fingers come out, the thunder becomes a summons, and the tempest becomes what it always was: *a ṣayyib* falling on a heart thirsty enough to stand out in it.


**Rainstorm: Provision and Peril from One Sky**

The parable's sky is the believer's own sky. The storm — ṣayyibah, the cloudburst — is the same water that brings the fruits of 2:22, and the parable's terror lies in that identity: the party caught in it has placed itself where mercy arrives as flood. Sūrah an-Nūr shows the same sky working in slow motion for those who look at it with belief: "Do you not see that Allah gently drives the clouds, then joins them together, piling them up into masses, from which you see raindrops come forth?" (24:43). Gently driven clouds are revelation's ordinary mercy; the storm is what that mercy becomes for a people whose only response to it is to stop their ears. One sky, two weathers — the difference is the listener's posture.

The identity also explains the parable's fearlessness before the charge of cruelty. The Qur'an never presents the storm as gratuitous; it presents the deafness as chosen first. A messenger's warning is the rain's herald, and the people who drive their fingers into their ears have already told the sky how they intend to receive it.

**Fingers in Ears: The Comedy of the Defence**

The parable's psychological detail is merciless. At the sound of every thunder-clap, the fingers go into the ears — "for fear of death" — as though the danger were a sound one could refuse. The gesture is the exact portrait of denial's method: not argument with the thunder, not shelter from the storm, but the removal of the warning's access to the ear, while the storm itself continues overhead. The Book has already shown fingers plugged against lesser calls; here the fingers are against the clap of revelation itself, and the comedy is the strategy's futility: the deaf man will still be wet.

For the believer, the verse exposes a reflex worth naming: the temptation to stop one's ears at uncomfortable truth while remaining in the storm's open field. The Qur'an's alternative is never ear-stopping but ear-opening — the hearing that lets the clap finish its work, and the movement that follows the flash to shelter. Faith, in this parable's physics, is simply staying un-deafened.

**Encompassed, Not Merely Watched**

The parable ends with a change of scale: "And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺." (2:19) The fingers are in the ears; the storm is overhead; and above the storm is an encompassment the storm only illustrates. The Qur'an's word is not watching but surrounding — the doctrine the Book states flatly elsewhere: "To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And Allah is Fully Aware of everything" (4:126). Encompassment means the stopped ear never stopped the knowledge; the strategy of deafness was never once a strategy against the only audience that mattered. The verse quietly closes every exit the parable's actors thought they had built.

The word also dignifies the believers' position inside the same circle. The encompassing God is not a distant observer of the storm but the one who sets its boundaries — which is why the next verse can promise that the lightning snatches sight only at His leave, and why the parable's last word is power rather than rain. The reader leaves the storm knowing who owns the sky.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:20

> **It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight. Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still. Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Blinding Flashes: The Episodic Heart**

The storm parable concludes with its most psychologically exact diagnosis. The lightning is so fierce that *yakādu al-barqu yakhṭafu abṣārahum* — "it nearly snatches their sight": the flash meant to illuminate temporarily *blinds* — the familiar phenomenon of night-eyes that cannot receive a sudden intense brightness. Into this scene the verse places the hypocrite's strange, telling rhythm: *kullamā aḍāʾa lahum mashaw fīh* — "whenever it flashes for them, they walk in it" — *wa idhā aẓlama ʿalayhim qāmū* — "and when it darkens over them, they halt." Walk when it flashes; halt when it darkens. The commentators, mapping the figure onto the hypocrite's faith, found this to be the most precise picture of the *episodic religious life*: belief activated by flashes, suspended between them. When a quickening event occurs — a death in the family, a crisis, a Friday sermon that pierces, a Ramadan, a narrow escape — such a man "walks": he prays, he resolves, he reforms with a speed that startles his own household. When the flash passes and ordinary darkness returns, he halts: the prayers drift, the resolves dissolve, the reform is quietly unpacked and put away. His religion has no continuous power source; it lives entirely off the storm's intermittent electricity.

**Flash-Activated Faith and Its Modern Names**

No generation has had more technology of intermittent flashes than ours, and the verse reads like a diagnosis written yesterday: the man whose religiosity spikes at funerals and subsides by the third day of condolence; the Januarist who reforms every Ramadan and repents of his repentance by Shawwal; the youth whose weekend at a religious conference produces a week of dedication and a month of evaporation; the donor whose charity waits for viral catastrophe before it moves. The phenomenon the verse analyzed in lightning we now manufacture industrially — highlights, notifications, alerts, worship-snacks compressed into shareable intensity — while the slow, un-flirty work of *habit* — the daily five prayers at their times, the monthly mortgage of zakāh quietly paid, the unwitnessed pre-dawn repentance — attracts no crowd and produces no flash. The verse's merciless insight is that a religiosity that requires a lightning-bolt to move is *still the storm's subject*, not its beneficiary: it walks only when circumstances provide the current, and it is therefore not religion but *reaction*.

**Hearing and Sight: The Provisional Reprieve**

The verse's penultimate clause deepens the severity: *wa law shāʾa Allāhu la-dhahaba bi-samʿihim wa abṣārihim* — "and had God willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight." The commentators catch two notes here. First, the sheer contingency: the faculties by which these people are still walking-and-halting — hearing the thunder, glimpsing the lightning — are on lease; nothing obliges the Lessor to renew. The present tension between the verses is deliberate: verse 7 described certain faculties as already sealed, and the repetition now threatens the completion of the operation. Second, the subtle mercy of the conditional itself: "had He willed" means He *has not yet willed it* — the door, for the living hearer, is still open; there is still time to stop being the man of flashes and become the man of steady light. Ibn Kathīr read the clause precisely as a final notice served inside the parable's courtroom — a notice whose service is itself an act of clemency.

**"Powerful over All Things": The Closing Signature**

The verse signs off with its first explicit divine name in the passage: *inna Allāha ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr* — "Truly God is Powerful over all things." The name is the logical lock of the whole storm: the fingers in the ears (v. 19) are absurd because no faculty can be withheld from the One whose power has no exceptions; the flash-dependent walking is fatal because the One whose flash you exploit holds the switchboard. But the name also softly turns the parable over: the same unlimited Power that can remove the faculty can *restore* it — the divine name *al-Qadīr* is cited throughout the Book as the ground of both dread and hope. The believer who discovers himself inside the parable — the episodic man, moving with the flashes and halting with the dark — is given by the closing signature the exact petition his condition requires: a prayer to the All-Powerful to make his light *continuous*. The Prophet ﷺ regularly prayed:

> *"O God, place light in my heart... and enlarge my chest, and illumine for me my affair."* (from the comprehensive supplications of light — al-Bukhārī 6316; Muslim 763)

That is the storm parable reversed: not waiting for the sky to flash, but receiving from the Lord of the sky a light installed within the breast, so that the walking continues after the last peal of thunder has fallen silent.

**From Parables to Address**

With this verse the sūrah closes its second portrait-gallery. Eighteen verses have mapped the three human types — the reverent (2–5), the sealed (6–7), and now the double-hearted in full cartography (8–20). The exercise was never gossip about dead factions; the sūrah has been holding up triptychs to its every reader. And having now positioned every hearer somewhere inside the three frames, the Book does what it has not yet done in the sūrah: it turns and addresses all of humankind at once — *O mankind* — and issues the first universal command of the longest sūrah: worship your Lord.


**Walking by Flash, Standing in Dark**

The verse anatomises episodic faith: "Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still." The hypocrite has no guidance of his own; his motion is borrowed from crisis. When the community is winning, when the flash of events illuminates the road, he walks; in the dark stretches where faith must supply its own light, he plants his feet. The Book elsewhere poses the standing question of such people: "Do people think once they say, “We believe,” that they will be left without being put to the test?" (29:2) — the question being the sentence's whole argument, since the flashless dark is precisely the test the claimant assumed he would never face.

Every believer's faith has flash-days and dark-stretches, and the verse does not mock the walking; it identifies what is missing — the guidance that would let the man walk in the dark. The sūrah's own remedy is supplied in the five-act portrait: certainty of the unseen is the lamp that does not depend on weather,

**The Reprieve: Sight and Hearing Still in Place**

The verse's center holds the theology of delay: "Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight." (2:20) The faculties the hypocrite still uses are on a reprieve that the Lord can end at any instant, and the reprieve is not favour but rope — the Book's consistent doctrine of respite, which 3:178 reads as prosperity spun out like a rope. The parables have shown the man refusing light; the clause reveals that his very instruments of refusal run on borrowed time. Every clap he refuses to hear, he hears; every flash he refuses to follow, he sees. The severance he is building toward is entirely available to the One whose patience he is misreading.

Here the verse gives the believer his own corrective. The senses with which he still can hear the call and see the road are the same faculties — and the correct use of a reprieve is what the fire-parable's survivors did with their light: they walked while the walking was possible.

**Most Capable of Everything: The Formula Counted**

The verse closes with the sūrah's power-signature: "Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything." (2:20) The formula returns at the abrogation verse — "Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything?" (2:106) — at the pardon verse (2:109), at the qiblah-verse's gathering (2:148), and at the accounting verse (2:284). Five placements, all at moments where creatures confront something that looks fixed: a verse's law, an enemy's envy, the direction of prayer, the secrecy of hearts. The formula's message at each is identical — the apparent fixture is subject to the One whose capability lacks nothing — and its placement here tells the reader what the storm and the lightning always were: instruments in unhindered hands.

Counting the formula disciplines interpretation. Where a reader might read the parables as nature's autonomous violence, the signature declares the storm's Owner; where he might read the reprieve as weakness, the same words close the verse. The Book signs its difficult passages precisely so that no interpreter can mistake what they presuppose.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:21

> **O humanity! Worship your Lord, Who created you and those before you, so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Command of the Longest Sūrah**

After twenty verses of portraits, the Book lifts its voice for the first time in al-Baqarah to address not Muslims, not believers, not Quraysh, but the entire species: *yā ayyuha al-nās* — "O mankind." And the first word delivered to all humanity in the sūrah that contains a significant share of all revealed law is not a legal ruling, not a threat, not a datum of doctrine — it is the command at the root of every other command: *uʿbudū rabbakum* — "worship your Lord." The sequence is as deliberate as a foundation's: before the human being is told anything else to do, he is told in Whose direction to stand. Al-Ṭabarī notes that this is, within the order of al-Baqarah, the very first imperative of the chapter — and that the chapter's choice of where to begin its imperatives is itself teaching: the longest book of law in the Qur'an starts with the *relationship upon which law rests*, not with the law. Every subsequent legal verse — fasting, marriage, trade, war — will be an application of this founding, orienting relation; without it, they would be mere rules.

**Worship Exclusive by Reference to Creation**

The command is immediately grounded, and the ground is not *who God is* in abstract majesty but *what God has done* so intimately that no hearer can disclaim it: *alladhī khalaqakum wa alladhīna min qablikum* — "Who created you, and those who came before you." The verse's argument moves in Allah's classic direction within the Book: lordship proven by creation, worship owed to lordship. If He made you — your body from dust, your heart from nothing, your breath a gift renewed each second — then the most elementary honesty assigns the direction of your ultimate gratitude, fear, hope, and obedience to the actual Maker and not something else. The commentators call this the *proof of servanthood by creation*: there is no creature who can sit for the exam this verse administers and emerge with innocence — because none made himself. The Qur'an presses the point in the next verse with the household furnishings of existence itself. The logic is so plain the Book records even the idolaters conceding it (*"If you ask them who created you, they will say: God!"* — 43:87), which means the verse's real dispute with humanity is never *about* creation — it is about whether a creature's admitted origin will be allowed to issue its necessary consequences.

**Your Lord, and None Other's Lord**

The possessive is subtle and tender: *rabbakum* — *your* Lord. The creature is not told to worship an alien Owner negotiating from outside, but his own Rabb — the One who has been *his* from before his memory, who raised him stage by stage (the meaning of *rabb* as *murabbī*, nurturer, discussed under 1:2), who was feeding him in a womb whose address he never knew, who schooled his infant heart, who ordered his provision to this very hour. The Book's polemic is framed, accordingly, not as the imposition of a new allegiance but as the recall of an existing one — not a conquest of the will but a settling of an old account. And the addition of *those who came before you* universalizes the argument across time: the God commanding you is the God of your entire ancestry and of every departed soul you loved, so the call carries the weight not of novelty but of inheritance — the same call every one of your forefathers heard, answered, or evaded, and by which they now stand recompensed.

**That Haply You May Be Reverent: Worship as the Machine of Taqwā**

The verse ends by naming worship's fruit: *laʿallakum tattaqūn* — "that you may be reverent" (acquire taqwā). The commentators note the grammatical turn: *laʿalla* — literally a particle of hoping — is here, as everywhere it speaks of God's purpose, the naming of a consequence intended and expected, not of uncertainty (on God "hoping," al-Zamakhsharī's resolution is the classical one: the hope is attached to the subject's attainment, and from God it amounts to a promise). The theological payload is decisive: taqwā is the pre-condition of guidance (v. 2) — and *worship is its generator*. The circle is now closed: the Book will guide the reverent, and worship is how reverence is made. Devotion's five daily stand-bows, its dawn-fasts, its night-watches, its recitations, are thereby shown not to be arbitrary taxes exacted by a demanding Deity but a prescribed *curriculum of reverence* — a training of the guarding-instinct that is the human being's only real safety-equipment for a dangerous path. In Qur'anic anthropology man is not first a thinker who may choose to worship, but a worshipping being whose entire order of flourishing or ruin hinges upon getting worship's address right; the verse commands nothing other than *what man was made for* — as though a great engine's Manual opened by instructing the operator to plug it into the true source of power. Everything else in al-Baqarah, and in the religion, is an unfolding of this first imperative — and the reverent of 2:2 are simply those who heard it first and obeyed.


**The Address Widens to the Species**

The parables end and the Book turns, for the first time in the sūrah, to the whole species: *O humanity!* The previous twenty verses sorted mankind into portraits; the address now steps over every sorting and calls the lot. The Qur'an's largest congregational call returns at the sūrah's fourth chapter with creation itself as its ground: "O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord Who created you from a single soul, and from it He created its mate, and through both He spread countless men and women." (4:1). The pattern is deliberate — when the Book wants every ear, it names the common origin. No genealogy, tribe or century qualifies for the summons, and none exempts from it.

The widening also retro-organises the portraits. They were not classes of humanity but routes through it; the species-address announces that every reader of every portrait is being offered the same next verse. 

**The Argument From Creation, Not From Covenant**

"Worship your Lord, Who created you and those before you" (2:21) — the summons rests on origination, the one credential every human being shares. Israel's covenant has not yet been named, the Kaʿbah is chapters away; before any covenant comes the fact that the one summoned was made. And the Book states the making's purpose in the plainest verse of the creed: "I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me." (51:56). Worship is not a tax on existence; it is the existence's stated function, and the command of 2:21 simply instructs the creature to do the thing it was shaped for. The logic leaves the idolater without his usual retreat: his carved gods made nothing, demand nothing, and explain nothing of his own hands.

The phrase "and those before you" widens the argument across generations. The dead who worshipped other things were made by the same Lord who now commands worship, and their monuments are the sūrah's later exhibits. Creation, not history's majority, is the standing reason; the verse asks each reader to place himself in a line of the made, not of the making.

**So That You May Become Mindful: The Purpose Clause**

The command carries its purpose openly: "so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺" — worship as the engine of taqwā. The sūrah's second verse had already named the Book's beneficiaries — a guide for those mindful — and verse 21 now shows how such people are manufactured: not by argument alone, but by the discipline of worship performed at stated hours before the One who made the worshipper. The Qur'an uses the same purpose-clause for the fast — "so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺" (2:183) — welding the two great trainings of the religion to one output: mindfulness that outlasts the act itself.

The clause also explains worship's psychology in terms the modern reader recognises. Attention follows rehearsal: the man who interrupts his day five times to stand before his Maker is being shaped in the intervals as much as in the standing, the way a traveller's step is set by his destination long after he has looked at the map. Taqwā, the careful mindfulness of 2:2, is the habit of the rehearsed heart — and verse 21 is the habit's first prescription.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:22

> **˹He is the One˺ Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy; and sends down rain from the sky, causing fruits to grow as a provision for you. So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah ˹in worship˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A House Fitted for Its Tenants**

Having grounded worship in creation generally, the verse now walks mankind through its dwelling, room by room, as a steward tours a tenant through a furnished house: *alladhī jaʿala lakum al-arḍa firāshan wa al-samāʾa bināʾan* — "Who made for you the earth a bed of repose and the sky a canopy." The metadata of the images reward exactness. *Firāsh* is what is spread beneath one for rest — mattress, carpet, bedding: the earth is introduced to man not as a battlefield nor even primarily as a field of labor but as a *resting-spread*, stability engineered for habitation. And *bināʾ* — the sky as *built structure*, a roofed edifice lifted over the bedding below. The Qur'an repeats the pair elsewhere with the explicit note of purpose — *"And the sky We raised as a protected ceiling (saqfan maḥfūẓan)"* (21:32) — and the believer's ear catches that *maḥfūẓ*, *guarded*: the roof of the world is not merely high, it is *maintained*. The verse thus exhibits existence as a *hospitality scene*: before man was taught any command, man was already a guest — carried on a spread floor under a guarded canopy in a dwelling he did not furnish, did not design, and could not have secured. Worship, the verse implies, is not first the adoration of a distant Sovereign; it is the house-guest's elementary gratitude to the Host of the world, stunningly overdue.

**Water and Fruit: The Hospitality Served**

The tour proceeds from architecture to service: *wa anzala mina al-samāʾi māʾan fa-akhraja bihi mina al-thamarāti rizqan lakum* — "and He sent water from the sky, and brought forth by it, of the fruits, provision for you." The chain is exact: water descends → fruit ascends → provision arrives. The whole biological economy of the human table is compressed to a prepositional arc, and the arc terminates always at the same word: *lakum*, *for you*. The commentators dwell on *thamarāt* (fruits) as the suqrah beneath the table’s vocabulary — the word standing for all produce, and by extension for inward sustenance too, since the fruit is the plant's offering of itself at its sweetest — and upon *rizq* as the Book's master-category under which every genuine good of life is gathered: air, bread, family, faculty, faith under one heading. The verse thereby encloses the hearer in a single sweeping unanswerability: there is no single thing in hand — no grain of rice, no date, no breath — whose ultimate custody-trail does not lead back to this Provider. Al-Bayhaqī records the Prophet ﷺ as having trained the Muslims to trace even their smallest articles of food back through this very chain:

> *"...then it was said: O Messenger of God, what is the greatest sin in the sight of God? He said: That you set up a rival to God, though He created you."* (al-Bukhārī 4207; Muslim 86 — the report of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd that stands behind this very verse's closing)

**Equals: The Sin the Verse Names**

The verse's remarkable end locks its whole hospitality-tour into jurisprudence: *fa-lā tajʿalū lillāhi andādan wa antum taʿlamūn* — "so do not set up equals for God, while you know." *Andād* (sing. *nidd*) are counterparts, co-sharers, equivalents — namely idols, made-things raised to the rank of the Maker. The closing participial clause — *wa antum taʿlamūn*, "while you know" — is the knife of the verse: it identifies idolatry not as ignorance corrected by information but as knowledge betrayed. The first hearers were not atheists; they acknowledged Allāh as creator, provider, sender of rain (43:87). Their shirk was practical, not theoretical: to know the House's Furnisher and yet to burn incense to His furniture. The verse makes *shirk*, at root, a crisis of *integrity* — the encounter of a known truth refused — rather than merely a primitive metaphysics, and thereby remains freshly diagnostic in any age: wherever the heart knowingly assigns any created thing the Creator's right of ultimate dependence, fear, hope, or obedience — career, state, wealth, desire, self-that-would-be-god — the oldest sin is back in operation under a modern inventory.

**The Logic of Exclusivity**

The prohibition's logical anatomy deserves a word, because the verse privileges the modern reader with an argument rather than merely a command. The argument: a universe this *fitted* — bed below, roof above, service from above, a table set below — indicates one Fitter, not a committee. Multiplied gods divided in dominion would produce divided provision; the very unity of the household — every chain of custody ending at the same Host — testifies to the Host's unity. Hence the Qur'an elsewhere draws the argument to its celebrated point: *"Had there been in them gods other than God, they would both have been ruined"* (21:22). The practical instruction then flows exactly: because the hospitality is unified, the gratitude must be unified; to thank the many for what the One provided is the grossest misdirection of thanks, a thank-you note mailed to the wrong address.

**Provision and Reverence in Ordinary Life**

The verse's operational verse-footings — bed, roof, rain, fruit — are all features of the absolutely ordinary. They are beneath and above every human being at every hour: you are sitting on the firāsh now, carried under the bināʾ now, drinking the māʾ in some transformed state now. That is exactly the pedagogical genius: the Book places the evidence of its claim not in rare epiphanies but in the standing frame of a human afternoon, so that the act of returning to God can begin at any instant — in a kitchen, on a commute, under any sky. One of the Prophet's ﷺ most famous thank-yous was uttered over nothing more exotic than water and bread:

> *"All praise belongs to God, who fed us and gave us drink, and made us Muslims."* (al-Tirmidhī 3457)

Worship, by the logic of this verse, is the un-blinkered seeing of the ordinary; and shirk, by the same logic, is the chronic forgetting that the roof has a Roofer. The verse ends where all the sūrah's verses end: at the door of taqwā — the reverence that the Holy One fittingly receives from guests sheltered, fed, and informed.


**The Same Furniture Named Twice**

Verse 22's household is described again, nearly word for word, at the close of Sūrah Ghāfir: "It is Allah Who made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy." (40:64). When the Qur'an repeats a description this exactly — earth as residence, sky as construction — it is presenting a settled fact of the creation's architecture, the way a deed repeats the boundary-stones of a property. The two verses also share their next move: provision. 2:22's rain and fruits are 40:64's "He has provided you with what is good and lawful," and both verses end by turning the furniture into a claim upon the tenant: the Maker of the residence is the Lord who may be served in it.

The repetition lets the reader weigh the terms. A residence implies tenancy; a canopy implies the open road beneath it; rain and fruit imply a provider who feeds without being fed. The idolatry the verse forbids — setting up equals — is, on these terms, the tenant filing a second deed to the same property in another owner's name, an act absurd on its face and yet the standing temptation of every settled people.

**Knowingly: The Adverb That Divides the Guilty**

The prohibition's precise form is: "So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah ˹in worship˺." The adverb is the verse's dividing line. The tradition has always distinguished the one who sets up equals in confusion, or in the inherited worship of his fathers unexamined, from the one who does it knowing — the Iblīs of 2:34, who refused in full knowledge of the command — and the Book's severest verdicts are reserved for the second class. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān makes the line itself an invitation across it: "O People of the Book! Let us come to common terms: that we will worship none but Allah, associate none with Him, nor take one another as lords instead of Allah." (3:64). Common terms exist precisely because the knowing sin and the confused neighbour are not the same case.

For the believer, the adverb is a standing audit of comfortable syncretism — the private arrangements by which a man keeps the creed on his tongue while giving other things functional lordship over his choices. The verse does not forbid reverence for created things; it forbids installing them as equals, knowingly, in the one office the residence's deed reserves for its Maker.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:23

> **And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Standing Challenge**

After opening the door of worship upon the argument from creation (vv. 21–22), the Book turns to its own *credentials* and delivers what has become in Islamic thought the most famous audition invitation in the history of letters: *wa in kuntum fī raybin mimmā nazzalnā ʿalā ʿabdinā fa-ʾtū bi-sūratin min mithlih* — "And if you are in doubt about what We sent down upon Our servant, then bring a sūrah like it." The challenge is remarkable in its precision. It does not ask doubters to *believe* blindly, nor to admire, nor to submit to authority; it invites them to do the one thing every confident skeptic claims he can do with any human artifact: *make another one*. Strike one sūrah — one chapter, and the Book elsewhere reduces the required size to a mere fraction of the Qur'an (*ten likened sūrahs* in 11:13; *one* here and in 10:38) — with the same observed properties, and the whole claim collapses. The verse then closes the exits: *call your witnesses besides God, if you are truthful*. "Witnesses" (*shuhadāʾ*) here is glossed by the commentators as the challengers' allies, helpers, and patrons — the finest rhetors, poets, and patrons of letters who could be assembled. The test is: recruit whomever you like, pool all the resources genius and patronage can summon, and still produce one chapter.

**Why the Term Is "A Sūrah"**

The unit of the challenge — a *sūrah* — has drawn the commentators' exact quantification: that is, an assembly of Qur'anic discourse comparable in scale to the smallest chapters, some eighty or so words, weighing only a breath — as short as *"By the time. Indeed man is in loss..."* (Sūrah 103, three lines). The challenge thus reduces the burden to its barest floor: not a book, not a chapter of average length, but *something like a dozen verses long at minimum*. The Qur'an's point is that the gap between it and all other Arabic prose-poetry is not quantitative but *qualitative* — apparent at once in a sample of any size — so the smallest fair sample suffices for demonstration. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, and the writers of the science of *iʿjāz* (inimitability) built upon this verse the doctrine that the Book's incapacitating force is intrinsic to its texture: at every scale — its letters, its word-choice, its syntax, its rhythm, its teachings, its prophecies, its fitness with the human soul — what issues from it is of a different order from what issues from human composition, as water from the well differs from the picture of water.

**"Our Servant" as the Miracle's Frame**

Two words of the verse guard the miracle's meaning: *ʿabdinā* — "Our servant." The Qur'an is careful, in the very moment of its proof, to set the Prophet ﷺ on the correct rung: the Book was sent down *upon* a servant; its excellence is therefore not attributable to the man but to the Descender. The implicit argument was one the first audience could verify from personal biography: an unlettered merchant from Mecca, untrained in the schools of eloquence, unlearned in the poetry of Diwān, does not at the age of forty suddenly begin dictating — across twenty-three years, without revision sessions, in texts delivered piecemeal amid war, migration, bereavement, and administration — the most exact-controlled Arabic composition ever produced. The Prophet's ﷺ defense of the event was always the verse's own: I am servant, bearer, and transmitter; the eloquence you cannot reach is Signer #1's voice, not mine. The commentators accordingly emphasize that the miracle lies in the *words*, not in the bearer — which is precisely why the challenge is issued against a *text*, a challenge anyone at any time can take up.

**The Historical Silence of the Challenge**

The verse's force becomes palpable when the responding centuries are consulted. The first hearers of the challenge were the most eloquently gifted community the world may ever have seen — the Arabs of the *Muʿallaqāt*, men who had raised poetry to their supreme art and who now had every motive to answer: reputation, tribal honor, the whole ancestral order, and soon their very survival. Their response is a matter of record: *not one* composed response survives — not a verse of attempted imitation from the festival halls of Quraysh — although the later tradition does preserve one lonely, instructive exception: the mock-"surah" of the impostor Musaylimah, preserved in the books as a tragicomic failure of mimicry in content as in cadence. The silence of the golden age of Arabic eloquence — a silence that chose, at last, the sword over the pen — has always stood in Muslim argument as history's own submission of the verdict. The Book says the equivalent elsewhere in a sentence: *"Say: if men and jinn gathered to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce its like, even if they backed one another"* (17:88). Ibn Taymiyyah states the use-meaning of that recorded silence plainly: the refusal of the masters of a language to take up a challenge that would cost them nothing but effort is itself a confession better than an attempted failure.

**Reading "If You Are in Doubt" as an Invitation**

The verse's opening words are important as a final observation: *wa in kuntum fī raybin* — "*If* you are in doubt." The challenge is *issued* to doubt. Doubt, in the verse's own epistemology, is not haram — it is a standing human condition that the Book does not rebuke but *address*: the Book proposes a fair, concrete, falsifiable-looking procedure to anyone who wonders about its source: evaluate its texts by the test every other artifact submits to — *can the like be made?* The believer inherits from this verse both a claim and a posture: the claim that the Book is unique at the level of its making — and the posture of one entirely willing to place the claim on exhibit. The sūrah will now turn to the other side of the challenge: the outcome for those who, knowing what the challenge asserts, refuse the proving and proceed with rejection. The next verse states it without ornament: the Fire.


**The Challenge's Later and Harsher Forms**

The challenge of 2:23 is one rung on a ladder the Qur'an descends deliberately. Sūrah Yūnus lowers it to a single chapter: "Produce one sûrah like it then, and seek help from whoever you can— other than Allah—if what you say is true!" (10:38). Sūrah al-Isrāʾ removes the ladder's last rung and calls all of creation at once: "If ˹all˺ humans and jinn were to come together to produce the equivalent of this Quran, they could not produce its equal, no matter how they supported each other." (17:88). The Book's argument moves from the whole (2:23) to the part (10:38) to the species-wide impossibility (17:88) — each step making the standing offer harder to refuse and harder to meet. The reader of 2:23 is therefore reading the ladder's full-length form, addressed first.

The ladder also answers the liar's charge built into 10:38 — "He made it up!" — for a forged scripture is exactly the thing a coalition of all speakers should be able to match in part. The challenge's precision is its genius: it does not ask for beauty or length, which are arguable, but for a matching unit of the same kind, which either exists or does not.

**The Historical Silence of the Answer**

The challenge stood for twenty-three years of public recitation in the most poetry-conscious market on earth, and the record of the period is the record of its failure. The exegetical tradition preserves the closest any opponent came: al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, the Quraysh's own arbiter of eloquence, heard the recitation and confessed that these recitals were not the words of a poet — an account the classical commentators (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr) carry as a near-contemporary verdict. His people's answer to his confession was label-work rather than production. The challenge's silence has never since been broken; fourteen centuries of Arabic genius have amended everything the community owns except this text's arrangement.

The verse frames the silence with a warning rather than a taunt. The failure to answer is not scored as a loss in a contest but presented as ground for the fear of 2:24 — the refusal of a standing, answerable test. The Qur'an's confidence here is of a specific kind: it does not silence its critics; it hands them a pen.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:24

> **But if you are unable to do so—and you will never be able to do so—then fear the Fire fuelled with people and stones, which is prepared for the disbelievers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verdict That Forecloses Itself**

Having thrown open a fair challenge and closed every exit of pretense, the Book now delivers the challenge's outcome with a startling grammatical performance: *fa-in lam tafʿalū wa lan tafʿalū* — "and if you do not — *and you will not*." The first clause sets the condition; the second clause forecloses it before the sentence even ends. The doubling is not redundancy. As the commentators explain, the second clause is not another guess about their behavior but a revelation of foreknowledge: *lan tafʿalū* is God's own declaration of what the challengers will in fact never do — not a prediction-sealed suspicion but the Almighty's acquaintance with the hearts of the eloquent men who had every motive and none of the means. Al-Zamakhsharī lingers here: the conditional *fa-in* becomes, in God's mouth, the very vehicle of certainty — the verse is decisive not because intimidation replaces argument, but because the Book *knows* its opponents and states their incapacity as fact. The verse is thus the Book's *summation before the jury*: after the evidence of the challenge, the court pronounces.

**A Fuel of Men and Stones**

Then comes the recompense for the refusal: *fa-ittaqū al-nāra allatī waqūduhā al-nāsu wa'l-ḥijārah* — "then beware the Fire whose fuel is people and stones." The analysts of the image have always observed its deliberate starkness: a fire's *waqūd* is normally firewood or coal — material consumed to yield heat — but this Fire is fed on what ordinary fires do not feed on: *men*, and *stones*. "Men" is straightforwardly the disbelievers, those who refused the challenge and remained upon rejection. The "stones" have been read along two convergent lines of classical interpretation: on one, they are the idols — the carved stones worshipped beneath and beside God (Ibn Kathīr favoring this reading amongst others), so that the verse depicts worshippers burnt together with their worshipped, each a share of a single pyre, the parody of every temple's sanctuary. On the other, the stones are literal stony fuel of Hell's own geology — the sulfur of brimstone or black stones of the deep pit — a fuel of vastly greater density and heat than anything earthly fires consume. Both readings converge on the same truth: the ordinary fire of this world is a mere whiff of that blaze, for this fire burns with fuel no human fire can even consume. The Book elsewhere gives the Fire custody of the items of secular pride:

> *"Certainly you ˹disbelievers˺ and whatever you worship instead of Allah will be the fuel of Hell. You are ˹all˺ bound to enter it."* (Qur'an 21:98)

**Fear as a Command: The Praiseworthy Warning**

The imperative *fa-ittaqū* — "then be fearful, guard yourselves against" — frames the whole prohibitive side of the verse in the active vocabulary of taqwā: fear here is not neurosis but the rational response to a declared, specific danger. The tradition's proverb crystallized the argument: he who is forewarned and perishes has perished by his own negligence, not by ignorance. The Prophet ﷺ made the same logic the standing order of his own nights:

> *"O people, fear God; *man will look on what he has sent ahead of him*... whoever can shield his face from the Fire even with a fragment of a date, let him do so."* (Muslim 1017, from the farewell-era admonitions)

The Prophet ﷺ made the same concreteness famous in the same register of warning: despite *all* the unseen's abstraction, the response prescribed is utterly practical — a deed, a gift, a shield. Fear is made into agent of works.

**The Fire's Pre-Preparedness and Justice**

The clause *uʿiddat li'l-kāfirīn* — "which is prepared for the disbelievers" — has a cold geometric comfort to the believer's mind: Hell is not improvised upon the condemned; it was *prepared*, *uʿiddat*, in advance, as though fittingly and measuredly ready. The preparation-language is the same the Book uses for Paradise — *"prepared for those mindful ˹of Allah˺"* occurs repeatedly (3:133) — and the symmetry is laden: both destinations are *fitted*, made ready for their people, each a custom-made dwelling. Even in the architecture of the afterlife there is no slapdash: the justice of God is measured and the dwelling of each soul is pre-built upon its own works. And the word *li'l-kāfirīn* — "for the disbelievers" — assigns the address: the Fire is for those who *covered* (kafarū) — those who met the clearest of challenges and hid from it in the cave of their own refusal.

**A Sentence That Should Cool Any Sentence Against It**

As the challenge-side of these verses warned the arrogant master of rhetoric with *produce the like if you can*, this verse adds solemnity's second weight: the refusal of that test is not a merely intellectual defeat — it drags the loser somewhere real. The logic closes exactly: he who has not produced the proof of his challenge, and will not, bears the charge of confidence-without-evidence — the precise structural sin the Qur'an calls *kufr*: covering what one knows to be true. The sentence of the verse is thus utterly proportioned and utterly fitting: the Fire is for those who refused to be *answered*, and it is "men" precisely because the men knew — and it is "stones" because, in their refusal, they preferred their stones. The believer leaves the verse with the exact fear the Prophet ﷺ asked his community to carry as reverence's drummed-in wisdom: the fear that keeps the hands from unprofitable trade (2:16), the mouth from mockery (2:14), and the ears free of fingers (2:19) — the healthy protecting fear that between man and the pyre stands no guard but God's warning, now fully and fairly given.


**Hell's Wardens Named in the Verse of the Household**

The Fire whose fuel is people and stones is not unmanned, and the Qur'an names its staff in the verse every household is taught: "Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones, overseen by formidable and severe angels, who never disobey whatever Allah orders—always doing as commanded" (66:6). The verse of 2:24 tells what the Fire burns; the verse of aṭ-Ṭaḥrīm tells who stands over it and what their character is — obedience without lapse. The pairing removes the last consoling fantasy: that a fire, being a force, might be bargained with, escaped by cleverness, or exhausted by its own burning. These are keepers, and keepers who do not sleep.

The same verse welds the warning to responsibility on earth: protect yourselves and your families. The believer who recites 2:24's fuel-formula is being told that his first defence against it runs through his own house — through what is taught, watched and permitted there — before it runs through the mosque.

**The Worshipper and the Worshipped in One Fire**

The Qur'an identifies the fuel's two classes at a stroke: "Certainly you ˹disbelievers˺ and whatever you worship instead of Allah will be the fuel of Hell." (21:98). The fire of 2:24 — people and stones — is thereby explained: the people are those who refused the challenge, and the stones are the idols they preferred, the worshipped and the worshipper entering one furnace as one cargo. No verse in the Book argues against idolatry with colder economy.

The verse's audience is worth noting: the "you" is the disbelievers of Makkah, addressed through the Prophet's recitation — yet every later reader overhears the principle. Whatever is served instead of Allah, whether carved or conceptual, shares the destiny of the carved: it cannot save its servants from the fire it is itself assigned to, and the service given to it is the service whose reward the fire consumes.

**Threat, Then Promise: The Book's Alternating Cadence**

The verse ends on the Fire, and the next verse begins — before any breath — with Gardens under which rivers flow. The alternation is the sūrah's cadence from here to its end: covenant beside warning, mercy beside severity, each given immediately after the other so that neither can be quoted alone. The opening of the promise is already visible from this section's threshold: "Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow." (2:25). The Book does not dwell in threat; it uses threat the way a physician uses the name of the disease — precisely, once, and for the sake of the cure named in the next line.

The cadence also trains the reader's fear into its correct shape. Fear in the Qur'an is never an end state; it is the initial velocity of flight toward mercy. The believer who feels the Fire of 2:24 is meant to be moving already toward 2:25 — and the sūrah's structure, which never lets the two verses be far apart, is the movement's map.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:25

> **Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow. Whenever provided with fruit, they will say, “This is what we were given before,” for they will be served fruit that looks similar ˹but tastes different˺. They will have pure spouses, and they will be there forever.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**After the Warning, the Open Door**

The first full alternation of fear and hope in the sūrah closes on hope. Verse 24 ended with a prepared Fire; verse 25 opens with prepared Gardens — *jannāt* — and the balance is Qur'anic *method*, not mood-swing: the Book never leaves the inhalter of bad news suffocated, because the intention of warning is never despair but *movement*, and movement requires a destination. The imperative of the verse is itself notable: *wa bashshir* — "*give glad tidings*," spoken to the Prophet ﷺ. The messenger is commanded not only to warn but to *announce* — his ministry's content is, in half of its own self-description, *bashīr* (bearer of good news) as much as *nadhīr* (warner). And the recipients of the announcement are not the spiritually eminent but *those who believe and work righteousness* — the two plain verbs of the entire religion joined by "and": conviction and conduct, faith and fruit.

The tidings are first delivered in one sweeping noun: *jannātun tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār* — *gardens with rivers running beneath them.* The commentators catch the image's exact geography (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī): the rivers run *below* the gardens — the water is not stagnant marsh on the level, but flowing streams *beneath* the elevation of groves and palaces. In the desert hearer's imagination nothing declared irreversible abundance like moving water *under* the gardens: in Arabia, water was the one permanent precondition of any garden, and here it is assured *permanently flowing*. The image's core message is *security of abundance*: the dweller of this garden will never again know drought.

**The Fruit That Is Both Familiar and New**

The verse's subtlest gift comes in its account of the garden's fruit: *kullamā ruziqū minhā min thamaratin rizqan qālū hādhā alladhī ruziqnā min qablu* — "Every time they are provisioned from it with a fruit, they say: 'This is what we were provisioned with aforetime (in the world)'" — and the Book adds: *wa utū bihi mutashābihan* — "and it is brought to them in resemblance." The commentators unfold two riches here. First, a theology of *continuity*: the dweller of Paradise *recognizes* the fruits — they bear the same names as the figs, dates, and pomegranates of earth — because the life of the world is not abolished in the Hereafter; it is *translated*, carried over in identity of kind and transcended in experience. The verse dismisses the anxious thought that the unknown life to come annihilates every familiar joy: the names remain; the reality exceeds. Second, a law of *resemblance with difference*: *mutashābih* — the fruits resemble one another and their earthly namesakes in form, but differ in taste and transcending perfection — explained by the commentators variously as: same appearance with ever-novel flavor; or identical excellence across all fruits, none inferior; or the resemblance is itself increasing delight at each reception, since the "remembrance" of the worldly fruit is renewed with every taste, multiplied by the comparison with the garden's far-surpassing reality. Ibn Kathīr's celebrated reduction is: nothing is common between the fruits of the world and the Garden's but the names.

The spiritual meaning is easily brought home: the believer's habits in this world — his patience, his fasts, his charity, his interior fight — are not *erased* by heaven but are *there fulfilled*: his life's many small obediences will return to him there as provisions whose names he recognizes and whose taste is God's finished answer to their unfinished labor in the world.

**Spouses Made Pure and the Permission to Enjoy**

The verse next answers perhaps the most-asked question about the Afterlife in every sincere circle: *wa lahum fīhā azwājun muṭahharah* — "and for them therein are spouses made pure." The commentators explain the purity in both physical and moral registers: freed from the impurities the world couples to intimacy — menstruation, excreta, illness, distasteful blemish of body or conduct — the companionship of the Garden is *delight without repugnance*. The tradition has always treated this verse with pastoral gentleness against a certain false piety: God presents bodily companionship of the highest and purest order as part — not the totality, but a real part — of the highest reward, sanctioning thereby the human hunger for pure intimacy as *holy in its end*, not shameful. The joy of the Garden is spiritual and *does not flee the human form*: it is the human condition finally innocent, finally unashamed, finally whole.

The language of permanence then crowns the whole: *wa hum fīhā khālidūn* — "and therein they shall abide." Abiding (*khulūd*) is the Book's word for that perfect absence of endings — the very thing everyone in this world most wants after wanting the immediate goods. Every human eros — for pleasure, for intimacy, for rest, for home — is at last answered by the one thing this world could never add to any of them: *it does not end*.

**The Use of the Tidings in This Life**

The practical Prophet ﷺ built this verse into the believer's ordinary psychology with his most famous consoling hadith. When the Companions once trembled at the mention of the world-passing away:

> *"God says: I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has never occurred to a human heart."* (al-Bukhārī 3244; Muslim 2824 — the ḥadīth qudsī commentators constantly pair with this verse)

And, at the other pole of daily consolation, he ﷺ taught the *satisfaction-with-a-fragment*: what one sends forward of good deeds, though they are worth nothing in this world, compounds into the Garden's abundance. The believer of every age, living in an interval of famine or plague or the crushing ordinariness of labor, prays this verse when his tanks are empty — and in so doing obeys the command: receive the glad tidings.


**The Tidings and What They Are Made Of**

The sūrah's first promise arrives in the imperative — "Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good" (2:25) — and the good news is described with the restraint of an eyewitness rather than the excess of a salesman: "Gardens under which rivers flow." (2:25) The description returns, nearly whole, in Sūrah Āl ʿImrān: "Those mindful ˹of Allah˺ will have Gardens with their Lord under which rivers flow, to stay there forever, and pure spouses" (3:15). Beyond the description the Book declines to go; the Prophet ﷺ was told in a report the community learned early that the reward contains what no creature has sampled: “I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no heart of man has conceived” (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2824, from Abū Hurayrah).

The verse ties the tidings to two works only — believing and doing good — which is the sūrah's own five-act portrait compressed to a formula. No lineage qualifies, no wealth purchases, no eloquence substitutes. The promise is the first the Book issues in order, and its recipients are defined exactly as the guided of verse 5 were defined; the reader who matched the earlier portrait already knows whether the verse is addressed to him.

**Recognition Without Satiation**

The parable's psychology is the most human thing in the passage: whenever provided with fruit they will say that it is what they were given before — "for they will be served fruit that looks similar ˹but tastes different˺" (2:25). Memory and novelty are balanced to the grain — the fruit resembles what memory holds, and exceeds it in every mouthful. Earth's pleasures decay by repetition; the appetite dies of familiarity. The Garden is built on the opposite arithmetic: "eternal is its fruit as well as its shade" (13:35) — supply without exhaustion, freshness without the loss of the known. The believer's experience of worship already runs on this currency: the prayer repeated daily for decades never tastes of yesterday.

The closing clauses complete the offer: "They will have pure spouses, and they will be there forever." Purity is the word's work — companionship with nothing of earth's mixed motives in it — and permanence is the verse's last word, the one property no created joy has ever had. Every love of this world carries an expiry the lovers refuse to read; the verse offers the one companionship and the one residence with no term set.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:26

> **Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito or what is even smaller. As for the believers, they know that it is the truth from their Lord. And as for the disbelievers, they argue, “What does Allah mean by such a parable?” Through this ˹test˺, He leaves many to stray, and guides many. And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious—**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Divine Freedom to Illustrate through the Small**

This verse came down as an answer to a sneer. The commentators report its occasions in three overlapping accounts — the hypocrites mocking the parables issued against them (vv. 17–20), some People of the Book scoffing that a God who employs a fly (22:73) or a spider (29:41) in His argument must lack dignity, or the idolaters voicing the same objection. The response cuts at the sneer's premise: *lā yastaḥyī Allāhu an yaḍriba mathalan* — "God is not ashamed to strike a parable." The verb *yaḍriba mathalan* (hurling an example) is the Book's technical idiom for sacred pedagogy — the embedding of an eternal truth in a familiar scene. The verse teaches that the dignity of a proof lies in its truth, not in the social prestige of its materials. A teacher who refuses to explain through humble things reserves truth for the observation decks of the self-styled respectable; God, for whom the gnat and the galaxy are equally creatures, speaks through whatever instructs. That this pedagogy occasions no embarrassment is put into the Prophet's own idiom elsewhere:

> *"Indeed, God is not ashamed of the truth (al-ḥaqq)."* (al-Bukhārī 130; Muslim 317)

The Prophetic phrase belongs to a different passage of law, but the principle is one: truth outranks ceremony wherever it appears.

**Why a Gnat? The Greatness of the Negligible**

The selection of *baʿūḍah* — the gnat, the midge, among the least prestigious of visible creatures, "or what is smaller still" (*mā fawqahā*, understood by al-Rāzī and others as "what is beyond it in smallness") — is not a concession but an argument. The Qur'an repeatedly forces the hearer's gaze down the scale of being, because the wonder of creation is not concentrated at the top: the fly whose manufacture *all the false gods together cannot imitate* (22:73), the spider's deceptively engineered but structurally flimsy house (29:41), the ant with a queen, a nation, and an organized economy (27:18), the bee with a divine coordination called *waḥy* (16:68). A modern age that has put gnats under electron microscopes has only confirmed inside the parable's premise: the "negligible" creature, magnified, displays engineering of humbling sophistication — wing-mechanics, sensory arrays, chemical signaling — none of it assembled by the gnat. The smallest datum is, for the honest observer, the largest question: *who equipped this?* The one too proud to wonder at the small has thereby testified that his pride functions as an eclipse of the Real — the very condition the sūrah has been diagnosing since verse 6.

**One Parable, Two Harvests**

The verse's central theological disclosure comes next: the same parable *guides many and misleads many* — *yuḍillu bihī kathīran wa yahdī bihī kathīran*. The operative teaching is that revelation is not rendered inert by refusal: heard and refused, it *advances* the refusal into ruin. The Book presses the same nonlinear truth elsewhere — *"it increases some of them in faith"*, *"it increases them in foulness unto their foulness"* (9:124–125) — exactly as rain is a single water and yet, falling on different soils, yields from one a harvest and from another a crop of thorns. The creative/constitutive character of the Qur'an's address is here: the parable reveals the hearer. Believers, encountering the gnat-parable, *know it is the truth from their Lord* — not because the parable came with a certificate, but because their hearts are pliant enough to be taught by whatever comes from God; disbelievers respond with the dismissive question — *"What did God mean by this?"* — which the Book records as itself the symptom, not a request for explanation. The reaction *is* the diagnosis; the parable, which does not change, is the litmus by which hearts disclose their nature.

**"He Misleads None but the Iniquitous": The Boundary of Misguidance**

The verse ends with the guard-rail the theologians never allowed themselves to lose: *wa mā yuḍillu bihī illā al-fāsiqīn* — "and He misleads by it none but the iniquitous." *Fīsq* — the root being, in Arabic idiom, the date's emerging from its skin, the pebble's slipping from the fingers — names moral *egress*: the fāsiq is one who has *broken out* of obedience's enclosure. The qualified clause thus bounds the agency of divine misleading to a subject predisposed by his own prior exits; God does not mislead the uncommitted and the seeking, but those who have already broken fidelity. As with the seal (2:7) and the disease (2:10), divine action follows the human initiation, confirming and completing what the creature chose. The tradition's systematic theologians (Ashʿarite and Māturīdī alike) hold this as the settled boundary: guidance and misguidance are both divine acts, but misguidance is never first; it is always *an answer*, judicial and real, to a preceding human abandonment. Understood this way, the gnat-parable functions as a warning-sign posted at theology's sharpest corner: do not ask what God meant by the small things — ask, urgently, why you are the sort of person who finds it satisfying to ask.


**Every Kind of Lesson: The Parable's Charter**

The verse opens with a divine disclaimer of fastidiousness: "Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito or what is even smaller." (2:26) The embarrassment is the audience's, not the Speaker's, and the Book later states the principle the disclaimer rests on: "We have certainly set forth every ˹kind of˺ lesson for people in this Quran, so perhaps they will be mindful" (39:27). A revelation that claims to address every mind must be free to illustrate at every scale; a message that spoke only in the grand would abandon the servant as thoroughly as one that spoke only in the small. The mosquito-parable is thus not a lapse in dignity but a claim about where dignity comes from: from truth fitting its subject, whatever the subject weighs.

The scale of the illustration also serves the verse's polemic target. An audience that demanded marvels could always excuse its unbelief as fastidiousness; the Book removes the excuse by making the smallest creature carry the decisive fork. The test is no longer whether the example impresses but whether the hearer will be taught by it.

**The Fork in the Verse's Middle**

"Through this ˹test˺, He leaves many to stray, and guides many." The parable does not merely decorate the divide already drawn between the reverent and the sealed; it manufactures the divide, in real time, in the hearer. The believers hear the mosquito and know "that it is the truth from their Lord"; the disbelievers hear it and ask, "What does Allah mean by such a parable?" — the scoffing question of men who have decided that whatever puzzles them cannot be meant. One illustration, two harvests, and the harvest reveals the ground it fell on.

Every reader of the sūrah stands somewhere on this fork. The psychology is familiar enough from ordinary instruction: the student who wants to learn asks the small question until it opens; the student who wants to scoff asks it only to close it. The verse's promise is that no one meets the parable neutrally — the hearing itself sorts the hearer, which is why the same Book softens and hardens in the same week of reading.

**None to Stray Except the Rebellious**

The verse guards its doctrine with a boundary clause: "And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious." (2:26) The straying of the previous clause is therefore never arbitrary; it is the destiny of a character already chosen — the fāsiq, the one who breaks through the limit the way water breaks a bank. The Qur'an elsewhere refuses the fatalist reading in the plainest terms (29:2): do people think that once they say *We believe* they will be left without being put to the test? — testing, guiding and leaving are all responses to conduct, not decrees before conduct. Verse 26's fork is planted where the rebellion is, not where fate deals.

The clause also consoles the teacher. The caller to Islam watches some listeners grow softer and others harder at the same words, and the Book explains the divergence without blaming the call: the parable finds each hearer as his own rebellion or receptivity made him. The messenger sows; the ground answers for itself.
