## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:27

> **those who violate Allah’s covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained, and spread corruption in the land. It is they who are the ˹true˺ losers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Covenant and Its Breach**

The sūrah now names the iniquitous of verse 26 by their characteristic operations — three verbs that describe not occasional lapses but a settled method of being: *yanquḍūna ʿahda Allāhi min baʿdi mīthāqih* — "they break God's covenant after its solemn binding." The double noun — *ʿahd* (the agreement) and *mīthāq* (the solemn confirming, from a root of strength and thickness) — marks a covenant already contracted and then *re-inforced*, so that its breach is a breach at the deepest level of commitment recognized in Arabic. The commentators read the referred covenant across three classical lines of interpretation, all ultimately one: the primordial covenant disclosed to every human soul before embodiment — *"And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their progeny, and made them testify concerning themselves: 'Am I not your Lord?' They said: 'Yes, we testify'"* (7:172), whose breaking is every refusal of innate monotheism; or, in the nearer history of the Arabs, the solemn oaths they swore that were a messenger ever sent to them they would follow him more readily than any former community (35:42) — followed by the Messenger's arrival and their refusal of him; or, for the People of the Book, the standing covenant to safeguard the revelation entrusted to them and to recognize and support the prophet it foretold. All three are the Book's one pattern: a solemn bond with the Divine, ratified, then torn open.

The tradition holds the operative principle plainly: showing up for the covenant is the believer's only description of himself, and half-measures are not mentioned. God prescribed that testimony and shrank it into the most binding word Arabic has for the human condition — *fitrah* — so that breach of covenant is breach of the covenant *of being human*.

**Severing What God Commanded Be Joined**

The second verb moves from the vertical bond with God to the horizontal fabric of creation: *wa yaqṭaʿūna mā amara Allāhu bihī an yūṣal* — "and they sever what God has commanded to be joined." The passive construction — what God "has commanded *that it be joined*" — is broad enough for the classical commentators to bring under it, legitimately, several orders of obligation, and al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr note them all: the ties of kinship — *arḥām* — which the Book explicitly places in the register of God's command: *"Fear God, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs (arḥām)"* (4:1), and whose severance the Book names the veritable definition of the corrupt — *"would you then, if you were turned away, spread corruption in the earth and sever your family ties?"* (47:22); the joining of faith to practice, of this life to its sequel — severed in the hypocrite's systematic dual bookkeeping; the joining of the community's members around the covenant, of which severance is precisely the fasad of verses 11–12; even the joining of Muslim to Jew through shared kinship — al-Mawardī and others noting that the Arabs and the children of Isaac were kin — and the joining of every soul to the fellowship of the prophets across time. In the Book's own taxonomy of social evils, *severance* is the common element; in its taxonomy of goods, *joining* (*ṣilah*) is the master-word — whence the womb-tie is *ṣilat al-raḥim*; whence the Prophet ﷺ reordered heaven's arithmetic around this single social fact:

> *"The womb (raḥim) is suspended from the Throne, saying: Whoever joins me, God will join him; and whoever severs me, God will sever him."* (al-Bukhārī 5988; Muslim 2554)

The hyperbole-defying claim of that report — a bond that binds the human family being joined to the throne of God — is how seriously the religion takes the anti-severance of verse 27.

**Corruption upon the Earth as the Third Operation**

The third clause rounds the three-vocal chord: *wa yufsidūna fī al-arḍ* — "and they work corruption upon the earth." The verse thus gathers in one sentence the three orientations of wrong the sūrah has already exhibited in the hypocrites: toward God (breach of covenant), toward fellow-creatures (severance of bonds), and toward the general theater of life (spreading fasād). The corruption clause makes one further connection explicit: earth-wide mischief is not a separate species of sin but the *fruit* of covenant-breach and bond-severance. A civilization of persons keeping their vertical and horizontal bonds does not produce fasād; fasād is what flows from the shattered junctions upstream. The classical commentators accordingly read earth-wide corruption as the *syndrome* whose root causes are the broken covenant and severed bonds, not as a local disease.

**"It Is They Who Are the Losers": The Commerce Completed**

The verse's sentence — *ulāʾika hum al-khāsirūn* — deploys the restrictive formula met at 2:5 (*they alone*), now reversed from felicity to forfeiture. *Khusr* — loss — is the commerce-word the Book uses as the summative opposite of faith's profit (cf. 2:16 and the transactions of loss in 35:39; 39:15; 45:5). *Khāsirūn* is also better translated "the bereft" than merely "the bankrupt": the loser in the Book loses at last the one thing he could not replace — himself, his Hereafter, his true gain. And perhaps the precise weighting the verse gives the three operations is its final lesson: God's accounting does not isolate the *spectacle-sin* (the fasād that makes headlines) while overlooking the quiet breach of covenant and the unwitnessed severing of kin; the eternal ledger counts all three operations as one compound loss, and it enters the loss in the account of the *agent*, not of the spectacle. For the ordinary Muslim reader, the verse is a single-page invoice: any untreated covenant-breach — prayer abandoned, promise to God lapsed — plus any open kinship wound — plus a tolerating attitude toward mischief — and the account is already running at a loss.


**The Kinship Tie the Book Defends Everywhere**

The middle crime of this verse — breaking "whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained" — names the duty the Prophet ﷺ made a promise of provision: “Whoever wishes that his provision be expanded and his life be extended, let him maintain ties of kinship” (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2067; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2557, from Anas ibn Mālik). The tie is not sentimentality in the Book's law; it is a covenant of its own, wired into sustenance and time. The verse's lossers — the truly lost — are defined first by covenant-breaking with God and then by tie-severing with kin, and the order is itself teaching: the two breaches are one reflex seen from two angles, faithlessness toward the Giver and faithlessness toward His distribution of relatives.

The modern household supplies the parable's applications without effort. Kin severed over inheritance, aged parents rationed to a quarterly call, cousins known only as disputes — the verse refuses to file these as private style. A community is a lattice of obligations God has ordered joined; the verse names the man who cuts lattice-lines a corruptor, whatever his mosque-adjacency.

**Why the Three Crimes Travel Together**

Covenant-breaking, tie-severing and corruption of the land are listed in one breath, and the breath is the argument: the three are one syndrome at three scales. The covenant is the tie above; the kinship tie is the covenant's local branch; the corrupted land is what remains when both are cut. Sūrah ar-Raʿd lists the same trio as one people's biography (13:25), and the Book's consistent pattern is that no man keeps the vertical covenant while cutting the horizontal one for long — the faith that will not honour God's bonds will not honour His placement of brothers, and the wreckage lands in the visible world. "It is they who are the ˹true˺ losers" — the commerce-word closes the portrait, the man having severed the only relationships that could have profited him.

The verse therefore gives the believer a diagnostic trio for any age of breakdown, including his own. Where covenants dissolve, check the kinships; where kinships are cut, expect the land itself to show it. Repair runs the same road in reverse, which is why the Book's social teachings — the orphan, the neighbour, the relative's right — are never mere ethics but the maintenance of a covenant structure.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:28

> **How can you deny Allah? You were lifeless and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die and again bring you to life, and then to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Astonished Question**

The verse opens with one of the Book's signature interrogatives: *kayfa takfurūna bi'llāh* — "*How* can you disbelieve in God?" The *kayfa* here is not an inquiry seeking information but the interrogative of astonishment and rebuke — the sort of question that demerits its own answer because no rational answer is available. The commentators note its register: it is spoken to human beings in their capacity as *reasonable creatures*, as though the Book were bewildered at an anomaly in creation — the creature who ought to be the most grateful proving instead the most forgetful. The rhetorical construction implies that disbelief is not an opinion one happens to hold but a logical *impossibility*: if the premise is that one was dead, then alive, and owes every breath to the Life-Giver, the conclusion of indifference or rebellion has no room to stand. The question thus plants disbelief where the Book always diagnoses its final dwelling — not in the intellect but in the will's refusal to construe clear evidence.

**The Four Stations of Existence**

The astonishment is then argued explicitly by reciting the soul's own itinerary — four stations each of which is beyond the soul's power: *wa kuntum amwātan fa-aḥyākum* — "and you were dead, and He gave you life"; *thumma yumītukum* — "then He will cause you to die"; *thumma yuḥyīkum* — "then He will give you life"; *thumma ilayhi turjaʿūn* — "then to Him you shall be returned." The commentators read the first death in two registers without contradiction: either as the state of nonexistence before one was — the nothingness from which one was called into being, the condition the Book itself describes man as having emerged from: *"Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing remembered?"* (76:1) — or as the formless condition of one's physical stuff in the loins of fathers and the dust of earth, before the arranging Word made a hearer out of it. Al-Ṭabarī gathers a philological note that deepens both registers: in Arabic idiom the utterly forgotten thing is called "dead," so that the first station is the death of not-being-remembered — the zero before we had a name. The mystics would later extend this to the metaphysical register, Ibn ʿArabī and his school reading in the first "death" the condition of nonmanifestation *within Divine Knowledge* — hidden in God's eternal knowing of us before our actual formation, a "death" not of sheer nothing but of not-yet-being-shone-upon. All three readings serve the argument equally: there was a "you" before you existed in your self-givenness at all, and the one who summoned you from any of those zeros can certainly do it again.

The second station — earthly death — is stated with characteristic simplicity: it is no accident; *He causes you to die* (*yumītukum*). Death is God's deliberate action upon each soul individually, not an impersonal decay of matter. And then the return station is given the same simplicity: *thumma yuḥyīkum* — *then* (not "if") — He will give you life, and *to Him you are returned*, the riding of death into the presence of the Life-Giver. The four-fold structure is repeated in the sūrahs precisely as this verse states — most compactly at 40:11, where the resurrected confess with their own tongues what they used to deny: *"Our Lord, You have caused us to die twice over, and given us life twice."*

**The Argument for Resurrection Built into the Recital**

Embedded inside the four stations is the Book's fundamental argument for bodily resurrection — an argument not merely asserted but endless debated with doubters elsewhere in the Qur'an:

> *"And he strikes for Us a parable, and forgets his own creation. He says: 'Who shall give life to bones when they are decayed?' Say: 'He shall give them life who originated them the first time.'"* (Qur'an 36:78–79)

The verse's logic: whoever executed the first *impossibility* — a hearer called out of nothing — has established, *a fortiori*, the lesser impossibility of recalling the hearer out of the tomb. The second summoning is lesser in every measurable way: the materials still exist, the template is known, the power is proven. It is for this reason the astonished *kayfa* is attached to disbelief and not to resurrection: the strange event is not that the Dead should live again — for the Dead have already lived once, at someone's beckoning — but that those summoned from nothing should imagine the Summoner incapable of summoning twice.

**The Return as the Whole Point**

The final clause folds the itinerary into its destination: *thumma ilayhi turjaʿūn* — "then to Him you are returned." The return (*rujūʿ*) in the Book is the rendezvous of the whole series — the meeting at which the summons/vocation issued at the first station is finally answered with the account of what was done with the Sonship-gift of life. It is the theological difference between Islamic resurrection and every cyclic or absorptionist eschatology: the return is not dissolution into the Whole, but *return to a Person*, the Owner of every stage of the journey. The believer is therefore trained by this verse to carry the map at all times: behind him a nothingness from which he was called; beneath him a life that is loaned; ahead of him a death that is appointed, a resurrection that is promised, and a Return that is personal. The Prophet ﷺ taught the perfect practical use of it:

> *"O people, remember often the destroyer of pleasures: death. For no one remembers it in straits but that it widens for him, and no one remembers it in ease but that it narrows upon him."* (al-Tirmidhī 2307 from Abū Hurayrah; graded ḥasan)

Remembering the four stations does to the soul exactly what the verse did to logic: it sits the heart before an Owner whose bookkeeping neither the first summons nor the second can escape, and makes disbelief — virtual or practical — impossible for an honest mind.


**Two Deaths, Two Lives: The Verse's Arithmetic**

"You were lifeless and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die and again bring you to life, and then to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned" (2:28). The verse counts the states — lifelessness, life, death, life — and the counting is confirmed by the risen themselves: "You made us lifeless twice, and gave us life twice. Now we confess our sins. So is there any way out?" (40:11). The first passage from lifelessness into life was the creature's making; the death in the middle is the wage of the trust assumed; the second raising is the argument's whole point, because the second life is the one denial calls impossible. The Book's position is blunt: the second creation is no harder than the first, and no one was consulted about the first.

Sūrah al-Mulk supplies the verse's purpose-frame: "˹He is the One˺ Who created death and life in order to test which of you is best in deeds" (67:2). Death in this arrangement is not the failure of the design but a stage of it — the hinge between the two lives, and the test's examiner. A man who accepts the verse's arithmetic lives differently at once: the days between the two births stop being everything, and start being the work.

**How Can You Deny: The Question as Diagnosis**

The verse does not argue; it asks — "How can you deny Allah?" — and the question performs the kufr-word's second sense, ingratitude. The man being addressed owes his present consciousness, his intervening life and his coming account to the One he declines; denial is therefore not a conclusion but a refusal to notice a benefaction in progress. The Qur'an presses the point through the resurrection's critics with the shortest possible demonstration: the man who watches his own first creation has already watched the thing he calls impossible. The verse's confidence rests there — not on a syllogism the doubter might outmanoeuvre, but on a fact the doubter is using to doubt it.

The closing clause — "to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned" — adds the verse's social dimension: all, without exception, the grateful and the ungrateful, the denier and his evidence. Return is not a threat aimed at one class but an appointment set for the species, and the verse asks its reader to decide which direction he will be walking when the appointment arrives.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:29

> **He is the One Who created everything in the earth for you. Then He turned towards the heaven, forming it into seven heavens. And He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Created For You": The Earth as Endowment**

The verse opens with a clause whose reach is total: *huwa alladhī khalaqa lakum mā fī al-arḍi jamīʿan* — "He it is who created for you everything that is in the earth, all of it." The commentators pause over the little word *lakum* — "for you" — the letter of benefit: the mineral veins, the soil strata, the waters, the beasts, the plants, the breathable air — none of it is a cosmic accident awaiting a tenant; all of it is a prepared estate addressed to humanity. The majuscule "He it is" — the Divine Name at the front — keeps the endowment from degenerating into entitlement: the earth is given *for* us, but gains its meaning only from the Giver. The tradition reads this "for you" in two directions at once: as permission — the earth's lawful fruits are granted for use, food, clothing, dwelling, and work — and as discipline, since what is received "for you" is received under terms. Al-Zamakhsharī and the moralists of the commentary tradition add that the clause is an open-ended argument for gratitude: whatever the eye falls on of the earth's furnishing falls under the universal quantifier *jamīʿan* — "all of it" — and every particular instance is included in the original endowment; every berry, every spring, every seam of iron descends from this single sentence.

**Then the Seven Heavens**

From the earth the verse rises: *thumma istawā ilā al-samāʾi fa-sawwāhunna sabʿa samāwāt* — "Then He turned towards the heaven" (2:29), forming it into seven heavens. The commentators discuss the staging: the earth's creation precedes the heavens' in the telling (with parallels at 41:9–12, where the earth and its mountains are formed in days, then the ascending smoke of the primordial heaven is fashioned into seven firmaments, "and He revealed in every heaven its affair" (41:12)), because the human addressee looks *upward* — the verse follows the natural gaze of the creature standing on his endowment. *Istawā ilā* here carries its ordinary sense of "turning toward" — the direction of divine purpose and crafting — distinct from the *istiwā* ʿalā al-ʿarsh (20:5) of the Throne, which is of a different order. The "seven heavens" the commentators take as seven real heavens, confirming the ḥadīth of the Prophet's ﷺ Night Journey (al-Bukhārī 3207; Muslim 162 onward), in which he ascended through the seven and met a prophet at each gate — Adam in the first, then Jesus and John, Joseph, Idris, Aaron, Moses, and Abraham at the seventh, beneath the Lote-Tree of the Boundary. Whether "seven" enumerates distinct levels or also connotes, as the Arabic idiom allows, completeness layered upon completeness, the verse's point is stability and order: the heavens are *fa-sawwāhunna* — "fashioned, proportioned, made even" — the same artistry verb as at 87:2 ("Who created and proportioned"), fitting canopy to canopy with no flaw, echoing 50:6: "Have they not looked at the heaven above them, how We built it and adorned it, and it has no rifts?"

**"And He Is Knower of All Things": The Seal of the Verse**

The closing clause — *wa huwa bi-kulli shayʾin ʿalīm* — "and He is Knower of all things" — seals the whole creative survey with the attribute that most concerns the creature addressed: the God who stretched the earth beneath and the seven above is not an artisan who wound a mechanism and withdrew; His knowledge accompanies everything eternally — every secret of the soil and every orbit of every sphere, and (as the commentators tenderly add) every thought of the creatures He called into being "for" all this. The placement of the clause is apt: after asserting the totality of creation "for you", the verse asserts the totality of His knowing — so that the next verse's divine declaration of a *khalīfah*, and the whole risk-fraught enterprise of the human story, is already covered by the One who misses nothing. For the believer, the fusion of the two clauses is the measure of daily confidence: the same Lord whose knowledge encompasses all things has prepared all things for me — and the trust this breeds is precisely the garden-soil from which the next verse's great announcement will spring: man, old of nothing, is about to be named the deputy of the Knower of all things.


**Everything in the Earth, For You**

"He is the One Who created everything in the earth for you" (2:29). The preposition is the verse's theology: the earth's goods are addressed, not merely available — mountains for stability, rivers for carriage, plants for food and medicine, the whole inventory marked lakum, for you all. Sūrah Hūd grounds the duty in the same claim: "He ˹is the One Who˺ produced you from the earth and settled you in it" (11:61) — settled, not parked. A tenant who reads the deed this way manages rather than mines, and the Qur'an's later laws — the lawful and the good of 2:168, the prohibition of waste — are the tenancy's conditions written out. Provision implies a Provider, and a Provider implies instructions.

The claim also quietly answers the idle question of what the earth is for. In the verse's grammar the planet is furniture in a house built for its tenants: its scale matches human life, its materials match human need, its rhythms match human work. A creature who finds the world convenient has already met the argument of the convenience's Author.

**Then He Turned to the Heaven: The Order Question**

"Then He turned towards the heaven, forming it into seven heavens." The order — earth's creation named first, heaven's forming second — was noticed early and read with care. The commentators (al-Ṭabarī among them) explain that the verse names earth's creation first because the account is organised around the tenants' provision rather than the builder's chronology; Ibn Kathīr reads the heaven's forming as its completion from an earlier state, the smoke of 41:11 made into layers. The ʿulamāʾ did not let the particle thumma force a contradiction with the verses that name heaven's creation first (79:27–30), because sequence in a deed's description is not sequence in the deed: the Trustee may describe the house by its rooms, not by the day each was bricked.

The verse's own ordering has a pastoral logic worth keeping: it begins where the reader stands. The hearer in Makkah is standing on the earth, eating its fruits, and is then lifted by the verse's turn — "then He turned towards the heaven" — from the table to the ceiling. Creation is narrated as an act of hospitality, and the guest is walked from what he touches to what he only sees.

**Seven Heavens and the Knowledge of All Things**

"Forming it into seven heavens" (2:29) — the number the Book keeps elsewhere with an audit attached: "˹He is the One˺ Who created seven heavens, one above the other. You will never see any imperfection in the creation of the Most Compassionate" (67:3). The layers are harmonics of one structure, and the challenge of 67:3's second half is the reading discipline this verse trains: look, and keep looking, at what is made. The verse of al-Baqarah seals itself with the epistemic clause — "And He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things" — so that the theology of the built world ends where Islamic theology always ends: the Maker's knowledge exceeds the made, and the made is precisely the lesson He has arranged.

For the believer, the verse folds cosmology into devotion. The seven heavens are not a diagram to be defended but a ceiling to be acknowledged; the doctrine of the verse is doxological. The man who recites it at prayer's beginning is reminded that the house he prays in has a roof he never built, and that its Builder knows what he is about to ask.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:30

> **˹Remember˺ when your Lord said to the angels, “I am going to place a successive ˹human˺ authority on earth.” They asked ˹Allah˺, “Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood while we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness?” Allah responded, “I know what you do not know.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Announcement of the Vicegerent**

With this verse the sūrah lifts the curtain on the most consequential scene in Muslim anthropology: *wa idh qāla rabbuka li'l-malāʾikati innī jāʿilun fī al-arḍi khalīfah* — "When your Lord said to the angels: I am placing a vicegerent on the earth." Before there was any man to address, there was this heavenly announcement: God fore-declared His plan — *jāʿil*, "I am placing," the resolve of the Creator before the act. *Khalīfah* is a deputy, one who comes after another and represents him, exercising an entrusted authority under, never instead of, the Owner of the authority. The commentators distinguish two complementary senses already pressed by the early generations: humanity succeeds the earlier inhabitants of the earth — many of the Salaf name the jinn who dwelled there before — and, ever more profoundly, man's very vocation on the globe is *deputyship unto God*: to rule it, build it, keep its trusts according to the will of its King, in the global stewardship that Islam will later christen *ʿimārat al-arḍ* — the civilizing of the earth. The verse thus lays down the whole religious image of man in Islam with one word: not an intruder upon the planet nor a wicked afterthought of natural selection, but a commissioned officer — heaven-confirmed even before his clay had dried — with a mission from the Throne itself.

**The Angels' Question and God's Answer**

The angels respond to the announcement with a question that has been debated by the commentators for fourteen centuries: *a-tajʿalu fīhā man yufsidu fīhā wa yasfiku al-dimāʾ* — "Wilt Thou place therein one who will work corruption in it and shed blood?" Carefully: the question is not a rehearsal of doubt — no angel argues with God — but, as al-Rāzī and the classical tradition explained it, a plea for disclosure, voiced in wonder: how does this fit Your wisdom? Their information may have come from God's own telling, or from watching the earth's previous tenants, with their blood and turmoil. And alongside their question they offer from their own register the only possible alternative-vocation they know: *wa naḥnu nusabbiḥu bi-ḥamdika wa nuqaddisu lak* — "while we hymn Your praise and call You holy" — we already perform worship at the highest pitch: what need for this new species, who will do what we never do? God's answer is legendarily short: *innī aʿlamu mā lā taʿlamūn* — "I know what you do not know." He does not refute their information (the corruption and blood they foresaw would indeed come); He asserts the missing half of the ledger that they cannot see: from the loins of this bloodying, corrupting clay would rise Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, prophets and martyrs, lovers who would worship as no angel could — sinners repenting at dawn, the feeble forgiving — and in that second half of the ledger, the whole enterprise is justified. God was buying, at the price of all the wrong, something He treasures more: *repentance freely chosen*, *faith in the Unseen by one who cannot see*, the worship of a creature who may go otherwise.

**The Vicegerent's Charter for Every Child of Adam**

Applied to every son and daughter of Adam, the verse becomes the charter of human orientation within creation: each person who says "I am a Muslim" has implicitly said "I accept the deputyship": the earth his parish, God's laws his terms of commission, man's flourishing his charge. The early Muslims took the verse with utmost seriousness: Ibn ʿAbbās and his peers saw in it the primordial basis of all ethics of rule; the Sufis drew from it the science of the vicegerent's *beautiful servitude*: the khalīfah is God's shadow upon earth in the sense that what God loves he loves, what God hates he hates, what God gives he expands. Al-Junayd and the wayfarers recover the angels' question within every soul: before each new responsibility comes the question — *shall I, who may corrupt, take this up?* — and God's answer within the soul is the same: *I know what you know not* — the divine trust that made the human venture worth the clay. The believer's anxiety about his own weakness — what if I fail? — is answered from the verse's own logic: the Vicegerent who announced the risk knew the cost before any angel calculated it, and His *I know* stands at the end of the ledger, not at the beginning — so the believing deputy lifts the trust, trembling, hoping — as Abū Bakr did on the day of the Prophet's death and as Umm Waraqah did in her prayer-recitations — trusting that the One who said *I know what you know not* has already factored the whole of human history into the wisdom of this appointment.


**The Office Named Before the Officer Exists**

"I am going to place a successive ˹human˺ authority on earth" (2:30) — the verse announces an office, khalīfah, before naming its holder, and the sequence is doctrine: the trust precedes the trustee. The Qur'an elsewhere shows how heavy the office is: "Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they ˹all˺ declined to bear it, being fearful of it. But humanity assumed it" (33:72). Successive authority — generation after generation of stewards — is the term's other half: the earth is not a possession transferred but a post handed on, each holder accountable for the shift he served. The honour of the species and its audit are the same fact read from opposite ends.

Reading the office this way reorders the modern argument about man and nature. The sūrah's own gallery — Noah, Abraham, Moses — holds the same office under different commissions, each audited at the end by the terms of the trust, and the audit keeps the word from hardening into property. The vicegerent is not the proprietor whose will is the law of the estate; he is the deputy whose will is accountable to the Owner's instructions. The ecological wreckage of the age of entitlement is, in this verse's terms, a staffing failure — the deputy acting as owner — and the repair begins with the deed's vocabulary.

**The Angels' Question and Its Ground**

"Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood while we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness?" The question is not mutiny; the commentators (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr) report it as inference: the angels argued from the one precedent they had seen — the jinn's corruption — and asked the Owner whether He meant to repeat the experiment. Their stated alternative is worship: the praise and holiness they proclaim are the entirety of their activity, the occupation of beings with no appetites to serve. The contrast is the verse's engine: a creature whose whole day is glorification asks what use a bleed-and-corrupt species could be.

The question also teaches what angels are. They do not resist the decree; they request its wisdom, and their request is framed entirely in God's own terms — corruption, blood, glorification. A heaven populated by questioners of this quality is itself a datum about the Owner: He populates His creation with beings whose obedience is intelligent enough to see why the new creature is troubling.

**I Know What You Do Not Know**

Allah responded, “I know what you do not know.” (2:30) The answer is the ʿaqīdah's hinge: divine knowledge is not the sum of angelic observation but a different order of sight — the interior, the future, the ends. The next verses display the difference in action: where the angels saw a species' capacity for blood, God saw the creature who could be taught the names and could carry the trust through repentance. The sentence is the Qur'an's standing answer to every argument that human nature's catalogue of crimes disproves its choice: the catalogue is known to the Chooser, and was known when the choice was made. Election and foreknowledge are not embarrassed by history; history is the museum of what foreknowledge elected with open eyes.

For the believer, the verse converts into humility about his own verdicts. The angels, sinless and brilliant, lacked the datum needed to judge the human project; the believer who writes off a person, a people or himself on current evidence is using less information than the sentence claims the Lord has. The verse instructs the community to hold its judgements as provisions — revise-able, and owed to the One whose knowledge of what a soul can yet become is the verse's quiet promise.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:31

> **He taught Adam the names of all things, then He presented them to the angels and said, “Tell Me the names of these, if what you say is true? ”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Curriculum of Names**

The proof of God's *"I know what you do not know"* (2:30) begins immediately with Adam's own education: *wa ʿallama ādama al-asmāʾa kullahā* — "and He taught Adam the names, all of them." The enjoyed irony deserves a moment's attention: the angels have just protested their ceaseless glorification; God's counter-exhibit is not a miracle of power but a lesson in language — *teaching*. What were the names? The commentators range broadly, as our source records: Ibn ʿAbbās — the names men use in daily speech, "man, mountain, sea, kettle"; Mujāhid — the names of everything; al-Ṭabarī's preferred reading — the names of Adam's progeny and their kinds, carried by the masculine pronoun the verse uses; al-Rāzī — all languages, of which later men's tongues are mere preferences. Whatever the inventory, the theology is fixed: knowledge of names is the root of all dominion and all worship — for to name a thing is to hold it in thought, address it, use it, and finally *call upon God by* revealed Name upon Name. Adam's endowment is the very grammar of stewardship in the previous verse: the deputy on earth must know the things deputized to him; and the worshipper must know the Names by which he worships — *"Allah has the Most Beautiful Names. So call upon Him by them" (7:180)* (7:180).

**Names Displayed Before the Angels**

Then comes the examination that vindicates the divine investment: *thumma ʿaraḍahum ʿalā al-malāʾikati fa-qāla anbiʾūnī bi-asmāʾi hāʾulāʾi in kuntum ṣādiqīn* — "then He laid them before the angels and said: tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful." Whether "laid them" means the realities named or the names themselves is debated (both readings have their scholars: al-Ṭabarī for the named beings, many for the names set out); God's summons is exact: *if you are truthful* — if your implied claim of superior fitness is true, then speak these names. The test gently magnifies what the angels missed in their question at verse 30: they had posed objection in the currency of praising-power (we hymn, we sanctify), and God tests at the very level of knowledge, in which they lack. The tradition has always read deeper lines here: the angels asked, in effect, *what need is there of this creature when there are we?* — and the test discloses that need: the creature's vocation operates through a mode of knowledge (synthetic, linguistic, all-embracing, appointed to acquire and to *name* — to gather the scattered world into one consciousness) that the angels, each fixed in his single station as the Book describes them ("each has a known station," 37:164), do not possess. Ibn ʿArabī, in the famous development within the esoteric tradition, coins the limit: the angels are like the individual faculties of man — each excellent and each veiled from what exceeds its station — while Adam is the synthetic being who can reflect together what no faculty can reflect singly; he is therefore capable of the Names — all Names — even the Name by which the totality of the Divine is answered: *God*, which is the goal of all naming.

**Knowing, Address, and Prayer**

For the reader, the verse re-defines knowledge itself in religious measure. The first thing Adam learned, he learned *taught by God* — *ʿallama* — so that at the very root of human knowledge stands Revelation: knowledge descends from heaven, and the mind of man is made its student before ever it is anything else — a doctrine standing at the origin of every later Islamic harmonization of revelation and reason: reason is a gift whose first lesson was delivered by the Teacher Himself, and whose life is renewed whenever knowledge is received in *adab* before the One from whom it comes. The Sufi commentator among our sources draws the link into the inner life: man must use the names to *address* — and the highest address is prayer. The Prophet ﷺ taught the very naming of God as the heart's worship, saying, in the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah:

> *"God has ninety-nine Names, one hundred minus one: whoever enumerates and embraces them (aḥṣāhā) enters Paradise."* (al-Bukhārī 2736, 7392; Muslim 2677)

Ahṣāhā means to stand upon them, fold them into memory, and call upon them — the sustained echo, in every reader's prayer, of the day when the father of mankind stood before the assembly of heaven and, first among creatures, *recited names*.


**The First Curriculum: The Names**

"He taught Adam the names of all things." The first instruction the race receives is vocabulary — the mastery by which things are held in the mind, distinguished, and addressed. The commentators divide on the content of the lesson: names of all created things, the specific names of the angels, or the names of the very objects then set before the court (al-Ṭabarī carries the readings; Ibn Kathīr synthesises). On every reading the substance is identical: Adam received knowledge no creature present possessed, taught directly by God, and the capacity that distinguishes the species — language, reference, the power to name — is dated to its first father and its first lesson. Human speech, in the Qur'an's account, is not evolution's accident but heaven's curriculum.

The verse also dates the dignity dispute. The angels' question concerned corruption; the answer concerns capacity, and the capacity is intellectual before it is moral. The choice of the species is justified first by what it can know — the rest of the sūrah will spend two hundred and fifty verses filling that knowing with law, story and warning.

**The Test Posed to the Angels**

"Tell Me the names of these, if what you say is true?" (2:31) — the challenge-formula the sūrah had already used on the scripture-deniers at "produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true" (2:23). The Book's idiom of proof is consistent: the claimant is invited to perform what he claims to know, and inability is allowed to speak. The angels, who had argued from corruption to unworthiness, are shown a capacity they lack; their inability is not humiliation but information — the demonstration the questioner had asked for, run in the opposite direction. Heaven's court is scrupulous with evidence even when the accused is the species the angels doubted.

Notice what is not tested. The angels are not asked to glorify better, nor to praise longer; they are asked for the names, the one thing their worship-filled existence had never required. The lesson for every community is embedded in the format: the excellence one lacks is often adjacent to the excellence one has, and the purpose of a test is to locate the gap honestly.

**Knowledge as Taught, Never Owned**

The scene's epistemology is stated by the angels themselves in the next verse — "We have no knowledge except what You have taught us" (2:32) — and it is the verse's quiet revolution: in heaven's court, knowledge is a received trust, not a possession. Adam's superiority consists in having been taught; the angels' honesty consists in knowing the provenance of what they have. Every later science of the Muslims — the chains of transmission, the isnād culture that checks every report's teacher — is this verse institutionalised: nothing is claimed without naming where it came from, because nothing is truly self-made.

The modern reader meets the verse at the exact point his own culture finds uncomfortable: expertise without acknowledged debt. The verse does not denigrate learning; it dates it. The man who knows the names of things holds what Adam was given — and the gift's first property, in heaven's account of it, is the humility of the recipient, which is precisely what the angels display and the verse commends.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:32

> **They replied, “Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Angels' Confession**

Tested with the names they could not recite, the angels answer with a sentence that became, in the Islamic tradition, the constant formula of every knower who reaches the limit of his knowledge: *qālū subḥānaka lā ʿilma lanā illā mā ʿallamtanā innaka anta al-ʿalīmu al-ḥakīm* — "They said: Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us; truly You — You alone — are the Knower, the Wise." The confession is carefully built in three movements. First, *subḥānaka* — the declaration of God's transcendence above every insufficiency: since they themselves had fallen short, the failure sends them upward, not downward — awe at His plenitude rather than dismay at their limit. Second, *lā ʿilma lanā illā mā ʿallamtanā* — the admission that frames the whole anthropology of knowledge: *all* knowledge, angelic and human, is derivative; there is no other fountain — the angels refuse even the dignity of having partly-owned knowledge: no, it is all *what You have taught us*. Third, *innaka anta al-ʿalīmu al-ḥakīm* — the paired Divine Names closing the confession: He is the Knower — total in reach — and the Wise — total in placement: not only does He know all things, He knows where everything belongs, which is why His plan for humanity (the question of 2:30 already answered in deed) is wisdom itself, before ever the creature understands its reasons.

**A Prayer Taught by Angels**

The tradition seized upon the sentence's continued liturgical life. The Prophet ﷺ was heard in his prayer of the night — standing long in recitation, as ʿĀʾishah and Ḥudhayfah report — opening his *qiyām* with extended glorifications exactly of this genus:

> *"O God, to You belongs praise; You are the Light of the heavens and the earth and those in them; and to You belongs praise. You are the Sustainer of the heavens and the earth and those in them; and to You belongs praise..."* (Muslim 769, from Ibn ʿAbbās's overnight at his aunt Maymūnah's)

And in the Islamic intellectual tradition the angels' sentence became the standing epigraph of the sciences: the scholars of every age wrote *wa mā tawfīqī illā bi-llāh* and recited these words at the close of every learned labor, because the central Muslim doctrine of knowledge — *ḥubb al-ʿilm* — is bounded at both ends by that confession: all you know is taught; all that remains is His. The scholars pointed also to the angels' exquisite *adab*: when knowledge fails, they move instantly into glorification — the direct reversal of arrogance, which, failing, moves into self-defense. From the angels the believer learns the reflex that saves every studying mind: when reaching the limit, do not bluff and do not bluster — *Honestly: we have no knowledge except what You taught us; and You are the All-Knowing, the Wise.*

**Knowledge, Wisdom, and the Creature's Consent**

There is also a structural lesson within the story's sequence: the angels' confession is itself the fulfillment of God's announcement at verse 30 — *I know what you know not*: asked to recite what only Adam could recite, they now *confess* with their own lips the divine sentence they had then heard; and by their confession the contest between the two species closes: Adam's peculiar endowment (names, synthesis, deployment of earth) stands publicly justified. The pairing at the end — *al-ʿAlīm al-Ḥakīm* — seals the larger meaning for every reader who, like the angels, one day confronts a divine decree his heart questions: the One who determined it is both Knowing and Wise, which together entail that the decree sits in the perfect place even when we cannot yet see the placement. The angels' sentence thus became Islam's reflex of *taslīm* — consenting serenity — to say, with the angels, in the day of every mystery: *Glory be to You — we only know what You have taught; You are the Knower, the Wise.* Such words, carried in the mouths of creatures, veil no ignorance in shame; they convert it into the deepest knowledge of all: the knowledge of God.


**The Grammar of Glorification**

"Glory be to You!" — subḥānaka, the word by which creation declares its Maker free of what does not befit Him. The angels' exclamation is the Qur'an's first recorded speech, and its grammar teaches the discipline before its content: glorification is negative theology in the serving sense — the creature removes from God the deficiencies of the creature, ignorance chief among them. The same verb returns at the sūrah's later crises — the idolatry charge (2:116), the offspring slander — and its work is always the same: to place the Owner of knowledge beyond the category in which the objectors have filed Him.

That the first words of heaven's first speech are words of transcendence settles something about worship's order. Before petition, before praise of specific mercies, the creature's first act is to secure the boundary: God is not like what He made. The angels, nearest to Him, begin there — and the believer who opens his own supplications with the same word is joining the oldest habit in the creation.

**The Confession That Defines the Creature's Knowledge**

"We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise." The verse is the Qur'an's epistemology compressed to a confession: nothing is known except by instruction, and the Instruction-Giver's knowledge is not quantitatively but categorically beyond the instructed. The angels — the most knowing of the seen creation in the Book's economy — locate every item of their knowledge in teaching received. The confession is also the test's answer: asked for the names they had not been given, they answer with the provenance of the names they had. Knowledge in heaven's court is always cited. The scholars' own method obeys the same grammar: every chapter of law on testimony and teaching opens from received knowledge, never from self-authority, because the first knowers in this Book are told what they know rather than claiming it. So the confession stands as the race's first lesson and its standing rule of learning.

For the life of the mind, the verse builds better than it appears to. The scholar who works from this confession checks his sources, dates his debts, and holds his conclusions with the confidence instruction permits rather than the pride possession imagines; the community that teaches its children this verse first has inoculated them against both credulity and arrogance before the first textbook opens.

**The Praise No Creature Can Count**

The angels' formula — glory, limitation, instruction, wisdom — was given its fullest echo in the Prophet's ﷺ own prostration. ʿĀʾishah found him one night long past her side of the bed, his forehead on the ground and his words the confession of a creature before uncountable praise: “O Allah, I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your anger, and in Your forgiveness from Your punishment, and I seek refuge in You from You. I cannot count Your praise; You are as You have praised Yourself” (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 486, from ʿĀʾishah). The hadith and the verse agree on the arithmetic: created praise, however long, cannot exhaust its object, so the creature surrenders the accounting — Your praise is what You say it is. The angels said it at Adam's lesson; the Prophet said it at the height of his devotion; the believer says it between.

Placed beside 2:30's "we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness," the verse completes the circuit: the glorification the angels offered as their case for exclusion is the very posture the human being is being taught. The species the angels doubted will spend eternity in the angels' own first sentence — and the verse is where the sentence was learned.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:33

> **Allah said, “O Adam! Inform them of their names.” Then when Adam did, Allah said, “Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Adam, Tell Them": The Vindication of Clay**

Now comes the proof of the investment: *qāla yā ādamu anbiʾhum bi-asmāʾihim* — "He said: Adam, tell them their names." With no fanfare and no special effect, the man of clay proceeds to recite what the noblest angels could not. The commentators note the Divine gentleness with which the demonstration is arranged: God does not declare Adam superior; He *has Adam speak*, and the exhibition itself decides the case — the celestial court hears the truth from the mouth of the new creature, and the objection dies without a rebuttal needing to be spoken. The scene also contains a hidden form: just as the angels' own confession at verse 32 answered in word what God had promised in word ("I know what you know not"), so here His promise is answered in *act*: *when he had told them their names* — the deed seals the exchange and the prophecy of verse 30 stands visible before all.

**"Did I Not Say?" — The Rebuke Clause**

Then the sealing sentence: *qāla alam aqul lakum innī aʿlamu ghayba al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍi wa aʿlamu mā tubdūna wa mā kuntum taktumūn* — "Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal" (2:33) Two claims of knowledge are here joined. The first is the maximal claim: *ghayb al-samāwāt wa'l-arḍ* — the Unseen of the heavens and the earth, nothing enclosed from Him in either realm (see also 35:38; 49:18). The second claim reaches into the interior of the witnesses themselves: *mā tubdūna* — what you angels made manifest (their hymn, their question) — *wa mā kuntum taktumūn* — and what you were concealing. What had the angels concealed? The commentators offer several conscientious conjectures: the judgment in their hearts that no creature God could create would outrank them; or the reluctance Iblīs, for his part, was storing up against any creature honored above him — in which case the sentence is also a quiet address of exposure to the concealed founder of revolt, hearing his own secret quotation in heaven's court. The scholars further observe the tense: *kuntum taktumūn* — *what you **used to** conceal* — as if the concealment had gone on inwardly for a while before the speech at verse 30 disclosed even a portion of it; and God's notice takes account of both words and silences. The clause thus completes the education of the angels: not only does God know what they lack (names), He knows what they hide — and His plan for Adam, impugned in question 2:30, was laid from the first in full command of both their ignorance and their secrets.

*The Verse's Counsel for the Soul*

For the reader, the verse becomes a twofold mirror. In one direction it vindicates God's confiding in man: never let the interior accuser say "you, what could God want with you?" — for the assembly of heaven publicly heard the answer: the divine trust is seated in precisely this creature of clay. In the other direction, the verse is a commandment of truth-telling, especially in prayer: the Lord who knew in advance what the assembly disclosed and what it concealed stands before each believer with the same two registers always open. Al-Ghazālī's counsel in the *Iḥyāʾ* — *"Meet your Lord with what you would present to Him from your exterior matched by your interior"* — is the piety of this verse: since concealment before God is a category-error (my hiding-place, in the courtroom where everything is already produced), the believer's only rational policy is transparent confession: *I have no veil against You, Lord; You know what I disclose and what I conceal.* And precisely this emptiness of all cards, laid openly before the Knower, is what repentance is — for the angels' concealment, confessed, became their restoration; and Iblīs', defended to the end, became his doom — as the very next verse will show.


**The Demonstration Completed**

"O Adam! Inform them of their names." Then when Adam did, Allah said, "Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?" The scene's method is the argument's method: God does not merely assert the difference between His knowledge and the angels' — He stages it, lets the angels attempt what they cannot, lets Adam perform what he can, and then asks the question whose answer everyone present now knows. Revelation argues by demonstration where demonstration is available; the verse is the Qur'an's epistemology in narrative form, and its confidence is the confidence of a Teacher who can arrange the exam.

The closing question also converts the angels' doubt into instruction. They asked whether the new creature was worth the risk; the answer they received was a lesson in what they themselves did not know, delivered without reproach. The verse's gentleness to the questioners is part of its teaching: in heaven's court, being wrong is instructable, and the instruction ends with the wronger knowing more than before he asked.

**The Secrets of the Heavens and the Earth**

"I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth" (2:33) — the claim that outranks the angelic observation post. The angels patrol what is; the Owner holds what is hidden in it. The Qur'an makes the same distinction a command to the disputers of revelation: "Whether you conceal what is in your hearts or reveal it, it is known to Allah" (3:29). The verse of Adam's lesson thus grounds the doctrine the sūrah will need constantly: the sealed hearts of 2:7, the mockery said in private of 2:14, the thoughts of 2:284 — all rest on the knowledge displayed here as the reason the human trust could be assigned. The One who assigns the trust knows what each trustee will do with it.

There is mercy in the ordering as well. The secrets clause comes attached to a moment of vindication, yet it is spoken to teach rather than to shame: the angels are being shown the difference, not punished for it. The verse models how the community should hold its own knowledge-supremacy moments — demonstration, not humiliation, with the lesson's content made explicit enough to correct the next question before it is asked.

**What You Reveal and What You Conceal**

"I know what you reveal and what you conceal." (2:33) The clause widens the doctrine from things to hearts, and the address shifts within the verse — from the angels' question to every future hearer. The Book of which this is the fourth verse will be, two hundred and eighty verses later, the book that says "Whether you reveal what is in your hearts or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it" (2:284); the fourth verse already carries the epistemic ground the later verse will carry as law. Interior and exterior are one ledger in the Creator's sight, and the opening chapter of the race's history is dated to the moment that fact was published.

For the reader, the clause is both warning and refuge. Warning, because the private room of 2:14 was never private; refuge, because the concealed repentance, the hidden endurance, the secret charity of 2:271 are equally legible where they are done for Him alone. The verse that opened the race's file is also the first page of its comfort.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:34

> **And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,” so they all did—but not Iblîs, who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Command and Its Single Exception**

The honor seems already established by the names, but God confirms it with a gesture from the angels themselves: *wa idh qiḥnā li'l-malāʾikati usjudū li-ādama* — "and when We said to the angels: Prostrate before Adam." The prostration commanded was not worship of Adam — worship-prostration belongs to God alone — but the prostration of *honor and salutation* at His command, an ordinance permitted in that dispensation and later abrogated in the law of Muḥammad ﷺ, in which no prostration is made except to God — the Prophet ﷺ explicitly said:

> *"Were I to command anyone to prostrate to anyone, I would command the wife to prostrate to her husband"* (al-Tirmidhī 1159; Abū Dāwūd 2140 — graded *ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ*),

— a speech that upholds the distinction precisely: honor can be paid to men in the fiqh of speech and bow, but *sujūd* is worship and is for God alone. The angels prostrate; the scene's whole mass kneels; *illā iblīs* — *except Iblīs*. Three verbs then meter his fall: *abā* — he refused (he did not merely fail, he declined); *istakbara* — he waxed arrogant (the ascent of pride, visibly measured in his own word of 7:12 — "I am better than he: You created me from fire and created him from clay"); *wa kāna mina al-kāfirīn* — "and he was among the disbelievers." The last verb the commentators weight with extreme care: *kāna* — "he was" — not "he became" — signifying that pride had already existed concealed within him; the refusal did not create his kufr, it exposed it — just as the angels' secret thought ("we are more noble") was already known to God at verse 33. Thus the first sinner in creation was not moved by an external tempter; the tempter *became himself* through an interior motion all creatures know: comparison.

**Of Jinn, Not of Angels**

The Qur'an itself settles the identity the later folklore muddied: *kāna mina al-jinn* — "who was one of the jinn" (18:50) — not a fallen angel (angels, on soundest doctrine, do not disobey God's commands, 66:6). The commentators note that the odd reports of an angelic tribe for Iblīs contradict this verse and rightly belong to the accreted tales. The practical lesson is even more pointed: Iblīs, the jinn, had *risen among the angels* by thousand-year devotions — the hadith-literature describes his services near the Throne — and was the scholar of the celestial assembly; and it was precisely this work and this rank that birthed the fatal seed: *I am better.* All the externals of piety — the congregation, the vigil, the prostrations of ages past — had never yet been tested at the one sitting where his inner secret was at issue: *the honor of another instead of his own.* The tradition's verdicts upon Iblīs run uniformly here: al-Junayd declared him the father of *every* spiritual pride among the sons of Adam, the first to object to God's wisdom with a syllogism ("fire is nobler than clay"), and thus the father of *all analogies posed against the Text* — the beginning of *qiyās* used to overrule command. The fall was therefore at root a fall of *reason used in revolt*: the mind that had memorized all names except the one Name by which the self is surrendered.

**The Standing Warning for Every Worshipper**

The tradition never treats this verse as ancient biography; it is read in the first person: in every refusal of God's command waits the same three verbs. The Prophet ﷺ warned his community of the presence of the same motivation under every dress: he ﷺ said,

> *"No one enters Paradise in whose heart is a mustard-seed's weight of pride"; a man said: but a man likes his clothes fine and his sandals fine. He said: "God is Beautiful and loves beauty. Pride is to despise the truth and to scorn people."* (Muslim 91, from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd)

Despising the truth — Iblīs' motion exactly: the truth came to him from above; he weighed the truth against himself and scorned the asker ("am I to prostrate to what You created from clay?"). Conversely, prostration itself — the very gesture the one creature refused — became, in Islam, the believer's most distinctive prayer-part: the Qur'an's last such image for the faithful is that they *"prostrate and seek bounty from God"* (48:29), and the Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"The servant is nearest to his Lord when he is prostrating: so multiply supplication therein."* (Muslim 482, from Abū Hurayrah)

The morality of verse 34 thus resolves into one daily decision reproduced a billion times a day across the earth: kneel, or reason with the command; and the road of *I am better* is the road in which feet bristle against the earth — while the road of *usjudū* is the road in which God lifts the prostrating head up to the height His praise belongs to.


**The First Prostration in the Qur'an's Order**

"Prostrate before Adam" — the command to the angels is the Qur'an's first recorded command to created beings, and its nature was settled by the tradition's earliest care: the prostration is salutation and honour, tahiyyah and takrīm, not worship, for worship is due to the One who commanded it alone (the reading carried through al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr from the Companions' generation). The command is repeated at Sūrah al-Isrāʾ with the objection attached: "Should I prostrate to the one You have created from mud?" (17:61) — mud, the lowliest of materials, the point Iblīs will make into his case. The prostration law of later Islam — none to any creature — is thus fixed by the exception that broke it: honour was commanded once, worship was never transferred, and the two were distinguished forever by the one creature who confused them.

The scene also sets the species' honour in its place: the angels bow to the father, not to the race's achievements. The honour is conferred before any work exists to earn it — before the first harvest, the first prayer, the first child. Dignity in the Qur'an is a birth-gift with duties attached, not a wage the species has negotiated.

**The Refusal Named Three Ways**

"But not Iblîs, who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful." The verse names the act three times in one breath: abā — refusal; istakbara — the arrogance that makes refusal possible; and the verdict, unfaithful, one of the kāfirīn. The three terms are the anatomy of the first sin and of every sin after it: the will says no, the self-importance supplies the ground, and the covering — kufr's literal sense — drops over what was known. The Qur'an's psychology never improves on this compression; the sūrah's later portraits of the hypocrite, the disputant and the mocker are all this verse unpacked at length.

The verdict's weight deserves a pause: the refusal is counted as unbelief, not as disobedience merely, because what was refused was a direct command of the Lord with no interpretation available. The verse thereby defines the edge every later soul walks near: a creature who knows the command and declines it has not merely erred — he has filed himself, by his own act, in the wrong register of beings.

The verse's refusal-count — one command, one holdout — teaches by its proportion. Every creature in the heavens prostrated; the exception is numbered, named and quoted, so that no reader may imagine a revolt of many or a negotiation of terms. The Book's monotheism is on display in the arithmetic itself: a command from the One has no minority report, and the single dissenter is recorded not because his case is strong but because the reader's own case will sound exactly like his. When the sūrah's later covenant scenes show a whole people listening while a faction refuses, the grammar is already here at the race's first assembly — the many faithful, the one recusant, and a transcript that preserves both for judgement.

**One of the Jinn: His Origin Settled**

Was Iblīs an angel who fell, or something else? The Qur'an answers in the same chapter that reports the prostration: "so they all did—but not Iblîs, who was one of the jinn, but he rebelled against the command of his Lord" (18:50). The exegetes built on the ruling: the refusal that arrogance produced is a jinn's refusal, not an angel's, for the angels "never disobey whatever Allah orders" (66:6). The distinction matters theologically — it protects the angels' sinlessness, and it dates the existence of the jinn, with their capacity for command and rebellion, before Adam. The tempter of the race is therefore not a rebel from heaven's hosts but a being of fire whose kind knew obedience and declined it, which is why his argument in 17:61 is the aristocrat's: mud against flame.

The verse's placement is also its argument: the origin-clause arrives in the narrative of the prostration itself, not in a separate genealogy. The Qur'an refuses to let the tempter be mysterious; he is classified at the scene of his crime, so that no later reader can romanticise him into a tragic angel or minimise him into a symbol. He is a jinn who was commanded, refused, and was renamed by his refusal.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:35

> **We cautioned, “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Home and Its One Boundary**

The scene turns from the assembly to the settlement: *wa qiḥnā yā ādamu uskun anta wa zawjuka al-jannata wa kulā minhā raghadan ḥaythu shiʾtumā* — "O Adam: dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat of it freely — abundantly, at ease — wherever you two will." The dispensation is one of unmeasured generosity: the gift is a Garden and the charter over its fruits is a word of abundance — *raghadan* — full, sweet, unthinned. Then comes the stipulation that carved the first law in human history: *wa lā taqrabā hādhihi al-shajarata fa-takūnā mina al-ẓālimīn* — "but do not approach this tree, lest you be among the wrongdoers." The commentators weigh each chosen syllable: not "do not eat," but *do not approach* — a boundary placed at *distance*, for sin, as the jurists and saints both say, is safest fenced before the last inch; and *fa-takūnā mina al-ẓālimīn* — "then you would be among the wrongdoers": in that order, the duo would have *joined a class*, for the self in sinfulness is always enrollment, never a single trespass. What the tree might have been — wheat, grape, fig — the reports differ among and al-Rāzī leaves unsolved; the Book refuses to name it, because the drama does not depend on botany but on obedience: the one withheld thing in an open Garden tests the son of Adam on the precise point at which his vicegerency distinguishes itself from an animal's grazing: can he limit himself for Another's sake?

**"His Wife": Companionship by Creation**

The verse records the first married address in revelation: *anta wa zawjuka* — "you and your wife." The Book consistently presents the woman as *couple*, never as accident: created from the same soul ("O mankind... who created you from a single soul, and from it created its mate," 4:1), she is named in the original charter of dwelling, not appended after the fact. The Sufi commentator of our source, al-Qushayrī, notices the singular verb and singular address placed over both: the Garden is one home founded as a *togetherness*; and this quiet grammar is part of the point: the first marriage in creation was planted inside the blessing, not outside it — companionship was given *in* Paradise before the trial, lest any husband or wife later say that test and tenderness could never occupy the same roof. The Prophet ﷺ, at the end of the other history of dwelling, said of this pair's later worship-keeping:

> *"The most complete of the believers in faith are the best of them in character; and the best of you are those best to their women."* (al-Tirmidhī 1162; Aḥmad — *"khayrukum khayrukum li-nisāʾihim"*, graded *ṣaḥīḥ*)

**Of the Garden's Where and the Approach Clause**

Where was this Garden? — the question on which, as our source records, al-Rāzī ends with his characteristic wisdom: "the proofs are weak and contradictory; so one should cease, and refrain from being categorical; and God knows best." The majority of the commentators took it to be the eternal Garden itself; others, reasoning from 20:118–119's pair ("neither hunger nor nakedness, neither thirst nor heat") and from the need for a *descent* at expulsion, took it to be a garden of discipline on high, or an earthly one; the scholars of tafsīr have left the issue open where the Book left it open. Far more pregnant, for practical religion, is the verse's great clause: *lā taqrabā* — *do not approach*. From it the jurists of Islam deduced the most important of their fiqh principles: *sadd al-dharāʾiʿ* — the blocking of means: whatever typically delivers a man to the forbidden is itself fenced as a warning-zone, and the Prophet ﷺ phrased the same pattern as law, in the reports recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

> *"The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters... whoever is cautious of the doubtful matters has preserved his religion and his honor; and whoever falls into them falls into the unlawful — like the shepherd who pastures around the sanctuary: he is on the verge of grazing into it. Truly every king has a sanctuary, and God's sanctuary on His earth is His prohibitions."* (al-Bukhārī 52; Muslim 1599, from al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr)

Between God's "eat of it freely" and "do not approach," the first dispensation of mankind is the pattern of all subsequent: an open abundance to enjoy and one marked-off place not to touch; the dignity of man — made khalīfah precisely by the power of obedience — is appointed to hold at that fence, whether it stand around a tree in a Garden or around a neighbor's marriage, around the property of an orphan, around the sanctity of the mosque, around the ears and eyes of his prayer: the first test of Adam's children is always this one.


**The Same Terms at the Seventh Sūrah**

The dwelling-command is repeated, nearly word for word, at ˹Allah said,˺ “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat from wherever you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.” (7:19) — the identical permission and the identical single prohibition. The Book therefore tells the fall twice, in two chapters, with one difference: here the wife is given before the warning; there the same order holds. The repetition is a signature of the Qur'an's most consequential narratives — the covenant of 2:63 recurs at 2:93, the favours formula recurs — and the reader is meant to test the two tellings against each other, since a story told twice identically except at its edges is telling the reader where the weight lies.

The pair of tellings also disciplines speculation. Neither verse names the tree, describes its fruit, or locates the garden beyond calling it the Garden; the apparatus of folklore — apples, wheat, a specific river — arrives from elsewhere and is at best reconstruction. The two verses' agreement in silence is itself information: the event's lesson does not depend on the tree's botany.

**The Only Name the Tree Ever Carries**

The Qur'an never identifies the tree — and the one name it ever receives comes inside the tempter's own advertisement: "O Adam! Shall I show you the Tree of Immortality and a kingdom that does not fade away?" (20:120). The naming is his salesmanship, not God's information; the same speech calls the tree's fruit "the tree of wrongdoing"? — no, the Book's own voice at 2:35 calls only approaching it wrongdoing. This asymmetry is the verse's quiet lesson: the only certainty about the tree's identity is that it was marketed as endless life, and the marketing is what made the approach wrong. Desire supplies the labels; the command had only said do not approach.

For the reader, the scene sets the pattern the sūrah will repeat at every covenant: a broad permission fenced by one clear line, a deceiver who enlarges the fence's significance, and a verdict that turns on the line rather than on the appetite. The believer learns here to measure temptation not by the object desired but by the boundary drawn.

**Eat Freely: The Width of the Permission**

"Eat as freely as you please" (2:35) — the permission is stated with the same breadth the sūrah later gives the whole earth: "O humanity! Eat from what is lawful and good on the earth" (2:168). Islam's table begins in the Garden as generosity, not austerity: one prohibition inside an open world. The commentators note the rhetoric — the permission's breadth is what makes the single fence intelligible; a religion that forbade broadly would need no deceit to break it, but a religion of abundance tests whether the creature can keep one line while surrounded by yes. The first human act of religion is therefore an act of restraint at a single point, performed amid plenty.

The shape of the command also teaches the shape of the law that follows it. The sūrah's later food-legislation — carrion, blood, swine, theslaughter-name — is the Garden's one fence scaled to a fallen world: still generous, still specific, still single-purpose. The believer who finds the law restrictive reads the verse's order backwards; in the Book's own order, abundance comes first, and the fence is drawn inside it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:36

> **But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in, and We said, “Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Whisper and the Slip**

The enemy whose concealment God had exposed at verse 33 now performs his one triumphant act: *fa-zallahumā al-shayṭānu ʿanhā* — *and Satan caused the two to slip from it* The fuller parallel accounts give the method: whispering (*waswasah*, 20:120; 7:20), the oath of lying — "I am truly your sincere advisor" (7:21), and the two false promises: "Your Lord has forbidden this tree to you only to prevent you from becoming angels or immortals" (7:20) — desire for immortality and angelic rank, the two lures attached to the very human condition the khalīfah had been given. The slip-verb — *azalla*, to make slide — the commentators notice: the fall from obedience is never a leap but a *slip*: the forbidden aspires first as a small smooth place, and the feet are gone before the mind has acclimatized. The word of the Book has no false certainties: *and he got them out of what they were in* — from the easiness of the Garden to the labor that is the earth; from where no hunger and no nakedness (20:118–119) to where both were coined for mankind. The Islamic telling preserves, however, the decisive difference the Book itself will lay down in the next verse: not "original sin" passing downward, but a slip of a pair who will repent *before they descend*; their descent to earth is not the piling of their transgression upon their children but the commencement of the work for which Adam was created khalīfah in verse 30 — a destiny, the angels' question notwithstanding, to which the slip was not the undoing but the rough opening chapter.

**"Get You Down" — To Earth, Not in Disgrace Alone**

The command — *ihbiṭū* — "get you down" — is voiced across the participants in the plural the commentators variously count as addressed to Adam and Eve, or to them and Iblīs' angry line as well; what no commentator misses is the phrase that follows: *baʿḍukum li-baʿḍin ʿadūw* — "some of you enemies of others": the enemylines of man-against-man and man-against-Satan established at the first descent. But the sentence continues in tones not of exile only but of provision: *wa lakum fī al-arḍi mustaqarrun wa matāʿun ilā ḥīn* — "and for you on the earth is a dwelling-place and enjoyment for a time." *Mustaqarr* — a residence and settling; *matāʿ* — valid use-enjoyment; *ilā ḥīn* — until its fixed hour: the Book builds the *whole dignity* of the dwelling back into the descent: earth is not God's refuse-pit; it is the grantee's appointed home of work and proof — exactly the station for which verse 30 had named earth's khalīfah. The dwelling is timed — *until a while* — a while that the commentators map in three directions: to death, to Judgment, to each man's appointed hour; but all three are the same lesson: the earth is a dwelling rented for a term, not owned for eternity, and whoever treats the term as the estate errs in the first follower's own way.

**The Slip Translated into Every Soul**

The tradition applies verse 36 to daily life under two heads. First, *the whisper is repeated*: in every temptation the same two promises recur — if you eat of this you will be large, permanent, angelic beyond your limit — and the repentant heart learns to hear them as they are: "the same whisper, the same promises, the same slide" — as the Prophet ﷺ echoed in his description of Satan, most lately translated to the inner format, saying (through his own ḥadīth qudsī recitation of God's word):

> *"God said: I have created My servants hanīfs (inclined to God), but the devils came to them and turned them away from their religion..."* (Muslim 2865, from ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār — the Prophet's long account of the creation and the stratagems against the creatures)

Second, *the descent is overcome by repentance*: Adam's fall, recovered through God's pardon next verse, became for the Muslim tradition the primordial lesson that the child of Adam is never judged by having slipped — "all the children of Adam err" (al-Tirmidhī 2342, as below) — but by what he does after the slide: dwell in the bitterness and blame the whispers, or call upon the Lord in the words his father first composed: *Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves*. Between those two destinies the whole field of human religious history lies, and the Book wastes not one verse mourning the Garden: what descends from verse 36 is not doom but the *workplace*, with its rent and its term, while the gate of return opens immediately above the worker's head in verse 37.


The verbs also fix the parties and the blame with a precision the later traditions often blurred: "But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in" — both of them, equally, led out; and no verse assigns the first sin to the woman. The Arabic's slip-word, zaʿalla, describes a foot that skids on smooth ground — sudden, unmastered, relational to the surface — and the Qur'an uses it for this event only here and in the parallel tellings, as if the vocabulary itself refuses the rhetoric of monstrous guilt. A slip is recoverable in a way a plunge is not, and the recovery is the very next verse's business.
