In application — and the tradition has always extracted practical instruction from this difficult verse — the Muslim is taught to sanctify his table by the Prophet'sﷺ own table-adab: to utter the basmalah before meals, never to revile any food placed before him, to eat from the near portion, to eat with three fingers and lick them, to thank after food, and never to refuse what is presented except through religious necessity:

> *"The Prophet ﷺ never disdained any food: if he liked it, he ate it; if he disliked it, he left it — without finding fault with it."* (al-Bukhārī 3563; Muslim 2064, from Abū Hurayrah)

That one ḥadīth is the practical image of v. 61 negated: no commentary about the plate, no impatience with sameness, no depreciation of provision for want of greater variety. The tradition also built upon v. 61 the famous *ṣabr*-counsel of hearing no one complain while God gives: the believer eats what is sent from heaven today — manna of the grain, the date, the slice — in the trust that thanks for the same food *tomorrow* is more blessed than the exchange of positions that other, leafy, spice-heavy dishes promise. And the verse's closing doom — abasement, poverty, wrath — looms over ingratitude at the table of God's bounties as over contempt of the signs: the believer who refuses contempt of provision escapes, by the verse's own mechanisms, both.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:62

> **Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians—whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Verse That Widens the Horizon**

After twenty verses recounting the failings of the Children of Israel, the Book suddenly swings the gate in the other direction: *inna alladhīna āmanū wa-alladhīna hādū wa'l-naṣārā wa'l-ṣābiʾīn — man āmana bi-llāhi wa'l-yawmi al-ākhiri wa ʿamila ṣāliḥan fa-lahum ajruhum ʿinda rabbihim* — "Truly those who believe, and the Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabeans — whosoever believes in God and the Last Day and works righteousness shall have his reward with his Lord." The listing order itself carries a quiet lesson: the Muslims are named first — "those who believe" — but then three named communities outside Islam are placed alongside them under a single salvific formula. What is required is then stated without any communal label at all: *whosoever believes in God and the Last Day and works righteousness*. The commentators note that the verse's grammar moves from group names to the indefinite *man* — "whosoever" — as if to say: salvation is not the property of a name on a register but the consequence of three realities meeting in one soul — faith in God, faith in the Last Day, and righteous action. The promise at the end — *wa lā khawfun ʿalayhim wa lā hum yaḥzanūn* — "no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve" — is the sūrah's own recurring formula for salvation, already given to those who follow God's guidance (2:38), to whoever submits his face to God while doing good (2:112), to the friends of God (10:62), and to those who hold fast saying "Our Lord is God" (46:13). The verse thereby enrolls all who meet its conditions, by whatever community they are historically labeled, into the same security the Book promises its own believers.

**Who Were the Sabeans?**

The Sabeans — *al-ṣābiʾīn* — presented the commentators with a genuine puzzle, and the sources preserve a spectrum of identifications. The word was derived variously from *ṣabaʾa*, "to go from one religion to another" (the pagan Arabs reportedly called the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ a *ṣābiʾ* in this sense, one who had left the religion of his forefathers), or from a root meaning "to rise" or "emerge," as stars rise. The candidate communities proposed by the commentators include: people with no recognizable rite or book who yet testified that there is no god but God; worshippers of angels who recited the Psalms; a group who had departed from the religion of the People of the Book; a people who believed they followed the religion of Noah; and astral monotheists who venerated the planets. In early Islamic history, the star-influenced community of Ḥarrān in Syria adopted the name "Sabean" to claim the Qur'anic status attached to it, as did the Mandaeans of southern Iraq — a baptizing monotheist community honoring John the Baptist which survives to the present day. The practical import of the commentators' honesty here is itself instructive: faced with an obscure category, the scholars mapped possibilities rather than forced a verdict, leaving the boundaries of the term to God's knowledge — a modesty instructive whenever the verse is later invoked in debates over who may be "saved."

**Al-Ghazālī on the Reach of Divine Mercy**

The most celebrated classical meditation on this verse belongs to Imām Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī (d. 1111) in his treatise *Fayṣal al-tafriqah* ("The Decisive Criterion"). Al-Ghazālī argued that unbelievers are not a single rank before God: those who know the Prophet's teachings and virtues with clarity and still deny him deserve the name denier; but what of the Byzantine Christian or the far-off Turk of his day who had never authentically *heard*? How could a man be faulted for not investigating a figure he had only ever heard described as "the great liar," any more than a Muslim would investigate one rumored to be a false prophet? To have heard the *name* Muḥammad while having heard only the opposite of his true attributes is, in effect, not to have heard at all. Birthplace, upbringing, and social experience mediate every person's access to religious truth; and where access was obstructed, God's Mercy is wider than human gatekeeping. This principle — that God judges persons by the truth that genuinely reached them and by their response to it — has remained the mainstream theological temper of Sunni Islam on the salvation of non-Muslims, protecting two truths at once: the decisiveness of Islam as the religion accepted by God (3:85), and the boundlessness of God's mercy toward those cut off from a sound summons.

**Reading the Verse Without Abusing It**

The classical tradition walked carefully between two misreadings. On one side, al-Zamakhsharī attempted to confine the opening phrase "those who believe" to hypocrites who only claimed belief — an interpretation most commentators rejected, since nowhere else does the Book use "believers" ironically. On the other side, some commentators simply glossed "believes in God" as "accepts Muḥammad and his Law," effectively folding the verse back into a single community — yet, as the source commentary observes, a Christian who affirms Muḥammad's message is no longer simply called a Christian, and the verse's plain listing of communities under one salvific condition will not dissolve. The sound path, held by the generality of the scholars, honors both rails of the verse: first, that this is not an abrogated permissibility but the Qur'an's own repeated position (cf. 3:110; 5:48; 5:69; 22:67–69); second, that its promise is conditional — real belief in God, real expectation of the Last Day, and real righteous works — not a blanket endorsement of every religious label as such. The household rule given to the believers in the later Madinan period is a fitting commentary on the verse's spirit: when a Jew greeted the Prophet ﷺ with a mumbled curse, and ʿĀʾishah answered angrily, the Prophet ﷺ corrected her and taught the response of dignity: when a delegation of the People of the Book greeted him with distorted words, he answered simply:

> *"Wa ʿalaykum" — "And upon you"* (al-Bukhārī 6028; Muslim 2163).

Justice of speech toward other communities, confidence in the width of God's judgment, and clarity about one's own covenant: these three together are the manner in which the Qur'an itself teaches this verse to its believers.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:63

> **And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from you and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Mountain Over Their Heads**

The remembrance-cycle resumes with one of the most dramatic images in the whole address: *wa idh akhadhnā mīthāqakum wa rafaʿnā fawqakum al-ṭūr* — "and when We took your covenant, and raised the Mount above you." The word *al-ṭūr* — noted by al-Ṭabarī as originally Syriac for "mountain" (*jabal*), yet by the Prophet's time a fully naturalized Arabic word — is the Qur'an's usual name for Sinai, the theater of Moses' commissioning. The classical commentators for the most part read the scene literally and with awe: God uprooted a mountain and held it suspended over the Israelites like a canopy, terrifying them into acceptance of the covenant they had hesitated to take — see the parallel accounts at 2:93, 4:154, and 7:171, the last of which adds that they thought it was "falling upon them." The source commentary also registers a more measured reading: the phrase may parallel the English idiom of a mountain *looming* over people — wrapped in smoke and fire and violent trembling as Exodus 19:16–19 describes Sinai on the morning of the theophany, when the congregation was forbidden even to touch its base on pain of death. Either way, the spiritual geography is the same: the covenant was not taken at a negotiating table but beneath an overshadowing majesty, so that Israel would know that the Torah they accepted was no matter for casual handling.

**"Take Hold with Strength" — The Terms of Take**

The command spoken under the mountain is precise in its verbs: *khudhū mā ātaynākum bi-quwwatin wa-dhkurū mā fīhi* — "Take hold of what We have given you with strength, and remember what is in it." The commentators gloss "with strength" as *earnestly*, *obediently*, with full resolution to act — not a limp receipt of scripture but a gripping of it. The two commands together define the anatomy of every covenant between God and a people: first *reception with commitment*, then *remembrance with continuity* — taking hold, then keeping in mind, generation upon generation. And the purpose clause returns to the sūrah's master-word: *laʿallakum tattaqūn* — "that haply you may be reverent," the very goal announced at the sūrah's opening for its whole guidance-project (2:2, 2:21). Revelation's aim is not information but *taqwā*; the mountain was raised not to display power but to impress upon a people that what they held was heavy — weight-bearing, life-shaping, demanding the strength of ongoing obedience rather than the weakness of admiration at a distance.

**Raised Hands and a Raised Mountain**

The scene carries within itself a sober law of how covenants with God are sealed: the greater the mercy offered, the more fearsome the setting in which its terms are delivered. Grace, in the Biblical and Qur'anic imagination alike, does not arrive as a tame suggestion; it arrives wrapped in smoke and shaking, because the souls receiving it must be woken into seriousness. The Prophet ﷺ instructed his community in this same seriousness concerning what they themselves were given, telling them that the believer who reads the Book and *acts* is blessed, while warning consistently against the thing this verse was given to prevent — treating revelation as a recital without grip. Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr both draw the moral across to the Qur'an's own custodians: what was said to Israel under the mountain — *take hold with strength; remember what is in it* — is said with yet greater force to a community whose Book descends upon a heart and is meant to descend upon conduct. The believer who memorizes and does not act re-enacts the hesitation under the looming mountain; the believer who receives with strength fulfills the very pattern the mountain was raised to secure.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:64

> **Yet you turned away afterwards. Had it not been for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you, you would have certainly been of the losers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Turning Away Beneath the Mountain**

The verse records the bewildering aftermath of the scene just described: *thumma tawallaytum min baʿdi dhālik* — "then you turned away after that." After *that* — after the covenant was sworn beneath a raised mountain, after the command to take hold with strength, after the theophany of smoke and trembling that no onlooker could have slept through — the response of the addressed generation was still turning aside. The commentators read this turning as the pattern soon enacted in the history that follows: the postponements, the calf, the distorting party, the bargaining over obligations — the long behavioral record the sūrah has been recounting since verse 40. The juxtaposition is deliberate and devastating: the covenant sealed under the most fearsome conditions Scripture records is followed, almost immediately, by indifference. It is as though the verse closes off, once and for all, the theory that human beings turn to God because the evidence is overwhelming; a people can stand beneath a suspended mountain and still wander away by evening. Conviction is not manufactured by spectacle; it is maintained by the heart's continuing remembrance — which is exactly what had been commanded: "remember what is in it" (2:63).

**Saved Not by Themselves**

The second half of the verse names what intervened between that turning-away and destruction: *fa-lawlā faḍlu Allāhi ʿalaykum wa raḥmatuhu la-kuntum mina al-khāsirīn* — "and were it not for God's Bounty upon you, and His Mercy, you would surely have been among the losers." The Book names two shields: *faḍl* — bounty, the gratuitous extra that no desert earns — and *raḥmah* — mercy, tenderness toward the undeserving. Between the turning-away and the loss stands nothing of Israel's own doing; the verse itself denies them any credit: had matters run on merit, the ledger would have closed in ruin. The commentators apply the same grammar to the Prophet's community: the believer between his sin and his doom has only this same twin shield — bounty from God and mercy from God — and this is why the tradition grounds all hope in exactly those two names and never in works-in-themselves. The Prophet ﷺ taught this dependence in memorable terms:

> *"No one shall enter the Garden by his works." They said: Not even you, O Messenger of God? He said: "Not even I — unless God envelops me in bounty and mercy."* (al-Bukhārī 6467; Muslim 2816, from Abū Hurayrah)

**The Losers and the Believer's Ledger**

"Among the losers" — *al-khāsirūn* — is the Qur'an's commercial term for those who came to the end and found the account emptied. The verse's logic distributes a precious lesson: escape from loss is never narrated as Israel's achievement, nor as any believer's vigilance, but as God's bounty and mercy closing over human lapse — which is precisely why the sūrah keeps saying of pardoned generations, "We pardoned you... that haply you may give thanks" (2:52). For the reader in the Prophet's community, the verse transforms the lengthy censure of Israel into a mirror of hope and warning at once: warning, because turning-away after covenant is a documented human possibility and not a theory; hope, because the document also shows bounty and mercy pursuing generations who turned. The verse leaves the believer with a double practice that the tradition has always joined: take hold with strength of what God has given — the command of the previous verse — and cling without shame to the bounty and the mercy, the confession of need that this verse makes perpetual. One without the other repeats the old failure beneath the mountain and falls into the other extreme of presumption — the two missteps between which the Book keeps steering its community.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:65

> **You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath. We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sabbath and the Trick**

The address turns now to an event of which its hearers were not ignorant: *wa la-qad ʿalimtum alladhīna iʿtadaw minkum fī al-sabt* — "and you have indeed known those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath." The fuller narrative is given in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf (7:163–166): a coastal village of Israelites was forbidden to fish on the Sabbath, and found that the fish, by divine trial, came thronging to the surface only on that day and stayed away the rest of the week. Some of the people devised a stratagem — digging channels and pools on the day before, trapping the fish on the Sabbath without technically "catching" them, and collecting the catch the day after — thus honoring the letter of the prohibition while gutting its intent. The Qur'an's verdict upon the stratagem fell: *fa-qiḥnā lahum kūnū qiradatan khāsiʾīn* — "Be you apes, outcast" — *khāsiʾīn* meaning driven away, abased, expelled from nearness. The commentators note the deeper religious context: the Sabbath had been imposed as a day of consecrated rest upon these people after they refused the Friday that the earlier prophets' communities honored; the day of privilege became a snare when treated as a technicality to be gamed rather than a gift to be received.

**What the Transformation Means**

What exactly happened when the command "Be you apes" was spoken? The commentators transmit two principal readings. The prevailing early view takes the words at their full weight: the transgressors were outwardly transformed, becoming apes in body as a sign and a punishment, after which they perished within days leaving no progeny — a reading al-Ṭabarī transmits with its supporting reports. Mujāhid, among the earliest authorities, held a sobering inward reading: "Their hearts were transformed, though their bodies were not" — comparing the case to the Qur'an's description of Torah-bearers who do not carry their scripture as "an ass bearing books" (62:5): the likeness is real at the level where the crime occurred — in the heart that preferred cleverness to obedience. Al-Qurṭubī records a rhetorical construal as well: "Be, then, as you have chosen to be — apes," in the manner of the divine irony of 17:50, "Be you stones or iron." The Book itself places all such images in a single moral family along with the spider of 29:41, the dog of 7:176, and the braying ass of 31:19: to live beneath one's humanity is to take on, by likeness, the form of the lower — and numerous ḥadīth describe some people raised on the Last Day in animal forms answering to what ruled them within. Whichever reading is adopted, the essential verdict stands: *legalistic cleverness against a known command of God is not sophisticated piety but dehumanization* — the self subtracting itself from the rank of those addressed as "O children of Adam."

**The Sin of Hīlah — Outsmarting the Law**

The jurists gave this episode a technical name — *al-ḥiyal al-mamnūʿah*, forbidden stratagems: arrangements that preserve the outward form of a command while annihilating its substance, and this Sabbath-trick became their archetype in Islamic law. The Prophet ﷺ warned his community against precisely this ancestral error:

> *"Do not commit what the Jews committed, making God's prohibitions lawful through petty stratagems."* (reported by Ibn Baṭṭah and others; graded with weakness in its chain by some scholars, but corroborated in meaning by the Qur'an's own censure here and in 4:46, 5:13, 7:163–166, and widely cited in this sense by the jurists)

The verse's enduring admonition to later believers is plain: God is not honored by ingenuity at the boundary — by interest re-named, by vows made to be broken, by fasts kept in letter while the tongue and eye fast from nothing. The Sabbath-breakers did not deny the command; they obeyed it with a loophole, and were told to be apes — creatures that mimic human form without human substance. The likeness is the judgment: mimicry of obedience is itself the punishment, because it vacates the obedient act of the spirit that made it human. The tradition bid its community instead toward the other pole — honoring the spirit with the letter: the one who gives a day to God, a fast, a prayer, entirely, without carving a private channel for his desire inside the divine fence, is precisely the one whom the verse's counterpart promises shall not be driven out, but brought near.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:66

> **So We made their fate an example to present and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Punishment That Outlives Its Day**

The verse seals the Sabbath episode by explaining what God made of it: *fa-jaʿalnāhā nakālan li-mā bayna yadayhā wa mā khalfahā wa mawʿiẓatan li'l-muttaqīn* — "so We made it an exemplary punishment for what lay before it and what lay behind it, and an admonition for the reverent." The word *nakāl* denotes a punishment so striking that it restrains others — a deterrent written into public memory. The commentators unpack the phrase "for their time and for times to come" along several complementary lines: it can mean for the people present at the event and for generations after them; for those dwelling in the environs of the town, literally those in front of it and behind it; or for the sin committed at that moment and for sins of its kind yet to come. In every construal the point is constant: God's response to the Sabbath stratagem was not a private rebuke but a landmark — a fixed post erected in history so that every later community negotiating with a divine command would pass it and take its bearings. The village on the coast became, by divine decision, a permanent exhibit.

**Admonition Addressed Specifically to the Reverent**

The verse then names the ones who actually profit from the landmark: it is *mawʿiẓatan li'l-muttaqīn* — "an admonition for the *reverent*." The word *mawʿiẓah* in Qur'anic usage runs on a spectrum from tender counsel (as at 3:138 and 5:46) to stern reprimand; here the deterrent force is obviously uppermost, yet the Book declines to say "an admonition for all people," choosing instead the God-fearing as the class it benefits. The scholars and spiritual writers have long drawn the intended distinction: warning-signs in history do not convert everyone who passes them — many read the account of the Sabbath-village and walk on with amusement or dismissal — but the *muttaqīn*, those who carry taqwā, read the same sentence and change their road. Just as the sūrah declared at its opening that the Book guides, specifically, the reverent (2:2), so its darker exhibits also function: they are curatives only in hearts already soft enough to be take warning. Thus the same event is at once a *nakāl* for the transgressors and a *mawʿiẓah* for the reverent — terror descending on one group, instruction descending on another, from a single act of God.

**The Believer Trained by Landmarks**

For the later community this verse quietly establishes a whole discipline of reading history: God leaves punitive signposts standing among the nations — drowned Pharaohs, scattered confederates, Sabbath-villages — and expects the God-fearing to be taught by them rather than to repeat each lesson at first hand. The Prophet ﷺ once articulated this very principle of learning through the exhibits of others:

> *"The believer is not stung from the same burrow twice."* (al-Bukhārī 6133; Muslim 2998, from Abū Hurayrah)

The sting of the Sabbath-village need never be re-invented: its record stands open, and the reverent pass it, slow down, and straighten their conduct with the commands they know. Where verse 65 described the punishment, verse 66 describes its preservation — the transgression was in *their* time, but its custody as a warning belongs to all times, and its bride — admonition — is handed specifically to those who fear God. The verse thus closes the episode the way the Qur'an closes so many of its narratives of former peoples: not as antiquarian history, but as current correspondence addressed to the taqwā-bearing reader centuries after the nets were cut on the coast.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:67

> **And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow.” They replied, “Are you mocking us?” Moses responded, “I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Command Without a Reason Stated**

With this verse the sūrah begins the five-verse narrative that lent the whole chapter its name: the story of the Cow — *al-Baqarah*. *Wa idh qāla mūsā li-qawmihi inna Allāha yaʾmurukum an tadhbahū baqarah* — "And when Moses said to his people: God commands you to slaughter a cow." Note how the command arrives: bare, unexplained, without stated purpose, without background. At this point in the narrative the hearers are told nothing of the unsolved murder that the sacrifice will expose (2:72–73); Moses simply transmits a divine instruction that makes no apparent sense. This is the Book's deliberate narrative technique: the reader is placed exactly where the people stood — in front of an order whose wisdom is completely hidden — so that the reader must choose the same thing the story is examining: whether divine commands require our prior understanding to deserve our compliance. The response comes at once: *qālū a-tattakhidhunanā huzuwan* — "Do you take us in mockery?" The people heard an apparently irrational order and concluded that their prophet must be jesting — the first reflex of minds that measure God's directives against their own sense of the sensible.

**Moses' Refuge: Not Among the Ignorant**

Moses' answer is one of the great prophetic one-liners of the Book: *aʿūdhu bi-llāhi an akūna mina al-jāhilīn* — "I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant." The commentators unpack the force of *jāhil* here with precision: in the Qur'an's vocabulary, *jahl* is not mere absence of information. As the source commentary emphasizes, it is a *disposition against knowledge* — a willful, patterned resistance to what God says, a pathological preference for one's own knowing. The Qur'an repeatedly uses the word this way: Noah warns his son "lest thou be among the ignorant" (11:46) though the son possessed full practical intelligence; Joseph fears being "among the ignorant" (12:33) should he incline toward temptation. Moses is therefore not saying "I refuse to be stupid"; he is saying: *I refuse the posture in which a man, confronted with God's plain speech, rearranges it into something answerable to his own judgment.* Mockery of a prophet's instruction belongs to that posture — and it is precisely that posture from which the prophet seeks refuge in God. Notably, Moses does not begin with rebuttal and explanation; he begins with *aʿūdhu bi-llāh* — refuge-taking — modeling the prophet's and the believer's first move under provocation: fall back into the shelter of God before answering men.

**The Background the Verse Withholds**

The early exegetical tradition (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr) supplies the story's hidden premise, which the Qur'anic narrative deliberately discloses only later: a wealthy elder among the Israelites had been secretly murdered by his own heir, and the tribes were casting accusation upon one another, no witness able to resolve it (2:72). Moses was implored to ask God for a means of identifying the killer — and God's answer was this command: slaughter a cow. Seen in retrospect, the apparently arbitrary order was in fact the address of the exact crisis tearing the community apart; the people, not knowing what was folded inside the command, received it as a joke. This structure contains the story's first great lesson before the questioning even begins: *divine commands often arrive as wrapped solutions*; the wrapping looks irrelevant because the crisis it answers lies in the Unseen, and the command's wisdom stays invisible until it is obeyed. The believer's parallel recurs daily: a prayer whose timing interrupts him, an abstention whose utility he cannot trace, a zakāh whose arithmetic seems to subtract — each arrives like a bare cow-command, and the human reflex voiced in this verse — "are you mocking us?" — waits ready on the tongue of every age. Moses' refuge is the escape: hold the command, refuse the posture of the *jāhil*, and wait for the verse's later unfolding, in which the slaughtered beast raises the dead.

**"Slaughter a Cow" and the Ordinary Height of Tests**

Finally, the commentators note the plainness of the object chosen — a cow, the most ordinary animal of an agricultural people. The test of Israel was erected not on something splendid but on something from the farmyard, because the essence of the test was not the object but the posture toward the Commander. In the history of revelations God has repeatedly placed the decisive tests in humble containers: a tree in a garden, a wooden ark, an infant in a basket of reeds, a cow in a pasture. The measure of a community is taken not by its response to glory but by its obedience in front of the ordinary. This verse is therefore remembered in the tradition under the sober sign that the frivolous question — "do you take us in mockery?" — is not an Israelite specialty but a standing temptation inscribed over every unexplained command: and Moses' answer remains the standing medicine: refuge in God from the company of the deliberately unknowing, received before any reply is formed.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:68

> **They said, “Call upon your Lord to clarify for us what type ˹of cow˺ it should be!” He replied, “Allah says, ‘The cow should neither be old nor young but in between. So do as you are commanded!’”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Question: Negotiating with the Command**

Instead of rising to obey, the people open negotiations: *qālū adʿu lanā rabbaka yubayyin lanā mā hiya* — "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may clarify for us what she is." On its face the request sounds reasonable — there are thousands of cows; which one? But the commentators unanimously hear in the question something else: evasion dressed as exactness. The command had left the field entirely open — *any* cow would fulfill it, as the Prophet ﷺ later stated plainly: "Had they taken the nearest cow and sacrificed it, it would have sufficed them." The demand for clarification therefore functions here not as piety seeking precision but as delay seeking a pretext. It is the reflex of a will that has no intention of complying and so converts obedience into an investigation, hoping the order will dissolve in the process. Underneath the religious vocabulary — "call upon your Lord for *us*" — the commentators detect a familiar irony: the God whose command has just arrived is addressed as Moses' Lord rather than theirs, a small verbal distancing that betrays the heart's position even inside a pious-sounding request.

**The Answer Narrows the Gate**

God answers the question — and the answer itself is the lesson: *qāla innahu yaqūlu innahā baqaratun lā fāriḍun wa lā bikrun ʿawānun bayna dhālik* — "He says: she is a cow neither old nor without calf, middling between them." No longer any cow in the herd: now she must be neither aged nor first-calved, but exactly in life's middle. With every question the specification tightens, and with every tightening the number of qualifying animals shrinks — the commentators observe that by the story's end only one cow in the land will qualify, owned by one widow, priced beyond measure. The people are learning by experience the principle their descendants' scholars would generalize: he who asks God needless questions is answered with needless difficulty; the questioner's demand for granularity becomes his own narrowing gate. And God seals His answer with the exasperated closing of a commander who has now given two communications where one sufficed: *fa-fʿalū mā tuʾmarūn* — **"so do what you are commanded."** The imperatives multiply as the heart delays: where the first command was simply "slaughter a cow," the answering clause must now add, in effect: *stop interrogating; act.*

**The Middle Path Hidden in the Specification**

Even the content of the specification preaches. *ʿAwān bayna dhālik* — "middling between them" — describes a cow balanced between the extremes of age, and the spiritual commentary of Ibn ʿAjībah finds in it the golden description of the soul that responds to God: not the old soul whose habits have calcified past change, nor the heedless young soul that feels immortal and sees no need for repentance, but the soul in its middle season — supple enough to turn, awake enough to know it must. The image harmonizes with the Book's own preferred register of balance: a community "of the middle" (2:143), a path between prodigality and stinginess (17:29), a religion of ease that is never flaccid. The people's first question had asked *what* she is; God's answer quietly replies describing *the kind of soul* that succeeds with Him: the one in the middle of life and of disposition, neither hardened by time nor dissipated in vanity — and the command to act *now*: "So do what you are commanded." The believer reading this verse is trained in a reflex precisely opposite to Israel's: when God speaks, close the interrogation chamber and open the door of execution — before the field of cows narrows to one and the sky itself must be petitioned for每笔 detail that delay was never going to honor anyway.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:69

> **They said, “Call upon your Lord to specify for us its colour.” He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should be a bright yellow cow—pleasant to see.’”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Question: The Interrogation Continues**

Having received one clarification, the people return for another: *qālū adʿu lanā rabbaka yubayyin lanā mā lawnuhā* — "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may clarify for us what her color is." The pattern of verse 68 now repeats and hardens: answered once with the specification of age, they ask about color — and the quality of their questioning begins to reveal itself fully. A community genuinely ready to obey would find the age-specification more than sufficient to go and seek; a community not ready, finds the specification only a prompt for the next inquiry. The commentators remark that each successive question — age, color, condition, purpose — is directed not at carrying out the command but at *postponing* it: interrogation as a technique of delay. Behind the religious phrasing stands the ancient bargaining posture of a will unwilling to yield: make the instructions complicated enough, and perhaps the command will become impracticable; perhaps the prophet will tire; perhaps the whole thing will go away. God, however, answers again — He does not abandon them to their shuffling but matches it with yet further specificity, which is itself a form of patience mixed with exposure: the more they ask, the more clearly their resistance is documented.

**The Yellow Cow: Beauty Specified**

The divine answer is now positive and vivid: *innahu yaqūlu innahā baqaratun ṣafrāʾu fāqiʿun lawnuhā tasurru al-nāẓirīn* — "He says: she is a yellow cow; bright is her color, pleasing to the onlookers." *Ṣafrāʾ* is a yellow tending toward the intensely golden; *fāqiʿ* conveys a pure, saturated, unmixed brightness; and the description closes with a feature no ordinary purchase-search would ever require: *tasurru al-nāẓirīn* — her color gladdens whoever looks at her. Where the people asked a technical question, God answered with an aesthetic of perfection: not merely "yellow" but a yellow so complete that the sight of her gives joy. The commentators observe two things here. First, the continuing narrowing: age-middling, yellow, pure, dazzling — the qualifying cow is becoming nearly unlocatable; delay is being priced at rising expense. Second, the divine irony: God, who could have crushed the impertinent interrogation, instead answers with a description of beauty radiant enough to shame the questioner's scattered pretext — as if to say that the comrade of hesitancy is ugliness, and the comrade of obedience is a splendor that delights the eye. The specifying does not cease because obedience is engaged; the specifying ceases only when the community moves.

**Ibn ʿAjībah: The Beauty of the Purified Soul**

The esoteric readings of this verse make the cow's specifications into a mirror of the human self. Ibn ʿAjībah, in his spiritual commentary, reads the required animal as the ego-soul that must, in the symbolism of this story, be slaughtered to set the heart free: the soul must be *beautiful* — *ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿ* — bright-pure of its blemishes, cleaned of every admixture by the water of repentance, before it is fit to be surrendered to God; and the beauty that *pleases the onlookers* is the visible serenity of the purified self whose lightens the faces around it. Whatever one makes of the allegorical method, its practical kernel is sound and widely received in the tradition: the thing that God most readily accepts in sacrifice from His servants is not the cheapest thing they can find to part with, but the thing made whole and beautiful — the heart slain of self-love, given up when most radiant. And the verse teaches the same lesson from the other side: God's answer came dressed as a garden of yellow splendor not for the cow's sake, since a hide suffices Him, but to teach these bargainers what manner of people obeys Him — the people whose worship is not the poorest they can make it, but the purest: prayers offered with beauty (*iḥsān*), remembrances spoken with presence, fasts kept in beauty, so that on the encountering of the deed, the onlooker is gladdened. That is the quality of the sacrifice that ends the interrogation: *bright, unmixed, gladdening to those who behold it.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:70

> **Again they said, “Call upon your Lord so that He may make clear to us which cow, for all cows look the same to us. Then, Allah willing, we will be guided ˹to the right one˺.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Question: Confusion as a Strategy**

The interrogation advances to its third round: *qālū adʿu lanā rabbaka yubayyin lanā mā hiya inna al-baqara tashābaha ʿalaynā* — "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may further clarify for us what she is; cows are much alike to us." The plea now wears the mask of helplessness: having been told her age and her color, they protest that the description could still match many animals — "cows all look alike to us." Yet by verse 69 the specification already stood at *a middling-aged, intensely yellow, unblemished cow whose sight gladdens onlookers* — hardly the profile of an ordinary herd. The commentators remark that the claim of similarity is a pretense allowed to stand in the narrative because it exposes its own machinery: behind every "we need more guidance" lies the unspoken "we need more time." Their closing phrase — *wa innā in shāʾa Allāhu la-muhtadūn* — "and if God wills we shall surely be guided" — sounds like docility, yet taken in context it rings strangely: guidance is being solicited *while standing in the very act of declining* the guidance already given twice. The Book here initiates its readers into a recurring religious phenomenon: the vocabulary of submission used in the service of postponement, *in shāʾa Allāh* spoken not as trust but as deferral.

**Guidance Responds to Movement**

The spiritual logic hidden in their own phrase deserves attention: "if God wills we will surely be guided." True — but the Book elsewhere binds the asking of guidance to the stepping toward it: *"As for those who strive in Us, We shall surely guide them to Our ways"* (29:69) — guidance is promised as a consequence of movement undertaken, not as a substitute for it. The people in this narrative were asking for still more light while rooted in place; and God answers the third petition — which He did — while their feet remained where the first command had found them. The commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr) distill the lesson of these tripled questions into a principle that the Prophet ﷺ would later enunciate with his community: *"Whoever asks about what has not been forbidden and burdens himself with excessive questioning, is only making his religion hard upon himself."* This is the very instinct the Prophet countered when he taught his Companions:

> *"Leave me as I leave you; those before you were destroyed only by their excessive questioning and their disputing against their prophets."* (al-Bukhārī 7288; Muslim 1337, from Abū Hurayrah)

And his positive rule stands opposite the Israelites' example:

> *"When I forbid you something, avoid it; when I command you something, do of it what you are able."* (al-Bukhārī 7288; Muslim 1337)

**"Do of It What You Are Able" — The Medicine for Interrogation**

The verse's deep counsel to later believers is therefore double. First: the soul that truly intends compliance asks only the questions compliance requires — "what is commanded?" once; then movement. Second: the soul that asks past the point of need is usually manufacturing a complication in front of an obligation it dislikes — one more color, one more condition, one more "cows are alike" — and each manufactured complication returns as divine tightening, verse by verse, until the easy command stands wrapped in conditions the questioner himself authored. The destiny of the interrogating community in this story is to stand, at the end of the interrogation, facing a *single unique unfindable cow*; the teaching of the later Prophet to his community is the counter-medicine: *take the command at its first simplicity and move — guidance accompanies the movers.* It is precisely this reflex that the believer cultivates in prayer, in abstention, in honesty at the cost of advantage: not "show me more, then I may act," but the vow of the better disciples elsewhere in the Book: *samiʿnā wa aṭaʿnā* — "we have heard and we obey" (2:285). The third question in verse 70 is the mirror-inversion of that vow: *we hear, and we ask again* — and the story of the Cow unfolds as the long price of that second answer.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:71

> **He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should have been used neither to till the soil nor water the fields; wholesome and without blemish.’” They said, “Now you have come with the truth.” Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Final Specification — An Unworked Cow**

The last answer completes the narrowing: *innahā baqaratun lā dhalūlun tuthīru al-arḍa wa lā tasqī al-ḥarth, musallamatun lā shiyata fīhā* — "she is a cow not broken to plow the earth, nor to water the tillage; sound, without blemish." The specification is now total: the cow must be *untrained*, never yoked, never set to labor; *whole*, free of defect; and *unstreaked*, of one color without a spot of another. The commentators note the intersection with the Biblical ordinance of the red heifer (Numbers 19:2), which likewise requires an animal "without defect, in which there is no blemish, and on which no yoke has been laid" — the unyoked animal signifies that what is given wholly to God cannot previously have been worn in the service of anything else. But in the context of this narrative's five-verse sermon, the cumulative point predominates: by the end of the questioning, the children of Israel stood obliged to find a *single* beast in the entire land matching all five accumulated descriptions — middling in age, intensely golden, dazzling to behold, never worked, and spotless. The tradition records that only one such cow existed — in the keeping of a widow (or, in other tellings, an orphan) — and that its price rose accordingly to the proverbial limit: her owner asked her weight, then her hide's weight, in gold. Delay had multiplied the cost of obedience from *any cow at hand* to a fortune gathered with difficulty. Hesitancy is the most expensive negotiator a believing people can hire.

**"Now You Have Brought the Truth"**

The people's response at last: *al-āna jiʾta bi'l-ḥaqq* — "Now you have brought the truth." The commentators note the unintended confession inside the phrase: "now" implies that what preceded was somehow less than clear — though every earlier specification had come from the same Lord through the same prophet. Al-Ṭabarī glosses the sentence simply: *now you have made it plain to us.* The phrase thus seals the story's diagnostic: a people that receives five communications where one contained all needed truth congratulates itself at the end for finally receiving clarity — mistaking the accumulation their own delay demanded for the prophet's eventual precision. There is an enduring pastoral lesson here for every community of believers: the God whose first word was sufficient will keep answering questions — He is patient, and every answer is true — but the questioner's "now at last it is clear" is really testimony against his own slowness, not against the earlier answers. The Book's praise elsewhere always belongs to those who respond at the first clarity.

**"They Slaughtered Her — But Almost Did Not"**

The narrative's closing clause delivers the whole moral in five words: *fa-dhabaḥūhā wa mā kādū yafʿalūn* — "so they slaughtered her, but they almost did not." Even after the three rounds of questioning, after the unique beast was located and purchased at its legendary price, the community's compliance trembled on the knife-edge of reversal — "they almost did not do it." The commentators explain the near-refusal variously: the burden of the cost; the fear that the murder's exposure would ignite scandal; the residual reluctance that questioning had been designed to protect. Whichever account is taken, the clause survives as the Book's own verdict on the entire episode: this obedience nearly miscarried at the final inch, and what saved it was simply the act having been started. The Prophet's ﷺ summary of the story — transmitted through Abū Hurayrah and others, and recorded with a stopping-chain in collections such as that of al-Ḥākim and cited by the exegetes with the usual caution regarding attribution — crystallizes the lesson for all later hearers:

> *"Had the Children of Israel slaughtered any cow at all, it would have sufficed them; but they made it hard upon themselves, so God made it hard upon them."*

Spiritually, Ibn ʿAjībah reads the completed specifications as the full portrait of the soul that is finally given in sacrifice: unyoked to the world's plowing, unstreaked by mixed motives, of an unbroken single color of devotion — surrendered at last *"and almost it was not surrendered"* — because the ego dies, even at the end, by the slimmest margin. The believer reading this verse is taught to close the gap the Israelites kept widening: hear, and act — early, cheaply, joyfully — before the command nearly dies on the edge of "almost."

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:72

> **˹This is˺ when a man was killed and you disputed who the killer was, but Allah revealed what you concealed.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Crime Finally Named**

With this verse the Book discloses what the five-verse story of the Cow had kept veiled: the original crisis. *Wa idh qataltum nafsan fa-ddāraʾtum fīhā* — "And when you slew a soul, and cast the blame upon one another regarding it." The early tradition (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr) fills the outline: a wealthy man of the Israelites was killed in secret — by his own nephew-heir, in the most commonly transmitted account — and the body laid where others would be suspected. With no witnesses and no resolution, the tribes began hurling accusation at one another; the verb in the verse — *iddāraʾtum*, you thrust and parried blame among yourselves — depicts precisely a community throwing a corpse's guilt back and forth like a hot thing no one will hold. Human justice had reached its absolute limit: one dead man, and every hand pointing elsewhere. It was from this impasse that the appeal went up through Moses, and from this impasse that the strange command — "slaughter a cow" — had descended. Read now with the background revealed, the whole previous interrogation acquires an uglier edge: while the people cross-questioned colors and ages, a murderer sat among them watching the delay he had every motive to prolong.

**"God Is the Discloser of What You Were Concealing"**

The verse's hinge-clause delivers its permanent doctrine: *wa-llāhu mukhrijun mā kuntum taktumūn* — "and God is the Discloser of what you were concealing." The concealing had layers: the murderer concealed his own hand; the accusers concealed their suspicions and their motives; the community concealed its unwillingness to bear the cost of truth. Against this entire architecture of concealment the Book sets one divine attribute: *Mukhrij* — the One who brings hidden things out. The structure of the narrative thus becomes the working-out of a single sentence of doctrine: the most elaborate human operation of hiding — a perfectly secret murder, a community primed to quarrel, a delay engineered through pious questions — ended in public exposure by the least likely instrument in creation, a slaughtered cow. The commentators extend the clause beyond the episode into the universal law it states: there is no act so concealed that it lies outside the disclosing power of God; concealment before men may succeed for a season, but concealment as such is provisional, because the final custody of the hidden belongs to the One who brings it out — either in this world, as here, or at the Day when *"what is in the breasts is sifted out"* (100:10).

**The Cool Logic of the Solvable Cold Case**

For the believing community this verse functions as a perpetual instruction concerning hidden wrongs. First, it teaches that unresolved injustice is an open file in God's court, not a closed one: the case that exhausts every human forum still has a Judge. The tradition enshrines this confidence in the prayer it taught for wrongs beyond human redress — and in the Prophet's ﷺ own words about the supplication of the wronged:

> *"Fear the supplication of the one wronged, for between it and God there is no veil."* (al-Bukhārī 2448; Muslim 19, from Abū Hurayrah)

Second, the verse teaches the community that blame-storming — *iddārāʾ* — is itself a symptom of the unconfessed wrong: when every group casts the guilt on another, the guilt is ordinarily nearest the ones casting hardest, and the healing of the community begins when the concealment is abandoned. The murdered man in verse 72 is every unsolved injustice; the tribes hurling blame are every community that prefers accusation to confession; and the clause that stands over the whole scene — *God brings out what you conceal* — remains, for the reverent reader, half a terror and half a comfort: a terror to the one who still hides, a comfort to the one slandered in secret, who can leave his file with the Discloser and walk free.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:73

> **So We instructed, “Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow.” This is how ˹easily˺ Allah brings the dead to life, showing you His signs so that you may understand.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Strike Him with Part of It": The Impossible Instrument**

The command that resolves the mystery is one of the most startling sentences in the Book: *qulnā iḍribūhu bi-baʿḍihā* — "Strike him with part of it." The *him* is the corpse; the *it* is the slaughtered cow; the *part* was, as the early commentators transmit (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr), a limb or portion of the sacrificed animal — some traditions name the tail-bone or a piece of the thigh. When the living portion touched the dead man, life returned: the victim rose, named his killer, and died again. Consider what God chose to hang the whole resolution upon: not a relic of holiness, not a prophet's staff — but a fragment of a butchered animal whose selection had been the object of five verses of obstinate haggling. The instrument of revelation's most public vindication was the very object the community had almost refused to acquire. The commentators draw the structural lesson immediately: divine omnipotence is most luminous when it employs the most negligible means — contact with a dead animal's part animates a dead man — so that no observer can attribute the outcome to the instrument, and every observer must attribute it to the Commander of the instrument.

**"Thus Does God Give Life to the Dead"**

The verse itself seizes the episode and generalizes it: *kadhālika yuḥyī Allāhu al-mawtā* — "THUS does God give life to the dead." The particle *thus* — *kadhālika* — converts a single astonishing event into a standing demonstration of a universal power: *in this manner*, by sheer command, by contact of the least instrument at God's bidding, the dead are raised. The verse is thereby installed among the sūrah's cumulative proofs of the Resurrection — alongside the rain reviving the dead earth (2:164), the man who passed the ruined town (2:259), and Abraham's request to be shown the quickening of the dead (2:260). The Prophet ﷺ himself drew the same analogy in the ḥadīth transmitted in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, when a man asked him how God brings the dead to life:

> *"Have you passed by a valley and found it barren, then passed by it again and found it verdant?" He said: Yes. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Thus does God revive the dead."* (cf. al-Bukhārī 4937; Muslim 2800 — narrated regarding God's combining of the resurrection with the earth's renewal)

The sūrah's argumentation is cumulative and consistent: the God who greens the dead valley, raises the slain man at the touch of the sacrificed limb, and will, *thus*, raise the entire dead on the Last Day. The internal logic of the sign is exactly proportioned to its audience: a people disputing over a corpse were shown, in the case of that very corpse, the power they would later be asked to affirm concerning all corpses.

**"That Haply You May Understand" — And the Heart It Raises**

The closing clause — *wa yurīkum āyātihi laʿallakum taʿqilūn* — "and He shows you His signs, that haply you may understand" — frames the miracle, as it frames all miracles in the Book, as *pedagogy*: the raising of the dead man was not performed for the dead man's sake but for the understanding of the living onlookers; the signs are curriculum, and the intellect is the address. The spiritual commentators — al-Qushayrī, al-Nīsābūrī, and others — extend the verse's pattern inward in the tradition's customary manner: the dead man is the heart killed by heedlessness; the sacrificial cow is the ego-soul slaughtered by obedience; and the contact of the slain beast with the slain man is the quickening that visits the heart when the lower self has been sacrificed — in al-Qushayrī's words, *"whoever slaughters his soul with sincere striving, God brings his heart to life with the lights of direct beholding."* The allegory rests on the verse's own stated mechanics: the slaying of one thing is made, by God's appointment, the life-instrument of another. For the ordinary believer the practical residue is simpler and lies on the surface of the narrative: never despise the small instrument God appoints — a fast, a coin, an act of obedience as ordinary and undignified-looking as a cow — for the Book has just demonstrated that resurrection itself, and the overturning of the most secret injustice, once arrived by the touch of exactly such a thing.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:74

> **Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers; others split, spilling water; while others are humbled in awe of Allah. And Allah is never unaware of what you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Then Your Hearts Hardened" — After All That?**

This verse is the hinge of the whole Banū Isrāʾīl address, and its opening word carries the shock: *thumma qasat qulūbukum min baʿdi dhālik* — "THEN your hearts hardened after that." After *that* — after a dead man rose and named his murderer before their eyes; after the sea, the manna, the springs, the mountain — the response of the witnessed hearts was not softening but *qaswah*, hardness. The commentators point out that the indictment spans two generations at once: those who witnessed the raising and were unmoved, and the Prophet's contemporaries who heard this very recital and remained unmoved by its recital; the verse deliberately leaves both in range of its "your." The Book thereby establishes the darkest law in its anthropology: signs do not mechanically soften; they *can* be outlasted. A heart may sit in the front row at a resurrection — the raising of the slain man in the episode just finished is, structurally, a front-row resurrection — and walk out exactly as calcified as it entered. Everything the sequence of verses 40–73 catalogued was publicly displayed; and the diagnosis at verse 74 is that the display failed — not for defect in the display, but for a chosen rigidity in the witnesses. This is the midpoint warning of the sūrah, placed precisely at the center of the longest address to Israel: the peril of the people of a previous Book is not their ignorance but their *inurement*.

**Like Stones — Or Harder**

The comparison then compounds: *fa-hiya ka'l-ḥijārati aw ashaddu qaswah* — "being like stones, or harder still." The Book and its commentators are careful with the particle *aw* — "or": it does not here express doubt but corrective escalation — they are like stones; no, *harder*, because the verse immediately proves that stones themselves contain more softness than these hearts. Three classes of stone are then named, and each is an implicit rebuke: *some stones burst and rivers gush from them* — recalling the twelve springs struck from the rock at 2:60, rock that yielded water at one tap, while these hearts yielded nothing at the raising of the dead; *some split and water issues* — a lesser response, but response nonetheless; *and some crash down from the fear of God* — the commentators connect this with the theophany at 7:143, when the mountain crumbled at God's disclosure to Moses, and with 59:21: *"Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled, rent asunder from the fear of God."* Earthly stone, in other words, has a documented record of three grades of response to God — gushing, leaking, and collapsing in awe — while the addressed hearts exhibit none. The Prophet ﷺ, whose eyes saw the animateness of creation more truly than most, confirmed the Qur'an's world of sensible stones when he said of one boulder in the ravines of Makkah:

> *"I know a stone in Makkah that used to greet me with salutation before I was sent as a prophet; indeed, I know it even now."* (Muslim 2277)

A creation in which stones greet prophets and mountains humble themselves is a creation in which the deadened heart is not a natural object but an anomaly harder than nature.

**"God Is Not Heedless of What You Do"**

The verse closes with the standing reality under which every hardening takes place: *wa mā Allāhu bi-ghāfilin ʿammā taʿmalūn* — "and God is not heedless of what you do." Heedlessness — *ghaflah* — is precisely the state the Book diagnoses in man; the closing clause asserts its absolute impossibility in God. The hardening may be unnoticed by the hardened — that is the self-concealment of *qaswah*, that the heart no longer registers its own rigidity — but it is never unregistered. The tradition preserved the counter-discipline against this condition in the Prophet's ﷺ own most frequent spontaneous dhikr, the one vouched in the Ṣaḥīḥ as his constant speech:

> *By the Changer of the Hearts, establish my heart upon Your religion.* (al-Tirmidhī 3522 — the Prophet's constantly repeated supplication, "Yā muqalliba al-qulūbi thabbit qalbī ʿalā dīnik")

The nightly and daily use of that prayer is the community's practical admission of the verdict of verse 74: hearts change, and their hardness or softness lies in a Hand, not in their own possession. Ibn al-Qayyim, meditating on this verse in the classics of spiritual medicine, remarks in effect that the heart's hardness begins with abandoned remembrance: moisture follows dhikr as water follows the spring-stone of 2:60, and the same verse teaches despair of no one — for if God made *rock* gush with rivers, he is not asking the believer to despair of *any* heart, only to take refuge from Him against its staying stone. The address to Israel ceases here to be merely historical: *then YOUR hearts hardened* — the pronoun stands open to every reader with a Book on his shelf and a warmth gone from his prayer.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:75

> **Do you ˹believers still˺ expect them to be true to you, though a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Consolation Wrapped as a Question**

The address now swivels from the children of Israel to the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions: *a-fa-taṭmaʿūna an yuʾminū lakum* — "Do you then hope that they will believe you?" The verse is a pastoral intervention: the early believers in Madinah lived next door to the People of the Book, shared a scriptural vocabulary with them, and naturally hoped proximity and kinship would ripen into shared faith — the hope of every missionary age. God's answer corrects the arithmetic behind that hope: how can you expect belief from a people among whom a party has already done the worst thing that can be done to revelation — *yasmaʿūna kalāma Allāhi thumma yuḥarrifūnahu min baʿdi mā ʿaqalūhu wa hum yaʿlamūn* — "they hear the Word of God and then distort it after they had understood it, knowingly"? The sequence of verbs is the indictment: they *heard* the revelation; they *understood* it — the act of distortion began only *after* understanding; and they distorted *knowingly* — with full consciousness of what they were doing. Distortion born of ignorance would be error; distortion after comprehension and knowledge is treason against the truth — and treason of that order, God tells His hoping community, is not the soil from which your expected harvest of belief will grow.

**What Is Taḥrīf? Text or Meaning?**

The verse is one of the handful in the Book (with 2:59, 3:78, 4:46, 5:13, 5:41) on which the Islamic doctrine of scriptural *taḥrīf* — the corruption of earlier revealed texts — is built, and the tradition's internal debate over its nature is itself instructive and worth stating accurately. *Taḥrīf* lexically derives not from *ḥarf* (a letter of the alphabet) but from the root meaning *to slant, to incline, to deviate from axis*. The early commentators largely understood the distortion at issue as a distortion of *interpretation* — the scholars of the community slanting the meanings of a text they transmitted intact — an approach al-Rāzī defends with the practical argument that wholesale alteration of widely-circulated prophecies (such as those foretelling the Prophet, cf. 7:157) would have required an implausible universal conspiracy; the corruption he posits is subtler and more dangerous: a normative tradition of reading that drifts from the original sense while the words stay on the page using the same ink. Later polemicists, especially Ibn Ḥazm in the fifth Islamic century, pressed the stronger thesis of actual textual alteration. The mainstream resolution encompasses both: some distortion is verbal (as 2:79 will describe: writing a book and saying "this is from God"), and some is hermeneutical — and the present verse's own phrase, *"after they had understood it,"* points hardest at the second: the crime requires comprehension of the authentic sense as its prerequisite. The tradition also specifies the candidate offenders here: many of the commentators identify them with the party of elders who heard God's Word directly at the Mount (cf. 2:55) and then parleyed it down for their peoples — the attenuators at the source.

**Hope Realigned, Not Abolished**

The verse is not forbidding hope; it is re-placing it. The Prophet ﷺ and his Companions were being taught the mature mission-economics the Book repeats at other crises of expectation: *"Perhaps you will consume yourself following after them, in grief, if they do not believe in this discourse"* (18:6); *"Let not your soul go out in regrets over them"* (35:8). The teaching is precise: the preacher's hope may not be staked on outcomes among people whose track record with revelation is known — that stake would crush the preacher when the outcomes fail. Hope is lawfully placed in God, in the duty to convey, and in the open possibilities of individuals — and indeed a Salmān al-Fārūsī and an ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām did come over from exactly these communities, one outcome the verse's structure leaves fully open, aiming its rebuke at the *expectation of the collective*, not at the doors of any returning soul. The verse is therefore remembered in the tradition under the head of the consolations: it steadies the preacher, dignifies the refusal he meets, and transfers the burden of the outcome to the only place it can be borne: to God, who disclosed this people's history so His messenger would not suffer their refusal as a verdict on the truth of his call.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:76

> **When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But in private they say ˹to each other˺, “Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you, so that they may use it against you before your Lord? Do you not understand?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Faces, Two Speeches**

The Book now exposes the interior duplicity of a particular circle among the Madinan Jews with a scene so psychologically exact that it needs little elaboration: *wa idhā laqū alladhīna āmanū qālū āmannā* — "when they meet those who believe, they say: we believe" — *wa idhā khalā baʿḍuhum ilā baʿḍin qālū a-tuḥaddithūnahum bi-mā fataḥa Allāhu ʿalaykum* — "and when they are alone with one another, their own rebuke one another: do you tell them what God has disclosed to you, that they may dispute with you about it before your Lord? Do you not understand?" Al-Ṭabarī and the early commentators identify the speakers as hypocrites of the Jewish community of Madinah: men who spoke the language of affiliation with the Muslim gatherings — affimrming that Muḥammad was indeed a prophet, while internally reserving that he was "not a prophet sent to us" — and who, in the confessional of their own company, censured one another for precisely the acknowledgment that their public affirmation implied. The logic of the secret reproach is exquisite: *you affirmed him — but that affirmation can now be produced as evidence against you on Judgment Day — so why did you admit it?* Their keeness to keep the truth unusable extended even to policing their own public statements; they wished the very uttered fact of the Prophet's authenticity to be recalled to silence, lest it convict them.

**"What God Has Unveiled to You" — The Threshold They Knew They Stood At**

The phrase at the heart of the verse — *mā fataḥa Allāhu ʿalaykum* — "what God has unveiled/opened up to you" — is interpreted by the commentators on two complementary levels: what God had *vouchsafed* them in their scriptures concerning the coming prophet (the descriptions and prophecies, cf. 7:157), or more broadly *what God had made accessible* to them of knowledge, judgment, and command. Either way, the phrase is a tacit admission that they stood in possession of an unveiling — and the argument among them was whether *repeating it to the Muslims* was strategically wise, since what had been disclosed could be cited before God: *li-yuḥājjūkum bihi ʿinda rabbikum* — "that they may use it in argument against you before your Lord." That clause glows with unintended theology: the hypocrites themselves state the eschatological rule — knowledge disclosed to a man becomes evidence against him at the Judgment. This is precisely the Book's own doctrine of the culpability of the informed rejecter: *huujah* is established by the arrival of knowledge (4:165), and the duty to believe is proportioned to what has been unveiled. In other words, the speakers of this verse are condemning themselves out of their own strategy: their desire to *not hand the Muslims evidence* acknowledges that the evidence, once delivered, is binding in God's court.

**The Exposure of Double Speech as Ongoing Good News**

Rhetorically, the verse's last taunt — *a-fa-lā taʿqilūn* — "Do you not understand?" — answers its own speakers as a divine echo: they finished rebuking each other with that very question, and the Book repeats it back at them. The commentators note the irony-structure: the circles calculating how to avoid self-incrimination are conducting their calculation in total ignorance of the fact of being overheard — the next verse (2:77) delivers the answer immediately. For the believing community of every age, verse 76 performs two works simultaneously. First, it validates the experience of being received with smiling affirmation and private duplicity: the Prophet ﷺ met this face-to-face, and its exposure in the Book dignifies every later believer who encounters double-speech in religious life, teaching them to weigh professions of belief calmly and not be surprised when warm public phrases are disavowed in in-camera gatherings. Second, it warns the same community against becoming the thing described: saying "we believe" in the congregation while privately policing one another against acting on revealed knowledge — scolding a zealous believer: *why must you take the text so plainly? The others will use it to press us!* — which is precisely the catechism of institutionalized duplicity the verse has immortalized. Among the Prophet's ﷺ counsels preserved for exactly such conformism is the constant little prayer:

> *"O God, I seek refuge in You from knowledge that does not benefit."* (Muslim 2722 — in the Prophet's daily refrains of refuge)

Knowledge that would benefit yields action; knowledge hoarded so as not to testify against oneself is exactly the thing this verse brands as the costliest misunderstanding on earth.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:77

> **Do they not know that Allah is aware of what they conceal and what they reveal?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Single Question That Collapses the Whole Strategy**

There are shorter verses in the sūrah, but few that do as much work per word: *awa-lā yaʿlamūna anna Allāha yaʿlamu mā yusirrūna wa mā yuʿlinūn* — "Do they not know that God knows what they conceal and what they declare?" The scene of verse 76 — the private caucus, the plan to keep the Muslims from learning what the scriptures said — is dissolved by a single question. The calculation had been entirely horizontal: *if the Muslims learn what has been unveiled to us, they will use it against us.* The verse hangs one vertical fact over the entire caucus: the Keeping they feared was already complete; the hidden things were already inside the knowledge of God before the cloak was drawn. The commentators (Ibn Kathīr and others) note that the formula of this verse is one of the Book's standing refrains — *"Say: whether you conceal what is in your breasts or disclose it, God knows it"* (3:29); *"He knows the secret and the most hidden"* (20:7); *"He knows what is in the heavens and the earth, and He knows what you conceal and what you declare; and God is Knower of what is in the breasts"* (64:4) — and its insertion at exactly this point in the narrative is the sudden drawing-back of the curtain over the whole scene: the private conversation had a Listener.

**The Knowledge That Includes Intention**

The verse's pairing — *what they conceal and what they disclose* — maps onto the two faces of verse 76 with precision: the disclosed face of "we believe" and the concealed face of the inner caucus, both already fully known. This is the deeper cure that the Book applies to double-mindedness: the hypocrite's strategy presupposes an audience — the public, the congregation — and a backstage where accounting stops; the verse abolishes the backstage. God's knowledge of the disclosed word is the standard of the revealed word's integrity; His knowledge of the concealed word is the standard of the revealed word's sincerity. The scholars of spiritual discipline in the tradition — al-Muḥāsibī, al-Ghazālī — grounded their entire practice of *murāqabah* (vigilant self-watchfulness) in texts of this exact pattern: the believer trains himself to conduct every internal caucus — the weighing of whether to speak the truth, whether to act on what he knows — *in the knowledge that the caucus is already attended*. Verse 77 is thus the quiet charter under which all the Book's orders of sincerity operate: nothing proposed in secret is unrecorded; nothing dissembled in public is uncatalogued.

**Fear and Comfort of an All-Knowing God**

It is central to the Qur'anic presentation of divine omniscience that it functions with two registers at once — and the believing community is expected to draw both. For the plotting circle of verse 76, the knowledge of God is *exposure*: the record stands complete. For the believer maligned or misrepresented, the same knowledge is *vindication*: no account kept by enemies can omit the only entries that matter. The Prophet ﷺ habitually steadied his smaller early community with exactly this register of the all-knowing God when their situation looked overlooked: *"Do you think, perchance, that God does not know those of you who strive…?"* (cf. 9:16) — the question always arrives with the structure of verse 77, always converting the fog of secrecy into brightness. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported in the early tradition (al-Ṭabarī) to have said of just such assertion-verses: *"It is among the strongest consolations of the believers."* The verse is one sweeping clause: two verbs of concealment and disclosure, and the divine knowledge closing over both — the end of the caucus, and the beginning of *taqwā*, which is, at its most elementary, the permanent remembrance that God knows the thing behind the thing. The reader can practice this verse, literally, at the next thinking-distance: before finishing reproving others in his own private caucus for what they said in public, know that the caucus is public already — that is the sanity, and the mercy, of verse 77.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:78

> **And among them are the illiterate who know nothing about the Scripture except lies, and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Masses Behind the Scribes**

Having exposed the distorting scholars (v. 75) and the calculating hypocrites (vv. 76–77), the Book now turns to the ordinary people who followed them: *wa minhum ummiyyūna lā yaʿlamūna al-kitāba illā amāniyya wa in hum illā yaẓunnūn* — "and among them are the unlettered, who do not know the Book except by hearsay, and they do nothing but conjecture." Al-Ṭabarī and the early authorities take *ummiyyūn* here in its ordinary sense — people unable to read and write, commoners who had no direct access to the text of their own scripture. Notably, an opinion attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās reads the term differently — as a people who possessed no authentic book from God yet wrote one themselves and ascribed it to Him — but al-Ṭabarī and the generality of the commentators set this aside, since in the Arabic idiom *ummī* denotes the non-writing person (related, as the philologists see it, to *umm*, mother: one still at the level of birth-state, untutored by letters). The social picture the verse paints is then sharply three-tiered: at the top, scholars who *know* and distort; in the middle, politicians who *know* and suppress; beneath them, a populace that has no access at all and receives its religion second-hand. The verse's mercy is that it does not accuse the unlettered of the scholars' crime — it explains them: their knowledge of the Book is *amānī*.

**"Nothing but Hearsay": The Religion of Amānī**

*Amānī* (sing. *umniyah*) — rendered here as "hearsay" — denotes that which is wished, repeated, recited from hearsay: material the ear receives without the eye verifying it on a text. Al-Thaʿlabī glosses their whole scriptural knowledge as *what their scholars tell them*; and the commentators connect the content of their *amānī* with the very claims the sūrah has to correct in the coming verses: that the Fire will touch them only a few numbered days (v. 80), that none enters the Garden but a Jew (v. 111), that intercession and ancestry will discharge the individual's account. The pattern is universal: when a community's mass knows revelation only through the pipeline of an untransparent clerisy, its faith becomes an anthology of wishes — comforting slogans, tribal immunities, and distant hopes — untested against the page. The verse registers no rage at them, only diagnosis: *wa in hum illā yaẓunnūn* — "they only conjecture"; theirs is the guiltless guilt of the uncritical: conjecture standing in for certainty, desire standing in for knowledge. Yet the diagnosis carries consequence: God does not exempt the uncritical from the destiny their conjectures earned them, which is precisely why the Book insists on direct access to revelation as a communal right and duty.

**The Ummī Prophet and the Recited Book**

There is a luminous counterpoint the tradition has always treasured here. The same word — *ummī* — is the title God gives His final Prophet: *"those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet"* (7:157). The Prophet ﷺ himself embraced the descriptor in the ḥadīth recorded in al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

> *"We are an unlettered community (ummah ummiyyah); we neither write nor calculate."* (al-Bukhārī 1913; Muslim 1080 — regarding the tally of the lunar month)

But what a difference of standing between the two *ummī* states: the unlettered of verse 78 possess only *amānī* — they cannot verify what the transmitters relay; the Unlettered Prophet possesses *waḥy* — revelation itself, recited verbatim, preserved without his ever having apprenticed to pen or book, so that the very absence of letters in the Messenger becomes proof of the letter's divine origin: his Book is not hearsay he gathered but speech he received. And the community he formed was taught to remove the conditions of verse 78 from itself: literacy around the Book became a worship-adjacent virtue; the Companions wrote the verses down within his lifetime; and the tradition of verification — never taking a transmitted "from God" without examining its transmission — became the spine of Islamic learning. The believer who cannot himself inspect the sources is, in the terms of this verse, *ummī* toward them; knowledge of the Book at second-hand is *amānī* unless anchored in what has demonstrably come down. Hence the lifelong posture the verse prescribes: *read your Book; do not let your religion be hearsay.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:79

> **So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, “This is from Allah”—seeking a fleeting gain! So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they have earned.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Double Woe**
