Of all the indictments in the Banū Isrāʾīl address, this is the fiercest in its form: a vowel of doom pronounced twice. *Fa-waylun li'lladhīna yaktubūna al-kitāba bi-aydīhim thumma yaqūlūna hādhā min ʿindi Allāh* — "Woe to those who write the book with their own hands, then say: this is from God" — *li-yashtarū bihi thamanan qalīlan* — "to sell it for a paltry price" — *fa-waylun lahum mimmā katabat aydīhim wa waylun lahum mimmā yaksibūn* — "woe to them for what their hands wrote, and woe to them for what they earn." *Wayl* is the Qur'an's cry of woe — and the commentators add a darker note transmitted in a ḥadīth (accepted by many of the commentators, treated with caution by critics such as Ibn Kathīr) that *Wayl* is also the name of a valley in Hell into which the disbeliever falls for forty autumns before reaching its bottom — so that the cry is simultaneously a sentence and a destination. The scene described is the industrial face of the distortion exposed at verse 75: men who set pens to parchment, produced texts of their own composition, and retailed them to the ignorant as scripture — the commentators transmit accounts of scholars who sold such writings to credulous Arabs of the peninsula, and of custodians who overwrote the descriptions of the coming Prophet in their copies, turning revealed text toward whatever their patrons would pay for. The anatomy of the crime is complete: *authorship* (write with their own hands), *ascription* (this is from God), and *commerce* (sell it for a paltry price).

**"For a Paltry Price": The Economics of False Scripture**

The phrase *thamanan qalīlan* — a small, miserable price — became one of the tradition's canonical expressions for every transaction in which the things of God are traded for the things of the moment, and the jurists and moralists extended it far beyond parchment: the preacher who trims a ruling for a sponsor's fee; the scholar whose fatwa follows the signature; the reciter whose tongue is for hire against the truth; the trustee who patches revelation to fit the market. Imām al-Ghazālī makes this phrase the axle of the final book of his *Iḥyāʾ*, describing religion's scholar-merchants as sellers of what cannot perish for what cannot last — and noting the precise malice of the commerce: the buyer thinks he is purchasing God, while the seller knows he is selling paper. Against this stands the Prophet's ﷺ own categorical refusal of every religious wage — and his instruction to the community that the Book of God and the call to prayer must never be retailed at a price for their ministering. The tradition institutionalized the lesson in distinct ways, teaching that knowledge carried for money alone loses its light: the transmitter must not monetize the message, nor live falsely off it. Verse 79 thereby becomes the criminal code of religious fraud in Islam: forgery of the divine attribution is named, alone among ordinary wrongs, with the double *wayl* — woe down the pen, woe down the purse.

**The Earning of the Hand and the Earner**

The closing clause splits the woe into its two objects: one for *what their hands wrote* — the forgery itself — and one for *what they earned* — the proceeds and the entire moral income of the career. God thus implicates both the product and the profit; the forged page is not neutralized by the worthy use of the money it brought. The commentators widen "what they earn" to the totality of what the trade yields — the standing, the deference, the sect, the immunity to correction — everything bought by the profession of speaking for God falsely. For the later believing community, the verse speaks most sharply to two standing dangers. First, the writing hand: every age has its equivalents — a scholarship that re-labels opinion as revelation, translations that smuggle ideology into the text called "God's Book," trainings that teach students to *produce* authority rather than *transmit* it. Second, the buying public: the unlettered of verse 78 were the market; the duplicators of verse 79 the supply; and the chain is broken only where a community recovers the habit of verification — the tradition's own first act of kritik, from the isnād sciences onward, being nothing else than God's people refusing to buy every page that says *"this is from God."* Against the paltry price of the forger, the verse implicitly sets the other commerce the sūrah will praise at length: a trade with God alone (2:16, 2:207, 61:10–11), whose price is never paltry because its buyer is God.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:80

> **˹Some of˺ the Jews claim, “The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Have you taken a pledge from Allah— for Allah never breaks His word—or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Comforting Calculation**

The Book now reproduces, verbatim, the favorite consolation of the hearsay-religion diagnosed in verse 78: *wa qālū lan tamassanā al-nāru illā ayyāman maʿdūdah* — "and they say: the Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days." The commentators transmit the several versions in which this claim circulated among the Jews addressed: that their punishment would last only forty days — matching the days of the calf-worship — and then another people would inherit the Fire (some added, in a bitter grace-note, that the inheritors would be the followers of Muḥammad); or forty years, matching the wilderness wandering; or seven days, one for each age of the world's seven thousand. The arithmetic differs; the comfort is constant. This is *amānī* in full bloom — the hearsay-glacier of a community that has ceased to stand before scripture and now stands before its own wishes: a fixed, brief, survivable sentence, after which ancestral glory resumes. Note also the choice of verb: *lan tamassanā* — the Fire will not even *touch* us — the lightest verb of contact available, as though eternity's terror could be minimized by diction as well as by duration. The Book's answer will come in the next two verses; here it begins by demanding evidence.

**"Have You Taken a Covenant from God?"**

The divinely dictated response is forensic and inescapable: *qul attakhadhtum ʿinda Allāhi ʿahdan fa-lan yukhlifa Allāhu ʿahdah* — "Say: have you taken a covenant from God? — for God never breaks His covenant" — *am taqūlūna ʿalā Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn* — "or do you say about God what you do not know?" The argumentation is one of the sūrah's masterstrokes of dialectic — precisely the form of argument the tradition calls *ilzām* (binding by the opponent's own standard): the only thing that could guarantee a seven-day Fire is a covenant from God Himself, because only God's engagement can bind God; *and the verse grants the premise* — if you have such a covenant, it will indeed be fulfilled, for God never betrays His engagements. But of course no such covenant exists; the "days numbered" were never signed by anyone but hope. The syllogism leaves only the alternative clause standing: *you say about God what you do not know.* The commentators note that this final designation — speaking of God without knowledge — is itself classified by the Book among the gravest of sins, paired with idolatry at 7:33; the comfortable sentence about a short Hell is thus not a harmless optimism but a lie against the Throne.

**The Doctrine the Verse Guards**

What is at stake in demolishing the "numbered days" is not the possibility of finite punishment — Islamic theology in fact holds that punished *believers* may in the end be extracted from the Fire, on grounds entirely different (the intercessions and the divine mercy, established on other texts); what is at stake is the *source* of the claim. Salvation-arithmetic is not a thinkable right: no community is issued a sentence-cap in advance of the Judgment; no ancestry, scripture-custody, or denominational register fixes the duration of anyone's account. The Book's own parallel censure at 3:24 repeats the present claim and labels it what it is: *dhālika bi-annahum qālū lan tamassanā al-nāru illā ayyāman maʿdūdatin wa gharrūhum fī dīnihim mā kānū yaftarūn* — "that is because they said 'the Fire shall not touch us except for days numbered' — and they were deluded in their religion by what they used to fabricate." The delusion is self-authored — *mā kānū yaftarūn*, "what they used to fabricate" — the standing signature of *amānī*: first the wish fabricates, then the fabrications delude, then the deluded call it faith. Against every such arithmetic the verse sets only two lawful positions: either a covenant attested by God — and no community on earth possesses one limiting what He shall do — or the humble silence that concludes the verse: *it is not given to us to say of God that which we do not know.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:81

> **But no! Those who commit evil and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Balā" — The Refutation Word**

God's answer to the numbered-days fantasy begins with a particle that the Qur'an reserves for demolitions: *balā* — "Nay / Indeed rather" — a word that does not argue but overturns, used in the Book precisely where a prior assertion must be not merely corrected but reversed (as at the great sermon-clause 2:177, and at 21:26, 30:8). What is then set down is not a communal verdict but an individual law, stated with the universal quantifier the numbered-days claim had fraudulently emptied: *man kasaba sayyiʾatan wa aḥāṭat bihi khaṭīʾatuhu fa-ulāʾika aṣḥābu al-nāri hum fīhā khālidūn* — "whosoever earns evil, and his sin closes around him, those are the Companions of the Fire, abiding therein." The sentence moves from *man* — "whosoever" — to *ulāʾika* — "those" — with no communal label anywhere in between: the determinant of the Fire is not tribe but the two conditions named. Before judging those conditions, it is worth registering the frame the Book has just rebuilt: Paradise and Fire are here being assigned on principles any honest outsider can audit — *earning* and *envelopment* — two categories of deed and state, replacing the fantasied principle of membership.

**Earning Evil; Being Encircled by Sin**

The commentators unpack the two clauses. *Kasaba sayyiʾah* — "earns an evil" — is frequently specified as the earning of *shirk*, association of partners with God, the one evil that the Book identifies as determinative of destiny (4:48, 4:116); on this reading the verse states that eternal Fire belongs to the idolater. But the clause is broader in wording than its leading gloss, and al-Ṭabarī carries it to any grave sin persisted in. The second clause supplies the discriminator: *aḥāṭat bihi khaṭīʾatuh* — "his sin surrounds him, closes in upon him" — an image of total encirclement, like a besieged city with no gate left open. The commentators draw the discriminating lines here: the man whose sins encircle him — whose life is enclosed by his evil such that faith and repentance find no opening; who dies in his sins without repentance; whose decisive character is dark rather than light — is the companion of the Fire; whereas the believer who sins — a real sin, even a grave one — while faith, shame, and return still occupy ground within him, is *not* encircled: the siege-lines of sin never close into a ring. The verse has thereby quietly produced the classical theology of major sin in Sunni Islam: the *kāfir* in decisive orientation abides in the Fire; the believing sinner's permanence there is not pronounced by this sentence — which is why the following verse (2:82) can hasten to its counterpart without contradiction.

**The Ruin of Decisiveness and the Windows Left Open**

Of the verse's abiding lessons to the believing reader, three are permanent. First, *diagnosis matters to prognosis*: sins must be read by their trajectory — isolated, repented, intermittent, or encircling, encompassing, continuous. The tradition's own formulas of mercy assume the difference: God does not ask of His servants that they not be stung, but that the sting never close into siege; hence the standing command — *"follow the evil deed with a good one; it will wipe it out"* (al-Tirmidhī 1987, *ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ*) — the mechanics of keeping the circle from closing. Second, *membership saves no one*: the law of verse 81 is explicitly trans-communal — the man addressed by the numbered-days claim is judged under the same formula as the man addressed by the Gospel or by this Book. Third, *the Book does not teach presumption in either direction*: as the Christian-derived epigram and the streets of Madinah alike learned, it teaches the border zone — fear and hope, with neither the complacency of the numbered-days man nor despair, since for every sin other than decisive encirclement the gate of repentance stands open until the sun rises from the west (cf. 39:53). Verse 81 is therefore best read as the Book's great level-setting on judgment: a universal, individual, conduct-discriminating law, fair to every son of Adam, and closed to every fantasy that some registry in heaven already has the sentence-length penciled in.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:82

> **And those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Counter-Mirror**

The verse is the exact structural opposite, clause by clause, of the verse it answers (2:81): there, *whosoever earns evil and is encircled by his sins* — here, *wa-alladhīna āmanū wa ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt* — "those who believe and do righteous deeds"; there, *Companions of the Fire* — here, *aṣḥābu al-jannah* — "Companions of the Garden"; both sealed with the same two words: *hum fīhā khālidūn* — "abiding therein." The symmetry is the doctrine: heaven and hell are not assigned by two different bureaucracies — ethnicity for one case and merit for the other — but by a single moral law in two polar outcomes, stated in identical grammar so that no reader can pretend the Book measures its friends and strangers on different scales. Note, further, the verse's minimal composition: *belief* plus *righteous works*. No third clause; no communal registration; no genealogical stamp. In the sūrah's longest address to the People of a former Book and its own new community at once, the Book sets down the complete formula of salvation in six Arabic words.

**"Believe and Work Righteousness" — The Book's Joined Pair**

The pairing in this verse — *āmanū wa ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt* — is the most repeated conjunction in the entire Qur'an, occurring some sixty-two times in this exact grammatical neighborhood, and the tradition universally reads the repetition as defining: faith declared without works is not the Book's saving faith; works performed without faith are not the Book's righteousness. True *īmān*, in the classical definition the scholars converged upon, is assent of the heart, profession of the tongue, and action of the limbs — it increases with obedience and decreases with sin — and *ʿamal ṣāliḥ* is precisely faith become flesh: prayer, alms, truthfulness, kinship-keeping, patience. This verse is among those cited to establish that the believer who commits a grave sin does not thereby leave the fold — his works may be deficient while his faith abides — a position held against the Khawārij, who demanded works as the very existence-condition of faith, and against the Muʿtazilites, who invented a mediating rank and consigned the grave-sinner to perpetual Fire. The mainstream of Sunni Islam, Ashʿarī and Māturīdī alike, holds the tension this verse-pair creates exactly as the Book holds it: the believer who works righteousness is a Companion of the Garden, abiding; the believer who sins gravely is under the will of God — not above the Garden and not confined to the Fire; the decisive encirclement of verse 81 belongs to kufr, and its decisive deliverance in verse 82 belongs to faith conjoined with righteousness. The Book knows both certainties; the tradition has guarded both.

**"Abiding Therein" and the Consolation of Surety**

The closing phrase — *hum fīhā khālidūn* — deserves the same weight here that it received over the Fire: eternity, no exit visa, no second move. The Garden's companions are in it forever; not on probation, not in transit, not in a provisional lodging pending review. For the believer laboring under the sūrah's long demand-list — covenant, prayer, alms, all the commands that have been enumerating since verse 40 — this closing clause is the divine seal pressed over the whole ledger: *the address was long, but the promise at its end is permanent.* The consistency of the formula throughout the Book is the tradition's ground of assurance: not one of the sixty-two occurrences of this pair closes with a conditional; every one closes with a permanent. The Prophet ﷺ taught his community to live inside that permanence with the good opinion of God that runs the whole practice of hope: when his Companions asked about their works and their weaknesses, the Prophet ﷺ preserved the border-zone of hope and action together, declaring as reported in al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

> *"No one among you shall be saved by his works... but God shall enter His mercy upon whomever He wills; so do works in moderation and gladness, and be of good cheer: no one shall be expelled from the Garden who truly believed, though his works lagged."* (cf. al-Bukhārī 5673; Muslim 2816 — the combined sense of the Prophet's parallel sayings concerning works, moderation, and the mercy that finally envelops)

Verse 82 is therefore the verse under which the believing community finally rests from the arithmetic-fears of verse 80: not a numbered-days sentence to outwait, but an unnumbered home to inherit — for faith, and righteous work, and the mercy of the Lord who named the pairing.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:83

> **And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺, “Worship none but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy; speak kindly to people; establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.” But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away—except for a few of you—and were indifferent.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Covenant That Reads Like a Summary of Scripture**

With this verse the sūrah returns to the covenant-material of verses 63 and 40, now presenting its *content* in a compact creed-and-conduct charter: *wa idh akhadhnā mīthāqa banī isrāʾīla lā taʿbudūna illā Allāha* — "and when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: you shall worship none but God" — then, in clauses with the verbs carried by the first: "and toward parents, goodness; and toward kinsfolk, orphans, and the indigent; and speak to people in a goodly way; and establish prayer and give zakāh." The commentators and theologians of the Qur'an's literary form long ago pointed out the significance of the items chosen: the list is not specifically Mosaic in the sectarian sense but *universal-scriptural* — it reads like a digest of the Qur'an's own great ethical codes at 6:151–153 and 17:23–39, the passages some scholars rank among the *muḥkamāt*, the clear mother-verses on which everything else turns. The same triad recurs within our own sūrah at 2:177 as the definition of righteousness for Islam: God first, then parents and the circle of dependent humanity, then prayer and alms. The covenant taken from Israel is therefore stated in the very terms of the covenant taken from the Muslims — one moral architecture in both dispensations — refuting in advance the notion that this sūrah's address to Israel is tribal polemic; it is a shared syllabus being examined for fidelity.

**Parents First Among Men; Speech Reaching All**

The ordering within the list preaches. After God alone, the very first human creditors are the parents — *bi'l-wālidayni iḥsānan* — lit. "and toward parents, *excellence*" (the predicate nominative, as the grammarians note, carrying an understood verb: *act excellently*). The precedence is the Book's consistent one — 17:23, 31:14, 46:15 — and the duty extends, as the commentators insist, to parents who are unbelievers, Abraham's restrained courtesy toward his father (19:42–48) being the standing example; the ḥadīth raises the rank further, the Prophet ﷺ saying:

> *"Paradise is beneath the feet of mothers."* (al-Nasāʾī 3104; Aḥmad — a saying whose chain has been debated by critics, while its import is secured by the Qur'anic texts themselves and by sounder reports such as Muslim 2548: *"The mother... then the mother... then the mother"* in answer to who most deserves good companionship)

Then comes the dependent circle — *dhawī al-qurbā*, the kin; *al-yatāmā* the orphans, defined in the customary Islamic sense as minors bereft of their father; *al-masākīn*, the destitute — the three classes named every time the Book enumerates financial and social obligation. And then a duty of the *tongue* that the mind might not have expected wedged among the financial items: *wa qūlū li'l-nāsi ḥusnan* — "and speak to people in a goodly way" — to *people*, unqualified, Jew and pagan and believer alike. The commentators gloss this goodly speech as everything the tongue owes its neighbors: the call to God given gently, the command of right uttered without rancor, greeting answered, harshness refused. Only after speech come the two sacraments: *aqīmū al-ṣalāh wa ātū al-zakāh* — the same pair Islam received; so that the consent asked of Israel ends where the consent asked of the Muslims began (2:43).

**"Then You Turned Away, Save a Few"**

The covenant's epilogue is the Book's familiar grief: *thumma tawallaytum illā qalīlan minkum wa antum muʿriḍūn* — "then you turned away — save a few of you — while you were averting." Two things stand out for the believing reader. First, the exception clause: *save a few* — the Book does not narrate even the darkest periods of Israelite history as total apostasy; remnant-theology is built into the Qur'anic telling of Israel (cf. 3:113–115; 7:159), and the "few" who held covenant — the steadfast elders, the veracious scholars, the Salmāns and ʿAbdullāh ibn Salāms of later generations — are precisely the ones the coming verses (and later sūrahs) repeatedly vindicate. Second, the doubled verb of aversion: *tawallaytum... muʿriḍūn* — you turned the back, averting; two images of deliberate rotation away from the altar. The tradition applies the verse's warning to the ummah of Muḥammad in the plainest terms: *this* covenant — God alone, parents, kin, orphan, poor, good speech, prayer, zakāh — is not Israel's burden but humanity's; the Muslims received it at 2:43 and 2:177 and the daily shahādah itself; and the turning-away of a people who had it in writing is the Qur'an's standing caution to every later people who will *also* have it in writing. Whoever keeps this eight-clause covenant recited daily in his home and his manners has the substance of every revealed ethic in his keeping; whoever shelves it inherits, by the verse's own measure, the label the verse closes with: *muʿriḍūn* — a people averting while the syllabus lies open.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:84

> **And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant that you would neither shed each other’s blood nor expel each other from their homes, you gave your pledge and bore witness.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Covenant of Blood and Home**

The remembrance-cycle now reaches the covenant clause that will, in the next verse, be turned into the sūrah's sharpest reproach: *wa idh akhadhnā mīthāqakum lā tasfikūna dimāʾakum wa lā tukhrijūna anfusakum min diyārikum* — "and when We took your covenant: you shall not shed your own blood, and you shall not expel yourselves from your homes." The odd reflexive phrasing — "your *own* blood," expel "*yourselves*" — is deliberate and central: it legislates the community as a single body, so that the blood of any member is *your own* blood, and the exile of any member is *your own* exile. The commentators note that the dual prohibition mirrors the consummated compact of any coherent people: internecine killing absolved, internecine banishment absolved — the two fundamental crimes against any community being bloodshed within and expulsion from the circle. Then the verse records the ratification: *thumma aqrartum wa antum tashhadūn* — "then you acknowledged [it], while you bore witness": the addressed generation is reminded that this clause was not merely issued *at* them but *sworn by* them, whether as agents present at the original ratification or — as al-Rāzī allows — as heirs who inherit the witness of their forefathers by membership in the same covenant-people.

**The Madinan Background**

Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī supply the scene in which this covenant-clause became a live reproach. In pre-Islamic Madinah, the Arab tribes of Aws and Khazraj were locked in generations of feuding; each had Jewish allies — the Banū Naḍīr and Banū Qurayẓah with the Aws, the Banū Qaynuqāʿ broadly with the Khazraj. When war flared between the Arab tribes, Jew fought Jew upon opposite sides, driving their co-religionists from their homes, demolishing quarters, taking captives — and then, in the strange moral compartmentalization of tribal politics, the same community would afterward *ransom* the very Jewish captives whose expulsion they had abetted, citing their own revealed law against leaving a believer in enemy hands. The covenant's plain terms — no bloodshed within, no expulsion within — stood sworn and witnessed; yet on the ground, alliances with pagan tribes had silently outranked them. The verse therefore re-churches the covenant clause into the record because the community had learned to carry it in the scroll while voiding it in the street.

**The Sins of the Fathers and the Sins of the Self**

The source commentary inserts here a meditation on communal guilt that has become one of the sūrah's most instructive lines of thought: the Book's address uses *you* across generations — "when We took *your* covenant... then *you* shed blood" — speaking to men born centuries after the swearing. The fairness of that address, the commentary argues, rests on the way community identity actually works: whoever glories in his people's heritage and claims its victories as his own cannot, in justice represent, disclaim its crimes; group identity is a package — its covenants, its assets, and its liabilities — and the individual who enlists in the identity enlisted in its account. Beyond that, traits are transmitted across generations not usually by blood but by imitation: children reared among the treacherous learn treachery as they learn speech, and so the crimes of the fathers descend upon the children — not as doom but as *inheritance of habit*, from which the only discharge is repentance and a deliberate counter-tradition of virtue. A community, the commentary continues, can be re-moralized from above only by the rare interventions of prophets, saints, and sages; left to itself, it will keep the character of its progenitors. The believer's response to this sociology is double: he disowns in his heart the crimes of whatever people he belongs to — deploring them, dissociating from them — and he labors to be the infusion of virtue rather than the conduit of the inheritance. Even so, he may share the consequences of his community's sins as a neighbor shares the fire in a neighbor's house — which is why the Book makes the covenant *communal* ("your blood," "your homes"): because breaches by some are paid by all, and the covenanting individuals are pledged to build the kind of community in which breach is the exception and ratification is the rule. Into that pattern of thought the believer today reads his own ancestral and national liabilities — and recommits the covenant at the level where it is always kept or broken first: in what he will permit his own street, his own house, his own faction, to do to the members of his own body.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:85

> **But here you are, killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin and aggression; and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you as captives, you still ransom them—though expelling them was unlawful for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest? Is there any reward for those who do so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment? For Allah is never unaware of what you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Contradiction Exposed**

The covenant of verse 84 now becomes a bill of indictment: *thumma antum hāʾulāʾi taqtulūna anfusakum wa tukhrijūna farīqan minkum min diyārihim taẓāharūna ʿalayhim bi'l-ithmi wa'l-ʿudwān* — "then you — the very same people — kill your own and expel a party of you from their homes, conspiring against them in sin and enmity." The pronoun *hāʾulāʾi* — "you, these very ones" — is, as the Arabicists note, a gesture of astonished pointing: the covenant-witnesses are themselves the covenant-breakers. Out of the same body sworn to one blood, killing proceeded; out of the same compact that guaranteed homes, expulsions were carried out — and not privately, but *taẓāharūna ʿalayhim*, in allied conspiracy, sin (*ithm*: the wrong itself) stacked upon enmity (*ʿudwān*: the aggression in it). Then comes the exposure of the theater-contradiction for which this verse is chiefly remembered: *wa in yaʾtūkum usārā tufādūhum wa huwa muḥarramun ʿalaykum ikhrājuhum* — "and if they come to you as captives, you ransom them — though their expulsion was forbidden to you." The Madinan Jews, allied to feuding Arab tribes, would fight against their own co-religionists, help drive them from their houses, take them captive — and then scrupulously fulfill the scriptural duty of ransoming captives afterward. They kept the law that cost them money and broke the law that cost them alliances; they were obedient in the chapter that redounded to their credit and renegade in the chapter that pressed their politics.

**Believing in Part of the Book**

This is the verse from which the tradition draws its pointed phrase and its standing warning: *a-fa-tuʾminūna bi-baʿḍi al-kitābi wa takfurūna bi-baʿḍ* — "Do you, then, believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?" The clause has become the Qur'an's canonical diagnosis of *selective religion*: faith practiced as à-la-carte acceptance — the believer strong where the text favors him, silent where it obliges him against his interest. The commentators note that *kufr* here is not naked denial of God but the functional unbelief implicit in rejecting a binding portion of revelation while professing the rest — "a degree of kufr inseparable from hypocrisy and immorality of that order," as the early authorities put it — the very "disbelief" later named *kufr dūna kufr* ("a unbelief short of unbelief") by Ibn ʿAbbās in the tradition's discussions of 5:44–47. And the sentence upon selective religion is then stated as a general law, not a historical remark: *fa-mā jazāʾu man yafʿalu dhālika minkum illā khizyun fī al-ḥayāti al-dunyā* — "what is the recompense of whoever among you does that, but disgrace in the life of this world" — *wa yawma al-qiyāmati yuraddūna ilā ashaddi al-ʿadhāb* — "and on the Day of Resurrection they shall be returned to the severest punishment." The double rendering — disgrace below, torment above — binds the worldly degradation of the community that voids its own law (faction against faction, and all the humiliations division invites from outside) to the eschatological consignment awaiting the individuals who authored the voiding. And the clause that ended verse 74 returns to give the sentence its warrant: *wa mā Allāhu bi-ghāfilin ʿammā taʿmalūn* — "God is not heedless of what you do."

**The Checklist Turned Against the Selective Heart**

For the believing community, verse 85 functions as the sūrah's standing examination of religious selectivity, and the tradition applies it with no tribal limiter: whoever prays but cheats, fasts but backbites, honors the ransoming-chapter of the law while voiding the no-bloodshed chapter, is under the grammar of this verse. Al-Ghazālī's *Iḥyāʾ* lists as the daily marks of the same disease: rigor in the disciplines that are seen, and latitude in the disciplines that cost; eloquence about other people's neglect and silence about one's own; a fiqh of convenience in which every ruling that touches wealth, status, or faction is the one ruling forever under "review." The Prophet ﷺ aimed the same lens at his own community with an arresting image: the man who appears in this world having held to one part of the Book will come on the Day of Judgment with the scriptures themselves testifying:

> *"God wrote faith between the eyes of the believer"; and the Prophet ﷺ said: "A servant does not truly believe until his heart and his tongue are upright; and he shall not enter the Garden in whose neighborhood a neighbor is not safe from his harms."* (cf. Muslim 74; al-Bukhārī 48 — close wordings of the composite descriptions of incomplete faith)

The verse's universal law — that partial belief has a worldly disgrace and a final severity — stands as the Book's perpetual audit of every piety that is impeccable in the chapters it likes and blank in the chapters it dislikes. The medicine is the verse's implied opposite: whole-Book religion — belief seamless across the scroll — in which no chapter is ransomed at the price of another, since God, who is not heedless, reads the book of our deeds entire.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:86

> **These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world. So their punishment will not be reduced, nor will they be helped.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Invoice of the Transaction**

The Book closes this unit of judgment by naming the trade that produced it — *ulāʾika alladhīna ishtaraw al-ḥayāta al-dunyā bi'l-ākhirah* — "those are they who purchased the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter." The Qur'an's commercial idiom here is carefully chosen: not merely that they preferred the world, but that they *acquired* it — made the Hereafter the purchase-price, handed it over the counter, and walked away with the perishable goods. The sūrah had already introduced this metaphor of commerce at its opening (2:16): *ulāʾika alladhīna ishtaraw al-ḍalālata bi'l-hudā* — those who purchased error at the price of guidance; here the commodity is simpler and the stakes total: the world, for the entire Hereafter. The commentators note that the verb's grammatical form implies a completed transaction — a done deal: this is not the warning-siren of a choice not yet made but the divine postmortem on one already executed. The sad content of the deal is then its two closing clauses — *fa-lā yukhaffafu ʿanhum al-ʿadhābu wa lā hum yunṣarūn* — "the punishment shall not be lightened for them, nor shall they be helped": no mitigation and no assistance — every door of relief closed, since the two traditional sources of escape (a lighter sentence; a helper-intercessor) have both been spent already, in the purchase.

**Why the Two Closures?**

The commentators point out the precision of the two negations. *Lā yukhaffafu* — no lightening — answers every hope of the "numbered days" arithmetic dismantled back at 2:80: the Fire's abatement, intermission, respite from its worst — the small mercies of shade or pause that even the punished in the Book sometimes describe as scant relief — will not be given them. *Lā hum yunṣarūn* — they are not helped — closes the second door: no friend, tribe, patron, or intercessor will step forward on their account — this is the verse's echo of 2:48's triple refusal (no intercession, no ransom, no help). In other words, the negative half of the great ledger of this whole address to Israel is balanced exactly: they purchased a currency (the world's goods, its faction-victories, its paltry prices) in which no Hereafter-denominated help is tradable. The clause runs parallel through the Book in its closing cadences: 3:56 — the same verdict on those who prefer; 16:107 — "that is because they preferred the life of this world to the Hereafter, and God guides not a people ungrateful and false."

**The Merchant Inside Every Listener**

For the later believing community, the verse is kept not as history but as ledger-practice. The spiritual tradition insists that its category — purchase of the world at the price of the Hereafter — is indexed not once per life at death, but trade by trade: every sin of greed knowingly concluded, every alliance ratified at the expense of a known verse, every deferred repentance swapped for a present convenience — small invoices of one vast currency-exchange shaping one vast outcome. The Prophet ﷺ, teaching his Companions the worth of the two commodities, gave them the pocket-calculus in the briefest ḥadīth of the class — a saying out of the treasury of Tirmidhī, *ḥasan* in grade:

> *"What is the world to the Hereafter? It is like what one of you puts his finger into the sea: let him observe with how much of it it returns."* (al-Tirmidhī 2321)

A finger dipped into the ocean lifts its small film of water; the rest of the sea is what remains behind. That is the world; that residue, the Hereafter. And the Prophet ﷺ lived the arithmetic when, outlasting want through all the lean years of Madinah, he still died with his coat of mail pawned to a Jew for grain (al-Bukhārī 2916), leaving as his estate no dirhams and no dinars but only prayer-mats: the material was the residue; the Garden was the purchase. Verse 86, read beside that dying-out of the Prophet into the Garden, is the invoice against which every believer prices the world: *a finger's film of water paid for by an ocean* — the most ruinous trade ever closed under the sun.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:87

> **Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. Why is it that every time a messenger comes to you ˹Israelites˺ with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some and killing others?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Unbroken Chain**

With this verse the address performs its great panoramic summary of Israel's entire prophetic history, compressing a millennium into one sentence: *wa la-qad ātaynā mūsā al-kitāba wa qaffaynā min baʿdihi bi'l-rusul* — "We gave Moses the Book, and We sent a succession of messengers after him" — *wa ātaynā ʿīsā ibna maryama al-bayyināti wa ayyadnāhu bi-rūḥi al-qudus* — "and We gave Jesus son of Mary the clear proofs, and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit." The commentators unfold the picture: from Moses and his Torah, through the long chain of prophets sent within the Mosaic dispensation — David, Solomon, Elijah, John, and their fellows — men who brought no new religion but called back to the one religion and its Law; and finally Jesus, son of Mary, bearer of the Gospel and of those *bayyināt*, manifest proofs — the healing of the sick, the raising of the dead, the bird of clay quickened into flight (3:49), the telling of hidden things — reinforced by *rūḥ al-qudus*, identified by most of the commentators as the Archangel Gabriel, the same Spirit by whom revelation lives and hearts are quickened, whether the quickening be of bodies raised or of intelligences nourished. The whole span — Moses to Jesus — is presented as one continuous act of divine care: no century unvisited, no generation without a witness.

**"Whenever a Messenger Brought What Your Souls Did Not Desire"**

Then comes the pivot — and it is arguably the most penetrating sentence in this entire address: *a-fa-kullamā jāʾakum rasūlun bi-mā lā tahwā anfusukum istakbartum* — "Is it not so that whenever a messenger brought you that which your souls did not desire, you waxed arrogant?" Note what the verse does *not* say: it does not charge them with rejecting messengers who came with obscure speech, or doubtful credentials, or ambiguous signs. The criterion of rejection is located with surgical precision: *what your souls did not desire* — *mā lā tahwā anfusukum*. The messengers were audited not by scripture but by appetite; the verdicts against them were issued not from the Torah-scroll but from the self's *hawā* — its wish and its want. And against the Book's own principle that revelation authenticates the prophet, the community inverted the procedure: the prophet was made to authenticate *their* desires, and when he failed that audit, they rejected him. Upon that inversion, the consequences climbed their grim ladder: *fa-kullamā... istakbartum farīqan kadhdhabtum wa farīqan taqtulūn* — some you denied, and some you slew. Arrogance first; then denial — the verbal disposal of the inconvenient messenger; then killing — the physical disposal. The same ascent recurs through the history the sūrah has been recounting: the calf was *hawā* enthroned; the slaughter of prophets was *hawā* consummated; the rejection of Muḥammad ﷺ was *hawā* up-to-date.

**The Sufi Mirror and the Lizard's Hole**

The spiritual commentators of the tradition — al-Kāshānī and others — are emphatic that this sentence, addressed outwardly to the Jews of Madinah, is intended to be read inwardly by the Muslims who hear it recited: God succeeds His messengers with saints and sages in every age, and the same soul that measured prophets by its desires will measure the truth-tellers of its own time by the same test — and call them liars when they inconvenience it. The Prophet ﷺ himself prophesied that his community would re-walk the road of the earlier communities with uncanny fidelity:

> *"You shall surely follow the ways of those nations who were before you, span by span and cubit by cubit, so much so that if they entered a lizard's hole, you would enter it too." We said: O Messenger of God, the Jews and the Christians? He said: "Who else?"* (al-Bukhārī 3456; Muslim 2669, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī)

The verse's enduring lesson, therefore, is not an inventory of one people's failures but the exposure of a mechanism resident in every son of Adam: desire is a standing rival-revelation. It issues its rulings steadily, in the voice of plausibility, and appoints its own criteria for prophets, preachers, and texts. The believer who would escape the pattern of verse 87 has only one safeguard, the same one the sūrah has carried from its first page: revelation as the measure of desires, never desires as the measure of revelation — the heart trained to say, when the Messenger brings what the soul dislikes, what the better answerers said: *samiʿnā wa aṭaʿnā* — "we hear, and we obey."

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:88

> **They say, “Our hearts are unreceptive!” In fact, Allah has condemned them for their disbelief. They have but little faith.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Our Hearts Are Covered" — The Defense of Sealed Doors**

The verse now quotes the answer the addressed community gives to the Prophet's ﷺ call: *wa qālū qulūbunā ghulf* — "Our hearts are *ghulf*." The Arabic word is rich and worth dwelling on: *ghulf* (sing. *aghlaf*) primarily means *covered, wrapped, sheathed* — as a sword in its scabbard — and the commentators transmit two complementary readings of what the speakers meant by it. The first: *our hearts are covered over*, sealed in wrappings, so that what you present cannot enter — a plea that they would believe if only they could; their organ of faith is shuttered, and the shutter is not of their making. The second reading (Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, al-Thaʿlabī) hears the same word as a boast: *our hearts are already full* — vessels so stocked with the knowledge of their scripture that they stand in no need of any further message. Both senses — the heart saying "I cannot" and the heart saying "I need not" — are ancient defense-postures of refusal, and the tradition has always recognized them as twins: incapacity pleaded by the willful, and fullness pleaded by the proud. Either way the move is identical: the speaker describes his own unbelief as a *condition befalling* him — an enclosure he inhabits passively — rather than as an act he commits.

**God's Correction: Not Covered but Cursed**

The Book answers with its corrective reversal: *bal laʿanahumu Allāhu bi-kufrihim* — "Nay — God has cursed them for their disbelief." The direction of causation is the whole doctrine here: the sealing, where it exists, is not the *cause* of their disbelief but its *consequence*; they were not prevented from belief by a covering, but covered because they had disbelieved — the same law given its full statement in the parallel verse 4:155: *"Nay, but God sealed them because of their disbelief."* The cursing (*laʿn* — expulsion from mercy) thus answers to *kafara* (they disbelieved) in the order of responsibility: the human act precedes the divine response. The verse's closing clause then seals the diagnosis with a phrase of withering economy: *fa-qalīlan mā yuʾminūn* — "for little do they believe" — which can bear both readings the commentators note: they believe *but little* — their faith is fractional, declining, residual; or *few of them believe* — the community-wide gesture of faith occurring only in scarce individuals. Both are censure: the plea of covered hearts is answered not with sympathy for a handicap but with exposure of a record.

**The Longing Heart Is Not Sealed**

The source commentary adds a spiritual distinction of great pastoral value, which the tradition has steadily maintained: the claim of the sealed heart must be tested by its *tone and its tears*. The man who says "my heart is covered" while comfortably refusing every summons is the speaker this verse rebukes; but the man who says "my heart is dark, I feel far from God" while *longing* for the light — his statement is not the same utterance at all, for a completely sealed heart cannot know it is sealed; the grief of distance is itself the evidence of an aperture left open. Al-Junayd and the masters of the path taught exactly this consolation for troubled believers: awareness of the covering is God's mercy announcing that the cover is incomplete. The Prophet ﷺ taught his community the prayer that addresses the faculty directly, into the hand of the One who governs it:

> *"O Controller of the hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion."* (al-Tirmidhī 3522 — of which he ﷺ explained: "There is no heart but that it lies between two fingers of the All-Merciful")

That prayer is the believer's daily answer to the word *ghulf*: he refuses both postures of this verse — the comfortable claim of inability and the boastful claim of sufficiency — and instead petitions the Only Hand that turns hearts, knowing that a heart's covering is kept or removed by the same Lord who sealed the doors of the arrogant and who opens the doors of every returning servant, as promised: *"I am as My servant thinks of Me, and I am with him when he remembers Me"* (al-Bukhārī 7405; Muslim 2675). The prayer of the longing heart is never refused entry; the plea of the self-satisfied heart is what the verse calls *little belief*.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:89

> **Although they used to pray for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists, when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺, they rejected it. So may Allah’s condemnation be upon the disbelievers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Arrival of the Long-Awaited Book**

This verse narrates one of history's strangest reversals. *Wa lammā jāʾahum kitābun min ʿindi Allāhi muṣaddiqun li-mā maʿahum* — "and when there came to them a Book from God, confirming what was with them" — the "Book" is the Qur'an, described by its essential posture toward the scripture already in the Jews' hands: *confirming*, not cancelling; attesting the Torah's truth, not contradicting it. And then the parenthesis that gives the verse its irony: *wa kānū min qablu yastaftiḥūna ʿalā alladhīna kafarū* — "and aforetime they used to seek victory, by means of him, over those who disbelieved." The commentators (Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī) preserve the picture: the Jewish tribes of pre-Islamic Madinah, living among idolatrous Arabs who repeatedly worsted them in quarrels, would tell their opponents, in effect: "A prophet is coming — his time is near — by whom we shall be granted victory over you, and we shall cut you down as ʿĀd and Iram were cut." In some transmitted versions they offered prayers in their own gatherings: *"O God, send this prophet whom we find described in our Book, that we may punish these idolaters"* — invoking, by name and description, the very figure whose advent their scriptures foretold (cf. 7:157). The idolatrous Arabs of Aws and Khazraj therefore knew of the awaited prophet *from the Jews* — a debt of knowledge that the former pagans did not forget, and later threw back in their neighbors' faces: "You used to pray for conquest over us by means of Muḥammad — and now here he is."

**When the Recognized One Arrives**

Then the reversal: *fa-lammā jāʾahum mā ʿarafū kafarū bihi* — "when there came to them that which they recognized, they disbelieved in it." The commentators underline the verb: *ʿarafū* — they *recognized*. The refusal was not based on a failed identification; the description matched — the time, the signs, the substance of the teaching, the very truth they had once coveted — and precisely *that which they recognized* became the object of their rejection. The verse thereby diagnoses the new motive without yet naming it (verse 90 will name it: envy): what changed between the prayers and the fulfilment was not the message but the messenger's tribe — the awaited prophet arose among the Arabs, not among them — and the recognition was swallowed by resentment. Al-Rāzī moderates the claim slightly, allowing that the *recognition* could also mean recognition of prophethood's general marks rather than of an itemized personal description, but the Book's own logic is maintained either way: they disbelieved in what they knew to be true. The verdict descends at the end of the verse in its most impersonal, judicial form: *fa-laʿnatu Allāhi ʿalā al-kāfirīn* — "and the curse of God is upon the disbelievers" — stated not as insult but as sentence: expulsion from mercy is the settled decree upon kufr as such, whoever performs it.

**The Warning Etched in Reversal**

For the believing community this verse has always carried a double-edged instruction. Outwardly it vindicates the Prophet ﷺ beyond any plausible propaganda: his advent was anticipated in the scripture of his neighbors, and the former pagans of Madinah could attest that testimony — a convergence difficult to counterfeit and preserved in the early accounts of the city's conversion. Inwardly it warns every community that possesses a Book: the knowledge of revelation is no guarantee of love for revelation. A people may know, describe, anticipate, even invoke by prayer a coming truth — and still, upon arrival, find that the truth's *address* (to whom it came, from whose mouth, at what cost to standing) governs their response more than the truth itself. The scholars of the path have drawn from the verse its standing caution for the religiously learned: the peril of the well-informed soul is that recognition itself will be mistaken for acceptance — that a heart can describe prophecy perfectly and still, on the day, turn its back on the Prophet it described. The verse therefore teaches the Muslim's careful habit of thanksgiving for guidance: since recognition, unaccompanied by submission, is recorded here as the final rung before the curse, the believer continually asks God to keep learned knowledge from hardening into a museum of truths admired and resisted — and to let recognition always ripen into embracement, as it did for those Madinans of both communities whose hearts, upon recognizing, were moved to believe.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:90

> **Miserable is the price they have sold their souls for—denying Allah’s revelation and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants! They have earned wrath upon wrath. And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Motive Named: Envy**

After recording the rejection, the Book now performs the autopsy and names the disease: *bi'samā ishtaraw bihi anfusahum an yakfurū bi-mā anzala Allāhu baghyan an yunazzila Allāhu min faḍlihi ʿalā man yashāʾu min ʿibādih* — "Evil is that for which they sold themselves: that they disbelieve in what God has sent down, out of envy (*baghyan*) that God should send down of His Grace upon whom He wills of His servants." At last, the engine behind verses 87–89 stands exposed: *baghy* — envy crossed with transgressive resentment. The commentators specify its content: certain of the Jews of Madinah considered prophethood an Israelite patrimony — the lamp had burned in their house for centuries — and that the divine gift should pass to an Arab of the line of Ishmael struck them not as error but as *affront*: God had distributed His favor to the wrong recipient. The verse's phraseology is precise about the object of envy: it is not the Prophet's person they contested but God's own freedom of bestowal — *that God should send down His Grace upon whomsoever He wills*. Envy of the Prophet was thereby a quarrel with the Bestower: the envier appoints himself auditor of divine generosity and rules the appointment invalid. It is in its way a second tower of Babel: man's tribunal convening to judge God's choice of servants.

**The Commerce of Envy and the Currency of Grace**

The verse frames the envious act in economics — "they sold their souls" — and it picks up the sūrah's own currency-language (2:16, 2:86, 2:102): the soul spent itself to purchase kufr, and the Book's formula *bi'samā ishtaraw bihi anfusahum* — "evil is that for which they sold their souls" — marks the transaction as the worst bargain struck in the whole address, which is why the phrase is repeated verbatim at the end of the Babylon passage (2:102): the soul in exchange for tribal pride; the Hereafter for a census-fix. Opposite the sold soul, the verse names what was refused: *faḍl* — Grace, bounty, the surplus of God's giving — the same *faḍl* in which the believing sinner places his whole hope at 2:64 ("were it not for God's *bounty* upon you, and His mercy"). Human destiny, the sūrah thus teaches in its two currencies, divides between those who live upon grace and those who resent it; and envy toward grace is not an ordinary vice among others but the direct negation of the soul's only true wealth. The jurist-theologians add the verse's corrective to the old prophetic-lesson of lineage: prophethood was never an estate passing by blood-fief; God *sends His Grace upon whom He wills of His servants* — *ibād* here a term of honor, as on the tongue of the Qur'an whenever it praises (2:186, 2:207; 25:63).

**Wrath upon Wrath**

The outcome is stated in the rather terrifying image of accumulation: *fa-bāʾū bi-ghaḍabin ʿalā ghaḍab* — "so they returned burdened with wrath upon wrath." *Bāʾa* means to return home carrying a load; the sentence pictures the enviers arriving at the end of their transaction with a double burden: the commentators enumerate the two wraths variously — wrath for the calf and wrath for rejecting Jesus; wrath for disbelieving the Torah's own content and wrath for rejecting the Qur'an; wrath for the first corruption and wrath for the second rejection (Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī) — but all agree on the principle: *repeated light refused becomes repeated darkness earned*; one wrath was the price of one choice, and the second choice doubled it. The verse closes with the eschatological note: *wa li'l-kāfirīna ʿadhābun muhīn* — "and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment" — and the commentators draw out the significance of *muhīn*, humiliating: the destiny answers to the crime; the crime was a pride-offense — the refusal to bow where God had not crowned the expected crown — and the punishment is correspondingly the shattering of pride, a torment whose essence is *humiliation*, in exact moral counterweight to the exaltation envy had claimed for itself.

**The Believer's Inoculation Against Envy**

For the believing community the verse is a standing inoculation. The Prophet ﷺ so ranked *ḥasad* among the destroyers that he closed a famous ḥadīth with its somber image:

> *"Beware of envy, for envy consumes good deeds as fire consumes firewood"* — or, in the parallel wording — *"as fire consumes grass."* (Abū Dāwūd 4903 — a ḥadīth whose chain is graded hasan, and whose sense is corroborated throughout the tradition)

And the Prophet ﷺ taught the jealous-hearted to give themselves the medicine of this verse: when God gives a brother a bounty — knowledge, standing, provision — the believer's business with that bounty is twofold: pray for its increase upon its bearer ("bless him in it"), and ask of the Bestower His grace for oneself — because *faḍl* is not rationed by allocation but poured by will, and the envious burgle only themselves out of the distribution. God's answer to the claim that He sent prophecy to the wrong quarter was simply that *He sends down His grace upon whom He wills among His servants* — and the believer so receives that sentence that his entire worship becomes a series of little assents to God's freedom: glad when the Qur'an came from a hillside cave in Ḥijāz rather than from any academy; glad when rain falls on a stranger's field; glad whenever grace descends anywhere, since the rain belongs, after all, to God.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:91

> **When it is said to them: “Believe in what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “We only believe in what was sent down to us,” and they deny what came afterwards, though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures! Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Why then did you kill Allah’s prophets before, if you are ˹truly˺ believers?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Slogan of Partitive Belief**

The verse isolates and quotes the community's central formula of self-defense: when told *āminū bi-mā anzala Allāh* — "Believe in what God has sent down" — they reply *nuʾminu bi-mā unzila ʿalaynā* — "We believe in what was sent down *to us*" — *wa yakfurūna bi-mā warāʾah* — "while disbelieving in all that lies beyond it." The commentators (al-Ṭabarī and others) parse the phrase *mā warāʾah* as everything *after* or *other than* the Torah — the Gospel, and now the Qur'an. The slogan's cleverness is its pious sound: loyalty to one's own revelation is presented as the ground for refusing any other. Yet the Book immediately attaches the fatal double fact: *wa huwa al-ḥaqqu muṣaddiqan li-mā maʿahum* — "though it is the truth, confirming what is with them." The rejected Book does not oppose the cherished Book; it authenticates it. The custodian's claim "we stand by our own scroll" is therefore falsified by the content of his own scroll itself, for the Torah they profess testifies to the very Prophets they reject — and the Book proceeds to prove the emptiness of the slogan by the community's own history with the prophets who came *within* it.

**The Devastating Counter-Question**

The divinely dictated rebuttal is one question: *qul fa-lima taqtulūna anbiyāʾa Allāhi min qablu in kuntum muʾminīn* — "Say: then why did you slay the prophets of God aforetime, if you were believers?" The commentators note the rebuke's precise structure: the slain prophets of the old covenant were themselves Israelites, sent within the Mosaic dispensation, commanding nothing but fidelity to the Torah. If loyalty to "what was sent down to us" were truly the community's governing principle, those prophets — bearers of exactly that revelation — would have been its most honored men. Instead they were killed: Zechariah and John in the Gospel memory, Uriah in Jeremiah's day, Isaiah in the traditions, and the long line mourned in the Book's own repeated phrase (2:87; 3:21; 4:155; 5:70; cf. Luke 13:34: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets"). The counter-question thereby unmasks the slogan: *fidelity to the Torah* cannot be the motive of a people whose own Torah-faithful prophets lie dead at their hands. The motive is the one named in verse 90 — envy and pride — wearing Torah-loyalty as a garment. The argument's form is a standing model of Qur'anic *ilzām*: binding an opponent by the consequences of his own stated principle until his true ground is visible.

**Selective Belief and the Believer's Own Slogan**

For the later community of believers, the verse functions as a mirror at two removes. First, communally: Islam is the religion of *all* the revealed books — "who believes in God and... His Books" (4:136) — and the Muslim who would use his own Book to negate the authentic missions of Moses and Jesus repeats, in mirror, the error of those who used the Torah to negate his Prophet; the Book gives his community charge over *belief in the whole*, naming negation of any prophet as a species of the very kufr the verse denounces (4:150–151). Second, individually: the heart has its own version of "we believe in what was sent down to us" — a private partitive belief in which the believer accepts the verses that comfort and hesitates before the verses that oblige. The tradition's name for full-spectrum faith is stated in the Book itself: *"We make no distinction between any of His messengers"* (2:285) — and just as the verse demands of a scripture-people belief in everything the scroll-people was sent, the same demand assesses the reader of this sūrah: the Qur'an believed in part — comfort taken, summons declined — is the slogan of Madinah repeated at the level of the single soul. Faith's true speech is the whole-verse assent: *āmannā bi-mā unzila* — "we believe in what has been sent down," without the addition *"to us,"* and without the disbelief in whatever lies beyond the familiar.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:92

> **Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Proof and the Betrayal**

The verse tightens the argument of verse 91 to one piercing datum of history: *wa la-qad jāʾakum mūsā bi'l-bayyināti thumma ittakhadhtum al-ʿijla min baʿdihi wa antum ẓālimūn* — "Moses came to you with the clear proofs; then you took up the calf after him, while you were wrongdoers." The *bayyināt* — the manifest demonstrations — are enumerated by the commentators (Ibn Kathīr and others): the staff that became a serpent and swallowed the magicians' ropes; the hand drawn forth white and luminous; the sea split into wall-like paths; the cloud that shaded the camp; the manna and the quails; the water struck from rock. Against that solid front of evidence the verse places a single counter-image: the golden calf — *al-ʿijl*. And the chronological cruelty of the choice is in the verse's own words: *min baʿdihi* — *after him*, while the prophet was still alive, merely absent up the mountain for his appointment with his Lord (the fuller telling at 7:148–155; cf. 2:51). The rhetorical effect is devastatingly simple: after *that* — proofs upon proofs, mercies upon mercies — this people before the mountain did *this*. The verse is thus the compressed inventory of the irrationality of unbelief: no amount of evidence had ever yet purchased even the duration of one absence of the prophet from the camp.

**"While You Were Wrongdoers" — The State Within the Act**

The closing clause adds the moral light in which the act must be seen: *wa antum ẓālimūn* — "while you were wrongdoers." The circumstantial construction (the ḥāl), the grammarians explain, does not excuse or mitigate; it aggravates: the deed was done *in the state of* ẓulm, unrightedness, wrongdoing, the very quality already expounded as ingratitude-in-action at 2:51 and as the essence of shirk at 31:13 ("association is a tremendous ẓulm"). Their idolatry, in other words, was not a stumble of the ignorant but the act of a will already positioned against the covenant. The commentators adduce this verse as one of the fixed texts by which the sūrah indicts the whole repeated pattern: sign → relief → forgetfulness → substitution; and they locate in it, too, the foreshadow of the community's posture toward the later prophets — the refusal of Jesus and of Muḥammad ﷺ — for the soul trained to replace a living prophet's charge within forty days does not suddenly learn constancy in forty centuries. The calf is the template of all subsequent substitution: a God-shaped thing, made by human hands, embraced while the true Lord's prophet is briefly out of view.

**Idols Constructed in Absences**

For the believing reader, the verse's deepest practical sense lies in the phrase *min baʿdihi* — *after him*, in the gap while the prophet was away. The spiritual writers note the standing lesson: fidelity is measured in the prophet's absence — and the Prophet ﷺ is absent from his community in every generation after his passing; the believer lives, each hour, under the conditions of the Israelite camp at Sinai: the caravan of proofs lies behind, and the mountain-voice has gone silent. What a soul *does* with that silence is its whole religion. The Companions at the Prophet's death enacted the faithful alternative to calf-taking: Abū Bakr's ﷺ cry — already cited in this commentary at 2:51 — "worship God, for God lives and does not die" — was the ummah's refusal of every ʿijl fashioned in grief: personality, nostalgia, doubt. The Prophet ﷺ had himself foreseen the post-absence test and planted the criterion that survives him:

> *"I have left among you two things; you will never go astray so long as you hold fast to them: the Book of God and my Sunnah."* (al-Muwattaʾ, Book 46, 3; al-Ḥākim 1/93 — its wording debated by hadith critics while its substance stands guaranteed by the Qur'an's own commands to follow the Messenger)

Every later calf is cast from the gold of the Prophet's absence — the ornaments of old habit melted while the mountain-voice is not immediately heard: a revered sheikh obeyed against the text, a custom defended against the Sunnah, a desire enthroned against a verse. The lesson of 2:92 is thus renewed with every age: it is not the amount of the evidence, but the temper of the heart between his signs and his return, that decides whether the community stands in the covenant or dances round the calf.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:93

> **And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and obey,” they answered, “We hear and disobey.” The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts because of their disbelief. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “How evil is what your ˹so-called˺ belief prompts you to do, if you ˹actually˺ believe ˹in the Torah˺!”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"We Hear — and We Disobey"**

The verse returns to the mountain-covenant scene of 2:63, but this time it records what verses 63–64 had left unspoken — the community's actual answer: *wa qālū samiʿnā wa ʿaṣaynā* — "They said: we hear, and we disobey." The phrase is one of the most quoted inversions in the Book: by changing a single letter of the required response — the believers' *samiʿnā wa aṭaʿnā* ("we hear and we obey," 2:285) into *samiʿnā wa ʿaṣaynā* — they converted the formula of faith into the formula of rebellion. The commentators debate whether the words were spoken with the tongue or only uttered by the state of their conduct, and the sounder view embraces both: whether by speech or by behavior, the covenant received under the suspended mountain was answered with refusal — a refusal all the more damning for its frankness: not "we cannot" but *"we disobey."* The scene thus crowns the whole sequence: beneath the most fearsome terms ever attached to a revelation's acceptance, the response placed on record is rebellion articulated to God's face. And the Book will forever measure communities by the two one-letter-apart answers: the people of *aṭaʿnā* — "we obey" — and the people of *ʿaṣaynā* — "we disobey."

**Drinking the Calf into the Heart**

Then the verse renders one of its most haunting images: *wa ushribū fī qulūbihimu al-ʿijla bi-kufrihim* — "and they were made to drink the calf into their hearts, because of their disbelief." The commentators (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī) explain: the calf itself is not drunk; it is the *love* of the calf that was poured into their hearts until they were saturated — as a drink pervades the thirsty body, so the love of the idol pervaded their inner make-up. The image fixes the anthropology of idolatry for all of the tradition: the idol is first *imbibed* — loved, craved, internalized — and only afterward *worshipped*; by the time the golden statue stood in the camp, the calf had long been present inside them. The same metaphor instructs the Prophet's ﷺ ḥadīth about the two hearts:

> *"Trials are presented to the hearts like the reed-mat, strip by strip: whichever heart imbibes them, a black spot is fixed in it; whichever rejects them, a white spot is fixed in it, until there are two hearts — a white one like the smooth stone, no trial harms it as long as heavens and earth endure; and a black one, dust-colored like an overturned vessel, recognizing no right and rejecting no wrong, save what its own passion pours into it."* (Muslim 144, from Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān)

Whether the heart drinks *fitan* or drinks the *ʿijl*, imbibing is the mechanism: whatever the heart is made to absorb shapes its color and its destiny. The calf-worship was thus not a lapse of practice but a state of the inner cup — a heart already filled with the drink of the substitute.

**"Evil Is What Your Belief Enjoins" — The Irony Verdict**

God then commands His Prophet ﷺ to deliver the epigram that milks the whole irony from the scene: *qul biʾsamā yaʾmurukum bihi īmānukum in kuntum muʾminīn* — "Say: evil is that which your *belief* enjoins upon you — if you *are* believers." The name *īmān* is here spoken back at them in devastating quotation: you call this faith — and *this* faith commands you to reject, to slay prophets, to drink the calf, to answer the covenant with *ʿaṣaynā*? Then let us examine the belief by its commands: any *īmān* whose actual injunctions are disbelief, idolatry, and murder stands exposed as not faith at all. Ibn ʿAjībah, in the register of the spiritual commentary, reads the irony inward for the Muslim listener: the soul filled with the world and its ambitions has its own counterfeit "belief" — its own named-īmān that habitually issues the permissive rulings passion desires — and such a heart, whatever its profession, is under the verse's sentence: the belief is measured by what it *commands*, not by what it claims. The tradition takes the verse, therefore, as a standing audit of every believer's operative faith: not what creed does your tongue recite, but what does your pattern of choices command and permit? For the genuine faith — the faith named again at 2:82 (belief plus righteous work) — enjoins only good; and the discrepancy between professed and operative belief is precisely the gap this closing verse of the mountain-cycle holds open for every reader to step into, examine, and, by God's mercy, close.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:94

> **Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively for you ˹Israelites˺ out of all humanity, then wish for death if what you say is true!”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Challenge of the Private Paradise**

The Book now carries the argument to its sharpest edge — a formal public challenge: *qul in kānat lakum al-dāru al-ākhiratu ʿinda Allāhi khāliṣatan min dūni al-nāsi fa-tamannaw al-mawta in kuntum ṣādiqīn* — "Say: if the Abode of the Hereafter with God is exclusively yours, to the exclusion of other people, then long for death, if you are truthful." The claim being tested is the one the community had asserted in their literature of *amānī* — that Paradise belonged to them as a private possession, sealed off from the rest of mankind (cf. 2:111: "None shall enter the Garden but such as are Jews or Christians"). God's answer is dialectical elegance: take the claim seriously, and its rational corollary follows immediately. For a man whose eternal dwelling is *assured*, death is merely the door to his palace — and a sane man does not dread the door of his palace; he wishes it open. Therefore: *long for death*. Truthfulness has a simple signature here: the exclusive-heir should find every hour of this life a swindling delay. The parallel challenge appears at 62:6 in nearly identical terms, confirming that this was a standing instrument of the Prophet's ﷺ public engagement with the People of the Book in Madinah.

**The Logic of Assurance — and the Islamic Refusal of Presumption**

The commentators (al-Rāzī, al-Thaʿlabī) articulate the theology embedded in the challenge: the demand to long for death is not a command to suicide — the Islamic tradition explicitly forbids wishing for death as a personal impulse, the Prophet ﷺ having taught: *"Let none of you long for death on account of an evil that befalls him; but if he must, let him say: O God, give me life as long as life is better for me, and cause me to die when death is better for me"* (al-Bukhārī 5671; Muslim 2680) — but rather an *audit of certainty*. The world is divided, by this verse, into two conditions: the man certain his next dwelling is the Garden, who should rationally yearn — and the man who *does not* yearn, whose clinging to this world is the involuntary confession that his claimed certainty is not real. The Jewish interlocutors' refusal of the test (verse 95) thus reads as the Book's own demonstration of the hollowness of their exclusive claim. But the knife cuts in both directions: the verse installs, at the root of the doctrine of salvation, a principle decisive for Islam — *presumption about one's own destiny is itself a heresy of confidence*; the Book nowhere authorizes any believer, of any community, to sign his own certificate of election. Islamic piety therefore walks the exact opposite posture: not the swagger of the assured elect but the Prophet's own refrain — *works done in hope and fear* — with death loved not as the certificated but prepared for as the accountable.

**Between Longing and Working**

The tradition holds the balance of this verse with an entirely characteristic piety. On one side, the believer is forbidden despair and forbidden terror-led paralysis: death, for the friend of God, portends the encounter the Prophet ﷺ described when he said that whoever loves meeting God, God loves meeting him (al-Bukhārī 6507; Muslim 2683 — already cited in these commentaries at 2:46). On the other side, he has no license for the presumption verse 94 punctures: his secure inheritance is neither claimed nor counted until his Lord signs the account, and so his humanity between the two knows only one safe posture — the working hope. Rābiʿah al-ʿAdawiyyah's reported prayer-vocabulary distills the classical Sufi answer to the challenge's either/or: *"O God, if I worship You from fear of the Fire, burn me in it; and if from craving for the Garden, bar me from it; but if for You Yourself, then withhold not Your Eternal Beauty"* — attested in the literary record with debated chains but universally received as the spirit of the tradition's reply: the true lover has no need to certify his inheritance; he is too busy loving. In that spirit the verse's challenge settles into the believer's conscience not as a dare but as an examination: where the heart finds no longings for the meeting whatsoever, it should ask what precisely it has laid up in the unseen account — which is exactly the file the next verse will open.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:95

> **But they will never wish for that because of what their hands have done. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verdict of the Untaken Challenge**

The Book answers its own challenge, speaking the community's response before they utter it: *wa lan yatamannawhu abadan bi-mā qaddamat aydīhim* — "but they will never long for it, ever, because of what their hands have sent forth." The commentators dwell on the tense and the cause. The tense is absolute: *lan... abadan* — never, at any time — a divine prediction that no such longing would issue from them, and historically it is reported that none among the addressed scholars took up the dare; the proposal of a mutual imprecation (*mubāhalah*, on the reading mentioned by Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī) stood unaccepted. The cause is stated without euphemism: *bi-mā qaddamat aydīhim* — because of what their hands have *sent ahead*. The Book's idiom for one's works as sent-forth cargo — what goes before a man into the Unseen and awaits him there — appears throughout (3:30; 18:57; 75:13): death is feared not in itself but as the encounter with one's own forwarded freight. The unspoken truth of the refusal is thus confessed on their behalf by God Himself: they will not long for death because, at some depth inaccessible to their own slogans, they *know what is packed in the hold* — the calf, the slain prophets, the doctored scrolls, the covenants voided — and no community's public assurance of election can silence the private inventory of the hands.

**Conscience Under the Doctrine of Election**

There is a profound psychology of religion in this verse, which the commentators and spiritual writers draw out: the claim of exclusive salvation could not survive ten seconds of interiority. Outwardly the community professed the private Paradise; inwardly the same hearts, when invited to hasten to it by the shortest path, shrank — and the Book reads the shrinkage as unbelief's reflex confession. The verse thereby reacts a standing principle: *every professed certainty is tested by the prospect of its verification.* Whoever is sure his freight is good leans toward the shore; whoever hangs back from the shore tells you his certainty was decoration. This is also why the verse's final clause is not a threat but a diagnosis: *wa-llāhu ʿalīmun bi'l-ẓālimīn* — "and God knows the wrongdoers." The ending assigns the now-exposed people to their class: unwillingness to meet God was never the modesty of humility — it was the recognition of deeds, and God names the doers of those deeds *al-ẓālimīn*, the wrongdoers, with the same general term under which the whole address has been sorting them since verse 51. Between their lips and their ledger, God stands knowing both.

**The Believer's Sent-Forth Cargo**

For the Muslim reader the verse is not a piece of disputation-history only; it is a working rule of piety. The same inventory-question is posed to every believer in the tradition's daily meditations: *"Take account of yourselves before you are taken to account; weigh your deeds before they are weighed for you"* — a saying of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb transmitted in the early exhortations (cf. al-Tirmidhī's collection of zuhd-reports) — enacts precisely the mechanism of verse 95 in the direction of healing: the freight audited in time need not be feared at the landing. The Prophet ﷺ taught his community the merciful version of the same inventory, attaching repentance to it in a way that changes the cargo's contents:

> *"By the One in Whose Hand is my soul, if you did not sin, God would remove you and bring a people who would sin, then seek God's pardon, and He would pardon them."* (Muslim 2749, from Abū Hurayrah)
