And ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd preserved the Prophet's ﷺ saying that translates the freight-language into the language of feet — the sending members of verse 95's "hands":

> *"The two feet of the son of Adam shall not move on the Day of Resurrection until he is asked about five..."* — his life, his youth, his wealth, and what he did with his knowledge (al-Tirmidhī 2416, *ṣaḥīḥ*).

The believer auditing his five accounts regularly is precisely un-learning the posture of verse 95; he is storing freight he will be glad to meet, so that when his longing for the encounter comes — and the Book does not forbid him that longing but only its presumptuous version — it will be the yearning of a man who has audited, repented, and hoped in the mercy of the One who *knows the wrongdoers* and loves the repentant.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:96

> **You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people, even more than polytheists. Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years. But even if they were to live that long, it would not save them from the punishment. And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Superlative of Clinging**

The Book proceeds to measure the depth of the refusal just recorded: God predicts to His Prophet ﷺ — *wa la-tajidannahum aḥrasa al-nāsi ʿalā ḥayāh* — "you will surely find them the most greedy of all people for life" — *wa mina alladhīna ashrakū* — "[more so] even than those who associate partners with God." The comparison is startling and was meant to be: the idolater of Makkah, who believed in no resurrection and thus had every "reason" to cling to this one existence, is outstripped in life-hunger by these heirs of prophets and covenants. The commentators note the superlative construction and what it implies: greed for mere duration — not greed for knowledge, not for worship, not for completion of good — becomes the diagnostic sign of the community measured. The inner logic is the same as verse 95's: the man who *received* the promise of an after-House, then shrank from mortality anyway, reveals that his real worldview has silently collapsed into the materialist's — heaven is on his tongue, and extinction in his bones. It is among the Book's sharpest exposures of the split between professed cosmology and lived cosmology.

**The Wish of a Thousand Years**

The verse then quotes the wish itself: *yawaddu aḥaduhum law yuʿammaru alfa sanah* — "each one of them wishes he might be granted a life of a thousand years" — and then stamps its futility: *wa mā huwa bi-muzaḥziḥihi mina al-ʿadhābi an yuʿammar* — "though a long life would not budge him one inch from the punishment." The commentators remark the quiet precision of *muzaḥziḥ* — to dislodge, to shift by inches: what the thousand years cannot do is not remove the punishment wholesale but *shift it any distance at all*; time is simply not a currency in which sentence-distance is measured. Whether "a thousand" echoes the Persian millennial cycles observed by some of the commentators, or simply signifies the longest imaginable span, the arithmetic is the same: postpone the reckoning by any factor — a decade, a century, a millennium — and the reckoning's *proximity* is unchanged, for what falls due at the end of a thousand years is, at the end, exactly as near as it was on the day the wish was made. The verse therefore converts the wish for longevity into the starkest kind of bad bargain: all that extension buys is a lengthened courtroom-corridor, ending at the identical bench.

**And God Sees What They Do**

The unit closes with the same standing warrant that ended verse 85 and the trial-scene of verse 74: *wa-llāhu baṣīrun bi-mā yaʿmalūn* — "and God sees whatsoever they do." The commentators register the watchfulness-attribute here as the fitting closure: the men of the thousand-year wish labor at evasions under an Eye that misses none of it — flight within the field of vision of the Judge is flight inside the courtroom. The tradition binds the closing verbs of this cluster of verses (vv. 94–96: *knowing*... *aware of the wrongdoers*... *seeing what they do*) into a single doctrine for the believer's conscience: audit is total and continuous; nothing about the ledger is awaiting readability at a later scanning, and no chronological postponement alters its contents. The believing community is therefore trained by these three verses to the contrary wish: not the length of life but the soundness of it. The Prophet's ﷺ own practice of measure in such matters was reported by Ibn ʿUmar, who said the Prophet ﷺ took him by the shoulders and said:

> *"Be in this world as though you were a stranger or a wayfarer"; and Ibn ʿUmar added: "When evening comes, do not await the morning; and when morning comes, do not await the evening; and take from your health for your sickness, and from your life for your death."* (al-Bukhārī 6416)

That is the spiritual inversion of verse 96: the believer counts himself a passer-through and packs accordingly; the thousand-year wish belongs to the man who thinks he owns the road. Between the two stances, the verse plants the standing reminder that length of days is not an exemption, and that its requester is seen — all through the years of the request.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:97

> **Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it—a guide and good news for the believers.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Objection of the Declared Enmity**

The occasion of this verse, preserved in the early tradition (Ibn Kathīr and others), is one of the most revealing dialogues of the Madinan period. A group of Jewish scholars questioned the Prophet ﷺ with precise, testing questions that — as they themselves admitted — only a true prophet could answer, and his answers matched what they knew. Then they asked: *who brings you the message?* He answered: **Gabriel**. At that, they demurred: had he said **Michael** — the angel of mercy and of Israel's patronage in their literature — they could follow him; but Gabriel, associated in their received tradition with war, chastisement, and the destruction of cities, they accounted their enemy. In a parallel report, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb heard the same distinction from Madinan Jews and was struck at the notion of finding one of God's two near angels a friend and the other a foe — and upon returning to the Prophet ﷺ, found this verse already revealed. The commentators set the background in the wider Jewish angelology of the era: Michael exalted as Israel's advocate (Daniel 10:13–21; the later rabbinic literature), Gabriel assigned the sterner commissions — the destroyer of Sodom in the Midrash, fire to Michael's snow. The Book's answer refusals the entire premise of angelic partisanship in one verse.

**The Vindication: What Gabriel Actually Brought**

The divine reply does not argue about Gabriel's temperament; it simply enumerates his delivery: *qul man kāna ʿaduwwan li-jibrīla fa-innahu nazzalahu ʿalā qalbika bi-idhni Allāh* — "Say: whoever is an enemy of Gabriel — for it is he who brought it down upon your heart, by God's leave." Then the cargo is itemized in three clauses — *muṣaddiqan li-mā bayna yadayh* — "confirming what was before it": the content Gabriel conveys is not a novelty hostile to the Torah but its confirmation and seal; *wa hudan* — "a guidance" for every seeking person; *wa bushra li'l-muʾminīn* — "and glad tidings for the believers." In other words: the angel these scholars counted an enemy of their people is the very courier of the final good news their own scriptures anticipated; the enmity stands self-refuted by the freight. The commentators add the theological point quietly embedded in *bi-idhni Allāh* — *by God's leave*: Gabriel is not a free contractor of punishments or an autonomous power; he is a commissioned servant conveying and executing only by permission — so that hostility toward *his* office is, materially, hostility toward *his Sender*, which is precisely the deduction the next verse will make explicit.

**The Heart onto Which It Descended**

One more phrase in the verse deserves the tradition's long meditation: *ʿalā qalbika* — "upon *your heart*." The Qur'an consistently names the heart, not the brain, as the landing-place of revelation (26:193–194: "the Trustworthy Spirit brought it down upon your heart"), and the spiritual tradition built upon this its whole epistemology of the interior: revelation settles first in the Prophet's heart — the organ of direct knowing — and from his heart to his tongue, and from his tongue into the hearts of his community. The believer who recites the Book with presence is re-enacting the line of transmission on his own scale: from page to tongue, from tongue to heart; hence the tradition's insistence that recitation without the heart is incomplete communication of the same spirit. And the verse's final two nouns nominate the posture in which the recitation must be received: as *hudan*, guidance — to be followed — and as *bushra*, glad tidings — to be rejoiced in. The enemy of Gabriel is therefore, in the final analysis, anyone who meets this descent with enmity; the companion of Gabriel is anyone who meets it with the two acts named: guidance accepted, tidings believed — and his heart, like the heart it first descended on, becomes one of the places where the Spirit comes down.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:98

> **Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel, and Michael, then ˹let them know that˺ Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Law of Alignment**

The verse generalizes verse 97 into a total law: *man kāna ʿaduwwan li-llāhi wa malāʾikatihi wa rusulihi wa jibrīla wa mīkāl* — "whoever is an enemy of God and His angels and His messengers, and Gabriel and Michael" — *fa-inna Allāha ʿaduwwun li'l-kāfirīn* — "...then God is the enemy of the disbelievers." The sequence is deliberately telescoped: enmity at *any* point of the chain — toward God Himself; toward His angels as a class; toward His messengers as a class; toward the two angels named — compounds and resolves into a single verdict: the enmity of God toward the disbelievers. The commentators first dispense with a grammatical fallacy: the naming of Gabriel and Michael after the angels does not imply they are other than angels, just as the Qur'an names dates and pomegranates after "fruit" (55:68) — a particular singled out after its genus for honor. It then states the verse's symmetry, which is its essence: hostility is *reciprocated*, not merely recorded. Whatever man makes himself an enemy of God's side, he finds God arrayed with the other side of the war. The verse is the dark mirror of the Book's famous assurances of alliance — "God is the Protector (walī) of those who believe" (2:257) — and of the Prophet's ﷺ report of the divine warning in the ḥadīth qudsī repeatedly quoted by the commentators under this very text:

> *"Whoever shows enmity to a friend (walī) of Mine, I declare war upon him."* (al-Bukhārī 6502, from Abū Hurayrah)

**Pick Neither Angels Nor Prophets**

The verse also legislates a permanent rule of belief that the earlier communities had violated and the later community is warned against: *no selection among God's commissioned beings*. One may not follow Moses and reject Jesus; follow Jesus and reject Muḥammad ﷺ; honor Michael and despise Gabriel. Belief is an undivided allegiance to the whole divine side — God, His angels, His messengers — precisely the creed the believers themselves profess and the Book praises at the sūrah's close: *"We make no distinction between any of His messengers"* (2:285). The Madinan scholars' political angelology — kindness from Michael, sternness from Gabriel, therefore preference for one — is thus diagnosed as a sundering of God's unity on the angelic plane, the same fragmentational instinct that verse 85 had diagnosed in their partitive belief in the Book. A heart that says "yes" to what is gentle in God's service and "no" to what is stern in God's service has not yet understood that both come from the same Lord — the mercy of Michael and the severity of Gabriel are two expressions of one Will, and enmity toward either is enmity toward the One who sent them both.

**God's Enmity as the Last Dread**

The closing clause is the heaviest in the whole unit: *fa-inna Allāha ʿaduwwun li'l-kāfirīn* — "God is indeed the enemy of the disbelievers." The commentators and devotional writers alike treat the sentence with trembling: it is dreadful not as an image of pique but as the description of an alignment — the man who has set himself against the divine side discovers that every protection is now on the far side of the line he drew. All defense that ever stood between him and ruin — providence, intercession, mercy, time — proceeds from the side he has made his enemy. The verse thus stands as the terrible counterpart of the tradition's greatest glad-tidings: just as God *befriends* the believer and fights his battles — *"the servant draws near to Me... until I love him; and when I love him I am his hearing by which he hears and his sight by which he sees"* (al-Bukhārī 6502) — so, on the other side, He *opposes* the disbeliever, and nothing in the universe stands on the disbeliever's side of that opposition that could help: for the helper too is God's. Faith, in the light of verse 98, is simply the stance of being found, at one's death, on the side that God is on — and the sūrah has spent ninety-eight verses teaching that the price of that stance is one thing only: *do not pick among His angels, His Books, and His messengers; take the whole of what God sent, from whichever angelic hand and whichever prophetic tongue it came.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:99

> **Indeed, We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ clear revelations. ˹But˺ none will deny them except the rebellious.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Signs Beyond Dispute**

After the whole survey of objection — the plea of covered hearts, the calculus of envy, the partisan angelology — the Book states its summary judgment: *wa la-qad anzalnā ilayka āyātin bayyināt* — "We have indeed sent down to you clear, self-evidencing signs" — *wa mā yakfuru bihā illā al-fāsiqūn* — "and none disbelieves in them except the iniquitous." The phrase *āyāt bayyināt* gathers, in the commentators' reading (Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī), both the revealed verses themselves and the entire constellation of proofs around the Prophet's person: the conformity of his description with what the earlier scriptures had foretold, the manifest qualities of his character, the Qur'an's own inimitable splendor — signs whose clarity is such that they bear their evidence in themselves, needing no intermediary advocate. A *bayyinah* is what *makes plain*: these signs are not clues requiring a detective but lights requiring only eyes.

**"Only the Fāsiqūn Disbelieve" — The Diagnosis of Rejection**

The second half of the verse assigns unbelief its address with arresting directness: the only ones who deny such signs are *al-fāsiqūn* — the iniquitous, those who have stepped out (from *fasaga*, to exit, as a date exits its skin) from the circle of obedience. The verse thus states one of the sūrah's most consequential doctrines: unbelief before manifest signs is not an intellectual verdict but a moral event. The Book does not here call the rejecters *juhhal* — ignorant — nor *mubtalūn* — perplexed; it calls them *fāsiqūn* — people in a state of *exit*. The commentators unfold the implications with care: this is not the claim that every non-believer harbors conscious malice — the Qur'an itself repeatedly distinguishes the stubborn from the ignorant, the leader from the led (see, e.g., 9:101; 33:67–68) — but the claim that when signs of this clarity are met with refusal, something in the will has already moved first: a prior commitment of desire, status, or interest that the sign is not permitted to disturb. Rejection, in such cases, is the *fisq* protecting its positions. The sentence is thus a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ in the same register as 6:33 ("We know that what they say grieves you; yet it is not you that they belie — it is God's signs that the wrongdoers deny") and a description of mechanism: faith failed not because the light was faint but because the eye was shut from within.

**The Mirror for the People of the Book and After**

For the sūrah's first audience, the verse firmly closes the dispute of verses 87–98: nothing in the enmity toward Gabriel, the envy of the Arabs, the nostalgia for exclusive covenant has any footing in evidence — the signs stand clear, and only the state of *fisq* accounts for seeing them and walking away. For the ummah that received this sūrah as its own charter, the verse holds a sobering secondary application, repeatedly drawn by the tradition's preachers: the Book in the hands of the Muslims is likewise *āyāt bayyināt* at home among them, and the same law — that refusal of plain light is a moral event — assesses every heart that hears verses it dislikes and quietly steps out of their circle, one small exit at a time: the neglected obligation, the evaded text, the redescribed sin. Al-Ghazālī heard in this verse the whole pathology of the scholarly self-deception he anatomizes in the *Iḥyāʾ*: knowledge so luminous that only *fisq* can bar it, paired with a person so practiced in *fisq* that the luminosity no longer reaches the street. The verse's word of mercy within its severity is that *fisq* is a door that opens inward as well: the same Book that names the exiting ones commands them to return — *"O you who believe, repent to God with a sincere repentance"* (66:8) — and the one who turns from fisq to repentance re-enters by the same door he left, to find the clear signs as clear as on the day he first saw them.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:100

> **Why is it that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside? In fact, most of them do not believe.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Pattern of the Broken Compact**

The verse opens with the interrogative of astonished confirmation used repeatedly in this address: *awa-kullamā ʿāhadū ʿahdan nabadhahu farīqun minhum* — "Is it not so that whenever they enter into a covenant, a party of them casts it away?" The verb *nabadha* — to hurl something behind oneself contemptuously, to fling aside — is the Book's chosen term for covenant-violation: the compact is not cautiously renounced or apologetically renegotiated; it is *thrown away*, like a thing worthless. The occasion of revelation preserved by the commentators exhibits the pattern threefold. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Thaʿlabī transmit that some of the Madinan Jews objected, "We made no covenant concerning Muḥammad specifically" — a narrowing the verse answers by recalling the general covenant to follow God's messenger *whenever* he comes (cf. 3:81), which the community had affirmed for generations: the awaited prophet was indeed expected to be an Israelite, but nothing in the covenant of fidelity made obedience conditional on his tribe. Others connect the verse to their actual treaty with the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah, cast aside when alliance with the Quraysh suited the hour (cf. 8:56–58; 4:51–52). Al-Rāzī rightly generalizes beyond any single incident: the verse describes an abiding behavior-pattern — *kullamā*, *whenever* — the conditional of repetition: covenant after covenant, compact after compact, the same motion of casting away.

**"Most of Them Do Not Believe"**

The closing clause delivers the statistic: *bal aktharuhum lā yuʾminūn* — "nay, most of them do not believe." Its precision has been treasured by the commentators: the Book does not say *all* of them — the remnant acknowledged at 2:83 ("save a few of you") and vindicated at 3:113–115 ("they are not all alike; among the People of the Book is an upright community") is here mathematically preserved: covenant-treachery is the majority's pattern, not the community's essence. The diagnostic link between the two halves is the theology of the verse: *breach of covenant is not a breach of etiquette but of faith* — which is why the Book explains the castings-away with the words "most of them do not believe": the compacts disintegrate because the interior state that alone gives compacts weight — faith, whose covenant-substance is reverence of the covenant's Witness — has itself disintegrated. A man can fling a document away only if the guarantor of the document is already gone from his accounting. The scholars of the spirit, al-Ghazālī foremost, extended this to the whole of the religious life: prayer-promises, repentance-promises, fasts volunteered and abandoned — each is a little covenant, and their repeated fracture betokens the same failing root, not bad time-management but thinning *īmān*.

**Keepers of Covenants: the Muslim Counter-Vocation**

The verse's opposite pole is one of the defining virtues of the Prophet's ﷺ own community — covenant-keeping as a creedal mark of the believer. The Book will crescendo to that mark at the sūrah's end among the qualities of the delivered: *"those who keep their covenant when they covenant"* (2:177), and praise the people of fidelity at 3:76: "Nay — whoever keeps his covenant and is reverent, God loves the reverent." The Prophet ﷺ made treaty-fidelity the very test of religion's presence, saying in the tradition at al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

> *"The signs of the hypocrite are three: when he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks it; and when he is entrusted, he betrays."* (al-Bukhārī 33; Muslim 59, from Abū Hurayrah — and in the version of Ibn ʿUmar: *"...even if he fasts and prays and claims to be a Muslim"*)

That ḥadīth is this verse transposed from the historical register to the personal: every believer's oath, appointment, marriage-contract, treaty of work, is a *mīthāq* under the same Witness; the habit of keeping small covenants is precisely the habit of remaining in faith, and the habit of breaking them is the slow motion of the *nabadha* — the flinging hand — this verse has immortalized. The community that inherits this sūrah is thus summoned to be the people from whom no covenant, once given, is ever taken back: secure in the promise of their Prophet that God Himself takes up the sides of the man upon whom men can rely: *"the believer is he whom the people trust with their blood and their wealth"* (al-Tirmidhī 2627; Aḥmad — graded *ḥasan*).

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:101

> **Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them— confirming their own Scriptures—some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs as if they did not know.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Messenger They Miscalculated**

The verse completes the election-cycle opened at verse 89 with almost the same framing and damningly different emphasis: *wa lammā jāʾahum rasūlun min ʿindi Allāhi muṣaddiqun li-mā maʿahum* — "and when there came to them a Messenger from God, confirming what was with them..." — the divine credentials are set out exactly as before: a messenger *from God*, whose content is not contradiction but confirmation of their own scripture. Then the response: *nabadha farīqun mina alladhīna ūtū al-kitāba kitāba Allāhi warāʾa ẓuhūrihim* — "a group of those who had been given the Book cast God's Book behind their backs." The commentators first settle whose book was cast: al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī argue (against those who would limit the phrase to the learned alone) that it is the *Torah* itself that was thrown aside — for it is "those given the Book" who do the casting, and what was cast is "the Book of God" in their keeping, specifically insofar as it contained the descriptions and glad tidings of the prophet to come (cf. 2:99; 7:157). They did not merely reject a new Scripture; they discarded their own old Scripture at the precise page where it testified to Muḥammad ﷺ. The gesture — *behind their backs* — is the contempt of total reversal: the scroll held facing the world in public is, in the moment of decision, swung out of sight. A book carried before the face is a testimony; a book flung behind the back is a burden disowned.

**"As If They Know Not"**

The verse's closing clause is one of its most debated and most devastating: *ka-annahum lā yaʿlamūn* — "as though they know not." The commentators hear in it a deliberate irony. These are the *knowers* par excellence — the community of scholars and readers — and the Book records that at the decisive juncture they acted in the manner of men who do not know: they cast their own testimony aside with the insouciance of the illiterate in whose hands a sacred page is mere paper. Two readings flow from the clause, both intended: first, their conduct was that of ignorance — from the outside, one would say such men had never read; second, their hearts had arrived at a functional knowing-not — for knowledge that does not restrain the hand from betrayal has already crossed, in the Book's psychology, into knowing's opposite. The verse is thus a standing diagnosis of *knowledge decoupled from conduct*: it does not argue that information was missing; it records that information ceased to govern. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, and the spiritual commentators after them cite verse 101 in the whole dossier of the tradition's warnings about the scholar whose learning adorns him without binding him — the category the Prophet ﷺ described as the first contestants of the Fire in the ḥadīth of the three judged first on the Last Day:

> *"...and a man who learned knowledge and taught it and recited the Qur'an: he will be brought, and will enumerate his favors and acknowledge them — and He will say: what did you do in them? He will say: I learned knowledge and taught it, and I recited the Qur'an for Your sake. He will say: You have lied — you learned that it might be said, 'a scholar'; and you recited that it might be said, 'a reciter'; and it was said. Take him to the Fire."* (Muslim 1905, from Abū Hurayrah)

**The Scroll Behind the Back in Every Age**

The tradition is unanimous that the verse's application is not caged in its occasion. Whoever possesses revelation and treats its inconvenient pages as though they were not there — shelved, bracketed, "contextualized" until silent — re-enacts this verse's gesture with his own copy of the Book. The reverent handling of scripture, as the sūrah itself taught at 2:63–64 and repeats here, is not the uplift of ceremony but the submission of conduct — *taking hold with strength*. Between the two images — the Book held before the face and the Book flung behind the back — the Qur'an stretches the entire choice of every scripture-possessing community. And it records, as cold comfort that is actually warm in reality, that a *group only* (farīq) did the casting: the remnant of the believing scholars — the ʿAbdullāh ibn Salāms, the mukhaṣṣaṣ readers who recognized and embraced — are the counterfigure of the verse: men who found their own Book, at the page of the promised Prophet, and *brought it forward*.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:102

> **They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon. Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved. They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon. The two angels never taught anyone without saying, “We are only a test ˹for you˺, so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith.” Yet people learned ˹magic˺ that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband and wife; although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will. They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them—although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter. Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls, if only they knew!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**What the Slanderers Said of Solomon**

The verse begins by exposing a false attribution: *wa ittabaʿū mā tatlū al-shayāṭīnu ʿalā mulki sulaymān* — "and they followed what the satans recited against the kingdom of Solomon." Certain circles — the commentators explain — circulated the tale that Solomon's extraordinary dominion (the winds, the jinn, the subjugation of peoples; cf. 21:81–82; 34:12–13) had been founded on sorcery, and that writings of his occult art, buried beneath his throne, were exhumed after his death and spread abroad. The Book pronounces the historical verdict with a clarity that has protected Solomon's prophethood in the creed of Islam ever since: *wa mā kafara sulaymānu wa lākinna al-shayāṭīna kafarū* — "Solomon did not disbelieve; the satans disbelieved." The Empire of Solomon was prophecy and miracle, not spellcraft; the sorcery was the satans' curriculum — *yuʿallimūna al-nāsa al-siḥr* — "teaching the people sorcery," and the formula of the slanderers reversed the roles: prophets do not traffic in occult manipulation; *satans do*, and then they write their school's diploma in the prophet's name.

**Hārūt and Mārūt: the Babylon License and Warning**

Then comes the strange and much-debated reference: *wa mā unzila ʿalā al-malakayni bi-bābila hārūta wa mārūt* — "and that which was sent down upon the two angels at Babylon, Hārūt and Mārūt." The commentators transmit a spectrum of accounts — colorful legends of two angels sent to earth (some tales in later literature embroidered the episode beyond recognition, which Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī firmly set aside as foreign accretions). The verse's own deliverable, however, is historically and theologically precise without any furnishing: at Babylon, through two angels, occult arts were let into the world *as a test* — *wa mā yuʿallimāni min aḥadin ḥattā yaqūlā innamā naḥnu fitnatun fa-lā takfur* — "they would teach no one until they said: we are only a trial; so do not disbelieve." Whatever the channel's form, the moral signature is the angels' standing preface: the art is a *fitnah* — a trial — and acquiring it for ends against God is *kufr*. The tradition also notes what sort of sorcery is actually meant across the manifold senses of *siḥr* — illusion and sleight-of-hand, the manipulation of hidden cosmic correspondences, persuasion that bewitches the judgment — and gives the example the social reality of premodern magic made primary: *fa-yataʿallamūna minhumā mā yufarriqūna bihi bayna al-marʾi wa zawjih* — "they learn from them that by which they separate a man from his wife" — sorcery not as spectacle but as the targeted destruction of covenant and love.

**"But They Harmed No One Except by God's Leave"**

Into the middle of the report the Book interposes its sovereignty-clause, the keystone of Islamic teaching on all hidden harm: *wa mā hum bi-ḍārrīna bihi min aḥadin illā bi-idhni Allāh* — "but they do not harm anyone with it except by God's leave." The verse thereby nails the wall against every later superstition: no spell, no practitioner, no eye, no hidden force possesses autonomous power; the dark arts operate — where they operate — within the same decree that governs rainfall and death. The believer's response to fear of the unseen world is thus never panic but *taqwā*, and the Prophet ﷺ supplied the canonical practice: al-Bukhārī and Muslim record that the Messenger ﷺ would say every morning and evening and at retirement the three protecting sūrahs — al-Ikhlāṣ and the two "seekers of refuge" (al-Falaq and an-Nās) — blowing over his palms and wiping what he could of his body:

> *"Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak... Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind"* — recited three times, *"sufficient for you against everything"* (al-Bukhārī 5017; Abū Dāwūd 5082; al-Tirmidhī 3575: *"ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ"*).

The same Prophet ﷺ forbade the other pole of the disease: *"Whoever goes to a soothsayer and believes what he says has disbelieved in what was sent down upon Muḥammad"* (Aḥmad 2.408; Abū Dāwūd 3904 — its chain debated, its ruling echoed by parallel stronger reports). To fear sorcery beyond God's leave disbelieves the verse; to seek it out disbelieves the warning the angels themselves pronounced.

**The Purchase That Has No Share**

The verse closes with its own application of the sūrah's master-metaphor: *wa la-qad ʿalimū la-mani ishtarāhu mā lahu fī al-ākhirati min khalāq* — "they knew full well that whoever purchases it has no share in the Hereafter." The buyer of sorcery knows he is buying — with money, with teachers' fees, with his soul — and the verse assesses the trade with the phrase already delivered at 2:90: *wa la-biʾsa mā sharaw bihi anfusahum law kānū yaʿlamūn* — "evil indeed is that for which they sold their souls, if only they knew." *Khalāq* is a portion or share: the merchandise of Babylon pays in this life and cancels the buyer's lot in the next. Ibn ʿAjībah and al-Kāshānī, in the spiritual reading the tradition has long appended here, draw the final lesson back into the heart: every soul possesses a "Solomon" — the spirit seated in dominion when God is obeyed — and a troop of "satans" — the desires reciting their counter-book against the kingdom; and the art worth guarding against most is not the witch at Babylon's gate but the counter-recitation by which the appetites teach the heart to pull apart what God has joined: man and wife, brother and brother, the believer and his Lord. Against all of it, the verse fixes the one lawful address of fear: *inna-mā naḥnu fitnah; fa-lā takfur* — the trial warns before it teaches, and salvation lies in refusing the purchase altogether.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:103

> **If only they were faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, there would have been a better reward from Allah, if only they knew!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Road Not Taken**

After the long, heavy reckoning with Babylon, the Book pauses to state, in one aching counterfactual, the alternative that stood open the entire time: *wa law annahum āmanū wa-ttaqaw la-mathūbatun min ʿindi Allāhi khayrun law kānū yaʿlamūn* — "Had they believed and been reverent, a recompense from God would surely have been better — if only they knew." The commentators note that the two conditions named are the same irreducible pair that govern the whole sūrah: *īmān* — belief, the inner orientation of trust and assent — and *taqwā*-reverence, the outer discipline of restraint from what God's light forbids. No third condition is ever added: belief alone, in this address, is the invitation itself; reverence, its acting out. Against the *mathūbah* — a recompense that is literally a "return-reward," a wage coming back to the doer — stands everything the preceding verse documented them purchasing: magic-knowledge, Babylon-tuition, the wrecked marriages of others, and their own souls thrown into the bargain. The verdict is sheer arithmetic: God's *mathūbah* is *khayr* — simply *better* — better than the fees of sorcery, better than the voyeuristic superiority of knowers of the occult, better than anything the satans ever advertised.

**"If Only They Knew": the Two Knowledges**

The closing clause repeats the sigh that has run through the episode like a leitmotif — *law kānū yaʿlamūn* — "if only they knew." And that sigh is informative, because the verse above established that they *did* know the Hereafter stakes: "knowing that whosoever purchases it has no share in the Hereafter." Two different knowings are being distinguished. At verse 102 they had *ʿilm* — the informational knowledge of the exchange-rate; at verse 103 they lack *maʿrifah* — the realizing knowledge in which a known thing is weight-bearing in the heart and shapes conduct. The whole spiritual tradition, from al-Muḥāsibī to al-Ghazālī to the commentarial exhorter of every age, is a commentary on this distinction: knowledge that merely reports and knowledge that *reorders*. The sorrow of the clause — the divine near-exclamation over the wasted intelligence of the libertine — is that the gap between the two knowledges is not an information gap but a love gap: the thing known is not yet believed-in, so it does not steer, so it loses every daily contest with the appetite that is believed-in. The verse is thereby set down as one of the Book's great encouragements of return: it stares at a crowd of occultists, mockers, and covenant-breakers and tells them that as far as God is concerned the matter is still expressible as *"had they only... they would have"* — the invitation alive in the grammar of the impossible that is, actually, very possible, because it is conditioned only on *belief and reverence*.

**Mathūbah: the Wage God Himself Pays**

The commentators dwell on the sweetness of the specific noun: not bare *ajr* (wage) but *mathūbah* — that which comes *back* (from *thāba*, to return) — the pay that returns to its laborer, has a special tenderness: as though God's promise were of wages that *find their way home* to the worker. The tradition spreads the image in the Prophet's ﷺ descriptions of how deeds return to their doer clothed in light, and how the Lord Himself receives His returning servants: *"Whoever draws near to Me by a handspan, I draw near to him by an arm's length; and whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him hastening"* (al-Bukhārī 7405; Muslim 2675 — the ḥadīth qudsī already referenced in this commentary at 2:88). Verse 103 therefore stands as the merciful exit-door of the entire Babylon passage: after detailing the worst spiritual commerce on record, the Book tells its readers that the profit-and-loss column on the other side is and always was open, its sums better, and its paymaster reliable — needing only the two currencies delivered daily in the shahādah itself: belief, and the reverence by which belief visibly walks.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:104

> **O believers! Do not say, “Râ’ina.” [Herd us!] But say, “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!] and listen ˹attentively˺. And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turn to "O You Who Believe"**

With this verse the sūrah pivots away from the extended address to the People of the Book and opens the first of the eighteen *Yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū* — "O you who believe" — direct addresses that will structure the whole rest of the chapter. The first lesson delivered to the believing community concerns something as granular, and as telling, as *one word of speech*: *lā taqūlū rāʿinā wa qūlū unẓurnā* — "Do not say *rāʿinā* ('attend to us'), but say *unẓurnā* ('regard us'), and listen." The background, preserved across al-Ṭabarī and the early commentators, is a small drama of language: the believers were accustomed, when asking the Prophet ﷺ to repeat or hold a point in his teaching, to say *rāʿinā* — "give us your ear." In the dialect of Madinah the word could also bear a mocking undertone, and some of the Jews of the city — like schoolboys listening for the pun — had seized on the resemblance of the believers' *rāʿinā* to a slur (as the parallel verse 4:46 takes note of Jews "twisting words from their contexts," saying *rāʿina* with a spin that turned the honorific into an insult) — turning the Companions' innocent request into an occasion of ridicule. God's answer is characteristic of His training of the new community: He did not censure the believers' intention; He simply *changed their word* — the sound-alike was retired, and the unambiguous *unẓurnā* ("look upon us, regard us") put in its place.

**The Sunnah of Vigilant Speech**

The commentators draw the permanent principles of the verse. Al-Ṭabarī treats it alongside the other Prophetic refinements of vocabulary — the retiring of gray words for noble ones — as a legislation of the *semantics of the community*: the ummah is to speak in a register so clean that no enemy can pun upon it, no sneering interpreter can twist it, no ambiguity invites sneers. Al-Rāzī connects the verse with the broader legislation of address at 24:63 — "do not make your calling of the Messenger among yourselves like your calling of one another" — as one edifice of adab toward the Prophet ﷺ: his attention is to be requested with reverent words, never with the familiarity of an equal. And the spiritual tradition extends the lesson to ordinary piety with an exactness the scholars summarize as *ḥadhdhar al-ʿibārah* — caution in formulation: since even *innocent* expressions were replaced to guard the community's reverence, how much more must the believer police words whose undertones are not innocent: the sneering diminutive, the sneaky euphemism, the winked obscenity. The door of the Prophet ﷺ was the first place the community learned that God cares how we *say* things; the tongue, as the soundest collections put the Prophet's own saying, is among the first of the two organs between which he guaranteed Paradise: *"Whoever guarantees me what is between his jaws and what is between his thighs, I guarantee him the Garden"* (al-Bukhārī 6474).

**"And Listen": the Closing Clause That Transposes the Whole**

Then the verse pivots inward: *wa-smaʿū* — "and *listen*." The commentators (al-Thaʿlabī and others) gloss it in two complementary senses: listen to the Prophet's ﷺ speech, since you ask him to "regard us" — the requesting of attention obliges attention in return; and listen *inwardly*, for the same utterance — *a single letter* — distinguishes the two famous formulas of verse 93: the one letter between *samiʿnā wa aṭaʿnā* ("we hear and we obey") and *samiʿnā wa ʿaṣaynā* ("we hear and we disobey") — which is exactly the order of magnitude of the correction in *this* verse as well: one word for another, one letter for another, one hearing for another. A community being trained by God learns that greatness is adjudicated at the level of the small things: vocabulary, tone, *one-word* habits. And the closing verdict — *wa li'l-kāfirīna ʿadhābun alīm* — "and for the disbelievers a painful punishment" — restores the horizon: sneering punners and their like in Madinah are not merely rude; they are under a different sentence from the believers, whose destiny is being shaped, syllable by syllable, by the most careful Teacher in history — down to the very words they say when they ask to be heard.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:105

> **The disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord, but Allah selects whoever He wills for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Who Begrudges the Descent**

This verse, addressed to the young Muslim community of Madinah, reads them the map of their neighbors' hearts: *mā yawaddu alladhīna kafarū min ahli al-kitābi wa lā al-mushrikīna an yunazzala ʿalaykum min khayrin min rabbikum* — "Neither the disbelievers among the People of the Book nor the idolaters wish that any good should be sent down upon you from your Lord." The "good" — *khayr* — sent down from the Lord, the commentators (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī) agree, is revelation itself — the descending guidance, verse by verse, upon the Prophet ﷺ and through him to his people. The verse thus diagnoses the actual posture of the two neighboring camps of Madinah and Makkah: it is not that they have *judged* the revelation false on evidence and therefore reject it; it is that they *prefer* that no revelation descend at all — that heaven stay quiet, that the Arabs receive no Book, that this particular grace fall, if it must fall, upon some other quarter. The wish-verb — *yawaddu* — is the quiet give-away: beneath all argumentation sits a *desire about the fact of revelation*, and desires of that order precede and manufacture the arguments that then defend them.

**God's Jealous Freedom in Granting Mercy**

The divine answer to corporate begrudging is divine freedom: *wa-llāhu yakhtaṣṣu bi-raḥmatihi man yashāʾ* — "but God singles out for His mercy whom He wills." *Raḥmah* here, as the commentators gloss, is the mercies of prophethood and revelation — the special mercy of being chosen as the vessel of God's address. The verb *yakhtaṣṣu* — designates exclusively, singles out — answers the desire of the grudgers with a grammatical finality: the designation is God's affair, exercised by His will, not by the approval of communities, and not channeled by ethnic or scholarly seniority. The full stop of the verse then rests on the divine attribute that makes such freedom forever rational: *wa-llāhu dhu'l-faḍli al-ʿaẓīm* — "and God is Possessed of Tremendous Bounty." Because the Giver is inexhaustibly bountiful, His giving where He wills is never a withdrawal from anyone else — the lamp lit in Arabia dims nothing in Jerusalem. The verse therefore contains in itself the answer to the whole doctrine of envy (vv. 90, 109): what one community stubbornly calls preference is, from God's side, the operation of an abundance no arithmetic can corner.

**The Believer's Serenity Before Begrudged Grace**

For the believing community the verse is both shield and mirror. As a shield, it inoculates the community against being wounded by the fact that neighbors begrudge their glad possession of the Book: the begrudgement is ancient, predicted, and entirely compatible with God's favor; God's singling-out is not voided by the neighbor's sigh. The believers of, e.g., the age of the Prophet ﷺ, heard from this text that their possession of revelation was God's *faḍl ʿaẓīm* — tremendous bounty — and that their neighbors' regressive wishes were to be met not with reciprocal hatred nor politics of display but with the quiet gratitude of an address from the Throne: grace received, bestowed, sustained. As a mirror, the verse asks every believer: when you see the gifts of God descend elsewhere — on another person's family, another scholar's insight, another community's revival — do you wish that no good had been sent down? The heart's recoil from *others' rain* is the first symptom of the spiritual illness this verse has named in two great communities. The cure is the verse's own ending: God is the Tremendously Bountiful, and the proper response to His giving anywhere is *hoping in the same Faḍl*, not resenting it. The Prophet's ﷺ own prayer, reported among the comprehensive supplications, captures the posture: *"O God, I ask You of Your bounty (faḍl)"* (Muslim 2722) — to ask of *His* bounty is to confess that nothing given to another empties the store from which our own provision pours.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:106

> **If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Abrogation: God's Prerogative over His Own Speech**

This verse stands as the Qur'an's own permission-slip for one of the most debated instruments of its legal life: *mā nansakh min āyatin aw nunsihā naʾti bi-khayrin minhā aw mithlihā* — "No sign do We abrogate, or cause to be forgotten, except that We bring better than it or the like of it." The word *naskh* — abrogation — carries, as the philologists note, a range that runs from transcription (the Qur'an itself as a *copy* of its heavenly archetype in the Preserved Tablet, 85:22) to the sun's erasure of the shadow and the wind's obliteration of footprints — and from that range the tradition distilled its legal-technical meaning: the setting aside of an earlier revealed ruling by a later one, with the earlier text often remaining in the Book as a record of the road the community has walked. The philosophical point is stated in the verse itself: abrogation is not improvisation, still less indecision — it is God's *exchange*: *We bring better than it* — for the community's good and its stage of growth — *or like unto it* — equal, when the change confronts the believers with the test of which voice they follow when two divine words stand across one ruling. Then comes the grounding interjection: *a-lam taʿlam anna Allāha ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr* — "Do you not know that God is powerful over all things?" Abrogation is thus annexed to omnipotence: the One who can command whatever He wills can also retire whatever He wills, in wisdom, at the appointed time.

**The Rules of the Science**

The mainstream science that grew from this verse developed its safeguards with care, and they deserve exact statement, since the term is often abused in loose hands. First, *naskh* properly operates on *rulings* — commands and prohibitions — not on the Book's narratives, its theology, its descriptions of God and the Last Day; no faith-truth, no prophet-story, no promise like 2:62 can be "abrogated," for God's speech about reality is timelessly true. Second, the jurists over centuries sharply disagreed about the *extent* of abrogation: Shāh Walī Allāh of Delhi narrowed the instances to five; Jalāl al-Dīn al-Suyūṭī counted twenty-one; Ibn al-Jawzī had spun the list out to two hundred forty-seven — and a minority strain, represented by Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī and harmonized by many modern scholars, held that proper legal naskh has not occurred within the Qur'an at all, that apparent conflicts resolve as specification, qualification, or temporal stages of a single divine pedagogy. Third, the commentators distinguish kinds: the abrogation of a ruling while the text remains (the commonest); the abrogation of the text while the ruling stands (the famous stoning-report attributed to ʿUmar, treated with great caution by the hadith critics); and the abrogation of both (the suckling-report of ʿĀʾishah). The intelligent Muslim need not decide the scholars for them; what the verse itself demands is simpler: confidence that whatever God ruled, whenever He ruled it, and whatever He later brought, stands inside the open eye of *better or equal* — not the cadence of a changeable God but the curriculum of a *wise* One.

**"Cause to Be Forgotten": Mercy within Loss**

The verse contains a second and tenderer provision in its *aw nunsihā* — "or cause it to be forgotten." The commentators preserve the reports and the spiritual reading: in one narration, two men complain to the Prophet ﷺ that they once could recite a sūrah he taught them and now cannot bring a letter of it, and he answers: *"It is among what has been abrogated and forgotten — so let it be"* — attested with the caution the report-chains require but consistent with the verse's plain warrant: God not only retires legal dispensations; He may also, in wisdom, *lift a portion of memory from the community's heart*, as He willed to keep — under strict human custody — what He willed to keep, and to let recede what He would not have recited to the end of time. The devotional tradition, faced with a believer's grief over a forgotten sūrah or a lapsed memorization, has always answered from the spirit of this clause: memory itself is administered by God, and His books are not balanced by the accountant's method; what He causes to be forgotten was not negligence-on-your-part alone, and the whole Book in the end remains in the guarded Tablet and in the guarded community. Al-Ṭabarī's analogy to verse 93 — "they were made to drink *the love of* the calf" — suggests the grammatical shape here too: what is brought "better" may be the *ruling* of the sign rather than the sign itself. In either construal, the verse ends where every sovereign clause of this kind ends: with the tidings of *qudrah* — *God is powerful over all things* — which is to say: the speaker who retires a ruling is the same speaker who first issued it, keeps the ledger of His own speech, and will be found, at the end of His pedagogy, to have given every generation precisely the words and the rulings that were, for them, *better*.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:107

> **Do you not know that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah, and you have no guardian or helper besides Allah?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Basis of the Divine Pedagogy**

The verse stands as the theological warrant for everything verses 105–106 asserted about God's freedom in giving His mercy and exchanging His signs: *alam taʿlam anna Allāha lahu mulku al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍ* — "Do you not know that God's is the dominion of the heavens and the earth?" Al-Ṭabarī notes the rhetorical drift of the address: it begins as a question to the Prophet ﷺ — *dost thou not know* — and then widens to take in all human beings in its second clause, a shift in address frequent in the Book (cf. 33:1–2), by which the Prophet's affirmative is made the model and refraction-point of every hearer's affirmative. The sovereignty predicated is *mulk* — full, operative kingdom: not a titular kingship above a bureaucracy of independent causes, but the possession and effective rule of *everything in heaven and earth* — the spinning stars, the rising rain, the hearts of kings, and the instruments of revelation; the same sovereignty the whole cosmos acknowledges at the end of this sūrah in the verse beloved above all verses: *"His is whatsoever is in the heavens and the earth"* (2:255).

**Neither Walī Nor Naṣīr After Him**

The second clause states the universal human condition in the vocabulary of alliance: *wa mā lakum min dūni Allāhi min waliyyin wa lā naṣīr* — "and you possess, apart from God, neither protector nor helper." *Walī* is the patron-guardian who shelters, accompanies, and watches; *naṣīr* is the succor who reaches you in extremity. To say that mankind has *none of either* outside of God is not to say that human beings cannot protect or help one another — the Book consistently honors human protectors — but that no created guardian operates independently: every walī among men is himself under God's sovereignty, every helper himself first needs help. The structure of divine protection is therefore direct at the root: beneath every protecting roof is God the real Protector; beneath every rescuing hand is God the real Helper — and when a man *exchanges* God's patronage for a creature's, he has not relocated to another shelter but has stepped out of the category of the protected altogether. The verse's logic folds back upon its environment: it follows the claim of abrogation (v. 106) because abrogation is precisely *the exercise of mulk* — the King with absolute disposal of His Own words now bring what is better or equal; and it precedes the challenge about futile demands on messengers (v. 108) because the demanders are only dreaming of a new sign-sender when the whole earth and sky already belong to the Sender.

**The Consolation in Absolute Sovereignty**

The tradition further takes from this verse its primary spiritual training — *tawakkul* — in the classical sense: the heart's deliberate leaning upon the only Support that cannot itself fall. If sovereignty is God's alone and if neither protector nor helper exists outside Him, then the believer's account with every lesser power — wealth, status, plan, patron — is settled: they are means within His rule, not alternatives to it. The Prophet ﷺ voiced the principle in the beautiful words reported by Ibn ʿAbbās, when he ﷺ sent him out on a day and taught him:

> *"Know that if the whole community were to gather to benefit you with anything, they would not benefit you except with what God had written for you; and if they were to gather to harm you with anything, they would not harm you except with what God had written against you. The pens have been lifted and the pages have dried."* (al-Tirmidhī 2616 — *ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ*)

That is verse 107 for the heart. And its address-opening, *dost thou not know*, is God's own call to each reader: you *do* know — the knowledge is native, not exotic. The verses of this sūrah — from the Sovereign's sending of the Book to the Sovereign's care in exchanging its rulings — presuppose and renew that knowledge: the King unto whom the heavens and the earth belong is your only guardian and your only help, and in that being your one all — *ḥasbunā Allāhu wa niʿma al-wakīl* ("God suffices us, and what a beautiful Guardian," 3:173) — lies the believer's whole peace in the world and in the world to come.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:108

> **Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger as Moses was asked before? But whoever trades belief for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question-Genealogy That Destroys**

The verse puts to the believers a question about its own earlier-readers: *am turīdūna an tasʾalū rasūlakum kamā suʾila mūsā min qabl* — "Or do you wish to question your messenger as Moses was questioned aforetime?" The commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr) unfold the actual forms the demands took: the Children of Israel asked Moses to bring God out into visibility (2:55); to produce for them a god they could see, as the idol-peoples had their gods (7:138); to carve out for them a stream from the rock with twelve distinct springs (2:60) — all demands upon the *prophet* as though he were a subcontractor of marvels, all prefaced with the excuse of needing unaided confirmation. Among the Quraysh the parallel demands were floated daily: let him split for us the hill of Ṣafā into gold, let him make rivers burst in the barren valley, let him bring a Book that opens springs; and God's answers in His Book consistently diagnosed the requests as what they were: not thirst for evidence but thirst for *refusal-by-postponement* — the same interrogation-as-evasion described at the sūrah's Cow-episode (2:67–71) and warned against in principle at 5:101: *"O you who believe! Ask not about things which, if disclosed to you, would trouble you."* The Prophet ﷺ made the genealogy explicit in his own summarized diagnosis:

> *"God disliked for you three things: gossip, the squandering of wealth, and much questioning;... the people were destroyed before you only by their many questions and their quarreling with their prophets."* (al-Bukhārī 2408, 5977; Muslim 593, 1337 — composite of the two classical reports already cited at vv. 70–71)

**Exchanging Belief for Disbelief: the Terrible Commerce**

The verse then seals its warning with the sūrah's general law of exchange, stated as a principle unrestricted to one community: *wa man yatabaddal al-kufra bi'l-īmāni fa-qad ḍalla sawāʾa al-sabīl* — "whoever exchanges belief for disbelief has surely strayed from the even path." On the grammar of the exchange-verb — *tabaddala* — the commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) note that the formulation can run in two directions, and here runs from the better to the worse: the one who *gives away* faith and *receives* disbelief — the same terrible commerce the sūrah has already charged as purchased error at 2:16, as purchased world at 2:86, as sold souls at 2:90 and 2:102. What makes this purchase maddest of all is its object: not some far-away Hereafter commodity alone but the path under one's feet — *sawāʾ al-sabīl* — the *even*, *middle*, *level* way, flattened for walking; the exchanger forfeits the very road. The spirit of the legal tradition found in the verse a standard rule by which to measure all the specious "objective inquiries" its own approach to revelation engenders: an inquiry conceived *in* faith ends in worship; an inquiry conceived *in* refusal ends, regardless of answer, in the next question — and the succession of questions is the slow-motion of the exchange itself.

**The Law of Salamah — Safe Passage for the Believers**

The verse's practical deliverable into the daily life of Muslims is the Prophet's ﷺ own repeated catechetical rule, already quoted in this commentary at verse 70:

> *"What I have forbidden you, avoid; what I have commanded you, do of it what you can; for those before you were destroyed only by the multiplicity of their questions and their disputations with their prophets."* (al-Bukhārī 7288; Muslim 1337, from Abū Hurayrah)

The related ḥadīth — *"The most criminal of Muslims in respect of Islam is the one who asked about something that was not forbidden, whereupon it became forbidden because of his asking"* (al-Bukhārī 7289; Muslim 2356) — records the terrible irony the Cow-episode had already demonstrated: unnecessary questions can *write new law*, and the questioner's own query becomes his constraint. The milder faces of the same science deserve mention too: the Companions asked plenty of questions — about orphans, about charity, about the months — and sūrah-revelations came down upon their asking (e.g. 4:127; 33:35; 58:1–4); and the tradition praises the question *aimed at practice* as against the question aimed at escape. Verse 108 therefore tells the believers to examine, in the moment of asking, the child of which genealogy their question is: the genealogy of "cows" — questions that multiply specifications and narrow the gate — or the genealogy of guidance — questions that become tomorrow's deed. The safe traveler on the even road is precisely described: the one who says to whatever God's messenger brings: *what am I to do with this?* — and does it.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:109

> **Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them. Pardon and bear with them until Allah delivers His decision. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Wish Driven by Envy**

Continuing the disclosure of motivations begun at verses 90 and 105, the Book now speaks it plainly to the believers: *wadda kathīrun min ahli al-kitābi law yaruddūnakum min baʿdi īmānikum kuffārā ḥasadan min ʿindi anfusihim* — "Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after your belief — out of envy from within their own souls." The commentators specify the historical soil: after the setback at Uḥud — when the Muslims suffered reverses — some of the Jewish neighbors taunted the Muslim converts from among their people with the outcome, and the taunts did in fact turn a few souls back to their former religion (Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī). But the phrase that the tradition has memorized as the permanent diagnosis lies within the verse itself: *ḥasadan min ʿindi anfusihim* — "envy *out of their own souls*" — not out of a mounting of evidence, not out of zealous error, but rising entirely from the interior, from the nafs' unwillingness to see grace descend where it had not expected it. The verse then records the final cruelty of such knowledge-illumined envy: *min baʿdi mā tabayyana lahumu al-ḥaqq* — "even after the truth had become clear to them." This is the darkest data-point of the entire address: clarity arrived, was achieved, was inhabited — and envy still operated *within* the knowing. Information, the sūrah has argued from verse 63 forward, is not the medicine against this disease; only reverence is.

**"Pardon and Forbear" — the Command to Bear**

Onto such a scene the Book legislates a surprising community-emotion: *fa-ʿfū wa-ṣfaḥū ḥattā yaʾtiya Allāhu bi-amrih* — "so pardon, and forbear, until God brings His command." The two verbs are distinct: *ʿafw* — effacing pardon, the wiping of the offense from official record; *ṣafḥ* — forbearing disregard, the turning of the cheek-page without retaliation. The commentators describe the command's setting: the Muslim community, still in its minority-trial years in Madinah, was being commanded to master a novel form of strength — not the repayment of affront but its deliberate effacement, *while they wait for God's direction*: *until God comes with His Command* — that is, until God legislates the next statute for the community (and many commentators note that the mandate of defense and fighting would come later, at 2:190, 22:39, in due time — which is part of why the verse is called by some a *mansūkh* or conditioned command). But the enduring religious content of the verse exceeds its occasion: Islam's default posture toward personal enmity and slights is pardon — *ʿafw wāṣil* — while justice and defense are institutions, not instincts. The Prophet ﷺ embodied the verse's pardon in the most famous scene of the Meccan entrance: standing before the city that had tortured and starved his community, he asked, *"What do you expect me to do with you?"* — and, in the account preserved in the Sīrah literature of Ibn Hishām, answered them with Joseph's own sentence from the Book: *"No reproach upon you this day; God forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful"* — "Go, you are free." Every believer living beneath the sneer of a greater number, the mockery of knowledge, the obstinate envy of neighbors, is folded by verse 109 into that same stance: pardon deliberate, forbearance chose — *until God comes with His Command.*

**"God Is Powerful over All Things" — the Promise underneath**

The verse closes with its paired refrain from verse 106: *inna Allāha ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr* — "Truly God is powerful over all things." The repetition is no accident but a promise placed underneath the command to forbear: the community obeying *fa-ʿfū wa-ṣfaḥū* is never asked to forbear because they are too weak to reply; they forbear because the power-case has been transferred to a higher court. The One Powerful over all things will preside over the account; their part is to keep the shoulders of forbearance, His part is the coming of the Command. The tradition has always comforted its minorities with this exact stance: patience in place, pardon in the heart, and attentive hope to the Father of outcomes — knowing that on the day this sūrah's warnings ripen, the verdict will fall exactly along the lines the Book has been drawing: *"but God is powerful over all things"* — and those who preserved their religion amid the pulls-to-apostasy will find the One to whom they transferred their case to have been the most powerful and most just of advocates.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:110

> **Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Prayer and Alms as the Two Pillars of Fortitude**

Following the double command of pardon and forbearance, the Book attaches its own standing prescription of strength: *wa aqīmū al-ṣalāta wa ātū al-zakāh* — "and establish the prayer and give the zakāh." The pairing is the sūrah's refrain — issued to Israel's remnant at 2:43, recited in their covenant at 2:83, and now issued anew to the believers — and the commentators note the doubled fitness of the sequence: the steep assignment of *ʿafw* and *ṣafḥ* requires spiritual nourishment, and nothing nourishes reverence like the prayer standing fed throughout the day and the wealth flowing outward through the hands of zakāh. Prayer is the vertical deed which re-binds the servant to his Lord until the load of the forbearance becomes bearable; almsgiving is the horizontal deed which turns the community's inner economic life into mercy — both together acting as the community's standing hedge against the envy and taunts detailed in verse 109. The believer who prays five times a day and pays his zakāh and feels the weight of the mockery around him is taught here to see that weight as part of a prescription God had already filled — the old pair, offered again.

**Sent-Ahead Good Found With God**

Then the verse opens the Book's perpetual maxim of cosmic accounting — a sentence the tradition has cherished as a complete financial theology in nine words: *wa mā tuqaddimū li-anfusikum min khayrin tajidūhu ʿinda Allāh* — "and whatever good you send on ahead for your souls, you will find it with God." The Quran's commerce-language here is deliberate and recurring (cf. 73:20; 75:13; 3:30): deeds are not *lost* behind you; they are *sent ahead* — a courier-service toward the only secure vault, where they wait for their owners at the landing. The commentators (Ibn Kathīr) gloss the promise as *a promise encoded as a description*: the statement of fact *is* the guarantee — nothing spoken here is rhetoric; good sent never fails of arrival. The verse instructs the believer to mentally *escort* each prayer, each coin of zakāh, each swallowed retort of verse 109's forbearance, into the future — watching it pass out of his hands and arrive in God's custody — and the heart so trained need not tally its wealth on this side of the grave: *you will find it with God.*

**He Sees: the Companion Clause at 73:20**

The closing warrant is the sūrah's familiar refrain already encircled three times (vv. 96, 74, 85): *inna Allāha bi-mā taʿmalūna baṣīr* — "surely God sees all that you do." The source commentary appends a precious practical transmission here about the Prophet's ﷺ own recitation: a Companion reported hearing him read the parallel verse of 73:20 — *"and whatever good you send ahead for your souls, you will find it with God, better and greater in reward"* — and he would stop there and add from himself: *innahu baṣīr* — "verily He is All-Seeing" (*yarāhu jamiʿan* — "He sees it all"). The commentary notes the larger habit this attests: the Prophet ﷺ paused mid-recitation whenever the verse's content called for a response — glorifying at verses of glorification, supplicating at verses of supplication, prostrating where prostration came — receiving the Book not as a text under voice but as a living transaction between the Reciter and the Lord whose words were being recited. For the reader of this sūrah, verse 110 thus seals the program of vv. 105–109 in a single daily cycle: pray, give, send good ahead under the certainty of one divine seeing, and bear with pardon what the envious send back; for God — who sees all you do — already stands in custody of all the good you send.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:111

> **The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof if what you say is true.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Exclusive Claim Quoted**

Having already recorded their claim of covenant-privilege (v. 80's numbered days) and of unique sonship with God (to come at 5:18), the Book now sets down the fullest form of the community's exclusivism: *wa qālū lan yadkhula al-jannata illā man kāna hūdan aw naṣārā* — "and they said: none shall enter the Garden except one who is a Jew or a Christian." The commentators note the verse's quiet irony of pronouns: each community claimed the gate for itself — the Jews reading it of themselves alone, the Christians of themselves alone — so that the verse's grammatical indifference exposes both claims at once, and verse 113 will directly show them leveling the identical accusation of nothingness against *each other*. The Book then names such theology by its own term, repeated from verse 78: *tilka amāniyyuhum* — "those are their own wishes/the empty hopes they cherish" — *amānī*, the consolation-fictions of hearsay necessity, the same category under which the sūrah had already written down the claims of numbered days and the fables of the self-writing scribes. The existence of such a sentence in a scripture is not proof of its truth; it is proof of a *community* narrating itself into safety.

**"Bring Your Proof": Islam's Standing Demand for Burhān**

The verse's answer is command: *qul hātū burhānakum in kuntum ṣādiqīn* — "Say: bring your proof, if you are truthful." With that imperative the Qur'an delivers into the hands of every believing generation its most celebrated epistemic one-line requirement: *burhān* — demonstration, evidence, the evidentiary argument that if produced must be produced in public before the eye (the root *baraha* is the morning's brightness) — Ibn Kathīr and the commentators glossing it simply as *the decisive proof*. The demand is not made as a rhetorical device but as a permanent jurisdiction of the faith: *every claim about the afterlife must stand or fall by its evidence*; the Book's repeated pattern — 21:24, 23:117, 27:64, 28:75 — extends the demand universally: *bring your burhān* is Islam's answer to every ungrounded theological assertion, whether it come from a neighbor, a tradition, a charismatic teacher, or from the believer's own wish built into a doctrine. The phrase *in kuntum ṣādiqīn* — "if you are truthful" — sets the trial's single axis: truthfulness must submit to demonstration, or withdraw. The tradition's scholars point out that Islam does not merely tolerate this demand — it grounds itself upon it: the Qur'ans's own challenge to bring its like (2:23; 10:38) is the same weapon turned toward its own bearer, the mark of a Book that does not fear its own test.

**The Verse That Demolishes Gatekeeping**

The wider theological function of verse 111 is its quiet demolition of *gatekeeping* as a salvific category. The next verse (2:112) will state positively who is in the Garden — "whosoever submits his face to God, while being excellent" — and the tradition read the two verses as the Book's canonical two-step: first demand proof of the gate-keeper (v. 111), then state the door's actual dimensions (v. 112). In Islamic teaching, entrance to the Garden is in no man's gift and no tribe's monopoly — not even the ummah of Muḥammad's own: the Prophet ﷺ taught his innermost household the same principle in the clip whose address-name became proverbial, there in al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

> *"O Faṭimah daughter of Muḥammad, O Ṣafiyyah aunt of the Prophet — do deeds for yourselves, for I can defend you not at all before God."* (cf. al-Bukhārī 2753, 3071; Muslim 205 — in the Prophet's public warning at the conquest of the Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib)

If the Prophet's own daughter and his own aunt are excluded from the gate by blood, then *every* insider-claim of "none enters the Garden but he who is one of us" stands shown for what the Book calls it: *amānī* — wishes. The judgment of who enters is God's alone, pronounced in His court on the day when all *burhāns* are laid out; and the believer's posture, taught by verse 111, is to rest his only stay upon his own evidence of submission to God, not upon his address of birth — the very ground cleared for the next verse's universal answer.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:112

> **But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Door's Actual Dimensions**

After the verdict on wishes, the Book states the door: *balā man aslama wajhahu li-llāhi wa huwa muḥsinun fa-lahu ajruhu ʿinda rabbih* — "Nay — whosoever submits his face to God, and is a doer of excellence, his reward is with his Lord." The demolition-particle *balā* — used at 2:81 — once again blows the prior assertion off the table, and the replacement is built of two conditions, which the tradition treasures as the sūrah's clearest formulation of the complete religious life. First: *aslama wajhahu* — *he submits his face*: the commentators explain the face as a man's noblest and most-expressive part, so that to offer the face means to offer the whole being in sincere surrender — al-Ṭabarī: body and acts together; al-Rāzī: an allusion whose highest form is the Muslim's own prostration, the placing of forehead and nose — the face's summit — upon the ground before the Lord. The tongue of the verse is the very root-noun of islam itself: *man aslama wajhah* — "whoever makes islam of his face." Second: *wa huwa muḥsin* — *while he is excellent in his doing*: submitted inside, excellent outside — the twin that Ibn Kathīr maps exactly onto the accepted two conditions of every deed: sincerity toward God and conformity with His measured Law.

**Reward with the Lord, and the Double Exemption**

The promise attached to the pair is this sūrah's standing one (2:38; 2:62): *fa-lahu ajruhu ʿinda rabbih* — "his reward is with his Lord" — *wa lā khawfun ʿalayhim wa lā hum yaḥzanūn* — "and no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve." The language of deposit is once again deliberate: the reward is not left in the hands of communities with their gate-keys; it is *with his Lord*, in the safest vault in existence — and the double exemption from fear and grief returns the heart to the two borders of time which the verse 38's charter already guarded. The Book thereby keeps its vow that no community's *amānī* decides the guest-list of the Garden: the guest-list is written by submission and excellence, fixed with the Lord, and re-declared over and over through the sūrah's promises with the same two amen-promises: no fear, no grief.

**The Tradition's Two Wings of Acceptance**

The commentators' debate recorded in the source commentary is instructive and is best set down plainly. Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī, as our source notes, confine the acceptance-formula by *conformity to the Law*: deeds of a Christian monk, though sincere, lack conformity to the revealed measure; in their view the muḥsin within Islam's dispensation must act upon the Book and the Sunnah — while others of the authorities read the plain expression as laying down the rule in principle: sincere submission and excellent action as such. The difference between the readings is real but not infinite — the tradition's general solution is housed inside the doctrine of reward, not in the definition of door: God *alone* is the weigher in the end (29:4-5; 99:7-8). What no commentator diminishes, because the text does not diminish it, is the absolute reach of the clause to *man* — *whosoever*: no determination by tribe, sect, school, or party. The Prophet's ﷺ clip on the two wings makes the creed of acceptance one line, through Jābir from the Prophet ﷺ:

> *"No soul believing in God and the Last Day and doing righteousness shall fear..."* — and in the greatest of the genre: *"Whoever says lā ilāha illa llāh sincerely from his heart shall enter the Garden"* (al-Bukhārī 6507; Muslim 28 — the ahadīth of sincere testimony, its wordings already used and guarded at vv. 62 and 82 of this commentary).

Verse 112 is thus fixed in Muslim consciousness as the Book's own charter of the middle way between the gatekeepers and the gatekeepers' enemies: it is not "none shall enter except the Jews or the Christians"; it is also not "every hope is enough"; it is exactly this: *submission to God* — the face given wholly — *with excellence in following* — deeds sent soundly — and the Lord's own four-word seal upon the end: *no fear, no grief.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:113

> **The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on” and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,” although both recite the Scriptures. And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺. Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Mutual Annulment Between Reciters of One Book**

The verse records the scandal of mutual rejection between the two scripture-communities: *wa qālati al-yahūdu laysa al-naṣārā ʿalā shayʾin wa qālati al-naṣārā laysa al-yahūdu ʿalā shayʾin wa hum yatlūna al-kitāb* — "The Jews say: the Christians stand upon nothing; and the Christians say: the Jews stand upon nothing — while they recite the Book." The commentators note the point of the reciting-participle with great exactness: both parties *recite* scripture — and scripture itself gives the lie to both accusations; the Torah borne by the Jews bears witness to Jesus, and the Gospel borne by the Christians presupposes and confirms Moses.
