Ibn Kathīr observes that when the delegations of Najrān and of Madinah traded these sentences in the Prophet's ﷺ hearing (the reported occasion of this verse's setting), each side was pronouncing a verdict that its own Book could not sign: the Jews saying the followers of the Messiah — whom their own scriptures describe — have nothing; the Christians saying the bearers of the Torah — upon which every verse of their Gospel stands — have nothing. The Book's closing sigh over the matter recalls the sūrah's own diagnosis: *kadhālika qāla alladhīna lā yaʿlamūna mithla qawlihim* — "thus used to speak, in words like theirs, those who do not know" — preceding pagan generations trading exactly the same exchange of mutual nullification; the learned communities of scripture merely added footnotes to the taunt of the unreached. And al-Kāshānī's re-reading, in the book of esoteric commentary which the Sufi tradition passes down, sets the two renouncements side by side as a diagram of imbalance: a people veiled from the inward by clinging to the outward, and a people veiled from the outward by clinging to the inward — and similar deviations besetting every lion-split inside Islam itself.

**God Will Judge Between Them**

Upon the shouting scene the Book descends with a rare and quiet gait: *fa-llāhu yaḥkumu baynahum yawma al-qiyāmati fīmā kānū fīhi yakhtalifūn* — "so God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that in which they used to differ." The commentators emphasize that the cancellation of man's nullifications doesn't come from man's tribunal: not by the sentence of the Prophet ﷺ in their hearing, not by the sword of any later majority: *God* will judge — with full evidence — on the one Day. The category of such deferred arbitration belongs to the most important religious law of the Qur'an's intercommunal theology; the exact same charge is pronounced over the differings of Christians at 3:55, of sectarians at 5:48 and 6:164, of the very takfīri quarrels at 10:93 and 16:92, of Jews and Sabians and Magians and the idol-folk at 22:17-69, and it closes the whole list at 39:3 and 46. In the realm of its own law, Islam sets a double boundary as a result of that deferred jurisdiction: on one side, the stakes are genuine — the Book does not fold Christianity and Judaism into Islam nor Islam into them; on the other side, the final *reconciliation of contested claims* belongs to the Day when all evidence becomes one digit under God's gaze — and the earthly business of the believer is *not* the organic foreclosure of the difference but the submission of every named party's claims to God's adjudication-by-truth. The Sufi tradition and the legal tradition meet at the same door: our confession inside this life is the truth as the Book teaches it, held without fudging; our *sentencing of souls* is left on the docket of the Day.

**The Mirror of Negatives**

For the Muslim community the verse also functions as a watchtower over its own internal speech. The scholars and saints long ago applied it to the ummah's own differences: the habit of declaring "so-and-so's madhhab has nothing," "such-and-such a shaykh is nothing, while we have something" — all of it shows the same disposition the verse diagnoses in the two renouncing communities, and the same covenant of deferral applies: God judges between the carriers of the dispute concerning what they differ in. A community gathered by one Book — as the Jews and Christians were gathered, in God's intention, by the thread Torah-Gospel-Qur'an — must recite its Book *against* its renouncements, not as an instrument of them; the Torah testifies to Jesus, the Gospel confirms Moses, and the Qur'an confirms both and regulates all (cross-confirmed at 5:48: "a guardian over them"). The believer practicing verse 113 reads the others' books with the respect of traffic in a family, debates the points of difference with burhān rather than contempt, and entrusts the court of last judgment to God — with whom the Prophet ﷺ lodged every disputed case in the formula of the covenanting prayer:

> *"My Lord, judge [between us] in truth; and our Lord is the All-Merciful, the One whose help is sought against what you allege."* (21:112 — the Prophet's ﷺ commanded supplication over every difference)

—a prayer built entirely on the deferral: witnesses called today; the verdict left with the Arbiter.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:114

> **Who does more wrong than those who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship and strive to destroy them? Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear. For them there is disgrace in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Worst Wrong: Blocking the Houses of God**

This verse opens with the Qur'an's standing formula of superlative interrogation — *wa man aẓlamu...* — "who does *greater wrong* than..." — the Book's manner of marking a crime's top rank: *mimman manaʿa masājida Allāhi an yudhkara fīhā ismuhu wa saʿā fī kharābihā* — "than one who prevents the mosques of God from having His Name remembered in them, and strives for their ruin." The *masjid* — from *sajada*, to prostrate — is, etymologically, simply "the place of prostration"; the Book names with this word both the Temple in Jerusalem ("the Farthest Mosque," 17:1) and the Kaaba in Makkah ("the Inviolable Mosque," 2:144; 5:2), and the commentators divide over the referent: al-Ṭabarī holds for the Temple destroyed by Romans, some with connivance; others for Ḥudaybiyah's prevention of the Prophet's ﷺ pilgrimage in 6 AH, when the Makkans barred the Muslims from the Kaaba itself; al-Qurṭubī widens the verdict to every house of worship from which God's remembrance is barred; and Ibn Kathīr adds the profound general point: the idolators' filling of the Kaaba with idols was *already* its ruin — a house of God emptied of God's oneness is demolished even while its walls stand. The verse thus unites outer siege and inner profanation under one superlative: to stop God's Name being remembered in His houses — by arms or by idols — is the deepest ẓulm on the scale.

**Entering in Dread; Disgrace Below, Punishment Above**

The verse then disposes the legal and the eschatological sides of the case in two clauses: *ulāʾika mā kāna lahum an yadkhulūhā illā khāʾifīn* — "those ones — it was not for them to enter them, except in fear": the rightful tenure of God's mosques belongs to the reverent, not to bar-armies and idol-fillers — the commentators gloss it variously (as their proper disposition of trembling worship, or as their expected fate of entering upon fear and tribute in the conquered future) — and *lahum fī al-dunyā khizyun wa lahum fī al-ākhirati ʿadhābun ʿaẓīm* — "theirs is disgrace in this world, and theirs, in the Hereafter, a tremendous punishment." The commentators transmit the Prophet's ﷺ standing comfort under the first half — a supplication regularly on his lips:

> *"I seek refuge... from disgrace in the present life and from the punishment of the grave"* and *"O God, I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done and the evil of what I have not done"* (al-Bukhārī 6367-68, 6377; Muslim 2702, 2706, 2708 — the class of refuge-prayers by which the Prophet fenced his community against the khizy of this verse)

— while the second half simply consigns the matter of the siege-lords and the profaners to the same scale as in vv. 85–86: no mitigation, no escape. The tradition's jurists built from verse 114 the standing law of the sanctity of houses of worship: no barring the doors of God's mosques against His servants, and no violence inside them — the Prophet ﷺ pronouncing in the conquest of Makkah that fighting is unlawful in its sanctuary forever (al-Bukhari 1834; Muslim 1353), and the sūrah itself, at 2:191, declaring: *do not fight them at the Inviolable Mosque until they fight you there.*

**The Mosque of the Heart**

The spiritual commentary of the tradition — al-Qushayrī and Ibn ʿAjībah, in the two registers our source joins — carries the verse inward in one final step: the believer himself possesses a *masjid* — the heart that was made for God's remembrance — and the same superlative applies to whatever blocks God's Name from within it: the heedlessness that bars the heart, the false desire that strives for its *kharāb*. In that reading the verse's legislative shape stands unaltered: the heart should be "entered" by its Owner only in reverence — *innā* in the idolatrous sense superadded — and the man who bars God's remembrance from his own interior mosque is the worst of wrongdoers *against himself*, sharing the vv. 61–86 formula: the outward siege of buildings and the inward siege of remembrance are tried on the one scale. The standard counsel of the wayfarers becomes the verse's wall-plaque: *keep the mosque of your heart populated with the Name or the punishing dust creeps in; and God is All-Seeing of whatever you do against His houses — stone or spirit.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:115

> **To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah. Surely Allah is AllEncompassing, All-Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**East and West in One Hand**

The consolation for verse 114's profanation arrives as a doctrine of boundless presence: *wa li-llāhi al-mashriqu wa'l-maghrib* — "to God belong the East and the West." The whole compass of the heavens' rising and setting points — every hemisphere, every horizon — is His property; the Lord cannot be evicted from any territory by the ruin of any building, for the Book calls Him elsewhere "Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests" (55:17) and "Lord of the easts and the wests" (70:40). And the consequence for the believer's worship is drawn at once: *fa-aynamā tuwallū fa-thamma wajhu Allāh* — "whithersoever you turn, there is the Face of God." The commentators read the clause on two interlocking registers — and both routes lead to comfort: first, the practical register of the qiblah. The early community had once prayed toward Jerusalem, and after this general reassurance, 2:144 would appoint the Kaaba; but the present verse stands as the everlasting guarantee underneath every particular statute: the God addressed is not confined within any direction, so that the traveller, the battle-worn, the lost, and the mount-rider can pray genuinely toward the Face they cannot geographically hit, with God's own license, on the same basis as the Prophet's ﷺ instruction for the canonical prayer at its most desperate choice: *"If you fear an enemy, then on foot or riding"* (2:239) — the nearness of God is not hostage to the orientation of the road outward.

**"There Is the Face of God" — the Heart of the Clause**

On the second register — the doctrinal — the commentators negotiate the phrase *wajhu Allāh* ("God's Face") with the same reverent care the tradition shows in every mention of the Divine Attributes. The majority of the interpreters read it here as presence, direction, and God's goodpleasure: there — wherever you turn in lawful prayer — is God's facing you, the qiblah of His acceptance. Al-Rāzī argues from the clause itself God's utter non-corporeality: a body occupies one place, cannot be in all directions at once; that the Face can be met in every turning is among the strongest proofs that God is not a body anywhere in space, but encompasses and transcends it — being with His creatures wherever they are (57:4; 58:7) while nothing at all is His like (42:11). The spiritual tradition has always further received the verse among its texts of the divine *all-ness* toward creation: All things perish save His Face (28:88); all that is on the earth passes away — and there remains the Face of your Lord, Possessed of Majesty and Bounty (55:26–27); He is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward (57:3). From these affirmations the Sufi commentators framed their celebrated doctrine of God's presence-to-all-things — the vision the great commentators defend as *not* the dissolving of the Creator-creature distinction, for the Face remains His, but the negating of every "where" in which He would be absent. Under verse 114's ruined mosques therefore stands this verse's indestructible answer: the Lord whom barricades cannot reach cannot be barricaded against the turning worshipper — for *wheresoever you turn, there is His Face.*

**All-Encompassing, Knowing — and the Mosqueless Prayer**

The verse seals itself with the pair of Names perfect to its comfort: *inna Allāha wāsiʿun ʿalīm* — "God is All-Encompassing, Knowing." *Wāsiʿ*, the commentators note, is at once vast and unstintingly generous — God whose mercy has no edge: *"My mercy encloses all things"* (7:156); *"truly your Lord is of vast forgiveness"* (53:32) — and ʿAlīm whose knowledge tracks every worshipping direction turning toward Him through every confusion and fog-bound night. Al-Rāzī draws the paired names back into the episode of verse 114: though mosques be ruined, remembrance cannot be blockaded, for the Encompassing One is never absent from the place of the turning. The tradition then reads this pair of verses as the consolation of every believer whose mosque was ever shut, whose prayer-hall was ever occupied, whose minaret was ever silenced — to which the Prophet's ﷺ own sentence concerning the whole earth gives its final coloration, preserved in al-Bukhari and Muslim:

> *"The earth has been made for me a masjid (a place of prostration) and a purifier; so wherever the prayer-time comes upon any man of my community, let him pray."* (al-Bukhari 335, 438; Muslim 521)

Every spot of the globe thereby became one masjid by the gift — because East and West are God's, and the Face is met at every turning, for the worshipper who prays, in the field or the ruin or the corner of the bedroom, with the believing certainty of this verse.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:116

> **They say, “Allah has offspring.” Glory be to Him! In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth—all are subject to His Will.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Claim Surveyed and the Immediate Tasbīḥ**

The Book now compounds together — deliberately — a family of claims from separate quarters: *wa qālū ittakhadha Allāhu waladan subḥānahu* — "and they said: God has taken a child — Glory be to Him!" The commentators carefully mark that the "they" gathers several goatways at once: the Christians' doctrine of divine sonship for Jesus (addressed at 4:171; 5:17, 72; 9:30; 19:34-35), the extreme claims made of Ezra ʿUzayr in some Jewish circles of the Prophet's century (9:30), and the Arab pagans' allocation of daughters to God among the angels (16:57; 37:149-153; 43:16-19; 52:39). Against them all, the same immediate response: *subḥānahu* — the tasbīḥ — which the grammarians (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī) explain as carrying simultaneously glorification and *disassociation*: "far exalted, remote above all that they allege." The tradition has always heard in the interjection the faith's instinctive reflex: before all argument, the very soil of the claim — that the Creator has a need-structured, derivative, species-relationship with a creature — is repudiated by a word whose entire force is: *transcendence*.

**His Absolute Ownership and the Servanthood of All**

Then the correction rests on two premises stated as facts broader than the controversy itself: *bal lahu mā fī al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍ* — "nay — to Him belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and the earth": the entire catalogue of candidate "children" — Jesus, Ezra, the angels — fall within the possessive; a property cannot beget its Owner, an owned thing is by self-definition not the Owner's peer — *kullun lahu qānitūn* — "all are devoutly obedient to Him." The commentators unfold *qānitūn* through its fiqh of reverence: compliance, humility, standing-in-presence, held silence — the angels' own comportment before the Throne. Ibn Kathīr links the clause's inclusive sweep with 13:15's manifesto: "to God prostrate all who are in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly" — while al-Qurṭubī adds the eschatological register: at the Resurrection the *qunūt* will be visibly total, as every creature stands, wordless, in sheer compliance. The alleged candidates thus testify *against* the claim from within their own stations: the Messiah — far from disdaining — is God's servant (4:172), the angels brought-nigh are worshippers (21:26-27, 43:19), and Ezra (ʿUzayr) was never, to his own people, what the extremist fraction claimed.

**The Kalām Core: Why No Sonship Is Possible for God**

The source commentary gives here the classic theological argumentation at its most direct, and it is worth setting out at its native length, for it became the germ of the systematic kalām of the schools. Al-Rāzī's four arguments are representative of the mainstream Ashʿarī and Māturīdī teaching: (1) whatever is called God's offspring is either eternal or originated in time; if eternal, nothing distinguishes "father" from "son" (both being necessary and without beginning) so the terms collapse; if originated, then it is *created* before — and a created thing cannot qualify as the proper son of the Creator, who in Himself has no begetting; (2) offspring is of the progenitor's species — human from human, lion from lion — and would require the offspring to share, in kind, the divine essence in a way that demands the divisibility and composition of the Divine Essence, whereas God is one and not composed; (3) offspring among creatures answers to needs — continuity, comfort, protection against senescence — none of which can be predicated of the Self-Sufficient (al-Ṣamad) — and God declares of Himself:

> *"Say: He is God, One; God, the Self-Sufficient Besought of All. He begot not, nor was He begotten; and none is comparable unto Him."* (112:1-4 — the sūrah the Prophet ﷺ pronounced equal to one third of the Qur'an, al-Bukhari 5013, 5015)

(4) the Book, refusing the claim at its root, teaches the alternative attribution: whatever exaltation God bestows upon Jesus is sonship-in-no-wise — only "a word from Him, and his name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary" (3:45-51; 4:171) — and the same gift of unbegotten generation by *Be!*, about to follow at verse 117, making the claim's physical logic superfluous: God creates sons for Himself by command, not by begetting; the Messiah was created by the word *Kun*, as Adam before him (3:59).

**Devout Obedience as the Believer's Posture**

The closing noun — *qānitūn* — passes from the verse to the Muslim devotional vocabulary as the ideal of *qunūt* — the long standing of humbled obedience — descending directly into the Sunnah's own prayer-parts: the Prophet ﷺ, whom God's Messenger described as *raising his palms* in the witr of the night, praying the supplication named from his own tradition *duʿāʾ al-qunūt*:

> *"O God, guide me among those You have guided, and grant me safety among those You have granted safety, and take me as Your friend among those You have befriended... You decree, and none decrees against You; he whom You befriend is never abased, and he whom You oppose is never honored. Blessed are You, our Lord, and exalted."* (Abū Dāwūd 1425; al-Tirmidhī 464; al-Nasāʾī 1745; Ibn Mājah 1178 — graded *ḥasan-ṣaḥīḥ*)

Verse 116 thus contributes both the faith's most compact disproof of all doctrines of divine offspring and its positive devotional answer: "all are devoutly obedient to Him" — and the believer so answers, joining his own *qunūt* to the chorus of the heavens and the earth, and disassociating his Lord from every need with the tasbīḥ of the verse: *subḥānahu.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:117

> **˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and the earth! When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!” And it is!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Badīʿ: Maker Without a Model**

The answer to the claims of sonship completes itself in a Divine Name that rules them out by definition: *badīʿu al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍ* — "the Originator of the heavens and the earth." The commentators dwell on the precision of *badīʿ*: to originate *without precedent*, to bring forth what never before had an example — God does not need a father to have offspring, for He is Himself the One from whom first-instance existence ever comes: every "first" in creation descends from His *badʿ*. The Name is joined, in the sūrah's own logic, to everything that precedes: how could the One who brought the heavens and the earth out of absolute un-likeness — no blueprints, no materials, no prior pattern in which to copy — possibly be folded into the procreative economy of His creatures? The verse is the theological vault-key to 2:116: the candidates for "sonship" belong to the order of *originated* things; the Originator is of the wholly different order — the one in whom origination itself begins — and al-Rāzī's strategy is precisely to demonstrate that the predicate "offspring of X" presupposes the very genus-and-need structure which *badīʿ* has just excluded from God entirely.

**Kun Fayakūn: the Sovereign Word of Creation**

The verse's closing clause is the celebrated educational formula: *wa idhā qaḍā amran fa-innamā yaqūlu lahu kun fa-yakūn* — "when He decrees a thing, He but says to it: Be! — and it is." The commentators unfold its senses without forcing the metaphor beyond the Book's own usage: God creates *without labor, without process, without intermediate means*: no clay must first be gathered by the Hands' tools, no millennia must accrue before the thing arrives; the command itself brings the commanded into being as the speakers' *be* puts the servant's work in motion — except that God's Word does not merely command but *causes-to-exist*: the call and the existence are in immediate conjunction: *fa-yakūn* — "and it is." The same formula repeats in the Book's expositions of creation, providence and resurrection — 6:73; 16:40; 36:82; 40:68 — and stands behind Islam's most compassionate creeds of ease: the Lord whom men sought to configure into father, craftsman, or molder is none of these needs-bound agencies; whatever He wills, *is*. The tradition's spiritual writers especially treasure the non-delay structure: no awaiting of helpmates, no dependence upon conditions thought physically necessary — for the Divine Speech is alone the sufficient condition of the willed thing, as the Book sets down at the great dyad:

> *"When We will a thing, Our word to it is but: Be! — and it is."* (16:40; 36:82)

**The Answer to the Months of Waiting**

Applied to the whole dispute of vv. 116–120 — that God must have had help to create His prophets and His Book's heroes — verse 117 resolves the file: Jesus does not have to be begotten to be honored, for God created him by the same *Kun* by which Adam was created from dust (3:59); Ezra does not have to be a "son" to be God's *ʿabd*; angels do not have to be "daughters" to be near-stationed servants — the whole family-tree of possible exaltations grows from the Word *Be!*, and no genealogy is needed to explain it. For the believing heart, the Name *badīʿ* and the formula *Kun fa-yakūn* become two of its most frequent consolations in daily need: whatever is impossible by the laws men know is a small thing before the Originator's command — as the Prophet ﷺ was taught to answer the dismay of his own companions when the road seemed to stop before a pit:

> *"God wills not a thing but that it is; and whatever God has willed, surely comes to pass"* — and with the Prophet's own sigh of trust by which Ḥudhayfah transmitted it: *"God is Sufficient for me; there is no god but He; upon Him I rely; and He is the Lord of the tremendous Throne"* (Abū Dāwūd 5081; graded *ḥasan*)

The verse is thereby stored in the believer's memory against every day of impossibility: no need travels to God's action by laborious roads; the Originator speaks — and what was not, *is.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:118

> **Those who have no knowledge say, “If only Allah would speak to us or a sign would come to us!” The same was said by those who came before. Their hearts are all alike. Indeed, We have made the signs clear for people of sure faith.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Timeless Taunt**

The Book turns now to a demand as old as prophecy itself: *wa qāla alladhīna lā yaʿlamūna lawlā yukallimunā Allāhu aw taʾtīnā āyah* — "those who do not know say: if only God would speak to us, or a sign would come to us." The commentators note the deliberate vagueness of the actors: "those who do not know" may be read as the pagan Arabs, the Christians, some of the Jews — or every class of persons for whom the description holds (al-Ṭabarī). The ambiguity is deliberate and forever-renewed: the demand for direct divine speech or a bespoke sign is not the property of one community but the standing reflex of ungrounded hearts. Al-Ṭabarī and others make the further diagnosis: the sentence is not a sincere question but a *taunt* — a demand manufactured to be refused, so that refusal can become the excuse for continued unbelief: just the genre of requests catalogued at 4:153 ("we will not believe you till we see God openly") and 17:90–95 ("we will not believe you till you cause a spring to burst for us from the earth"); the Book has already told the Prophet's community the genealogy of that hunting-party in the challenge of the cow (2:67–71) and the demand of sight at 2:55.

**"Their Hearts Are Alike" — One Unbelief Down the Ages**

The divine answer is not to grant the demand but to unmask its genealogy: *kadhālika qāla alladhīna min qablihim mithla qawlihim tashābahat qulūbuhum* — "thus spoke those before them in words just like theirs; their hearts are alike." The Clause *tashābahat qulūbuhum* — "their hearts have made themselves similar" — is one of the sūrah's most-pondered psychological puzzles. The commentators draw the lesson with economy: unbelief does not keep coming up with new arguments; it recycles one — because the engine is never the argument but the heart's condition; and the same condition brings forth the same speeches across millennia, across continents, across languages. The ploy of specially-requested signs thereby collapses upon the identity of the asking heart: not a deficiency of evidence moves it — the Book, at the time, was delivering the most magnificent evidence of all in the gradually-compounded composition of the recited Qur'an itself — but the *prior decision* not to believe, dressing itself in a request for more proof: and the same heart in every century asks in the same accent. The tradition has always taken *tashābahat qulūbuhum* as both a rebuke and a consolation: rebuke, because the Prophet's ﷺ caller after them must not take each recycled taunt as fresh argument; consolation, because the heart-fellowship of belief is likewise one across the ages — you are never alone on your path, for the hearts of the certain are a single caravan through time.

**Clear Signs for the Certain**

The verse closes with the decisive placement of evidence: *qad bayyannā al-āyāti li-qawmin yūqinūn* — "We have already made the signs plain for a people who have certainty." The commentators capture its logic: the signs have not been withheld; they have been *clarified, in public* — but clarity goes home only in certain hearts. Certainty (*yaqīn*) here is not the fruit of argumentative accretion but the heart's posture toward the already-delivered revelation: the Book's abundant arrangement, its readiness of proof and its tightly-woven meaning, stand in full view; among a people made of *those who are certain*, the ready plainness of the signs finds ready eyes, while beneath the taunting requests of "those who do not know," the clarification runs off like water off stone (cf. v 74). The tradition has always treasured the verse as the seal of the road already marked out in vv. 108, 109, 118, and, shortly, 120: the end is not that every question is answered but that the certainty-bearing souls — *li-qawmin yūqinūn* — are already brought to rest by what has been given. The Prophet ﷺ praised such certainty as the highest degree of faith, in the core of the Jibril-hadith of al-Bukhari and Muslim: faith's root *iḥsān* is *"that you worship God as though you saw Him; and if you see Him not — He sees you"* (al-Bukhari 50; Muslim 8) — and his companions would say, reciting the reports of certainty in the Quran: *"This is the faith of the people of certainty"* — the station where the signs suffice because the heart already knelt.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:119

> **We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺ as a deliverer of good news and a warner. And you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Sent With the Truth: the Prophet's Charter**

Unto His Messenger — amid the taunts recycled in verse 118 — God declares his charter in full: *innā arsalnāka bi'l-ḥaqqi bashīran wa nadhīrā* — "indeed We have sent you with the truth, as a bearer of glad tidings and a warner." The two offices named — *bashīr* and *nadhīr* — form the Book's standing pair of the prophetic ministry (6:48; 17:105; 34:28; 4:165): the prophet holds out the promise in one hand and the warning in the other; he is neither a dreamer detached from consequences nor a fire-alarm detached from mercy, but precisely both, in one breath, so that the human heart's two engines of hope and fear are both engaged by one mouth. And the charter's first clause, *bi'l-ḥaqq* — "with the truth" — is the decisive one: the carrier is measured by what he carries; the Prophet carries the truth, so that the office is not personal invention but commissioned conveyance. The commentators underline the letter of consolation this charter delivers to the messengers under taunt: your duty is deliverance of truth, not the manufacturing of acquiescence.

**"Thou Wilt Not Be Questioned About the Inhabitants of Hellfire"**

Then comes the relief whose comfort generated a whole family of parallel assurances in the Book: *wa lā tusʾalu ʿan aṣḥābi al-jaḥīm* — "and you shall not be asked about the companions of the Hellfire." The commentators read the clause in the sense given by its kindred verses: *you will not be held responsible for the fate of those who refused hearing* — just as 2:272 ("guidance is not upon you; God guides whom He wills"), 18:6 ("will you destroy yourself over them with grief?"), 35:8 ("let not your soul go out with regrets over them"), 88:22 ("you are not a warder over them"). The teaching establishes one of the sūrah's — and the religion's — most humane rules of preaching:*the preacher answers for fidelity, not for harvest*. The rejection of the hearers is never laid on the faithful messenger — no, not even upon the Seal of the messengers, whose "guidance is only in God's hand, who guides whom He wills" (28:56: *"You guide not whom you love"*); still less shall it be laid on any preacher after him.

**The Burden Lifted From Every Caller**

The tradition's field of applications from verse 119 is very large, and it has always been used with frequency for two pastoral purposes. First, directly unto the Prophet ﷺ himself at the time of his deepest anguish over the stubbornness of his people: to Muḥammad ﷺ himself, standing at the graves of the Makkan dead after Uhud and grieving over the obstinacy of those who had rejected him, this verse and its kin became the Master's own answer: *deliver the truth; I will deal with the hearers* — so that the Prophet could pray: *"O God, forgive my people, for they do not know"* — while being relieved of the further burden of their accountability classing. Second, to every subsequent caller in Islam — every teacher, parent, imam — the verse has always given back the peace of a measured charge: you are a *bashīr* and a *nadhīr*: carry the twin office faithfully, and leave the combustion of the furnace-souls to the just weighing of God. The Prophet ﷺ voiced the same consolation concerning the day of intercession and judgment, in the long hadith of the intercession at al-Bukhari and Muslim:

> *"God will say: O Muḥammad, lift up your head! Ask, you shall be given; intercede, you shall be granted intercession" — and the Prophet ﷺ shall intercede for his community, saying, upon the beam beyond: O Lord, my community! my community!"* (al-Bukhari 3340, 4712, 7440; Muslim 193, 322 — from the long narrative of Abū Hurayrah and Anas ibn Mālik)

The messenger-destiny the sūrah assigns him at verse 119 thus ends not in detention before the question "why did they not believe?" but in the lifted head and the cry of mercy upon the bridge: *my community!* — and for every lesser messenger the same separation of roles holds: his duty the clear conveyance, God's sole province the reckoning over the souls of flame.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:120

> **Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith. Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.” And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against Allah.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Impossibility of Contentment**

The Book now states to the Prophet ﷺ, with great directness, the terminal fact of his interlocutors' hearts: *wa lan tarḍā ʿanka al-yahūdu wa lā al-naṣārā ḥattā tattabiʿa millatahum* — "the Jews will not be content with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their *millah*." The commentators note two features. First, the double negative (*wa lan... wa lā*): the discontent is perpetual — no degree of kindness, treaty, eloquence, or partial accommodation would ever produce the coveted *riḍā*, for the demanded price is full submission to the other's *millah* — a term the philologists gloss as more than opinion: the creed, the way, the religious law that defines a community (cf. 2:130, 135; 4:125; 6:161). Second, the *target*: the demand is addressed personally to the Prophet ﷺ — *until you follow* — the pressure to convert the messenger being the surest way to subvert the message; and the commentators attach the verse to the negotiations and sulks that followed the change of the qiblah from Jerusalem to the Kaaba (al-Thaʿlabī), when some offered truce-readiness if he would bend the nascent community back toward their forms.

**"The Guidance of God Is THE Guidance"**

The answer reduces the issue to one clause that has descended into the marrow of Islamic certainty: *qul inna hudā Allāhi huwa al-hudā* — "Say: *the guidance of God — that is the guidance.*" The construction deliberately repeats the word, excluding by grammar every rival subject: God's guidance is not *a* guidance among many, to be bartered beside the millahs; it is *the* guidance, the genus, the entirety. The verse then sounds the full weight of what apostasy would mean — not with the threat merely of the world but with the sūrah's own standing double negation from verse 107: *wa laʾini ittabaʿta ahwāʾahum baʿda alladhī jāʾaka mina al-ʿilmi mā laka mina Allāhi min waliyyin wa lā naṣīr* — "and were you to follow their caprices after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have against God neither protector nor helper." The commentators rightly insist that the conditional is *rhetorical honorific*, addressed to the Prophet as the most honored warning possible — for the Book itself had already declared the Prophet's certain maintenance under God's protection (5:67's "God will protect you from the people") — so the addressee of the threat-clause in its effective application is everyone *following the Prophet*: to the ummah listening over his shoulder the verse says: if *he*, with all his nearness, would lose both guardian and helper by following their caprices — what of the ordinary man?

**Caprice vs. Knowledge — and the Ummah's Own Warning**

The verse pairs two cognitive terms that the tradition has long treated as the poles of religious epistemology: *ahwāʾahum* — their *caprices*, the desires of the soul dressed as reasons, *hawā* — and *alladhī jāʾaka mina al-ʿilm* — "the knowledge that came to you": given knowledge descending from the sky. The Muslim afterlife of verse 120 is therefore entirely about the choice between *hawā* and *ʿilm*: for him the pressure to be "contented" — by interlocutors, neighbors, majorities, fashions — is merely the modern dress of the verse's prohibition: to bend his religion until the bystanders are placated is precisely the millah-following paid at the price of guidance. But al-Ghazālī and the tradition's great preachers further warn against the tamer form: the re-describing of one's *own* piety so that its edges round off at the very points where God's guidance meets the neighbor's displeasure — a padding of caprice in religious costume. The direction of verse 120's solution is identical to that of vv. 105–109: the believers' relief does not come by pleasing the unwilling neighbors but only by holding God's guidance as *the* guidance, *hudā Allāhi huwa al-hudā* — and thereby remaining within the paragraph of vv. 107: having protector and helper, not of silver, but of God — neither of which can be found *against* God after the knowledge of God has come.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:121

> **Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed. It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it. As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Recite It as It Should Be Recited"**

The verse shifts from the taunters to the true receivers: *alladhīna ātaynāhumu al-kitāba yatlūnahu ḥaqqa tilāwatih* — "those to whom We have given the Book and who recite it as it should be recited." The commentators explore the object-clause in two directions that finally converge: to whom does "the Book" refer, and what is *ḥaqq al-tilāwah* — the truth/due of recitation? For al-Ṭabarī and many of the early authorities, the first referent includes the People of the Book — the learned among the Jews and Christians — who are challenged to follow their own scripture fully (and following the Torah in full, on the Book's testimony at 7:157, necessarily means following the Arabic prophet when he comes, since the Torah commands it); for others, the addressees of *ātaynāhum al-kitāb* are the Muslims given the Qur'an. The beauty of the verse permits either and demands both: entrusted-scripture followed *in truth* brings belief. Al-Rāzī draws out the conditions of true recitation as the tradition catalogues them: humility and understanding beyond mouth-service — while many of the commentators cite the alternative verbal meaning of *talā*: *to follow*, in step, behind a guide — *who follow it as it should be followed*: the true recitation of scripture is the obedience of conduct it commands.

**Recitation Amounting to Faith**

The consequence of true recitation is then stated as a simple copula: *ulāʾika yuʾminūna bih* — "those — they believe in it." The verse thereby delivers a doctrine the tradition has never let go: *genuine contact with God's Book produces faith*; and conversely, the failure of scripture's impact on a reciter is not proof against the Book but the sign of a recitation stopped halfway — read by the lips, not yet followed by the feet. Ibn Masʿūd is reported in the early tradition to have defined the true recitation in conduct:

> *"By Him in whose hand is my soul, the true recitation of it is that its lawful is held lawful and its unlawful held unlawful, that it be recited as God sent it down, and that it not be twisted away from its places."* (cited by al-Ṭabarī under this verse, among the reports of the Salaf) The tradition thereby forever connects the tilāwah with everything after it: reading is an act of *following*: the Qur'an is to be rehearsed into conduct — a devotion whose opposite, as the commentators warn, is the prophet's own complaint at 25:30: *"O my Lord, my people held this Qur'an as something abandoned."* ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd's summary, in another report both in the early tafsīr and the later akhlāq-collections, describes the same truth from the side of deeds:

> *"The Qur'an was sent down so that people might act by it; and they have taken its recitation itself as the work."* — and the Sufi commentators after him add the complementary direction: only the recitation of the whole heart, humble before the voice, becomes inward increase (al-Sulamī's *Ḥaqāʾiq al-Tafsīr* at this verse).

**"Whosoever Does Not Believe in It — They Are the Losers"**

The verse ends with the inevitable: *wa man yakfur bihi fa-ulāʾika humu al-khāsirūn* — "and whoever disbelieves in it — those, they are the losers." The name *khāsirūn* — already used at 2:64 and at every ledger's end — settles the calculation the verse has made: after encounter with the Book, there is no neutral column remaining; belief or disbelief, balance or loss. The tradition also preserves the hadithic portraits of the two kinds of carriers. In al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

> *"The likeness of the believer who recites the Qur'an is that of the citron: its fragrance is pleasant and its taste is pleasant"* (al-Bukhārī 5020; Muslim 797)

—and, in the same reports, the hypocrite who bears the Book while hollowing it is likened to the colocynth: bitter of taste, without fragrance. The corollary of the sūrah's own rules firmly proposes verse 121 as a continuous yardstick: the Book given to any generation of believers — its throne the meditation-room of the heart, its soil the reenacting feet — ever divides those whom it meets into the two classes named: *those who believe in it*, and *the losers.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:122

> **O Children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you and how I honoured you above the others.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Refrain Rings Again**

The address that opened the Israelite cycle at verse 40 and closed the rehearsed catalogue at verse 47 sounds again here — verbatim — after more than seventy verses: *yā banī isrāʾīla udhkurū niʿmatiya allatī anʿamtu ʿalaykum wa annī faḍḍaltukum ʿalā al-ʿālamīn*. Within the sūrah's architecture the repetition is architectural, not redundant: it marks the boundary between the two great panels of the address to the People of the Book. The first panel (vv. 40–121) recounted delivered mercies and betrayed covenants, unfolding the community's record as cautionary history; the second (vv. 122–141) redraws the whole family-line, re-rooting both communities in Abraham — their common father — so that neither Jews nor Christians nor the new community of Muslims can claim the patriarchal franchise as private property. By repeating verse 47 exactly at this gate, the Book recalls all the earlierevidence into current account: you have heard the whole trial-record; now hear the final argument, which concerns your own father Abraham.

**Memory as Doctrine Once More**

The command *udhkurū* — *remember* — lands upon the same theology expounded at verse 47: gratitude is not a passive emotional note but a corporate discipline of memory, the act that keeps covenant visible through time; and *faḍḍaltukum ʿalā al-ʿālamīn* — "I preferred you above the worlds" — retains here its earlier established meaning: preference in *their* historical frame, among the nations of their age — with prophets, scriptures, deliverances poured out abundantly, a temporal deputising of light, not an eternal assurance. Al-Qurṭubī's rule, cited at verse 47, bears setting down once more here in the sūrah's own reprise: the preference is theirs *in the ages of their fidelity* — and the verse positions the reader at its threshold precisely where the condition will be transferred in the coming verses from the tribe of the custodians to the creed of Abraham itself: whosever follows that creed inherits the favor. The reprise is thus at once a summons of history and a laying of a foundation for the Abraham argument: remember what was given, because what is about to be proved is that the same grace now flows by another channel, opened to all who keep the covenant of the father of the three communities.

**The Pedagogy of the Recurring Sentence**

The commentators note that the Qur'an teaches by refrain, as a teacher repeats the thetical sentence at the opening of each class; and its return after the longest interval in the sūrah (from 47 to 122 — some seventy-five verses of argument) comes at the moment the hearers are being invited to a new decision. The static between 47→48 and 122→123 is exactly the content surveyed: the whole inventory of the sea and the manna and the calf and the cow and the distortions and the covenants and the clear signs and the envy — all of it now bracing into this second frame, so that when the refrain sounds, it sounds with the weight of all that has been proved. In this, the address leaves one further lesson for every teacher after it (the tradition of the Prophet's own sermons echoes the same technique: structures that return upon themselves, as well as repeated sentences whose meaning thickens with every return): God's pedagogy toward His servants' hearts revisits its critical theorems until they hold; and the second "O Children of Israel" arrives not as an alien exhortation but as a familiar doorway — their own sentence greeting them for the last time before the family line is opened to Abraham.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:123

> **And guard yourselves against the Day when no soul will be of any help to another. No ransom will be taken, no intercession accepted, and no help will be given.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verdict Named Again Before Abraham**

The twin of verse 48 returns with one subtle reordering of its triplet of refusals: *wa-ttaqū yawman lā tajzī nafsun ʿan nafsin shayʾan wa lā yuqbalu minhā ʿadlun wa lā tanfaʿuhā shafāʿatun wa lā hum yunṣarūn* — *"and be mindful of a day when no soul shall recompense another soul in any way; nor shall a ransom be accepted from it; nor shall intercession avail it; nor shall they be helped."* At verse 48 the order was intercession, then ransom; here it reverses to ransom, then intercession — the commentators read the exchange as purely rhetorical variety signifying exhaustiveness: every door an escape-artist might try is named and sealed, in whatever order: no surrogate to stand in, no wealth to pay in, no advocate to speak in, no rescuer to reach in. The repetition at the pivot into the Abraham section is a calculated warning: before the patriarch is brought forward — the very man in whose genealogy both contesting communities seek shelter — their common father is introduced under a sky in which genealogy wins nothing: *the sons of Abraham will be judged, as every soul is judged, inside the ledger of what they themselves earned.*

**The Solitary Ledger**

The tradition holds this pair of verses (48 and 123) as the sūrah's twin gateposts upon judgment-day-solitude — and fleshes the scene with the Prophet's ﷺ own dramatic presentations of it. ʿĀʾishah reports the Prophet standing in the night while his soul trembled and teaching his community the scene of the Day, in the narration of al-Bukhari and Muslim:

> *"You shall be gathered barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised." I said: O Messenger of God — will the men and the women not look at one another? He said: "The matter is too tremendous upon them on that day for that."* (al-Bukhārī 3349, 6527; Muslim 2961)

On that day, the Prophet ﷺ elsewhere teaches, each soul stands with its own scroll — *"read your record; sufficient is your soul this day as reckoner against you"* (17:14) — and no duplicating of guilt is permitted in either direction of the balance.

The tradition's theology of intercession, expounded with care in the address at verse 48, holds unanimously on the two verses: the refusal of surplus-help is not the denial that the Prophet's ﷺ shafāʿah exists — for the Book establishes it promised (17:79) and the Sunnah describes its ranks (and the believers' shared resort to it) — but the denial that any of the help-forms function *independently of God's permission and desert*: no *compensation* by substitution (one soul carrying the load of another), no *ransom* purchasable (the sūrah has already forbidden every millenary bargain), no *intercession* benefiting of itself (only by God's leave — 2:255, 20:109, 39:44). The tradition's trace of the line is exact: as al-Bukhari preserved, the Prophet ﷺ at the grave finality of that day will say to the last: *"myself, myself"* — while the creation runs from Adam to Noah to Abraham to Moses to Jesus, each answering *"I have no warrant for this — go to the other"* (al-Bukhari 3340; Muslim 194) — a narration in which the rule of our verse is already exemplified: not refusal by the prophets, but the matter's carrying only at God's permission.

**Twin Gates Closing the Frame**

The function of verse 123 before the Abraham cycle is finally to settle the criterion of all the arguments about to come: when the Prophet ﷺ exposes the Abrahamic root of the true religion (vv. 124–141), he does so — the Book's own logic requires — liberated from every claim of *group-inheritance*: the Day when souls are faced with God, with their own works, without advocate or bail, is the very Day under which Abraham will be counted the friend of God and those who follow his creed his true *millah*. The verse therefore serves as the hyphen that links the genealogical debate with the final evaluative sentence of the unit at 2:134 and 141 ("that is a community that has passed away; theirs is what they earned and yours is what you earned"), closing every later hope of community-salvation-by-tribe, and opening the door, alone, to the creed of Abraham and the bookkeeping of deeds.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:124

> **˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments, which he fulfilled. Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model for the people.” Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?” Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Trial by Words**

The Abraham narrative opens at its summit — with a trial *completed*: *wa idh ibtalā ibrāhīma rabbuhu bi-kalimātin fa-atammahunn* — "and when Abraham's Lord tested him with certain words, and he fulfilled them." The commentators, as the source records, differed over what the *kalimāt* were, and the tradition's honesty preserves the field. Some of the early authorities named the commandments of bodily devotion and purification — circumcision and the laws of cleanliness that entered religion through Abraham's practice; others, the rituals of pilgrimage — circumambulating the House, running between Ṣafā and Marwah, casting the stones; others yet, the severest fissures of Abraham's life — the fire made cool (21:68–69), the migration, above all the command to sacrifice his son (37:102). Because the text does not itemize, the commentators conclude modestly: the trial was real and entire, whatever its items — and the essential is the second verb: *fa-atammahunn* — "he completed/fulfilled them all." The Book has its own parallel at its other praise-register: *wa ibrāhīma alladhī waffā* — "and Abraham, who fulfilled" (53:37) — and it is exactly this *entireness* of execution that the verse makes the qualification for what is about to be granted: imamate follows fulfilment; leadership of mankind is the prize of total response, not of wish or status.

**The Imamate of Mankind**

God's response crowns the completed trial: *qāla innī jāʿiluka li'l-nāsi imāmā* — "He said: I am making you an imam for mankind." *Imām* — the one placed at the front to be followed — becomes here one of the highest titles in sacred history: Abraham is appointed, in al-Tirmidhī's phrase within the tradition's commentaries, *the Imam of the people of tawḥīd*, the model-dam at the head of the three faiths: Judaism through Isaac and Jacob, Christianity through the line, Islam through Ishmael — in this verse all three spiritual nations are gathered under one man. The Shiʿi tradition receives the term in its fullest theological load — the imamate as a divine appointment and a divine covenant (*ʿahd* in the verse's own noun) — and the Sunni majority receives it with the same text and a lighter ontology, but on the exact this: *imamate is God's gift, and His covenant runs by desert.* Abraham — the pattern of fathers — immediately asks for it as a patrimony: *qāla wa min dhurriyyatī* — "and from my progeny?" The prayer is the most natural of fathers' prayers: let the mantle run down the generations.

**"My Covenant Does Not Include the Wrongdoers"**

The answer demolishes every hereditary franchise in one sentence: *qāla lā yanālu ʿahdī al-ẓālimīn* — "My covenant does not include the wrongdoers." The commentators reflect on what the clause establishes: *nāla* — to reach, attain — God's covenant is not an estate descending by blood; it is *reached* only by the qualified. Not all of Abraham's progeny would be virtuous — the Book itself states it plainly at 37:113: "among their progeny are the good-doer and the one who plainly wrongs his own soul" — and the covenant in the verse is thereby explicitly made merit-structured, not genealogy-structured: prophethood, imamate, covenant — none of them are in the gift of race. The application to the dispute the whole sūrah is arbitrating was and remains obvious to every commentator: the Jewish and Christian claim upon Abraham (vv. 135, 140) can never be a patrimony-claim; what Abraham received, he received after *atammahunn* — entire fulfilment of the divine words — and whoever claims his mantle must come by the same road. The Shiʿi imams (the fifth and sixth, in the transmission of al-Ṭabarī) cited the verse to the same end: God does not appoint and does not ratify an unjust imam — covenant and ẓulm are exclusive. And the tradition joins to the verse the Prophet's ﷺ own description of the two statuses as they actually descended in Abraham's seed — *righteous sons and wronging sons* — in the hadith of the best generations:

> *"The best generation is mine, then those who follow them, then those who follow them"* (al-Bukhari 2650–51; Muslim 2533–34) — and after them, *"a people bearing false witness"* — the tree inheriting both branches, each by its own earning, as the verse vows to every would-be heir of Abraham thereafter.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:125

> **And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer.” And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The House: Rendezvous and Sanctuary**

The scene now opens upon the building that would define Abraham's city and the compass of Islam: *wa idh jaʿalnā al-bayta mathābatan li'l-nāsi wa amnan* — "and when We made the House a place of return for mankind, and a sanctuary." *Mathābah* — from *thāba*, to return — is no ordinary noun; the commentators unfold it: the Kaaba is designated the *place of return-pilgrimage* — the lodestone to which the hearts and feet of the believers are drawn back recurrently, returning because they first turned there, yearning because it never leaves the heart once seen. The tradition's image is that of a magnet and pivot: the lives of prayer that had been steering toward it day and night through the qiblah of 2:144, the Hajj processions of the ages returning into it, and the yearning-travelers of every century streaming toward its black square — its *mathābah*-nature visible in every epoch of the religion. The second predicate, *amnan* — "and a security, a sanctuary" — names what the desert around it bore from Abraham's day: the sanctuary-law the commentators describe vividly: fearful men took refuge there, bloodshed ceased at its bounds, and its dignity was respected amid the feuding tribes of Arabia with a reverence older than the idols of the Arabs — until the Prophet ﷺ, at the conquest of Makkah, pronounced over the city its eternal status in the narration of al-Bukhari and Muslim:

> *"This city God has made inviolable on the day He created the heavens and the earth: inviolable by the sanctity of God until the Day of Resurrection. Its thorn-trees are not to be cut down, its game is not to be chased, its lost things are not to be picked up except by one who announces them; and fighting in it is permitted to no one after me."* (al-Bukhari 1834, 2439; Muslim 1353, 1354)

**"Take the Station of Abraham as a Place of Prayer"**

Within the House, a second command names the stone: *wa-ttakhidhū min maqāmi ibrāhīma muṣallan* — "and take the Station of Abraham as a place of prayer." The commentators record two readings of the Station: the famous stone adjacent to the Kaaba — believed to bear the imprint of Abraham's feet from the building-season and housed at its fixed station today — and, by extension, the rites of Station *unto* the pilgrimage as a whole (cf. 22:26–32 for the same Abrahamic rites). The reports preserved by al-Ṭabarī describe its dramatic consecration: the Prophet ﷺ took ʿUmar by the hand and walked him to the stone — *"this is the station of Abraham"* — and ʿUmar asked: shall we not take it for a place of prayer? and the Prophet ﷺ answered: he had not been so commanded — but *before that day was done our verse was revealed*, and the station was thereby inscribed into the mosque's own worship: two rakʿahs after the circumambulation at the station, a rulering that became the standing sunnah of the ṭawāf for every pilgrim to this day — one of the few pieces of fiqh whose *occasion of legislation* is so fully contemporaneous.

**"Purify My House" — Abraham and Ishmael at Work Together**

Then the third command gives the cycle its hands-on covenant: *wa ʿahidnā ilā ibrāhīma wa ismāʿīla an ṭahhirā baytiya li'l-ṭāʾifīna wa'l-ʿākifīna wa'l-rukkaʿi al-sujūd* — "and We charged Abraham and Ishmael: purify My House for those who walk around it, and those who retreat in it, and those who bow and prostrate." Two details the tradition never fails to treasure. First, the covenant is laid on *father and son together*: the Ishmael-line is established within the House's consecration itself, before all later faction-claims. Second, the purification commanded — cleansing the House of idolatry and doubt, per al-Ṭabarī — names the same vocation the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ, of Ishmael's n-th line, would discharge millennia later, breaking the three-hundred-and-sixty idols of the Kaaba at the conquest of Makkah: the covenant's circuit returned to its givers' descendant: *from the purification of Abraham and Ishmael, to the re-purification by the Prophet of them both.* The three classes of servants named map the settlement of the mosque to this day: *al-ṭāʾifūn* — the circumambulators — and *al-ʿākifūn* — the ones who cling there in retreat: *iʿtikāf*, the Prophet's own practice in the last ten days of Ramaḍan (al-Bukhari 2026; Muslim 1172) and the root-pattern of every subsequent spiritual seclusion (*khalwah*) within Sufism — and *al-rukkaʿ al-sujūd* — **the prayers themselves** with their double geometry of humility, bowed and prostrate: all three registered under the covenant before the House's final consecration was even seen. Verse 125 is thus read by the tradition as constituting: the House itself as pivot, the station as chapel, the covenant of purification as heredity, and the family of worshippers as the community of every later age converging on the same spot with the same three deflections of the body and the soul.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:126

> **And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure and provide fruits to its people—those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day.” He answered, “As for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves for a little while, then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire. What an evil destination!”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Father's Prayer for the Barren Valley**

The Abraham cycle adds civic founding to ritual founding: *wa idh qāla ibrāhīmu rabbi ijʿal hādhā baladan āminan wa-rzuq ahlahu mina al-thamarāti man āmana minhum bi-llāhi wa'l-yawmi al-ākhir* — "when Abraham said: my Lord, make this a land secure, and provide its people with fruits — those of them who believe in God and the Last Day." The scene, at its fuller parallel in 14:37, is the desert valley of no cultivation, Hagar and the infant Ishmael left there by God's command — *"a valley without tillage, at Your Sacred House"* — and Abraham's prayer for the settlement that would rise there covers two needs with prophetic directness: *security* — *baladan āminan*, a land at peace, from which fear is lifted (and the tradition links the granting with the sanctuary-law of verse 125: God did indeed make it inviolate, so that a man might walk to prayer through centuries of tribal war in peace) — and *provision* — *fruits*, in a valley that grew *nothing*, and which the tradition describes as thereafter served by caravans' abundance, by the divine answer at Mecca's market tables — the valley with no tillage becoming, in al-Ṭabarī's phrase, *a valley supplied by all the earth*; and above all the gushing of Zamzam under the infant's heels, God's literal liquid answer to Abraham's prayer for water.

**The Interruption: "Whosoever Disbelieves"**

One feature of the verse stopped the commentators with admiration: Abraham *limits* his prayer: feed — *man āmana minhum* — *"those among them who believe."* And God — as it were — corrects the patriarch's pious narrowness in the middle of the scene: *qāla wa man kafara fa-umattiʿuhu qalīlan thumma aḍṭarruhu ilā ʿadhābi al-nār* — "He said: *whosoever disbelieves — him too I shall give enjoyment a little while*; then I shall compel him to the punishment of the Fire: an evil arrival." The exchange is one of the Book's most discussed doctrines of provision (*rizq*): God's feeding of the world is *not* restricted by faith — bread in this world descends upon believer and disbeliever alike, for God is the Provider of all His creation (11:6); but verses of this type are also the Book's locations for teaching the doctrine of *imlāʾ* — God's granting of respite: brief enjoyment, then the compulsion toward the reckoning; as the same pattern is repeated at 3:178 ("We grant them respite only that they may increase in sin") and the Psalms' long-pondered mystery of the prospering wicked is resolved: *prosperity here is not endorsement; it is the short, free time before the account.* The commentators note Abraham's silence after the answer and its lesson: the patriarch did not contest God's provision for the unbelievers — he had asked what his father-heart wished; God's provision is wider than any father-heart — and his real gift to his progeny was secured in the next verse's prayer (v. 128): *make us submitters to You.*

**Fruit, Security, and the Citizen-Believer**

The tradition has drawn verse 126 deeply into Muslim civic self-understanding: Abraham's prayer named security and provision as the citizen-form of the city he was devoting to God — *amn* and *rizq* — and the Prophet's ﷺ community ever afterward measured every true blessing of a polity by the pair, the Prophet himself compressing them into his best-known supplication for nations and homes:

> *"O God, make us enjoy our hearing, our sight, and our strength as long as You keep us alive, and make our heirs from us; and make our vengeance upon those who wronged us, and help us against those who held enmity toward us; and do not make calamity strike our religion; and do not make the world the greatest of our concerns, nor the extent of our knowledge."* (al-Tirmidhī 3502 — *sahīh* — the Prophet's long duʿāʾ for his city and his ummah, always recited with the rest of the companions over fearful days)

And the verse's final sentence — *wa biʾsa al-maṣīr* — "an evil journey's end" — completes the grid for every society thereafter: security and fruit are real gifts, thankworthy and prayer-worthy; but they are interim gifts, and their entire ethical salience is contained in what their possessors set into the *next* life by their use of them. The City of the Prophet stands witnessed in both: made secure and fed to this very day by Abraham's prayer, and warned — as the next verse will show its founders themselves warning themselves — to know that the valley is a place of *return-thither* not the final destination: it awaits, as everything in this world awaits, the journey's end.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:127

> **And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael, ˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord! Accept ˹this˺ from us. You are indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Father and Son, Trowel and Prayer Together**

The cycle's most tender scene opens with a construction-site: *wa idh yarfaʿu ibrāhīmu al-qawāʿida mina al-bayti wa ismāʿīl* — "when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House, and Ishmael." The verb *yarfaʿu* — was *raising* — chose the imperfect of ongoing action: the commentators represented the two figures passing stone to stone, the father upon the wall, the son below; many also recalled the lore that, in another layer of tradition, the foundations went back to Adam himself — a House rased by the flood and *re*-founded by Abraham rather than initiated from void (al-Ṭabarī records the lore, judging it chain-weak history, while many of the commentators preserve it as worthy pious memory; the Book itself stands behind only what is fixed: Abraham and Ishmael *raising* the foundations). But the tradition's perennial astonishment at the scene lies elsewhere: the Qur'an immediately tells us that *while* they built, *while* their hands were in the mortar, *their tongues were in prayer*: *rabbanā taqabbal minnā innaka anta al-samīʿu al-ʿalīm* — "Our Lord, accept from us; truly You are the Hearing, the Knowing." Work and worship were not two periods of their day: the lifting was prayer, and the prayer was lifting.

**"Our Lord, Accept From Us" — the Builder's Humility**

The commentators draw from this prayer what they call the great lesson of *khashyat al-ʿadam* — fear of non-acceptance: if Abraham the Ḥanīf, and Ishmael the purified, finishing the very House of God at the command of God, still feared that their work might not be accepted, how can the later believer ever rest confident concerning the acceptance of his prayers, his fast, his zakāh? ʿĀʾishah heard the same trembling theme in the Prophet's own house — he recited 23:60, "those who give what they give with hearts quivering that they will return to their Lord" — and, when she asked whether these were the thieves and adulterers, who rightly tremble, he answered:

> *"No, daughter of al-Ṣiddīq: rather they are those who fast, and pray, and give charity, and yet fear that it may not be accepted from them — those are the ones who vie in the good works."* (al-Tirmidhī 3175 — *ṣaḥīḥ*; also transmitted in the two Ṣaḥīḥs' sense of *trembling in giving*: al-Bukhari 5052)

The prayer's theology is thereby laid down for every believer after Abraham's house: no work is so sacred that its *acceptance* is assured by its own nature; acceptance dwells with the Recipient, whose hearing surveys the work's *qawl* and whose knowledge searches its *niyyah* — *al-samīʿ* of every word of supplication and *al-ʿalīm* of the heart's hidden calculus when it lays its stone.

**The Answered Foundations**

The tradition traces the specific range of the twin names named at the prayer: *al-Samīʿ* — *Hearing*: God heard the whispered *taqabbal minnā* while the trowel was moving; *al-ʿAlīm* — *Knowing*: God knew the project behind the project — the father building for his son, the son for the child of the promise, the city for the final prophet — and accepted with all three depths of hearing: the Kaaba stands at the compass-center of Islam some four thousand years later, with the verse itself recited daily in the circumambulating-circle by millions who are Abraham's distant answer, and through whom the two names keep verifying the two builders' petition in every lifetime: *God heard, and God knew, and God accepted.* The spiritual tradition draws the lesson to every act of service: *build*, and *pray* — for the hands build and the Recipient answers; every mosque raised thereafter, every good work launched, enters under Abraham's petition at its laying: *Our Lord, accept from us; You are the Hearing, the Knowing.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:128

> **Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You and from our descendants a nation that will submit to you. Show us our rituals, and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Builders' Prayer for Submission**

Still standing on the scaffolding of the House, father and son continue praying — and the order of their petitions is the tradition's unforgettable proof-text on what a founder of God's House first asks for: not for its walls, but for their own souls: *rabbanā wa-jʿalnā muslimayni laka wa min dhurriyyatinā ummatan muslimatan lak* — "Our Lord — make us two *muslimān* to You, and of our progeny a community (*ummah*) *muslimah* to You." The commentators mark the deliberate doubling: Abraham — the very man God had pronounced to have *fulfilled* the words at 2:124 and honored with imamate — asks to be *made* a muslim: submission is not an achievement remembered but a sustenance begged, never graduated beyond; even the priests of the house must petition to remain its worshippers. And the gift asked for the progeny is deliberately communal: *ummah muslimah* — not scattered individuals but a *community* characterized by submission — the seed-prayer of the ummah of Muḥammad, which the Book says elsewhere that God chose and named *al-muslimīn* by this very name (22:78: "He named you al-muslimīn, before and in this"), and which verse 129 will narrow down to the very prophet of that chosen community.

**Muslim as Universal, Not Tribal**

The verse stands on the tradition's register of texts proving the universality of *islām* as a name and posture — the commentators here, as the source records, treat the verse with 2:131–32 and 2:136 as the chain demonstrating that *islām*-submission is the primordial religion, the one constant of God's dealings with all prophets: not a seventh-century start-up but the eternal covenant renewed in the line of prophets — *"the religion in God's view is islām"* (3:19). Abraham here coins the name afresh within the Abrahamic shop of the House: *muslim* as the participial vocation of the House-builder, and *ummah muslimah* as its congregation. Upon this register the whole subsequent debate on millah in vv. 130–140 is won: when the sūrah is summoned to answer "be Jews or Christians," the Book's rebuttal is in the etymology these verses themselves record — Abraham was neither; Abraham was *muslim* — and the name of *islām-submission* is recovered from his prayer rather than from any later fortification of tribe or sect.

**Rites Shown by God; Return Relented By God**

The two remaining petitions bind religion's two hands: *wa arinā manāsikanā* — "and show us our rites" — the word *manāsik* covers the pilgrim stations of raw devotion (from which Ḥajj's rhymes are all later named), the commentators noting that, whatever documentation Abraham had, he asked the rites to be *shown* — because worship, in Islam's perpetual dictum, is *tawqīfī*: received, not invented; the pilgrim stations by which the community would serve the House through all ages were scheduled in heaven before the houses of earth — and then: *wa tub ʿalaynā* — "and relent toward us": the prayer closes, amid the work of God's own House, with tawbah-requested! The spiritual commentators note the depth of the humility: even the builders of the very shrine of tawḥīd ask for return-forgiveness: no work, however high, cancels the servant's standing need of pardon; and the Names sealing the prayer are the same pair that closed Adam's own first tawbah at verse 37: *innaka anta al-tawwābu al-raḥīm* — "You are the Oft-Returning, the Merciful" — the letters with which the father of the prophets binds his family's post-days to the same mercy on which the father of mankind began the whole human story.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:129

> **Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, AllWise.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prayer That Waited Two Thousand Years for Its Answer**

The climax of the builders' duʿāʾ is a request for a very specified descendant: *rabbanā wa-bʿath fīhim rasūlan minhum yatlū ʿalayhim āyātika wa yuʿallimuhumu al-kitāba wa'l-ḥikmata wa yuzakkīhim* — "Our Lord — raise up in them a messenger, from among them, who recites Your signs to them, and teaches them the Book and the Wisdom, and purifies them." The commentators and historians of revelation converge upon one reading: this is nothing less than the *founding prayer for the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ*, lodged within the foundation masonry of the Kaaba by his great ancestor. Its four content-clauses describe Islam's ministry in detail with a precision only sealed prophecy could write: a messenger *from among them — the Ishmaelite Arabs*; reciter of the signs; teacher of the **Book** (the Qur'an) and **the Wisdom** (the Sunnah — al-Ṭabarī and the majority; the pairing also receives a wider register — scripture and understanding — as with Jesus at 3:48, 5:110); and *purifier* — one who takes souls from the soil of Jahiliyyah and cleanses them with tawḥīd. And God — as the Book itself carefully shows — answers this prayer *verbatim*: at 2:151, the divine speech declares *"As We have sent among you a messenger from among you, who recites to you Our signs, and purifies you, and teaches you the Book and the Wisdom..."* — the very same words, in the very same order, and with the *ka-mā* ("just as") that ties promise to fulfilment. The worldly span between the prayer and its spoken answer is measured in millennia; in God's word it was immediate: the verse's unanimity on the matter among the commentators is little short of a testimony to the art of the composition: two generations read 2:129 and 2:151 side by side as the *proof that the Qur'an was God's latest answering witness of a prayer made atop those very walls.*

**From Among Them: the Wisdom of a Home-Grown Messenger**

The commentators emphasize the prayer's qualifier *minhum* — "from among them." God could have commissioned angels or transferred the office back to a distant tribe; Abraham asked — and God ratified — that the seal come from within the waiting people: one whose tongue is theirs, whose customs they know, whose veracity they verified for forty years before his claims — *"indeed a messenger has come to you from among yourselves"* (9:128). Abraham thereby unknowingly builds the criterion into the Kaaba's very walls: the Arab prophet, from the sons of Ishmael, of the Banū Hāshim — among the people who at this very moment stand around the foundations — would arise out of them not as conquest but as kin: *minhum* both in tribe and in moral familiarity. The Prophet ﷺ described his status under the same signature in the famous hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim:

> *"I am the answer to the prayer of my father Abraham, and the glad tidings of Jesus."* — *"anā daʿwatu abī ibrāhīm wa bushra ʿīsā"* (Aḥmad 2/129; al-Ḥākim 2/342 — graded *ṣaḥīḥ*; widely received among the commentators on 2:129)

In that four-word claim the entire theology of verses 124–151 compresses: the imamate of Abraham (2:124) is no tribal pride but the seed of a world-sign: the House-founder prayed for its Prophet, and God, in 2:151, *textually* granted it.

**Mighty and Wise: the Seal of the Prayer**

The names closing the verse — *innaka anta al-ʿazīzu al-ḥakīm* — "You are the Mighty, the Wise" — complete its logic: the granting of such a prayer required *ʿizzah* — absolute power to bring forth a messenger from the barren house of Ishmael upon this schedule and humble valley — and *ḥikmah* — the wisdom that delayed it exactly to its hour, when the scripture of Israel had been handed down, the Gospels prepared, the trade roads of Arabia bricked, the unlettered community matured to receive an unlettered prophet (7:157). The tradition folds this pair of Names into the believer's accustomed closure upon every divine answer: God's timing is never late for those who build and pray — *two thousand years of mortar-dust on the stones*, and the answer stands there today, recited by hundreds of millions: *he taught them the Book* — and they carry him daily in the prayers of Abraham and every son of Abraham thereafter.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:130

> **And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool! We certainly chose him in this life, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Creed Declared**

Having made the Abraham narrative into the widest register of the covenant, the Book states its conclusion with the standing interrogative of condition-refusal: *wa man yarghabu ʿan millati ibrāhīma illā man safiha nafsah* — "and who but a foolish soul turns away from the creed (*millah*) of Abraham?" *Millah*, in the commentators' register (as with 2:120), is more than a religious brand: it is the community-forming *way* of faith — its law, its orientation, its public life. The verse has thereby settled the definition, for the whole remainder of the sūrah's debate with the People of the Book, of *whose* way is to be followed: not the creed attributed to Abraham by tribal invention, but the creed *he had* — the primordial, unbent surrender the sūrah has been describing since verse 124. And the verdict upon the refusal is calibrated for maximum effect: not *unbeliever*, not *sinner* — *safih* — foolish, light-headed, the man of the emptied scale: *safiha nafsah* — to cheapen one's own soul, to handle the priceless goods of the self as though they were weightless (cf. 4:5, where the *safīh* cannot be trusted with property): One who turns from Abraham's creed, says the verse, is quantified as a soul squandered by its own owner — the same young pathos of self-destruction the sūrah will name again at 6:12 ("those who have squandered their own souls in ruin suffer loss upon loss").

**Chosen in the World; Named Righteous in the Next**

The verse then seals the quality of the creed rejected by establishing the rank of its bearer in both worlds: *wa la-qadi iṣṭafaynāhu fī al-dunyā wa innahu fī al-ākhirati la-mina al-ṣāliḥīn* — "We chose him in this world, and he is, in the Hereafter, of the righteous." *Iṣṭifāʾ* — divine selection, choosing out — is the Book's rank-word for the best of God's friends: Adam was *chosen* (20:122), Moses *chosen* (7:144), Mary *chosen* (3:42), the seal of the prophets *chosen* (35:32) — and Abraham's being *chosen in the world* means his special favor and office among so mightily many: the friendship of God, the imamate of mankind, the consecrating of the House, and the furnace made cool; while *in the Hereafter he is of the righteous* overturns every possible line of doubt about his eternal standing: the genuine creed-bringer is not merely celebrated in this life; he is numbered with the *ṣāliḥīn* in the next.
