The two pillars, taken together, define the creed of Abraham as proven at both ends of existence: tested in this world, ratified in the other — and therefore cannot be dismissed by any man who fancies that history and eternity each hold separate bills.

**The Believer Between Safh and Iṣṭifāʾ**

The tradition hears verse 130 as one of the sūrah's pressure-points against every descendant of Abraham after him — and as a protection against the reflex of religious amusement toward the names *Jew* or *Christian* as though either could properly own him. Al-Qurṭubī and many of the commentators draw the practical bearing from it for the community of Islam: upon the continuity of Abraham's sharīʿah and Muḥammad's; many of the cleanliness and ḥajj statutes of the Prophet ﷺ are cited from Abraham's practice, and the Islamic legislator declared at the point of the change of prayer-direction:

> *"The best prayer after the obligatory ones is the night prayer"* — *"afḍalu al-ṣalāti baʿda al-farīḍati qiyāmu al-layl"* (Muslim 1163) — the link of the deep of night in which Abraham's own dream was born, alive still in the house of Muḥammad.

The *safīh* of the verse, by contrast, is every person to whom the costliness of Abraham's creed is unwelcome because it demands more than his comfort — of whom the sūrah has already spoken in the catalogue of the numerated-days fantasists (v. 80), the millennial wishers (v. 96), and the bargain-makers of Babylon (v. 102): all three specimen-pages of the same refusal. The tradition hears in the verse's framing the standing counsel of the saints to their disciples in every age: *own your soul, or you will be owned*; not to turn from the Abrahamic creed is the only way to keep the soul from folly — for in that register, everyone is either a clinger to Abraham's way, or the squanderer of a foolish soul; and the Book now invites its readers to count themselves, in the very next verse, among the community built upon a patriarch better than chosen: *who heard "Submit!" and submitted* — asverse 131 will now show.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:131

> **When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**One Word of Command, One Word of Answer**

The tradition holds verse 131 as the briefest and most perfect creed in the Book: *idh qāla lahu rabbuhu aslim qāla aslamtu li-rabbi al-ʿālamīn* — "when his Lord said to him: *Submit!* — he said: *I submit to the Lord of the worlds.*" The commentators note its compressed architecture: God's utterance is *one word* — *aslim* — the bare imperative with no qualifications, no provisions, no ornaments; Abraham's answer is likewise one complete act — *aslamtu* — "I submit" — with the submission's destination defined by the divine names it deserves: *li-rabbi al-ʿālamīn* — "to the Lord of the worlds" — not to the tribal idol or the burning star or the decrees of the age, but to the *Rabb* and Cherisher of every realm: and the commentary-tradition, from al-Ṭabarī forward, highlights the absence of delay: no "grant me a sign first," no "clarify the cows first": the answer arrives *when* the command arrives — the very grammar of instantaneous faith. The verse does not linger on what was commanded; the commentators read this, plausibly, as the submission to the same words whose fulfilment had been celebrated at 2:124 — or, more comprehensively, to the whole summation of his trials and the covenant-trials — the fire, the sacrifice, the family, the House, all the *kalimāt* contracted into one divine summons: *aslim.*

**Islam Defined on Abraham's Lips**

The tradition invokes verse 131 as the charter of the name *islām* before Islam's historical millennium: the same words the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ was commanded to bring were first spoken by a man at the furnace and the altar of sacrifice, thousands of years before Madinah: *"the religion with God is islām-submission"* (3:19), and *"whoever seeks a religion other than islām, it shall never be accepted of him"* (3:85). Al-Qurṭubī classifies the verse among those verses demonstrating that the sharing of *islām* runs across the line of prophets: every messenger was commissioned to deliver the same summons — *my people, submit to the Lord of the worlds* — and only the legal rites governing each age differed. The equation completes the verse's own feedback-loop with the whole Book: when the final Prophet ﷺ was asked at the Angle of the mountain, "What is islām?" he answered in the hadith of Gabriel, reported in al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

> *"Islam is that you bear witness that there is no god but God and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of God, and establish the prayer, and give the zakāh, and fast Ramaḍan, and make the pilgrimage to the House if you are able."* (al-Bukhari 8, 50; Muslim 8 — the Jibril-hadith)

and when the question was answered by the *īmān* (beliefs) and then by *iḥsān* (excellence), the thing's name was unchanged: *islām* — the one surrender asked of Abraham, articulated in his descendants as the five pillars, recited daily for the billions of Ummah-e-Muslimah that verses 128–129 had petitioned.

**Summons and Response in the Believer's Day**

For the reader the verse is a standing school of the soul's hearing: God enters each day as He entered Abraham's: *aslim* — Submit! in whatever form the day's call comes — the dawn call, the discovery of a duty, the summons to a costly act of righteousness; and the soul's great discipline of *isti'āna* (2:45) consists precisely in answering the call before the interpreters assemble: *aslamtu li-rabbi al-ʿālamīn.* From the Book to the saints' books, the tradition has never tired of praising the directness of the patriarch's syllable: in al-Ghazālī's Iḥyāʾ, at the opening of his analysis of *taubah*, Abraham's answer is the model against every delaying response: "Have you *submitted*? Then you have received everything, for submission is the beginning of every acceptance." And the Prophet ﷺ, decreeing the same for his own community, compromised the exact grammar of verse 131 into his command to the bedouin, reported in the two Ṣaḥīḥs:

> *"Submit — *aslim* — and you are safe."* (al-Bukhari 7281; Muslim 133 — in response to the man asking for what saves)

*Aslim* to the Lord of the worlds: *aslamtu*; and commit no bet on the hesitation — the two words alone are the whole roll of the faith: Abraham heard and Abraham answered, and the garden of covenants began out of those five letters.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:132

> **This was the advice of Abraham—as well as Jacob—to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this faith; so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Bequest of the Fathers**

The submission Abraham had made became, at the end of his life, the last testament he handed down: *wa waṣṣā bihā ibrāhīmu banīhi wa yaʿqūb* — "and Abraham charged his sons with it, as did Jacob." The verb *waṣṣā* — to entrust a bequest — is the Book's term for the final, binding charges dying men make (cf. 4:12; 5:106): the patriarchs' will to their descendants was not land, not flocks, not the treasure of the valley — but *this* — *bihā*, "with her" — the feminine pronoun pointing to the word and way of the submission just defined in verse 131; Abraham's estate was *islām*. Jacob — Israel himself, Abraham's grandson — receives the same charge in the Book as an independent witness, that its substance come not from one grandfather's wishful memory but from the household of prophets across generations: the great chain of *waṣiyyah* — testament upon testament — delivering one religion from Abraham, to Jacob, to the Tribes, each father contracting upon the sons in the hour of his death: *yā baniyya inna Allāha iṣṭafā lakumu al-dīna fa-lā tamūtunna illā wa antum muslimūn* — "O my children: God has chosen for you the religion — so do not die except in submission."

**Chosen of Your Religion: the Election Notice**

The middle clause deserves a full pause: *inna Allāha iṣṭafā lakumu al-dīn* — "God has chosen for you the religion." The commentators unwrap its election-bearing grammar: the same root *iṣṭafā* that marked Abraham out at 2:130 ("We chose him") now falls upon *the religion chosen for his sons*: the choosing reaches the children through the way itself — the one God has selected for them and sealed with His own election; and the tradition learns from the clause the dignity of bearing Islam: compliance with it is not a self-invented allegiance it is a divinely chosen thing carried — God chose *this* religion for Abraham's children — the verse thereby overturns any notion that Islam is a little set of private postures: it is a divinely elected *dīn*, substantially the same as it was at the camel-train halts of the patriarchs, and only its modes of obligation are time-tailored by God's wisdom. The tradition also reads the charge at home: Abraham and Jacob did not *discourse* their children into the faith, but — as the word *waṣṣā* carries — *bound* them as a final command: the ḥadīth, with similar spirit, frames the believer's household obligation in everyday terms at the Prophet's own tongue:

> *"Command your children to pray at seven, and discipline them in it at ten"* (Abū Dāwūd 495; Aḥmad — graded *ḥasan*),

and — as the masters of the tradition never tired of reminding — the child is easier bound in his early days than after his skull has hardened in the school of the age: it is the dying duty of every parent to see to it that his children enter the next world in *muslimūn*.

**"Die Not Save in Submission"**

The verse's final clause became one of the most repeated deathbed injunctions of the entire religion: *fa-lā tamūtunna illā wa antum muslimūn* — "so do not die except while you are in submission." The commentators lay out its practical force: "die" is stated as the final particle of life: whatever one does before, the *end* belongs to submission — the clause enshrines what Islamic piety calls *ḥusn al-khātimah* (the good ending), thereby central to the ummah's ars moriendi: because the ending hour is the one carrying the final register of the soul, the daily question of a believer is not only *how do I live?* but *in what state might death find me at any hour?* — prayer-time, sin-time, iḥsān-time: every hour is a possible last hour; the Prophet ﷺ stated the doctrine of the end in the unequivocal ḥadīth of certainty:

> *"Every servant is raised up upon what he died upon."* (Muslim 2866; Aḥmad — *"kullu ʿabdin yabʿathuhu Allāhu ʿalā mā māta ʿalayh"*)

And another golden thread of the same qur'anic covenant is the Prophet's saying of the last words of the dying:

> *"Whose last words are *lā ilāha illa llāh* enters Paradise."* (Abū Dāwūd 3116; graded *ḥasan* — and in Muʿādh's account in Aḥmad, with details of the Prophet's instruction to remind the dying)

The verse has thereby defined the whole of Islamic religion at its two poles: the establishment of daily submission — *islām* as begun living — and the guardianship of its resting-hour: let no child of the patriarchs ever conclude in anything else — *fa-lā tamūtunna illā wa antum muslimūn.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:133

> **Or did you witness when death came to Jacob? He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?” They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers— Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac—the One God. And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**At the Bedside of Israel**

The Book summons its hearers to a scene no living reader attended: *am kuntum shuhadāʾa idh ḥaḍara yaʿqūba al-mawtu idh qāla li-banīhi mā taʿbudūna min baʿdī* — "or were you witnesses when death came upon Jacob, and he said to his sons: what will you worship after me?" The rhetorical question — *were you there?* — is among the sūrah's debating instruments that the commentators name with special notice (cf. 46:8; 19:98: "do you perceive any one of them, or hear from them so much as a whisper?"): it defends the historical truth told in the Book neither by tradition-custody alone nor by the disputants' archives, but by the God who was witness when no scribe stood; and it strips from the adversary the one ground he thought he held: private tribal memory. The setting is intensive with piety: Jacob — *Israel*, after whom the nation was named — on the bed of his passing, gathers his sons around him, twelve boys and the offspring of twelve, and asks not of their provision but of their worship; the primordial father interrogating the after-world over the shoulders of time: *what will you worship when I am gone?*

**The Sons' Creed: One God, and to Him We Submit**

The answer of the sons is the sūrah's sextain of the patriarchal creed delivered in one breath: *qālū naʿbudu ilāhaka wa ilāha ābāʾika ibrāhīma wa ismāʿīla wa isḥāqa ilāhan wāḥidan* — "we shall worship your God, and the God of your fathers, Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac — One God" — *wa naḥnu lahu muslimūn* — "and to Him are we submitters (*muslimūn*)." The commentators note the chain's theological precision: the sons name *Ishmael* — the uncle — *before Isaac*, and they name him *a father* of Jacob's line of faith, acknowledged by the verse itself as standing in the same creed: the Ishmael line is not a side-branch outside the promise, but stands *within* the creedal genealogy of the sons of Israel themselves, the same creed: *one God* — *ilāhan wāḥidan*: the word's indefiniteness deliberate, as the commentators long pointed: not "God," proper-nounized into a tribal patron — *the* God of Abraham — but God-as-God — deity as unity — *ilāhan wāḥidan* as a confession of abstract tawḥīd to be sealed against every subsequent tribalization. And the sons complete the creed exactly where verses 131–132 had stationed it: *and to Him are we muslimūn.* The entire debate of the sūrah with the two reading-communities is hereby sealed over the graves of the patriarchs: the community that calls Abraham's and Jacob's sons theirs has heard them say *muslimūn* — and the community whose Book tells the tale without that word has been reading its own creed back into the house of the prophets.

**A Testament for All Who Come After**

The spiritual tradition and piety of the Muslims raised this scene into one of the ars moriendi's master-icons: the dying man entrusting his pivots to his family — and *asking them*, so that the creed issue from their mouths and not from his: the Prophet ﷺ, approaching his own death, having fortified his house with the same succession of charges, left his community comparably bound with the book of God and his Sunnah in the farewell sermon at ʿArafah (al-Bukhari 375-76, 1650; Muslim 1218, 2950), and the tradition's custom has ever since been to gather at the bedside of the dying — reading Yā Sīn, reciting the shahādah — asking one another, in Jacob's spirit, in what state of submission they stand — and hearing from the children and grandchildren the same answer; and the believer attends in the deepest hour of the family estate: *not wealth, not lands, not fame — faith* — the only legacy to survive the grave, the one the patriarchal ancestors of the whole triad of communities knew — *yā baniyya, inna Allāha iṣṭafā lakumu al-dīn: we shall worship your God, the God of your fathers — one God; and to Him are we submissive.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:134

> **That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Boundary of the Generations**

After the deathbed scene of Jacob, the Book plants its celebrated gate-stone between the age of the patriarchs and every later claimant: *tilka ummatun qad khalat lahā mā kasabat wa lakum mā kasabtum wa lā tusʾalūna ʿammā kānū yaʿmalūn* — "That is a community that has passed away; theirs is what they earned, and yours is what you earned; and you shall not be questioned about what they used to do." The commentators (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī) identify the verse's elegant three-part settlement: first, *khalat* — "it has passed" — the patriarchal age is closed behind its own actors: Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes have crossed the bridge of their days and stand beyond our ballots; second, *lahā mā kasabat* — "to it what it earned" — their accounts travel with them, credits and debits set in their own sealed columns; third, *lakum mā kasabtum* — "to you what you earned" — your accounts likewise, opened separately, filled with the currency you yourselves mint. The word *kasaba* — to earn, to acquire — the commentators note with the full range of its Qur'anic freight: not only *gain* in the sense of profit but also *commit* in the sense of imputation: the soul is the earner of both its golds and its rusts, each entry credited to its earner.

**The Doctrine of Personal Accounts**

The corollary arrives in the final clause: *wa lā tusʾalūna ʿammā kānū yaʿmalūn* — "you shall not be asked about what they used to do." Al-Qurṭubī and the commentators mark it as the deliverance of the verse: responsibility across generations is *severed* at the ledger-level — the descendant bears no tribunal for his ancestor's sins, nor does he inherit a covenant-credit by the mere fact of descent. The verse thereby demolishes, in a single sentence, both the Jewish concept of inherited Israelite favor and any later Muslim temptation to rest in the glory of ancestors: *no community is saved by its genealogy.* The Book will sound the same doctrine at 6:164 ("no bearer of burden bears the burden of another") and at 53:38-39 ("that no soul laden bears the load of another, and that man shall have only what he strives for"), but the verse's setting amid the Abraham-controversy gives it its argument-sharpened edge: the ancestors cited as character-references — Abraham was neither Jew nor Christian — cannot serve as witnesses either way: *their* accounts are theirs, *yours* is yours, and the court will not ask the sons of Jacob whether their fathers were better than their fathers' sons were.

**Heritage as Argument, Not Alibi**

The verse is not, however, the erasure of heritage; the tradition has always distinguished the two uses of the past that this same sūrah makes mandatory: as *argument*, the old stories are load-bearing — the sūrah itself has just argued from the covenant at the Mount, the lengthy record of the cow, the destiny of Sabbath breakers; as *alibi*, history is refused — no son of a prophet is saved by his grandfather's blood, no descendant of sinners condemned by theirs; the ancestry supplies material to *reflect* on, never a verdict to *rest* on. And the sentence's phrase — *tilka ummah* — "that is a community" — receives frequent notice in the tradition as the Qur'an's consolatory way of doing the past: rather than rubbing the dead generations' wrongs across centuries (into perpetual recrimination against their descendants), the Book assesses them *there*, and instructs the living: you have accounts of your own to answer — *tend to them.* Ibn Kathīr's citation-verse of 5:105 in the parallel context abides as its canonical footnote:

> *"O you who believe! You have charge of your own souls; he who has gone astray cannot harm you if you are guided"* — the heresy of the patriarchs defunct by *khalat*: the present hours engaged to the verse's third column: *lakum mā kasabtum.*

**The Believer Facing Forward**

For the believing community the verse cures a double disease of the religious present: the unjust condemnation of one reading of scripture by the other communities' sons, and the unjust self-congratulation in the sons' own glory-story. Abraham was ḥanīf; his children's children — in covenant or in rebellion — are judged new at every sunrise: *yours is what you earned.* The Prophet ﷺ left the universal gate of this verse as explicitly open as the verse itself, in the famous line reported by al-Tirmidhī and others:

> *"All of Adam's children err, and the best of the errers are the repenters"* (al-Tirmidhī 2342; Ibn Mājah 4251 — *ḥasan*; already cited at 2:52) — the gate still open, the accounts still writing, the verdicts still possible — until the day the ver verdict-stamp falls: *you will not be questioned about what they used to do.*

Verse 134 thus plants between the Abraham-cycle and its extension at verse 141 the steadying rule: look back to harvest wisdom; look forward — the ink of *your* column is still wet.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:135

> **The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No! We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright—who was not a polytheist.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Competing Invitations**

The Book now records the two counter-invitations cast at the Muslims in Madinah: *wa qālū kūnū hūdan aw naṣārā tahtadū* — "and they said: become Jews or Christians, and you shall be guided." Al-Rāzī marks the scene's structure: this is not a joint profession of openness; each community was calling the Muslims to *its own* fold, presenting its own name as the sole gate of *hudā* — guidance — and the Book has already shown that the same two communities openly judged the other as *standing upon nothing* (2:113). Addressed separately, each call had a plausible force: "be Jews" came from the oldest house of covenant; "be Christians" from the most recent mission — each could summon scroll and genealogy. The answer God dictates is an eviction from both alternatives without even a moment's accommodation: *qul bal millata ibrāhīma ḥanīfan* — "Say: rather — the creed of Abraham, the Ḥanīf" — *wa mā kāna mina al-mushrikīn* — "and he was not of the idolaters."

**Ḥanīf: the Word Chosen to Name the Third Way**

The central term of the answer is one of the most beautiful words in the religious vocabulary of the Qur'an, *ḥanīf*, and the commentators and philologists cluster around it with unusual reverence. At root it carries *inclination* — a turning *toward* — but in the Qur'anic register it names the man inclined from all crookedness *toward the straight*, devoted to God and upright: "making his way sound toward God" — the lexicons and commentators variously glossing it *mustaqīm* (strait-standing), *qānit* (devoutly obedient), *muslim* (submitter), *hanīf* as the epithet that joins them all. In the pre-Islamic Hijaz the word already designated the religious nonconformists among the Quraysh who had refused idolatry before Islam arrived — men like Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl and others who said: *I take the creed of Abraham* — and the Book adopts the term to define Abraham's creed as the religion older than every later fracture: primal, unidolatrous, God-inclining, exactly the *fiṭrah* — the native disposition — that God had fastened into mankind and to which the same word is attached at 30:30: *"so set your face to the religion, ḥanīfan — the fiṭrah of God upon which He formed mankind."* Abraham's creed is thus identified with the very genetic code of religion, not with another brand among brands: God does not answer the two invitations with a *third* alternative of the same kind; He recovers the *original* of which both alternatives are subsequent modifications.

**"He Was Not of the Idolaters": The Line of Exclusion**

The final clause — *wa mā kāna mina al-mushrikīn* — *"and he was not of the idolaters"* — seals the answer by excluding the one trait that would dissolve God's whole pedagogy: whatever the two contestants add to Abraham — sonship-claims, angel-daughters, calves, triads — they share, in God's word, the genus of *shirk*; and Abraham — the man who told his people at 6:79, *"I have turned my face to He who created the heavens and the earth, ḥanīfan — and I am not of the idolaters"* — is God's own counter-example to every such add-on. The tradition reads this verse together with 3:95 and 4:125 and 16:123 — the Book's consistent pattern of framing Islam as *the creed of the Ḥanīf Abraham* — and notes that the Prophet ﷺ himself cited the same credential of his call from its very first day, in the tradition of ʿĀʾishah at the start of descent of revelation:

> *"Never did the Prophet ﷺ suspect any rite was better than the one he called to... he never bowed to any idol in his life"* — with Waraqah ibn Nawfal's certification as the early recognizer: *"this is the Nāmūs sent down upon Moses"* (al-Bukhari 3, 4953, 6982; Muslim 160 — the canonical reports of revelation's beginning, always read beside 2:135 by the tradition).

**The Answer That Matures Every Later Temptation**

Verse 135 thereby gives the ummah its standing answer for every age: *lā hūdan, lā naṣārā — bal millata ibrāhīma ḥanīfan.* Neither tribal creed nor imperial creed — but the creed of the father, sound, unbent, endlessly renewed: and the firm exclusion clause teaches its delicate double duty: toward the people of the Book — *respected inheritors of Abraham through our scripture's own account* — yet toward their shirk-elements and the shirk-elements of every age: *he was not of the idolaters* — so neither are we. The believer in every generation stands at the same fork with the same reply prayer-shaped by Ibrahim's own invocation at Sūrah 12 and Sūrah 60:

> *"My Lord, make me firm upon Your religion... I have turned my face to You; I am the first of the submitters — and I am not of the idolaters."* (cf. 6:79; 6:162-63 — Abrahamic-path phrases sealed into the Prophet's own prayer)

“Say — rather the creed of Abraham, ḥanīfan": the standing answer, at every subsequent gate of religion-history, for all who count themselves Abraham's millah to the last day.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:136

> **Say, ˹O believers,˺ “We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us; and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants; and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and other prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them. And to Allah we all submit.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Believers' Creed Announced**

God now directs His Prophet and the community to *say* — openly, heraldically — the answer to the exclusivist calls of verse 135, in a creed-verse that would echo at the sūrah's close (2:285): *qūlū āmannā bi-llāhi wa mā unzila ʿalaynā wa mā unzila ʿalā ibrāhīma wa ismāʿīla wa isḥāqa wa yaʿqūba wa'l-asbāṭ* — "Say: we believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us, and in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes" — *wa mā ūtiya mūsā wa ʿīsā wa mā ūtiya al-nabiyyūna min rabbihim* — "and in what was given to Moses and Jesus, and in what the prophets were given from their Lord" — *lā nufarriqu bayna aḥadin minhum wa naḥnu lahu muslimūn* — "we make no distinction among any of them, and to Him we are submitters." The asbāṭ — the Tribes — al-Rāzī and the commentators explain as the twelve tribes of Israel from the twelve sons of Jacob, sibṭ carrying the sense of *grandchild*; the creed thus reckons by families of prophets rather than by scrolls alone. The commentators note the exact inverse of the verse the sūrah had diagnosed at verse 85: the charge against the custodians there was *do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?* — here the believing community proclaims its wholeness: *all* of God's prophets, *all* of God's revealed gifts, without partition. The verse is placed on the believers' tongues by express command: it is the identity-creed of the ummah, spoken outward in a three-religion city that had just asserted two tribal counter-claims.

**"We Make No Distinction" — The Key Clause of Prophetic Equality**

The tradition fastens upon the creed's central weapon: *lā nufarriqu bayna aḥadin minhum* — "we make no distinction among any of them." The distinction condemned — as verse 285 will repeat — is the selective reception of prophets for reasons of tribe, era, or community: God sent them, and the believer refusals to sort them into accepted and rejected. The Book prohibits distinction *among them* while itself distinguishing them in rank *by God's own Word* — "these are the messengers: We preferred some of them over others" (2:253) — but rank belongs to God's assessment, and duty toward them to the believer's non-distinction: *each prophet asks no smaller measure of assent than the whole truth he brought.* The commentators cite in confirmation the large harmonizing verse 42:13: "He has prescribed for you as religion what He enjoined upon Noah, and what We revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: that you uphold the religion, and do not divide in it." And the press of verse 136 into Islamic doctrinal life is total: the articles-of-faith catechism — "faith is to believe in God, and His angels, and His books, and His messengers, and the Last Day, and the decree" from the Jibril-hadith at al-Bukhari/Muslim — was memorized in accordance with its own scriptural basis precisely here and at 4:136 and 2:285.

**Said by the Believers Every Day**

The spiritual tradition notices especially the opening of every clause in the first person plural: *āmannā — we believe — wa naḥnu lahu muslimūn — and we, to Him, are submitters:* the answer is not a dissertation but a *we*, the ummah presented as one body declaring its faith in the face of separate gate-claims. To say this verse following the Prophet's own daily recitation of the sūrah was, and remains, to recite the ummah's public confession, exactly as his Companions did after him; and the tradition records that the Prophet ﷺ heard its lines returned on the lips of his own community as the standard answer to the People of the Book, in one of the interchanges al-Bukhari preserves from the Madinan period:

> *"When the verse was revealed — 'say: we believe in God and what was sent down to us...' — the believers were commanded to say: we believe in God, and in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus, and in what the prophets were given by their Lord: we make no distinction between any of them — and they used to say it."* (al-Bukhari 4488; Muslim 28 — commentary in context of 3:84's same creed, widely cited under our verse by the mufassirūn)

Verse 136 thus supplies the creed-side of the millah-answer: the creed of Abraham repeated on the lips of Muslims is the *whole-undivided belief in all the prophets*: it is the answer, spoken every day since Madinah, to all who demand partition of God's messages.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:137

> **So if they believe in what you believe, then they will indeed be ˹rightly˺ guided. But if they turn away, they are simply opposed ˹to the truth˺. But Allah will spare you their evil. For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Like of Your Faith**

This verse as the linchpin of the whole Abraham-block measures the dispute's two possible outcomes against the creed the believers have just been given to say (v. 136): *fa-in āmanū bi-mithli mā āmantum bihi fa-qadi htadaw* — "if they believe in the like of what you believe in, they are guided indeed." The commentators take care with the word *mithl* — "the like of": not the sense that the object of faith admits comparison with God — the Book asserts *laysa ka-mithlihi shayʾ* (42:11) — but that the community of those called from the earlier Books *affirms the same truth-content* the Prophet's community affirms, a full and undivided confession like the creed just spoken: God, the prophets all, the revealed books all, and the Day all — or, as al-Rāzī allows, belief in the *undistorted* Torah and Gospel (the same *taḥrīf*-question at 2:75), which content would be "the like of" the Muslims' Book. The conditional thus fixes one standard: not *become Jews*, not *become Christians* — the two millah-claims collapse — but *affirm this same, whole faith*. Whoever comes over by that creed is guided as communities of faith; whatever community holds to less than that creed stays inside the line drawn by verse 85.

**And If They Turn Away: Schism Named, Sufficiency Promised**

The opposite branch follows with extraordinary consolation: *wa in tawallaw fa-innamā hum fī shiqāqin fa-sa-yakfīkahumu Allāh* — "if they turn away, they are only in schism — and God will suffice you against them." *Shiqāq* — cleavage, breach, from *shaqq*, to split — is the Book's deep diagnosis word: the turning-away isn't the fruit of superior knowledge; it is the condition of *split*: a cut between these people and the truth, between them and the believers, between them, in the end, and their own Book's testimony (cf. 22:53; 38:2; 41:52, where the same term recurs at the great boundaries of separation). The Prophet ﷺ and his community are thereby told to read rejection within a new map: the rift-lines are no longer drawn between party and party, believer and dissenter within a small community: they are drawn against God's own order — and so the burden of the confrontation is immediately transferred to the side it must be: *fa-sa-yakfīkahumu Allāh* — "God will suffice you against them." The verb *kafā* — to be sufficient, to fill the need, to discharge fully what is due — belongs to the Book's repertoire of assurances (3:173's "God suffices us"; 8:62; 9:59; 33:48): the commentators illustrate how God's sufficing had already worked between the lines of the Madinan struggle: His sustaining-restraint of the enemies' plotting (33:25), their confounded counsel at the Confederates, the providential retreats of the malevolent Jews of Madinah, all read by the tradition as the divine sufficiency assured at verse 137 made visible.

**The Names Sealed on the Suzerainty of Help**

The verse is sealed with the twin attributes of audit: *wa huwa al-samīʿu al-ʿalīm* — "and He is the Hearing, the Knowing." *Samīʿ*: the invitations, the offers, the negotiations, the whisper-device — all remain within His hearing; *ʿAlīm*: the motive-parts of schism — the envy at verse 90, the tribe-emptying at 140 — remain within His knowing. For the later believing community verse 137 establishes the rule by which the Prophet's ﷺ ummah has ever judged its disputes with bigger communities: the Muslim's duty is the clear proclamation of the *whole* creed (v. 136); the counterpart's fork — to accept its like, or to turn into shiqāq — is theirs; and the believer's peace over the outcome is not via anxiety but via the sovereign sufficiency named: *fa-sa-yakfīkahumu Allāh.* The tradition is rich with the Prophet's own praxis of the sufficiency clause; among many instances, at the fearful days before al-Khandaq and at the backlash against the Ḥudeybiyah hardship, the Prophet ﷺ would commit the whole case to this formula, praying aloud:

> *"O God, revealer of the Book, swift in reckoning, defeat the confederates; O God, defeat them and shake them."* (al-Bukhari 2933, 4115; Muslim 1742 — from Ibn Abī ʿAwfā's report of the siege of al-Khandaq)

And the verses of the Book had already pledged, in the days to come: *God will suffice you against them* — and He did, at the cost of the historic record that stands in all the books. Thus verse 137 closes the Abraham-block on its universal terms: the faith is issued wholly; those who accept its whole are entered into the guided path; those who split apart receive not an angry campaign but the name of their schism — and the believers receive quite simply the full sufficiency of their Lord.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:138

> **This is the ˹natural˺ Way of Allah. And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way? And we worship ˹none but˺ Him.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Coloring of God**

The verses of the Abraham-block now flower into one of the Book's most singular metaphors: *ṣibghata Allāhi wa man aḥsanu mina Allāhi ṣibghah* — "the baptism of God — and who is better than God in baptism?" — *wa naḥnu lahu ʿābidūn* — "and we are worshippers of Him." The central word *ṣibghah* derives from *ṣabagha*: to dip cloth into dye, to color a fabric through-and-through by plunging it, and the commentators unfold the term's reach with a reverence hardly otherwise shown. Al-Rāzī and the grammatical tradition gloss it *the coloring* of God, or *the religion* of God; al-Thaʿlabī's reading — the *fiṭrah*, the primordial nature with which God dyed human beings at their making — became the tradition's favored explanation, since the same word-family connects naturally with 30:30 — "the fiṭrah of God upon which He formed mankind" — and with verse 135's *ḥanīf*: both are the primordial configuration of the soul, delivered at its first weaving, prior to every later dye. The verse's phrase has thereby historically linked the two back into one: the baptism of God is the fiṭrah of God, the creed of Abraham is the fiṭrah-instituted creed — the religious life does not stain the fabric of the soul from outside but restores it to its *original color*.

**Baptism God-Given, Not Man-Given**

The commentators are explicit about the verse's positioning against the Christian rite whose name the Arabic still keeps: some, in the Madinan moment, see the wording as a measured answer to the cultivation of Christian baptism: the washing in water is of men; the true baptism — the coloring of the soul by God — is from God. And the question that follows — *wa man aḥsanu mina Allāhi ṣibghah* — "and who is better than God in baptism?" — places the rival dye-works side by side in open comparison, binding the two senses of the word (baptism as washing and baptism as coloring) into one devotional verdict: no rite nor sacrament by human hands matches the coloring that God hastens onto the soul itself at creation's loom and re-colors in the repentant believer at every return. The tradition extended the image in the mystics' way of reading: al-Sulamī's community describe the one whom God's dye has fixed as safe against every washing-off by the age: tribulations and societies wash daily at the soul's surface; but the fiber dyed by God at the root cannot be re-dyed: "Whoever bears God's ṣibghah — the world leaves his color unchanged."

**"And We Are Worshippers of Him" — the Sign of the Dyed Soul**

The clause completes the baptism's evidence: *wa naḥnu lahu ʿābidūn* — "and we — to Him — are worshippers." The critics inside the commentary tradition take care that the verse not be read as a slogan: the soul dyed by God evidences the color by the life of worship — *ʿibādah* — not by the profession of the dye. That joining — God's coloring completed in man's worship — makes the verse one of the tradition's most beloved capsule-definitions of religion entire: not a doctrine arrived at by wisdom-ascents alone but by *plunging* beneath God's own hand, and not a rite whose sign is emergence from water alone, but the whole conduct of *ʿubūdiyyah*: service lived out. The commentators standing with the Prophet's report understand the verse as having its action-form prescribed in the same diction of coloring God gives the soul: the shahādah itself — the confession formula by which the believer is dipped — together with all the prayers and pillars that make the color fast. The tradition reads all this as the full reply-dose of verses 135–136 to the twin millah-invitations of Madinah: our baptism is not your option-menu of sects; it is the dye God put into the unspoiled material of man *before* any choice between the millahs was ever conceived — and so the Book commands the saying with the declarative cadence this verse itself shows: *the ṣibghah of God; and who is better than God in ṣibghah? — and we are worshippers of Him* — thereby sealing the entire Abraham-unit in a sacred color the Book repeats daily on the tongues of believers: *God's dye, no other dye.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:139

> **Say, “Would you dispute with us about Allah, while He is our Lord and your Lord? We are accountable for our deeds and you for yours. And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**One Lord, No Room for Dispute**

The debate of verses 124–138 now reaches the sentence of recusal God puts on the Prophet's lips: *qul atuḥājjūnanā fī Allāhi wa huwa rabbunā wa rabbukum* — "Say: will you dispute with us *concerning God* — when He is our Lord and your Lord?" The commentators note the dismantling precision of the question. Disputation over religion proceeds, ordinarily, upon a claim that the deity to whom appeal is made is *ours* in a special way — the property of a millah; the verse cancels the presupposition at once: the God of Abraham — the very God invoked as their warrant by both Jews and Christians — is equally the Lord of the Muslims; whatever may divide the disputants, it cannot be *God*: He belongs indisputably to both sides. Whatever the rhetoric of tribal custody-myth, argument about God from a party on the pretext of ownership of God collapses at this arithmetic: *wa huwa rabbunā wa rabbukum* — He is our Lord *and* your Lord.

**Unto Us Our Deeds: the Demarcation of Works**

The verse then legislates the second demarcation after the demarcation of Lordship: *wa lanā aʿmālunā wa lakum aʿmālukum* — "unto us are our deeds, and unto you are your deeds." The Book is following the same ledger-law set down in verse 134 — each community earning its own register — but now fixes it *between* the contesting communities, drawing the line of judgment as one of conduct rather than of nomenclature. "Our deeds" points to the substance the believer must answer for; "your deeds" to the substance the adversary must answer for: the judgment that decides the *real* merit of the dispute will not be weighed with genealogies in the scales but with deeds. The third clause, in turn, takes the demarcation to its purest point: *wa naḥnu lahu mukhliṣūn* — "and *we* — unto Him — are sincere/oath-true." *Mukhliṣūn* comes from *ikhlāṣ*: the purification of worship from every adulteration — from tribal advantage, from party status (the People of the Book's *amānī*-economy), from display, from every second motive — until one's religion is God's alone. The commentators read in this clause the preferential self-description God Himself commands the believers to utter: *we* — unlike the tribe-counted faith — have only one customer for our Islam: *the One whom we and you both call Lord* — and to Him alone are our deeds sincere.

**The Tradition's Treatise of Ikhlāṣ, Built on This Clause**

The tradition never lets this verse go. The *muḥājj* — disputation — of verses 135–140 is made here to terminate not in the adversary's refutation so much as in the believers' self-assessment: the Prophet's ﷺ community re-read the verse's third clause as the standing question of their own piety: is our religion *sincere* — mukhliṣ — toward *Him*? The hadith-collection's foundational text of intention likewise stands behind this first chapter of every manual of devotion:

> *"Actions are but by intentions, and every person shall have but what he intended"* (al-Bukhārī 1; Muslim 1907 — from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb: *innamā al-aʿmālu bi'l-niyyāt*),

and Imam al-Nawawī's collection of forty traditions places it appropriately as the first of the forty; and the science of purification — that the act should ask for no second gaze — is articulated on this very verse by the Sufi writers from Sahl al-Tustarī and Junayd onward. The Prophet's supplications contain part of its practical school, in the treasury of the refuge-litanies reported at al-Tirmidhī and others:

> *"O God, I seek refuge in You from practicing shirk while knowing, and I ask Your forgiveness for what I do not know."* (Aḥmad, al-Ṭabarānī — the Prophet's famous *duʿāʾ al-shirk al-khafī*, corroborated across the tradition as part of the refuge-litany for hidden showing-off)

The tradition equally records the comfort for the hidden worker, so that the deed unseen is registered without audience: *"Conceal your charity as you conceal your sins"* (cf. the believer-counsels of the Salaf at this verse and 2:271): the stripping of audience — *naḥnu lahu mukhliṣūn* has to pass no tribunal but God's.

**Dispute Terminated at the Same Lord**

The practical liturgy the verse teaches over every later religious debate is exact: one, not to get entangled in dispute *about* God as though God were a party's property; two, to draw the discussion always back into the partisan-free ground of deeds; three, to end the debate with its very end: *we are sincere to Him*: the community confesses itself into a purifying practice while reserving the judging of the other side to the same Lord — and let God's Day pronounce: sincerity shall be weighed, and deeds shall decide. In the Madinan context the verse functioned exactly so: it closed the barter-of-credentials offered in verses 113 and 135 ("the Jews say... the Christians say... be Jews or Christians") with neither answer-to-answer nor quarrel-to-quarrel, but the declaration of the only ground on which disputing communities can stand without quarreling about God: the ground of One Lord, separate ledgers, and sincerity toward Him alone. Thus the Abraham-block ends its polemic in the way Islam always chooses to end debates: *with the confessional of its own fidelity, and with God's Day as its court.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:140

> **Or do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants were all Jews or Christians?” Say, “Who is more knowledgeable: you or Allah?” Who does more wrong than those who hide the testimony they received from Allah? And Allah is never unaware of what you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Anachronism Exposed**

The Book now carries the argument of the Abraham-cycle to its decisive blow — a question whose mere asking annihilates it: *am taqūlūna inna ibrāhīma wa ismāʿīla wa isḥāqa wa yaʿqūba wa'l-asbāṭa kānū hūdan aw naṣārā* — "or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes were Jews or Christians?" The very phrasing makes the absurdist charge visible: these men lived centuries before Moses, millennia before Jesus; the names Jew and Christian are themselves products of later history — *Yahūd* from Judah son of Jacob and the southern kingdom, *Naṣārā* from Nazareth in Galilee — so that to call Abraham a Jew, or Isaac a Christian, is to dress genealogy in clothes that had not yet been woven. The parallel at 3:65–67 spells the same logic for every hearer: "The Torah was not sent down nor the Gospel until after him — will you not understand?... Abraham was neither Jew nor Christian, but rather a *ḥanīf*, a *muslim*, and he was not of the idolaters." The tradition has always treasured verse 140 as the most elegant refutation of retrojective religious branding: *the prophets are not the property of the denominations erected after them.*

**"Do You Know Better, or Does God?"**

Then the second sentence of the verse delivers the epistemological verdict: *qul a-antum aʿlamu am Allāh* — "Say: do you know better — or does God?" The commentators point out that the Book does not here merely counter-assert the patriarchs' true creed (it has already done so at verses 131–133); it removes the whole file from the claimants' archives: if the people with scriptures claim the patriarchs, the Book's own question collapses the epistemic frame — no historical tradition of theirs reaches those generations with any authority; only God's own verbal witness reaches them, and He *has* witnessed: they were neither; they were ḥanīf-muslims. The same epistemic question stands at the root of the tradition's doctrine of evidence (v. 111's *bring your proof*): the contested ground of sacred history belongs to God's testimony; what isn't in His knowledge, no tribe-claim can cover.

**Concealing a Testimony from God**

The verse closes with the universalized sentence that has echoed far beyond the debate in Madinah: *wa man aẓlamu mimman katama shahādatan ʿindahu mina Allāh* — "and who does greater wrong than one who conceals a testimony he has in keeping from God?" *Shahādah* — testimony — as the commentators read it (Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī alternately): either the testimony God Himself bore in the earlier scriptures — that the patriarchs were pure monotheists, and that a prophet like Moses' description would come — which the custodian-scholars held in their copies and concealed (so their hiding is not ignorance but suppression, and thus ẓulm par excellence); or, by light extension, the Muslims' own scripture-born testimony concerning God's truth, which to conceal is likewise a wrong of the first degree. Either way, this verse became one of the central Islamic texts legislating the *illegality of religious suppression*: to sit on evidence concerning God, while bidding men talk of God — the commentators lay out how the verse's question-form (*who does greater wrong...?*) marks its crime as maximal among the wrongs the moral sense can size: witness-sitting is not silence; it is *theft from the court of truth*. The tradition speaks of it through the hadith of deliberate misdirection:

> *"Whoever is asked about knowledge and conceals it, God will bridle him with a bridle of fire on the Day of Resurrection."* (Abū Dāwūd 3658; al-Tirmidhī 2649 — regularly cited by the mufassirūn under this verse among the laws of testimony)

**"God Is Not Heedless" — The Closer That Judges Every File**

And the ending of verse 140 restores the sūrah's most severe formula once more (2:74, 2:85): *wa mā Allāhu bi-ghāfilin ʿammā taʿmalūn* — "and God is not heedless of what you do" — the same words that stood at the end of the cow-story and of the partial-believers' indictment now standing over the whole Abraham file: concealment is of no avail where no file is closed; the Lord is the unforgetting Auditor of every scroll's every reading. Together verses 135–140 thereby accomplish the full counter-position of the Abraham-cycle: the creed of Abraham (*ḥanīfan*, not Jew nor Christian), the believers' whole-covenantal creed (v. 136), the two branches of schism or guidance (v. 137), the true baptism (v. 138), the one-Lord disavowal of disputation (v. 139), and the patriarchs' release from posthumous branding (v. 140) — so that verse 141 can now re-plant its central axis of "that is a community that has passed away," as the section closes with the second planting of its Shibboleth of judgment from verse 134.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:141

> **That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verse Planted Twice**

The sentence of verse 134 returns — verbatim — to close the Abraham block exactly as it had closed the scene of Jacob's deathbed: *tilka ummatun qad khalat lahā mā kasabat wa lakum mā kasabtum wa lā tusʾalūna ʿammā kānū yaʿmalūn* — "that is a community that has passed away; theirs is what they earned, and yours is what you earned, and you will not be questioned about what they used to do." The commentators note the framing's purpose: the Abraham cycle began at verse 124 with the trial and the imamate, and on both sides of its roll of patriarchs — Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Tribes — the Book erects the same identical fence: *look back, harvest the wisdom; but no account travels except its own.* At verse 134 the fence had closed the scene of Jacob's charge to his sons; here it closes the entire debate over their identity: since neither Jew nor Christian can claim the patriarchs by name (the patriarchs had passed away before the two names were born), and since no one will stand trial for another's deeds anyway, the whole genealogical franchise is doubly voided — first by anachronism, second by the law of personal accounts.

**Its Twofold Emphasis for the Two Readers**

The tradition reads the repetition as a deliberate doubling of the lesson upon both poems of the audience. To the People of the Book, who defended their community by their lineage, the verse is spoken as the closing of the argument: Abraham was ḥanīf, and they have no share in the quality of his deeds unless they share his creed — and "you will not be questioned about what they used to do" means equally "their righteousness will not cover your rejection." To the Muslims — the third community descending in faith from the same Abraham — it is spoken as the standing caution: *you too* will not be judged by Abraham, nor by Muḥammad ﷺ, nor by the sixty-two repeated promises of paradise to believers prior; you will be judged by *what you earned* — and the verse shapes the Muslim community's self-description at its very origin as a community *working out its own ledger*, freed precisely by inheritance from the temptation of charter-righteousness. The Prophet ﷺ confirmed the discipline in a word reported from Abū Hurayrah by al-Bukhari and Muslim:

> *"If God wills good for a servant, He puts him into action." — It was said: How does He put him into action? He answered: "He guides him to righteous work before death."* (al-Tirmidhī 2142 — *ḥasan*; in the same form-class as the Prophet's standing instructions that the ledger is closed at the deed, not at the blood-line)

**A Gate Left Standing at the Cycle's End**

In the architecture of the sūrah, the repeated verse serves as the architrave of the whole Abraham panel (vv. 124–141): Abraham has been secured for the universal religion; the tribes have been located with their prophets; the two competing communities have been answered; and the believers' creed (v. 136), baptism (v. 138), sincerity (v. 139) and testimony (v. 140) have been sealed in God's court. The ending twin-verse, planted at both its pillars, frames all of this within the one permanent roadway: *you are a community passing through — like them — and your record is inked by your own hands.* The tradition's preachers so often read the verse at funerals and in exhortations because it pronounces the solitary dignity of the individual believer among all these great names: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob — all passed; *your* scroll is open *now*. With verse 141's exact planting, the sūrah shuts the door on the Abraham-file — *you won't answer for them* — and turns its page to the great transition of the qiblah, in which the believing community is about to receive its own orientation — open-eyed before the God who has ever judged men by questions no genealogy can answer.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:142

> **The foolish among the people will ask, “Why did they turn away from the direction of prayer they used to face?” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “The east and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah. He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"What Has Turned Them?" — The Taunt Arrives**

With this verse the sūrah opens the qiblah transition — and the Book chooses to begin, not with the legislation of the change, but with the talk the change would provoke: *sa-yaqūlu al-sufahāʾu mina al-nāsi mā wallāhum ʿan qiblatihimu allatī kānū ʿalayhā* — "the fools among the people will say: what has turned them away from their qiblah that they used to follow?" The commentators establish the background: the Prophet ﷺ, after the Hijrah, prayed toward Jerusalem for a period (the reports vary between thirteen and twenty months; most mention sixteen or seventeen) — the qiblah of the Jews of Madinah — while his heart longed for the House of Abraham. The Book, before recording the longing and the turn (v. 144), plants the opposition's jeer in advance so that the sūrah itself is the first to speak of it. The speakers are named *al-sufahāʾ* — *the fools*: al-Ṭabarī records the taunt's several authors — the hypocrites asking "what is wrong with you, that you have a qiblah and then change it?"; the Jews saying "Muḥammad longs for his homeland — had he stayed with our qiblah we would have thought him the one we await"; the pagans of Makkah saying "Muḥammad has wavered in his religion" — every faction framing the same small-mindedness in its own dialect, and the Book summarizing all of them under one adequate name: of what truth do these taunters carry a key, that they measure God's directing by the direction taunted?

**"To God Belong the East and the West"**

God's dictated answer is the very phrase already carved at verse 115; now applied with full legal weight: *qul li-llāhi al-mashriqu wa'l-maghrib* — "Say: to God belong the East and the West." The commentators nail the doctrine: no direction is holy in itself — not Jerusalem, not Makkah — but direction becomes the qiblah *because God appoints it*; His command sanctifies the place, never the place His command. The objection's whole energy ("they changed direction!") thereby dissolves: if the East and the West are God's, obedience to His appointment while facing any direction is the same obeisance — the qiblah is wherever God turns the face. Al-Rāzī takes the verse as knocking out at its root the essentialist assumption that a spot of earth can be *intrinsically* worship's direction — and the tradition's jurists point out that Islam's own fiqh ratified the lesson forever: the command of the direction is a *statute*, not a tenant of the land; and the verse replies to the taunters not with an argument about geography at all, but with the divine sovereignty over all the compass-points.

**Obligations and Their Changes**

The transition the word *will say* introduces is also the first of the sūrah's great confirmations of the same doctrine God had announced at 2:106 — the abrogation or replacement of rule by rule. The commentators are agreed that the qiblah change belongs to the core examples of *naskh* in the science: Jerusalem prayed toward, then Makkah — and the question-answer frame of verse 142 defends not the *development* (God knows what He is doing from all eternity) but the *submission*: the same worshippers who turned at God's word toward Jerusalem will turn at God's word toward the Kaaba — and believers bow before *both* statutes because both proceed from the same Command. The Prophet ﷺ lived the verse's practicality the day the reply became sunnah: in the middle of the afternoon prayer at the tribe of Banū Salimah, the congregation turned mid-ṣalāh at a caller's cry from the new-heeling and completed the prayer toward Makkah — that mosque still named, as the source records, *Masjid al-Qiblatayn*, the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs — the most literal living monument to the doctrine of verse 142: *there is no qiblah but God's facing.*

**"He Guides Whom He Wills"**

The verse closes with the creed of guidance: *yahdī man yashāʾu ilā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm* — "He guides whom He wills to a straight path." The commentators note the answer doubly barbs the taunt of the fools: first, the guide of the community is not the qiblah but God; He guided the believers to Jerusalem and guided them on to Makkah, by deed of His choice, not of their wandering; second, the straight path's *straightness* is measured not by any meridian of earth but by the Guide's appointment: the same God who makes the ant's tiny path straight across the wall and the star's vast circuit true across the sky knows what direction His worshippers should face — and in every age the faithful of many cities, unable to determine the direction mathematically, have been reassured by the liberal tradition of this law: *"what lies between the east and the west is qiblah"* (al-Tirmidhī 342, Ibn Mājah 1011 — guidance reports of the Salaf cited at this verse by the mufassirūn): direction as precision-burden is released; direction as obedience stays: *God is the East and the West — and He guides whom He wills to a straight path,* just as He guided a handful of poor emigrants, facing each other beneath a roof of spread cloaks at noon in Madinah, to the House of their father Abraham by word of their faithful caller from a far tribe, mid-prayer, with every tongue ready and every eye turned the same way, at once.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:143

> **And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community so that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you. We assigned your former direction of prayer only to distinguish those who would remain faithful to the Messenger from those who would lose faith. It was certainly a difficult test except for those ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah. And Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith. Surely Allah is Ever Gracious and Most Merciful to humanity.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Middle Nation Named**

In the very architecture of the qiblah transition, the sūrah plants the ummah's signature-line: *wa kadhālika jaʿalnākum ummatan wasaṭan li-takūnū shuhadāʾa ʿalā al-nāsi wa yakūna al-rasūlu ʿalaykum shahīdā* — "and thus did We make you a middle community (*wasaṭan*), that you may be witnesses over mankind, and the Messenger a witness over you." The commentators explain *kadhālika* — "thus" — as tying the naming to three possible analogues: just as the Kaaba is the world's center, so are you the middle people; just as We appointed the qiblah, so too We appointed your rank; just as We guided you, so too We made you *middle*. The Prophet ﷺ himself glossed the word in the tradition: *wasaṭ* here means **ʿadl** — *just* — and the commentators supply why: in the Arabic idiom the *middle* of the people is their choicest, and true justice dwells between every pair of extremes: courage between rashness and cowardice, generosity between prodigality and miserliness; between every legalism and every license the middle nation stands with its just balance. The apologists of the ummah through the centuries have read inside the naming a spiritual geography: between Judaism's accent upon law and Christianity's accent upon love stands Islam's proportion of both; between this world and the last stands its twin concern (the Prophet ﷺ prayed: "our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter"); and this *middle* ends in the figurehead of a witness: the community is balanced precisely so that it can be God's scale over the rest.

**Witnesses Over Mankind — and the Messenger Over You**

The tradition's great exposition of this clause lies in the ḥadīth of the Day of Witnessing, transmitted in al-Bukhārī from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, a passage the mufassirūn repeat at this verse without exception:

> *"Noah will be called on the Day of Resurrection, and he will say: Here I am, at Your service, my Lord. God will say: Did you convey the message? He will say: Yes. Then his people will be asked: did he convey it to you? They will say: No warner came to us. God will say to Noah: Who bears witness for you? He will say: Muḥammad and his community. And they will bear witness that he conveyed the message."* — and the Prophet ﷺ then recited: *"Thus did We make you a middle community, that you may be witnesses over mankind, and that the Messenger may be a witness over you"* (al-Bukhari 3339, 4487 — occasion-report expressly tied to 2:143 by Ibn Kathir and the mufassirūn)

— and the Messenger's witnessing over his own community stands on the same semantics — he will testify upon them, and his four-witness covenant was given the beautiful reported saying: *"God will cause to enter Paradise any Muslim for whom four witnesses testify"* — ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb asking "even three?" — "even three" — "even two?" — "even two" — "and I did not ask about one" (al-Bukhārī 7474; Muslim 2478 — however one grades its chain, the covenant of witnesses thereby belongs to this verse's architecture). The tradition thereby installs the *middle* quality into Islamic identity as an office of arbitration: to be *wasaṭan* is to be God's balancing-point, entrusted with testimony — living *witness* in the world in both directions of the Arabic noun's meanings: *being* a witness (giving account of God's religion truly to mankind) and *being witnessed* (made visible as God's living evidence before mankind), as al-Rāzī's register under our verse recites.

**Appointed Only to Distinguish**

Then the sūrah discloses the inner purpose of the entire qiblah episode: *wa mā jaʿalnā al-qiblata allatī kunta ʿalayhā illā li-naʿlama man yattabiʿu al-rasūla mimman yanqalibu ʿalā ʿaqibayh* — "and We appointed the qiblah you had been following only that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns on his heels." The commentators deal carefully with *li-naʿlama* — *in order that We may know*: as the kalām tradition notes, God's knowledge *already* comprehends the future; the verse's own counsel in the commentaries is that *to know* here means *to let be seen in time*: the fixed divine purpose was to give the community a *test in the open sky* in which followers would be distinguished from heel-turners *as public fact*, that God's verdict be made in the evidence of deeds rather than in His eternal foreknowledge alone. And the verse records the weight of the move: *wa in kānat la-kabīratan illā ʿalā alladhīna hadā Allāh* — "though it was a tremendous thing, except for those whom God guided" — the commentators observe from this verse the candor of the Book, striking in all religious history: the Lord openly calls the change — of liturgical habit, of direction, of long-disciplined posture — a *heavy thing*, and describes faithful flesh as finding struggle within it: a record no rival scripture sets on its own face, uttered in the same breath that confirms the change as God's own appointment.

**"God Would Never Let Your Belief Be in Vain"**

Then the verse's final mercy-clause sounds, the verse from which the tradition has drawn inexhaustible consolation: *wa mā kāna Allāhu li-yuḍīʿa īmānakum* — "but God would never let your belief go to waste." The commentators explain: the believers who had prayed toward Jerusalem and died before the change — as when some Companions tearfully asked: "what of our brothers who died facing Jerusalem?" — hear the answer: God does not waste *īmān*: the prayers prayed toward the old qiblah, in obedience while the old qiblah stood, are safe within the account. The master-commentators generalize the clause still further: *īmān* here is glossed *prayer*, by consensus of the salaf — and every prayer prayed in direction of obedience is refused no harvest by God: the verse was revealed to dry the eyes of the believers, crying over the buriers of the months of the old direction: God is not in the business of writing off true worship done during the term of an earlier command. Voluntary fasts kept, night prayers stood, pilgrimages walked — all are drought-proof here: *inna Allāha bi'l-nāsi la-raʾūfun raḥīm* — "Truly God is, toward mankind, Kind and Merciful": the Names closing the verse are themselves chosen for tenderness — *Raʾūf* the extreme of mercy, *Raḥīm* the grain of it — and the tradition repeats from this clause the standing comfort of a ummah that has passed through every era's qiblah-pivots together: *no sigh obeying God's direction is ever lost: God wastes no heart-turn, no facing, no prostration done in the right moment at the right word of His Messenger.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:144

> **Indeed, We see you ˹O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven. Now We will make you turn towards a direction ˹of prayer˺ that will please you. So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque ˹in Mecca˺—wherever you are, turn your faces towards it. Those who were given the Scripture certainly know this to be the truth from their Lord. And Allah is never unaware of what they do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"We Have Seen the Turning of Thy Face": God's Watcher-Speak**

The verse opens with an intimacy the commentators never cease to treasure: *qad narā taqalluba wajhika fī al-samāʾ* — "We have seen your face's turning in the heaven." Over months at Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ — praying toward Jerusalem at God's earlier command — would gently raise his face toward heaven, waiting, yearning, hoping for the word that would turn him toward the House of his father Abraham; and God recorded that He *saw* the yearning: the Watching Creator, as it were, speaks in the Prophet's own register of filial tenderness — *We see your glancing* — before granting the prayer. The commentators hear in it the pledge that no pious yearning of the righteous messenger goes unnoticed: the One with the sight of the eyelid's least flutter has been watching the face of the Most Honored all along, and declares it in a verse preserved to the Day of Resurrection.

**"A Qiblah Thou Shalt Love"**

God then grants the wish with exactness of fit: *fa-la-nuwalliyannaka qiblatan tarḍāhā* — "We shall surely turn you toward a qiblah you will delight in" — *fa-wallī wajhaka shaṭra al-masjidi al-ḥaram* — "so turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wheresoever you are, turn your faces toward it." The commentators record the granting's tenderness: the qiblah is appointed not barely as a duty but as a *delight* — *tarḍāhā* — tailored to the Prophet's own native longing: the Kaaba of Abraham and Ishmael, of whose valley the Prophet's city is built, of whose lines his own blood carries. *Shaṭr* — "toward, in the direction of" — the Arabic-speaking commentators explain, means the precise *facing* — establishing, as the jurists developed it, the exactness of fore.direction for those in Makkah itself and the line-following elsewhere in the world: the direction for every community of prayer is set from the Kaaba's own location outward. From this verse grew one of the tradition's most subtle intellectual disciplines — the qiblah-calculation of Islamic astronomy and geometry, in which mathematical astronomers down the millennium labored over the minutiae of great-circle bearings from every city on earth, the jurists accepting approximation at distance while requiring exactness in proximity to the House — with the old maxim of the scholars, "between the east and the west is qiblah" (already mentioned at 2:142), covering the less certain cases.

**The People of the Book and the Fit Between the Houses**

The verse closes by reading the secret of the change itself into the record of the earlier scriptures: *wa inna alladhīna ūtū al-kitāba la-yaʿlamūna annahu al-ḥaqqa min rabbihim* — "and those who have been given the Book indeed know that it is the truth from their Lord." The commentators report what this knowledge meant in Madinah: the descriptions in the Torah and the prophecies of the awaited Prophet included his orientation toward the Kaaba — the ancient creed of Abraham — so that the change of qiblah was itself part of the recognition-mark: the new Prophet would restore the House his father built; and the sages of the People of the Book who assessed Muḥammad ﷺ could verify his truth from the qiblah itself (among the sign-points by which some scholars were said to recognize the fulfillment). The verse thus turns the change from a domestic ordinance of the fledgling community into a sign-credential of the Prophet's mission; and the seal of the verse returns its formula from verse 140: *wa mā Allāhu bi-ghāfilin ʿammā yaʿmalūn* — "and God is not heedless of what they do" — watchful over the response of friend and foe alike.

**The Longing That Shapes the Qiblah**

The spiritual tradition has always treasured the verse as the account of a *watchful Lord granting a longing heart*: the Prophet's turning of his face, scanning the sky, is the visible posture of every servant who feels the pull toward God's House in his prayers — and the verse reveals his answer did not arrive by decision-taking but by gift. Al-Qushayrī captures the heart of its teaching: God saw His Beloved's gaze lift, and He couldn't hold him waiting — the divine *qad narā* — "We have seen" — has ever since taught the faithful that the Lord of the Throne watches the smallest movement of His servants' faces toward Him: no glance is lost, no sighing for the House unseen. When the believers, in every age since, line their city's streets and raise their hands — turning *shaṭra al-masjidi al-ḥaram* — the orientation itself re-enacts the original moment: a face turned where God was pleased to turn it, from the first day the verse came down on the emigration's first year at the mosque of Banū Salmah, at noon — and the faithful turned, already in mid-prayer, toward the House.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:145

> **Even if you were to bring every proof to the People of the Book, they would not accept your direction ˹of prayer˺, nor would you accept theirs; nor would any of them accept the direction ˹of prayer˺ of another. And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, then you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Every Sign Would Not Suffice**

The verse states the impossibility of satisfying the recalcitrant neighbors with evidence — *wa la-in atayta alladhīna ūtū al-kitāba bi-kulli āyatin mā tabiʿū qiblatak* — "and even if you brought those who were given the Book *every sign*, they would not follow your qiblah." The commentators set this with the sūrah's long-established diagnosis of active rejection (2:75, 2:108): the sticking-point was never a sign-deficit; the People of the Book knew, as verse 144 said, that the qiblah came from God — but knowing never gets past a heart resolved against following; God will not multiply signs among those whose prior verdict is already fixed, for the sign-inventory serves to confirm the believer, not to engineer the rebel. To the Prophet ﷺ the clause serves the exact consolation given at 2:118/119: *you are not accountable for the refusal of those who have decided to make their own will the criterion* — not even an unlimited budget of signs would change them.

**The Qiblah Compass as a Sign of Separated Ways**

The verse then untangles the whole geometry of the dispute, in a statement whose precision the commentators treat as one of the Book's least-noticed masterpieces: *wa mā anta bi-tābiʿin qiblatahum wa mā baʿḍuhum bi-tābiʿin qiblata baʿḍ* — "and you are not a follower of their qiblah, nor are they followers of one another's qiblah." Three propositions are laid out: the Prophet ﷺ does not follow *their* qiblah (the Jerusalem of the Jews); *they* do not follow *each other's* qiblah — the Jewish-Christian division on direction itself betraying that "their qiblah" is not even one qiblah: Jerusalem for the one, the East for the other (for the Christians of the region prayed toward the rising sun); and the only one left for the Prophet — the Kaaba — is the qiblah where the whole matter is *converged* upon God's own appointment. The neatness of the proposition — even the accusing parties don't agree among themselves — is quietly turned by God into the sign of a truth not acquired by the wind of whichever neighbor's fashion: in the face of their disagreement, the Prophet is not to gravitate toward any of the contestant directions, but only toward the House the change-verse of 2:144 established.

**"After the Knowledge That Has Come to Thee"**

Then comes the severest second-person address of the entire passage: *wa la-ini ittabaʿta ahwāʾahum baʿda mā jāʾaka mina al-ʿilmi innaka idhan la-mina al-ẓālimīn* — "and were you to follow their caprices after the knowledge that has come to you — you would then be among the wrongdoers." The commentators note again that the conditional is honorific-address — the Prophet ﷺ, by God's promise (5:67), would never follow the caprices — with the universal lesson built upon the impeccable example: if *the Prophet* following *hawā* after knowledge would be *ẓālim*, how much less safe is any lesser claimant? The complement of *hawā* and *ʿilm* is the same as at 2:120: furnished knowledge from God's descent, followed *after* by subjective solutions patched to the pattern of the age — the constant danger of a tempted religion, pressed at the borders it shares with the greater society of its time. The school of tafsīr often cites here the verse from the Prophet's own counsel to the community at large:

> *"The truest word the Arabs have is the verse at the end of Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ: *'And that the poets, the perverse follow them — do you not see that they wander in every valley, and that they say what they do not do? — save those who believe and do righteous deeds...'* " (Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī — al-Bukhari 3360 — the Prophet reciting 26:224–227 on the teaching of *hawā* against *ʿilm*, classically cited beside 2:145 by the fiqh-and-tafsīr tradition on the boundary between following and being led)

**The Believer's Definite Qiblah**

The spiritual commentary of the tradition has always applied verse 145 at the heart of the worshipper: God has set you a definite direction — refuse every wind. The *hawā*-crossings are perennial features of every religious life: the age's own qiblah, the majorities' drift, the minor schisms (whose directions, like the communities of Madinah, disagree even among themselves) — the believer's remedy is the same God's-tracked phrase: *innaka idhan la-mina al-ẓālimīn* — the self becomes *ẓālim* the moment it delays God's appointment for anyone else's caprice. Every believer is commanded to shake away the *other directions* entirely from the heart, so that — as the Sufi commentators put it — *God's qiblah and the worshipper's gaze may coincide, in the city of truth, in one direction* — and the verse stands in the tradition's teaching as the final fencing of the divine appointment's distinctness: *no qiblah shared, no following-thereafter of caprices; the believer's facing is sound only by God's own directed word.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:146

> **Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children. Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Recognition as Sure as a Father's of His Child**

Following the claim of the qiblah's vindication, the Book states the degree of recognition the People of the Book possessed of the Prophet ﷺ himself: *alladhīna ātaynāhumu al-kitāba yaʿrifūnahu kamā yaʿrifūna abnāʾahum* — "those to whom We gave the Book recognize him as they recognize their own children." The commentators unfurl the weight of the comparison: a father's recognition of his own sons is not inference — it is the most immediate, undoubtable knowledge a man has: upon sight, without hesitation, without confusion over resemblances. The verse thus testifies from Heaven that the learned of the People of the Book, who possessed the descriptions of the awaited Prophet in their scriptures (7:157: "whom they find written in what they have of the Torah and the Gospel"), knew him with first-person certainty: scrutinizing his biography, his age, his character, his marks, they could not fail to place him correctly. Ibn Kathīr (and others of the tradition) preserves the famous corroboration from the historical reports: ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām — the most learned of Madinah's Jews before his Islam — said upon view of the Prophet: *"I knew him the moment I saw him more surely than I know my own son"* — the very identification this verse speaks of — and the accounts of his conversion are carried in the sīra and the tafsīr of this verse from al-Ṭabarī forward.

**The Tragedy of Recognition Concealed**

Then the Book immediately adds the heartbreak of its report: *wa inna farīqan minhum la-yaktumūna al-ḥaqqa wa hum yaʿlamūn* — "and yet a group of them conceals the truth while knowing it." Recognition did not crumble because of knowledge's lack but because of *katm* — deliberate concealment: the same word that ran through the sūrah's indictments of scribal conduct (2:42; 2:140; 2:159): there is a class among them who, with recognition fully equipped, still chose to sit upon the evidence.
