Al-Ṭabarī reads the qualification *farīqan* — *a party*, not *all of them* — as the verse's careful precision (the same qualification as at v. 100): the indictment in the sūrah is always of the *acting* concealment, never of the entire community; those among them who did the concealing are registered with God as the knowing suppressers, and the recognition nonetheless remained, in the tradition's memory, a living gate for every other learned man of their people. The famous record of scholars from among them who *did* translate recognition into confession — Salmān al-Fārsī from the Gospels, ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām from the Torah, the monk Baḥīrah from earlier — is preserved as the standing reason the sūrah always says *farīq* — a *group* — not *all.*

**Lessons for the Readers of Every Age**

The spiritual tradition mines this verse in two directions. In the first, it is a warning against trusting mere *recognition-power*: men can know by sure sight and still deny: the knowledge that does not flourish into surrender is — *kamā yaʿrifūna abnāʾahum* — a child-known shewn of its share of the Father's speech; and the concealed truth, though so carefully secreted, stands as the final witness against the conscience that hid it (2:140: "who does greater wrong than one who conceals a testimony from God?"). In the second, it is the solemn description of all who hold, without acting upon, God-given knowledge of the truth; and the tradition's counsel at this verse runs in al-Ghazali's word that the supreme danger of the learned is that they will know deeper than they act — the man recognizing truth while laying it under — as the case in this very verse becomes, in the end, the man whose own recognition voices the final verdict against himself at the Degree of deeds.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:147

> **˹This is˺ the truth from your Lord, so do not ever be one of those who doubt.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Shortest Completeness of a Counsel**

With the whole debate over the qiblah closed and the recognition of the readied work laid down, the sūrah turns inward with the briefest of stressings: *al-ḥaqqu min rabbika fa-lā takūnanna mina al-mumtarīn* — "the truth is from your Lord — do not, then, be among the doubters." The commentators note the verse's striking economy: no polysyllabic elaboration, no subordinate arguments; a declarative and an imperative, tied together as one mental act. Forenamed of truth is its very sufficiency for the Prophet's address — it is from *your Lord*: the Lord who answered the face-turning, granted the Kaaba at its longing, rendered the Taunt and the question of the fools futile in the verses just past — He is the truth's postmark, against the fools' taunt, the millah invitations, the doubters' reasoned suspension, and the Not-Understood verdict: *every* witness of the whole tract proclaims the signature of the same Sender.

**Lā Takūnanna: The Prohibition of the Twin-Grid**

"Do not be among the doubters" — *mumtarīn*, those of doubt (*miryah*) — is built with the strongest prohibition form in the language — the *lā* of emphatic veto within a doubled assurance, the musajjal of absolute injunction — and the commentators build from it the normative rules of Islamic certainty: externally, do not join the company of those whose piety is at work only among clouds of air-testing (the same verse echoes at 3:60: "the truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters" after the controversy over Jesus; and 11:17; 29:68 — the same voice standing at many summits of the Book); internally, do not become one of them in your own heart. For doubt, the masters of certainty in the tradition explain, is of two families: doubt of the intellect *suspended* before evidence — natural in the seeker before finding, and forgiven by the arrival of truth — and doubt of the will *protected* against evidence — the disease of the recalcitrant for whom no amount of readiness-from-evidence suffices, because their refusal is a difference not of proof but of stance. The believer is forbidden *this* doubt, and taught its opposite: *yaqīn* — certainty — two verses before and eleven chapters after, the same praise-signature being repeated of the People of Certainty: "We made clear the signs for a people who are certain" (2:118) — certainty being the signature verse at the end of the whole intellectual passage.

**The Prophet's Confidence as the Ummah's Rule**

Since the injunction is addressed, in its surface, to the Prophet ﷺ — for whom doubt was never to be supposed — the tradition has always read the verse as the standing promise that when the Lord issues truth, His servant passes beyond the mere private certainty into the authority of it — as the ḥadīth oft-quoted by the mufassirūn at such verses has already made the ritual point in the tradition:

> *"None of you believes until what I have brought is dearer to him than his family, his wealth, and all the people."* — and: *"I have left to you what if you hold to, you will never go astray — the Book of God."* (Muslim 44, 2408 — part of the famous definitions of faith and certainty; classically cited whenever the sūrah or 2:285's *ṣadaqna* formulas occur at their word-to deed crossings)

If the Prophet himself must be commanded *not to doubt* the truth that was descending, the community behind him — reading his prophetic steadiness — receives its standing counsel as a supplication of gratitude of its own: *my Lord, anchor us in Your truth; make us not among the doubters.* So the believers read verse 147 as the epigraph of their certainty: *It is from your Lord; it is beyond the suspending shift of any He in front of a taunt* — and with that footing, step forward from the qiblah transition into the next revealed charge: turn steadfast, like one upon a straight path, with no deviation of doubt behind.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:148

> **Everyone turns to their own direction ˹of prayer˺. So compete with one another in doing good. Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together ˹for judgment˺. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Each Has a Wijhah"**

The sūrah closes the geometry-talk of directions with the most elegant summary: *wa likullin wijhatun huwa muwallīhā* — "and for every one there is a direction (*wijhah*) toward which he turns." The commentators lay out the several congruent readings (al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān): the *wijhah* may be orientation itself — every community oriented toward a facing, and the believers' facing is now the Kaaba by divine appointment — or, as al-Rāzī's school developed it, the *wijhah* of each soul is its *orientation-system*: every claim to religion, indeed every human being, has a *toward* to which it inclines — principled or corrupt — and the Book recognizes the outward plurality with inward severity: no *wijhah* is sacred by its practitioner's holding, only by the appointment it answers. The statement also checks the dispute of verses 142–146 in its final count: after all the talk of qiblahs, the Muslims are told that every tribe's compass-post is now beside the point — the race is elsewhere.

**Vie With One Another in Good Deeds**

Then the orienting verb transfers: *fa-stabiqū al-khayrāt* — "so vie with one another in good deeds" — *fastabiqū* (from which the old Arabic *sabaqa*, to outrun in a race): the Book directs the community of the believers, in the moment the compass-talk is concluded, to re-direct their competitive effort: not toward directions, not toward proof-points, nor toward counter-taunts, but toward al-khayrāt — the goods, deeds, efforts — each one racing the other *through* plain righteousness itself. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī make the normative rule from the phrase: since all directions may be argued over, God re-points the community into the race that cannot be argued: the one of *works-worship* — the fasts, the charities, the awakened wills — and so the entire qiblah dispute is closed not by final proof but by re-prioritization: the Muslim stops being provoked over directions long enough to surpass in goods.

**"Wheresoever You Are, God Will Bring You All Together"**

The verse's conclusion powers the race toward the one outcome that waits over all: *aynamā takūnū yaʾti bikumu Allāhu jamīʿan* — "wherever you may be, God will bring you all together" — and the commentators read in it the worldwide compass of the Judgement: no direction distances any from that assembly — not believers facing their Kaaba, "fools" at their taunts, recalcitrants in their barred files: *all* will be brought, from every part of the earth into one convocation, and the compass-rose made into a point. The clause seals the verse with its own signature-name: *inna Allāha ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr* — "truly God is powerful over all things" — the same formula that had answered the Millah-invitations in 2:20, 2:106, and now 2:148: for the God powerful enough to raise all scattered knees to one Day, the compass-directions of the earth are not obstacles — *wheresoever* they turn their faces, they will be brought, and on that Day neither argument over directions nor forgetting of deeds will rescue anyone among them.

**Ummah Building Through Fastabiqū**

The tradition never wore out verse 148's mandate. The school arrives through it at the deepest Islamic disciplines of *competitive good*: the Salaf read in its command the spending-race of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar (the latter resolved to out-spend the former, fell short, and learned the frankness of the moral pay-offs; the Prophet ﷺ judged: "no sun rises until Abū Bakr surpasses" — the narratives record in detail the spend-and-counterspend of the greatest two of the Companions, in al-Ṭabarī and the sīra), and likewise the standing race of the Companions in imān-secret, ṣalāt, ḥajj, dhikr: every Muslim is commanded to be *intentionally* behind no one in khayr — the verse excusing no standing rank at the back and excusing no boast at the front — *fastabiqū*: the race is *open*; in God's scoring it is always on — but the crown-chart of the race, the race's end-point is the unification God pronounces at the close of the verse: the Day when *all* will be gathered. The race is to be won in time, while all the scattered feet are still traveling across many directions, for no direction will slow the universal convocation ahead.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:149

> **Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. This is certainly the truth from your Lord. And Allah is never unaware of what you ˹all˺ do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Whencesoever Thou Goest Out"**

With verse 149 the sūrah re-issues the qiblah command in one of its most comprehensive formulations: *wa min ḥaythu kharajta fa-wallī wajhaka shaṭra al-masjidi al-ḥaram* — "from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque." The commentators read *min ḥaythu kharajta* in the fullest sense: from whichever place the Prophet ﷺ emerges — house, road, journey, land — the facing obligation is attached to him and, through the second-plural-form of verses 144, 149–150 read together (*wa ḥaythu mā kuntum fa-wallū wujūhakum shaṭrah*), attached also to every believer behind him. The phrase binds the direction of prayer to the believer across every transit: journey prayers, field prayers, prayer in stations and in hostels: God's appointment is universal, and the Kaaba becomes the single landmark constant across every terrain the believer crosses. The jurists derive cleanly from this verse and its companion the whole fiqh of direction: the duty is present even to the one who does not know where the House lies — the facing is at its appointed *shaṭr*, and the duty of every traveller is only the sincere effort at the facing; in al-Shāfiʿī's school and Ibn Ḥanbal's, the searching for evidence of the qiblah in lands far off — by stars, by contours, by localized knowledge of caravan-routes — became the broad discipline the ṣalāt-hadith's word "between the east and west is qiblah" culturalized (so the scholars of every land could legislate the facing).

**The Truth From Thy Lord**

The verse then announces the deep reason of the command: *wa innahu la'l-ḥaqqu min rabbik* — "and indeed it is the truth from your Lord." The formula binds the direction-burden to its all-important source: *the direction itself, now, is God's revealed truth* — not an accommodation, not a tradition, not a retrojection: *divine truth*. The commentators (al-Ṭabarī in particular) tie it to the truth-claim that the Book has made for itself at 2:147: the same *truth* that descends as verses, *the same truth* descends as directive: the command to turn is one form of the truth — *all* revelation is the truth of the Lord, and *this* one happens to face men toward a square stone sanctuary on earth. By such a narrative the Kaaba's centrality is sealed as revelation-truth inside Islam's creed — never merely as a regional landmark, nor a monumental conservatism.

**"God Is Not Heedless"**

And the verse's close adopts the formula-seal for the third time in the qiblah-block (2:85, 2:140, 2:144): *wa mā Allāhu bi-ghāfilin ʿammā taʿmalūn* — "and God is not heedless of what you do." The commentators note that the whole qiblah-manufacturer, with its passion over directions, is here held to the Judgment's scrutiny: facing is not for the earth-watching Yahūd, nor for the Naṣārā observers of minarets, nor for the careful churches: the Kaaba-ward turning is performed while remembering *God sees* — and the verse which appoints the direction itself fixes, by its very seal, the direction of the heart above the direction of the body: God is not heedless of the turning, of the yearning, of the obedience shown between both — and since it is toward the truth from the Lord that the flesh turns in prayer, the straight and the crooked in the *directions* receive no verdict but from the *unheedless* God. With verse 149, the twofold appointment has been certified behind its formula of Truth; the sūrah moves in the next verses (150–152) to the further ordinance — to the prayer-direction in every place, in the Company even of its enemies — expanding the obedience into the total decree of 2:150's bare, all-embracing sweep.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:150

> **Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. And wherever you ˹believers˺ are, face towards it, so that people will have no argument against you, except the wrongdoers among them. Do not fear them; fear Me, so that I may ˹continue to˺ perfect My favour upon you and so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Full Universal Tie**

Verse 150 doubles the directives of both 144 and 149, fusing them into the single, fully-exhaustive form the commentators call the settling verse of the qiblah ordinance: *wa min ḥaythu kharajta fa-wallī wajhaka shaṭra al-masjidi al-ḥaram wa ḥaythu mā kuntum fa-wallū wujūhakum shaṭrah* — "whencesoever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wheresoever you may be — you believers — turn your faces toward it." The twofold precision binds the singular Prophet's obligation and the plural community's obligation into one form: whether departure, movement, journey or standing: the Household or the field; in Madinah and abroad; by night and by day — the appointment is *at-haythu* — wherever. Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī and the fiqh tradition trace just how total the coverage is: from this verse the whole qiblah discipline of a worldwide religion is transcribed — travelling believers, camped armies, spread-out villages, isolated tens of thousands of miles — until the one House becomes, by God's algebra, the center toward which every prayer everywhere on earth inclines.

**"No Argument Against You"**

Then the purpose-clause is given in an ascription of evidentiary finality: *li-allā yakūna li'l-nāsi ʿalaykum ḥujjatun* — "so that the people may have no argument against you" — *except* those among them who are wrongdoers: *illā alladhīna ẓalamū minhum*. The commentators align the clause with the verse's neighbors: once the Muslims prayed toward the Kaaba, the People of the Book — the Jews of Madinah who had claimed Jerusalem for their own and charged the Muslims with divided religion — were left without a ḥujjah, an argument: the very qiblah of Abraham had been re-anchored by God's appointment inside a community of Abraham's faith; there was no longer any grouse, no counter-charge, nothing remaining to say. *Except* the wrongdoers: the recalcitrant whom no sensible direction satisfies; no ḥujjah is cut off from the wrong-hearted — their argument does not reside in the intellect in the first place, but in the will (the same diagnosis the sūrah rendered at 2:108, 2:118, 2:145). The tradition's career with the clause is equally breath-taking: the leaders of the Muslims, in every age, refused to count every criticism at face; the same clause is cited through each generation's account of who ought to be feared within God and who need not be flattered: the believers settled their qiblah as God appointed — and with that settled their differential toward the *people's* opinions in matters of worship.

**Fear Me — and the Completion of Blessing**

The verse then returns to the blessed formula-pair — *fa-lā takhshawhum wa-khshawni* — "so do not fear them — fear Me": the customary exchange of fears that had already sealed the sūrah's oaths to Israel (2:40–41): fear none whose argument depends upon refusing your obedience, but fear the One whose obedience you perform. And with it comes the *ultimatum plenitudo* echo: *wa li-utimma niʿmatī ʿalaykum wa laʿallakum tahtadūn* — "and so that I may complete My blessing upon you, and that haply you may be guided" — the same completion-of-blessing formula as at 2:40 (with "remember My Blessing that I bestowed on you"), now tied to the qiblah itself: in turning the community's prayers fully into the axis of Abraham's House, God's blessing on the believers receives its completion — the perfecting of *ʿibādah* they had prayed for from the days of the emigration onwards. The commentators note that the sequence is the last of its family before the verse changes function and the sūrah moves on to new material at 2:152: with verse 150 the round is closed: the obligation of worshipping toward the Sacred Mosque, the judgment upon opponents of the appointment, and the final mercy attached — *haply you may be guided* — are now sealed together as the total of God's discourse on its appointed direction. From the Muslims ever since, the phrase lives in every walll: turn your faces wheresoever — and God completes.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:151

> **Since We have sent you a messenger from among yourselves—reciting to you Our revelations, purifying you, teaching you the Book and wisdom, and teaching you what you never knew—**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Abraham-Prayer Fulfilled**

At verse 129, in the middle of the Kaaba's construction, Abraham and Ishmael had raised hands and asked: *rabbanā wa-bʿath fīhim rasūlan minhum yatlū ʿalayhim āyātika wa yuʿallimuhumu al-kitāba wa'l-ḥikmata wa yuzakkīhim* — "and send among them a messenger from among them, reciting to them Your signs and teaching them the Book and the Wisdom and purifying them." Here, at verse 151, the Book answers the prayer by placing it — word for word — inside the mouth of God as a gift already conferred in the Prophet ﷺ: *kamā arsalnā fīkum rasūlan minkum yatlū ʿalaykum āyātinā wa yuzakkīkum wa yuʿallimukumu al-kitāba wa'l-ḥikmata wa yuʿallimukum mā lam takūnū taʿlamūn* — "even as We sent among you a messenger from among you, reciting to you Our signs, and purifying you, and teaching you the Book and the Wisdom, and teaching you what you knew not." The *kamā* — "even as" — is placed in exact resumption: the conducting clause of v. 152 will follow; the master-commentators note the Book's own precision that the verse is counted inside the same bridging figure, rather than as a merely repeated petition: what was prayed *through* Abraham's covenant is now confirmed *from* God, as promise-and-fulfillment framed in Himself — *and the community reads the Prophet's mission not as charity newly-decided, but as the deliberate answering of the very prayer its foundation-builder had prayed with his son*. The Prayer of Abraham concludes thus, delivered: the messenger from amongst them — Ḥaḍrat Muḥammad ﷺ — is the answer to the builders' supplication in the valley of Makkah.

**The Fourfold Curriculum Again**

The enumeration re-issues the mighty fourfold line (already spelled at verse 129): recitation (*yatlū*), purification (*yuzakkī*), teaching of Book-and-Wisdom (*yuʿallimu al-kitāba wa'l-ḥikmah*), teaching of the unknown (*yuʿallimukum mā lam takūnū taʿlamūn*) — and everywhere the commentators reiterate the singular pedagogical fields the Prophet's ministry brought with him. The recitation is the recitation of verses whose *conveyance* itself opens hearts into sūrahs of Islam (the original functions of *tilāwah*); the purification is the inner washing of hearts from the idols and habits of Jahiliyyah (as with the pre-Islamic Companions and the emergence of the purified generation); the book's and wisdom's teaching is the Book of God both as revealed speech and as the correct grasp, the *ḥikmah* being the Prophet's sunnah, glossed by Ibn ʿAbbās and the majority of the mufassirūn as standing member of the tradition; and the final phrase — "and teaches you what you knew not" — is expressly classed by the commentators as the crown of the sequence: for the Prophet ﷺ was not sent merely to rekindle forgotten scripture but to introduce an ummah that had been *ummiyyah* — *unscriptured* — into stores of knowledge *mā lam takūnū taʿlamūn* — knowledge of God's Names, of the Judgement, of the laws of the covenant of religion, of the hidden histories of the prophets, of the moral secrets of the heart — nothing of which the Arabs had carried. The examples pour in from every seat of tafsīr: verses of the afterlife, of the angels, of the scales and the books of deeds — *every* one of them part of that vast treasury of the unknown that revelation unfolded through Makkah and Madinah until the religion stood complete (5:3).

**The Prophet's Ministry as One Complete Gift**

The tradition is especially fond of verse 151 because of the *concision* with which it catalogues the Prophet's functions. Reading it together with the parallel at 3:164 ("God was truly gracious to the believers when He sent among them a messenger from among themselves...") and 62:2 ("it is He who sent among the unlettered a messenger from themselves..."), the sūrah and the wider Book make a triple announcement of the same fourfold gift — the mufassirūn explain that the repetition is no redundancy but the station for gratitude the Book never wishes to pass by: the gift itself is repeated *so that the audience thanks with full formula after full formula*. The believers' loftiest teachers — among them the Salaf's commentary teachers from Ibn ʿAbbās down to al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī — regard the verse as a total order for the Muslim community's education-system: recitation before purification; purification before teaching; teaching of the Book before deepest wisdom; and the whole fourfold work unwrapped not by the men of Madinah but by the Prophet first — the teacher plenipotentiary sent as the answer to the Kaaba-builders' prayer — the circle of giving drawn fully closed by the *kamā* of verse 151: the binding of the builders and the Revealer's response into one ummah, the same ummah that had stood beneath that House since the very day of its raising, waiting for the prayer to be answered — and now, in the Prophet ﷺ, answered indeed.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:152

> **remember Me; I will remember you. And thank Me, and never be ungrateful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Consequence of Being Supplied Everything**

The Abraham-cycle and the qiblah-unit close their long arc upon the verse the tradition calls the covenant of remembrance — *fa-dhkurūnī adhkurkum* — "so remember Me, I shall remember you" — the conclusion of the discourse whose every verse has been the spelling-out of its premise: God has given faith (v. 136), direction (v. 144), appointment (v. 150), the Prophet (v. 151): so the answering call of all such gifts is singular — *fa-* ("so") — *remember Me.* The commentators lay out the covenant's exactness: the servant's remembrance is by the heart, the tongue, and the limb of worship; God's remembrance in reply is by grace in the world, mercy at death, and glory upon the Day of Presentation (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr). The verse then doubles the care of the covenant-doctrine into its second arm — *wa-shkurū lī wa lā takfurūn* — "and give thanks unto Me, and do not be ungrateful to Me" — or, with the other flank of the reading, "do not disbelieve in Me": the same lettering of *kuf* (ingratitude and unbelief born of the same root) weaving the two counsels together, as the sūrah has been weaving them since verse 40. Ibn Kathīr records the balanced maxim of the salaf upon the paired clauses: *God remembers him who remembers Him, increases him who thanks Him, and punishes him who is ungrateful-disbelieving.*

**The Greatest Reciprocity**

The tradition has marked the verse as Islam's single most treasured proclamation of *mutual remembrance*: the servant lifts God into his little memory — and the Lord of the Worlds is the guarantor that — by the measure of His majesty — the servant is into *His* memory: surely the greatest of all disproportionate returns, the Imam Ibn al-Qayyim reasoned, in the whole of obedience. And the Prophet ﷺ brought home the verse's majesty with the celebrated sacred-hadith reported in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, which belongs among the foundations of the tradition at this verse:

> *"God — blessed and exalted — says: 'I am as My servant thinks Me to be, and I am with him when he remembers Me; whoever remembers Me within himself, I remember him within Myself; whoever remembers Me in company, I remember him in a company better than it; whoever draws near to Me a handspan, I draw near to him an arm's length; whoever draws near to Me an arm's length, I draw near to him a fathom; whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running.'"* (al-Bukhari 7405, 7505; Muslim 2675)

The commentaries hold the verse as the great charter-text of *dhikr Allāh* — the sustained remembrance of God — the practice from which the whole later map of Islamic devotion has arisen: the dhikr after prayers (33:41–42), the dhikr of the witr-night, the gathering-dhikr of the mosques, the solitude-dhikr of the cell: its every corner was pledged under God's own signature here; and every mystic-wash of Islamic soul-culture — al-Muḥāsibī, Junayd, al-Qushayrī, al-Ghazālī, Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh — circulates upon this exact circuit: remembrance-God-ward met by remembrance-God's-own: the current flows round and returns within the covenant named in the two words *fa-dhkurūnī adhkurkum*.

**Gratitude as the Spine of Faith**

The twin-clauses of gratitude and the ban on ingratitude are the very pair the sūrah introduced at its Blessing-sermons to Israel (2:40: "remember My blessing that I bestowed upon you," vs. 2:61: "they were stricken with humiliation and need and returned with wrath from God") — and what now descends upon the Muslims is the positive solution: the ummah of the Prophet ﷺ is to tread the line-perimeter of thanksgiving rather than the line-perimeter of ingratitude. The whole tradition's doctrine of *shukr* — standing between Islam's two posts of ṣabr and ṣalāh — re-unrolls at this verse: thanksgiving, Ibn al-Qayyim's doctrine runs, is for the eyes upon the gift rather than upon the finger-size of the gift: the believer sees the infinitely greater visible gift — guidance, qiblah, the Book, the Prophet, *and was charged with nothing: only remembrance* — and so he stands between the mountains of blessing and the yoke-light remembrance: the smallest of exchanges. The verse thus seals the entire covenant-structure the sūrah carried from its first Blessing-sermon forty verses back: gifts bestowed; covenant demanded; remembrance levied; ingratitude outlawed — *fa-dhkurūnī adhkurkum wa-shkurū lī wa lā takfurūn* — the believer's everyday work, the Book's everyday grace, joined in one verse in the Lord's direct speech forever.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:153

> **O believers! Seek comfort in patience and prayer. Allah is truly with those who are patient.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Remedy Announced Again**

The verse stands as the second of the identical counsels of the sūrah, its first having been addressed at verse 45 to the Children of Israel: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū istaʿīnū bi'l-ṣabri wa'l-ṣalāh inna Allāha maʿa al-ṣābirīn* — "O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer: truly God is with the patient." The commentators register both the repetition and its new assignee: verse 45's address to the *Bani Isra'il* finds in verse 153's address to *the believers* its completed parallel: the same remedy, dispensed first to the forerunner-community, is now administered by name to the successor-community; the Book has given Israel the map, and now gives the Muslims the full levy. The verb *istaʿīnū* — *seek help* — is deliberately selected: patience and prayer are not here one discipline among others: they are summoned as *the help* — the believer's pair of auxiliaries in the full campaign of religion: patience in the campaign's waiting, prayer in the campaign's drawing nigh: the marching and the supply, the standing-fast and the running-forward, issued together.

**The Three Patiences of the Ummah**

The commentary tradition, from al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī down to Ibn Kathīr, neatly folds the whole of the predicate into its three serial provinces: *ṣabr* — (1) upon obedience — *al-ṣabr ʿalā ṭāʿat Allāh* — in the constancy of prayers and fasts, of alms and ḥajj — where pacing, remaining, unmoved rebuilding carry the arc of the will through years of worship; (2) from disobedience — *al-ṣabr ʿan il-maʿṣiyah* — the unyielding refusal of sinful roads even where the doors stand open, a patience of restraint the salaf called the submissive-shield of the pious; (3) upon the decreed injuries — *al-ṣabr ʿalā aqdār Allāh* — the heart's agreement not to fold, bankrupt, or curse under soreness and calamity: loss of dear ones, ruin of health and wealth, wounding in God's cause. The verse itself stands upon the shallows of the sūrah's next verses: verses 155–156 follow with the inventory of those third-kind calamities (fear, hunger, loss of wealth, of souls, of fruits); the same overlap reappears at 3:186, 3:200, 90:17, 103:3. And God is *with the patient* — *maʿa* being regarded by the commentators above as the cousin of *maʿiyyah* — "with-ness": not bare nearness of location but the divine accompaniment of agency, help, and confirmation: the One who commands patience declares Himself present in the room where patience is carried out.

**The Prophet ﷺ and the Double Staff**

The tradition records the covenant-lived quality of the counsels through the Prophet's own examples — the years when he stood the nights in prayer until his feet swelled (as his Companions report, with ʿĀʾishah asking why when God had forgiven everything; he answered: "shall I not be a grateful servant?" — al-Bukhari 4836; Muslim 2820) and when he met every weight — the scoffing of the poets, the siege of Abū Ṭālib, the loss of Khadījah upon the same months as the loss of his uncle — *with prayer and patience* handshake-working: so his community grew upon the pair. And the Book's counsel was universally channeled through the generation into the two great supports: prayer, and patience — the two paragons linked at the very moment the Prophet ﷺ taught that one of the most fragrant human acts was to wrestle with the two weights of endurance and turning-Godward upon every adversity — his own every circumstance of discipline, suffering, and construction harnessed under the twin laws of the verse, so that the community could inherit them in age after age, long after his ﷺ return to his Lord, as every believer's measuring-rod: till today the Muslim says upon every intricate issue, *Patience and Prayer: God is with the patient:* the two-armed staff of the Book's counsel still borne by the faithful through every difficult century.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:154

> **Never say that those martyred in the cause of Allah are dead—in fact, they are alive! But you do not perceive it.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Word Forbidden**

The sūrah now places a new subject under discipline — the tongue's word over the fallen in God's path: *wa lā taqūlū liman yuqtalu fī sabīli Allāhi amwāt* — "and do not say of those slain in God's cause: they are dead." The verse alights — the commentators record — upon the deaths of the Muslims at the battle of Badr and then at Uḥud, and above the generation-carrying memory of the slain of every subsequent campaign of Islam: the Book lifts the fallen out of the category of the dead, not eliminating their deaths but outlawing the language of absence over them. The commentators note the claim's exact and narrow point: it is not said, "they never died," but rather, do not *say of them* as you say of the dead: this is why the same correction is then grounded on their inner state: *bal aḥyāʾun wa lākin lā tashʿurūn* — "No, they are alive — but you do not perceive it." The correction diverges — not into the afterworld's promised future (where the question of resurrection-life remains for all the righteous), but into the *now*, the hidden and present: they are alive at present in the manner the tradition explains, and the failure rests with us, not with them: *wa lākin lā tashʿurūn* — but *you* do not sense it.

**The Oasis of the Green Birds**

The tradition's own commentary — the celebrated hadith of the Companions — is now the largest support to the verse; carried in Sahīh Muslim, al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Ḥanbal from Ibn Masʿūd, it supplies the interior portrait of that life beyond perception:

> *"The spirits of the witnesses are in the bodies of green birds, moving through the Garden where they will; they alight upon lamps hanging beneath the Throne — and your Lord will then glance toward them and say: What do you desire? They will say: O Lord, what should we desire, since You have given us what You gave to none in Your creation? And when He sees that they have nothing to ask, they say: We desire to return to our bodies in the abode of the world, that we may be killed for Your sake once more — seeing the rank of martyrdom. The Lord will say: I have written that they shall not return to it."* (Muslim 1887; al-Tirmidhī 3010)

— and the same ḥadīth stands glossed by the parallel reports at al-Ṭabarī that describe them as white among white, spirits flying the shade of the Throne among fruit and rivers: the *green birds* are the body-interim of their journey between dying and the full resurrection: the eagle-like report of interstellar mediating life of the best of believers in God, before the greater day; and the hadith stands without fault in every Muslim child's hearing from Medina forward to the present — the consolation with which Islam has gone to her own slain at every front for all the centuries.

**A Death That Is Not Forfeit**

The mufassirūn adduce of the verse a strict doctrine: the witnesses' bodies have indeed ceased this world, in the sense the earth receives; the life the verse proclaims is a life of the soul begun at the moment of martyrdom — a barzakh-life — about which al-Ghazālī (and the tradition as a whole) writes that neither the body residents in the grave, nor the soul hung on the scales of the Day, can contain it: it is a fifth region, appointed for martyrs, and referring to the same hidden life that the tradition treats at 3:169 ("alive with their Lord, provided for"). The judgment the Book makes inside the two verses is formed upon the rectitude of the language rather than upon a metaphysics of details: do not say "dead"; the witness lives. And the spiritual-counsel level of the verse runs down to every subsequent century of suffering believers: by God's word in verse 154, the martyrs of His cause in every nation, language and century are accompanied out of the language of absence into the living, thriving, busy paradise of the moment between their death and their rising: *bal aḥyāʾun wa lākin lā tashʿurūn* — but the senses in this world comprehend them not — though God knows them, sees them, greets them, and awaits sending them back to their tenderest reward on the Day the skies open for the resuming of every true name.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:155

> **We will certainly test you with a touch of fear and famine and loss of property, life, and crops. Give good news to those who patiently endure—**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Notification of the Trial**

The sūrah intimates, before the trial arrives, the trial's arrival — and in God's own established way it gives the news in advanced citation: *wa la-nabluwannakum bi-shayʾin mina al-khawfi wa'l-jūʿi wa naqṣin mina al-amwāli wa'l-anfusi wa'l-thamarāt* — "We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth and selves and fruits." The commentators mark the verse's pacific forewarning between the prescription of patience at verse 153 and the reward at verse 157: the believer is told the coming so he can ready the station; and the exact map of the coming test is issued: *fear* — dread of the enemy, dread of insecurity, dread upon the course of life; *hunger* — literal scarcity of bread, and all famine's narrower relatives; *loss of wealth* — reversals of the purse and of trade; *loss of souls* — the deaths of friends, relatives, beloved helpers (as Ibn Kathīr makes sure the verse's exact scope covers), and, for some readings, one's own faculties compromised by illness; *loss of fruits* — the shortfalls of crops and gardens, and the loss even of children, whom the commentators call with the verse's tenderness *the fruit of hearts*. Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr both count the five enumerated kinds in the tradition's standard catalogue of the epitomes of worldly hurt — the circle of misfortunes that concentrate every category by which the believer is made to feel a leave-taking amid all his earnings.

**The Trial's Measure in the General History**

The verse is also read by the commentators against the wider file of the sūrah's decrees: the Quraysh (who had been established in the sanctuary of Makkah) had been protected by God's blessing from fear and hunger (106:4: "who has fed them against hunger and made them secure from fear") — and an ungrateful town was to wear hunger and fear as a garment (16:112) — so that the verse at Sūrah al-Baqarah stands over the world of the believers as the universal *ibtilāʾ*, the trial struck open against every soul under Heaven's laws: the world's conditions will not come by exemption to a community that, by its account, is to work harder than all that preceded it: it is the proving-ground of the promise made at verses 29–30 of al-ʿAnkabūt: *a-ḥasiba al-nāsu an yutrakū an yaqūlū āmannā wa hum lā yuftanūn?* — "Do people imagine they will be left to say 'we believe,' and not be tested?" — and the verse herewith answers: no; the trial is issued, with a severity scaled to the strength of the tried — and even the weights of the trial are told in the plainest currency of everyday living: fear, hunger, goods, lives, fruits.

**Tidings for the Patient Only**

Then the verse breaks out of the enumeration to the opening of its great promise: *wa bashshiri al-ṣābirīn* — "and give glad tidings to the patient" — the full citation-of-glory being deposited at verse 157; and here the tradition fixes its relationship to the terrifying five kinds: these are not given to choose; only the response is given to be chosen — and the word *ṣābirūn* is the faithful word by which the future is folded into the present: whoever is patient under the test is being included in advance into the register whose check is signed in 2:157: blessings from the Lord, mercy from the Lord, guidance certified for the register-marked self. The commentators praise the choice of the verb *bashshir* — *give glad tidings*: the very word of good news, the same root by which Heaven creakş the gates of Paradise open — and the Prophet ﷺ is expressly commanded to himself perform the duty of glad-tiding, so that the announcement be laid down not as a general maxim but as *the personal good-news carried by the Messenger to his community, person by person, at every loss*. And it is preserved in the tradition how the Prophet ﷺ practiced the very verse upon his own wounded community at Uhud, after the death of his dearest uncle Ḥamzah and so many of his beloved Companions:

> *"How excellent a community you are, that God tells me to give you good tidings..."* (from the consolatory teaching of the Sahīḥ on the patience-clauses; al-Ṭabarī records its connection to our verse — and the discipline stands through the generations of Islam)

and the general lesson of patience by initial blow — *inna al-ṣabra ʿinda al-ṣadmati al-ūlā* — was its performed law by the whole generation: al-Bukhari 1283, 1302; Muslim 926 — from Anas ibn Mālik: "the Prophet ﷺ said: *Patience is at the first blow*": the habit of the heart measured not by the measured reconciling of the final year, but by the state of the first moment of the blow — the sudden gesture with which the soul breaks or holds — and on this foundation the Prophet ﷺ built the whole civilization of losses and rebuildings in his community — the most fearsome categories of grief remade into gain — upon the small seed of five words of the Book of God.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:156

> **who, when faced with a disaster, say, “Surely to Allah we belong and to Him we will ˹all˺ return.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Saying That Carries the Patient Through**

The verse defines the patient of verse 155 by the very word spoken under the affliction — *alladhīna idhā aṣābathum muṣībatun qālū innā li-llāhi wa innā ilayhi rājiʿūn* — "those who, when a trial strikes them, say: truly we belong to God, and to Him we are returning." The commentators mark the saying's weighty anatomy: there are four entire theological affirmations set within it. *Innā* — "truly we" — is first the mind's acknowledgment of the misfortune as given to *us*. *Li-llāhi* — "belong to God" — restores ownership: we ourselves, our acts, our property, our kin, are all the property of the Lord (the sūrah's own parallel in verse 116: "unto Him belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and the earth"), whose gift and taking are both right. *Innā ilayhi rājiʿūn* — "and to Him we are returning" — sets the eye upon the ultimate state: not to the dust of the grave nor to the wall of the years but *to Him* we are returning, and the return is the theme that precedes its statement in verses 210 and 281 of the same sūrah ("unto God are all matters returned"; "beware a day when you shall be returned to God"). The muṣībah — the affliction-event — is placed in the verse as the *occasion* of the résumé of belief, not as the occasion of the heart's collapse: the whole loss is re-counted as a turning of the head upon a journey: we were given, and we are going; both poles belong to God.

**The Formula in the Practice of the Believers**

The saying itself — *innā li-llāhi wa innā ilayhi rājiʿūn* — has become, by God's decree through the Prophet's own language, the universal Islamic formula upon affliction. The famous hadith at Muslim (and the other Sahīḥ collections), from Umm Salamah, carries the full tableau of its performance's reward:

> *"If any servant is afflicted, and says: 'Truly we belong to God, and to Him we are returning — O God, reward me for my affliction and replace it for me with better' — God will surely reward him in his affliction and replace it for him with better."* Umm Salamah says: when Abū Salamah died, I said, what the Messenger of God ﷺ had taught me — then I said: and who is better than Abū Salamah? — and God gave me in exchange the Messenger of God ﷺ himself (Sahīḥ Muslim 918 — throughout the generations told as the supreme illustration of our verse's office)

Successive generations and languages have received the formula as its own house of refuge — so that by now the verse has become the living utterance of the Muslim peoples at births, deaths, and every catastrophe of the five kinds of verse 155 — the landscape of the loss crossed with a single Arabic sentence, the *istirjāʿ* — and it is a striking thing, the tradition's teachers repeatedly dwell upon, that the formula's utterance is itself a work of piety: the worshipper who speaks it at the catastrophe is *doing* faith in the very instant that the blow is falling, by God's own words in His own Book.

**Its Practice as Kindled Certainty**

The Sufi commentators adduce from the same verse a very careful analysis: the formula is not stoicism — it does not practice absence-of-pain — it practices holding pain in a holding-God's-room: as al-Ghazālī writes, grief remains grief, but *since the servant acknowledges God as owner and re-owner of both grief and grievee, grief is lifted into a station where it rebuilds his view of everything:* the filiations of the believer past, the loses of the future, all standing on the same ledger of outgoing and giving — *we are God's; we are returning to Him.* And within this calculus the tradition marks the faithful progress of the sufferers at Uhud and the many battles: those who said *innā li-llāh* preserved their sight of God in the crowd of their wounded; those who omitted it otherwise could not stand in the same crowd for looking at nothing but their losses. The verse's seminal teaching is then disciplined by the Book's own application: by this spoken word the afflicted believer moves instantly and literarily from the chaos of the mischance into the nomenclature of God, and his next step is already being walked into the greater plain where the belongings are final — *to God, returning.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:157

> **They are the ones who will receive Allah’s blessings and mercy. And it is they who are ˹rightly˺ guided.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reward Register of the Saying**

Following the saying by the faithful of the istirjāʾ formula at verse 156, this verse delivers its very register of reward: *ulāʾika ʿalayhim ṣalawātun min rabbihim wa raḥmah wa ulāʾika humu al-muhtadūn* — "those — upon them are blessings from their Lord, and mercy; and those — they are the guided." The commentators note first the threefold crown of the clause: (1) The *ulāʾika* is the demonstrative of loftiness in the Arabic — the verse summoning *them* above the rank of other, as it were by pointing upon their elevation from where the judgment sits; (2) the two gifts — *ṣalawāt* and *raḥmah* — and (3) *al-muhtadūn* — their guidance already realized — thereby sealing the rewards into the keys of religion's greatest designations.

**Ṣalawāt Min Rabbihim**

*Ṣalawāt* — plural of *ṣalāh* — is most often the prayer from man to God; but with the preposition *ʿalā* it is the mercy and praise proceeding from God toward man — the direction reversed. The commentators tie it firmly to the other usage in the Book — God bless *the Prophet*: "truly God and His angels send blessing upon the Prophet" (33:56) — and the stations where the Prophet is commanded to *yuṣallī ʿalayhim* — "bless them — your blessing is a comfort for them" (9:103) — so the two usages open its wings: from God to the people: mercy; from people to God: prayer; and upon these the tradition pronounces: at verse 157 it is God to the people: *ṣalawāt* as the multiple mercy and praising honour bestowed by the Lord: He praises them in the Highest Assembly, they are blessed upon the tongues of the angels, and from Him their recompense issues: the honour of every afflicted believer who has spoken the words of verse 156 in sincerity, given its citation in verse 157 as coming directly out of the Treasury of the Lord of the Worlds, without interference from any hand.

**And Mercy — an Unenumerated Grace**

And *raḥmah* — *mercy* — is included without a number of its forms: the commentators note the indefinite use — *wa raḥmatun* vagueliness unbuilt upon limbs or items — as the most embracing sign: God's mercy over the afflicted patient cannot be enumerated: it is the sea into which every river of reward flows: the lifting of the trial itself at its time, the accompanying peace upon the loss, the forgiveness tied to tribulation (cf. the hadith at Muslim: "no fatigue nor grief reaches a Muslim but God expiates some of his sins thereby" — al-Bukhārī 5641, Muslim 2573), the reward of patience at the first blow — all of it reckoned under the unbroken inlet of *wa raḥmah.*

**"Those Are the Guided"**

The last seal of the verse — *wa ulāʾika humu al-muhtadūn* — "and those, *they* are the guided" — restores the equation of verses 2–5 of the sūrah to its full close: at the beginning, the Book itself characterized the righteous as *al-muttaqūn*: "upon them is guidance from their Lord, and those — they are the successful"; now, having walked through the whole curriculum of the opening passages of al-Baqarah, the believer hears the same equation of guidance with their own *ulāʾika* of the tribulation-line: the effort is complete from the first promise of guidance to the last — they are the guided, guide-certified at the very moment the crises of life strike. And the tradition in reading all three verses together — 155, 156, 157 — preserves the school's further principle: the very articulation of the trials in *lā tubliwannakum* of verse 155 stands *as the most immediate reward of the believing community*: God has forewarned the faithful in the exact words of the kindled verse, so His trial of them comes as the test *they themselves* have been told of by Him — the whole sūrah now closed, for the time, on the paradox the companions of the Prophet ﷺ verified in their own battles: the affliction was not absence of God but descent of His blessing, and the driven roads of suffering became the above-ground instruments of guidance and mercy, at the nexus where the Lord of the Unseen folded back the veil of every believer's height, width, and depth of pain, and said — *to those: upon them are My blessings, and mercy, and they — they are the guided.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:158

> **Indeed, ˹the hills of˺ Ṣafa and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever performs the pilgrimage or minor pilgrimage, let them walk between ˹the two hills˺. And whoever does good willingly, Allah is truly Appreciative, All-Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Hills of the Mother's Running**

The Book now consecrates the two small hills by the Kaaba — Ṣafā (al-Ṣafā) and Marwah (al-Marwah) — declaring their rituals of God: *inna al-ṣafā wa'l-marwata min shaʿāʾiri Allāh* — "truly Ṣafā and Marwah are among the rituals of God" — *fa-man ḥajja al-bayta awi iʿtamara fa-lā junāḥa ʿalayhi an yaṭṭawwafa bihimā* — "so whoever performs the ḥajj of the House or performs the ʿumrah, there is no blame upon him to walk between them." The shaʿāʾir of God — the commentators of the Arabic expand the root sh-ʿ-r toward "that by which God is known": His signs, His appointed places, His sanctified movements — and upon these hills God places His seal because of what they carry: the testimony of Hagar (Hājar) running between them seven courses, searching water for her infant Ishmael whom Abraham had left in the barren valley at God's behest (cf. Genesis 21, retold in the tradition's sīra at this verse) — the mother's heart running, desperate, between two hills until Zamzam burst forth under the child's feet — every pilgrim thereafter walking in her hurried steps in the saʿy (the "course between walking and running," that motion the old Arabian idiom calls between full walking and running): the living re-enactment of her pas-de-deux with God. Ibn Kathīr adjudges the verse to establish what the ḥajj itself already had: the two hills continue as part of the pilgrims' course because they are tied into the Abrahamic narrative; and with that the Companions' own earlier hesitation — that the saʿy might be a leftover of pre-Islamic practice, or a superfluous itinerary — is itself resolved by the settled authority of God Himself.

**The Ḥajj, the ʿUmrah, and the Course**

The jurists derive from the verse the two great pillars concerning the saʿy across the whole ummah's schools: the Ḥanafīs (and with them the Mālikīs) counted the saʿy a duty of the pilgrimage owed but reparable by sacrifice, while the Shāfiʿīs and Ibn Hanbal's one of its pillars, without which the ḥajj's structure is incomplete — all schools, in the end, *performing* the course exactly — and the verse's *no blame* is read as removing all doubt from the rite, not as license to skip it: the Companions' last scruples were over precisely this (Ibn Kathīr preserves the relational telling that some feared the saʿy to be a Jahili rite — the hills having housed two idols in the pre-Islamic period — until the verse downcame to prove the association false and God's sign true). The well-known ḥadīth on the pilgrimage seals the rite forever:

> *"Make the course (saʿy) between them, for God has prescribed for you the making of the course."* (Aḥmad, al-Nasāʾī — carried by the mufassirūn and jurists under this verse as its working hadith — and the annual refrain since the Prophet's Farewell Pilgrimage)

**Volunteering Good Above the Marches**

Then the verse's close opens the march's scope to the larger field of volunteered goodness: *wa man taṭṭawwaʿa khayran fa-inna Allāha shākirun ʿalīm* — "and whoever volunteers good, truly God is Thankful, Knowing." The commentators (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr) explain *taṭṭawwaʿa* — the volunteering of supererogation — as the general class of deeds given beyond the commanded minimum, beginning in this very place with the ʿumrah itself, which performed outside the prescribed ḥajj-days became the ummah's standing course of voluntary pilgrimage worship; and the two names of God given in the close — *Shākir* (*Thankful*) and *ʿAlīm* (*Knowing*) — close the field with the two qualities of the Rewarder: the Thankful One giving for the volunteer far more than the volunteer's measure, and the Knowing One recording every intent and motion of even briefly-passed hearts upon Ṣafā's dusty slope. The scene the tradition preserves for our instruction is that of the Prophet ﷺ himself walking the same course — stepping from Ṣafā to Marwah, green cloths around his waist, reciting the very verse we read — and the ummah has walked in his steps ever since, the marble of the two hills now set within the stones of the enlarged mosque in Makkah, and millions run in Hagar's course every year — every one of them praying toward the same conclusion the Book has sealed above it: *God is Thankful, Knowing of all.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:159

> **Those who hide the clear proofs and guidance that We have revealed— after We made it clear for humanity in the Book—will be condemned by Allah and ˹all˺ those who condemn.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Crime of Concealing Clear Proof**

Following the exaltations of the patient in trials and the sanctification of Ṣafā and Marwah, the sūrah returns to the running reproach of the sūrah's theology-work: concealment. *Inna alladhīna yaktumūna mā anzalnā mina al-bayyināti wa'l-hudā min baʿdi mā bayyannāhu li'l-nāsi fī al-kitāb* — "truly those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance, after We have made it clear to mankind in the Book" — *ulāʾika yalʿanuhumu Allāhu wa yalʿanuhumu al-lāʿinūn* — "those — upon them is the curse of God, and they are cursed by the cursers." The bayyināt — the clarifiers, the proofs endowed with proof — and the hudā — the guidance itself — are two spaces of revelation: the proofs are its incontrovertible certainties; its guidance the map of life itself. The commentators read this indictment upon two fields. The narrow field runs again to the custodians of the People of the Book, continuing the files of Katm at verses 140 and 146 — those who had in their scriptures the clarity about the Prophet ﷺ, and refused it. The wide field runs beyond tribes — to every man entrusted with religious knowledge who keeps it from its people, inside any age and any land: for which the crime is one of the great offenses of the Book itself. And then the Punishment of the double curse: God curses the suppressers — and all cursers curse them.

**Whose Curse Is Meant?**

The commentators read the company of the cursers from several noble witnesses. Al-Ṭabarī, preferring angels and believers (the two with curse-capable standing), takes it as the great chorus joined by 2:161: God, the angels, and mankind all together: for concealment strikes against the guidance by which all mankind lives, so all those under guidance turn and curse the concealer. Al-Rāzī's field draws larger: even the *beasts* curse them — the beasts being of the chorus, as the salaf reports indicate, of whom it is said by the commentators of verses of this type that all creation upon the conveyor of God's sentence accompanies the curse: in the register of the Day, every soul misled through concealment arrives as a curse upon the concealer of its evidence, and the very dwellers of the Fire may well curse those who made them those whom they became, since Book and proof stand responsible no longer. The Prophet ﷺ said upon the same import (reported by Abū Hurayrah at al-Tirmidhī, with the companions' own saying attached):

> *"God does not seize knowledge by snatching it from people's hearts; rather He takes it away by taking away the scholars, until no scholars remain, and people take for leaders the ignorant, who when asked give answers without knowledge and thus go astray and lead others astray."* (al-Bukhari 100; Muslim 2673)

and the tradition stands thereby behind the seriousness of our verse: knowledge held back from the people is the kindling of their leading-astray itself, and the curse descends from all company upon those who would bury it after God had lifted it *into* the Book.

**The Condemnation Without Exclusion**

The spiritual tradition holds the verse as the second great rebuke of the ummah against the tyranny of the learned-class seated upon its wealth-of-knowledge as traders upon ware — the first being verse 42, "do not mix truth with falsehood, nor conceal the truth while knowing" — and now at verse 159, with the wrath of the Divine Curse itself attached. The commentators mark that ⁠— the curse (laʿna) in the Arabic — conveys in the Book both divine expulsion from mercy and the drive away of companionship (as at verse 161 and the companions' la'an formula) — so it is taught as the utmost theological sentence upon insight-burying: *God chairs the tribe of the cursers against the concealers of His light*. The next verse (160) will add the sole exception *save those who repent and make amends* — but verse 159 stands, for every scholar and for every household of the Book's preserver, exactly as it is: silent-downholding of God's light drawn is the heaviest stone laid upon a man's rolled-up soul — *ulāʾika yalʿanuhumu Allāhu wa yalʿanuhumu al-lāʿinūn* — and the tradition waits no disputes to recognize it. Nor does the believer flinch when he reads the formula of the verse as his own recital: it is the called-down benchmark for every heir of prophets and scholars since, and it stands and defends the Light in the lamp-stand of the chosen hearts, that they may light more hearts as long as the Lord intends for men to be guided.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:160

> **As for those who repent, mend their ways, and let the truth be known, they are the ones to whom I will turn ˹in forgiveness˺, for I am the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Exception Written In**

The thunder of the double curse in verse 159 does not fall without a gate left open — and the Book, as ever, plants its gate explicitly within the sentencing: *illā alladhīna tābū wa aṣlaḥū wa bayyanū fa-ulāʾika atūbu ʿalayhim* — "except those who repent, and make amends, and make clear: those — unto them I relent." The commentators mark the triad of conditions, which stand precisely over against the threefold crime of verse 159. Where the crime was *katm* — deliberate concealment of bayyināt — the first condition is *tawbah*: the inner turning, the admission to God of fault, the movement of the heart back through the door shut at the time of suppressing. Where the concealment had done structural damage — souls left unguided, communities left in the dark — the second condition is *iṣlāḥ*: the worker's repair of the damage-in-world, the "putting things right" the Arabic carries as its own duty: unfinished business actually finished, burned structures actually rebuilt, the wrong against truth actively overruled by the pen. And where the crime itself had been *silence* — the covering of truth inside speechlessness — the third condition is *tabyīn*: the making-clear of what was concealed: the former concealer must now himself speak the buried proof, in the open, with his own tongue, to the very people from whom it was hidden. The commentators (al-Ṭabarī forward) note the point: God ties the cure directly to the disease — the medicine is the precise reversal of the suppressing sin — and in so doing teaches the general rule: no repentance is complete without the restoration of the right which the fault had crushed, so far as restoration is possible.

**"Unto Them I Relent" — The Divine Singular**

Then come the verse's words of majestic embracing — *fa-ulāʾika atūbu ʿalayhim wa anā al-tawwābu al-raḥīm* — "those — I turn back to them; and I am the Relenting, the Merciful." Two observations the commentators never miss. First, the grammatical descent from the plural "We sent down" (v. 159's *anzalnā*) to the singular *I* — *atūbu*, *anā* — the Divine Unity stepping, as it were, out of the royal plural of majesty to meet the individual penitent at his personal repentance, singular to singular: mercy is not administered here from the Court's plural but from the One Merciful himself. Second, the naming — *al-Tawwāb*: He who turns back again and again — the superlative of the same root the repentant uses for his own turning: the tradition's noetic reading is celebrated: man turns to God once, and God turns to him seventy times; man's turning is the motion of a fallible creature, and God's turning is the motion of the Generous answering every motion toward Him — as the hadith runs in al-Bukhari and Muslim:

> *"God extends His hand by night for the repentance of him who sinned by day, and extends His hand by day for the repentance of him who sinned by night, until the sun rises from the west."* (Muslim 2759 — from Abū Mūsā, one of the standing proof-texts of al-Tawwāb cited at our verse and at 2:37 and 2:128)

**Across the Curse to the Name**

The school of tafsīr often pauses at the full flow of verses 159–161 to note the spiritual drama built into the order: the concealment-curse is not stated without its rescue-clause; the persistently disbelieving (v. 161) are stated under the curse precisely as those *not* of the resume-clause — those who *did not* repent — so that by the end of the trilogy the believer has been shown both that katm is cursed and that the curse's own Lord stands at the open gate of His names, waiting for the concealer who would return by tabyīn. The Prophet's own conduct with those who would once have been of the People of the Book-in concealment among Madinah's rabbis, having known the signs of him in their scriptures, is recorded by the tradition: when ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and such converts came forth with the buried knowledge, the Prophet ﷺ made no demand of them beyond the verse's own three: they repented, amended, clarified — and entered the fold clean: for him the gate was never shut. In the same manner the tradition extends the verse to the whole category of concealed knowledge — and the one who holds a hidden truth of God within himself is forever invited to take the three steps back out of concealment: *turn to God, mend the world you harmed, and speak the light you buried* — and the double name declared at the end guarantees the outcome: *He is the Relenting — al-Tawwāb — and He is the Merciful — al-Raḥīm* — the One whose mercy across tens of centuries never once denied its open gate to whoever knocked upon it.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:161

> **Surely those who disbelieve and die as disbelievers are condemned by Allah, the angels, and all of humanity.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Dying the Same as They Lived**

Following the gate-held-open at verse 160, the Book pronounces the sentence upon the other side — the heart sealed before the umbral closing of life: *inna alladhīna kafarū wa mātū wa hum kuffārun* — "truly those who disbelieve and die *while* disbelievers." The commentators take whole the final phrase — *wa hum kuffārun* — "while they are disbelievers" — as the verse's true loadstone: the charge is not simply disbelief but disbelief *carried into death*: the earlier gates all stood open (9140's Shahadah concealed, 159's curse with its tabyīn-rescue, 160's Relenting as close as the penitent's breath), and death arrives while the concealer still sits upon his concealment and the denier upon his denial, and opportunity's gate follows the body's breath in closing. The sentence that follows is expressed in one of the Book's fullest curses: *ulāʾika ʿalayhim laʿnatu Allāhi wa'l-malāʾikati wa'l-nāsi ajmaʿīn* — "upon them is the curse of God, and of the angels, and of mankind — all of them together." The *laʿna* — curse — whose sequence had been doubled in verse 159 (cursed by God and by cursers) is now tripled and sealed: God and His angels and all humankind take their positions, and the one unrepentant arrives at the Day with all three choirs against him.

**What the Curse Means**

The commentators explain the theology of laʿna with precision: to be *malʿūn* — under curse — is to be filled-out with divine expulsion from mercy: to stand outside the circle of the Godhead's raḥmah itself, with no approach allowed, having forfeited by chosen-transgression the relation of helping-listener to Lord. The angels' part in the curse is their supplication — the blessed assembly of the Highest agents, the bookkeepers of the soul-files, turning upon the adamant disbeliever with the prayer of repelling (so al-Ṭabarī); and mankind's part — *all of them together* — the commentators lay out as including both the curse of the prophets, and the curse of those they had themselves beguiled, and the curse of every believer upon every defiant unbeliever, and — as al-Rāzī explains — even from the ranks of the damned themselves the damned will hurl the la'an at one another for the misfortunes that each had loaded upon the other (29:25: "then on the Day of Resurrection you will disown one another and you will curse one another"). The verse completes precisely the theology of all humankind: humankind now the cohort of witnesses against the one whose record God has already sealed.

**The Prophet's Setting for the Laʿna**

The jurists, together with al-Qurṭubī, reliably attach to this verse the exact conduct of the Prophet ﷺ in his deployment of the laʿna: it is bound to the Hereafter, to the state upon arrival before God — and *not* given as a licensed pastime of speech in this world. The Prophet ﷺ restrained rather than extended the vulgar cursing of the disobedient — forbidding it upon the one already undergoing the veil of divine punishment, forbidding curses upon the repentant — and he taught that the one who is under the earth cannot be helped by the malediction of men: his account stands at God's seat, as the verses render it, with all the arrows of humanity — *not* with any man's own tongue. From this position the tradition structures the conduct that still governs: a believer leaves the sentence upon the unrepentant disbeliever where it stands — with God, the angels, and mankind at the Day of the Great Exposure — and attends to his own warm duty: the guidance of the still-living soul who may yet come toward the gate that will never close in its day. The verse's relentlessness — judgment upon dying-as-disbelievers — serves in the general teaching as the deepest spur of Islam's *daʿwah*: the muslim thinks whenever he sees a soul at risk, *that he may repent before death; because after death without repentance, the verdict of verse 161's concurrence is fixed* — laʿna of God, of angels, of mankind all together: and the curtain rises upon the Day whose concurrence no one can undo.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:162

> **They will be in Hell forever. Their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be delayed ˹from it˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Three Fixed Endings**

The sentence completes the triple-chambered judgment that verse 161 had prepared, in one brief constructions of the Book's most forbidding formulas: *khālidūna fīhā lā yukhaffafu ʿanhum al-ʿadhābu wa lā hum yunẓarūn* — "therein they abide; the punishment is not lightened for them; and they are not granted respite." The commentators lay each clause upon its place with care, since the Book's prohibition-triple forms together the triple foreclosure of every hope the damned might have secretly kept. *Khālidūna fīhā* — "abiding therein": the first closing on duration — the dwelling is permanent, no exit day is penciled upon the calendar, no transfer is decreed, no release follows upon a given epoch: the fire keeps them inside it as their permanent state (in the same diction as 3:116, 4:56, and so many others — the word *khālid* belonging to the Qur'an's fixed vocabulary of eternal duration). *Lā yukhaffafu ʿanhum al-ʿadhāb* — "the punishment is not lightened for them": the second closing on severity — no lighter hour, no afternoon's leniency, no twilight of the flames: the same punishment, in its fullness, without reduction of any kind, with the Book repeating the exact phrase at 2:86, 3:88, 16:85, 35:36, and 43:75 as if to multiply its impossible repetition before every reader. *Lā hum yunẓarūn* — "and they are not looked upon with reprieve": the third closing on time — the *naẓar* of respite, the look of God that would grant leisure and holdward, is withdrawn: no deference, no waiting-room of relief: the sentence is permanent and immediate forever.

**A Formula Answering a Specific Hope**

The commentators cast the verse into its argued context: the Book has already rejected the argument of naught (verse 80: "the Fire shall not touch us but for a few numbered days"), and the verse's every negation answers some whispered hope that had been nursed beneath recalcitrance in the days of the world — the hope that eternity's severity might lighten; the hope that the Inevitable might be at least postponed; the hope that the state of abiding itself might one day end — and the Book meets all three inside a single verse, affirming by its exact negations the immutable reality of the whole sūrah's opening pledge: the sūrah had guaranteed, at verse 39, that those who disbelieve and belie the signs would be *companions of the Fire, abiding therein* — and verse 162 has now narrated exactly what *khālidūn* means: no lightening, no respite: a fullness of doom matched to the fullness of refusal in the world, the exactness of scale the Lord creates to answer the exactness of unfaith: the Prophet confirmed the balance of both sides in his constant account of seriousness in the tradition:

> *"The most feared of what I fear for my community is every knowledgeable, fluent hypocrite."* — and with the eschatology from the great scene: *"If you knew what I know you would laugh little and weep much"* (al-Bukhārī 6485, 6486; Muslim 2359 — from ʿĀʾishah's account of the Prophet's visitation of the graveyard at Baqīʿ, among the standing accounts of the Book's eschatological realism)

**The Standing Counsel of the Verse**

Verse 162, the tradition understands, is not entered into speculation about a cosmology of torment: it is established for the changing of the reader *now*, the hadith-realization as the early Muslims called it for themselves — the Book as force. Muslim fatherhood and mother-love passed the verse through every Islamic century on the understanding that a believer could read verse 161 and verse 162 and be frightened into transmitting piety with his last breath, since the gates of repentance shut with the breath's leaving, as the Prophet's ﷺ positions on the sun's rising from the west (at 2:160) made the Prophet's teaching the canonical mark of the unshut gate of repentance. The tradition still holds the verse among the short recitals preached before sleep (the so-called *āyāt al-raḥmah wa'l-waʿd wa'l-waʿīd*), its every cluster of negations read before the Last Judgment's questioner: whether one's own life be one of repentance in time, or one of the habitation within which the verse has already shone its fixed final words — *they abide therein; the punishment is not lightened for them; and they are not granted respite* — and its lesson stands at the head of repentance-school: that the three closed doors are not God's cruel choices but the honest read-out of the choices which the condemned had made themselves, across years when every gate had been open before them.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:163

> **Your God is ˹only˺ One God. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Sermon in a Sentence**

In the very aftermath of judgment's transparency, the sūrah's voice returns to the most decisive declaration in all religion: *wa ilāhukum ilāhun wāḥidun lā ilāha illā huwa al-raḥmānu al-raḥīm* — "your God is one God; there is no god but He — the Compassionate, the Merciful." The commentators mark the verse as the most-recited of tawḥīd's grammar-lessons: three articles of grammar complete the fullest conceivable ontology. First: *ilāhukum ilāhun wāḥidun* — "your God is one God" — naming Him by the word *ilāh* (the generic name of deity) rather than by the supreme personal name Allāh — the theological point al-Ṭabarī expounds — so that even a one passing by *any god-concept* is told: yours is *one*; second: *lā ilāha illā huwa* — "no god but He" — the very formula of the shahādah itself, preceded by the emphatic negation of any others; third: *al-raḥmānu al-raḥīm* — the two Names of Mercy sealing it (the very pair of the basmalah), so the One God is introduced not as bare power or bare dominion but as the Lord of Mercy — His unity not bare arithmetic but loving unity: the two most-called-upon, most-loved of His names standing at the verse's conclusion, completing in one line the felicity of faith's whole sentence.

**Oneness as Freedom From Composition**

Al-Ṭabarī gives to *wāḥid* the fullest understanding of the Arabic: *one*, unique, indivisible, without parts — not made of things assembled, not shared among others — the duration without parts and without need and without partner, upon which the whole of tawḥīd rests. The yet larger school of Islam's theology over the centuries makes the precise point that God's oneness as it is delivered here is not an algebraic oneness — the number one which could be followed by two — but *real* singularity: nothing can be put beside Him, since every thing would thereby already be of another order; and nothing can belong to His likeness, since likeness among His nature would return the same One back into *differentiation* — and the tradition-verses gathered to it — 112's "He is God the One" — 59:22's assertion "He is God, there is no god but He" — stand in the same line of what the Book would later gather under its most soaring designation of throne: "He is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward" (57:3), all of them explicating the same irreducible declaration: **this God is one**, since gods among the believers of Madinah and Makkah had been many, but this God is not among them.

**The One God Under All of the Book's Teaching**

Commentators variously place verse 163 at the crux-link between the immediately foregoing judgment-unit and the coming displays of creation-signs at verse 164: the tawḥīd-statement precedes the world-signs just as *Wahhāb's* account precedes His bestowals — one God is announced first, then the catalog of His distributed works; and equally it closes the theological question verse 158 had notified: if Ṣafā and Marwah are the rituals of God, the One God, then all ritual and all bounty come from Him alone — there is no second Benefactor to pay double thanks, no alt-Helper to appeal over His head: gratitude belongs straight to Him alone. The pious tradition, in a word, treats verse 163 as among the reciters' verses: it was from the start read among the great enumerated marks of the Book; it is heard in tawḥīd classes by the young; and through the cats' mouths of century upon century its twin-mercy names have concluded every lesson of learned friends and pupils, *the Compassionate, the Merciful* — the names which have, after every judgment-scene and after every theology of unity, been chosen to bring home its uniqueness: a reminder of the deeper majesty that stands beneath every declaration of the Book: *one God, none but He, the Compassionate, the Merciful.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:164

> **Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth; the alternation of the day and the night; the ships that sail the sea for the benefit of humanity; the rain sent down by Allah from the skies, reviving the earth after its death; the scattering of all kinds of creatures throughout; the shifting of the winds; and the clouds drifting between the heavens and the earth—˹in all of this˺ are surely signs for people of understanding.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Grand Gallery Opened**

Following upon the declaration of the one God at verse 163, the Book swings open the grand gallery of His signs in creation — *inna fī khalqi al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍ* — "truly in the creation of the heavens and the earth..." — and the commentators describe the verse as one of the fullest single panoramas in the Qur'an, matching in reach only hisacles 3:190 and 30:20–27: *seven* registers of His works are unrolled, comprehending the galaxy and the grain of a boat's hull together: (1) the creation of heavens and earth — the frame itself, made from nothing and comprised of what any looking can see — (2) the variation of night and day — the alternation that ministers rest and labor — (3) the ships that run upon the sea with what benefits mankind — of the catalogue only the artificial thing (the commentators of tradition love to note), yet the one through which man is most conscious of divine ministration: the little shell between him and the unbottomed sea — the occasion of turning-to-God in storm which the Book records elsewhere (29:65; 31:32); (4) the water from the sky by which He revives the earth after its death — the rain on the dead plain; (5) the scattering therein of every beast — the replenishment of the world with its moving tribes; (6) the shifting of the winds — the change of their directions, gentle and rough, warm and cold; (7) the clouds subdued between sky and earth — the clouds made, like the ship, to course between the two terraces of creation, subjugated exactly as other things are named in the Book as being subservient to God or made subservient to man.
