The list: *āyāt* — signs: and the phrase ends with the quality of the community addressed: *li-qawmin yaʿqilūn* — "for a people who understand."

**"Signs for a People Who Understand"**

The commentators unfold the key phrase as the Book's own doctrine of the sign: it is not the display that makes the sign, but the meeting of the display with a people who *think*; *ʿaql* — the faculty of knowing-restraint, of binding conclusions to their causes — is what converts the night-day alternation into evidence. The astronomers among Muslims (from the Baghdad school through the Maghribi institutions) themselves read their own vocation in the verse's favoring: the heavens-and-earth, the night and the day — these are the very terms of their discipline: astronomy was in the Muslim world the most theological of all sciences because, read at the perspective of verse 164, its star-catalogues are *the catalogue of signs*; and the botanist, the hydrologist, the mariner, and the meteorologist of the old world each found their own page in it. The mystics read the same use of "sign" in reverse: the believer sees God *through* the sign, so that the view is transformed into vision — rain becomes mercy-descending; wind becomes the spirit's own movement, the Arabic rīḥ (wind) being cousin by root to rūḥ (spirit); clouds become the trucks of rain-bearing grace: the whole list turning into a single language addressed to the understanding — if the understanding has been turned to the One who sent it.

**The Answer to the Askers of Signs**

Al-Ṭabarī also preserves the occasion-reports tied to the verse: the idolaters were demanding a wonder — Ṣafā turned to gold (cf. verse 158's hill!) — and some were mocking: *how can a single God be sufficient for all mankind?* The verse's answer is therefore not silence but *re-direction*: the signs have not ceased; what has ceased is the demanders' footing: instead of one mountain in gold, the whole heaven and earth, the alternating hours, the ships of the sea, the living down of rain, the scattered beasts, the winds above, the clouds between — all of them are laid on the table as the answer to the jest: *the sign they ask for is what they are standing inside*. This same lesson — the refusal of the sign-faqirs while the earth groans under signs — is the very one still pressed through the Book's pages wherever unbelievers demand tokens: *the greatest sign is not wrought in a moment; it is sown all around the askers, every single day, for a people who understand* — and the Prophet's own pattern in his answers to sign-demands conformed to the Book's own teaching: when asked, he asked back for *reading*: for the Book and the existing signs — so the community refused from the first day the notion that God's own abundant display was anything less than demonstration — and the verse's closing word remains in every land where inquiry is in good health: *signs for a people who understand.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:165

> **Still there are some who take others as Allah’s equal—they love them as they should love Allah—but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more. If only the wrongdoers could see the ˹horrible˺ punishment ˹awaiting them˺, they would certainly realize that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is indeed severe in punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Rivals in the Love-Market**

After seven cosmic witnesses, the Book turns to the human heart's own response — and finds adultery: *wa mina al-nāsi man yattakhidhu min dūni Allāhi andādan yuḥibbūnahum ka-ḥubbi Allāh* — "among mankind are those who take, apart from God, equals; they love them as much as God is loved." The word *andād* — plural of *nidd* — the grammarians explain as the *like*, the peer, the counter-weight set opposite; al-Rāzī renders it *the competitor*: anything — stone or spirit, chief or throne, craved coin or craved status — adopted at a level stretching to God's own level in the soul, which thereby becomes the god's *competitor* within the heart's fidelity. The exact meaning of the love-comparison is given in all its polyvalent force (Ṭabarī, Rāzī): they love the rivals as they love God, dividing one love between the many and the One; or they obey them as they should obey God — the man chief of the tribe and the pagan fair after the idol taking God's share; or they invest them with the kind of love God alone should command — the love of perfect reverence and reliance. The assessment of the sūrah is thereby articulated in no evasive language: *shirk is love mis-spent*: the idolater does not merely get his metaphysics wrong; he places the heart's most valuable commodity — love — at a shrine of stone: *they love them as the love of God* — the very love due to the only true God dispersed among creatures and stocks.

**"Those Who Believe Love God More"**

Against this market, the believer's heart appears as the starkest contrast: *wa alladhīna āmanū ashaddu ḥubban li-llāh* — "but those who believe are more ardent in love of God." The commentators' reading of the comparative is carefully opened: the believer's love is greater than the idolater's love of his idols; and greater than any divided love the idolater may still owe to God alongside his idols; for the believer's love is concentrated — undivided — upon its true object: the only One. The tradition has made of this clause the gold-standard of the Islamic doctrine of divine love: *ashadd* — *strongest, tightest* — love-than-the-rivals', unwavering beneath all trials (2:155's tests serve, as the Sufis of every age observe, to burn strain out of even this love until what remains is pure: the afresh covenant of 2:156 flows from very love of God in the teeth of every loss). The Sufi commentators from Junayd to al-Qushayrī to Rūzbihān Baqlī build from the verse the whole economy of Islamic *maḥabba*: God's love for man guiding him; man's responding love to God exceeding his love for every other object; the love between God and servant closing at last where the divisions vanish (the famous *nawāfil*-hadith: "My servant keeps drawing near to Me through supererogatory deeds until I love him; and when I love him..." — al-Bukhārī 6502 — as the tradition's own sīra of love) — at which point the believer's love of God is flawless because counted with God's own.

**The Sight on the Day It Burned**

The verse closes upon the moment of final sight: *wa law yara alladhīna ẓalamū idh yarawna al-ʿadhāba anna al-quwwata li-llāhi jamīʿan wa anna Allāha shadīdu al-ʿadhāb* — "if those who do wrong could but see, when they behold the punishment, that power belongs to God altogether, and that God is severe in punishment." Al-Rāzī notes the optative reading: the verse may equally be taken as an address to the Prophet's vision — *had you seen* the wrongdoers *when they saw* the punishment: upon that day their resistant hearts perceive in full the market-collapse of every rival: their *andād* cannot shield; every human and stone power counted, *one single Power holds the whole account*: *al-quwwatu li-llāhi jamīʿan* — "power is altogether God's": the phrase closing all hierarchy-claims of heaven and earth; *and God is severe in punishment*: the quality the wrongdoers denied in the world, now standing before their eyes. The tradition has taught through this verse that the theology of *andād* is not settled in abstract reasoning but at the very moment of exposure: the day the counterfeit love-objects crumble, the soul sees in fullness which love had been the valid one — but it sees it too late for its own salvation: *would that they see now* is the verse's present-tense lesson to the living: every rival set up in the heart, when counted-upon at the world's edge, will prove as the stone idols of Makkah on the day of the conquest: mute and fallen.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:166

> **˹Consider the Day˺ when those who misled others will disown their followers—when they face the torment—and the bonds that united them will be cut off.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Scene of Disavowal**

Then — continuing the sentence of verse 165's *had they but seen* — comes the great cinema of the judgment: *idh tabarraʾa alladhīna uttubiʿū mina alladhīna ittabaʿū wa raʾaw al-ʿadhāba wa taqaṭṭaʿat bihimu al-asbāb* — "when those who were followed disavow those who followed, and they see the punishment, and the ropes are cut from between them." The commentators make clear the cast of the two troupes: *those who were followed* — the leaders of misguidance: the chiefs of idolatry, the satans, and more broadly every patron who set himself at the head of error and made himself an *andād*-rival of God (as Ibn ʿAbbās's school reads it: the old callers of all generations who cried away from God) — and *those who followed* — the rank-and-file of followers: the ordinary worshipper who had taken his creed from the mouths of the chiefs: and on the Day when the account-books are laid flat and every rope tested, the leaders of misguidance turn upon their own followers: *tabarraʾa* — "they disavowed" — a full renunciation upon that Day, with voice and heart united: *we have nothing to do with you* — the very words that the verse renders in the splash of the most mystical theater of the sūrah.

**The Ropes Cut**

The image of verse 166 turns upon the last word's meaning: *al-asbāb* — "the ropes, the bonds" — the plural ties that held the followers to their followed-chiefs — exploded in one blow. The commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī) count the *asbāb* variously: the family-bonds, the business-bonds, the affection-bonds, the deed-bonds, all of which, on the Day, no longer carry anything across: the network that once promised help in every strait is revealed as the brown and crackling fronds of a dried-out cane, snapping under the least strain. And it is yet sharper: it is the very ropes that were once hung from God to His creatures that were cut: nothing between him and God now holds, the follower had already snapped his own cord to God by setting up in His stead the idols now mocked in this very scene of mutual disavowal. The spiritual tradition reads the *asbāb*-severing with its own peculiar weight (the Sufis accordingly mark the whole worldly dependence on human means as the hanging of one's hope upon threads of asbāb that must be tested in the hereafter: daily *tawakkul* — trust in God — is precisely the training in dispensing with the rope-dependence that verse 166 will abolish): the believers' forewisdom is precisely to fore-cut the counterfeit cords of follower-followed while still in time, hanging their every weight instead upon the Hand to which every asbāb finally returns; and with that the verse closes its picture of the followers hung in the pall with no child-borne and no bail-bearer, their whole network "cut off from them," announced in the verse with God's own voice as the master of every assembly: rightful or wrong.

**The Punishment, Seen**

And *raʾaw al-ʿadhāb* — "and they see the punishment" — runs like a key through verses 165, 166 and 167: the seeing thrice repeated: the direct beheld thing — not rumor, not deduction — with the Book's repeated inscription of it as the Day's *act* of certainty: the false idols' ghost-economy collapses in their sight; the leader-follower formations turn traitor in their sight; the infernal depth arrives in their sight. The commentators from al-Ṭabarī to Ibn Kathīr notice the priority of the sight: it precedes every conclusion, every curse, every regret because it is the axis of certainty that was missing in the age of choice: when doubt ruled over them, truth was hidden; when they said, "we never believed," the truth was veiled — but now: seeing — and with it the whole chain of disavowal, regret, separation enacted. They shall see their leaders disclaim them; they shall see with their eyes the thing their flesh-hungered deeds had purchased; and in that seeing, they will know that God's declaration in verse 165 was ever true: *power belongs to God altogether, and God is severe in punishment.* The tradition carries the following sentence about the same Day from many standing accounts:

> *"When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, a crier will call: O people of Paradise! This will be eternity without death... and the people of the Fire will hear: O people of the Fire! This will be eternity without death."* (al-Bukhari 6548–6549; Muslim 2849 — the standing account of the abiding sealing, cited across the tafsīr tradition at verses of eternal residence)

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:167

> **The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, “If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us.” And so Allah will make them remorseful of their misdeeds. And they will never ˹be able to˺ leave the Fire.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"If We Had Another Turn"**

The drama of disavowal is now answered from the other side: *wa qāla alladhīna ittabaʿū law anna lanā karratan fa-natabarraʾ minhum kamā tabarraʾū minnā* — "and those who followed will say: if only there were for us another turn, that we might disavow them as they disavowed us." The word *karrah* — *a turn, a re-running* — is the Arabic language's own word for the second chance on the racetrack: let us return for another round; and the commentators explain the followers' request in full: *send us back, let us live again with this new knowledge — this time we will be the disavowers.* The classroom of the mufassirūn is careful about what *exactly* the regret consists in: it is not repentance (for repentance is the gate of God's mercy — and no version of this scene includes the word tawbah) — it is precisely the *Ḥasrah*, the burning regret of the man who sees the gated pasture from outside, the bitter wakefulness of the soul which, already inside the fire, computes all it has lost. This distinction is important for the understanding of the whole scene: God "shows them their deeds as ḥasarāt" — regrets — and it is told as a *showing*: He lays before them their own ledgers as the spectacle of every forgone good.

**Regret Shown, Not Felt Only**

The Book describes the sight *thus does God show them their deeds as a source of regret for them* — *kadhalika yurīhimu Allāhu aʿmālahum ḥasarātin ʿalayhim* — and the commentators turn the display over: it is not merely that they remember, but that the deeds are *presented* — the whole file of their lives hung before them as achieved ḥasarāt — as so many losses sent home: the occasions they neglected, the light they suppressed, the rival-loves abandoned late, each deed becoming a *Ḥasraḥ* — a regret rendering itself known. Al-Ṭabarī notes that the wish for a karrah will not extract them from their doom — for him this verse stands among the proofs that the punishment of the stubborn disbelievers endures: the wish itself is a tearing at the soul, but the gate is locked. And the commentators remember, in the parallel of 29:25 and elsewhere of the assembly of the fire-dwellers, that this talk of mutual cursing, disavowal, wishing to return, and refusal of release constitutes the scene-depth of the afterlife's knowledge — not as God's inventions imposed from without, but as the soul's own realized archive: the soul accusing itself, in the full transparent view of itself, that which it had truly been.

**Remedy for the Living**

The tradition of tafsīr turns about the verse as the pivot between followers and followed: faith by rope, obedience by rope, love by rope — the whole network of second-hand implementing — is the Book's great warning against: the believer does not build his heaven or hell upon the crowns of others, but upon his own turn: "if there were a turn" — the heeding outside of that word *if* is the greatest gift of verse 167 to the living: *there is a turn, and you have it; and you are in it now.* The Prophet's own insistent teaching remains the companion-clause of the verse, and the sūrah's two great consort-verses (the "unto Him all matters are returned" of 2:245, 2:281/2:210; "to Him we return" of 2:156) are written precisely against the tragic wishfulness of the karrah: return *before* the return is without return. The tradition's teachers of repentance have always preached this verse from a very precise angle: the disavowal the damned ask for — *we would disavow them as they disavowed us* — is set against the disavowal that reaches God in time: repentance for the leader-followed rope, in whichever form it recently hung around one's neck: cut the rope now, and your verdict will not be the karrah-sentenced wish of the fire: your karrah will be the day-by-day repentance of the living: *God grants other turns until the curtain falls and the rope of returns is pulled tight* — so the Pontiffs of piety in the community have urged upon every generation the repentance-doctrine of the Book: that God's gate of repentance — the *tawbah* promised to concealers (v.160) — never shuts to the living, but that the wishing of the dead is forever fixed.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:168

> **O humanity! Eat from what is lawful and good on the earth and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Universal Table Spread**

Turning from the fate of those who followed the ropes to the food that stands upon the whole earth, the sūrah now lifts the most comprehensive dietary address of the whole Book: *yā ayyuhā al-nāsu kulū mimmā fī al-arḍi ḥalālan ṭayyiban* — "O mankind! eat of what is lawful and good on the earth." The commentators mark both its breadth — *O mankind*: not only the believers; the permission belongs to the species — and its double-condition: *ḥalālan* (lawful) and *ṭayyiban* (good): the two-part sieve through which the food of the earth is drawn into Islamic life: *ḥalāl* — juristically released, adopted from the root's register of loosening/unbinding (the halter removed, the line untied: permission as a releasing of goods into the servant's use); *ṭayyib* — good, pleasant, wholesome — the food that can be enjoyed without hidden spoilage of body or spirit. And the double filter's very necessity — eating *of* (mithu *min*: *from*, partitive) — is read with the second clause of the verse: *wa lā tattabiʿū khuṭuwāti al-shayṭān* — "and do not follow the footsteps of Satan." The instrument of Satan's deception is stepped by the very word *khuṭuwāt*: footsteps — one small print at a time — the hook-implement of gradualism: the offenses of diet seldom come in a single stride; they creep in print by print, little tracks of justification: the words from an unclean quarter here, the doubtful plate there, until the whole course has been gone by the following of footprints.

**Occasion and Universal Rollout**

The occasion-reports connect the verse's descent both to its universal address and to its local application: al-Qurṭubī transmits that the idolatrous tribes of Thaqīf, Khuzāʿah, and Banū Mudlij had imposed upon themselves artificial fasts from certain animals (the same catalog of self-forbiddings the Book reproves in 5:103's listing of the inventors of baḥīrah and sāʾibah: cattle whose ears were slit or whose riders were tabooed out of the common diet by superstition), and the verse descended dismissing their religiosity of restriction: *eat of the lawful and good*: let no tribe make a liturgy of the forbidden where God never wrote one; but the whole unfolding of the verse leaves the law open to every age and nation: eat — then distinguish (good and lawful as paired requirements, cutting away equally the forbidden kinds and the spoiled kinds), and refuse Satan's stepping-stone seductions. The commentators supplement the occasion-report with the general divine-saying of the authentic hadith (Muslim 2865 — from ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār):

> *"God says: 'I created My servants as ḥanīfs (pure monotheists); then the satans came to them — diverted them from their religion, and forbade them what I had made lawful for them."*

— the exact diagnosis of the Thaqīf-type traditions: the ṭayyib-of-earth hold wrongfully fastened since the Devil's day of marriage to superstition.

**Food and the Answering of Prayer**

The teachers of piety invariably bring to this verse the import of the celebrated hadith of acceptance (carried by Muslim, al-Tirmidhī and others through the centuries at the head of the dietary tradition — the very instance the tafsīr cites here): a man stretches out his hands to heaven, having long journeyed — *My Lord! My Lord!* — *while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothes are unlawful* — *how then can his prayer be accepted?* — and the immediate companions' reading of the verse becomes practical in that very direction: eat ḥalāl and ṭayyib, that your duʿāʾ be heard; and the tradition adds the longer-standing mechanical account (attributed to the Companion tradition while the precise isnād's strength is debated): *one forbidden morsel* renders the body breaking itself upon godliness for forty days — whether literal or as the school-reading suggests, the scale of the bar-buffer grows with the morsel's repeated kind. The Sufi commentators, upon all of this, read the verse as the eating-discipline of the godly: eat ḥalāl *from* the earth that God has freely given — eat ṭayyib with thankfulness; and never make of your stomach the seat of a second religion either by superstition-restrictions nor by superstition-excesses: thus the footstep-avoidance of Satan carries all along the line of the believer's bodily life, and the verse is set to guard the heart not merely from polytheism's abstract rivals, but from the lawful-and-good forgotten — the very securities of the whole Islamic jurisprudence of food-and-drink grow out of this single, universal sentence, commanded to all men, now and always.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:169

> **He only incites you to commit evil and indecency, and to claim against Allah what you do not know.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Devil's Three Orders**

The verse now dissects the satanic voice in perfect serial: *innamā yaʾmurukum bi'l-sūʾi wa'l-faḥshāʾi wa an taqūlū ʿalā Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn* — "he only commands you to evil and indecency — and to say of God what you know not." The commentators unfold the full triad in order of rising gravity. First: *al-sūʾ* — evil: the whole field of the morally bad, the illicit profit, the hurt against neighbor, the false turning in the world: the Devil's daily concerns among the steps of transactions and desires. Second: *al-faḥshāʾ* — the grave decency-crimes: the Islamic scale's deeper crimes — licentiousness, flagrancy in sexual and bodily life — laid much lower than everyday evil but of the same satanic rope: in the Islamic man's ladder of temptation, *al-faḥshāʾ* hangs at the last branches: from evil-thought to evil-deed to evil-habit to open indecency: the footprints of the Devil's teaching (as the companion 2:168 already warned) travel from the one extreme to the other by khuṭuwāt, slender, seductive, repeatable. Third and greatest: *wa an taqūlū ʿalā Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn* — "and to say about God what you know not": the verse crowns the Devil's manual with the tampering of God's own file: the lying upon God — inventing lawful/unlawful on His name, attributing names and promises He never uttered, pretending commands and concessions without scriptural warrant — the very thing the foregoing verses have exposed (cf. 2:80's "few numbered days" talk; 2:135's millah-claims), which the Book will return to with the most fearsome framing at 7:33 and elsewhere: the three heads of the Devil's commission thus fixed: pull men into evil; pull men into shamelessness; pull men into lying upon God.

**The Theology of Uttering Without Knowledge**

The commentators notice the Book's own taxonomy: the order climbs — *evil*, *indecency*, then the utterance against God: the scheme of separate crimes converging into the last, which is held the most severe: for in saying of God *what you know not*, Satan works at the truth's own shrine: with evil he solicits the lower desires; with indecency he solicits the animal-shamelessness; but with unauthorised speech about God he solicits the very organ of religion: lying in God's name, inventing His said word, forging His image by guessing — the head of the Devil's work, for by it all the other crimes are justified *as religion*, so that his market stands finally equipped: sin *endorsed by the altar.* Al-Ghazālī's school follows the outline in many texts: the most dangerous of the gates of Satan is not pleasure nor greed but *the unauthorized word upon God* — and all the sciences of Islamic law and theology rise guardedly in the course of verse 169: the schools' insistence upon *it is not lawful to say of God's ruling what one knows not* — and the schools' citation of this verse at the question of the unlicensed scholar — confirm the verse's own placement: the third satanic order attacks the seat where God's authority should hold court within the mind: and where the mind begins to speak of God "what it knows not," ritual and creed at once become the Devil's own clay: divorce the truth of the shariʿa from evidence — and you hold immediately in your hand the Devil's own blind-fold.

**The Speech-Guarantee of Islam**

The tradition's subsequent application of the verse has been to all the major speech-fields of the religion — the hadith-scholar gives it with every caution before citing an unverified report; the faqih of law-book tradition cites it for every judgment sworn beyond evidence; the theologian cites it for every creedal guess passed off as doctrine. The Prophet ﷺ warned near the same file:

> *"Whoever says about God what he knows not has prepared his own seat in the Fire."* — and there is the Sufi's dread-echo within the heart: *"whoever speaks of the hidden knowledge before it is his from God loses the inner state."* (the former is al-Bukhari 137 and Muslim 1719's complement from the traditions about the fabricator upon God — carried at this verse across the tafsir tradition)

The believer thereby gathers from the verse's triad the grimmest arithmetic of Islamic speech-discipline: nothing in religion can legitimately be uttered upon God without His clear charter: lawful-forbidden, promise-threat, said-unsaid, all belong to the opening-name of God, who is within His own speech the sole authority — and the Devil's entire program, in its three departments, is here stripped of disguise by God's own naming of it: *he only commands you to evil and indecency, and to say of God what you know not.* The believer, knowing his three mandates, answers with the defenders' formula of the Sunna, not to utter without knowledge what he knows not of God: for no lie upon God can lie beneath a prayer Islamic accepted, and no religion is safe when its speech is built to order rather than traced from the skies.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:170

> **When it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.” ˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Calls and the One Refusal**

Behind the Devil's three commands stand the men who execute them, and the Book displays their formula: *wa idhā qīla lahumu ittabiʿū mā anzala Allāhu qālū bal nattabiʿu mā alfaynā ʿalayhi ābāʾanā* — "and when it is said to them: follow what God has sent down — they say: rather we follow what we found our fathers upon." The commentators first identify the company that was its historical carrier — the same pagan custodians of Makkah and the Jewish-campaigning mendicants of Madinah who ran within the sūrah's files of earlier indictments (v.14's following Satan; the Thaqīf-and-Khuzāʿah artificial prohibitions at v.168): wherever new Revelations press, the answer remains *we keep to what we found our fathers doing.* Yet the verse's own movement is broader than its Arabic happenings: *wa idhā qīla* — *whenever it is said*: the Book's whole pedagogical device is committed to the universalizing of the formula: the refusal that echoes among times unmentioned — the hellenized scribe in the sixth century who would not cross to the new Light; the court-theologian of the late ummah who would not return his charters to the sources; the modern ideologue, secure among his fathers' declarations of their own constructions — the same response-word echoes across fourteen centuries: *bal nattabiʿu mā alfaynā ʿalayhi ābāʾanā* — the Arabic *alfaynā* laying upon *found them* (the book's same *wajada*-foundation as heritage's finding: not inquiry, not proof — merely finding), the printed premise of traditionalism in all its forms — the Book breaking down each of the Twelve Tribes of StayingPut who judge religion by census rather than by God's descent.

**"Even If Their Fathers Understood Nothing?"**

The Book answers its heartbreaking fidelity with a question that sets reason against habit: *a-wa law kāna ābāʾuhum lā yaʿqilūna shayʾan wa lā yahtadūn?* — "what — even if their fathers understood *nothing*, and were not rightly guided?" The doubling is precise: *ʿaql* and *hidāyah*: the twin measures of the Book: to *understand* (the intelligence as the sectioning-grace), and to *be rightly guided* (the guidance by which understanding becomes a way): men seated in neither fathers nor sons — and the Book utters its question into all the future epochs: let a generation so worship tradition that *whether* their fathers had grasped anything is never asked — whereupon the Book's question follows them: *whose fathers? — why these, other than because they lived first?* The great question is placed in the form we call the argument of absurdity: *even if their fathers understood nothing and were not guided, would mere found-upon-ness stand as your ground?* — upon this question the Book had already laid its parallel at 5:104 ("sufficient for us is that wherein we found our fathers"), and again at 31:21, 43:22–24 — the sūrah standing in a whole line of verses by which Islam from the beginning stood as the *refusal of the ancestral veto*: the Prophet's own preaching against the pagans turned, from the very first day, on this verse's own counsel.

**The Islamic Measure: Tradition by Truth, Not Truth by Tradition**

The tradition adds anxiety's balance-wheel: for the verse is not an evacuation of the past itself (Islam is *rich* in the honoring of fathers — the sūrah's own Abraham-block had already praised the *millat of our father* in 2:128–129), but a sorting of *which* fathers are to be followed: Abraham — who had received understanding and guidance from God — *he* is to be followed (the Book's distinguishing the two kinds of ancestors-in-faith at 2:128 versus 2:170 is part of its exact anatomy of the idolaters' misuse of inheritance); the ignorant fathers whose only warrant is that they came before — *they* are not to be followed. It was exactly this sorting that the Prophet's people effected between the idolatrous generations and the patriarchal generations, and so Islam was shown from its beginning, by its own first sound, as not "breaking with tradition" in some abstract sense, but as *repairing tradition*: following Abraham while refusing Abu Jahl, following the Prophet while refusing the tribal captains who never opened their scriptures. And so the Muslims have kept their rule ever from this verse: tradition, in Islam, is to be measured by truth and not truth by tradition; and every ancestral practice, no matter how long built, is measured against God's descent — *what God has sent down* — with the understanding (*ʿaql*) and the guidance (*hudā*) of the Book: so that the community of faith may be held immune from the suspicion of 2:170: *even if their fathers understood nothing* — and so walk precisely on into the original light of what has been sent down.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:171

> **The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger’s warning˺ is like a flock not comprehending the calls and cries of the shepherd. ˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb and blind so they have no understanding.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Herder and the Herd**

The verse opens its parable immediately upon the heels of 2:170's fathers-blind adherence — and the simile is famous: *wa mathalu alladhīna kafarū ka-mathali alladhī yanʿiqu bi-mā lā yasmaʿu illā duʿāʾan wa nidāʾan* — "the likeness of the disbelievers is as the likeness of one who calls out at that which hears nothing but a summons and a shout." The commentators dwell on the ingredients: *yanʿiq* — the word of the shepherd's cry to his flock: the bleat-caller whose voice sends the immovable camel or the uncomprehending sheep hurdling onward; the creatures do not understand one word of the sounds themselves, and yet they trample onward by their noise: the flock-capacity is adequate only for noise and reply-to-noise. This is placed as the very likeness of the disbeliever's relation to revelation: the call of the Prophet ﷺ and of God falls upon them — and their response clusters as the aught attendance of cattle: hearing occurs; understanding does not; motion springs — they answer, they quarrel, they follow-by-habit — but the words themselves, with their meaning, enter nowhere: the carrying-through is absent because the mechanisms of their ears are filled with something else: the noise of their fathers' vocables (v.170) and the hum of the Devil's steps (v.168). The commentators point as well to the parable's twin positions: the harder reading makes the Prophet the shepherd calling at the heedless herd; the softer reading (al-Ṭabarī's register) makes the disbelievers themselves the *nāʿiq* — the shouter — calling at idols: each side listening to itself, both locked into a conversation without content.

**The Triple Sealing: Deaf, Dumb, Blind**

Then the verse completes the triple verdict by changing from simile to outright description: *ṣummun bukmun ʿumyun fa-hum lā yaʿqilūn* — "deaf, dumb, blind — they do not understand." The school notes the identical words as verse 18 within the sūrah's very opening (of the hypocrites there: *ṣummun bukmun ʿumyun*), except for the terminal qualifier: at 2:18's ladder of hypocrites the book had said *fa-hum lā yarjiʿūn* — "they shall not return"; here the book says *fa-hum lā yaʿqilūn* — "they do not understand": the two terminal clauses, parallel and distinguished, dissolve to the endeavor the whole sūrah teaches: the hypocritical hear-and-turn — the disbelieving hear-and-not-receive: the two dooms plant at the two ends of the same corridor: wherever the Holy Word is made the shepherd's bleat to be answered at noise-level alone, the heart has already taken the triple seal of ṣumm-bukm-ʿumy — the sensory abdication that is not organic but posited (the Book never says they are *by nature* deaf — all three defects are placed as *accomplished* after their own choice, verbs of sealing rather than statutes of nature: *they have made themselves deaf, dumb, and blind*), and its standard child — *lā yaʿqilūn* — *they understand not*: the final passivity-no-explanation of the sūrah's whole diagnosis since 2:6.

**The Parable in Every Age**

The verse is remembered by the tafsīr tradition just where parables of the divine discourse on hearing are given: with the prophets' words, with the Book's own calling to the creation, with the call of the believers: 2:171 teaching what lies beneath every Kaffir-turned: the ear is jammed at a medium — one hears, one does not receive: the medium between God and man closed by the triple seal — and the tradition of Islam preserves the complementary hadiths in which the praying believers are commanded at the moment of prostration *not* to recite at the moment the imam recites aloud, and counsel all and sundry instead: *listen* — *anṣitū* — the Quran's own remedy against the deaf heart of 2:171 (17:46's "We placed coverings on their hearts..."; 7:179's "they have hearts with which they do not understand..." — the same register): because the threefold clouding of the senses is not the end of God's remedies — it is the presenting-symptom: the Muslim's answer is at all times to scrub the ear by ḥusn al-istimāʿ, the heart by the remembrance of God (dhikr), the tongue by truthful speech: the heard word answered by hearing, the called one by answering, by the Light's own appointed training — for everyone who has been sounded with the call of God and responded *noiselessly*, in the dust of his fathers' footprints — for him in particular stands the verse's final double warning: *hearing and blindness, over him are they sealed — they understand not at all.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:172

> **O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided for you. And give thanks to Allah if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Mankind to the Believers**

The narrower service-address now follows upon the universal address of verse 168: where the whole of mankind had been summoned to eat what is lawful and good, here the *believers* are called to the specific pairing of eating and gratitude: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū kulū min ṭayyibāti mā razaqnākum* — "O you who believe — eat of the good things We have provided you" — *wa shkurū li-llāhi in kuntum iyyāhu taʿbudūn* — "and give thanks unto God, if it is Him you worship." The believers' address has its own distinct purpose-food: where the first address (v.168) was universal — eat-and-refuse-Satan's-footpaths — the second (v.172) is confederate: eat-and-thank, among those who recognize the provision's authorship: for it adds to the food the name of the One who had given it: *We have provided you* — God reading the eaters' whole rations book over His own signature: every morning's bread and afternoon's fruit set down, without intermediary in the accounting although through numberless hands in the agricultural journey, as *God's provision*, and the eating therefore coming before its questioning of identity: you who eat from the same Provider's table — worship only that same Provider. The thanksgiving the verse attaches has a particular diction: *shkurū li-llāh* suggests both words and deeds — acknowledged thanks of the tongue and succeeded thanks of a life spent in worship — and the subordinate clause delivers the question in the sharpest possible form: *if it is Him you worship* — pointed as it were into the worshipper's midriff: *if He is the One you worship, then let thanks be paid to Him* — for to have eaten from His provision while giving thanks at false altars is the very imbalance of accounts the sūrah has been weaving through its idol-rivals' section (2:165's *andād*; 2:170's fathers' marks): worship shows by thanks.

**Food as Primary Worship**

The verse is often read by the tradition's favorite provision-difference: some foods, al-Ṭabarī explains, are *ṭayyibāt* — the class of good things (clean, healthy, clean-gotten, God-given, of the pleasing kind); some are by contrast *khabīth* — the class of the loathsome, dirty, and corrupt (the same pair the Prophet's context defines at 5:47's forbidding of the khabīth to the booty-generation). The eating is thereby set by divine discourse within the infrastructure of worship rather than against it: *the meal itself* is mikveh of worship's chain — for the believers' obedience in eating the clean-given is itself a *ḥukm*: a judgment to be offered to God in the good things. Al-Ghazālī's spiritual tradition points out the precise subtlety: the food carries as worship only insofar as the thanks precedes it, accompanies it and follows it: food eaten with no thanksgiving-economy — with the basmalah omitted, the conversation profane, the satiety-masked forgetfulness — has no share in *wa'shkurū li-llāh*: the very middle of the meal from the heavens stands *bound* through thankfulness to God, and disconnected from Him, food is worship's counter-current: while connected through thanksgiving, even the bread-and-water meals of the ascetics are religious professional through and through.

**The If-Clause That Tests Every Mouthful**

The verse's ending — *in kuntum iyyāhu taʿbudūn* — "if it is Him you worship" — has carried through the centuries of tafsīr a most alarmed examining power: the very conditional sentence — the little word *in* ("if") — is granted by God to the believers as the *testing particle*: it is as if He, by spacing the thanks from the food by the *if*, instituted an examination-point upon every mouthful: *you who call yourselves worshippers of Me — trace the lines: is what you eat ṭayyib from My provision; do you give thanks for it at My name; do you eat as one who worships?* And the spiritually-taught commentators tie it to the community's standing formula of gratitude, the supplication reported directly from the Prophet's own table etiquette:

> *"The Prophet ﷺ said upon a meal: O God, bless us in what You have provided us, and shield us from the punishment of the Fire."* (al-Muwaṭṭaʾ and Ibn al-Sunnī's record of the Prophet's eating-remembrances, in the tradition of the bismillah-at-meal forms: Bukhārī records the command to recite the basmalah before eating at 5376)

"Whoever attains to recognizing the Provider in the provision," the commentators finally bring home, "already possesses the *if*-conditional of verse 172 fulfilled before even his first morsel is swallowed — the eating then colored from the start by the gratitude commanded in the verse — and from such mouths the morsel becomes a certificate of the faith whose worship is *God*, *only*, *always*."

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:173

> **He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity —neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—they will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Four-Chambered Prohibition**

With the general invitation settled, the Book destines the dietary map's hard borders, and the verse announces them with impressive economy: *innamā ḥarrama ʿalaykumu al-maytata wa'l-dama wa laḥma al-khinzīri wa mā uhilla bi-ghayra Allāh* — "He has only forbidden to you carrion, and blood, and the flesh of swine, and that over which other than God has been invoked." The school feels the exactness of the tradition's four pillars of prohibition: (1) *al-maytah* — carrion — the animal that dies of itself, unslaughtered, its death natural or accidental rather than human-manage; (2) *al-dam* — "the blood" — the effusive, poured kind, distinguished by the jurists from residual blood in flesh; (3) the flesh of swine — the species whole among the four categories, the juristic fine-points about which (such as whether necessity permits its fat where its flesh does not, in certain schools) never disturb the absolute species-wide ban of the flesh itself for this ummah; (4) *mā uhilla bi-ghayri Allāh* — what was consecrated to an other-than-God name: the animal slaughtered at idol altars, killed in the name of a shrine's dead relative or a tribe's practiced hedge-guardian. The commentaries add (with precision, and with Ibn Kathīr's generalization): the whole brief register of prohibition is given as binding *for this community*, alongside its exact siblings at 6:145 and 16:115, its fuller form appearing at 5:3: and the eaters of Islam are thereby set within neither the scrupulous extension-lines of the Jewish dietary law nor the pagans' arbitrary self-imposed taboos: they may eat everything of God's provision *except* these four — *innamā* — *only* these four: the confinement being itself divine mercy (as in 7:157's account of the Prophet who "permits them the good things and forbids them the corrupt things" — the ummah's rightful table filled, its margins sealed).

**The Emergency Clause**

Then the mercy-valve is opened within the very same verse: *fa-mani iḍṭurra ghayra bāghin wa lā ʿādin fa-lā ithma ʿalayh* — "but whoever is compelled by necessity, without transgressing or exceeding — upon him is no sin." The commentators mark the conditions: *iḍṭurra* — forced by hunger to the door of the instructed flesh, in a state below that of ordinary down-going: the comparison is drawn at once by the madhhabs into the teachings on the *ḍarūrah* — necessity-permits: the food thus eaten under true compulsion is neither *bāghin* — transgressing, aiming at the sin's own pleasure (eating out of desire and appetite rather than out of survival) — nor *ʿādin* — exceeding — eating beyond the measure of survival, treating the emergency as an opened granary. Within those two boundaries, the school establishes, the forbidden is released, and the forgiven and the merciful witness the inscription of the two names in the verse's very sealing: *inna Allāha ghafūrun raḥīm* — truly God is the Forgiving, the Merciful: the Forgiving being the Ghost of the act that annihilates; the Merciful the Godhead of the descent of a grace that not only absolves but preserves. The tradition applauds the mercy of the whole architecture: God's covenant was never the starvation-torture of the believers in wastelands separated from unlit fireside; He forbade categories, then opened them *under necessity*, making the forbidden itself the contingent exception-proof: the pattern of Islam's entire jurisprudence — *everything forbidden returns under true necessity* — is already sealed in its first prototype in this simple verse of al-Baqarah.

**Divine Economy as Virtue**

The Sufi commentary tradition attaches to verse 173 the further measure of provision-ethics: the fourfold prohibition is God's covenant to the believers to live from a table in which the dead, the bloody, the swinish, and the name-of-idols have no part: it shapes a body free of carrion's undertones and of idol-ritual's hidden sponsorship alike; and the Dispensation of necessity — a category for sudden collapse that had in it no permission to found a shop in the forbidden — is God's clemency as it were within the law, without relinquishing the law: the believer lives inside a *ḥalāl-rich* economy with the borders guarded from either side: borders guarded by prohibition, and borders guarded by a Doorless border-guardian: *our practice is no fruit of superstition, nor of affliction* (as al-Ṭabarī's school concludes): it is our covenant with the God of true provision and true mercy; and between the pillars of *innamā ḥarrama* and *fa-man iḍṭurra* the whole of Islamic law opens forever — *the law, absolute in its four barriers; the mercy, unspalled in its necessity-opening; and the God of both, forgiving and merciful.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:174

> **Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain consume nothing but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment, nor will He purify them. And they will suffer a painful punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Concealing-and-Selling: The Double Verb**

The verse joins the two sūrah-long blame-streams into one compound sin: *inna alladhīna yaktumūna mā anzala Allāhu mina al-kitabi wa yashtarūna bihi thamanan qalīlan* — "truly those who conceal what God sent down of the Book and *buy* with it a small price." The commentators note the Book's threading here of its two previous files: the concealment of verses 159–161 — the burying of revealed evidence — and the *purchasing* of verses 41, 79, and 175 — the financial trafficking in revealed speech. What this adds is decisive: the concealment now has a *price-tag*: the hiding was never arid intellectual reticence: it was commerced: the custodians discovered that, hid away, the buried truth gave them unprecedented command (the muftis' dues, the fattiers' offices, the professional advantages of being the sole keeper of the source of privilege) — in Ibn Kathīr's and al-Rāzī's terms, they sold the citizens' birthright for the stool asked of Esau: a portion of bread, the people losing what even the children of their Book possessed by right. And the judgment equates the internal price of the sale with fire: *ulāʾika mā yaʾkulūna fī buṭūnihim illā al-nār* — "those eat nothing in their bellies but fire" — the very expenses consumed are reckoned as mere flame-eaten in the making, on the very same analog the Book gives at 4:10 ("they shall eat fire in their bellies") on the consumed property of orphans: the body swallows what was spent by the soul-sale of God's words, and that what *becomes* within the hereafter fire itself.

**Silent God, Ungreeting God**

Then the three layers of their penal sentence are sounded — the first two spiritual and the third drawn from the tradition's most pitiless formulas: *wa lā yukallimuhumu Allāhu yawma al-qiyāmati wa lā yuzakkīhim* — "God will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them." The commentators have given patient analysis of this silence within the broader file of the same formulas (at 3:77 — with its own list: "God will not speak to them nor look at them... and theirs is a painful punishment"): for the Book *elsewhere* has God speaking at the Day: He questions enemies (15:92-93 — *by thy Lord we shall question them all*); He says to the dwellers of fire "Be gone, speak not to Me" (23:108); and yet here He withholds speech. Al-Rāzī's resolution — which enjoyed the school's widest favor — runs thus: the withheld speech here is of *greetings*: no word of salām, no word of reassurance, no word of praise: rather than no words *at all*: for the God who is lastly heard to say *Be gone!* still speaks only punitive speech: and al-Qurṭubī quotes the Arabic idiom: in ordinary speech *he did not speak to him* is said of the gravely angry. The suppression of purification — *lā yuzakkīhim* — runs the same way (a stroke above the whole class of human achievements): He will not declare them *tahir* — cleared and purified as the saved are declared purified: nor praise their actions: nor set right their misdeeds (the verb zakkā ambidextrously meaning to purify and to pronounce purified): the purifying sentence He will simply not speak — for concealment's lineage disqualifies forever the buried work: *we are as we are*. And so the last name comes in without variation: *wa lahum ʿadhābun alīm* — "and theirs is a painful punishment": the fourth element fixed as at all the verses of the same register (3:77 etc.): the *alīm* — the fiercely-painful — appended as the full completion of the sentence: silence from the Greeting Lord, purification withheld, and then pain held at its full measure — all of it earned by that single paltry-price sale of what had been the property of all mankind.

**The Verse in Islamic Ethics of the 'Ulamāʾ**

The tradition's own use of the verse has been consistent grave-side: the ulama of the ages have made verse 174 — memorized in sequence from generations of Madrasa lessons — the torment-verse of all concealment-tainted dispensers of religion: the imams of the Salaf cited it at every failure of tabyīn by those who held the offices of the knowledge-trade: and the school cites the Prophet's own warning about the fire-bridle for the concealer of knowledge — *"Whoever is asked about knowledge and conceals it, God will bridle him with a bridle of fire on the Day of Resurrection"* (Abū Dāwūd 3658; al-Tirmidhī 2649) — the canonical word upon knowledge-traders, present and accounted for in the tradition's reading of our verse. The verse's own sentence ties together God's silencing and the fire's consumption: *for those who buy God's words with a small price have already committed their bellies to the reckoning* — and this verse stands, after the Book's verses of tampering and the sūrah's many repeated reports of concealment, as the deepest picture of the trader's opposite-world: their eating is fire, their God is silent, their purification denied, and their punishment already named over them.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:175

> **They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment. How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Bad Exchanges Totalled**

The Book now computes the ledger of the concealment-sellers — and the sum turns out to be a pair of bankrupting exchanges: *ulāʾika alladhīna ishtaraw al-ḍalālata bi'l-hudā wa'l-ʿadhāba bi'l-maghfirah* — "those are they who bought error at the price of guidance — and punishment at the price of forgiveness." The verb *ishtaraw* — "bought" — continues the sharp imagery of trade-exchange already used at verse 16 ("they bought error at the price of guidance; their trade did not profit") and verse 86 ("they purchased the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter"), but now the verse completes the whole exchange-grid: *two* wrong trades are rung up. First: *al-ḍalālata bil-hudā* — error for guidance: the teacher's-deeds brokers took the misdirection-laden product home, and paid down the one commodity the world-homes of every conscience trade upon: the guidance itself given in the page of the Book. By them, the guide was paid away, the ḍalāl was purchased with it. And second: *al-ʿadhāba bil-maghfirah* — punishment for forgiveness: the thing the keepers of the Book held in hand — their possession of God's forgiveness — was equally transacted away: in its stead they received the final bill: punishment. The pairing, with its exact grammar of exchange, is stupendous — and the imam al-Rāzī reads the structure as its own science of trade-disaster: not every bad bargain is like another bad bargain, but *this* bargain is the distinctly worst — and the tradition remembers how the Prophet ﷺ drew from the tun of commercial beatitudes the mortified fact:

> *"The two parties of a transaction have the option of canceling the transaction, so long as they have not parted — if they were truthful and made things clear they were blessed in their transaction, but if they concealed and lied, the blessing of their transaction was obliterated."* (al-Bukhari 2079, 2110; Muslim 1532 — the Prophet's great rule of commerce, placed by the tradition at all of the exchange-verses of the sūrah: 2:16, 2:86, 2:175)

**The Fire-Suffering Question Form**

And then the verse's final clause switches its voice from ledger to exclamation — *fa-mā aṣbarahum ʿalā al-nār* — "how patient they are toward the Fire!" — or, *how shall they endure the Fire!* — a line the tradition understands in every open register. The underlying Arabic form — *mā afʿalahu bi kadhdhā*, the "how-X!" of amazement — is read first as genuine amazement at the exchange's madness: *who buys fire with water, error with guidance? What kind of commerce prepares such endurance for the Fire — what patience do they build for its flames?* Some, as al-Ṭabarī records, tease out the secondary senses: *what drove them to such a deed that the fire became their end; what endures them upon it?* — the fire-patience they will need cannot come at the price they paid it: God has no disdainful irony here: rather the verse voices the reader's own astonishment at people who, freely surveyed the two objects, chose the fireward — personifying, as in all the Book's trading-verses (2:16, 2:86–87, 2:175, 4:44), the household stevedore who carried the books' ships to seaward with a ship-load of hell-bricks in the hold. The commentators read the verse as a fitting postscript to the whole foregoing financial file: the exchanges of verses 41, 79, 86, 175 collectively becoming the Madina-market's final judgment: the people sold divine revelation, the meters of its price, its accurate handling, and its public availability for position, price, pride — and at last the record closes with the reaction of the watcher rather than of the judge: *fa-mā aṣbarahum ʿalā al-nār* — *how shall they bear the Fire* — the sentence of the whole financial file, the sentence that turns at last the books' insights into flames' insight.

**A Verse for Every Trader**

The tradition reads the verse with a vista right into the 21st century, as it was read at the beginning: every modern trade is similarly booked against its anti-trade, every worth sold today for a momentary petty price — the khutbah-giving distracted by market-cauoting, the witnessing weighed down by opposing advantage, the fatwa-trading by agencies of equidistance: it is all being *sold* — and the second witness is not the trader's enemy, but the trader's keeper of the real reckoning: God will not speak with such traders on the day of needing Him (2:174): but the sentence here is not ended with divine silence alone: God speaks elsewhere, but the listener of verse 175 is left with the fire — and the astonished whole creation at their fire-patience in enduring something already foreseen: *how shall they endure it?* — and the tradition has always answered the book's amazement with the believers' adage of fear: it is receivable no endurance for it: *the fire asked: how shall they endure? and they will not: but the question is set to burn the living conscience: Hold not the book; sell not the signs; and ask not what the price returns in the hereafter: the price already stands against the two goods of the believer: guidance and forgiveness.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:176

> **That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth. And surely those who differ regarding it are totally engrossed in opposition.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The "That Is Because" Bridge**

The heart of the concealment-trial now receives its causal articulation: *dhālika bi-anna Allāha nazzala al-kitāba bi'l-ḥaqq* — "all this — because God has sent down the Book in truth." The demonstrative *dhālika* — "that" — reaches back (as al-Ṭabarī decides) to the whole punishment-parade of verses 174–175: the fire-eating in bellies, the God-silence, the purification withheld, the painful punishment, the bankrupt exchanges — and names its first premise: the Book God sent is *in truth*, exactly what its readers must receive with the reverence due to truth's own descent. The commentators note the proposition's structure: the concealment-sellers' sentence is not laid down upon any local crime-scale but upon one of the largest truths of the sūrah: *God Himself* has made the Book true: to bury it, to carve it, to sell its pages at the petty price of Madinah's own marts is to wage war upon truth at its springhead: every later act — every tampering at verse 75, every exchange of phrases from their places, every "we hear and we disobey" — stands condemned under the one premise: *nazzala al-kitāba bil-ḥaqq*. The truth-in-the-Book means further, with the school of al-Rāzī, that the Book testifies to *God's own guarantee*: no part of it derives from failure, mixing, or misdirection: it descends *in* truth (together with it) and *upon* truth (witnessing to it abidingly), its integrity binding upon everything beneath it — the tafsīr noting: to measure the concealment's crime of verse 174, we need first weigh the truth of verse 176's first premise.

**Schism Pronounced on Dissension**

The consequence to the differers is then named: *wa inna alladhīna ikhtalafū fī al-kitābi la-fī shiqāqin baʿīd* — "and truly those who differ about the Book are in far-reaching schism." The *shiqāq* — the cleavage — is the exact same noun used at verse 137 (the schism of those rejecting the whole creed) and at 2:176's own sister-verses (22:53; 38:2; 41:52) — and it is now named with its adjective *baʿīd* — *far, deep, extended* — the split whose cuts run far from the Book's own line, far between factions, far between factions and God Himself. The commentators note its diagnostic weight: difference-in-the-Book is not treated simply as intellectual dissonance: it is *reported* as schism from the truth: the disputants differ over the one descent-from-God, but the Book calls it *splitting* precisely because the alternative to the Book's reception is no friendly diversity: the splitting is what happens when the truth-Book descends among people of parts: the people divide themselves apart by what they each fragmentarly hold — rather than unite behind what God sends whole. Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī allow the verse's deep extension: the Book here can be either the one in the custodians' own hands (the Torah-Gospel whose altered readings had inaugurated the schisms of v.75 and v.79) or the descent of the Quran itself (to which their disputants divided and their concealed friends invited division) — and in each case the verdict is the same: difference over God's true descent is schism.

Schism baʿīd — *far-reaching schism* — as the commentator Qatādah and others gloss the adjective, is not mere sect-splitting: it is *direction-splitting*: the differing parties travel their separate routes away from the One Descent, widening always the gap between themselves just as the gap widens between themselves and God: their chosen difference being the *baʿīd* — the far-distance — into which God naturally lets them travel when they choose to position their own roads against His one road.

**The Rule of the Single Truth-Book**

The tradition derives from this exact verse the standing rule: dissension that would be licit in the face of an ambiguous human ordinance becomes the cleavage-punishment when the Book actually descended in truth is in question — and the sūrah's *shiqāq baʿīd* formul closes its long polemic against selective reception (2:85), distortion (2:75), selling-with-small-price (2:41, 174), concealing (2:140, 146, 159), and caprice-following (2:120, 145) in one line: *differing over the Book* is not a pluralism: it is a schism whose line is drawn far from God. The Prophet ﷺ is recorded through the tradition in the general warning-neighborhood of verses like this whenever seemingly minor divisions multiplied into schisms among the believers themselves:

> *"Beware of excess in religion: those before you were destroyed by excess in religion"* (al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah — the standing contexts of the dangers of narrow dispute over God's own word, cited across the tradition at the warnings against multiplication of sects in the Book of Tribulations)

The community's emendation — dissension upon the Book never allowed to settle — is nested in the same file: the differing schismatics travel further and further from the one descent, the one truth, the one criterion — and with verse 176 completed, the sūrah's long polemic against the various tamperers stands at its natural rest: *the Book in truth* — and every differing moved into its opposite: *the schism, far-reached*.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:177

> **Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets; who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives; who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and keep the pledges they make; and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity, and in ˹the heat of˺ battle. It is they who are true ˹in faith˺, and it is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Opening the Verse of Birr**

This is among the largest single verses of the entire sūrah — and the Book earlier scholars have called its articulation among the fullest summaries of religion in the whole Qur'an (often standing beside 4:136 and 2:285's rounds of the articles of faith). The address opens by pulling away the whole recent qiblah-burden: *laysa al-birra an tuwallū wujūhakum qibala al-mashriqi wa'l-maghrib* — "piety is not the turning of your faces toward the east and the west." The commentators fit it naturally into its moment: the believers had just undergone the transition from one qiblah to another, the talk of turning-where had dominated every conversation, and the People of the Book — who had their own directional claims (the Jews westward toward Jerusalem, the Christians eastward toward the sun-rising) — regarded the direction as the center of the creed; the verse now strips direction from the throne of piety and installs piety's true occupant: *birr* — the obedience well-settled in the heart (al-Ṭabarī), the entire bundle of true righteousness — the man whose believing, spending, prayer, oath-keeping, patience are all working together toward the One Lord. The verse does not retract the qiblah-commandment — it repositions it: direction is compulsion of the Book's custody; *birr* is the total frame in which the turning takes its proper, subordinated place.

**The Five Creed-Articles Folded In**

The enumeration of piety's profile then runs as the comprehensible ladder of the entire religion: *wa lākinna al-birra man āmana bi-llāhi wa'l-yawmi al-ākhiri wa'l-malāʾikati wa'l-kitābi wa'l-nabiyyīn* — "piety is: he who believes in God, and the Last Day, and the angels, and the Book, and the prophets." The commentators mark the list as the complete list of the essential credits of religion — the very five enumerated in the Jibril-hadith's definition of *īmān* (al-Bukhari 8/50; Muslim 8): belief in God, in His angels, in His Books, in His messengers, and in the Last Day — given here in the similar order (with the appointed places of angels/Book reversed outside, but with content preserved). God's Book names the five behind the moral life of the soul in this verse: religion is not routed into limb-first obedience (the direction of prayers etc.) even before the five articles, but the whole body of obligations are set *upon* these articles: no one owns piety through an ablution or qiblah-connected schedule unless his believing reaches the full list: the critical turning is from turning East and West toward *turning-centric-God-and-last-Day* — the pivot from ritual-rivalry to the theological core the community calls its *creed*.

**Giving Despite Love: the Invoice of the Soul**

Then the obligation-clause follows and runs on as the conduct-catalog: *wa ātā al-māla ʿalā ḥubbihi dhawī al-qurbā wa'l-yatāmā wa'l-masākīn wa ibna al-sabīli wa'l-sāʾilīn wa fī al-riqāb* — "and gives wealth, despite his love of it — to kinsfolk, orphans, the needy, the stranded traveller, beggars — and for captive-freedom." The phrase has been analyzed into two possible strands of grammatical reading: (a) *ʿalā ḥubbihi* — *despite loving it*: the giving what is dearest, the property wrested from the hand that cherishes it (cf. 76:8's same wording; the Book elsewhere says, "you will not attain piety until you spend from what you love": 3:92) — the position preferred in the older readings; and (b) *ʿalā ḥubbihi* — *on account of love of Him*: the giving because of the love of God — in which case the verse ceaselessly proclaims the fatherhood of all meaning (with God the final ground — bountiful of the whole great donation-economy). The commentators note the listing's shape: start at kinsfolk, proceed to the orphan on whose behalf the Law inserts the most abundant protections (4:2, 4:6 etc.), then the utterly destitute (*masākīn*), then the *ibn al-sabīl* — the stranded traveller — the far-from-home wanderer whom the ummah classically bundled among the zakah-categories (9:60), then the *sāʾilūn* — the ones who ask openly — then the *fī al-riqāb* — the ransoming of captive necks, the freeing of men from slavery, the Book's undoubted passion to extinguish the captive-market from within.

The prayer-and-zakat clause then follows in expected pairing — *wa aqāma al-ṣalāta wa ātā al-zakāh* — "and establishes prayer and gives the alms": the constant Islam-hadith couplet the whole Book ties together innumerable times (2:43, 2:83 etc.), and the verse's middle station between the creed-side and the conduct-side: religion's twin pillars planted squarely: then the covenant-side — *wa'l-mūfūna bi-ʿahdihim idhā ʿāhadū* — "those who keep their covenant when they covenant": and then the patience-clause, returning the whole sūrah's patience-theme back inside the framework of the great profile: *wa'l-ṣābirīna fī al-baʾsāʾi wa'l-ḍarrāʾi wa ḥīna al-baʾs* — "the patient in poverty (*with al-Ṭabarī noting baʾsāʾ as the straitness of provision, while ḍarrāʾ the pressure of illness and circumstance), and in the time of conflict*": the al-baʾs clause meeting the sūrah's ancestors of tribulation at verse 155 (those tested by fear and hunger) and amplifying their patience into active conflict situations.

**"Those Are the Truthful"**

The verse closes in the two-part laying-down that stamps the whole profile with its final proper names: *ulāʾika alladhīna ṣadaqū* — "those are they who have been truthful: *their believing has lodged in deeds and their deeds in character*" — *wa ulāʾika humu al-muttaqūn* — "and those are they who are the reverent." The two names close the sūrah's own golden arch: *al-muttaqūn* — the very name with which the sūrah opened, at verses 2–5 ("a guidance for the reverent: those who believe in the Unseen, establish prayer, spend from what We provided, believe in what was sent down before, are certain of the Hereafter") — now given its fullest articulated census: the muttaqī hearer of verse 2 is *this* man of 2:177, and therefore ushered from the Book's introduction through the thick of every Madinan test and controversy into the full format — believing, spending, praying, promising, patiently enduring — and is adjacent-declared with its other name, never forgotten in the tradition: *al-ṣādiqūn* — the truthful. It is widely reckoned, summing-up the centuries of commentaries from al-Ṭabarī onward, that the verse presents Islam's fullest one-verse creed-and-conduct: when a later convert asks *what is Islam?* after verses 2–5, the text-answer is placed by God at this verse: *the creed, the spending, the prayer, the zakat, the covenant, the patience — followed by the truth-name, and the muttaqūn* — and the tradition's own name for the human being painted in this verse is the one it has reserved for this verse's own seriousness from every teacher's classroom in every age: *the verse of the whole piety*.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:178

> **O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set for you in cases of murder— a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female. But if the offender is pardoned by the victim’s guardian, then bloodmoney should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously. This is a concession and a mercy from your Lord. But whoever transgresses after that will suffer a painful punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Retaliation Anchored and Bounded**

The sūrah now enters the first of its largest testament-law furlongs — the penal code of murder — and announces with stunning scope the recombing of the world's blood-feud life: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū kutiba ʿalaykumu al-qiṣāṣu fī al-qatlā* — "O believers: retribution has been prescribed for you concerning the slain." The *qiṣāṣ* — lex talionis, the "tracking-cut" (qaṣaṣa = to retrace the track step by step) — the law whose decipherment the tradition has read most carefully again and again against the precedent of the Arabs' infinite vendettas: tribe killing tribe for one man's blood seemingly without end, with glorification in quantity and degenerative motive in which the best blood might be required for a low-ranked dead man. The Book declares the law *kutiba* — prescribed, written down — the Law written onto the horizons of retaliatory claim and fixed once and forever: in number within tally, in rank by rank: *al-ḥurru bi'l-ḥurri wa'l-ʿabdu bi'l-ʿabdi wa'l-unthā bi'l-unthā* — "freeman for freeman, slave for slave, female for female." The jurists' long commentary over these three parallel phrases (quoted again, over the dispute with Scripture's own heritage, at 5:45: "a life for a life, an eye for an eye...") judges the verse as symmetrical-limitation rather than literal confinity: no one but the killer pays, and no one takes one single drop of innocent blood: the pre-Islamic escalation into whole-tribe extermination is legally wiped from Arabia by three short parallel clauses — the records of the Basūs war and the Khazraj feuds, which Arabia remembered for generations, standing as testimony to the lawless order these clauses abolished.

**Pardoner's Handheld Restitution**

The verse then opens the *very door of mercy* — the Islamic constitutional pivot of diya and pardon: *fa-man ʿufiya lahu min akhīhi shayʾun fa-ittibāʿun bi'l-maʿrūfi wa adāʾun ilayhi bi-iḥsān* — "if one is granted some pardon by his brother, let there be honest following-up and payment to him in goodness." The commentators comment over the exact mechanics: the kinsman-avenger (walī al-dam) of the victim is given choice beside the dead — he may exact blood-for-blood, or take the *diyah* — the blood-money — or forgive: by that choice he may "pardon" his brother (the very kinship-reminding word the verse employs: *min akhīhi* — *from his brother* — the *language* of the sentence is employed over and against the language of revenge: a mere *brother* — sat behind the crime). Al-Qurṭubī and the fiqh tradition dwell on the wording: *let it be followed honorably* — pursuing it neither with harassing importunity nor with frills of abuse nor with the sowing-of-future-hatreds that vendetta nourished: *and discharge the payment to him in goodness* — the payers' part: handsomely paid, at the arranged time, without making criminal capital of delay or starvation: the Book thereupon settles its pair of conditions of an indebted pardon — *respect on both sides* — and reads the verse as itself the mercy-paraphrase: *dhālika takhfīfun min rabbikum wa raḥmah* — "that is an alleviation from your Lord, and a mercy" — the mercy of the statutory pardon-avenue the Book is putting into all hands, once and forever.

**But After Pardon, No Transgression**

And the warning clauses close the circle: *fa-mani iʿtadā baʿda dhālika fa-lahu ʿadhābun alīm* — "whoever transgresses after this — his is a painful punishment" — the fiqh's ground-rule: once the route of pardon-with-compensation has been invoked and the matter discharged, the transgressor (whether by renewal of vendetta, by vengeance upon the payment-receiving parents of the avenging victim, or by returning to capture a hostage of blood) shall bear God's named punishment. The tradition's larger commentary on the whole verse, across centuries from al-Ṭabarī to the moderns, is the sūrah's nodal contribution to the Islamic jurisprudence of blood (the jurists call it the verse of *ḥadd al-qatl*: the fixed law of the killing itself, the same text-perch from which determination of *intentional*, and *quasi-intentional*, and *accidental* homicide began); and the verste's two-headed mercy of noun *raḥmah* and noun *takhfīf* — *alleviation and mercy* — stand like two gates stood behind its measured retaliation, its *retribution* — meaning not the revenge but the measured legal response sanctioned by state — and its *pardon* — the voluntary, mercy-steeped power invested in the avenging next-of-kin. The ummah's commercial traditions notoriously celebrated this original gentle structure: *"the blood of all Muslims is equal"* (Ibn Mājah 2682, Nasāʾī — the saying of the Prophet cited in the fiqh by the Ḥanafīs in defense of the full-blood equality of believers at retaliation) — the legal balance already certified by God in the three parallels of rank in His address, and the interchangeable heaven-choice carried in His merciful hand of pardon and iḥsān.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:179

> **There is ˹security of˺ life for you in ˹the law of˺ retaliation, O people of reason, so that you may become mindful ˹of Allah˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Death as Lifeguard: The Verse's Paradox**

In the very middle of settling retaliation and pardon, the Book lands its boldest doctrinal paradox: *wa lakum fī al-qiṣāṣi ḥayātun yā ulī'l-albāb laʿallakum tattaqūn* — "and there is life for you in retribution, O possessors of intellect — that you may be reverent." The commentators (al-Ṭabarī at the head) unfold the paradox as the Brightest of all the Book's legal aphorisms, their argument running deliberately against the surface: retaliation *is* death (the putting down of the killer), yet precisely *in it* life is preserved: for the threat of strict measured retribution works as the greatest brake upon the whole murder-market: whoever might kill to gratify passion, enrich ambition, or answer insult counts now, by law, with the counting *the price of blood*: blood is not free blood anymore; its wage is the transfuser's own life. According to the economic order the Book installs here, putting the killer's life to the balance sheet of blood itself maintains the lives of the living: the possibility of execution dammed-back is the most potent wall against murder's onset — so the whole people ride under the protection of its presence: *in retribution there is life*. "Life" here therefore stands on two legs: deterrence — the life saved by the fear of retaliation; and equity — the life *dignified* by the measured contour the law writes around each blood spilled: neither tribes' vendettas nor rulers' whims are the curbs of murder: the curbs of murder are *execution proportional to the crime*, with no vendetta beyond: so qiṣāṣ stands as a system that *saves life far more than it takes*.

**To the Master's-Kernels of People**

The verse's internals are addressed to a special company: *yā ulī'l-albāb* — "O possessors of intellect" — literally, *possessors of the kernels* (the Arabic lubb being the kernel within the husk, as of a nut): the Book opens the cantor ahead again, and calls by their very metaphor the men of kernel-life: those who can descend beyond the husk of the matter into its pith. The phrase across the Book's registers (2:197, 269, 3:7, 190 etc.) becomes its stock-name for penetrating mind-kind: to them alone this paradox is declared — and the tradition points its own acuity back upon the reader: the paradox of *retribution-as-life* cannot be scanned at the level of the husk: the man born to the husk hears *killing is law*; but the men of kernel hear the deeper machinery: *legalized strictness in killing keeps killing low*: and by those pairs the whole jurisprudential ingenuity of the verse is transported: qiṣāṣ begins as law and ends as *peace-living*: taking one life to keep thousands from ever being taken: that is the arithmetic no lawless terror can ever achieve. And with the same kernel-insight the commentators end at the piety-phrase *laʿallakum tattaqūn*: the law is not mere terror-management for deterrence's sake: it is a reverence-generating wall: *so that you may be God-fearing* — living lives conditioned by the fear of God's lawful consequence, the reverence being the Book's own foundation under all its levels of law.

**The Penal Faith Educating the Whole Ummah**

The tradition has preserved with this verse the broadest of its moral lessons about jurisprudence itself: law — as God's Book executes it — is not a deterrent-only discipline, but a teacher of *taqwā*: the fear of God's justice *within* society; the believer is trained by the law's presence to stand in awe of the life God has made sacred (the following verse 6:151's exact doublet: "do not kill the life that God has made sacred save for cause") — and what began with "retribution is prescribed" at 2:178 is brought to full life-measure at 2:179: the law is not only abstract fairness, not only crime's remover: it is a *life-saver*: it is "life for you" breathed through the law's own winds: the whole of the Law, by the deepest law-vision of Islam's own lawyers of the heart, is a *ḥayāh* — the preservation of life's species and structures under God — from the most trivial penalty up to the loftiest law of blood.
