The teachers never tire of marking the formula's sharpness: *the killing is to preserve the not-killing*: the compensation is to preserve its un-need: the whole legal structure is to wake men into reverence: and by verse 179's lips the whole ummah was ushered from the feud-dark of their memories to the new daylight of a proportioned, mercifiable, taqwā-scented law of blood.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:180

> **It is prescribed that when death approaches any of you—if they leave something of value—a will should be made in favour of parents and immediate family with fairness. ˹This is˺ an obligation on those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Testament Command**

The sūrah's law-furlong now turns from the life-preserving representative-laws of blood to the custody of property at life's edge: *kutiba ʿalaykum idhā ḥaḍara aḥadakumu al-mawtu in taraka khayran al-waṣiyyatu li'l-wālidayni wa'l-aqrabīna bi'l-maʿrūfi ḥaqqan ʿalā al-muttaqīn* — "it has been prescribed for you, when death draws near to one of you — if he leaves good (property) — the bequest for parents and kinsfolk in an honorable way: a duty upon the reverent." The commentators explain the *waṣiyyah* — the testament — on its original footing: this address came down before the great inheritance-verses (4:11–12) had been revealed, so that the first Islamic estate-law stood simply herein: when a man dies leaving property, he is to command by will that his parents and near relatives be beneficiaries of a goodly, *maʿrūf* portion — *in the recognized, fair way* — not blowing the property away in exotic charities nor starving the immediate kindred: the old-world testament had often been a tribal charter-sketch of gifts to allies and crews (the Arab testament-precedent being notoriously loose), and the Book's first estate-law re-anchors the whole practice at *kin-love* and at *honorable measure* — *bi'l-maʿrūf* being the formula by which every neighbouring duty of kinship had likewise been bound in the Book's earlier address (2:83's covenant-clause and its triple-layer kin-charities) — the testament being the last act of the deceased's kin-love, and thus never scratching generosity-feuds, blood-burials, vengeance-assets, or their like. The closing *ḥaqqan ʿalā al-muttaqīn* — the "true right upon the reverent" — renders the testament's making not a mere good habit but one of the reverent's special duties: their final obedience beyond which their instruments of living have run out: the death-near will, here installed by the Book, is the soul's *very last* item of *taqwā* — a fitting summit assignment for the verse that began its law-file at *retribution* (v.178).

**The Third and Its Margin: The Hadith's Frame**

Then the commentators map the verse against the revelation's shape after the inheritance-sūrah came down (4:11ff): the famous *ḥadīth* — "no bequest for an heir" (*lā waṣiyyata li-wārith*: Abū Dāwūd 2870; al-Tirmidhī 2120; in the same tradition of the Prophet's sunnah) — was delivered upon the settlement of automatic shares, which rendered testamentary provision for statutorily-inheriting kin void; the Prophet's own decisive exchange with Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ — who, sick at the Conquest of Makkah, asked what he might bequeath ("shall I bequeath two-thirds?" — "No"; "a half?" — "No") — fixed the outer bound ever after for the whole tradition:

> *"One-third, and a third is much: it is better to leave your heirs rich than to leave them beggars at the doors of other men."* (al-Bukhārī 2733, 2742, 5449; Muslim 1628 — from Ibn ʿAbbās's report of the Prophet's answer to Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ at the Conquest of Makkah)

and the jurists never swerved: the whole bequest-movement of property in Islam is bounded by one-third (*thulth*), the jurists being agreed thenceforward that any bequest beyond a third requires the consent of the heirs themselves; and harmlessness inside the third was made the rule ever after: the whole bequest-economy of Islam bears therefore the imprint of God's appointment (2:180) plus the Prophetic bound — and the moral continuance of the verse into the era of share-law is fixed by the school's resolution: after the fixed shares, the bequest stands for (i) the non-heir relation, (ii) the charity-destination, (iii) the welfare-endowment — while the inheritance-verses stand for heirs — and the two texts thereby become complementary chapters of one complete law rather than competitors.

**The Word in Its Companions' Circle**

The tradition is full of the verse's worked examples: for the men of the generation who first received it, the testament was no supposition of theory but the day's deed: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb's bequest — recorded as *extensive* in the very letter that was brought to him (al-Buk plus) — the careful repayment of debts before bequests, the bestowing upon companions and provision for kin alike; likewise Abū Bakr's testament, known throughout the world. The verse is still repeated: *ʿalā al-muttaqīn* — "a duty upon the reverent" — every word of which became the salutation of the good death amid God's estate-heresy-without-finishes (the term commentators coined for the infinitely extended *waṣiyyah* that mindful Muslims must now give the conscious moment between life and death: *the will written in time, the kin given in maʿrūf, the duties remembered*). And here the commentators turn the verse to every age's ear: the death-bed is not the moment for extravagant charity; it is the moment for *maʿrūf* — the honorable: the reigned charity toward the immediate family, because revelation assesses their right at higher tension than the stranger-benefaction — the rule of charity-literature down the centuries (close-right first, then the wider circles), just as the doctrine al-Ghazālī gives voice to again and again in the beginning of the Kitāb al-Waṣāyā: *let your testament be written while your heirs await it, and let it close your days with the mention of God.* And so the believer lives to see his final estate duty discharged *in life* — by thinking of it early, by discharging debts quickly, by assigning his wills honestly, and by closing in his testament — the example of end-life's completion which the Prophet's own dying saw to completion — at the feet of the finished race.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:181

> **But whoever changes the will after hearing it, the blame will only be on those who made the change. Indeed, Allah is AllHearing, All-Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Tampering Executor**

Fast upon the testament-command comes the verse of its guarding: *fa-man baddalahu baʿda mā samiʿahu fa-innamā ithmuhu ʿalā alladhīna yubaddilūnah* — "whoever alters it after he has heard it — its sin is indeed upon those who alter it." The commentators point the pronouns with precision: the man has *heard* the will spoken aloud by the dying testator — he is the witness, the executor, the one to whom the dead man's last breath was entrusted — and then, once the tongue has silenced and the hand stopped writing, he reaches into the instruction and alters it: changing beneficiaries, shifting amounts, twisting counsel, inserting unasked lawyers'-words, quietly folding the will's meaning into a shape closer to his own pocket's preference — every such tampering is counted here by the Book with the most succinct of verdicts: the sin is *not* soured into the estate nor back upon the dead man; the sin falls exactly, tracelessly, inalienably, upon the hands that made the alteration — *innamā ithmuhu ʿalā alladhīna yubaddilūnah*: *upon them alone*, by a formula (the *innamā* of restriction) that bars every row of fingers from pointing at the dead man's paper: they cannot blame his parchment, his old ideas, the climate of his sentiments: it was theirs, the alteration; the sin is theirs.

**The Boundary Against the Executor's Pen**

The jurists' work within this text has been remarkably fruitful and specific: the verse is drawn — throughout al-Qurṭubī, and onward into the inherited traditions of Muslim estate-law — as the verse that *fixes the boundary at the moment of probate-discovery*: let kings, executors, and notaries beware: an ostensibly minor adjustment in a testament — the balancing of various heirs' shares, the redrawing of phrases "for better sense" — stands the dead man's official signature beneath God's own watching pen: and the tradition preserves the Prophet's weighty warnings about it, none more alarming than the chain of sayings concerning the falsifier of legacies:

> *"He who alters a bequest after hearing it bears upon himself the likeness of the one who introduces lying upon God."* — and upon will-forgery in general, the Prophet's saying among the terrible-major-sins formulas is recorded: *"The injustice (janaf) in bequests is one of the major sins (kabāʾir)."* (related traditions assembled by the mufassirūn and jurists under this verse; a family of reports to the same effect carried by the collections and cited by al-Qurṭubī at this verse and by every later writer on 2:181–182)

The verse's precise-cast seal — "Truly God is Hearing, Knowing" — places the two divine names at the top of the dead man's defense-council: *Samīʿ*: He *heard* — and the died will's words remain with Him unchanged, so the alternators now alter no private paper but a recorded statement; *ʿAlīm*: He *knows* — the court's stenographer of intent-from-circumstance, that remembers the testament when the alternator has long left it cold: the altered testament thereby joins the altered scripture (the sūrah's own strongest parallel being our verse 75's "they altered words from their contexts") in the same hearing-before-divine-recorder: the altering of the testament was never heard by the ones who buried him, but God's office had been listening.

**Shield of the Dying**

The tradition dwells upon the passage by its own emotional tips: the will is made at the greatest possible moment of human helplessness — the testator propped toward death, his voice measurable by a witness's ear alone, his properties held only by trust-custody: he cannot defend his words, cannot read alternators' handwriting, cannot sue under his own statutes. For this reason the Book rises here in the special posture it takes only when it warns fraud upon the falling: successors, executors, heirs, and collecting-agents are told with the express threat of verse 181: the man leaving are his testimony and the spoken wording, and God's two names stand in between the hearing and the knowing as the Charter's guarantee: *rewrite what you would in the books of men — the sin's address is written against you.* The hadith of the most beautiful expression of the good death is read in unison at this teaching-verse, for the man who has nothing left before the end but *his heirs' kindness*:

> *"It is better to leave your heirs rich than to leave them indigent, begging from other men"* (al-Bukhari, Muslim — revisit: above at verse 180 — re-cited in the jurists' system of heirs and bequests everywhere the general counsel of the good death is annualised under this verse)

with the same standing counsel: every executor who hears the will and loves God leaves his dead man's spoken words under God's two names, in the very form he heard them spoken, with their every comma untouched, their every clause sealed by the double finger of al-Samīʿ and al-ʿAlīm — so that the Trust of the Dead is carried through the hands of the living by the discipline of honor, honesty, and adherence to the dead man's words, exactly as the Book's statutes declared.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:182

> **Whoever suspects an error or an injustice in the will and brings about a ˹fair˺ settlement among the parties will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Executor's Exception**

Balanced precisely against the prohibition of verse 181 is the exception of verse 182 — and therein lies the Book's famous legal subtlety: *fa-man khāfa min mūṣin janafan aw ithman fa-aṣlaḥa baynahum fa-lā ithma ʿalayh* — "whoever fears from the testator some injustice (janaf) or sin, and so sets matters right between the parties — no sin is upon him." The commentators first situate the pronouns fully: *man* — the executor, the hearing witness, the responsible administrator of the estate; *janaf* — "leaning," injustice by iniquity; *ithm* — outright sin; the exception's sense is: not every alteration is the alteration of verse 181 — the guy who sees the dead man was *himself* tilting his testament toward wrong — hiding from the heirs their legal rights, diverting by predatory bequests, overusing the will as a pretext to squeeze out rightful women or poor children — he is not changed to adjust the dead man's wrong tilt into honesty. The verse gives its co-ordinates with the rarest precision: it's exactly because the boundaries of God's Law hold forever, that the fear of the testator's tilting entitles the executor to insert the law's straightness into the skewed testament: he is not the *alterer* of verse 181: he is the *straightener* of the Book's own commands. The commentators cite the example never absent from their teaching: a will directed overtly at bypassing the compulsory shares by designating an heir-in-Fact but an heir-in-camouflage — a will assigning to a daughter-in-law property that actually serves the son — constitutes the exact *janaf* for which verse 182's adjusting becomes a responsibility rather than an offense.

**The "Fearing" Prior to Action**

The school of law points out the care with which the verse identifies its own epistemic stage: *man khāfa* — "whoever fears": not mere suspicion, and not certain knowledge, but the executive'*s considered, documented fear: the executor has arrived at a convinced apprehension that the dead man's pen had been unfair — and then the school allows him to intervene (under the authorizing clause *fa-aṣlaḥa baynahum* — "and makes peace/right between them" — the iṣlāḥ, the reconciliation-work, the rebalancing): this is not the alteration the Book condemned; it is the extensive repair the Book had commanded at every opening of reconciliation (thus 4:114's praise of whoever mediates the better, and 4:128's treaty between spouses). The classes of reconciliatory intervention are spelled out in al-Qurṭubī: reduce an oversized bequest to the third, nullify a weaponized exclusion that stood as a thinly removed punishment, restore a legitimate excluded relative — each instance protected by the rule of verse 182's cadence: no sin upon him, the justice-overrides arrangement the Book determines in its own final verdict: *fa-lā ithma ʿalayh* — "no sin upon him."

**God's Names Sealed on the Case of Adjustment**

The verse closes by lifting the whole contested testament into the two most merciful of God's Names: *inna Allāha ghafūrun raḥīm* — "Truly God is Forgiving, Merciful" — the seal which brings the whole file to rest in the graces rather than the ledger: to the parties of every such estate, executor, heirs, testator, judge, are called to see that — behind the delicate jurisprudence of *wasiyyah* and its instrument-bearers — stands the One whose Forgiving is endless to men-at-peace and whose Mercy encompasses every error the fear of God attempts to correct with sincerity. The tradition attends to the deeper rule the seal sets under the entire testament-file: God's Forgiving guards the adjusting executor, lest honesty-built adjustments be made taboo by fear of the alteration-sin; God's Mercy guards the tilting testator himself, inasmuch as his unjust testaments can still be softened by the reconciler rather than left to be the sin-charged last signature with which he stands before his death. The verse is coupled thus into the sūrah's testament-architectural duo: verse 181 closes the door against fraudulent alternation — verse 182 closes the door against fraudulent closings of legal remedy — and the two doors together guard the small, tender business that a dying man commits to the Lord and his heirs: his will — designed to draw out the truth from the Law of all-life, adjusting itself to the strains of no man's sin against his own soul, and standing forever within the law that the Forgiving and the Merciful both surrounded.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:183

> **O believers! Fasting is prescribed for you—as it was for those before you—so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Fifth Pillar Announced**

The sūrah has already called out the prayer at verse 43; now comes the solemn installation at the heart of Islam of its sister act of devotion — the fast: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū kutiba ʿalaykumu al-ṣiyāmu kamā kutiba ʿalā alladhīna min qablikum* — "O you who believe! fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you." The commentators mark the verb-list's continuity with the Levitical pattern the sūrah follows: the same formula introduced the law of retribution (2:178) and now it introduces the fast: *kutiba* — *is written/prescribed* — the passive laying the legislation in God's own hand rather than the Prophet's or the community's: fasting is not a custom passed down from tribe to tribe — it is a divine inscription writing upon every subsequent covenant: the life of the soul from fast to fast. And the historical clause reads into its placement the identity-tradition of the fast across the ages: the word *kamā kutiba ʿalā alladhīna min qablikum* — *as it was prescribed for those before you* — making clear that this fast belongs to an unbroken chain: the many studs read into the pages of the former Scriptures (the Torah's Days of Atonement: Leviticus 16; the season's fasts of the prophets; the fast-days of the Christians with their own recorded forty days in the wilderness of Jesus): the tradition regards Islamic fasting not as an innovation on the meal-table of the religions but as the crowning branch of one single stem, planted in the very word that began the fast across the world with Adam and Noah, and declared in Abraham's line, and cleansed and confirmed for the Muslims at Madinah.

**The Fast and the Ramadan-Binding**

Within the verse's formative charter the commentators riffle its association with several elements of time and detail: whether the clause "as it was prescribed for those before you" measures the prescription by the *obligation* of fasting (the whole tradition of divine fasting from Noah through the prophets), by the *timing* of the fast (Ramadan approximations among the earlier communities), or merely by the *kind* (i.e., the abstention from food, drink and known human appetites with spiritual intent). The class of universal readings — what all commentators accept — is that the specific Ramadan fast of the Muslims (vv. 184–185 to follow) belongs to a specifically-Muslim reappointment: the form's time-set and month-set is new: and the obligation's core — the total daylight fast from dawn to sundown, the abstinence from food, drink, and sexual contact — is the Book's own sacred novel; but the very idea of fasting stands up vertical through Abraham's children of every millennium, the same as prayer and zakat: each people fasting through the mill of the From-One-Generator-schedule: *as it was prescribed for those before you*: the fast of Moses' forty days (2:51); the fast of ʿĀshūrāʾ (the Prophet's community fasting with the Jews at Madinah until Ramadan was declared); and the whole practice continuing in the Islamic heart until the present day.

**That You May Be Reverent — The Fast's Telos**

The purpose-clause arrives upon the verse with the same close-off flourish the sūrah has used through every law-unit of the passage: *laʿallakum tattaqūn* — "that you may be reverent/fast-fast the reverent": the *ḥikmah* of the fast is not any deprivement-deprivative but the *impartation of God-consciousness* (taqwā) — the faculty with which the sūrah opened — *ittaqu* as command at verse 21 etc., the muttaqūn at verse 2 — the fast being one of the best express-ways into it. The commentators anatomize the mechanism in a near-medical language: hunger scourges the body until it can no longer conspire with the lower passions; hunger cuts down the blood's attention to the subtle calls of gluttony and lust; the believer's nine-tenths of temptation proceed via the full stomach; by restraint of the body's two fitnas (food and sex) the fast mounts direct pressure upon the ward of God-consciousness, leaving it alone and uncluttered to hear and carry out what God commands; and the fast is called *sirr* — secret — between God and His servant in the tradition's own language — for its very license is invisible: no prostration in the mosque among the people, no charity's wealth passing hand to hand, no Khaninah of public practicing: the empty stomach is God's alone: He is the sole witness — and so the fast opens an interior hands-on solidarity with God that no outward public duty has: *lillāhi al-ṣiyāmu wa lahu ajruhu* — God is the fast's own: He is its reward: God said (in the ḥadīth qudsī reported in al-Bukhārī and Muslim from Abū Hurayrah):

> *"Every deed of the son of Adam is multiplied, a good deed receiving a tenfold to seven-hundredfold reward — God said: except the Fast, for it is Mine, and I shall reward it: he leaves his food and his drink and his desire for My sake. The faster has two joys: a joy when he breaks the fast, and a joy when he meets his Lord. And the smell coming from the mouth of the faster is better with God than the fragrance of musk."* (al-Bukhari 1904, 5927; Muslim 1151)

**Written for Self-Discipline, the Great School-Term**

And the verse is summed over the tradition-sea as the Lord-inscribed definition of taqwā-training: fasting is God's own daily curriculum over a full month (Ramaḍān, the month yet to be named in the next verse) whose stated academic objective is *laʿallakum tattaqūn* — *that you may be reverent*: no lost souls are hoped-for *in percentages* — but the whole congregation attains its degrees and doubles its portions of taqwā; and the tradition has tended its own solemn spectacle: the whole ummah is its graduating class provided *by the divine Inscription* with one curriculum for all, written in by God Himself at the threshold of every year. And so from the little scimitar-shaped hill villages of the Niger to the great cities, year after century, a billion people rise, one month annually, from dawn to sundown, by the sheer sway of *kutiba ʿalaykumu al-ṣiyām* — fasting *written* upon them: the largest mass educational enterprise in the history of the world has proceeded annually since the second year after the Hijrah, each year bringing forward its diploma upon tens of millions of hearts: *laʿallakum tattaqūn* — that you may be reverent — the School-Year's single name: Ramadan.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:184

> **˹Fast a˺ prescribed number of days. But whoever of you is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺. For those who can only fast with extreme difficulty, compensation can be made by feeding a needy person ˹for every day not fasted˺. But whoever volunteers to give more, it is better for them. And to fast is better for you, if only you knew.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Days Numbered" — The Measured Term**

The fast's first directive fixes its count: *ayyāman maʿdūdāt* — "for days numbered" — a phrase the commentators have treated with the abundant scholarship it drew. Two older positions stand beside one another: it means *a limited count* — either the month of Ramadan itself (the far commoner understanding, since verse 185 immediately names it), or the specific early days the believers were already fasting (the three days a month plus ʿĀshūrāʾ they had observed upon first arriving at Madinah) before the new full month was announced — *maʿdūdāt*: *not interminable, not mystically unbounded — from start to finish a count*: God Himself writing the numerals and therefore writing *the kindness* of a finite count: the fast is never lightly drawn beyond the suffering-frame of the believer's body: it is *days numbered*, and behind the numbering stands the Book's own luminous rule (to be spoken in verse 185): *God desires ease for you, and He does not desire hardship.*

**The Sick, the Traveler, and the Fed-Ransom**

The verse's second sentence then lays the mercy-ladders of the fast: *fa-man kāna minkum marīḍan aw ʿalā safarin fa-ʿiddatun min ayyāmin ukhar* — "if any of you is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days" — the two earliest and most widely graced exempted classes: (1) the sick: those whose fasting would damage the body — healing first; the fast waits; (2) the traveler: the one who physically out-travelling; the road is counted for him as hardship-qualifier — in both classes the day missed is re-set upon *a number of other days*: the same number as missed, at later days of the year. And the fulcient third class is given by the Book's traveling-school of law: *wa ʿalā alladhīna yuṭīqūnahu fidyatun ṭaʿāmu miskīn* — "upon those who can bear it — the compensating ransom of feeding one needy person." The commentators' studied unfolding of the Arabic *yuṭīqūnahu* (from the root ṭ-w-q: *to be able, to bear, to endue-with-effort*) supports both of the ancient readings that the fiqh of later centuries distilled: (a) those *really able* to fast — the whole class of the able-bodied — for whom the first stage of Ramadan's fast had been opened with the substitution-choice: fast, or feed one poor person for every day unfasted (the first revealed rule of the fast, which the later rule of verse 185 would tighten into direct fasting for all who were able); and (b) those able *only-barely* — those who *endure the fast with severe difficulty* — the old man and the old woman, the slowly sick, the pregnant and nursing women for whom the fast's burdens are not straightforward illness but heavy-load — for whom the compensating ransom remains standing now and always: the madhhabs differ as to whether (a) or (b) has priority, but all schools accept *yuṭīqūnahu* as carrying the burden-measure: *those who can bear it* being those whose bearing can survive only through ransom: and all schools agree, the ḥadīth of the Prophet supports it:

> *"At the beginning of the year, one had the choice between fasting and feeding a needy person each day, until fasting became declared wholly obligatory."* — so the Prophet's own account of the fast's tightening order within its first years (cited in the tafsīr and hadith works by Ibn ʿUmar and others, on the stage-by-stage grounding)

**"That You Should Fast Is Better" — The Verse's Counsel**

The last limb of the verse stands as its own culminating exhortation: *wa an taṣūmū khayrun lakum in kuntum taʿlamūn* — "and that you should fast is better for you — if you but knew." God Himself brings into the law-born verses its most serious recommendation: better it is indeed to fast — even when the ransom door is legally opened — because the *ḥikmah* of the fast is the shaping of the soul: feeding the poor is the mercy that *stands ready for the weak*, but the fast itself is the *worship*: *khayrun lakum* — better *for you*, not in external calculations but in the soul's sculpting; and the closing *in kuntum taʿlamūn* — *if you but knew* — is the same formula the sūrah had used at verse 103 ("had they but known" about Moses and the Jews' bargains), at verse 154, at 2:30, at 16:19 and so on: heaven's redoubled way of saying: *the arithmetic of the soul is known fully only to God; your fasting is measured against a gain you yourselves cannot compute*: so through the generosity of the law, verses 183–184 together set up the two legs of the fasting discipline: the *obligation* rooted in the universal human experience of the number of days; and the *mercy* rooted in the generation-bound and needy categories and then in the ransom-choices — both completed in the verse's own summing and also as the fast's deeper fabric: a worship whose numbers are God-inspired, whose needs are mercy-rooted, and whose advantage is known only to those who know.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:185

> **Ramaḍân is the month in which the Quran was revealed as a guide for humanity with clear proofs of guidance and the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺. So whoever is present this month, let them fast. But whoever is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺. Allah intends ease for you, not hardship, so that you may complete the prescribed period and proclaim the greatness of Allah for guiding you, and perhaps you will be grateful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Ramadan-Named: The Month of the Revelation**

For the first and only time in the whole Book the sacred month is named: *shahru ramaḍāna alladhī unzila fīhi al-qurʾānu hudan li'l-nāsi wa bayyinātin mina al-hudā wa'l-furqān* — "the month of Ramadan, in which the Quran was sent down as guidance for mankind and as clear proofs of guidance and of the Criterion." The commentators record the education's greatness in the very naming: the entire world-month is sealed *by the revelation*: its fast is not founded upon a milking-star season nor upon a tribe's commemorations but upon *the descent of the Quran*: the two blessings — the feast of fasting and the feast of the word — are united in the same month: the month when, at the Cave of Ḥirāʾ, the angel Gabriel began the descent of the verse-lines that would change the world (Quraysh's own narrator forever: *iqraʾ bi-smi rabbika* — "recite, in the name of your Lord who created"): the Muslim calendar's commemoration of God's own outbreak of speech in the night of Ḥirā, and then the whole *furqān* — criterion: the distinction of right from wrong unveiled across a subsequent 23 years of wordfalls — all begun in a single month: it is called in its own clear proofs of guidance: *hudan li'l-nās* — *as guidance for mankind*: not a private revelation for chosen subsets: and then *bayyināt* — *clear proofs of guidance*: the word-loops that make guidance's path plain at every crossing; and *al-furqān* — *the Criterion*: the balancing of the Book's own word: being by which the truthful cross and the liars fall: Ramadan thus holds for every later year of the earth's turning the one's truly great memory-year.

**Fast It — and the Exemptions of Mercy**

Then the verse's address intensifies into the personal command: *fa-man shahida minkumu al-shahra fa-l-yaṣumhu* — "whoever of you *witnesses* the month — let him fast it." The *shahida* — *to witness, to be present* — is decisive: the fast's law comes alive for the believer not merely when the month begins in God's Book, but when it arrives and is witnessed in the believer's own city and month-air: the month is seen entering (the sight of the new crescent) — and with its seeing, the duty falls on the one standing there: fast it: fast the whole count of the month. And the mercy-clauses are repeated from verse 184 in the fuller verse-of-law as the Book's own constitutional guarantees: *wa man kāna marīḍan aw ʿalā safarin fa-ʿiddatun min ayyāmin ukhar* — "whoever is ill or on a journey — a number of other days": the sick and the traveler stand among the exempted through the verse's own articulate sentence of law-mercy, and the repentance-pilgrims to the fit-missing days are registered as faithful fasters by the Book's own counterpart: no day is dropped from the duty; it is shifted; it is transferred; it is carried in the believer's scroll across the calendar with God's approval.

**"God Desires Ease for You"**

Then the greatest principle of the whole Islamic law is declared: the *ease-intent* of the Lawgiver: *yurīdu Allāhu bikumu al-yusra wa lā yurīdu bikumu al-ʿusra* — "God desires for you ease, and He does not desire for you hardship." The commentators never cease to open this principle into the whole foundation of Islam as law-legislating: the very existence of the exceptions — days of illness, traveling, feeding-ransoms, alternative days — is framed inside the very intent of God: He *desires* — a verb — the ease (*yusr*) — and negates — the ʿusr — the hardship; and the commentators' golden hours spread this principle out to every branch of law-sequence: the permissions (rukhṣah — license, rukhakh — easyening) are not accidents of overspill: they are the outworking of God's own express character in legislating: the veil of compassion over all of Islam's laws comes not from the men's democratic preferences but from the Godhead's own express character: *ease-intent* — and the verse's commentator's talk it through the ages at every gate of the law where the hardship-argument stands: God's Law is never hardship-imposed: He intends ease. And the tradition, over the ages, has preserved the verse-background in the Prophet's own passages of calm and mercy — al-Tirmidhī recording from many hands the fiqh-teachers' works:

> *"Make things easy and do not make things difficult" (yassirū wa lā tuʿassirū — al-Bukhari 69; Muslim 1734 — the standing rule of the Prophet's entire sunnah of easing)

and the Prophet's own giving the choice in the law's folds — shortening prayers in travel, combining them, breaking the fast by instruction to the sick and the traveler — are presented by the tradition as verse 185's very teaching in practice: the law was made to hold in the people's actual lives, not to crush them beneath its own grace.

**Completing the Count, Magnifying the God**

The verse's last clauses lock the whole fast down in its spiritual goals: *wa li-tukmilū al-ʿiddata wa li-tukabbirū Allāha ʿalā mā hadākum wa laʿallakum tashkurūn* — "and so that you may complete the number, and magnify God for having guided you, that haply you may give thanks." (1) *li-tukmilū al-ʿiddata*: so that you make the fast's count *whole* — the whole days of Ramadan completed as by the numbered-days charter (v.184); (2) *li-tukabbirū Allāha ʿalā mā hadākum*: so that you magnify God for His guidance — the days of the fast closing in the Festival-morning's great *takbīr* — the takbirāt of the ʿĪd: *Allāhu akbar Allāhu akbar* — "God is Most Great" — whose sparing the dreadful books had acquired under 6:82 and now fix upon God the praise His guidance merits; (3) *laʿallakum tashkurūn*: *that you may be thankful*: the whole amendment of the month — its physical restraint, its mercy-licenses, its closing blessings — is aimed toward *shukr* — thankfulness: the sūrah's own triune graces of the believer-foundation (ḥamd at 2:1-5; ṣalāh and zakāh at 2:43; shukr at 2:152 and 2:185) now rounding off to the fast's own crowning formula: *fast, that you may be reverent (v.183) — at the end of it, magnify God, and give thanks.* The fast's four-part nucleus — obligation's beginning (v.183), exemption's mercy (v.184), God's character of ease (v.185), thanksgiving's crowning (v.185) — has in the fourteen centuries since been the full engine of the observance of Ramadan anywhere the believers of the round of the earth watched the moon and cut-back the table: and on its second night, the Prophet's prayers at the Night of Power are still remembered (*laylatu al-qadr* — 97:1-5 itself its own night-concealed-wonder: *better than a thousand months*): and beneath it all, the believer stands and fasts, hearing God's south: *the month of Ramadan, in which the Quran was sent down... fast it.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:186

> **When My servants ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about Me: I am truly near. I respond to one’s prayer when they call upon Me. So let them respond ˹with obedience˺ to Me and believe in Me, perhaps they will be guided ˹to the Right Way˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verse at the Center of the Sūrah**

In the very middle of the fast-legislation — between the fast's mercy-licenses and the fast's night-rules — God plants the verse the tradition calls the *heart of the whole matter*: *wa idhā saʾalaka ʿibādī ʿannī fa-innī qarīb* — "when My servants ask you about Me — truly I am near" — *ujību daʿwata al-dāʿi idhā daʿān* — "I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me." The commentators tell us this placement is no accident: the verse floats alone inside the fast-block, unbunched with any topic of food, drink, or marriage, because *duʿāʾ — supplication — is the center of all worship*: the fast itself, as the Sufi commentary-writers note, is the year of the prayer's engine being turned to its fullest compression: the hungry, the thirsty, the night-singers, and the abstemious are the very people whose duʿāʾs ascend most swiftly — and so the Book, in the midst of explaining the fast, issues the answer to the fast's natural question: *is the Lord of all this fasting near us as we pray?* — and the answer comes back in God's own personal voice — unmediated, unworked, answered in the ordinary plural-singular, as though the Messenger had been asked by every single man of his town: **I am near**.

**Asked and Answered in One Breath**

The occasion-reports cluster around the giving-kindling question: al-Ṭabarī records that the Companions asked the Prophet ﷺ: *where is our Lord?* — *is He near that we may whisper to Him, or far that we must shout?* — and the verse came down directly as its answer: al-Rāzī and the variant transmitters record the Bedouin who asked: "Is our Lord near that we converse secretly, or far that we call aloud?" — the same teaching-trade of the Prophet's time, in the question whether prayer travels as it were by distance. The answer of revelation stands: *no intermediary*: *I am near* — even nearness itself being offered before any formula has been composed: *I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me* — the condition given in the Arabic is only the calling itself: caller, call, and the answer of God — between them the verse makes no mention of sponsor nor saint, deliverer nor door-keeper: God Himself near — answering *ujību* — the direct singular verb of His answering: no deputy's intercession; no queue; no fee: *the One who is near hears the whispered duʿāʾ and the shout alike* — indeed the Prophet is reported (carried at al-Bukhārī 2992, 6311; Muslim 2711) to have corrected his own Companions exactly at this point when they lifted their voices in prayer on a journey:

> *"You are not calling one who is deaf or absent; you are calling One Hearing, Near — and He is with you"*

**Duʿāʾ as Worship**

The tradition then built the whole library of Islamic devotion upon the word *duʿāʾ* as it is modified in this verse: the Prophet — said in al-Tirmidhī and its companion books — taught: *al-duʿāʾu huwa al-ʿibādah* — *supplication is worship itself* (al-Tirmidhī 2969; Abū Dāwūd 1479 — from Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr's account, authenticated across the collections): for in the duʿāʾ the soul presents itself as creature before Creator — nothing is shown of power, of wisdom, of martyr-zeal before Him: only the dependent appeal: and so the duʿāʾ — the simple call — is the very kernel of all worship — the fast itself is its thousand-hours' concentrated duʿāʾ, the ṣalāh itself is the timed duʿāʾ-atonement, the ḥajj itself the duʿāʾ-haven — and the saying of the ḥadīth qudsī is tied to it at once: *"Call upon Me: I will answer you — truly those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hellfire utterly humbled"* (40:60) — and Al-Rāzī's school never tires of marking the double-faculty: *ask — and let your faith lead you; respond — and let your belief be the answer's ladder*: the verse's final clauses — *fa-l-yastajībū lī wa-l-yuʾminū bī laʿallahum yarshudūn* — "so let them respond to Me and believe in Me, that they may be led aright" — marries together the duʿāʾ's two reciprocities: your call answered by God's answer; God's call answered by your response: *respond to Me* — by obeying what He has commanded (the fast, the charity, the pillars) — *and believe in Me* — so that the call itself be planted upon faith's own soil: the sum: *guidance, rashd* — the state of one whose every step is guided — is the end toward which calling and answering together carry.

**"When My Servants Ask" — The Servant-Direct Address**

The commentators note the verse's great distinction: it does not read *when mankind asks* but *when My servants ask*: *ʿibādī* — *My servants*: the possessive ascription — *Mine* — being itself the believers' greatest honor: the fast-wearied night-watchers, waking-parched far apart from their God, are named *His* in the most tender possessive short of the names of father and mother: they are enrolled in the servants' charter, three thousand children of the hours to whom this one sweet phrase belongs throughout the ages: *when My servants ask, I am near* — and with this Indivisible pledge the whole Ramadan-block of the sūrah closes its first leg: the fast was written for this listening nearness: the fast's purpose was taqwā; taqwā's highest side-throne is duʿāʾ; and duʿāʾ's royal promise is the verse: **I answer the caller when he calls Me**, the pledge that stands — the tradition says — against the whole file of mankind's fearful loneliness: since God Himself says it, no servant of the servants is ever again actually alone: the believer supplicates — and he is answered as surely as morning follows the night.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:187

> **It has been made permissible for you to be intimate with your wives during the nights preceding the fast. Your spouses are a garment for you as you are for them. Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves. So He has accepted your repentance and pardoned you. So now you may be intimate with them and seek what Allah has prescribed for you. ˹You may˺ eat and drink until you see the light of dawn breaking the darkness of night, then complete the fast until nightfall. Do not be intimate with your spouses while you are meditating in the mosques. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not exceed them. This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to people, so they may become mindful ˹of Him˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Alleviation Night**

From the nearness-and-duʿāʾ promises the sūrah returns to its fast-details with one of its most tender mercies: *uḥilla lakum laylata al-ṣiyāmi al-rafathu ilā nisāʾikum* — "you are permitted on the nights of the fast the approach to your wives." The commentary tradition immediately clothes the verse's arrival in its historical report: before this alleviation, the spouses of the Ramadan ummah had understood something nearer abstinence for the entire month — food and drink after sunset until the ʿishāʾ prayer (perhaps), and any contact with their wives postponed: and it is a known story of the Companionage of the first generation: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb himself confessed to the Prophet that he had broken the taboo upon a night of Ramadan; and others among the people had likewise slipped; and the verse's own word — *kuntum takhtānūna anfusakum* — "you were betraying yourselves" — is expounded by al-Ṭabarī and the whole school as the kindly accounting of that swerving: *you* — not the Law — *had placed your own souls in the impossible bind*: the demands you placed upon yourselves were unlivable — you betrayed yourselves by your own too-heavy assumptions: so God relieves you, without blame, in two movements: *fa-tāba ʿalaykum wa ʿafā ʿankum* — "He relented unto you and pardoned you": God accepts the general niggardliness of the Ramadan-spouses over before it was minded, then releases the nighttime with the single verse-word license. The verse in its own cadence records the *tawbah* — the turning-back — the very turning-as-to-come back at verse 128 ("You are the Relenting, the Merciful" — as Abraham's prayer) — *and the pardon ʿafw*: the Lord gives His back-turning and His pardons-together at the single first night the permission is delivered.

**The Garment of Marriage**

The metaphor-compression at the center of the verse is itself one of the most celebrated figures of the whole Qur'an: *hunna libāsun lakum wa antum libāsun lahunn* — "they are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them." The commentators never tire of opening its dimension — garment as concealment (each covers the other's faults and shames), garment as warmth (each being the heat-source of the other's soul), garment as nearness (touching skin to skin as the garment to the body), garment as beauty (each being the other's admiration-determining figure before the world), garment as protection (each screening the other from the world's dust and enemy-gleam): within the five-layered metaphor the verse finds not a treasury of provision-orders (as in 4:34) nor of reciprocal rights (as in 2:228's *aspects-hierarchy*) but *the very closeness of each to each*: husband and wife are for each other the covering against nakedness: *and what garment leaves a gap through which the cold can sweep in upon the wearer?* The tradition is so strong upon the intimacy of this verse that one cannot speak of marriage at any Islamic wall without its garment-imagery. Behind it lies the whole sūrah's counter-pole: the verse in which God's unity re-foundations marriage as the garment of *each* — not the covering of one upon the other as some pre-Islamic law-glass imagined, but the reciprocal wear of two souls, each the sheltering skin-of-comfort of the other.

**The White and Black Threads of Dawn**

The eating-window of the fast is set by the two loveliest benchmarks of the Book: *wa kulū wa-shrabū ḥattā yatabayyana lakumu al-khayṭu al-abyaḍu mina al-khayṭi al-aswadi mina al-fajr* — "and eat and drink until the white thread of dawn distinguishes itself from the black thread." The commentators situate the thread-imagery fully within the Arabic vocabulary: *khayṭ* is what a seamstress uses to join two pieces of cloth; the two threads mark the seam of night-and-day mingled at the edge of dawn: the white thread being the first glow-width across the eastern sky and the black thread the remaining darkness of night behind it: dawn becomes clear — safety reverts to its true etymon — between the two threads as they separate: the very natural measuring-instrument of every morning the whole ummah knows from birth. In the very making of this measurement the Prophet ﷺ had to instruct the early community upon a literal-readings: some early believers took it literally — reaching for actual white and black threads and holding them against the dawn — and the Prophet is handed down (in the records at al-Bukhārī and Muslim, widely cited at this verse) as laughing-strutting his friends toward its real sense: *it is the whiteness of the day and the blackness of the night — hold the fast against the sunrise not against a thread* — the Prophet's own Arabic of the chapter-tradition delivering lessons with the warmest humanity: and so the fast has since begun across fourteen centuries by the light alone: Muslims scanning the east for that seam-line of color-change, the room becoming lighter against the still-black western sky: the verse's own loveliness teaching the plainest physiology of Ramadan's first seconds.

**"Those Are the Limits of God"**

And the iʿtikāf clause closes the fast-unit's laws with its special last caution: *wa lā tubāshirūhunna wa antum ʿākifūna fī al-masājid* — "do not lie with them while you are in retreat (iʿtikāf) in the mosques." The retreat — the still-standing Sunnah of the last ten days of Ramadan, at whose heart lay the Prophet's custom and at whose end the rule governs Quraysh's whole later record — is thereby bound explicitly: even during the permitted night, the mosque-muʿtakif — the one cloistered in prayer and dhikr — is fenced off from his wives' field: the mosques are the space where law grammatically reasserts itself over the permitted: the retreat-to-mosque again remaps the believer's daytime-table into the wider remembrance: the verse moves from night-permits, to misgiving-mercy, to dawn-threads, to the rules of iʿtikāf, and closes its middle verse with its own bright absolute: *tilka ḥudūdu Allāhi fa-lā taqrabūhā* — "those are the limits of God: so approach them not": the ummah of Islam marked out by the two threads of dawn and dusk within God's *ḥudūd* — limits — the boundary-line whose crossing-avoidance is itself the love-servitude: and the verse ends with the sūrah's characteristic promise formula of verse 183: *laʿallahum yattaqūn* — *that they may be reverent*: the very aim set down at the fast-unit's first verse — and that, after the seal, the tradition continues repeating generation after generation in the moon-lit nights of Ramadan, while people recite the same word across the minarets of the world: *fast — keep to the limits — keep from the limits' approach — be reverent* — the Law of the Month now sealed on every gateway.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:188

> **Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly, nor deliberately bribe authorities in order to devour a portion of others’ property, knowing that it is a sin.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Devouring Forbidden**

From the law of the fast, the Book now opens its brief fierce chapter upon property — a subject of the utmost centrality to the whole Islamic order of the ummah: *wa lā taʾkulū amwālakum baynakum bi'l-bāṭili* — "and do not devour your property among yourselves falsely." The school of tafsīr has always emphasized the choice of the verb: *taʾkulūn* — *you eat*: property-eating as eating: for the wealth in the wallet bears within it not dry figures but bread, water, shelter: swallowed as the strong swallows the weak's bread — the taste-feeling of eating describing the physicality of the taking: *devouring by falsehood* as the whole wrong hunger of the earth: and the *bāṭil* — the false, the void, the null-and-void-metaphysically: the grab has no root among God's ordinances: so it doesn't slow down and becomes *nothing*: *navigated by deceit* the verse explains the whole domain of cheating of contracts, underground bribery, faked accounting, crooked sale, duress-coercion, takings-by-friendship and by office: all of it comes under *devouring-by-falsehood*: the head of the property-file opened right after its own pairing-file of the fast: the law of God protects the blood at 2:178, the balance of relatives at 2:180, and the property in the very next note.

**"Nor Proffer It to Judges"**

The second clause directly attack *the bribe-route*: *wa lā tudlū bihā ilā al-ḥukkāmi li-taʾkulū farīqan min amwāli al-nāsi bi'l-ithmi wa antum taʿlamūn* — "nor proffer it to the judges, that you may devour a part of people's property sinfully, while you know (better)." The verb *tudlū bihā* — to hurl, to offer, to throw *downward* — is read by the critics as chosen for the gesture of pushing a wrapped gift into the judge's lap: the briber *casting* his gift toward the responsibility-seat: and al-Rāzī and Ibn al-ʿArabī treat the clause as the *fiqh's open charter against judicial bribery*: to bribe the judge is not merely payment-influence — it is *using the state machinery to *eat* your neighbor*: the court becomes your teeth: and the conduct is reckoned under two sets of sins: (i) bribery of the judge as bribery of public office; (ii) accomplished injustice upon the victim — not accidental but *illustrated with* the victim's knowing: *wa antum taʿlamūn* — the knowing of wrongdoing assembled exactly where the Book's knife presses deepest: he who lies convincingly in the judgment-house still receives his measured fire-portion, having devoured what does not belong to him.

The tradition-enamoured school also brings in the Prophet's own saying about the judge's human frailty — carried at al-Bukhārī (6967, 7180-85) and Muslim (1713) from Umm Salamah — which is perennially placed at 2:188's lineage:

> *"I am only a human being, and litigants come to me; it may be that one of them is more eloquent in his argument than the other, and I judge in his favor according to what I hear. So whoever I judge for with anything of his brother's due, let him not take it, for I am only assigning him a piece of the Fire."*

**The Judge's Ruling Does Not Sanctify**

The jurists who teach from 2:188 derive directly from it (via Ibn Kathīr's and Ibn Qayyim's writings) the great ethical boundary-precept of Islamic legal civilization: *a judge's ruling does not make the unlawful lawful, nor render the lawful unlawful* — the holiness of the final decision does not attach to the moral status of the act: the bribed decision is morally void even when it enters the law-books: the Prophet's own saying — *I am but a man judging by what I hear* — is the supreme certification that the *courtday* is not the *heartday*: the first is the exchange by evidence and voices; the second by truth and conscience: the sin devoured by verdict stands still to be devoured on the Day of True Verdict. And the whole property-deployment of the verse — *among yourselves* — is fixed in the Book's own history of the ummah's rupture over property: the first fitnah of the Madinan history triggered by the Bakht (of the Companions after the Prophet's death, at the Fadak-legacy debate etc.) was in its kernel by the moral coaching of 2:188's stern discipline: *between you, among yourselves* — the pronoun plural of fellowship: the property being *yours* only to take when the Law lets you take; *bāṭil* — void — when it doesn't: the cheaters never cheat a stranger; they cheat their own selves, their own fellowship, their own "among-yourselves" — and they teach the witness of the ummah a lesson long-folded under twelve treaty-rule: *no law, no court, no fraternity legalizes what God's word made void.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:189

> **They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the phases of the moon. Say, “They are a means for people to determine time and pilgrimage.” Righteousness is not in entering your houses from the back doors. Rather, righteousness is to be mindful ˹of Allah˺. So enter your homes through their ˹proper˺ doors, and be mindful of Allah so you may be successful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question of the Moons**

The long stream of questions now asks a very simple one — tied both to the pilgrimage to come and to the fast just finished: *yasʾalūnaka ʿani al-ahillati qul hiya mawāqītu li'l-nāsi wa'l-ḥajj* — "they ask you about the crescent moons — say: they are appointed times for mankind and for the ḥajj." The commentators situate the question as rising through the same Madinan route as the other questions of the sūrah (the "they ask you" formula: 2:215, 2:217, 2:219, 2:220): the askers — the Madinan community around the Prophet — needed easily workable conventions for marking time: seasons of journeys, sea-states and festivals, planting seasons and fasting months, and especially of the pilgrimage: *what are the crescents for us?* And the answer comes back in the most basic of terms: **they are appointed times for mankind** — the Book's very flat-society solution: time is not portioned by paper but by the unowned celestial body that lights every road: *no need for astronomy-tables* — the crescent visible to the naked eye, consulted for free by merchants, travelers, farmers: *mawāqīt* — appointed signposts: the verse places the whole celestial chronology of Islam, the calendar of the holy month and the ḥajj, upon *what anyone can see*: the moon itself rises as the calendar's own governor — a calendar not of aristocrats but of everyone: and the wording answers the questioners with the simplest wisdom: the crescents are given as *time-marks*, not omens — to be used, not worshipped: nor feared nor adored for their phases — the sun and moon being God's two lights of counting (6:96's "He made the sun a radiance and the moon a light, and determined its phases so that you may know the count of years and the reckoning") — the moon belongs to God, and then only to mankind at the user's level of sky-timing.

**Houses from the Rear: The Old and the New**

The verse then passes immediately to a second instruction — unexpectedly riding upon a homespun parable given within the very same sentence: *wa laysa al-birru bi-an taʾtū al-buyūta min ẓuhūrihā* — "and it is not piety to approach houses from their rear." The commentators are well-informed about the story behind these words: in the days before Islam, the people of Madinah (and others in the circle) had held a superstition concerning the pilgrim's iḥrām state: that when the pilgrim returns from his journey back to his own home, he must not enter by his own door — but climb the rear wall or enter through the back, as though the door had in some way become ritually separated by the iḥrām; the practices inconvenienced men and disrupted houses, with wives, children, and household duties — and the verse arrived as the rectification: *that is not piety*: piety is not based on silences and weird door-routes: the door of the house remains the door the pilgrim enters by; the roof of the house the roof he needs to seek beneath. The verse's wider lesson — as al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī and later Ibn Kathīr all emphasize — is exactly the same instruction the Book repeats hundreds of times across all its dispensation: *superstitious self-ritual is not piety*: true piety is obedience-steady: come to houses *by their doors*: frontally, plainly, without maze'd contrivances: and by the very parable the verse signals the further thing the commentators say with some flourish: *knowledge comes to truth by its front, not over its back-wall*: men who approach the Book itself by self-entered secret passages (external hints, invented rites, ascetic exaggerations) are re-enacting the same mistake: the Book has a door: **the front door of the plain divine meaning: enter by it.**

**"Piety Is the Reverent"**

The verse then delivers the pivot-definition of *birr* of the whole passage: *wa lākinna al-birra mani ittaqā* — "rather, piety is he who is reverent." The Book's own tight antithesis answers both pillars of the two-part question: the crescent moons are time's reckoning — not God's shrines — and the rear-door frames are not piety — obedience is: piety depends neither on the astrologer's phase-charting nor on the taboo-keeper's contorted delicatesse: *birr is the heart that fears God.* And the verse ends by commanding their entry-habit and blessing their outcome: *wa-tū al-buyūta min abwābihā* — "come into houses by their doors" — with the final closing *wa-ttaqu Allāha laʿallakum tufliḥūn* — "and reverence God, that you may prosper."

The school clarifies two connected instructions of the verse's full text: (1) in the mosque and house and street, let all doors be entered frontally and lawfully (the Prophet's own sunnah of general door-entering: *if we separate, remember God; upon entering our home, invoke the name* — the general formulas the traditions at Abū Dāwūd carry constantly for leaving/entering of houses); and (2) in the heart, let all approaches to the Lord be *directly by the door revealed*: no detours around the front: the question of the moon-gazing is thereby gathered within the big answer to the sūrah's whole question-chapter (188–189–190's sequence): *the rituals* belong to God; *the timing* belongs to mankind at the sky; *the piety* belongs to the heart-reverent; and the doors of every house of God and house of man are to be used in full face, without crooks and detours — the secret crypt-keys of superstition flung down in the dust, in this verse and every other, until the doors themselves lead again into the open house of the Most Merciful — and then the blessing-word is pronounced upon those doors' entry forever: *laʿallakum tufliḥūn* — *that you may prosper* — prosperity being the second half of the philosophy the first half of the sūrah has been bringing forward since verse 5's parallel-clause: *the successful: the prosperous: upon them are guidance and them are the successful* — the whole destiny-shaped crown resting in this very verse of the crescent moons and the back-door forgotten making of men.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:190

> **Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you, but do not exceed the limits. Surely Allah does not like transgressors.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Verse of Qitāl**

This verse stands at one of Islam's most consequential thresholds: it is generally counted the **first verse of the Qur'an to permit fighting** — the legislation of jihād entering the sacred page for the first time after thirteen years of explicit Makkan teachings of non-retaliation: *wa qātilū fī sabīli Allāhi alladhīna yuqātilūnakum* — "fight in the way of God those who fight you" — and immediately, in the same breath: *wa lā taʿtadū* — "but do not transgress" — *inna Allāha lā yuḥibbu al-muʿtadīn* — "truly God does not love the transgressors." The commentators explain the legislative moment: in Makkah, the rule had been patience (the Companion-reports count the forbidding-of-fight passages as including 41:34 — "repel evil with what is better" — and 73:10 — "bear patiently what they say" — and 5:13 — "pardon them and forbear" — and 88:22 — "you are not a warder over them"): the community had been commissioned to forgive, to bear, to draw aside; but now, in Madinah, with the Makkans raiding on their borders, robbing their caravans, killing their husbandmen: God gave, verse by precise verse, the right of *self-defense* — *fight those who fight you* (and the commentators point to its companion-verse at 22:39: *permission is granted to those who are fought, because they have been wronged* — as belonging to the same first moment of the law). The Qurayshite perversion had already gone on for twelve years; at Madinah, the whole situation changed militarily and spiritually: the ummah was now ordered — not by a human king, but by *the Book* itself — to defend itself.

**In the Way of God — Fī Sabīlillāh**

The verse's condition — *fī sabīli Allāh* — "in the way of God" — is the commentary-tradition's constant drill-line: *why* the fight is to be carried on — not for vengeance nor banditry nor province-taking nor pride of tribe (the sīra-born Conflicts facing the Prophet were none of them aggrandizement-pursuits: they were the defense of a besieged ummah, and afterward the opening of breathing-space for a persecuted community); but *in God's own direction*: in defense of the religion, of the community's access-fairness, of the tithe of life on which the faith sustains its people. The entire Islamic jurisprudence of war arises from this single verse's three clauses and its garden: fight *only those fighting you* (the tribe-of-Bakr, Khuzāʿah alliances and the broken Ḥudaybiyah aggressions being its later unfoldings), *no transgression* — and by the words' own central placing of God — fight *for God, not oneself*.

**"Do Not Transgress" — The Boundaries**

The master-commentators never pass over the boundary-clause: *do not transgress* — *lā taʿtadū*: the verse that grants fighting bans brutality in the same clause: *iʿtidāʾ* — overrun, overspill beyond the limit — is immediately forbidden inside the very verse that opens the war-permission: and the tradition's whole conduct-in-war law unfolds directly: no killing of children, no killing of women, no killing of old men, no killing of the sick, the hermit, the monk of the cell (as Ibn ʿAbbās's rule at the school; the Companion-reported statutes of Abū Bakr's instructions at al-Māwardī's gathering), no mutilation of corpses, no cutting down of fruit trees, no burning of houses, no breach of treaty, no fighting against whoever restrains his hand or offers peace (as ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz's famous letter on this verse itself had instructed: *"fight not those who do not fight you"* — al-Ṭabarī). The Prophet ﷺ's standing address to his own commanders in every departing battle-file, preserved by the tafsīr and all the collections as belonging to the doctrine of verse 190:

> *"Fight in the way of God... but do not transgress, do not act treacherously, do not mutilate, do not kill children."* (Muslim 1731 — from Buraydah's report, from the Prophet's addresses at the departure of the armies)

**God Loves Not the Transgressors**

The ending of the verse — *inna Allāha lā yuḥibbu al-muʿtadīn* — is the classic *warning-signature* of the sūrah (already at 2:205, repeated at 2:190): the fight's law thereby stands upon the same ground-rules as the rest of the sūrah's laws: God's love-economy: He *loves* the virtuous (2:195), the repentant (2:222), the purifiers (2:222), the just (5:13), the patient (3:146), the trusters (3:159), the doers of good (3:148, 5:93), and those who keep reforming (5:64); and the transgressor is written inside the same Book's enumerations of whom He does *not* love — and so the soldier of Islam, like its judge, its writer, its craftsman, its merchant, knows that his department too possesses its own *love-test*: did my fighting transgress? — or remained *within* God's boundaries? The believers' army — the tradition shows — was the first in world history to enter battle burdened with law: the verse had struck the door for war open — and slammed the door against its transgressions: and the world's lay-learners across the centuries have been obliged to weigh Islam's conduct in its own scripture's own scales: *fight — but never transgress: God loves not the transgressors.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:191

> **Kill them wherever you come upon them and drive them out of the places from which they have driven you out. For persecution is far worse than killing. And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque unless they attack you there. If they do so, then fight them—that is the reward of the disbelievers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wheresoever You Come Upon Them**

The emergency order, given at the very hour the believers were preparing for their turn-back Ḥudaybiyah journey, now opens its second phase: *wa-qtulūhum ḥaythu thaqiftumūhum wa akhrijūhum min ḥaythu akhrajūkum* — "and slay them wheresoever you come upon them, and expel them from whence they expelled you." The commentators explain the direction of its measure exactly: those who had expelled them — the Quraysh, who barred them from the Kaaba and drove them in their flight from Makkah — those *may now be expelled in return*: the measurement exactly balanced: expulsion for expulsion: the verse's legal ground being the *lex talionis* at the scale of communal crime: not every idolater of the Peninsula, but *those who had expelled them*: the specific persecutors of the emigration-years standing now under the counter-order of the Book. And the *thaqifa*-word — *thaqiftumūhum*: the military-scouting "overtake," "come upon" in its richest register: hunt them out wherever your scouting overtakes them — the imperative sustaining its full force across the entire fighting-period until pardon or submission's alternative was reached: and the immediate context, as the commentators explain with exact historical reference — *do not fight with them near the Sacred Mosque until they fight with you there* — the second clause drawing the sacred-ground: even in the midst of this general battle-permission, the ḥaram stands inviolate: no strike falls within it until it is fallen first from the other side: God's sacred geography preserved even here in the thick of the defence-command.

**Fitnah Worse Than Slaying**

The great sentence of the verse arrives now — one of the most quoted clauses of Islamic law in the entire record: *wa'l-fitnatu ashaddu mina al-qatl* — "for strife is worse than slaying." The word *fitnah* is translated by the tradition across its registers: from the Arabic root's primary sense of *trial-by-fire* (the flame's testing of gold), the word is used in the Book and sunnah for religious persecution, for faith-breaking pressure, for the systematic destruction of a community's religion: the commentators at this verse gloss it first and foremost as the *persecution of the believers* — Makkah's systematic commission, over the banishing of the believers from their houses, their markets, their sanctuary, their free practice — *that* is worse than slaying: the *shirk* — the idolatry-enforcing scheme of Quraysh — is worse than the blood of battle: as the school always explains: blood swept from the battle-field leaves its family weeping; but *fitnah* — religion extirpated from a city's hearts — leaves its generations crumbling: the community by numbers is small; the community by religion is limitless: and so the verse sets over the two scales the authentic measurement: *fitnah*: the scorched-earth of the soul; *slaying*: the ruined house of the body — the first exceeds the second in the Court of God's measuring: and according to most schools of law and other than, the clause is understood equally as the *legal* justification of the 190-verse permissions: *were fighting not now permitted, the fitnah would roll the whole religion under* — so the fight is the mercy at its wider flare.

**The Sacred Precinct, Held Inviolate**

The verse's second half immediately reins in its own permissive scope *at God's House*: *wa lā tuqātilūhum ʿinda al-masjidi al-ḥarāmi ḥattā yuqātilūkum fīh* — "but do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you there." The commentators measure the immense condition: had the over-literal reading of verse 190's first clause been accepted at its plainest, fighting might have proceeded against Quraysh inside the very sanctuary the Arabs, from Abraham's day, had never permitted bloodshed: God blocks that reading immediately: *not in My sanctuary — until they attack you there*: *the Kaaba stays inviolable above every military command*: *even* the justified defense is held outside the House; and the clause then continues — *if they fight you within it, slay them* — the defense-permission itself standing even inside the sacred zone — for defense belongs to a wholly different nature from aggression and thus is allowed inside God's House; but the *first-hand* aggression *never* begins for the Muslims within God's House — never. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the verse becomes the first great answer of the Book to the military problem of the whole sacred-zone: *fighting does not cross its line, even in defense of Islam:* the dignity-of-place is set above the dignity-of-force, and so the City of the Sanctuary — the whole Meccan district (Mina and Muzdalifah and every furlong within the naming of the iḥrām) — has remained a peace-zone down fourteen-century living record of prayer-complying: and the verse ends its vial with the solemn recompense-formula: *kadhalika jazāʾu al-kāfirīn* — "such is the recompense of the disbelievers": the verdict against everyone who wages war upon God's house and God's community: and the Prophet's own line of the same register at the moment of re-entry into Makkah is remembered always at this verse:

> *"When the Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah on the Day of the Conquest, he declared: this city has God sanctified, and it shall not be lawful for anyone who believes in God and the Last Day to shed blood therein or to cut down its trees — save for me, for one hour of one day."* (al-Bukhārī 1834; Muslim 1353 — the Prophet's own documented phrase of the Day, with the greater tradition remembering the exact boundaries the Book set forever thereafter on the sacred zone)

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:192

> **But if they cease, then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Verse of One Breath**

After two full verses of commands, permissions, sacred boundary-markers and recompense-formulas, the sūrah plants a verse of only eight Arabic words — *fa-ini intahaw fa-inna Allāha ghafūrun raḥīm* — "but if they desist, then truly God is Forgiving, Merciful" — and the commentary tradition treats its placement with the most solemn gravity: the purpose of the first breath-of-air verse is to show *how quickly God's war is finished*: not gradually, not after forms and rituals, not after restitution-schemes nor tribunals; but *if they desist* — the moment the opponent's hand stops striking, the whole war-ledger reverts to its original two names: *Forgiving* and *Merciful*. The commentators keep the discussion near at hand: desisting here means the ceasing of hostility — of fighting and expulsion and fitnah — not necessarily the ceasing of difference of religion (with the schools' elaborate discussions of its scope: al-Rāzī confined it precisely to fighting and expulsion, as the clause directly connected to the violence); and the verse underlines the near-immediacy of divine pardon: no vestibule of repentance-days is required before the Names end the war: the Names' language's present-tension is the sharpest of assurances: God forgives now, God is merciful now: no wait-state; no probation; no review: God settles back into the names of His essential nature the moment the sword of aggressing falls silent.

**God's War Is Not Vendetta**

The tradition has dwelt upon the verse the whole mercy-architecture of Islam's war law (which had already been defined tightly by verses 190–191): the aggression is God's boundary-crossing; once its actor ceases, the track-back of God's vengeance does not extend: God's fight is *defense* in its terms — defensive in its cause, limited in its scope, wavering to mercy at the very drop of the enemy's blade: *fa-ini-ntahaw*: *if they desist*: the school constantly draw the balance-model: the outgoing correspondence stops at exactly the door where the in-going stopped: not thrust by conquest's unbounded appetites, not wave-tossed by victory's own cup: at the absolute halt of their striking, the law returns to *ghafūrun raḥīm*. The Prophet's own conduct on the greatest day of his vindication — the Day of the Conquest of Makkah, January 630 (AH 8) — and its tradition-famous speech of forbearance to the assembled Quraysh, belongs in technical terms to this very rule:

> *"Go; you are free."* — the Prophet's ﷺ own general amnesty upon the conquered city — the moment the whole past-war's account was settled in one sermon, and twenty years of persecution — drawing the whole file forthwith into God's names — was itself the most glowing sunnah-illustration of the verse's compact mercy: once they desisted, they were *tulaqāʾ*: freed on the ground of their own desisting, without recompense upon the years of battle and expulsion (from the Prophet's speech upon the Day of the Conquest, reported by al-Wāqidī and the histories and carried in the sīra and tafsīr of this verse, corroborated in the universal narrative of the conquest)

**The Believers Own No Highway to Revenge**

The tradition's jurists have built the verse into the extremity of Islamic war-law: after hostilities have legitimately ceased, Muslim armies are not permitted to exact *proportionate-retaliation* for old takings, nor *reprisal* for remembered suffering: *fa-ini-ntahaw* establishes their non-responsibility: the *ghafūrun raḥīm* seal closes the whole list of war-crimes-in-the-waiting at that one exhaustive clause: the codes of war and peace of the classical fuqahāʾ, Abū Yūsuf and al-Shaybānī and al-Shāfiʿī and al-Māwardī — every manual of *siyar* — anchors the end-state of hostilities to this verse's command of desisting: fighting lasts only as long as fitnah lasts: after the last blow, the Book counts nothing remaining but the two Divine Names — from beginning to end — *forgiving* and *merciful*: and the verse therefore stands solemnly before every later age of Islamic conduct: *God's peace is His own*: He is less sharp-edged than the mountain-tribes of man's own turbulence: He opens the gate of pardon the moment the foe's mace falls: *fa-ini-ntahaw — fa-inna Allāha ghafūrun raḥīm*: the entire Islamic warfare-doctrine compressed into eight sacred words.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:193

> **Fight against them ˹if they persecute you˺ until there is no more persecution, and ˹your˺ devotion will be to Allah ˹alone˺. If they stop ˹persecuting you˺, let there be no hostility except against the aggressors.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Terminus of Fighting**

Having placed its lines under one de-escalating seal, the Book now sets the precise endpoint of the fight: *wa qātilūhum ḥattā lā takūna fitnatun wa yakūna al-dīnu li-llāh* — "fight them until there is no fitnah, and religion is for God." The commentators examine both offices in strictest detail. The first — *ḥattā lā takūna fitnatun* — *until there is no strife/persecution*: the fitting measure of the state's war-limits: the fitnah of the pagans had for fourteen years prevented the believers' access to their own worship: they were routed out of their houses, their mosques, the House itself: *until no fitnah*: the field is leveled; the banished people come home; religion stands on its own feet. The second — *wa yakūna al-dīnu li-llāh* — *and religion be for God*: is unfolded with the greatest care by the classical commentators, and it belongs with the entire constitution of the law: religion-for-God as *the worship-state where God is truly served openly* — where He alone is invoked in His House without competitors: where tawḥīd stands unstifled among the citizenry; and their let-clause answers the whole defense-theory at once: religion being for God does not mean the whole earth forcibly converted in one crucible — the Book has its own explicit denial of religious compulsion (2:256: *lā ikrāha fī al-dīn* — "no compulsion in religion"): it means that God's own Word is allowed unhindered air — the fitnah against His worship dismantled — and His House stands *for Him* alone, uncrowded by idols: it is the *public* victory of tawḥīd, the *public* security of the believers' worship, the *public* dignity of the House — not the forced coalescing of every heart by the sword: and even that public victory comes to its measure at once when their attacking hands still: *fa-ini intahaw fa-lā ʿudwāna illā ʿalā al-ẓālimīn* — "if they desist, then there is no enmity, save against the wrongdoers."

**No Enmity Save Against the Wrongdoers**

The commentators grasp the final restrictive clause with the exactness of its wording: *fa-lā ʿudwāna illā ʿalā al-ẓālimīn* — *no enmity-aggression remains: save against the wrongdoers*: the *illā* — *except* — is the center-star of the verse: the defensive war against the persecutors is legitimated only against *ẓulm* — wrongdoing — against those who had begun and continued the aggression: once they stop, no enmity follows them into their current houses, nor against their children, nor against those who never participated: the school has never departed from pointing out that the exception-seal set itself deliberately against *wars-of-aggrandizement* and *tribe-of-different-tongues wars* — the wars people fight once their enemies fall silent, in order to *finish the job*: the Book sets in that very spot its exception: after their desisting, the only enmity *legitimate* is against recidivist wrongdoers — those who return to aggression — and even that enmity is lawful only through the state's legal re-assessment. The verse is thus read as the exact delimitation of all Islamic self-defense: *fight until the persecution is dismantled — fight until God's religion is genuinely served* — *and if they stop: stop*. And the legend of Islam's own past chivalries — its forbears at the Christian wars, a contrast the scholars of the great fiqh schools have often drawn, reading the verse as Islam's own standing charter — *stop at the second their enemies stop* — was the great recording of Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb's instruction to his own armies in Syria:
