> *"Do not betray, do not trespass, do not mutilate, do not kill a child nor an old man, do not cut down a burning tree, do not destroy a monastery... you will pass by people devoted in their cells; let them be in that in which they are devoted."* (the standing legal-instructions of the early conquests, assembled in al-Ṭabarī and the siyar-books, and carried by the tradition as the lived meaning of *lā ʿudwāna* at this verse)

**The Begun Will of Peace**

The tradition thus keeps this verse at the heart of the whole Islamic war-peace philosophy: since the *fitnah*-ended state and the true-religion state is its end, and the wrongdoers only its residual subject, from it emerges the whole legislation of truce, capitulation, dhimmah, treaty, peace-terms — *everything* filtered from the last clause of *fa-lā ʿudwāna*: the whole Islamic world of early peace-with-unbelieving-neighbors was the direct administrative application of the doctrines of verses 190–194 (al-Māwardī's siyar al-Sulṭāniyyah being the exhaustive archived system-registers of its widening-school). The Book's whole scheme thereby comes full circle: the fighting-permission opened in verses 190–191 marks the transitional hour of the first battle-authorization; the destination-marked fighting at 193 fixes Islam's war upon its true purposes and bars its false widening; and the desisting-end reads as the very peace-dispatch of God's own Names — *Ghafūr, Raḥīm* — in every age of war and peace of the believers: *until no fitnah, and God's religion stands by itself; and thence forward, no enmity, none, save against the wrongdoers alone.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:194

> **˹There will be retaliation in˺ a sacred month for ˹an offence in˺ a sacred month, and all violations will bring about retaliation. So, if anyone attacks you, retaliate in the same manner. ˹But˺ be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is with those mindful ˹of Him˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Month's Sanctity Reciprocal**

After the war-laws' structure was set, the Book turns to its own sacred timing — to settle the application of the fighting-rules inside the sanctuary of the calendar itself: *al-shahru al-ḥarāmu bi'l-shahri al-ḥarāmi wa'l-ḥurumātu qiṣāṣ* — "the sacred month is for the sacred month, and for inviolable things there is retribution." The commentators take the natural reading of the verse at its face: the sacred months — Dhu'l-Qaʿdah, Dhu'l-Ḥijjah, Muḥarram, and Rajab — in which the Arabs since Abraham's day had ceased bloodshed — are not disarmed *unilaterally*: if the enemy sheds blood during the sacred month, the month does not turn into the predator's hunting-blindfold: *the sanctity is reciprocal*: *they* broke it, and so they have released the month from its shelter for their account: blood shed in violation of sacred-season is answered in the sacred month, by the same *qiṣāṣ* — measured retribution — that holds for blood elsewhere: and the tradition runs back the concrete event: during the first Ḥudaybiyah march, some had suspected that they would be attacked in Muḥarram or Dhu'l-Qaʿdah while they themselves were barred from fighting by the sanctity: the verse thus answered the Muslims' exact apprehension: sanctity bound *both* sides — and if one side abandoned it, the second side's defense restored it against the wrongdoer. Al-Rāzī sums it up: *God's sacred times are not founded to give advantage to whoever cynically spurns them*: their binding is *ḥurumāt* — inviolabilities — held mutually: so long as the other side holds them; but not into self-destruction.

**Retribution in the Forbidden Things**

The second clause expands the principle's reach into everything else God made inviolable: *wa'l-ḥurumātu qiṣāṣ* — "and for inviolable things there is retribution" — and the retribution-pattern already pronounced at 2:178 (blood), 2:181 (testaments), and now 2:194 (sanctified days and things): the commentators unfold its field with broad strokes: *ḥurumāt*: the inviolable acts and estates of God's law — the sacred months, the sacred House-grounds, the state of iḥrām, the inviolability of the believer's blood, of his property, of his sanctuary; and the *qiṣāṣ* — retribution — is named over all of it in kind, in measure, in proportion: the violated sanctities are *answered* by the lawful instrument set in God's measure: never by fury's spontaneous overruns (like the pre-Islamic tribe-feuds) and never by the cynical blanking of the violators' account: *retribution in the forbidden things* is the Book's radical device of law: it plants a decisive contravening-power upon the side of violated sanctity itself, so that the covenant of inviolability never stands toothless before its cynics: *out of proportion shall no man respond, nor cynically shall any offense be unpunished*: retribution instead of chaos.

**Transgressed and Transgress Back — In the Same Measure**

The verse's third clause — *fa-mani iʿtadā ʿalaykum fa-ʿtadū ʿalayhi bi-mithli mā iʿtadā ʿalaykum* — "whosoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same measure as he transgressed against you" — is its own great charter of *legal proportion*: the phrase uses the very verb for sin (*iʿtadā*: transgress) as its own counter-agent's action: reply *in the same measure* — *bi-mithli mā*: with the like of what was done — neither more nor less. The Muslim response bears therefore the stamp of *mirrored equality*: as at 16:126's exact parallel ("if you punish, punish with like of that wherewith you were punished") and 42:40's ("the recompense of an evil is an evil like unto it"): *measure for measure* — the Book's whole law of defense standing so engraved: defense resets the offense only at the measure-notched: blood for blood (v. 178), treaty-break for treaty-break (2:193), sacrilege for sacrilege (2:194), as the mirror in the hand of the offended never expanding beyond what was wanted from the offender's own hand. And the Book then reads its believers the seal: *wa-ttaqu Allāh* — "and reverence God": the counteraction, though lawful, is not to loose the God-fearing rein upon even lawful force: within the mirrored retaliation God's own watchfulness stands over them, lest the lawful measure possess itself into vindictiveness — and the verse seals with the comforting clause-names: *wa-ʿlamū anna Allāha maʿa al-muttaqīn* — "and know that God is with the reverent": *maʿiyyah* — *withness*: being with them, guiding them, granting them His confirmations in war and peace — the very withness the believers will need in the difficult balances of the mirrored-response: measured by the exact clash bounded by God's boundaries, whose very limits are the ochlocratic counter to man's violent tide of vengeance: *my retaliation comes down at the toe of the line: my God is with me, and what I strike for measure I cannot exceed — for what I exceed in vengeance I cross God's own line.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:195

> **Spend in the cause of Allah and do not let your own hands throw you into destruction ˹by withholding˺. And do good, for Allah certainly loves the good-doers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Spend — Then the Second Command**

The verse opens with the sūrah's constantly recurring summons: *wa anfiqū fī sabīli Allāh* — "and spend in the way of God": spending as the Islamic stream of resources flowing from the believer out toward God's many causes — arms and expeditions, journeys and foundations, the feeding of Muslims and their supplies, the maintenance of the ummah's children and the infrastructure of worship: all of it cradled into the wide designation *in God's way*. The clause truly belongs with the whole chapter of defense and could be read as continuing the war-law stack of verses 190–194: fighting is not founded upon an army of mercenaries in a ledger's ink — it is founded upon the Muslims *spending their own substance* in God's way, from their own pens and purses: the believers' war is a citizens' war economically as well as militarily — financed from the charity-circle of the believers, by the purse of the community, without conquest's plunder to survive upon: *spend in the way of God* — for the defense the next verses will complete is fought from the hearts and the stores of the believers themselves, not borrowed on the world's terms.

**"Do Not Cast Yourselves Into Ruin"**

The next command is one of the most debated directives of the whole legal body of the sūrah: *wa lā tulqū bi-aydīkum ilā al-tahlukah* — "and do not cast yourselves with your own hands into ruin." The tradition preserves the *asbāb al-nuzūl* — occasion of revelation — in all its detail: during the compaign-time of the Prophet's expeditions, a Muslim charged the Byzantine lines alone and fell, and some Muslims said, *he destroyed himself: his casting was his own hand-casting* — upon which Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī spoke the hadith of the occasion, as it is preserved in the accounts of al-Tirmidhī and others, in its direct recorded wording:

> "This man has cast himself into ruin"? Abū Ayyūb answered: "O people — you do not know the verse as we who were with the Revelation know it: this verse concerns *us*, the Anṣār: when God gave victory to His Prophet's religion we said secretly among ourselves: *let us now return to our properties and rebuild what the war took from us* — and God revealed against it: *do not cast yourselves with your own hands into ruin*: *casting into ruin* means *staying with one's wealth, preferring wealth to spending in God's way,* not the man who charges the lines at the heart of God's war. (al-Tirmidhī 2972; Abū Dāwūd — the occasion-report universally cited by the tafsīr tradition at this verse)

So the verse counter-charges *against hoarding*, not against duty's costliest devotion: *casting* is *the refraining from spending*: burying gold rolls beneath one's own bed while God's cause stands in need: *that* is the casting-into-ruin the Book names. The mufassirūn then generalize its carrying: abandoning jihād itself under the wealth-argument of rebuilding one's house is casting into ruin; selfish-for-calculating-refusal of expenditures demanded by the cause is casting into ruin; and — Ibn Kathīr preserves the expanded meaning of the moral despairer — *the man who, thinking God will no longer forgive him, gives up striving altogether and drowns himself further in sin* — he also casts himself into ruin — not by the sin alone, but by the despairing-turning-away from the spending and the striving still within his reach: while the plain meaning remains for all believers: *everything* which by one's own hand brings ultimate destruction — physical, financial, moral-spiritual — is hereby forbidden: the Book pronounces its absolute guard over the souls' own future: *do not cast yourselves into ruin — not into pride, not into cowardice, not into despair, not into wealth-clutching nor into world-wreckage.*

**"And Be Virtuous — God Loves the Virtuous"**

And the seal of the verse is itself one of the seals of the Book's own nature: *wa aḥsinū inna Allāha yuḥibbu al-muḥsinīn* — "and be virtuous — truly God loves the virtuous." The word *iḥsān* is left in its most general register: the beautiful doing: and just as verse 112 had defined *man aslama wajhahu li-llāh wa huwa muḥsin* — "he who submits his face to God while being virtuous" has won his reward — so now the Book seals its three commands — spend, do not cast into ruin, be virtuous — with God's love declared upon the named: *He loves al-muḥsinīn*: the doers-beautifully: the hadith of Gabriel itself having made iḥsān the head of the religion's three-storeys (islām, īmān, iḥsān: al-Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8 — with the answer: "*iḥsān*: worship God as though you saw Him, for though you do not see Him, He sees you"): so with the sealing of verse 195, the fighters of the field are sent into war with God's love assessed precisely as the *higher* duty they fulfill within war: and the verse swings itself into its broader teaching: *spend* as the horizon of generosity closes and *do not cast* as the horizon of suicide despair opens, *and be virtuous between them all* — with God's love waiting on the name the believers bear when they have spent, have held, have lived, have fought, and have survived: *the virtuous — the loved of God.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:196

> **Complete the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage for Allah. But if prevented ˹from proceeding˺, then ˹offer˺ whatever sacrificial animals you can afford. And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its destination. But if any of you is ill or has a scalp ailment ˹requiring shaving˺, then compensate either by fasting, charity, or a sacrificial offering. In times of peace, you may combine the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage then make the sacrificial offering you can afford. Whoever cannot afford that ˹offering˺, let them fast three days during pilgrimage and seven after returning ˹home˺—completing ten. These offerings are for those who do not live near the Sacred House. And be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Complete for God**

Now the sūrah's ḥajj-commission comes before the reader all together – its length and detail answering the events of the Ḥudaybiyah era, when the threatened war had thrown itself between the Muslims and the Kaaba: *wa atimmū al-ḥajja wa'l-ʿumrata li-llāh* — "and complete the ḥajj and the ʿumrah for God." The small particle *li-llāh* — *for God* — carries the charge first: the ḥajj is not a spectacle nor tribal pomp nor trade-encounter: it is *for God*: as the traditions' favorite reported phrase had already defined it: *al-ḥajju ʿArafah* — "the ḥajj is ʿArafah" (the day the whole ummah stands in one plain before God — and if anything distracts to the level of vanity, the ḥajj has been emptied of its God). Second: the function of the verb — *atimmū*: *complete*: the command's own insistence has been resolved by the fiqh into the road-rule: *if you begin the ḥajj, you must complete it to its end*: a leaving-off mid-journey, a shortening by one's own preference, are not allowed: once the iḥrām is put on, its sacredness may only end at its proper end: the certification's very purpose is this: *the ḥajj is full of beginnings: God demands the ending.* And third: in the union of ḥajj and ʿumrah, the Book binds the lesser pilgrimage with the greater in its single command with the same explicit verb: *both*: the greater being fard (3:97's own settling clause), the lesser — most of the schools have taught — being the sunnah-muakkadah *so near to its way* that the verse's *complete* encompasses it in the same breath: while the Ḥanbalī and Shāfiʿī schools have even seen the sameness of the obligation — the scholars agreeing together only on their daily working: *ḥajj and ʿumrah both being commanded* — and every year since the conquest of Makkah the answers of faith have made their completeness testify to the book itself: millions leave their homes, both fulfilling together in God's name *both* the greater and lesser pilgrimage.

**The Hinderer's Offering — and its Scalp-Ransom**

Now the Book's mercy-interruption clause: *fa-in uḥṣirtum fa-mā istaysara mina al-hady* — "and if you are hindered — then such offering as is easy." The verb *uḥṣirtum* — contained, besieged, blocked — carries the exact loading of the Ḥudaybiyah moment itself: the road to Makkah being blocked by Quraysh's counter-draw, the pilgrims turned back at the very edge of their ʿumrah; and the Book's answer: *the journey hindered is not wasted* — the ummah whose iḥrām is put on, but whose road is barred, does not shave nor released iḥrām in the field of their hunting: rather: *send forward the offering* you can most easily bring — one sheep at minimum (or commensurate cow or camel, as is encouraged by the whole tradition) — *and until it reaches its place of sacrifice you do not shave your heads*: *wa lā taḥliqū ruʾūsakum ḥattā yablugha al-hadyu maḥillahu.* The commentators adduce the very action of the Prophet on the Ḥudaybiyah-plain itself: he commanded the sacrificing of the camels *there* — not at Makkah, but where the road was blocked — and then shaved, and the iḥrām was lifted where they stood, without the sanctuary ever being entered: *the pilgrimage that may not run forward may run backward in God*: *maḥilla* — the "place-of-reaching" of the offering — is read by one tradition as Mina itself, by another as the very place where substitution was made: — wherever God reaches it to its appointed destination in acknowledgment: wherever God knows the offering has discharged its soul. And the verse then enters the specific case of the afflicted pilgrim: *fa-man kāna minkum marīḍan aw bihi adhan min raʾsihi fa-fidyatun min ṣiyāmin aw ṣadaqatin aw nusuk* — "if anyone among you is ill or has an ailment of his head, then a ransom of fasting or charity or sacrifice." The early Muslims kept shaving difficulties before their very hands: men with lice (the simplest report: a man comes down his ḥajj with heavy scalp — the Prophet, at al-Bukhārī 1815-16; Muslim 1201, is reported to have ordered him: *shave and ransom by three days of fasting, or feeding six poor persons, or slaughter of a sheep*: the same three options from the book: and the merciful depth is immediate: the nowadays-itching scalp of the desert-pilgrim has its own charter of law laid down here: *nor are you to suffer the ailment through the end*: shave — and with your shaving God has His due: not all of God's law obligates suffering where the Lord has already accepted relief.

**Tamattuʿ — The Ten Days**

The verse then approaches the ecstasy-rules of its pilgrim-engine — the one the Book calls *al-tamattuʿ* — "enjoyment": combining the ʿumrah with ḥajj in the same journey, but leaving the first iḥrām between: *fa-man tamattaʿa bi'l-ʿumrati ilā al-ḥajji fa-mā istaysara mina al-hady* — "whoever enjoys the ʿumrah ahead of the ḥajj — such offering as is easy": the man who fully re-enters iḥrām between the ʿumrah and the ḥajj brings a hady back with him — animal-sacrifice: he reaps the two-year rewards in one journey's field, and this sacrificial-offering is the token of their union. Yet the Book's mercy-valve is opened here too: *fa-man lam yajid fa-ṣiyāmu thalāthati ayyāmin fī al-ḥajji wa sabʿatin idhā rajaʿtum tilka ʿasharatun kāmilah* — "whoever finds not [the means], then — a fast of three days during ḥajj and seven when you return": and the glorious close: *those are ten complete* — *tilka ʿasharatun kāmilah* — God Himself sealing the alternate to the substitution-scheme by His own arithmetic of wholeness: ten days of fasting standing for one sheep — the poor pilgrim already becoming, by God's own book-mathematics, *the same* in God's acceptance as the wealthy pilgrim who offers kine and camels. And the fit of the clause — *dhālika li-man lam yakun ahluhā ḥāḍirī al-masjidi al-ḥaram* — "this is for those whose people are not neighbors of the Sacred Mosque": the local Makkans receive no fast of ten days: the rule applies only to the travelers — for the whole point of the law's concession is that coming-from-a-distance carries its own easings in ritual-combinations: Makkan dwellers do not tamattuʿ — the two pilgrimages fall under one iḥrām — their economics of temple-visit already placing them miles nearer to the divine requirement than the travelers for whom the verse carries its mercy-count. And the Book's final pronouncement of its own heed: *wa-ttaqu Allāha wa-ʿlamū anna Allāha shadīdu al-ʿiqāb* — "reverence God, and know that God is severe in retribution": the strong-seal placed by the whole ḥajj-prescription squarely inside the watching God's own two eyes, so that nothing in the verse may ever be read as mere paper-law: its readiness to bear is also accompanied by God's own reading of its readiness: the mercy-provisions of God are not the loopholes of a hard Lawgiver, but the appreciation-lace of a Knowing One: and by them, travelers have crossed the desert times — the Ḥudaybiyah road — all the desert roads again — the completion-command on their tongues and the ten days of the substitute's counting inscribed on their foreheads, at the foot of the great House.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:197

> **˹Commitment to˺ pilgrimage is made in appointed months. Whoever commits to ˹performing˺ pilgrimage, let them stay away from intimate relations, foul language, and arguments during pilgrimage. Whatever good you do, Allah ˹fully˺ knows of it. Take ˹necessary˺ provisions ˹for the journey˺—surely the best provision is righteousness. And be mindful of Me, O people of reason!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Known Months**

The law of the ḥajj becomes bound first by its clock: *al-ḥajju ashhurun maʿlūmāt* — "the ḥajj is during months well known." Al-Ṭabarī and the companions of law lay down the conveyance with its old force: Shawwāl, Dhu'l-Qaʿdah, and Dhu'l-Ḥijjah are the head-months of the pilgrimage — their ten days' division, and specially (copiously announced in the schools in either form: the three whole months together, or the ten days of Dhu'l-Ḥijjah at their tail) — the iḥrām for ḥajj may never be safely drawn in any other month: the pilgrim entering its state in Rajab or Ramadan stays in it through the seasons to the Day of Assembly, the load of its regulations extending over half the year of anticipation: the Book itself thereby choosing the path of balance between the spontaneous piety of immediate entrance and the calendar-certainty of the sanctioned season: God's known months house a rhythmic assembly — that the pilgrims of the world can gather at God's House in a season-indexed covenant of months — just as Ramadan was made known by moon-sighting to every land so its appointed fast is known to happen at its right world-season: the ḥajj-season is fixed as well: its people return at the tenth of Dhu'l-Ḥijjah to prove the solemn words of their ancestors' pilgrimage in every year and by God's command.

**No Lewdness, Iniquity, Quarreling**

Now the charter's purpose: the code-iḥrām etiquette, conjoined in a threefold vivid outlaw: *fa-man faraḍa fīhinna al-ḥajja fa-lā rafatha wa lā fusūqa wa lā jidāla fī al-ḥajj* — "whoever undertakes the ḥajj in them — no lewdness, no iniquity, no quarreling in the ḥajj." The three realms gather, at the ḥajj's actual pilgrim-filed day, into one legislative breath: *rafath* — lewdness — the explicit sexual act or insinuating speech relating to it, outside the law's seal upon the covenant: banned inside the whole iḥrām state, while at the actual ḥajj the fit with one's wives themselves is deferred to later; *fusūq* — iniquity — the general sin: bantering, swearing, lying, backbiting, wrong-thinking spoken anyhow: *every sin* coming by tongue or act or secret net beneath the entire iḥrām state; and *jidāl* — quarreling — the arguing that trips into hotness (al-Qurṭubī with the genealogies of the desert ḥajj: the Quraysh parades atop the Station of Abraham boasting of their own lineage and the honor of their maṣāʾil, the tribes boasting over the founding-names of their lands — all of it cut out of the pilgrimage): the tradition's own clean working: the pilgrim enters the sanctuary at the high noon of passions stripped away, with the law establishing the barest etiquette from the pledge-person: *not to do what is lewd; not to enter upon any iniquity; not to trade words in quarreling*: the Prophet's own single verdict upon the ḥajj-pilgrimage stands as the Tradition's summary of this verse (al-Bukhārī 1521; Muslim 1345 — from Abū Hurayrah's account):

> *"Whoever performs the ḥajj without lewdness nor wickedness will return as on the day his mother bore him"*

— *ka yawmi waladathu ummuhu*: the famous phrase of salvation's zero-return: the pilgrim returns re-made, infant-bare of history's marks: and the commentary tradition never lets the word go down: *as-pure-as-newborn* — the verse's own purpose: *that no lewdness nor iniquity nor quarreling should accompany the pilgrim*: the consolidation of the ḥajj's spiritual calculus within a single ten-day transfiguration-period: the man of God having returned by God's hand to the mother-birth of true innocence.

**The Best Provision**

Then comes the famous line that all the preachers of the ages keep at the center of their ḥajj-sermons: *wa tazawwadū fa-inna khayra al-zādi al-taqwā* — "and make provision — for the best provision is reverence." The verse weaves twin structures differently: its surface counsel is plain needing — the pilgrim must saddle himself with provisions from his own home — the Book forbidding the pilgrim upon the road to become a beggar in his rīḥ-cloak: he must come with drink and food *from his storehouse*, clothing to change, a mount if he has it: *no reliance is to be made upon the heedless charity of the fellow-pilgrim nor on the bounty of arriving villages*: the wayfarers of the desert-pilgrimage carried this word as immediate practicality — no gas stations, no caravanserais, no organized rest-houses: and yet the scripture sends its deeper counsel immediately: *fa-inna khayra al-zādi al-taqwā* — *the best provision is reverence*: you may fill your saddle-bags with bread and salted meat, but you may not starve your soul: *provision of the spirit* takes the verse's center: taqwā (the sūrah's Golden Name from its first verse) is chosen as the *best* — the word *khayr*: not merely "a good" nor "a goodly": *the best*: *between all provisions a traveler may prepare before his death, between all saddle-bags of pilgrimage, between all procurable goods in the world and all foods of earth, the best provision that the pilgrim takes with him remains the fear of God.* Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ghazālī both water the whole verse almost every single chapter of theirs with its beauty: the pilgrim to Makkah readies himself with gold and beast of load; the pilgrim to God through death readies himself likewise: he appears before God — by the Book's plainest similitude — with the same two loads on his camel: whatever he carries of earthly goods and whatever he carries of the heart's provisions: and the judgment falls simply upon the better of the two: death's wayfarer is told to make provision of *taqwā*: for only taqwā survives the journey-forever of the afterlife: all worship and acts are bound together in the single provision: *make provision — the best of provision — reverence.*

**"Reverence Me, O Possessors of Intellect"**

The very seal of verse 197 closes — *wa-ttawqīnī yā ulī'l-albāb*: "reverence Me, O possessors of intellect" — even employing the further word whether *wa-ttaqu-ni* — "fear Me": the pivot-aided object: the possessors of the *albāb* — kernels — the men of intelligences able to bear the weight of the command (2:179 already addressing them on the city's heights of retribution-law): the Book confides the whole pilgrimage not just as ritual-route but as the finest practical exercise God has designed for the intact cultivation of reverence: the man in iḥrām's stripped sobriety — who cannot quarrel, nor brag, nor flirt, nor cut his hair, nor cover his head, nor whine, nor be alone with women — is being daily drilled in taqwā's soil in its own cognitive intensity — the *albāb* of men are made instead of being proven: *reverence Me*: the Book of God lifts the pilgrim to the very station of the men of intellect not by any increase in ritual-lineage but by the growing inward rigor of taqwā: 59:18's own solemn closing: *and fear God; truly God is aware of what you do*: at the end of the ḥajj-charter, as its commanding pronoun at its commanding word — *wa-ttaqu-nī* — *reverence Me* — the possessors of intellect receiving the same command the prophets receive: *do not learn of God's path with the outside alone but at the center of the heart*: and a billion pilgrims of the past 1400 years have precisely at this seat — the seat of the world-summit of rebounding intellectuality and devotion: *O possessors of intellect* — have received the greatest command of the Book of God and set forth with all saddle-bags, staffs and garments upon the straightest of all roads to God: *reverence Me — make provision — remember Me* — the trinity of tags closing God's pilgrimage-command for centuries over a billion shoulders of the Hujjaj of the world: *respect and holiness* — the twin columns: pledge and pillow: goal and shroud.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:198

> **There is no blame on you for seeking the bounty of your Lord ˹during this journey˺. When you return from ’Arafât, praise Allah near the sacred place and praise Him for having guided you, for surely before this ˹guidance˺ you were astray.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Commerce-Clause of the Pilgrimage**

The verse opens with the law of trade itself: *laysa ʿalaykum junāḥun an tabtaghū faḍlan min rabbikum* — "there is no sin upon you in seeking a bounty from your Lord." The commentators mark exactly what the clause means at the ḥajj's season: some of the first Muslims had imagined that trade during the pilgrimage was wrong — that commerce carried a corruption-corona from the circus of its merchants: and the verse was given to clarify: *no blame upon the pilgrims who trade, buy and sell, carry goods in or out of the sanctuary during the pilgrimage*: *bounty from your Lord* — *faḍl* — commerce itself being God's own bounty woven among the world's exchanges — so the seeking of profit by legal means among the pilgrimage crowds is not any desecration: it is *God's earthly bounty, lawfully in the pilgrims' path*: al-Qurṭubī recounts the consensus: to refrain is better spiritually — but to trade is not blame — and the phrase *faḍl* — bounty — becomes the argument made farther on against the ascetical eye with which the conquests of Islam had expanded their cities: the legitimacy of the market itself is God's street, and he who trades honestly in pilgrimate-days does not stop being God's man: the bounty of God *is His to give*, and He gives much of it in the transactions of His own House's circling-in-a-gap through markets and crowds of the larger cities of the great standing season of the year.

**"When You Pour Out From Arafat"**

Then comes the pivot of the whole ḥajj-day: *fa-idhā afaḍtum min ʿArafātin fa-dhkurū Allāha ʿinda al-mashʿar al-ḥarām* — "then, when you pour forth from ʿArafah, remember God at the sacred ground." The verb — *afaḍtum* — from *ifāḍah*: to pour out, to flow down en masse — captures the tide of pilgrims departing ʿArafah at sunset for Muzdalifah, the middle-ground between the plain and Mina — and the tradition probably passed its most famous transfiguration-state of the whole sojourn: hundreds of thousands, in one single white-clad flood, leaving the plain at once for the dusk-lit ground at Muzdalifah — with the verse's instruction: *remember God* — the whole crowd's strongest devotion to be the united-dhikr (remembrance) of the Sacred Land-mūment — the *mashʿar al-ḥarām*: *the hallowed station*: which some of the earlier commentators (as the tradition reports at al-Rāzī's register) read as the whole of Muzdalifah itself, others as a marked little hill within it — the hill of Quzaḥ — where the whole night of Muzdalifah is passed in prayer before morning breaks — the pilgrims sleeping on the open ground beneath God's own palace-arch, the moon above them, and God's own watchfulness over them throughout that holy night: the words of remembrance themselves being the pilgrim's staples of the ḥajj — *subḥān Allāh, al-ḥamdu li-llāh, Allāhu akbar* — the moonlit plain humming with their low chant even through the night.

**"As He Guided You"**

And, last of all, the verse claims the entire day's remembrance as the turning-point of the whole guidance-economy: *wa-dhkurūhu kamā hadākum wa in kuntum min qablihi la-mina al-ḍāllīn* — "and remember Him as He guided you — though formerly you were of those astray." The *kamā hadākum* — *as He guided you* — has been read both as a "remember Him *because* He guided you" (the Arabic *kamā* as comparative-ground: remembrance commensurate with the guidance) and as "remember Him *just as* He guided you" (remembrance matching the guidance's own measure): the commentators lock both readings in their solemn cadence: *we were astray — we were actually of the ḍāllīn* — and the grace of guidance is so sovereign that only a remembrance as strong as it can answer it: the converted Arab of Madinah recollects Makkah's still-living fleshy memories: their father's gods, their tribe's beat, their whole history of devotion to the vanity-idols ranged around the Kaaba — then looks at Mount ʿArafah and now stands on the field of Muzdalifah beneath God's sky — and invokes the act of *remembrance as if God Himself stood opposite him, watching*: *wa in kuntum min qablihi la-mina al-ḍāllīn*: *and how can the tongue praise less than the tour the Lord of the House has made from lostness to guidance?* The tradition has always preserved the verse as the very covenant-day of the ḥajj: on the Plain of ʿArafah, where the Prophet ﷺ stood on his camel asking about everything on the day of the greatest of sermons (as the accounts of the Farewell Pilgrimage lay out), the pilgrim tilts his head to Heaven to say his own thanks for the grace of the guidance whose very inch he was standing upon — *we were of the lost — and now we are here, pouring out in remembrance* — and the vow is made in all centuries' pilgrims' hearts that the remembrance will never cease: *dhikr-Allāh at the mashʿar al-ḥarām* — a remembrance issued when the whole world has fallen silent and the pilgrim-tide has already poured out from ʿArafah into Muzdalifah's dark amen.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:199

> **Then go forth with the rest of the pilgrims. And seek Allah’s forgiveness. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Whence the People Surge"**

Now the sūrah issues the very movement-order of the great day: *thumma afīḍū min ḥaythu afāḍa al-nāsu* — "then surge onward from where the people surge onward." The commentators immediately tie the verse's instruction to one of the most elaborately narrated occasions of the whole pilgrimage-theory among the first generation: the Ḥums — the name by which the Quraysh and their allied tribes of the Kaaba's neighborhood styled themselves, from a root carrying sincerity/devoutness — had in the days before Islam made a claim no other Arabic tribe made: *our tribe never leaves the ḥaram*: and so, when the pilgrimage-season drew its people to ʿArafat — which stands thirteen miles *outside* the ḥaram — the Ḥums remained behind at Muzdalifah, counting their exclusion from ʿArafat as piety: "we do not pray outside our own sacred land" — and thereby one tribe stayed home while thousands passed by them to the plain where God had chosen to meet His pilgrim-nations in the first place. When God's Messenger came upon the Day of Arafah to Makkah, the whole tribe of the Ḥums went with him — and this verse's instruction is read by the tradition as God's own follow-up: *go on the Day of Arafah where the others go — do not create your own liturgy of shrines against the one God has shown*: *min ḥaythu afāḍa al-nās*: from the very place where *the people* — al-nās — flood forth: God's House has not one particular family: its pilgrim-file is for *all the people* — Quraysh, Saqīf, Anṣār, the Bedouin, every generation of the earth — all performing what Abraham established for *all*: and at the Prophet's hand the whole separate ḥajj of the Ḥums was abolished for ever: their false piety of tribe-defending-claim was dismantled — Islam does not worship a geography set aside for certain high-born: *wherever the people surge, surge with them.*

**Abolishing Tribal Shibboleths in God's Name**

The tradition has always read the verse therefore as Islam's deep lead against the spiritual aristocracies: not lineage nor bond nor fancy of self-styled purity (the Ḥums, precisely, had claimed purity as their banner: *we are purity-people, we do not leave ḥaram*) cuts it with God's House: high-born pride functions exactly as the despised idol-competitors of the whole sūrah: the *nīd* — rivals — of verse 22 and the *andād* of verse 165: the "We are more special than others" of the Meccan elite is here seen to equip itself with the same abomination's logo as the pagans' gods: verse 199 is written against them: *afīḍū min ḥaythu afāḍa al-nāsu* — not one family transforms itself into the choice-few of God's pilgrims: but the people: the mass: the crowd. Islam is fundamentally the religion of *the people*: the weeping sinners, the weary Bedouin, the road-weary trader, the scarred slave, the husband and wife, the whole humankind: *its* pilgrimage is by definition the one where the ummah of God assembles itself — *with no one left behind believing his own tribe was too sleek for the plain*. And that day the Quraysh were stripped of one of the proudest boastings of the pagans, and forever admitted as one single rank in the ummah, one single file-of-pilgrims among the countless files of the people of God, with their arrogance stripped by the command of "the people": *then surge whence the people surge* — and no idol of tribe nor fancy remains standing.

**Ask Forgiveness — The Instructions of the Crowd-Day**

And its final clause binds the whole journey — for forgiveness: *wa-staghfirū Allāha inna Allāha ghafūrun raḥīm* — "and ask God for forgiveness: truly God is Forgiving, Merciful." The commentators mark the note's strange continuity: why *istighfār* — the *plea for forgiveness* — in the middle of a jubilantly victorious pilgrimage? The tradition's answer is incisive: because the final day of ʿArafah has revealed how far above man is God's own measure: after all the humility of iḥrām (hair gritty and uncovered), after the servant stands for nine hours in ʿArafah's sun, after the whole nation casts off its tribes' boasting by acknowledging their unbroken human state: the whole crowd has been placed back in soul-humility, and the very fact of pilgrimage's perils so punctures man's self-estimated sheet-cover of righteousness that the Book immediately offers the key the soul then holds: *stating yourself, asking forgiveness*: *fa-min dhālika al-yawm li-ghīri yawm* — from the day we were creatures, the whole affair of being pilgrims looks like sinlessness-side-by-side-with-sins, charity side-by-side with amends: and the crowd moves forward asking God for pardon — and the verse drives its central pair of Names — at the very center of the whole pilgrimage: *God Forgiving and Merciful*: not in the light of the sanctuary's hour only, nor in the multitude's external majesty only — but in the very fact that millions of men ask Him forgiveness *on one ground at one time* — *and His forgiving:* for the Lord's greatest of names still bears the vastness of the whole of mankind's repentances, however much He has pardoned before, now, or ever again.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:200

> **When you have fulfilled your sacred rites, praise Allah as you used to praise your forefathers ˹before Islam˺, or even more passionately. There are some who say, “Our Lord! Grant us ˹Your bounties˺ in this world,” but they will have no share in the Hereafter.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Rites Ended, Remembrance Continued**

The great ḥajj-sequence, which roamed from v.196's commissioning to v.199's pour-out, comes to its close not with ritual's ending but with remembrance's mandate: *fa-idhā qaḍaytum manāsikakum fa-dhkurū Allāha ka-dhikrikum ābāʾakum aw ashadda dhikrā* — "and when you have completed your rites, remember God as you remember your fathers — or with a more intense remembrance." The commentators outline the ancient background (al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī): among pre-Islamic Arabs, when the ḥajj days ended at Mina, the tribes assembled for the *customary bragging-matches of ancestry* — *our fathers were nobler; our swords sharper; our Tribe dead-laid more heroes into war* — the ḥajj-becoming-tribal-festival: genealogy beats outranking genesially beats: and the verse strikes its majestic blow at that very ritual: *when your rites end, let God* — not your fathers' liveries — *be the memory you carry back*: *fa-dhkurū Allāha ka-dhikrikum ābāʾakum* — *remember God as you remember your fathers* — the comparative *like* chosen by the Book itself: "as you remember" — for the Book never bans the memory of fathers themselves (Islam recognizes the fathers' line as the first natural bond: 6:151's own counsel: "be good to parents") — but it *compares* God's remembrance with it: the bragging of fathers is to be answered by the *remembrance of God: even as you remember them — *aw ashadda dhikrā*: or with still more ardent remembrance:* God has an argument for being remembered *more* than the fathers — the extents of His gifts exceeding all ancestral anchorages: so al-Rāzī's school hears the audacious grace of it: *the old Arabic dignity of the fathers was the deepest intimacy of the Arabs':* the verse takes it, shatters neither it nor its sweetness, and directs its whole thunderous warmth to the *Lord of the fathers*.

**The Alternative Reading: Children Calling out to Parents**

The school of the commentators forever preserved al-Qurṭubī's and others' precious counter-interpretation of the comparative: *as you remember your fathers* — read not the grown men's boast, but the small child's cry: *remember God as a child remembers his father*: with the frank dependence, the immediate whimper of need, the trust in a father's power and arrival, the instinctive lifting of arms for the lift of the father: as the small boy calls for his father when night gives him fear, with no hesitation that the father will not answer: in the same state of intimate helplessness, the believer calls upon God — *and God is the Father of fathers* — and the tradition builds upon this register with its favorite hadith of divine generosity beyond human:

> *"If you call upon God, call upon Him certain of being answered; and know that God does not accept the call of a heedless, distracted heart."* (al-Tirmidhī 3479 — teaching-filed circling around the every ummah's school of duʿāʾ — supported in the general Sunnah patterns because such supplications' full courses of necessity and fret join the same register the earlier commentaries gave to the language of remembering God *as the fathers are remembered*: the vernacular tenderness folded into the verse by God's own adjective)

**The One-Sided Prayer Exposed**

The verse then flashes its immemorial distinction between the prays of the world and the prays of the faithful: *fa-mina al-nāsi man yaqūlu rabbanā ātinā fī al-dunyā* — "for among mankind are those who say: our Lord — give us in this world" — *wa mā lahum fī al-ākhirati min khalāq* — "having for them in the Hereafter no share." The commentators draw the distinction starkly: there are supplications that stop at the borders of *this world* — the bread-eater's prayer, the pleasure-hunter's prayer, the stock-raiser's prayer asking yields and fortunes but nothing beyond: and the prayers of such prays end at the same borderline: no share — *khalāq* — no portion — in the Hereafter: the tragedy spelled out with absolute brevity: they are given; let them be given till the full supply is exhausted — but they shall have *nothing written* for them in the next world: the one-worldism prayer itself becomes the believer's mappost of the wrong-prayer-form — as the tradition later adds the equal condemnations of the one-world teachers of the plain-idlers: *one who prays for the world alone has pledged himself to one debt-closed settlement; the believer prays for both worlds* — the famous two-worlds duʿāʾ visiting its place at the verse following this (2:201) — and the sūrah's greatest teaching of prayer-balance thereby depends upon its exact equilibrium between the two sides: those who ask for this world alone; those who ask for both — the answer given in the next verse.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:201

> **Yet there are others who say, “Our Lord! Grant us the good of this world and the Hereafter, and protect us from the torment of the Fire.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two-Worlds Duʿāʾ**

Beside the one-worlders the Book now installs its own proper duʿāʾ of the ummah — the supplication destined to become among its most oft-repeated of all times: *wa minhum man yaqūlu rabbanā ātinā fī al-dunyā ḥasanatan wa fī al-ākhirati ḥasanatan wa-qinā ʿadhāba al-nār* The commentators mark its singular structure: it is the exact opposite — to the letter of its complement — of the one-world formulas of verse 200: there: *this world only*: here: *this world as well as the next world*: given the two-word specification *ḥasanah* — *good*: not wealth for its own store but *good:* the health of body being good here, the health of religion even better; household-peace being good here, the peace of a trembling-free relationship with God beyond; being without want here, being without wailing in the Plain of Reckoning at the far side. And the word *kinā* — *save/shield us from the punishment of the Fire* — pins its flight: the two blessings of two worlds are *not to be read as God's prize-outlay*: they are God's gifts tied at their last to the *rescue from Hell* — upon which all the other gifts' ultimate bears: for what is the good of this whole world if the Fire waits on the far bank, and what the good of a hundred years of prosperity when Judge closes the book? The verse runs to its end with a supplication that faces the Fire's flames ahead: *wa-qinā ʿadhāba al-nār* — *save us from the punishment of the Fire* — the fearful chapter of the daybook already drawn, God is asked, before the hooded tongues of doom ignite.

**The Prophet's Own Duʿāʾ Habit**

The tradition preserved the knowledge intact the greatest tribute of the verse: *it was the Prophet's own most-loved supplication* — the duʿāʾ most often on his tongue — as the Sahīḥ collections record across the generations: his intimate companions preserved its usage in him since his days of Makkah:

> *"The duʿāʾ the Prophet ﷺ used to pronounce most often was: O God! our Lord! give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and shield us from the punishment of the Fire."* (al-Bukhari 6389; Muslim 2690 — from Anas ibn Malik's own account — and its sway in the general duʿāʾ repertoire of the whole tradition: carried in all the subsequent books of supplication of Islam)

The general school drives home the weight: a duʿāʾ that was habit-carried by the Messenger of God — the summit-adiles of the ummah's devotion-buildings are *not* the gabble of formulas but the body of prayers the Prophet himself habitually spoke — has to be understood as the settled liturgy of the entire tradition: the pious of each century thereafter pick it up in the morning, in the night, in travel, in sickness, in the last phrase of wudu, at the close of the ṣalāh: the beloved-prayer of the Ummah's Head. Ibn ʿUmar is recorded attributing the verse's authority further out: *that it is a compressed spiritual request that comprehends everything*: *good here* encompasses all worldly good — of good health, of good provision, of good standing; *good there* encompasses the safeguard of the grave, Paradise, and God's pleasure — and the Fire-shield is both the deliverance and the grace of deliverance: the total form of blessing being so capacious that the school of law ever since has instructed both parents and children to read it *as their daily bread-prayer*, it eventually claiming the place of the ummah's most widely spoken supplication.

**A Prayer for Every Age**

The highest daub of commentary at this verse — at al-Ghazālī, al-Nawawī, Ibn al-Qayyim, and the Sufi commentators — has been at the relation of the verse's two parts: *how* the world-good and the hereafter-good may be yoked: the answer given to it by the Muslim theologians of every age: the balance of earthly and heavenly goods is accounted for in the verse's own grammar: *ātinā fī al-dunyā ḥasanah* buries the world-blessings deep as *good-things-therein* — not as *tax-withdrawals* — because all taste of the world is a gift *from God* (the *ātinā* — *give us* — being God's own): and *fī al-ākhirah ḥasanah* contains the good-things-there: the verse hangs the two *goods* on the face of the two worlds, with the *Fire-shield* itself guarding the junction between: and so God is asked not for goods at random, but for the two-fold good separate-tied-together: *one without the other is incomplete.* Never-mind the ancient divide of piety claiming that for this world is no share: for God wills *two-worlds-good* for every servant's prays: the Book casts against the one-worlders of verse 200 the very model with which their prayers are answered — the two-worlds petitioner at 2:201 — with the second generation of believers — for God will not leave the bridge un-crossed between our bread-gift and our Paradise-gift: *ātinā fī al-dunyā ḥasanah wa fī al-ākhirah ḥasanah wa-qinā ʿadhāba al-nār:* the greatest, most comprehensive, most human duʿāʾ of God the Ever-Giving.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:202

> **It is they who will receive a ˹heavenly˺ reward for the good they have done. Surely Allah is swift in reckoning.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Each Gets What He Wanted**

The verse now assigns the measure itself from the range of prayers just requested: *ulāʾika lahum naṣībun mimmā kasabū* — "those have a share from what they have earned" — *wa Allāhu sarīʿu al-ḥisāb* — "and God is swift in reckoning." The commentators are rightly careful over which of the two groups of verses 200–201 this *ulāʾika* — *those* — designates: does it mean the one-worlders ("have a share of what they earned" — a share only within the world), or the two-worlders ("a share from their earning" — both worlds fully met), or both? Al-Rāzī's reading is among the fullest — and most faithful — the truth: both groups receive *their own measurement from what they actually asked*: the one-worlder is given *his this-world share only*, the two-worlders *both shares*: God's reckoning being perfectly swift — *sarīʿ al-ḥisāb* — fast in perfect suchness of fitting: no trans-matching: nothing is transferred by accident from one account to the other: the one-worlder's demand is entered, the number written, the account delivered: and with no part in the Hereafter due or given, his ledgers are balanced — *swiftly*: and the two-worlders' account likewise fully settles them: the one-world-account holding some good things within the world — precisely while in the world — and no share hereafter: God's giving itself never defaults — but upon the two-hands of the *requested*: because the gift is *from what they earned:* God's judgement is measured, balanced, expedited, swift — *and each of them has been given according to what he himself asked*: He does not shortchange; He executes.

**The Accounting-Speed of God**

The phrase that has held the school spellbound throughout its tafsīr's centuries is the second clause: *sarīʿu al-ḥisāb* — God is swift of reckoning. The commentators open the sentence as a deep footnote of the divine audit: the account of human lives — every act, every motive, every hidden prayer — is kept not in slow-moving offices nor in books kept in numbers but in God's own instantaneous discernment: the full survey completed in no time — so that the whole account of the whole world at the Day of Resurrection takes no eons of cosmic delay — God is not ours to *wait-upon*: *sarīʿ*: the tradition always teaches: his eye does not wander; his registering does not dawdle: *everything is instantly there* — and the word's purpose at this verse-place is unmistakable: the one-worlders who asked for their bread-gift are measured *swiftly*: God's answer to their prayers arriving exactly within the one world-limit they themselves asked: no lag, no drift, no randomness: the judgment — *each after his asking* — registered instantly: so that no one can say he was never given: God's gifts are precise: the one-worlders asked of *their* scale, and from that scale God's speed-of-giving equally bestowed: but He did not reach beyond *their* scale: asked what they asked, and given what was asked: no one among mankind misreads God as either stingy or confused: He is the Perfect Filler of *what he asked* — and with *that* His account is already *completed instantly*.

**A Verse for the Soul's Judgment Days**

The Sufi commentators have always joined the verse immediately to every devotional station: the reading of accounts — not as some clever headline but as the *socket of faith*: *your life is a request:* God's gifts to you are the slow spill of the request's own file: every man has by God been given *what he asked of his life* — so the asker is told: if you ask of God — ask for two worlds: then God invests: if you ask for bread alone — ask and be fed: your account's margins and crack-flow are already served instantly: ask no more than you dare; ask for all the *worlds of the Lord*: *sharīʿ* is His account: instantaneous: but on every balance-page He deals your account by what your own soul asked for: and the believers' great preachers of the spiritual life — al-Qushayrī and Rūzbihān especially — never tire of the verse's unique teaching: God's reckoning is so exquisite (unseen, hidden in detail) that not the one-world-filed man nor the two-world-filed man can ever try the matter against God: the books will balance: their shares will be paid: the judgment made swift: and the whole matter — hence — falls *foreseeably upon mankind itself*: *the prayer for two worlds must be answered accordingly: every prayer's product comes with no detour: the balance-sheet of each asker is genetically preordered: and God is swifter in reckoning than every weapon of his hand.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:203

> **And remember Allah during ˹these˺ appointed days. Whoever departs swiftly on the second day is not sinful, neither are those who stay behind ˹till the third—seeking additional reward˺, so long as they are mindful ˹of their Lord˺. And be mindful of Allah, and know that to Him you will ˹all˺ be gathered.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Days of Tashrīq Named**

The Book continues its ḥajj-instructions from the Day of Arafah into its immediate sequel-days — the *Days of Tashrīq*: *wa-dhkurū Allāha fī ayyāmin maʿdūdāt* — "remember God in the days numbered." The commentators pinpoint them at once: the eleven, twelve, and thirteen of Dhu'l-Ḥijjah — the three days after the Day of Sacrifice (yaum an-naḥr, the tenth) that the pilgrims spend at Mina, stoning the three pillars (jamārāt) standing as the ritualized thrice-struck flags of Shayṭān's resistance at Abraham's own station; and the naming *maʿdūdāt* — *numbered* — appears already in the sūrah at verse 184, but now in holy designation: days so few — three — yet mighty: on them is the iḥrām-deserted ummah's plentiful leisure between the sacrifice's conclusion of ʿĪd al-Aḍḥā and the trek home: no interpretation replaces their essential seat: the three days of tashrīq, each day the pilgrim going out to the three pillars to cast stones — *seven at the first pillar, and seven at the middle; and seven more at the pillar of al-ʿAqabah* — the Prophet's own guidance:  and filaments of all of them announcing Allāhu akbar with every pebble lifted: the supplication in the full limbs of being — the arms, the voice, the stone — God's name elevated in the desert itself — thus the verse's general *remember God* being formed by the physical ritual of the believers' three days to its iconic bone-structure: stones, rising sun, fledgling city of tents, the ummah's own year-festival of idols-transfigured: *at every appointed stone — and every thrower, and every God-filled shout — the whole adornment of the memory of God descending.*

**Two Days or Three: The Counting Flex of God**

And the mercy-valve, once more, is set upon the whole arrangement with the utmost exactness: *fa-man taʿajjala fī yawmayni fa-lā ithma ʿalayh* — "but whoever hastens on after two days — no sin upon him" — *wa man taʾakhkhara fa-lā ithma ʿalayh* — "and whoever delays — no sin upon him." The commentators describe the exact rule: the pilgrim may depart Mina on the second tashrīq day (the twelfth of the month) — having stoned before sunset — and be *sin-free*, as statutorily as the pilgrim who remains for all three days: the option being given by God with full legitimacy: each course of action — two days or three — is of *equal* value: the Book issuing its waiver upon the two (and thereby settling for all ages to come what earlier had been the object of competing self-discipline-spirals: some advancing the three days as required, others the two, but God declaring both blameless) — *li-mani ittaqā* — *for the reverent:* for the god-fearing in either measure: the hajj was sent down from God not to crank open endless duty but to close the ummah's whole march of remembrance with mercy-bounded length: *whichever you do — leave on the second or stay to the third — you are obeying* — divine regulation within human measure: the choice limited to God-fearing measure and never licensed to anything more: and the studies of every madhhab have stayed gelled on that margin ever since: the Ḥanafīs and Shāfiʿīs, the Mālikīs and Ḥanbalīs read the verse with every law-school of Islam across all the centuries: hasteners may leave, delayers may stay: both sins-free, and the state itself God-decorated.

**"Unto Him Shall You Be Gathered"**

And then the verse, recovering its deeper meaning from its pilgrim-detail, rises to its very eschatological-pinpoint close: *wa-ttaqu Allāha wa-ʿlamū annakum ilayhi tuḥsharūn* — "and reverence God — and know that unto Him you shall be gathered." The *tuḥsharūn* — the great Day of *ḥashr*: gathering: unification: assembly — is here set as the Book's very *tertium*: the whole ḥajj — its blessing-days and its waivers — points not only back to Makkah's valley but forward to the Day Each Where in his Year's Case: that long-man-spread forward: *ilayhi tuḥsharūn*: the Day of the One-Day Plane: the verse suddenly swings the readers' whole geographical-vision upward: the ḥajj is *not* this mount of days, nor these necklaces of stones nor this Etiquette in Mina and Arafah — though all is holy — *or* this cancellation of their number-days: it is the great Gate of the great *Ḥashr* whose service-mould is here shaped: every pilgrimage in every year is drilling-beforehand: the raising-mass of the ummah of God from Mecca's plains is the preparing-mirror for the raising-mass of all mankind from the Dead Sea of the tombs: *O you who know the whole journey: unto Him shall you be gathered*: and with that perfect closing the Book's long ḥajj-cluster from verse 196 ends at the threshold of the final warning: its topics of traveling, provision, going, returning, lifetimes' store — *and at the last, the standing before Him* — all sealed with taqwā's own note admonition: *wa-ttaqu Allāh*. And the tradition has ever since preserved the twin-vibration for its practicing of the pilgrimage-season: every pilgrim at Mina, between pebble-toss and pebble-toss, in the assembling-sun's blaze, hears the verse's larger voice: *these days will soon be days past — and every later day a madhouse of leaves in flight; but the Days that the Lord awaits are also gathering-days: remember Him here as He shall remember you at the Plain of Standing: forget yourself here, and your days themselves shall forget you.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:204

> **There are some ˹hypocrites˺ who impress you with their views regarding worldly affairs and openly call upon Allah to witness what is in their hearts, yet they are your worst adversaries.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Speech That Pleases, Heart That Assails**

The sūrah now turns from the pilgrims' ease-filled ordinances to the opposite pole of humanity — the polished deceiver: *wa mina al-nāsi man yuʿjibuka qawluhu fī al-ḥayāti al-dunyā* — "and among mankind is the one whose words concerning this world's life impress you." The commentators (Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī) mark the wise choice of the starting verb — *aʿjaba* — to impress, to please, to cause wonder: the danger comes dressed in convincingness: his account of worldly affairs — trade, politics, cultivation, alliances — is fluent, agreeable, even delightful to hear: wisdom seems to pour from him. And with the very next clause the match between mouth and heart is broken before our eyes: *wa yushhidu Allāha ʿalā mā fī qalbihi* — "and he calls God as witness over what is in his heart": the man goes beyond speech into sworn testimony, invoking the All-Knowing Himself as guarantor of his sincerity — *God knows what is in my heart* — while God, who does know what is in his heart, immediately supplies the true reading of the oath: *wa huwa aladdu al-khiṣām* — "yet he is the fiercest of adversaries" — the most obstinate, most crooked in dispute (al-Ṭabarī glossing *aladd al-khiṣām* as the maximal capacity for hostile contention): the smoother the talk, the harder the enmity it conceals.

**Plausible Occasions, Universal Teaching**

The commentators name the reports that have been attached to this passage while insisting that its lesson be kept general. One report ties verses 204–207 to al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq al-Thaqafī — a man of fine bearing and silken tongue who presented himself before the Prophet ﷺ with every posture of attraction to Islam, swearing his affection by God — "God knows what is in my heart" — while carrying nothing of it within (al-Ṭabarī's account). Another account relates the passage to one of the Quraysh delegations' treacheries: some Makkans pretended interest in Islam and asked the Prophet to send learned men to teach them; when the delegation of teachers set out, they were ambushed and murdered on the road (al-Thaʿlabī's report). The majority of the mufassirūn, however, hold firmly to the universal horizon: these verses are not biography but a *category* — the portrait of a perennial human type: the man whose eloquence about this world wins every ear while his inner direction wars against every truth; so the Book does not say "this man" but *mina al-nās* — *among mankind* — throwing the warning-verb into every generation's marketplace of impressive talkers.

**The Believer's Ear Disciplined**

For the listening community the instruction is protective: *yuʿjibuka* — *he impresses you* — the second-person pronoun ranges wide: even the Prophet could be momentarily struck by the sheen — and if the impression might touch the Prophet himself, how much more the rest of mankind? The believers are therefore taught not to let eloquence do the work of evidence: speech about this world is a show-skill purchasable by anyone; what weighs in God's scales is the direction of the heart, which no art can renovate and no oath can falsify — for the very God invoked by the swearer is the One who reads hearts (59:22: "He is the Knower of the unseen and the seen") and here testifies against the oath's content. The sūrah has met this hypocrisy before — at its opening arsenal: "when they meet those who believe, they say, 'We believe'..." (2:14) — and now meets it again, in the middle of the law-book of pilgrimage and warfare, situating the hypocrite exactly where he likes to stand: at the doorway of every cause, fluent and sworn, ready to impress. The spiritual tradition made much of this placement: the pilgrim of verses 196–203 is told how to walk toward God; verse 204 shows the man who walks with his tongue toward everyone and with his heart toward no one — so that the checks of the iḥrām-road might sift the true seeker from the traveling actor. The believer's balance remains what the verse implies throughout: **listen to the words — but judge by the works**, for God alone is the Witness who cannot be fooled, and He has already answered the oath with His own verdict: *he is the fiercest of adversaries.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:205

> **And when they leave ˹you˺, they strive throughout the land to spread mischief in it and destroy crops and cattle. Allah does not like mischief.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turning Away and the Rushing**

The portrait of the smooth deceiver now shows what his real movement looks like the moment the audience's back is turned: *wa idhā tawallā saʿā fī al-arḍi li-yufsida fīhā* — "and when he turns away, he rushes about the earth to work corruption in it." The commentators read *tawallā* on two layers at once: he *turns away* — leaving the company of the Prophet and the believers, or merely leaving the gathering in which he performed his piety; and he *turns in enmity* — his heart wheeling from the faith outward (al-Ṭabarī carrying both senses). With the turn comes the *saʿy* — *he rushes*: the verb's freight of hurried, purposive activity is not lost on the tradition: corruption does not grow like weeds at his doorstep; it is *hustled into being* — the false witness runs, the inciter rides, the arsonist hurries: while the righteous soul moves deliberately and builds slowly, the worker of corruption sprints: evil finds this man industrious exactly where the good finds him absent.

**The Destruction of Tillage and Offspring**

The corruption's two favorite targets are named with an agrarian exactness that the commentators explain with great care: *wa yuhlika al-ḥartha wa'l-nasl* — "and to destroy the tillage and the offspring." Al-ḥarth — the sown field, the crop, the agriculture that feeds mankind; al-nasl — *offspring*: primarily livestock — the herds upon which the desert economy stood — though the majority also extend it to human progeny (Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī carrying both). The reports attached to verse 204's Akhnas-type give flesh to the portrait: the man is said to have passed by sown fields and grazing animals belonging to Muslims — and burned the fields and hamstrung the donkey. The mufassirūn generalize the two words into the very syllabary of corruption: *ḥarth* covers the productive order that sustains life — fields today, economies and institutions tomorrow; *nasl* covers the living line that continues life — the herds, the families, the generations: and the worker of corruption attacks always these two bases: *what keeps people fed, and what keeps people coming*: famine-making and lineage-breaking being corruption's oldest tools. The Sufi and reform-minded tradition has long read the pair still more broadly: the whole of human civilization stands upon the cultivation of earth and the cultivation of offspring — and corruption is discerned wherever these two cultivations are destroyed.

**"God Loves Not Corruption" — The Seal of All the Corrupt**

The verse ends with the divine verdict whose placement the commentators prize as the summary-line of the entire sūrah's corruption-thread: *wa Allāhu lā yuḥibbu al-fasād* — "but God does not love corruption." The same words that ended the hypocrites' self-exoneration at 2:11 ("they are the workers of corruption, but they perceive it not") and answered the corrupters' reform-claim at 2:12 now pronounce the love-sentence of God against the whole category: *fasād* — the rot of what was sound — is excluded from the divine love; and since God's love is the sole fountain of felicity in both worlds, the verse quietly assigns the corrupter his portion: he is cut off from the Love that matters. The tradition preserves the Prophet's own conversion of this doctrine into prayer-guard — the words of refuge recounted from his most frequent supplications:

> *"O God, I seek refuge in You from evil character and evil deeds and evil lusts."* (al-Tirmidhī 3592 — from among the Prophet's daily refuge-litanies — cited by the commentators and preachers in the very register of this verse's sealing-principle: character is where corruption begins, so the prayer for protection must reach it at the root)

And the ecological and social conscience of the modern tradition — standing squarely on this line of the Book — reads 2:205 among the founding charters of Islamic ethics of the land: *ḥarth and nasl* — agriculture and offspring — entrusted to mankind as vicegerents (2:30's khilāfah); their destruction by arson of any kind is not private but cosmic crime: the man who burns a field declares war on a covenant. With three strokes — a turning away, a rush, a double ruin — and one Name-verse of divine refusal, the Book leaves the silhouette of the saboteur fixed for all time on its page: **he rushes — and God does not love corruption**: every stride of his speed measured, and answered, from eternity.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:206

> **When it is said to them, “Fear Allah,” pride carries them off to sin. Hell will be their proper place. What an evil place to rest!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Admonition That Backfires**

The deceiver's portrait is completed by his response to the one remedy offered him: *wa idhā qīla lahu ittaqi Allāha akhadhathu al-ʿizzatu bi'l-ithm* — "and when someone says to him, 'Reverence God,' vainglory seizes him, with sin." The counsel itself is the shortest and most constant of the believing tongue: *ittaqi Allāh* — "fear God, be mindful of God" — the exhortation offered daily in mosques and markets, soft and free, requiring of the hearer nothing but humility. Yet in this man the softest word strikes the deepest wound — not of conscience but of *conceit*: *al-ʿizzah* — his sense of pride, tribal honor, personal eminence — seizes him *with sin* (*bi'l-ithm*), and the commentators gloss the seizure with precision: confronted with God's name, the hypocritical man feels *humiliated*, as though being reminded of God were an insult to his standing; pride rushes to defend the fortress, dragging him further into transgression: the word of guidance itself becomes, on his ear, a provocation to more sin. The diagnosis has lived at the very center of the Islamic science of the heart: an admonition received with resentment is the mirror that distinguishes the sick soul from the sound one — the sound soul softens at the mention of God (8:2: "when God is mentioned, their hearts tremble"); the diseased soul stiffens, and its pride *sins in the very act of refusing the cure*.

**"Hell Suffices Him" — The Completeness of Fit**

The sentence that follows is one of the Book's most chilling economies: *fa-ḥasbuhu jahannam* — "Hell is enough for him." The commentators attend to the verb-noun *ḥasb* — *sufficiency*: the same construction used positively — *ḥasbunā Allāh* — "God suffices us" (3:173) — is here turned upon the damned: what *suffices* him — what measures to him exactly, what fits him, what matches and answers his account in full — is the Fire. Al-Rāzī and the kalām tradition note this structural mirroring: man receives, in the end, *a sufficiency cut to his size*: for the righteous, God is the sufficiency that fills all need; for this man, Hell is the sufficiency that fills all his need of requital. And the mournful post-script seals the portrait: *wa la-bi'sa al-mihād* — "and an evil resting-place it is" — *mihād*, literally a *cradle*, a bedding prepared and spread: the commentators catch the savage irony of the word-choice: the cradle is where a child is softly laid down — this man's cozy abode *is Hell*: the bed he has been making for himself all his life through pride and corruption is the bed on which he shall finally recline. The verse thus answers the whole Akhnas-figure with his whole biography's last line: impressive talk (v. 204), industrious ruin (v. 205), pride-offended by guidance — and the cradle of Fire assigned as his due.

**The Medicine of Reminding**

For the believing community, the verse's placement constitutes a double instruction. First, the reminder must still be given: the Book narrates the man's rejection of exhortation precisely so that exhorters shall not judge their duty by its reception: the counsel *ittaqi Allāh* is owed to God, not to the hearer's temper — the Prophet's own charge being summarized in the famous saying that the religion is *naṣīḥah* (sincere counsel) —

> *"The religion is sincere counsel." We said: To whom? He said: "To God, to His Book, to His Messenger, to the leaders of the Muslims and their common folk."* (Muslim 55 — from Tamīm al-Dārī — the founding hadith of Islamic exhortation, always cited when rulings on counsel and its reception are discussed, including at this verse)

And second, the hearer mustnever receive counsel as this man did: the believers are trained from this very verse onward to greet the words of admonition with the praised counter-move — *this is for me*; self-accusation before self-defense: the pious predecessors' motto at such verses being Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb's: *"Take account of yourselves before you are reckoned with"* — because the man who is struck by his own sin at the door of counsel is already inside the house of mercy, while the man whose vainglory rises with offense at the very words "fear God" finds his cradle already laid. Thus verse 206 ends the three-panel portrait of the plausible destroyer — and the sūrah immediately sets its counter-portrait in motion: the man who *sells his soul, seeking God's Good Pleasure* (v. 207) — buyer and seller, face to face upon the same page of the Book.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:207

> **And there are those who would dedicate their lives to Allah’s pleasure. And Allah is Ever Gracious to ˹His˺ servants.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Counter-Silhouette**

Against the three dark panels (vv. 204–206) the Book now raises one luminous figure in a single verse — deliberately opened with the identical formula — *wa mina al-nās* — "and among mankind": *wa mina al-nāsi man yashrī nafsahu ibtighāʾa marḍāti Allāh* — "and among mankind is the one who sells his own soul, seeking God's Good Pleasure." The commentators luxuriate in the commerce-wording: *yashrī* — he *sells* — the true inverse of every bad bargain the sūrah has condemned (the purchase of error at guidance's price, 2:16; the purchase of this world at the Hereafter's price, 2:286's spiritual ledger): here the merchandise is the self and the price is *God's good pleasure* itself — and the trade is acclaimed by the tradition as the most profitable transaction ever recorded: a man gives the one thing he cannot keep — his passing self — to purchase the one thing he could never earn — the eternal satisfaction of his Lord. The Sufi commentators never stop at the secular sense of selling life in battle; *nafs* here is the soul with all its claims: a man *sells* his prides, appetites, comforts, vanities, his whole private economy — *ibtighāʾa marḍāti Allāh* — in the pursuit of a single good: the pleasure of God.

**Those the Tradition Remembered**

The mufassirūn set down several splendid occasions narrated for the verse's descent, and a universal purpose erected above them all. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, the second caliph, is reported to have commented on the seller's identity: *"a man who goes out commanding right and forbidding wrong — and is slain"* (al-Ṭabarī's transmission) — the brave enforcer of 3:104's community-duty, whose bargain costs him his life and buys him God's pleasure. Others relate it to the emigrants who left their wealth stranded in Makkah for God's way; others, memorably, to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib's night in the Prophet's bed on the eve of the hijrah — volunteering his body as the stand-in beneath the assassins' raised swords so that the Prophet could slip away toward Madinah (al-Thaʿlabī and the sīra literature) — the night when selling one's own skin was literal. The consensus, as always in the School — the reports illustrate, the verse legislates universally: everyone who pours out his self for God's good pleasure is inside this verse: the fasting reformer, the martyr, the quiet giver, the patient mother: *any man, any woman, any seller — the merchandise being nafs and the price marḍāt Allāh.*

**"God Is Kind unto His Servants"**

And the verse closes not with the seller's profit tabulated but with a Name-testimony — *wa Allāhu raʾūfun bi'l-ʿibād* — "and God is Kind unto His servants." The commentators note the tenderness of the closing: the seller, seemingly ruined by his own commerce (his soul spent away!), is handed over to the most tender care: *Raʾūf* — the intensest gentleness, the compassion that anticipates need (9:117 uses the same Name for the Prophet toward the believers; it is God's own Name at 2:143 already) — is appended exactly where the soul-seller needs it most: a man who empties himself for God's pleasure is met, at the empty place, by the Kindness that fills everything. The spiritual tradition has never wearied of this closing's logic: *no one sells his soul to God and finds himself bankrupt* — the Kindness of God settles the account with interest no trader computes: *bārak Allāhu lakum fī shirāʾikum* — *God blessed you in your bargain*, as 9:111 states of the believers' great transaction: "God purchases from the believers their souls and their wealth in exchange for Paradise" — the verse of the Garden-Price fixing forever the exchange-rate of the earlier revealed word here: the seller of his own soul has Heaven for price — and the Kind that receives his soul is the Gentle One whose care is world-spread.

**The Bargain Available to All**

The Sufi manuals read verse 207 as the completion of the sūrah's whole meditation on commerce: after error-purchasings (2:16), after withheld charity (2:268), after the forbidden avarice of swearing and blocking (2:224–225 to come), stands the page's single honored sale: the soul itself — *though it seems one's dearest capital yesterday* — sold gladly for God's Good Pleasure with eternity's ledger already settled. The Prophet's own summary of such self-offering appears in the records of 9:111's occasion:

> *"Rejoice in the bargain which you have concluded. That is the tremendous success"* — in the register of the tradition's readings of these twin commerce-verses (al-Ṭabarī transmitting the Prophet's salutation of *bushrā* — glad tidings — upon all who owned these verses' content of sale and purchase).

Thus 2:207 — the seller-of-his-own-soul at God's Good Pleasure-door — endures as one of the sūrah's most beloved portraits: the verse of men and women who, by the grace of the Raʾūf, have through the centuries sold all they had and gone on rich with the wealth of nearness to the Very Kind themselves: *and God is Kind unto His servants.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:208

> **O believers! Enter into Islam wholeheartedly and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. Surely he is your sworn enemy.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Summons of the Silm — Completely**

The long, turbulent bridge between the ḥajj-code and the sūrah's coming community-laws begins with one of the Book's most sonorous invitations: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū udkhulū fī al-silmi kāffah* — "O you who believe — enter into the *silm*, all of you — completely." The commentators weigh the two hinges of the command with great care. First, *al-silm*: most of the exegetes (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī leading) read it as *islām* itself — *submission* — the word al-silm sharing the root s-l-m with islām and both carrying the sense of total self-surrender; others (as Ibn Kathīr records) take it primarily as *entering into obedience* — the whole ecosystem of God's commands — while preserving the plain meaning *peace*: *enter into peace itself, wholly*: the three senses flow into one ocean: to be in Islam is to be in peace, and in obedience is peace fulfilled.
