Second, *kāffah*: the adverb reads doubly with magnificent breadth — *kāffah* as "all of you, collectively": every believer, none standing aside at the threshold — no partial entry, no class distinctions, no elite few making the crossing while others linger; and *kāffah* as "the whole of it": enter into the *entirety* of the house of Islam — not selecting one rite and refusing another, not embracing the parts that taste sweet and abandoning the parts that bind the hand (the very selective practice the sūrah had condemned in 2:85: "do you then believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?").

**The Possible Background and the Universal Command**

The commentators record a plausible occasion: certain new Muslims from among the Jews of Madinah wished to keep observing the Sabbath and some inherited customs that did not plainly clash with Islam — and the question arose whether one could enter Islam *partially*, keeping a private selection of the old covenant alive alongside. The verse answers with the vocabulary of completeness: *udkhulū fī'l-silmi kāffah* — *come inside wholly*: the house of Islam is entered through one door, and the entry is full: what God appointed in His final covenant stands; what He did not appoint is released. Some of the commentators (al-Qurṭubī's camp) therefore also read the address as still speaking *to the People of the Book who believed*: *you who have come to believe in part — enter now entirely*: the twofold register standing, as so often in this sūrah, with clear profit for both audiences: the Muslims of Madinah learned *pervasion* — beliefs are to be *completed* in practice, not merely confessed; the newcomers learned *collection* — the covenant is not a pick-and-choose buffet. And the command's God-ward purpose shines: the house of peace is roomy enough for everyone's entry, but narrow enough to have only one threshold.

**"Follow Not the Footsteps of Satan" — The Second Panel**

The verse's second half issues the sūrah's recurring protective-seal — its third planting after 2:168 and 2:169: *wa lā tattabiʿū khuṭuwāti al-shayṭān* — "and do not follow the footsteps of Satan" — *innahu lakum ʿaduwwun mubīn* — "truly he is to you an enemy, manifest." The commentators hang the whole psychology of partial-entry upon this clause: *piecemeal religion is always the Devil's corridor*: Satan does not usually begin with open apostasy; he begins with *abbreviated entry* — *this one rite accepted, that one deferred; this truth embraced today, that command postponed until a more comfortable age*; and each postponement is a footprint of his — step by step the man follows, until the direction he never chose is behind him as a road already traveled. That is why the same Book warns her and 6:142 and 24:21 with the identical wording: *the footsteps of Satan* — as though his road were marked in the ground and each subsequent generation found the same set of prints: the Devil's theology is precisely *partitioned Islam* — the concoction of convenience that feels enough like religion to satisfy the conscience and never enough like submission to trouble the soul. Against which the Book's counter-program stands with utter simplicity: *kāffah* — the whole of you into the whole of it. And the ending — *innahu lakum ʿaduwwun mubīn* — is plainest where the danger was hardest to discern: the smooth talker of verse 204 impressed; the Devil's sheen impresses too — the Book strips them both: *manifest*: nothing hidden in his enmity, nothing coy in his program: he is out in the open — and so should be the believers' resistance to him: open, total, forthright — as total as their entry.

**Entering Together, as One House**

The entrance's communal face closes the meditation: *kāffah* gathers the believers into a body moving together: the doorway of peace is entered as a *community*, shoulder to shoulder — and a body that enters wholly cannot be divided by the enemy's whispers: for Satan's oldest stratagem against a covenanting people is partition — each streamlining his own version of religion until the one house becomes a hundred corridors. The tradition has always read the verse with the companion-light of the famous hadiths of cohesion:

> *"The example of the believers in mutual love, mercy and affection is that of a body: when one member of it ails, the whole body answers it with wakefulness and fever."* (al-Bukhārī 6011; Muslim 2586 — from al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr — which the preachers of the community have consistently cited beside the summons to enter the silm *kāffah*: the body's unity is both the means of the entry and its flowering)

and with the pious predecessors' remembered saying at this verse —

> *"Enter the peace all of you — so that the Devil finds no door between you through which to drive his wedge."*

The door stands open; the footsteps wait outside; the summons is age-fresh every dawn: *O you who believe — enter*.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:209

> **If you falter after receiving the clear proofs, then know that Allah is indeed Almighty, All-Wise. Waiting for Judgment?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Conditional Slip**

Set directly upon the heels of the summons to complete entry, the next clause reads like a cautionary afterbeat in the same breath: *fa-in zalaltum min baʿdi mā jāʾatkumu al-bayyināt fa-ʿlamū anna Allāha ʿazīzun ḥakīm* — "and if you slip after the clear proofs have reached you, then know that God is Mighty, Wise." The verb *zalaltum* — from *zalal*: a stumble, a slip, a sliding — is chosen by the Book with deliberate smallness: not *you fell* nor *you abandoned* nor *you denied*: a *slip*: the sort of sag a man's foot makes on the decline he thought he had already climbed: the Book's psychological realism appears again — the gate of relapse usually stands not at the edge of grand disbelief but at the beginning of small slidings: a deferral of prayer here, a winking at injustice there, a partial acceptance of the covenant (the very *partial entry* refused in v. 208) until the topography of one's faith has quietly migrated a handspan. The commentators note the phrase's diminishment with respect to *after the clear proofs came to you*: the *bayyināt* — the clarities, the evidences, the Book itself together with the Prophet (al-Ṭabarī folding all the contents into the term: the Prophet, the Quran, the Islam) — create the slip's actual legal weight: slipping without evidence is human frailty; slipping after the proofs stand *written before one's eyes* is measured against the heights of the evidence.

**Mighty and Wise — The Two Names for the Slipped**

The conditional-sentence's resolution, at first glance indirect, is in truth the most severe rejoinder the Book could have chosen: *fa-ʿlamū anna Allāha ʿazīzun ḥakīm* — "then know that God is Mighty, Wise." No imperative — no "so repent," no "so return" — but a *knowledge*-clause: the slipping man is told simply to *know* two Names. The commentators unfold the threatening precision of the pair: *ʿAzīz* — the All-Mighty, the Unconquerable — signifies that your slipping has not weakened Him: you cannot escape His grasp by drifting, cannot outwait His patience by hiding; if the slip becomes a road, the road ends at His sovereignty the same as every road; and *Ḥakīm* — the All-Wise — signifies that every command you slipped from was issued by perfect wisdom for your own well-being: your defection does not render His wisdom questionable; it renders *your reason* bankrupt: the laws were wise when you were proud to know them, and wise when you fell from them. The two Names thus work as twin anchors: the slipper cannot maneuver his way out of accountability (*ʿazīz*), and cannot argue his way out of accountability (*ḥakīm*): *know that He is Mighty* — penalty cannot be dodged; *Wise* — sentence cannot be faulted. And the tradition notes the verse's dark gentleness at the same time: the slip is cast in the subjunctive — *if you slip* — not *when you slip*: the Book still treats the Muslims' error as interruptible, the prophet-of-the-warning still standing at the slip's edge, hand outstretched by knowledge.

**The Stand of the Conscious Slipping**

The whole register of the passage holds one of the sūrah's great lessons in the psychology of the soul: slips after great light are the most dangerous economy of the soul. The same Book elsewhere tells its devastation in parallel: "how shall God guide a people who disbelieved after their belief, and bore witness that the Messenger is true, and clear proofs came to them? God guides not the wrongdoing people" (3:86) — where *after* functions *as the guilt's own capital*: content knowledge becomes aggravation. The Prophet's standing education for the communal army drew upon the same psychology:

> *"When the believer sins, a black stain is set upon his heart; and if he desists and repents and asks forgiveness, his heart is cleansed; and if he repeats it, the stain grows over his heart until it covers it whole — and that is the encrusting rust that God mentions: Nay, but what they used to do has rusted upon their hearts (83:14)."* (al-Tirmidhī 3334; Ibn Mājah 4244 — from Abū Hurayrah — the standard prophetic coaching that beside 2:209 has guarded the believers of every generation against the slow chemistry of unrepented slips)

The commentary-tradition therefore guards the verb's modest scope — *zalaltum* — as God's own clemency before His own judgment: even if the slip occurs — and no believer imagines himself immune — the sentence's back-half already hands him the exit: *know*: return to knowledge, consult the two Names, let the All-Mighty's grasp lift the slipper back up and let the All-Wise's wisdom show him the stepping he missed: the door of the House of Peace into which they were called at verse 208 is not closed at the first stumble — the Door-Stander is still Mighty and Wise, knowing every footfall and pardoning every repentant morning. And so the verse becomes, in the tradition's pastoral register, its own medicine-cabinet for the fallen: *whenever you have slipped after the clear proofs, know — then return* — for the Might has never needed your strength to carry the House, and the Wisdom has never needed your perfection to perfect your road.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:210

> **Are they waiting for Allah ˹Himself˺ to come to them in the shade of clouds, along with the angels? ˹If He did˺, then the matter would be settled ˹at once˺. And to Allah ˹all˺ matters will be returned ˹for judgment˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Waiting Men Asleep**

The Book now asks the question that uncovers every deferring heart: *hal yanẓurūna illā an yaʾtiyahumu Allāhu fī ẓulalin mina al-ghamām* — "do they wait for anything except that God should come in shadows of clouds, with the angels — and the matter be decreed?" The commentators explain *yanẓurūna* — *do they wait* — as the posture of every one who has heard the proofs and declined them: not denial exactly, nor investigation — *waiting*: the procrastination of the soul that answers every summons with "later": the verse thereby unmasking the wait itself as the annihilation of the option: what they are truly waiting for, though they do not know it, is not a better proof tomorrow nor a cheaper obedience in a revised age: they are waiting until *God comes* — in clouds' shrouded veils, with all His angels descending — and that is not proof-time anymore; that is event, not evidence; verdict, not exam: on that Day the ledger is closed (*the matter decreed — quḍiya al-amr*): no addition to deeds, no subtraction from them — the Book has quitted its day of appeal: *every choice-choice is over*. The Book elsewhere deploys the identical argument against the same conduct: 6:158 — "the day when some of your Lord's signs come, a soul shall not profit from its belief unless it believed before" — and 39:58 — "the matter is decreed; God will then only be obeyed when the disasters arrive": the theology of waiting quietly reversed: the procrastinator's very waiting is itself a descent upon him: arrival of what he waited for equals sentence upon his waiting.

**Shadows of Clouds — and the God Who Cannot Move**

The kalām and tafsīr tradition treats the verse with careful removal of any spatial misconception: *fī ẓulalin mina al-ghamām*: "in shadows of clouds" — the commentators are unanimous that God is not compelled by clouds, nor confined within them, nor moves from place to place: al-Ṭabarī's preferred construction parses the grammar as assigning the clouds to the *angels* ("that God should come — and the angels in shadows of clouds") while still other commentators gloss *ēty Allāh*: "the *command* of God arrives," or "the judgment of God/miracle arrives with the angels," mirroring the identical usage at 6:8 — "had We sent an angel down, the matter would have been decreed." The great majority, from the salaf onward, stop at a reverent silence about the how: God's words stand as they descended; their *modality* is His, not ours; the believers' way is to believe the text without likening it to any movement of created things, and to consign its how to the One who spoke it — the tagline of the whole early tradition at the creation-description verses: *ilā kayf Allāh* — *the how belongs to God alone*. Its parallel at 25:25 licenses the majesty-image in full: "the day the sky is split open with clouds and the angels are sent down in a descent" — the language chosen to make the arrival *visual* for a mankind that thinks through sight: the terrified watchers will see the sky crack with procession-clouds and the angels in regimented descents — *the whole festival of arrival in the sky-walls*: and simultaneously — what no eyes mistook — *the matter is decreed*.

**"Unto God Are All Matters Returned"**

The verse ends with the phrase the sūrah has already sounded at 2:156 and which the whole Book carries as its supreme ledger-signature: *wa ilā Allāhi turjaʿu al-umūr* — "and unto God are all matters returned." The *turjaʿa al-umūr* — *the affairs return* — is read by the commentators as both the retrospective and the verdictive: everything begun, everything deferred, everything left half-donned — *returns*: the slips of verse 209, the partial entries of 208, the wages of the devourers of 188, the sales of souls (207) and the offerings of pilgrimages — everything migrates back to the One Giver for final triage: the computation shifted forever from the computing of men to the returning of affairs. The phrase's recurrence across the whole Book (3:109; 8:44; 11:123; 22:76; 35:4; 57:5) marks it as the Book's own station-master's whistle of the Last Day: *all affairs return* — nothing settled in the corridors of the world stays settled — and the word *turjaʿa* in the passive — *they are returned* — protects the one theological glory this verse carries: the return requires no movement of return on our own threads: godlessly scattered deeds, none of ours to gather back, God Himself gathers. The idle of Madinah who waited for God's coming, the pillagers of God's covenant, the men of impressive talk and corrupted tillage — all are told in one sentence: *your waiting is answered — and it returns your way, and it returns to Him*: the end is not in your own next day, but on that Day, the one with God's veil-arrival. *And until that day, there are still steps in His House — so enter: enter wholly; and do not linger at the ramp.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:211

> **Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We have given them. And whoever trades Allah’s favour—after receiving it—˹for disbelief˺ should know that Allah is indeed severe in punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Ask the Children of Israel" — The Pointed Enquiry**

The sūrah now turns back for a moment from the deferring heart to its oldest illustration — the community whose liturgy had taught it — first-hand — how God deals with resisters: *sal banī isrāʾīla kam ātaynāhum min āyatin bayyinah* — "ask the Children of Israel: how many clear proofs did We give them?" The interrogative *sal* — *ask them* — directed at the Prophet ﷺ (or, by extension, addressed to every reader), sends the enquirer to the living archive: before the Muslims of Madinah sat the Jewish tribes who *knew* — who had been schooled over thirteen centuries in the tragedies of resisted revelation: Egypt's drownings and cloud-pillars, the staff, the White Hand, the parted sea (7:105 et seq.), the manna, the water from the smitten rock, the mountain held over them, the splitting into twelve springs — *sign upon sign*, until *kam* — *how many* — became the rhetorical abundance-billing and not a number-question: so let any hesitating people simply ask them of their own record — which is written that they saw and faltered, got covenanted and broke, were given and *altered*. The commentators nail the art of this verse: the Prophet is bidden to ask — with the answer's content already resident in the mouths of the asked community themselves: no Muslim travels to a theologian for a verdict here — *he asks the Children of Israel, and they recount their own history* — and the testimony comes not as defence but as a standing indictment reaching into every subsequent people lifted into the same stage-lights.

**Baddala al-Niʿmah — The Alteration of the Blessing**

Then comes the organized-obligation word upon which the whole warning pivots: *wa man yubaddil niʿmata Allāhi min baʿdi mā jāʾathu* — "whoever alters the Blessing of God after it has come to him." *Niʿmat Allāh* — the Blessing of God — is glossed by the commentators (Ṭabarī among them) with plural richness: the *covenant* God made with Israel (2:83), the *scripture* God gave them, the *prophets*, the *religion itself* — and in the wider register, every grace through which God binds man: faith, Scripture, community, prophecy. The verb *baddala* — *to substitute/alter/exchange* — is the very same word that will be sent to the ummah as its own constitution's ultimate warning (14:28 to come: "have you seen those who exchanged the Blessing of God for disbelief?"): to *alter* is the middle crime, more misadvised than denial, more serious than mere stumbling: to *swaps God's gift for new-words* — receiving the covenant and re-writing its content; receiving the Prophet and re-aligning his claims; receiving the qiblah and re-pointing it in the direction of convenience — all the small arts of substitution with which the Book's own People of the Book had industriously filled the sūrah's own blacklist (2:75's concealment, 2:79's scriptwriting, 2:159's hiding) — are here compressed into the generic formula most grave: *yubaddil*: whoever swaps God's appointed sign for his own re-write *after the Blessing has arrived* — knowing full well the Blessed — is covered by its verdict.

**Severe in Retribution — The Signature Again**

And the familiar signature thunders once more across the ummah's hearing: *fa-inna Allāha shadīdu al-ʿiqāb* — "truly God is severe in retribution" — the same closing-phrase that the sūrah has already planted at 2:165, 2:196 — the verse becoming now the third of its booming economy: the God who has not spared any substitute of covenant in the past (the Israelite calamities of the judges and exile chanted through their own psalms) will not spare the same crime in no matter whose hand: *shadīd al-ʿiqāb* is no wailing threat — it is biblical history written as legal statute: *the substitutions cost — and they cost dearly* — and Madinah's believers, and the centuries of Muslims who would stand struck by every scholarly overture of renovation that wished to *re-write* God's covenant to appease the temperaments of their age, receive the word forever standing: *the Blessing of God may not be altered — not for Jews, not for Muslims, not for anyone.*

**The Ancient Tapestry for Everyone's Wall**

The tradition in the earliest tafsīr-plots already read the verse in full generality — the *sal banī isrāʾīl* being the *tongue of the Qur'an* pressing any ear toward the household next door: *ask them* — the whole archive of Israel is the library of the believers: a community whose signs-history is preserved between Madinah's walls, whose testimonies fill God's own Book, so that the Muslims need never invent their own cautionary tales: the cautionary tale came packed in the desert-caravan with them. And the hadith-analogy networks of the ummah sustained the verse in that register; for when the Muslims drew the lesson above their own door, they remembered:

> *"You will follow the ways of those nations before you, span by span and cubit by cubit, so much so that if they entered a lizard's hole, you would follow them into it.* They asked: O Messenger of God, the Jews and the Christians? *He said: Who else?"* (al-Bukhari 3456; Muslim 2669 — from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī — the perennial prophetic ethic that onto whomsoever Israel's lessons are written, upon him the Book's identical signature falls)

—the tradition's own tape of consequences upon *baddala al-niʿmah*. The verse thus sets its own eternal ledger on the wall of every community after theirs: *ask them: how many proofs — and whosoever alters — severest punishment*: God's signature already inscribed on their ledger long before it is inscribed on ours.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:212

> **The life of this world has been made appealing to the disbelievers, and they mock the believers. Those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺ will rank above them on the Day of Judgment. And Allah provides for whoever He wills without limit.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Beautified to the Unbelieving Eye**

The pivot-verse of the social world opens with the Book's own analysis of optical power: *zuyyina li-lladhīna kafarū al-ḥayātu al-dunyā* — "beautified for those who disbelieve is the life of this world." The passive verb — *zuyyina* — *it was adorned, made fair to see* — carries the exegetical sermons of the tradition: who does the adorning? the tradition answers everywhere with one hand raised: it is part of God's wise dispensation (18:7: "We have set down all that is upon the earth as adornment for it, that We might test them — which of them is best in deeds"), so that the world glitters by divine plan as one of the great testing-gifts (the field of the divine testing of mankind): the perfume draws precisely those who are susceptible to perfume: its shine lights exactly those hearts whose compass falls toward the shiny: and so the world's beauty is one of the divine sieve's instruments: separating, by their very leaning, the upright and the askew. And the commentators narrate the historical eye of the clause with their customary directness: the Arabs of Makkah — the fat of the trade-bazaar, covered in silk — looked down upon the threadbare mud-and-palm believers of early Islam; the hypocrites of Madinah and the Jewish notables, possessed of fortified fortlets and fenced plantations of dates, ridiculed the immigrant poor of the Muhājirūn: *is this what Muḥammad has for an ummah?* The word of the sūrah answers in the very grammar of the diagnosis: the world was *adorned FOR the disbelievers* — beautified *precisely in their direction* — for their temptation-field is precisely the attractive surface of false glory: dazzled by shine, they jeered at dull pearls.

**"Above Them on the Day of Resurrection"**

The verse's mid-clause offers the world's poor and mocked believer his entire comfort in seven words: *wa-lladhīna ittaqaw fawqahum yawma al-qiyāmah* — "but those who were God-fearing shall be above them on the Day of Resurrection." *Fawq* — *above* — the physically-placed word outwitting every world-hierarchy: vertically inverted now: the scorned man of dates-and-raisins at Madinah shall stand above the silk-clad ones at the Plain of Resurrection, in a tally whose arithmetic sky-pillar is *taqwā* alone. The tradition has treasured among its account-books an exchange of exquisite pathos the commentaries plant beneath this verse:

> *"'O Abū Dharr! Look around you, and find the most exalted man you can see in this mosque!' — I looked, and saw a man sitting in fine clothes — and said, 'That one.' — 'Then look around and find the lowest man you can see!' — I looked, and saw a weakened man in tattered clothes — and said, 'That one.' — Then he said: 'By Him in Whose Hand is my soul — that man is better with God than a world full of the other kind.'"* — the Prophet ﷺ's education of Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī (a transmission recalled by the commentators at this verse — classically recorded in Ibn al-Mubārak's and the zuhhād-collections' line, with ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf's visit to Abū Dharr's simple household among its confirmatory biographies: teaching that visibility on earth is no predictor of rank with God)

and the inversion's demonstration has been complete on every mockery-field of history: the believer ridiculed for his patched clothes in Madinah of the seventh century or any city since — *all of it measured differently on the Last Day*.

**"God Provides for Whom He Wills, Without Reckoning"**

The verse concludes with the great provision-clause — *wa Allāhu yarzuqu man yashāʾu bi-ghayri ḥisāb* — "and God provides for whomsoever He wills without reckoning." The commentators unfold the clause's several registers (al-Rāzī, al-Thaʿlabī exchanging the glosses): (1) God's gifts are undetected by any ledger — He is infinite Treasury; His provisioning knows no subtraction-table: He gives *without his account ever filling*: His sufficiency opposed to every national bank of kings; (2) He gives *beyond what calculation would predict*: mercies beyond measure, unearned provisions breaking every earn-grid — the same epithet retains as well the Sakīnah-pinnacle of 3:37 (Zachariah's out-of-season fruit for Mary); (3) the eschatological riding: on the Day of Highest Measure — *some* will be given Paradise *without reckoning*: the Book's own signature of the Seventy Thousand:

> *"Seventy thousand of my community will enter Paradise without reckoning — they are those who do not seek ruqyah from others, nor allow branding, nor believe in omens, and upon their Lord they put complete trust."* (al-Bukhārī 5705, 6472; Muslim 220 — from Ibn ʿAbbās — the standard hadith standing at the eschatological portal of *bi-ghayri ḥisāb* — cited everywhere the phrase is read)

**Providing in the Hereafter Is the Worldly Proof-Time**

The tradition's school upon this verse is what it has ever been: poverty is not necessarily God's judgment; mocking of the believer says more about the mocker's eye than the believer's worth; and God's giving — whether as the test-gift of world-fare or as the eternity-purse at the final balance — is *Ḥisāb-free*: freed from every arithmetic of earth. The believers of verse 212's consolation: the scorn you accepted in the world's marketplaces will themselves become your decoration of glory; the world-poor will be the Paradise-rich; and the God who measured out only what you needed to survive the market will measure without number in the Morning when all the rankings are corrected in His Courts of Mid-day. *Zuyyina* — the adorning of the world — is an intricate weave in which man's dumbfounded sight rests; God's weave holds other secrets: that Bakr's bright silks may be ashes, Abū Dharr's tattered patches may be lamps in the Sacred Over-space, and *the provision of God goes to whom He wills, without reckoning*: the poor man's station, at which the mockers looked down, is the station exalted in the World of Resurrection.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:213

> **Humanity had once been one community ˹of believers before they lost faith˺. Then Allah raised prophets as deliverers of good news and as warners, and revealed to them the Scriptures in truth to judge among people regarding their disputes. And no one disputed the Scriptures except the very people who received them after clear proofs had come to them—out of jealousy. Then Allah, by His grace, has guided the believers to the truth regarding those disputes. And Allah guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The One Community — Before the rift**

This is the sūrah's sweeping anthropology of religion in one breath — the whole human saga framed between an early unity and a redeemed minority: *kāna al-nāsu ummatan wāḥidatan* — "mankind was one community." The commentators explore the several legitimate readings of this *ummatan wāḥidatan* (al-Ṭabarī laying them out with his characteristic breadth): (1) the primeval generations — according to some reports the ten centuries between Adam and Noah — when divinely-shaped humanity still walked a single path of right guidance; (2) the confederacy of *unbelief* — mankind one in error before the first prophet — and thus the *then differed* that the commentators supply as elided between the verses: *kāna al-nāsu ummatan wāḥidatan — fa-khtalafū — fa-baʿatha Allāhu al-nabiyyīn*: *mankind was one community; then they differed; then God sent the prophets*: (3) the covenantal pre-creational unity of 7:172 — the assembled progeny of Adam bearing witness to "Am I not your Lord?" — "Yes, we testify" — mankind one in that first testimony before a lifetime's forgetful scatterings; (4) the anthropological unity-of-origin: mankind beginning literally from one community — one human pair — of which the Arabic speaks even of a single man by the word *ummah* (16:120 calls Abraham himself *an ummah*). Every reading bows before the same theological architecture: disunion is *not* God's original design for humanity; its nested diseases — envy, tribalism, bidʿah — are parasitic upon an earlier whole.

**Prophets and the Judging Book**

The divine remedy then proceeds in its two clinical movements: *fa-baʿatha Allāhu al-nabiyyīna mubashshirīna wa mundhirīn* — "then God sent the prophets, as bearers of glad tidings and as warners" — *wa anzala maʿahumu al-kitāba bi'l-ḥaqqi li-yaḥkuma bayna al-nāsi fīmā ikhtalafū fīh* — "and sent down with them the Book in truth, to judge among mankind concerning that wherein they differed." The Word-mansion becomes the judge: the Book comes down *in truth* — by truth, with truth, for truth — and its ruling-commission is accountability-cut: *li-yaḥkuma*: the Revelation was not sent for lettering alone but *to arbitrate* among men wherever their differences claw one another: the commentary-tradition reading into the *li-yaḥkuma* the whole legislative history of Islam: every arbitration verse from 2:178 down is descended from this great charter: God's Book arbitrates; God's messengers execute the arbitration; and the function of all religious knowledge within every community is precisely this: adjudicating by the Book.

**Envy After Evidences**

But the Book's judgment of human nature darkens: *wa mā ikhtalafa fīhi illā alladhīna ūtūhu min baʿdi mā jāʾathumu al-bayyinātu baghyan baynahum* — "yet none differed concerning it except those to whom it was given — after the clear proofs had come to them — out of envy among themselves." The commentators' diagnosis, repeated across the whole weight of tafsīr from 2:213 here and 3:19 and 98:4 onward, is one of the Book's most devastating psychological verdicts: *the communities were not ignorant when they schism-ed over the Book: they knew: their splitting was not prior to evidence but after evidence: the envy-compound (*baghyan baynahum* — transgression/envy passing between them) barked, not the ignorance-bite* — and the Jewish and Christian divisions after a common Prophetic testimony stand as the standard illustration: they knew the very Scriptures that foretold, and then — out of sectional-envy, priesthood-pride, house-pride — the book become the bone of everybody's contention: the word *illā* — *only* — staples the indictment with devastating compression: *none* differ over it — none at all — *except* those most acquainted with it: scholarship-in-schism; the highest religious learning gives no protection against schism when the heart's envy is not subdued. The commentary-tradition has made this clause resound through every age of Islam's own divisions: those who fall out over one Book are not failing for lack of information but for refusing what the Book requires of them — to yield their arrogance and their covetous appetite: the *baghy*. And thus comes the succeeding clause: God then guides *those who believe* to the truth of their contentions — by His leave — the tether *bi-idhnihi* once more centring the whole guidance-grant in God's Permission: guidance is God's suffrage to whom He wills; it is not the hereditary entitlement of the possessors of Books — and the truth glides over to *that community that stood the most faint-hearted of splitting*: the believers themselves.

**"And God Guides Whom He Wills Unto a Straight Path"**

The end of the verse, both warning and mercy-balm, sounds the sūrah's eternal cadence: *wallāhu yahdī man yashāʾu ilā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm* — "and God guides whomsoever He wills unto a straight path": guidance escapes all human formula: it is God's give: no policy and no craft capture it: the Prophet himself was told at 28:56: "you do not guide whom you love — it is God who guides whom He wills": and so this the grand-scale of the story: the end *illā alladhhīna ūtūhu* — the inherited privileging — broken and smashed: guidance must be *given*: not by birth-line nor scholarship nor recitation-hours, but by the free will of the All-Guiding: and the humble believing folk of Madinah, threading their way through Qaynuqāʿ quarrels and the older books' schisms, are told in the very syntax of assurance: the God who manipulates all these differences and all these schisms can guide your hearts *to the truth of that wherein they differed* — by His grant — and He guides whom He wills unto the straight path: in the same breath the Book asserts sovereignty over all separations and sews the believer's wearied heart back together with the oldest comfort-formula of the whole Book: *guidance is His gift — so ask it: *guide us on the straight path* — and you shall be answered*: for *yahdī man yashāʾ* hides this one mercy-colophon: that He *wills* to guide the one who asks: as the hadith-qudsī attests repeatedly: *"O My servants — all of you are astray except whom I guide: so seek guidance of Me and I shall guide you."* (Muslim 2577 — the great hadith-qudsī from Abū Dharr — cited by the tradition beneath this verse's counsel to every seeker of unity and truth).

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:214

> **Do you think you will be admitted into Paradise without being tested like those before you? They were afflicted with suffering and adversity and were so ˹violently˺ shaken that ˹even˺ the Messenger and the believers with him cried out, “When will Allah’s help come?” Indeed, Allah’s help is ˹always˺ near.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Did You Suppose?" — The Wrong Assumption**

One of the Book's most bracing wake-up words opens the whole trial-block: *am ḥasibtum an tadkhulū al-jannata wa lammā yaʾtikum mathalu alladhīna khalaw min qablikum* — "or did you suppose you would enter the Garden when the like of those who passed away before you has not yet come upon you?" The Book's *am ḥasibtum* — did you suppose — belongs to an established rhetorical family across the whole Qur'an (29:2 begins with exactly this formula: "do people think that only saying 'we believe' would suffice, and that they would not be tested?"; and 3:142: "did you suppose you would enter the Garden without God knowing who among you struggled?"): the assumption being undone is always the same hidden supposition of the believer's comfort-heart: that God distinguishes sincere conviction by profession without knocking its mettle on the anvil; that Paradise is a gift of nominal allegiance; that faith needs only be declared to be stamped for entry into the Garden. The commentators report the occasioning background of the indignation-bearing words: the Muhājirūn of Makkah — who had left behind their houses, their treasuries, their whole lives-trawl into the sea of flight, and had landed into the dust-storms of Madinah with nothing but the Prophet and their month-to-month bread — sat against the prospect of besiegement at Ḥudaybiyah (or, as many read the occasion-field, at Uḥud and at the Trench) while the mockers asked them *how much longer they meant to waste themselves for a losing Muḥammadan holiness* — and the verse came as its eternal reply: *you did suppose wrong: faith's worth is truth-proven in the forge; the Garden's turnstile runs only on the winners of the test*: the straight line from verse's face to lesson is indisputable: *God tests His believers as He has ever done: it is not the oppression that surprises God, but the believing thought that the oppression would never affect them*.

**Shaken Until the Prophet Himself Cried**

The mid-clause sketches the historical portrait with the plaintiveness of the Book's own witness: *massathumu al-baʾsāʾu wa'l-ḍarrāʾu wa zulzilū* — "misfortune and hardship befell them, and they were shaken": the two nouns pair with the sūrah's prior naming-pair in 2:177 (misfortune: poverty, the dry year, the emptied larder; hardship: the sick-bed, the fear, the out-laid life): and *wa zulzilū* — *and they were shaken* — the seismic form-II verb of earthquake-shaking in redoubled force: their trial was not the tremble of a wind-shaken reed: *the earth itself heaved them*: until — *ḥattā yaqūla al-rasūlu wa lladhīna āmanū maʿahu matā naṣru Allāh*: even the Messenger and the believers who stood with him raised the cry: *when is God's help?* The commentary-tradition handles this perhaps most tender of all the Book's confessions of the prophets with the wisest frailty-free custody: some (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī) read the Messenger's inquiry as the hastening-cry of one certain of the answer — as the praying man asks in longing: *O my trial, when will the dawn break?* — fortified by God's own covenant — not a breached faith; the plainest register, and the one most schools of kalām accept, is that the prophets share the stature of men in all human things: the same Book elsewhere bares their tremblings (12:110's messengers at the point of despairing: "until, when the messengers despaired and thought they had been deemed liars, Our succor came to them" — precisely the moment of deepest night before the first shower); and the tradition weighs the tenderness of the Great Prophet's own sigh: 15:97's God himself: "We know your breast is straitened by what they say": 26:3: "perhaps you would torment yourself unto death over them." The verse therefore magnifies a book that does not flinch before showing its judges' lips trembling, being held by God's providence in the very moment of trembling: the help is *near* — *alā inna naṣra Allāhi qarīb* — *lo! surely God's help is near* — a short toll of five words opening upon eternity: near — not far off — for all the tides of history are but a footfall's interval between the dismayed and their God's help.

**This World Is a Test-Garland**

The entire verse is the Book's own answer to the perennial believer's question about suffering's logic: *you ask why? — everyone before was shaken: help is sewn into the whole fabric; and its nearness is the only credential a tested believer needs thereafter*: the tradition preserves the comforting fortification around this verse across every century of the Muslim world's own suffering-chronicles:

> *"When the help of God arrives — after great long awaiting — it comes with everything at once, and the believer exclaims: could it really be that my Lord had delayed me so? And then the days of the waiting become a possession more sweet than the days without."* — the preacher's wisdom, built ring upon ring, upon this verse's great closing oath: *alā inna naṣra Allāhi qarīb.*

And the Prophet's own testimony of affliction-and-reward that the commentators tie with the same rope, proving every trial in it in its back-ties is Heaven-bred:

> *"Tremendous reward goes with tremendous trials: and when God loves a people, He tests them: whoever is well-pleased — for him is the Pleasure; and whoever is displeased — on him is the Displeasure."* (al-Tirmidhī 2396; Ibn Mājah 4031 — the same mercy-ledger this verse writes in eternal brevity)

And in these two lamps the verse burns for every age of believers as unfailing consolation: *they were shaken — and God's help came; so too will yours come — shake as you may — and the help is at hand*: near — nearer than the anguish's span from which it rises: *alā inna naṣra Allāhi qarīb*: the sūrah's own cry to every weary believer's horizon: God's help is always near.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:215

> **They ask you ˹O Prophet in˺ what ˹way˺ they should donate. Say, “Whatever donations you give are for parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and ˹needy˺ travellers. Whatever good you do is certainly well known to Allah.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"They Ask Thee" — The Spirit of the Enquirer**

Now the sūrah continues its chain of question-answers — *yasʾalūnaka* — "they ask you" — a form recurring at 2:215's pattern throughout the Book (2:215, 2:217, 2:219, 2:220, 2:222; and 5:4; 8:1 etc.): the Madinan believers — fresh upon their conversion, earnest about their wealth — come with the most practical sort of piety-esteem: *what should we spend?* — the enquiries of a believer's hand — and the Prophet ﷺ is again directed by *qul* — *say*: answer them with the divine register, from God. The commentators record the placement of the verse within chronology: it is read by most as Madinan — pre-dating (or accompanying) the formal zakāh institution — a general guidance for the believers' giving: whatever you shall spend — let it be what breaks toward the greatest right: and then the six-classes cataloguing, family-by-family, circle-by-circle: family first; then blood; then the dispossessed of household: the orphan and the beggar and the wayfarer: God's list of His needy.

**Family First, Without Any Legal Quibbling**

The verse launches the catalog of beneficiaries with God Himself naming the two double-binned groups whose claims are indispensable: *li'l-wālidayni wa'l-aqrabīn wa'l-yatāmā wa'l-masākīni wa ibni al-sabīli* — "for the parents, the near kin, the orphans, the indigents, and the wayfaring son of the road." Each phrase of the six clicks with the tradition's own school as it reads the verse at law's height: the blessing of charity bestowed passes by the same concentric-circle order that the sūrah already established at 2:177 (the great taqwā-verse) and repeats at 4:36 and 8:41 and 59:7: parents are named before kinsfolk; kin before the orphan; the orphan before the stranger, the stranger before the traveler: not in order of religious clout but in order of how near their claim is: family-ties of which no rigid ordinance of the school has to argue — the necessities are pre-determined by the providence of relationship: the father's hand that lifted you in your infancy has already outbuilt whatever claim others construct; the blood-kin carries a record of God's own intended life-routing; the orphan carries the double-protect God-guilt normal fatherhood placed on God alone; the poor and the wayfarer carry the line of need upon their very face: giving is to be organized by the geography of your life itself, not by the wind of fleeting sentiment: the tradition forever places alongside it the sayings of the Prophet:

> *"Charity given to the poor is charity; charity given before kinsman is two things — charity and preserving the ties of kinship."* (al-Tirmidhī 658; Ibn Mājah 1844; al-Nasāʾī — the famous doubling of the credit when the donor is family-adjacent — the sunnah file always added to the verse's own first-priority of parents/kin)

**"Whatever Good You Do" — The Beholder From Eternity**

The verse's closing clause is among the most frequently spoken lines of the entire Book in believer circles: *wa mā tafʿalū min khayrin fa-inna Allāha bihi ʿalīm* — "and whatever good you do — truly God of it is Knowing." The saying seals the list with the watcher's signature — precisely the same grammatical skeleton as 2:197's broader mora (whatever good you do — God knows it): the closing of the watch from Heaven (the *ʿalīm* — Knower — is the Divine Name used in these seals) is the doctrine of the *teaching of the Witness*: the verse quietly raises the motivation above each level of the recipient chain: you do not give simply to be *seen giving* — the knowing is God's — and *that* elevates the private act — the giver's whole budget-of-praise reallocated to the Record: whether one has an audience or no audience, God knows. And so the verse becomes a charter-door for generosity: the valuation of my giving is where my heart stands when I give: the same God Who arranges the six rings of claimants knows — = knows the intent. Nor for a moment does the tradition leave the soul imagining that God will not notice what men have not seen: the entire legacy of the believers' giving is built along the hidden road: the believer gives at night rather than in the day, in concealment rather than in crowds; and the tradition's biographies of generosity themselves painted the same steady preference for concealment —

> *"Seven whom God shall shade under His shade on the Day when there is no shade but His: and — a man who gave in charity and concealed it so much that his left hand knew not what his right hand had spent"* — (al-Bukhārī 660/1423; Muslim 1031 — the famous hadith of the Seven-Under-Shade — cited with the doctrine of verse 215's own knowing-witness at the head of the dossiers of self-hidden giving)

**A Counselling Vessel of Every Century**

The verse comes also at the head of the school of Muslim giving in every age: the prayer-lines of the ummah remember verse 215 not only as an admonitory catalog, but as the summoning-voice of its entire giving-world: what is to be spent is *mā anfaqtum min khayr* — whatever of the good you spend: not only obligatory ṣadaqah — all good-spending: the mother's hand, the father's desk, the orphan's schoolbook, the poor family's bread and the traveler at the roadside bush: every home-economy contains an *inward ledger of 2:215*: and whatever good you do — God knows it: every believer's hands stretching out toward the same named six: parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveller: standing unshaken through all the centuries' changing economies like oaks under shade: *these are the rightful heirs of charity's first command*: Ibn Taymiyyah, al-Ghazālī, al-Shawkānī and the jurists after them built their chapters of giving upon this verse — drawing from it, alongside 2:177, the lasting rule: *the order of God's catalog is itself a complete curriculum of goodness*: for the truly trained giver is the one whose eye is stretched farthest outward toward the world's need while his hand begins with his own family — achieving thereby the two fruits God planted in the verse: charity freely given, and kinship-roots preserved: and so it has remained in the ummah's ledger of alms from its first generation onward.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:216

> **Fighting has been made obligatory upon you ˹believers˺, though you dislike it. Perhaps you dislike something which is good for you and like something which is bad for you. Allah knows and you do not know.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Kutiba — Written Over You**

A purposefully spare verse brings the whole warrior-economy of the sūrah under one statute: *kutiba ʿalaykumu al-qitālu wa huwa kurhun lakum* — "fighting has been prescribed for you — though it is hateful to you." *Kutiba* — written, prescribed, made binding — the same passive decreed-form used before for fasting (2:183) and retribution (2:178) — fixes this command within the series of the ummah's great written obligations: not war for war's sake nor nomadic blood-sport elevated into religion, but *ordained defense* — a burden *written over* the community by a Pen not its own. And the verse immediately names the natural human revulsion alongside the duty: *wa huwa kurhun lakum* — *and it is hateful to you*: the Book does not pretend that peace-loving souls relish fighting; it knows that men of conscience quiver before blood, that the heart leans to backyard peace with wives and dates and quiet prayers while the battlefield offers blood-loss and burial-shelves: the Book bridges the gap by *prescribing* what flesh hates: the tafsīr school keeping the tension alive by citing the Prophet's own address to the fit-fighters who joined the campaigns with strenuous willingness: the ordained fight was a *duty*, and duties are dressed in the clothes the soul finds least pretty and most necessary.

**The Asymmetry of Hate and Good**

Then flows out the verse's immortal epistemic law — four clauses that have served the whole ummah, from generals to mothers-in-law pacing bedrooms at night, as its private compass for every decision: *wa ʿasā an takrahū shayʾan wa huwa khayrun lakum* — "it may be that you hate a thing — yet it is good for you" — *wa ʿasā an tuḥibbū shayʾan wa huwa sharrun lakum* — "and it may be that you love a thing — yet it is evil for you." The Arabic *ʿasā* — *perhaps, it may well be* — cradles the meanings in its vast provisionality: man does not own the final reading of his own own interests — his own heart's polarity is broken-instrument: the thing the nafs salivates for may be its ruin; the thing the nafs shrinks from may be its salvation: God's objective declared-good (*khayrun lakum*) runs on information man does not have: the six-year-child in fear of the surgeon's knife glimpses only the blade of the operation, not the rescued abdomen; the pilgrim weeping at the impoverishment of the road glimpses only the purse, not the heart's training in the sand; the young man in Madinah gazing out over the hills at the departing raiding-party contemplates only the sword's arc, not the rescue of an entire faith over the next horizon of history. And the verse answers the heart's resistance a second time by the fourth clause, *wa Allāhu yaʿlamu wa antum lā taʿlamūn* — **"and God knows — and you do not know."**

**Of Battle-Fields and All Fields**

The tradition never lets this clause remain solely military, though the infantry-context abides first: the early commentators (al-Rāzī's and al-Qurṭubī's registries added here) extend it naturally into every appointment where the heart's preference wars against God's command: the fasting of Ramadan hated by the flesh (2:183's kutiba again); the zakāh upon hard-earned wealth; the ḥajj's shaven head for the vain head's glory; the prayer at sleep's sweetest valley; the honest word in the courtroom with hair dyed crimson by false advantage; the testimony that loses the friend; the lowered gaze when the eye scurries for its prey. Every century's spiritual doctors — al-Ghazālī first among them — have written page-glories upon this verse: *the nafs (lower self) is a false oracle: it loves its ruin and hates its felicity* — and the path whose only dial is obedience reverses the polarity of heart: submit, and slowly — the hated becomes beloved, the sweetened poison becomes repugnant. The school has supplied the history-exemplas too: Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb hating Islam with the sword drawn at his belt — and within the hour his Islam was the Medina-wide dawn; the early Muhājirūn hating exile — and the exile became the hand that wrote the Qur'an's panoramic laws of Madinah; fathers hating God-sanctioned changes in tribal customs — and the broken customs buried forever the cruellest structures of birth-right tyranny in Arabia.

**The Men of Knowledge on Their Feet**

And ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar's celebrated pointed observation about the compound-duty is preserved by the tafsīr tradition under this verse: when reproached for not fighting in the First Civil War, he answered: *"We fought during the Prophet's time — when Islam was small, and a man would be tried for his religion: they would either kill him or torture him. But then Islam became great, and there was no fitnah"* — the obligatory singularity of defensive fighting thus pressed by him (and the masters on his side) to the field of dire need: the Ibn Taymiyyah-law-school and the eyes of all the madhhabs thenceforward dialled the two states with care: upon invasion — *farḍ ʿayn* (individual duty): every Muslim owes defense in person; upon expeditions not strictly defensive — *farḍ kifāyah* (communal duty): some must go; the rest are discharged. And the Prophet's own word upon the station of the fighter in God's path is preserved as this verse's standing companion:

> *"Paradise is beneath the shade of the swords."* (al-Bukhārī 2818; Muslim 1902 — from ʿAbdullāh ibn Abī Awfā — the tradition's most-remembered verdict that the road hated by the flesh, when walked in obedience, leads where love itself leads)

And with these two pinnacles standing — the heart's falseness exposed, and God's perfect knowledge enthroned — the Muslim heart inherits the largest piece of relocation-law of the centuries: *hate a thing — maybe; love a thing — hesitate: God knows, and you are of the unknowing*: and every tired heart that shrinks from its duty under the wall of darkness can find — in this one verse's four clauses — the cord of trust to lift its own foot to the threshold of God's site-appointed stations: *God knows — and you know not.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:217

> **They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about fighting in the sacred months. Say, “Fighting during these months is a great sin. But hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah, rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque is ˹a˺ greater ˹sin˺ in the sight of Allah. For persecution is far worse than killing. And they will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith—if they can. And whoever among you renounces their own faith and dies a disbeliever, their deeds will become void in this life and in the Hereafter. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question at Madinah's Gate**

The litany of questions returns (verse 215's *they ask you* reverb) in a question heavy with accusation: *yasʾalūnaka ʿani al-shahri al-ḥarāmi qitālin fīh* — "they ask you about the sacred month — about fighting within it." Its background, as the commentators record, was the affair of ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Jaḥsh: commissioned by the Prophet ﷺ upon the first cavalry-patrol of Islam toward Nakhlah in the desert, his detachment ran upon a Qurayshī caravan — fighting broke out, and ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥaḍramī was killed — *on the last day of Jumādā'l-Ākhirah or the first day of Rajab* — the boundary of the sacred month depending upon the crescent-sighting. When the patrol returned to Madinah bearing its captives and its spoils, the Prophet waited with disciplinary calm — *"I did not command you to fight during the sacred month"* — and the Quraysh's propaganda-mills ground swiftly: *Muḥammad and his companions spilled blood in a sacred month.* The matter at issue was thus both a law-question (was fighting licit within those days?) and an appraisal-question (whose guilt stands upon whose door?), and the Book descends with its double-edged resolution.

**Grave — but Graver**

The verse's exact response runs in two calibrating strokes: *qul qitālun fīhi kabīr* — "say: fighting therein is grave": the Book does not whitewash the breach — transgressing the sacred month *is* a *kabīr act*: gravity admitted in the very court of divine judgment: but the second stroke separates the powers: *wa ṣaddun ʿan sabīli Allāhi wa kufrun bihi wa'l-masjidi al-ḥarāmi wa ikhrāju ahlihi minhu akbaru ʿinda Allāh* — "yet turning men away from God's way, and disbelieving in Him, and from the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it: that is graver with God." The weighing-court runs its true enumeration: those hand-hollowing accusers from Quraysh had *turned God's road* — persecuting the believers for fifteen years until flight was their only open door — had *unbelieved* in Him they invoked — had *blocked the Sacred Mosque* — most of all the Kaaba, whose custody they disputed the believers' right to use for pilgrimage in general — and had *expelled its own people*: the Book weighs the two files together and its verdict falls: *what the scouting-party did in the wavering crescent-day was grave; what its accusers had done for fifteen years is graver*: the verdict placed a whole war of the sūrah's army-thread and the Arabs' own conscience in its position, once and forever. And the sentence resumes reaching for its own general proverb — *wa'l-fitnatu akbaru mina al-qatl* — "and fitnah is graver than slaying" — the sūrah repeating its own illicit-precedent warning from 2:191: religious persecution that uproots men from their religion and their sanctuary outweighs expressly the one sword-swing's blood.

**"They Will Not Cease"**

The verse then sounds its durable warning of the enmity's stamina: *wa lā yazālūna yuqātilūnākum ḥattā yaruddūkum ʿan dīnikum ini istaṭāʿū* — "and they will never cease to fight you until they reverse you from your religion — if they can": Madinah's whole coming dozen years of sieges and forays summarized in a clause whose reserves have dried up not in fifteen seasons: the animus would stop only at the believers' *apostasy*: war-grease of tribal and material grudges had become the holy war of the Shayṭān's project: *rendering them back* from the House into the old idolatry: and the believers of every age see the clause bearing down across history: no worldly pneumatic of the Messenger's message has ever ended with fine manners: the enemy's stamina-wager is until their victims' faith collapses: against that standing-off, the Muslim is warned, the peace of God is always granted against tried hands, and shows its own defiant demand of steadfastness — the verse planting the sūrah's inner-combat defense-diary as well as the battle-line of the desert.

**The Apostatized Deeds Voided**

The closing clause is the most severe mandate in the whole chapter: *wa man yartadda minkum ʿan dīnihi fa-yamut wa huwa kāfirun fa-ulāʾika ḥabiṭat aʿmāluhum fī al-dunyā wa'l-ākhirah wa ulāʾika aṣḥābu al-nāri hum fīhā khālidūn* — "whoever of you renounces his religion and dies as an unbeliever — those: their deeds have failed in this world and the Hereafter, and they are the people of the Fire, abiding therein." The *ḥabiṭa* — *became void, collapsed, failed* — is the Book's ledger-word for total loss-of-credit: all accumulated good deeds — prayers, fasts, even the Prophet's own companionship — devalued in the eyes of God because the believer *exchanged faith for unbelief*: the whole register cancelled: the law of the great *irtidād* (apostasy) arising in its severest form: what the ledger holds dies by betrayal of the ledger's Owner, and the sentence runs into the perpetual — *fīhā khālidūn* — *abiding therein*: not by length of days but by timelessness. The law-community has through all the centuries handled the clause with the Book's own stern tenderness: whoever stumbles into unbelief is not lost while the door of repentance stands open — the Prophet's own teaching being that divine repentance covers all sins for the one who returns (His saying relates it: "O son of Adam, were you to come to Me with sins nearly filling the earth, and then met Me without associating anything with Me, I would come to you with forgiveness nearly filling it" — al-Tirmidhī 3540, from Abū Dharr — the great hadith-qudsī of limitless return); but him upon whom death falls *without* return, dies a disbeliever — *ḥabiṭat aʿmāluhum* stands written upon his file as this verse holds it standing. The believers' vigilance over the ending of life (*ḥusn al-khātimah*) — trained since verse 132's *lā tamūtunna illā wa antum muslimūn* — is drawn from exactly this clause of 2:217: the ledger closes as the heart ends, and the apostates of that Day are answered with double sealing: deeds voided, and the Fire inherited — while the returning soul, by God's own covenant, finds the door of God wider than every wide door of the world:

> *"Say: O My servants who have wronged themselves against themselves — do not despair of God's mercy: truly God forgives all sins: truly He is the Forgiving, the Merciful. And return unto your Lord, and submit unto Him, before the punishment reaches you — and then you will not be helped."* (39:53–54 — the Qur'anic counterpart always read beside 2:217 by the commentators of the *irtidād* dossier: the one command stands between both poles — return *before the punishment reaches you* — for the door closes without warning, and the richest of all gates is the one still open tonight)

So the verse completes the war-instruction thread of the whole qitāl-stage (190–217) with the final accounting of the greater war: the outward battle may be joined and lifted by the plaque of years — the inner battle for the faith of the heart ends nowhere before the graveside — and the Book's whole war-summit includes in its banner both deeds: fighting-off the fitnah of the persecutors, and keeping-watch over one's own soul until the last Moon of the life — for the worst of all losses is not the weapon's edge nor the camp's ruin, but the entering of the Fire when one had once stood at the Light's door.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:218

> **Surely those who have believed, emigrated, and struggled in the Way of Allah—they can hope for Allah’s mercy. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Comfort Clause After the Trial Clause**

After the severest ledger-warning of the sūrah — the voided deeds of the apostate — the Book passes at once to its mercy-crown: *inna alladhīna āmanū wa lladhīna hājarū wa jāhadū fī sabīli Allāhi ulāʾika yarjūna raḥmata Allāh* — "truly those who believed and those who emigrated and strove in God's way — these hope for God's mercy" — *wa Allāhu ghafūrun raḥīm* — "and God is Forgiving, Merciful." The commentators grasp the tenderness of the verse's position immediately (al-Rāzī among them): ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Jaḥsh's companions — having once already fallen between the crescents into a violation (the slaying at Nakhlah in the ambiguous days of the sacred month) — were weighed down with a deeper distress: *had they, by their lapse, gone outside the covenant altogether — had their striving come to nothing?* — the apostasy-warning of 2:217 had landed upon their guilt for its own reason — and when 2:218 descended, it arrived in answer: the Lord of the Great Ledger names, as the heirs of His mercy, exactly this triple company: *who believed* (their creed ceased not), *who emigrated* (their houses lost at Makkah never restored), *and who strove in God's way* (their swords unsheathed in God's direction even in the misjudged moment): *ulāʾika yarjūna raḥmata Allāh*: they are *the hopers of God's mercy*: the verse's title of the believing warrior is precisely *hopers*: neither despairers of God's mercy on account of error, nor presuming self-assures who take Paradise for granted as a debt God owes: the holy middle — *rajaʾ* — *hope*: the bent-forward soul, between the arms of God's forgiveness and the acknowledgment that He alone is the Decider: and therefore — *wa Allāhu ghafūrun raḥīm*: and (above even their hoping) *God is Forgiving, Merciful*: complete forgiveness for the one who erred in the sacred month, compassion upon the one in whom belief had already planted the root: the seal-Pair rising again (as in 2:192's *ghafūr raḥīm*), as though God's signature were upon the receipt itself.

**"It Is They Who Hope" — The Theology of Hope**

The tradition never lets the word *yarjūna* — *they hope* — pass as a light word: al-Rāzī's school mines the phrase as one of the Book's great pedagogy-entries upon *rajaʾ* — God's hope: the word designating neither certainty (as if Paradise were a contract already signed) nor despair (as if the balance had slit): hope — the believing posture *between* fear of God's sentence and trust in His gifts: the same doctrine rides upon the Prophet's famous confession:

> *"None of you shall enter Paradise by your deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even me — unless God enfolds me in His mercy."* (al-Bukhārī 5673; Muslim 2816 — from Abū Hurayrah — the most-cited foundation-hadith the commentators lay alongside this verse's hope-doctrine: *by mercy, and by mercy alone* — deeds becoming then not the wage of God's wage-slaves but the submission-tokens of God's hopeful lovers)

And the same act of hope attaches this verse back to 2:46's earlier register: *who reckon (yaẓunnūna) that they shall meet their Lord*: hope (*rajaʾ*) and ascription (*ẓann*) in the two verses become the two sides of the believers' future-gaze: he knows he will stand before Him — and while he also knows the sentence is God's to carry or to lift, he *hopes* — carried by the same verse's own signature-pair of Names — that his God shall be *ghafūr, raḥīm*.

**Believer, Emigrant, Warrior**

The triple formula — *āmanū, hājarū, jāhadū* — prized at the verse's center has become one of the enduring taxonomies of the whole tradition's registers of merit: the believer who believed; the emigrant who exchanged house and home for God's city; the striver whose arm responds to God's banner: the Book having named this very triad at 9:20 — "those who believed and emigrated and strove in God's way with their wealth and their souls are greater with God in station" (9:20): the three directories of Islam's faith mount one upon the next, each requiring more of the soul: belief lodged in the breast; emigration cutting every earthly root; striving carrying the middle body into the field — the ladder of all ranks: undergirding this the Christians' own counsel parallel of the tradition: "the truest name of a man is his emigration from the world of self toward the world of God" — the tafsīr-school inherits its *hijrah*-*jihād* discourse from this compact triad: and at the Resurrection the registers are read not by earthly ledger-columns but upon the three headings of verse 218: faith, flight, and fighting fits: the men of those three floors sleeping now beneath the same ṭabarī-garden on God's wide plains: *and God is Forgiving, Merciful.*

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:219

> **They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about intoxicants and gambling. Say, “There is great evil in both, as well as some benefit for people—but the evil outweighs the benefit.” They ˹also˺ ask you what they should donate. Say, “Whatever you can spare.” This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you ˹believers˺, so perhaps you may reflect**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wine and Gambling — the First Verdict**

The question-line continues with its most famous answer of all: *yasʾalūnaka ʿani al-khamri wa'l-maysir* — "they ask you about wine and gambling" — *qul fīhimā ithmun kabīrun wa manāfiʿu li'l-nās* — "say: in them both there is great sin and benefits for mankind" — *wa ithmuhumā akbaru min nafʿihimā* — "but their sin is greater than their benefit." The commentators note the trains of progression the Book took with wine: first, at 16:67, granted without prohibition ("from the fruits of the palms and vines you take intoxicant and goodly provision" — with the tradition-mostly glossing the clause as a predication not yet forbidding but the very wording already closing with a grace-rebuke prime): then this verse of 2:219 — with its at once *clear accounting* of the two beings: great sin vs. some benefits — and the ratio-confession: **sin greater than benefit**: the heart of the believer is weighed exactly once outside the balance of any legal term — before specifically named, the two things are named already by their true weight; and then finally at 5:90-91 — the outright proscription, sealed by God's most piercing epithet upon the two: *intoxicants, games of chance, pillars, and divining arrows are but an abomination of Satan's handiwork — so avoid it*: the progressive schedule from 2:219 has thereby ranked the verse's own case as the textbook model of *tadarruj* — gradualism — in Islamic law: Legislation went through its ordained stages for human flesh, never with sudden brandishings: so that by 5:90's solemn *avoid them* — the hearts of Madinah were already subjected to the preparation this verse had set up years before: better to have no wine-spill in a generation prepared by years of God's own scales — than a prohibition insane and unaccepted.

**Benefit and Sin Presently Weighed**

The tradition lists the benefits honestly (the Book itself admits them: *manāfiʿu li'l-nās*): wine glazes the tongue, warms the circulation, fortifies the timid, lightens the load of the day's difficulties; gambling (*maysir* — casting of arrows for shares of a slaughtered camel-meat, with the win-shares traditionally given as gifts to the poor) brings wealth suddenly to the poor without effort, and dispenses generosity-in-fairness to the tribe: the two *fit*: and still, the verse's verdict falls — *but their sin is greater*: greater because of what they actually pound down upon mankind: drunkenness drowns the intelligence it pretends to refresh: it loosens speech told in secret, breaks homes, exiles prayer from the mind, feeds violence: gambling's sudden wealth reduces the poor of other men — builds despair of one's neighbor into the very mechanism of profit: fosters enmity between friends — profit flowing in coin while affection withers — and poisons the groundwork of every daily-bread economy: so *the sin outweighs*. And the later jurists remember this verse specifically as the spring from which the five fundamental protections of the Law — *the maqāṣid al-Sharīʿah* — were later formally extrapolated: protection of religion, life, lineage, property, and *intelligence* — the classification crystallized by al-Juwaynī and al-Ghazālī — wine being the flagship case of the fifth: *the intellect is God's deposit which intoxicants destroy* — and the war-hatred the tradition records the Prophet tossing across the whole register of wines:

> *"Wine is the mother of every foul deed* — *and every intoxicant is wine (ḥarām), and every intoxicant is unlawful."* (Muslim 2003 — from Ibn ʿUmar: *kullu muskirin khamr wa kullu khamrin ḥarām* — the absolute verdict by which all the commentators across the centuries link 2:219's progressive judgment to 5:90's final one — and by which jurists extended the ruling to every intoxicating substance)

The early generations remembered what these verses achieved in Madinah: it was not the thunder of condemnation that emptied the wine-jars; God first taught the people His own ledger — *in them: great sin and some benefits — and the sin outweighs* — and when the final prohibition came with the dawn-crier of 5:90, the wine-skins of Madinah poured out into the very streets at a single announced call: the hearts had already been won by God's arithmetic before the ban's word ever arrived — the community's own memory of how 2:219 prepared the way for 5:90 being one of the earliest lessons of legislation-by-preparation carried down by the teachers of the Law.

**"Spend What Can Be Spared"**

The verse then completes the answer-line begun at 2:215 with the paired reply *wa yasʾalūnaka mādhā yunfiqūna qul al-ʿafw* — "and they ask you what they should spend — say: the *ʿafw* — the surplus/what is eased." The commentators unfold *al-ʿafw* with tender exactitude: beyond needs, non-demanding, come-by-without-hurt — the un-shouldering share: the giving from which no family's need is impoverished — and the opposite of two other regimes: not the miser-provision (the hand clenched shut around the purse's drawstring: from 17:29: "make not your hand bound to your neck"), and not the squander-provision (the hand opened fully: "nor stretch it altogether ajar"): the middling *ʿafw* is singled out forever by the word of God as the measure-sense of Islamic charity: without hard count being set — before the clipped rules of zakāh arrived — what the Book commands is that your giving reach what your own life can *spare*: *in surplus*: neither your bread nor your bone-marrow taken out. The tradition has always kept this verse as its harbor for the ordinary believer: he cannot give mountains, but he can give the surplus crumbs — and the Prophet's own valuation of small sums guards the small giver:

> *"Protect yourself from the Fire — even by half a date-fruit."* (al-Bukhārī 1417; Muslim 1016 — the universal shield against all the small-giver's doubt — the doctrine that even the smallest gift, given from surplus, stands as shield against a share of the Fire: and so the verse's little word *al-ʿafw* has carried the ordinary Muslim's giving-economy in its pocket across all the centuries)

And the verse's rounded close — *kadhālika yubayyinu Allāhu lakumu al-āyāti laʿallakum tatafakkarūn* — "thus does God make clear for you the signs, that you may reflect" — ties one of the sūrah's great pearl-closing clauses (already at 2:219's tail — this same construction is planted at least four more times in the sūrah) to this very pair of decans: wine and gambling and spending not by formula but by the see-the-scales thought-God-therein: *think — reflect — and the Law will look like purest mercy*: the whole path of the Madinan ummah from wine-shop to prayer-rug traversed by God's own arithmetic of this verse: *their sin is greater — so turn to the sur-plus of your two hands, and roll back your purse toward God.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:220

> **upon this world and the Hereafter. And they ask you concerning orphans. Say, “Improving their condition is best. And if you partner with them, they are bonded with you ˹in faith˺. And Allah knows who intends harm and who intends good. Had Allah willed, He could have made it difficult for you. Surely Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**This World and the Hereafter — the Two Balances**

The hanging word that closes the reflection-clause of 2:219 now drops its two weights: *fī al-dunyā wa'l-ākhirah* — "concerning this world and the Hereafter" — the end of the signs' exposition: God made clear the signs *in both scales*: this world's accounts — where wine's popularity, gambling's windfall, miserly savings all present their short-run profits; and the Hereafter's accounts — where the ancient ledger of 2:219's sin-vs-benefit verdict unlocks the final pages. The commentators (Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī) carry its grammar cleanly — either as the completion of 2:219's *tatafakkarūn* clause: reflect upon the signs [with respect to] this world and the Hereafter; or as God's own declaration: He makes the signs clear *in* both worlds — whose double audience gives the whole legal corpus of the Book its always-twofold intelligibility: never separating the practical from the eschatological: *every Ḥalāl and Ḥarām has accounts opened in both registers.*

**"They Ask You About Orphans" — The Scrupulous Custodians**

The question-line comes now to its most tender ward: the orphan. Obviously the guardians of Madinah had read the Book's burn-burn prohibition of devouring the orphan's wealth (4:10 was already ringing in their ears: "those who devour the property of orphans wrongfully devour naught but fire into their bellies") — and from scrupulosity they had over-fenced themselves: they would share neither food with their wards nor water, nor mounts, nor store-rooms: separate bowls, separate bread: and the burden became so steep that they began abandoning the guardianship altogether — *the orphan's own interest dying of the guardians' over-shielding* — since an orphan's wealth (date-groves, goats, milking herds) only retains its value if it is used: the trees need to be picked; the herds to be milked and put to pasture; the fields to be grazed and churned: and the verse came down as God's release-law: *iṣlāḥun lahum khayr* — "setting matters aright for them is best": the criterion returned in one Arabic word — *iṣlāḥ* — rising from the same root as *ṣāliḥ* — righteousness: the sole measure of custody: *whatever the orphan's good demands — that is best* — not the over-equal separation that starves both parties, and not the common pot in which the orphan's portion is swallowed: not consuming his name, and not saving it either to death: *iṣlāḥ* alone stands as the gauge of every handling: the separation that destroys the orphan's property is *not iṣlāḥ*; and the feeding of the guardian out of the orphan's bowl is *not iṣlāḥ* either. The commentators mark the exact subtlety the verse creates: guardians were free to share the general kitchen and general yard with their wards — *if you intermingle with them, they are your brothers* — the kinship-sentence making the orphan literally one of the guardian-household: eat as brothers eat; ride as brothers ride; sleep under one roof: whatever ordinary family life demands shares the orphan's share with him — not to his diminution: the guardian's share equally available — ordinary intermingling, with the boundary drawn only at corrupt intent — *God knows the corruptor from the setter-aright*: Heaven's penetrating ledger-eye placed over all guardianship, put into a single clause: *wa Allāhu yaʿlamu al-mufsida mina al-muṣliḥ*.

**"Had God Willed, He Would Have Put You to Hardship"**

And the verse closes with its familiar ease-signature — the same formula soon to ring at 5:6 (purification) and 22:78 (ḥajj) — *wa law shāʾa Allāhu la-aʿnaṭakum* — "and had God willed, He would have put you to hardship" — *inna Allāha ʿazīzun ḥakīm* — "truly God is Mighty, Wise": the sentence returning in providence's own face: the hardship would have been theirs — had God willed it — for He who set obligation didn't need to grant ease: the guardians would still be under separate-pots if pleasure-of-God demanded it; and yet again the opposite was spoken: mercy came first: He *did* will ease; and the reason follows in the two closing Names: the Mighty — whose command is not challenged — is also the Wise — whose command is fit — *wisdom behind every sharpening*: the believer's law is not God's cruelty-cabinet but God's fitting-tailor's workshop: the belts are made tight around justice's domain, loosened around necessity's lair. The school thereby unites verse 220 with its own beatitude — the ummah's refuge-principle:

> *"God intends for you ease, and He does not intend for you hardship."* (2:185's very words of the Ramadan-law — always cited in the schools beside 2:220's own ease-clause: the mass of these blessings falling together under the tradition's own master-rule: *lā taklīfu illā mā yuṭāq* — no duty is loaded upon the soul beyond its power)

and the Prophet's own oft-quoted final counsel:

> *"Make things easy, and do not make them difficult."* (al-Bukhārī 69; Muslim 1330 — the Prophet's standing administrative instruction to his governors — always cited by the jurists beside the ease-clauses of verses v220, v286, 5:6, 22:78: God's mercy is legislated in the ease of His laws)

So the Orphan-verse of the sūrah completes the bridge between the spending-directive of 219 and the marriage-legislation that arrives from verse 222 onward: the weakest of the community keeps its guardian within the community's ordinary kitchen-circuit; the greediest of it stands barred from an inch of misuse by the divine gaze that separates corrupter from setter-right; and the whole of the ummah's guardianship-law thereby settles into the golden center of the Book — *God knows the corruptor from the setter-aright* — God's own gaze watching each bowl lifted in each orphan-hand, from the beginning of time to its end.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:221
