> **Do not marry polytheistic women until they believe; for a believing slave-woman is better than a free polytheist, even though she may look pleasant to you. And do not marry your women to polytheistic men until they believe, for a believing slave-man is better than a free polytheist, even though he may look pleasant to you. They invite ˹you˺ to the Fire while Allah invites ˹you˺ to Paradise and forgiveness by His grace. He makes His revelations clear to the people so perhaps they will be mindful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Matrimonial Borderline**

The sūrah's whole domestic-law chapter opens with the boundary that defends the household's faith itself: *wa lā tankiḥū al-mushrikāti ḥattā yuʾminna* — "and do not marry idolatrous women until they believe" — *wa lā tunkiḥū al-mushrikīna ḥattā yuʾminū* — "and do not give [your women] in marriage to idolaters until they believe." The double command, dispensed symmetrically in both directions — man-to-woman and woman-to-man — builds the first ummah-home's foundational decree: the marriage-window must open onto faith: *belief first, wedlock after*: the fire-lines of religious difference drawn not against the People of the Book wholly (5:5's later license for chaste women of the People of the Book is read by most commentators as a specification surviving this verse's general rule — the question of abrogation versus specification being the standard debate in the schools) but against the *mushrik* — the idolater who has none of the revealed covenants: for the household is the first school of the soul, and two discordant directions toward God — one toward the One God, one toward the shrine's stones — sets the children of the house upon a double road from their first prayer-lessons: the Book calling this choice by its real name in the verse's own verdict: *ulāʾika yadʿūna ilā al-nār* — "those are callers unto the Fire."

**"Though She Please You, Though He Impress You"**

The verse's mid-clauses plant the anti-preference test most sharply of all: *wa la-amatun muʾminatun khayrun min mushrikatin wa law aʿjabatkum* — "surely a believing bondwoman is better than an idolatress — *though she please you*" — *wa la-ʿabdun muʾminun khayrun min mushrikin wa law aʿjabakum* — "and surely a believing bondman is better than an idolater — *though he impress you*." The commentators ring out the shock: in the Arabia of status, finance, and tribe, a *slave* person — least in worldly dignity — is declared *better marriage-material* than the free noble idolater whose beauty or bearing draws the heart: the Book deliberately chooses the lowest of social ranks and lifts it above the highest: *khayr* — *better*: better for your soul, better for your house, better for your child's faith, better before the scale of God: the old aristocratic measures must give way now — *beauty passes, wealth circulates, tribes rise and fall — but a believing heart is the one dowry that does not melt* — the doctrine exactly parallel to Abū Dharr's fine-clothes-tattered-man hadith (already deployed at 2:212): and the two matched clauses — *aʿjabatkum* (though she please you) and *aʿjabakum* (though he impress you) — are declared in full symmetry: the bride-candidate's charm and the groom-candidate's impressiveness likewise kneel before the greater criterion of faith. And the social revolution the verse planted — *slaves by faith above nobles by idol* — is the witness of the entire abolition-doctrine carried throughout the Qur'an's whole emancipation program: God *here*, not in the shadows of any later century's conscience, *honors the lowly that choose Him*.

**Callers unto Fire; Caller unto Garden**

The verse's closing theology reduces the whole choice to its precise formula: *ulāʾika yadʿūna ilā al-nār wallāhu yadʿū ilā al-jannati wa'l-maghfirati bi-idhnih* — "those call unto the Fire, but God calls unto the Garden and forgiveness, by His leave." The commentators hold up the verbs' symmetry as the pinnacle of the verse's lessons: whomsoever you marry attaches you to a *calling*: spouses call — and their calling travels from one heart into the other — day by day the home's direction is tugged toward the caller: (1) toward the Fire: if the caller's compass is shirk, nothing else in his person matters: the house becomes the Fire's outpost regardless of feast-spreads and silk; (2) toward the Garden: if God's own call governs — *and God calls unto the Garden AND forgiveness* — the twin destination: Garden *and* forgiveness — the two petals of the one gift — and the *bi-idhnihi* (*by His leave*) repeating itself a third time upon the whole taxonomy-clause: even His general call requires His individual authorization: the same divine liberty that raised verse 213's version of guidance-rights: so let the believers seek, embrace, and pursue a house founded upon God's own call: *marriage undertaken as a road to the Garden* — the tradition retaining the Prophet's own marriage-charter alongside:

> *"A woman is married for four things: her wealth, her lineage, her beauty, and her religion. So marry the religious one — may your hands prosper."* (al-Bukhari 5090; Muslim 1466 — from Abū Hurayrah — the famous church-and-hall tradition that from the soundest of all principles judges over all marriage-choices in the Muslim world, laid out in every fiqh manual's own exegesis of verse 221)

And its final architecture — *wa yubayyinu āyātihi li'l-nāsi laʿallahum yatadhakkarūn* — "and He makes clear His signs to mankind, that they may remember" — resumes the pearl-closings of verses 219, 221's own register: the whole ummah's whole house-owner's duty here given its eternal ground: God does not herd His servants to His own statute by blind law: He *makes the signs manifest* — *that they may remember.* The marriage-threshold of verse 221 thereby stands open to both genders of the believers: chosen correctly, it leads to the Garden; wrongly — and the heart may burn in the Fire first-*called* into one's own house.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:222

> **They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about menstruation. Say, “Beware of its harm! So keep away, and do not have intercourse with your wives during their monthly cycles until they are purified. When they purify themselves, then you may approach them in the manner specified by Allah. Surely Allah loves those who always turn to Him in repentance and those who purify themselves.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"They Ask You About the Monthly Course"**

The question-line presses into the most intimate corner of the household's law — and the Book answers with a modesty met by no comparable ancient legislation: *wa yasʾalūnaka ʿani al-maḥīḍi qul huwa adhan* — "they ask you about the monthly course — say: it is a harm/hurt" — *fa-ʿtazilū al-nisāʾa fī al-maḥīḍ* — "so keep apart from women during the menstruation" — *wa lā taqrabūhunna ḥattā yaṭhurna* — "and do not approach them until they have purified" — *fa-idhā taṭahharna faʾtūhunna min ḥaythu amarakumu Allāh* — "and when they have purified, then go to them in the way God has commanded you." The wording's choices have occupied the commentators at every level: *adhan* — *a hurt, a harm* — glossed by most as the uncleanness of the blood itself, by others as the pain and distress the woman herself endures during it (al-Qurṭubī noting the verse's gentleness in assigning the condition's burden to her discomfort, not to her personhood); and *taqrabūhunna* — the approaching of vaginal intercourse — the prohibition landing exactly and only upon that act: *keep apart* never meant the banishment of the woman from the home: the pagan Arabs had fastened upon women's monthly state a right seclusion — separate bedding, separate dishes, sometimes separate quarters — as the customs of Jews and Magians in neighboring lands also dictated (the commentators citing the background-systems, Leviticus 15 and the Zoroastrian purification-codes alike): and the Prophet ﷺ, immediately after this verse's legislative edge was understood, refused the cast-out status altogether:

> *"Your menstruation is not in your hand"* — his answer to his wife ʿĀʾishah when she demurred from fetching a prayer-mat out of the mosque for him (al-Bukhārī 295; Muslim 298 — the standing hadith building beside the verse: the woman's condition does not touch her service of the household, her joints of family-life, her closeness in bed: only intercourse stops, and stopping one door in order for the woman's own repose, the rest remaining open in full tenderness)

— the school thus writing the whole cross-tabulation of household mercy here from the most reliable occasions: kissing, fondling, eating, sleeping: all permissible: the verse's full command is: *one named door closes until purity returns — and every other door stays open.*

**Purified — and God's Own Command**

Then the verse's completion instructs the resumption in divine terms: *fa-idhā taṭahharna*: *when they are purified*: the majority of the schools requiring the woman's own *ghusl* — the ritual full-body washing at the flow's cessation — as the renewed-approach condition (the Ḥanafī school's customary exception: after the blood-cessation, before ghusl, in cases of hardship): and the directive's own clause wraps the whole subject in God's own sovereignty: *min ḥaythu amarakumu Allāh* — *in the way God has commanded you* — the law of the intimate union is not left to heat, to fashion, nor to lust: its grounds are commanded: the vaginal gate among the others (the school being unanimous that the anal path is never opened for the husband, at any season) — and the entire regimen of conjugal life is brought into the same framework as prayer and fast: the household-boudoir serviced by revelation as the household-mosque is: *go in unto them in the way God has commanded you* — and the tradition's other regulations follow accordingly: every other conjugal act besides intercourse remains lawful and loved during the menstrual days; the woman's prayer and fast are deferred, but her faith is never thereby stained and no shame falls upon her: God's own laws guard her in every way during her season.

**Loves the Repenters, Loves the Purified**

And then the beautiful sealing-pair: *inna Allāha yuḥibbu al-tawwābīna wa yuḥibbu al-mutaṭahhirīn* — "truly God loves the ever-repenting, and loves the purified." The commentators instantly hear the double-joining of the verse's whole content with its closing Names: (1) the repenting — *al-tawwābīn*: those who keep returning to God over every trespass of His bounds, whenever flesh has slipped past the statute: (2) the purifiers — *al-mutaṭahhirīn*: those who purify themselves, keeping the fleshly avenues within God's own purity-word: the two categories conjointly encompassing the whole discipline of marriage-purity: the tradition reads the closing as the divine generalization *beyond* this verse's subject: God's own heart approves (here and throughout: 9:108's own shrine-moon equation: "wherein are men who love to purify themselves, and God loves the pure") — the rituals of Islam being God's loving-care for the house-body as for the soul: the pleasure-command of Scripture tailored equally to both sexes' welfare — *the wife given rest-days by God's own law* — and both called to one shared return, one shared purifying, one shared Loverhood of their Lord. And on this exact administration the Prophet's own post-washing law resounded sanctified:

> *the sunnah order being dispensed in plain terms among the Muslim household's teachers down the centuries — al-Bukhārī's and Muslim's entire *Book of Menstruation* (Kitāb al-ḥayḍ) standing as the evidence of the tradition's detailed devotion to every household-rule this verse plants*

— so that the tenderness of 2:222's entire disposition comes to be folded forever after into the Muslim household's season-life: the wife's monthly statute is God's own loving law; its appointed rest does not mark her as unclean but guards her harder days into repose; its purification-marked reunion is God's commanded wisdom: and above them both the two *love*-clauses hang as the lamps of the whole household-altar: *God loves the repentant — God loves the purified* — a verdict over the whole devotional life of the believing home.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:223

> **Your wives are like farmland for you, so approach them ˹consensually˺ as you please. And send forth something good for yourselves. Be mindful of Allah, and know that you will meet Him. And give good news to the believers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Tilth of God**

From the law of seasons the Book advances into one of its most famous images for marriage itself: *nisāʾukum ḥarthun lakum fa-ʾtū ḥarthakum annā shiʾtum* — "your women are a tilth for you — so come to your tilth as you will." The commentators unfold the verse's background and bearing with their usual completeness: the occasion-records (al-Ṭabarī's and Ibn Kathīr's chains) speak of questions carried to the Prophet ﷺ about married relations between the Muhājirūn husbands and their Anṣārī wives — the two communities' different ancient customs abutting (some Madinan families holding inherited squeamishness about certain unions-in-positions while immigrant Makkans followed their own broad customs) — and certain men asking the Prophet *how* union with one's wife was to be practiced: the verse returned the answer through the tillage-simile that immediately became Islamic jurisprudence's charter of marriage-intimacy: *nisāʾukum ḥarthun lakum* — *your women are tillage for you*: the word's whole symbolic weight banked not upon wife-as-property (the very simile is expressly *agricultural*, not chattel-lic: a field is *cared-for, protected, watered* — and a farmer's whole future stands inside its soil) but upon the elementary structure of fertility: a wife's purpose-enclosure bears *seed into harvest*: children, the harvest of the Joining of the two — the Book christening the marital bed immediately as the field of God's own appointed fruitfulness: and with its single permitted form — the Prophet's notice glossing the verse's own plain law in the reliable records (al-Ṭabarī's chain): *"a single orifice"* — the tillage-word itself guiding what is and is not the field — vaginal union, only: for a field's fruits only grow from its soil.

**As You Will — the Freedom of the Law**

The verse's next clause then grants the spouses their room in God's own desacralizing generosity: *fa-ʾtū ḥarthakum annā shiʾtum* — "come to your tilth however you will." The commentators (al-Rāzī at their head) draw the technical consensus with precision: *annā shiʾtum* — *as you will* — grants the *mode* and manner of the union the full field of conjugal freedom — any position, any posture of love-play and tenderness — but *not the avenue*: the reproductive-way of the metaphor is alone admissible (as the Prophet's own gloss *one orifice* had ruled): the school universalizing the verse as the abrogation of an ancient tribal modesty-conventions — not as a license for any and every unbridled appetite: the arena of the permissible *within* God's own gates proving itself wide enough for every lawful tenderness: man and wife belong to one another — the Book offers no third limb on which marriage is to be practiced — and the law of conjugal intimacy flows downstream from this gate: the husband to answer the wife's call, the wife to answer the husband's in like measure — each spouse owning a share of rights over the other (as verse 228 will set down: 'they are owed obligations the like of those they owe, in an honorable way'); and between them, the adab-literature of the later centuries developed the age-old courtesies of the marriage-bed around the Prophet's own instructions of gentleness, privacy, consideration, and the opening *bismillāh* — the small handholds of reverence running in the Muslim household from generation to generation.

**Send Forth for Your Souls**

But the verse, that has been passing through the law of the widest adult-topic of worldly living, suddenly turns its face fully toward the Hereafter-scales: *wa qaddimū li-anfusikum* — **"and send forth *[good]* for your souls"** — the marital command then preceded immediately by its charity-admonition: the conjugal bed is not the end of your husband-and-wife existence: the joined spouses must also *send forth* — *qaddimū*: forward-model of the same verb the Book uses for all the acts sent beforehand to the Hereafter (see 5:80's own register: woe to them for what their hands have sent forward: and 82:5's separate echo of the people's *what a soul has sent forward and held back*) — the households of the believers stacked not only in tonight but in the long furnishings of the Last Day's ship: the prayerful unions, the shared alms, the children raised upon God's remembrance — all 'sent before' through God's own accounting-funnel: so the believing couple rests on one bed of flesh and sows *two harvests* — the earthly one in their children and the heavenly one buried beforehand into God's wide treasury: *and yet, O zealous — send forth for your souls.*

**"Know That You Shall Meet Him"**

And the verse's triple-blessing seals it all: *wa-ttaqu Allāha wa-ʿlamū annakum mulāqūhu* — "and reverence God — and know that you shall meet Him" — *wa bashshiri al-muʾminīn* — "and give glad tidings unto the believers." The second-person swing here is startling even after the whole passage's sweep: from the most earthly of subjects, the Book turns at once to *mulāqīhi*: meeting Him: the man of the bedchamber hastens to be reminded that the man of Resurrection-field awaits on the same being: and the final charge — *bashshir* — *give glad tidings!* — is entrusted to the Prophet: after all the fears and ceilings of the statutes of sex, marriage, divorce, the Book returns to the good-news final soil: *tell the believers* — the household mightiest mans, lying in the levies and fasts of true obedience — that their portion in God's own grant is *gladness*: not restricted, not restricted — *bahja*: the gladness that the Prophet's prophecy passed as well in the compound-family's duplex seal:

> *"When a man comes to his wife, let him say: In the name of God — O God, keep Satan from us and keep Satan from what You provide for us; and if God decrees a child for them, Satan can never harm that child."* (al-Bukhārī 141, 6388; Muslim 1434 — from Ibn ʿAbbās — the Prophet's specific instruction for the first moment of union, and with it the guarded blessing upon the child conceived — the tradition's household-litany standing beside verse 223 through every believing century)

> *"And in the lawful union of one of you there is charity." They said: O Messenger of God — one of us fulfills his desire and has a reward thereby? He said: "Do you not see that if he had placed it in what is unlawful it would be a sin upon him? Likewise when he places it in what is lawful, it is a reward for him."* (Muslim 1006 — from Abū Dharr — the Prophet's own equation of the licit marriage-bed with *ṣadaqah*: the very register in which verse 223's *bashshir* — give glad tidings! — has been read by the tradition ever since)

— and with that the husbands of Madinah learned that their household-life stood directly beneath God's own satisfied gaze: and so ends the small, famous, unforgettable marriage-verse of the Book of God: *your women are a tilth to you — so come to your tilth as you will — yet send forth for your souls — and reverence God — and know that you shall meet Him — and give glad tidings unto the believers.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:224

> **Do not use Allah’s Name in your oaths as an excuse for not doing good, not guarding against evil, or not making peace between people. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Oaths That Block Goodness**

The household-laws of menses and intimacy are followed now by the law of the sworn word — the vault of every Arab community's public bond — and the verse opens it with a doctrine standing at every oath's exit-door: *wa lā tajʿalū Allāha ʿurḍatan li-aymānikum* — "and do not make God an *ʿurḍah* — a barrier/screen — for your oaths" — the commentators explaining *ʿurḍah* metaphorically: an obstacle, a cover set at the path, so that the man of the oath finds his own sworn words standing between himself and every duty of goodness: so he says: *I swore by God never to give charity — so I cannot give*; *I swore by God never to speak to my brother — so I cannot reconcile*; *I swore by God never to enter that mosque or join that brotherhood — so I cannot repent* — God's name itself thus brandished by the swearer as his own liberty's *shield*: the road-block between the man and the good deed God had always asked of him. The verse collapses the whole cheap stratagem: God is not your shelter for refusing righteousness: *you shall not make Him the sump-arm of the oath*: if the oath stands against piety, the oath must break, not piety — for God's name was never meant to be the accomplice of disobedience.

**Against Pious Deeds, Cross-Croyers, and Peace-Making**

The verse then fastens its doctrine onto the three standing pillars of Arab community-morality: *an tabarrū wa tattaqū wa tuṣliḥū bayna al-nās* — "to doing good (*birr*), being God-fearing (*taqwā*), and making peace between people (*iṣlāḥ bayna al-nās*)." The triad — the same *birr* the sūrah had defined at 2:177, the same *taqwā* syllabling throughout, and the same *iṣlāḥ* God had already placed in the mouth of Jethro at Hūd 11:88 — stands here as the sample-work of all oaths-that-disobey: the Book choosing piety, fear, and peace-making as the most conspicuously valuable goods a man's oath might block — since the public weal of every nomadic haqour around Madinah depended upon whichever peacemakers were still free to act — and the tradition's records of the verse apply it further into the mores of the new covenant of peoplehood bound together at Yaḥrib: *every oath that keeps a man from joining kin, from giving charity, from saying the true word, from mending strife between neighbors — every such oath is annulled before God's command.* And the school thereby built the famous maxim of Islamic ethics out of this verse: **no obedience to created beings that involves disobedience to the Creator** — the same principle the Prophet consecrated with an opposite-quoted air: *"there is no obedience in disobedience to God — obedience belongs only to what is good"* (al-Bukhārī 4340; Muslim 1840 — the identical doctrinal territory articulated at this verse and passed into the manuals of Muslim ethics as the settled law of conscience).

**The Prophet's Own Sunnah of Breaking the Oath**

The tradition brings the whole doctrine home in the Prophet's own practical statute — the prophetic answer to every man who discovers his swearing is now blocking his well-doing:

> *"Whoever swears an oath and then sees that something other than it is better, let him do what is better and expiate his oath."* (al-Bukhārī 6235, 6678; Muslim 1652 — from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī — the Prophet's standing universal-counsel, whose charge is codified by the jurists as 5:89's kaffārah system: feeding ten of the poor, clothing them, or freeing a slave; if one cannot manage it, a fast of three days: this kaffārah set exactly where the oath was locked in against the good)

So the very oath's breaking becomes God's mercy-rods: no believer is forever chained by the hasty syllables of his own mouth: when the oath works toward sin or against good, the door of expiation is placed (as 5:89 laid the legal requirements in official form): break the oath, make the expiation, and proceed with the good: *do not make God a hindrance*: the Lord's name cannot be pleaded as excuse for stagnation — and the verse ends with the great names *wa Allāhu samīʿun ʿalīm* — *God is Hearing, Knowing*: He heard the oath spoken; He knows whether the oath conceals a heart bent on good or bandaged in pretended piety, and He knows whether the swearer holds the oath itself up as his refuge against mercy: the Witness of every oath detailed within one syntax of hearing and knowing — so that the whole doctrine of oaths may be resolved in the same wise vocabulary the sūrah has already supplied its subjects-by-subject: God hears the oath, and knows the heart it screens.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:225

> **Allah will not hold you accountable for unintentional oaths, but for what you intended in your hearts. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Oaths Uttered Without Purpose**

Now the mercy-bonded side of the oath-law comes: *lā yuʾākhidhukumu Allāhu bi'l-laghwi fī aymānikum* — "God will not take you to task for the *laghw* — the vain, thoughtless, idle — in your oaths." The commentators unfold *laghw* in two registers which the law-books put to not much difference (al-Ṭabarī's and al-Qurṭubī's registries): (1) the habitual, reflexive expletive of everyday Arabic speech — *wa'llāhi* — *by God!* uttered in innocent emphasis at market and fireside, without a conscious oath being made at all — the Arabs' lifelong vernacular habit that causes a religious man to swear ten times in a day's conversation without the faintest intention of bond; (2) the oath sworn sincerely about a thing the swearer believed to be so, afterward proved otherwise: the honest-slip: he swore he had paid that debt — he still thought he had — and time shows the truth: no expiation is required of him, the school rules: *laghw* — the residue of all the oath-phrases custom and flow carry through his speech without any real *bond-making intent*: and God's covenant-adjuster declared by the verse: *no reckoning upon these*: the mountains of idle wa'llāhis and the small honest slips — all remitted — the Lord bringing no man to task about the breakage the tongue never intended.

**"What Your Hearts Have Earned"**

Then the boundary-line of every oath-law stands: *wa lākin yuʾākhidhukum bi-mā kasabat qulūbukum* — "but He will take you to task for what your hearts have earned": the line between *laghw* (idle oath-speak) and *ʿaqd* (a binding oath) — between the tongue-only and the heart-bond: whatever the heart truly wrapped itself around — consciously intended oaths accompanied by full consent and deliberate aim — *there* the covenant-law locks every lock: as 5:89 develops the orders in its own full juridical chapter, with both the ruling and the expiation (feeding ten poor of the middle sort of your own food, clothing them, freeing one slave; whosoever finds not, a three-day fast): the Book's whole architecture of the oath never tolerating any blur between the two fates: the empty words fly before the wind of God's kindness, the deliberate words chain the deceiver — until the deed's reckoning arrives upon the heart's own ledger: and then the heart that wrapped its ownership around the oath must sit in the dock of the verse's accounting: not the mouth's convenience but the heart's intent — so that the whole edifice of protecting the honor of sworn words rises from this one distinction, the tradition remembering upon this point the Prophet's assiduous illustration with the fly-thought:

> *"God will not call you to account for what is inadvertent in your oaths, but He will call you to account for what your hearts have earned" — the Prophet's own gloss on the verse — recorded of his teaching in every ancient tafsīr register upon this point (al-Ṭabarī's majmaʿ reporting it in the chain — the same condition the tradition guards in its jurisprudence of intentions everywhere: the heart carries the deeds, from the founding hadith *innamā al-aʿmālu bi'l-niyyāt* (al-Bukhārī 1; Muslim 1907) onward: the oath is only a small case of the whole code.)

**Forgiving, Clement — The Sealing Pair**

The verse closes upon two names whose pairing this sūrah has now fixed as one of its most reassuring descent-waves: *wa Allāhu ghafūrun ḥalīm* — "and God is Forgiving, *Bearing* — Clement." *Ḥalīm* — forbearing, long-suffering: the patient Pardon-Bearer who does not hasten the punishment even when the offence is real (the name's glory already observed noticeably at 2:235's omen-placement and again ahead of us at 2:263): the forgiven Heart's own watchful gratitude swells where it has just passed through the ocean of God's patience: He *could* take to task the smallest verbal error — every loose *wa'llāhi* of the day was a real bond — but He is *Ḥalīm*: bearing with the stumblers, the ceaseless bearers of the slips of the tongue; and *Ghafūr* — Forgiving: even the heart-bonds broken in sin-covered ignorance receive His pardon at knocking: so the Muslim is shaped by the laws of speech into two settled convictions: *how leniently God charges us* — and *how much He bears with us*: and the whole oath-discipline is fitted into these two Names' own pattern: a tongue careful with oaths — serious when it swears seriously, at ease with the harmless expletive — inscribed into the believing speaker's character at every day's end: *God is Forgiving, Clement* — the amnesty returning upon all the careless words of yesteryears: as the tribes of Madinah heard them first.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:226

> **Those who swear not to have intercourse with their wives must wait for four months. If they change their mind, then Allah is certainly AllForgiving, Most Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Oath That Imprisons a Woman**

The oath-laws now turn to the grimmest weapon a husband could wield without severing the marriage — the vow of abstention: *li-lladhīna yuʾlūna min nisāʾihim tarabbuṣu arbaʿati ashhur* — "for those who forswear their wives — a waiting of four months." The commentators sketch the pre-Islamic cruelty this verse came to end: the Arab husband, in anger or in scorn, would swear by God never to approach his wife again — but *not divorce her*: she remained suspended in the deepest marital dungeon ever devised in that time — neither wife approached, nor widow, nor free woman: unable to remarry because still married, unable to live as a wife because sworn off: and that suspension might *stretch for years*, her youth drying inside the legal oath's prison while the husband sulked elsewhere or took other wives. This was the *īlāʾ* — the jurisprudential term drawn exactly from this verse's root (*yuʾlūna* from *ālā*, to swear an oath of forbearance) — and God cut the cruelty's cord with a clock: **four months**.

**The Clock's Expiry Forces a Choice**

The verse's grace-mechanism runs with exact legislative sobriety: within the four-month window, the husband may *think again*: *fa-in fāʾū fa-inna Allāha ghafūrun raḥīm* — "then, if they return, truly God is Forgiving, Merciful": *fāʾa* — *to return* — the Arabic word itself carrying the nuance of *coming back from a wrong*, so that the verse gently frames the forswearing itself as something to be walked back from; and on the return God spreads His two Names: no disgrace remains on the home where the wrong oath was broken back into tenderness. But the clock's face means also its chime must be heard: once four months glimmer complete, the swearing husband has exhausted the law's patience — either he returns, or divorce falls due (the schools elaborating the mechanics: many holding that after the four months he must either resume the marriage or release her; some that the wife may seek judicial dissolution; most — with al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī's dossiers — that the waiting itself forces the resolution into one of the two channels): **no more suspended wives** — that is the verse's one-sentence reform charter. And the commentators note the clause's compass: the traditions read the forswearing most naturally as the abstention from the marriage-bed sworn in wrath — an oath of celibate-contempt — while some of the schools (Ibn Kathīr among them) generalize the ruling to *any* oath of shunning-harm sworn against a wife (silent-treatment vows and the like), and limit the terrible strictness to sworn intent to harm: God alone knowing what darkness lay in each husband's breast (2:227's own *samīʿ ʿalīm* to follow).

**A Mercy for the One Wielded Against**

The doctrine slotted within the sūrah's bigger frame is itself profound: the oath belongs to God; the wife does not. The pious sanctions of oaths cannot be turned into private devices of spouse-torment — precisely as 2:224 declared of God's name in general ("do not make God a hindrance through your oaths"): a man's oath is not his wife's cage: God set His clock upon every *īlāʾ*: four months to reconsider, then release or return: and if he returns, God — the verse does not fail to remind — is *ghafūr*: fully forgiving the man who lays his wrong oath down. The tradition preserves beside the verse the Prophet's own household wisdom upon marital angers in general:

> *"Let not a believing man hate a believing woman: if he dislikes one trait of hers, he will be pleased with another."* (Muslim 1469 — from Abū Hurayrah — the Prophet's canonical counsel against the dislike-swellings that produce the ancient forswearing: the wife not ironed flat by vow but acknowledged as a garden of mixed flowers)

So the verse stands in the sūrah as the first statutory protection of a wife's continuing life inside a faltering marriage — its four-month mercy shining forward through the whole later fiqh of women's rights: no woman of the Book shall lie the rest of her days under a man's suspended anger: God closes every such oath's prison with His own calendar.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:227

> **But if they settle on divorce, then Allah is indeed All-Hearing, All-Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Choice Visible at the Window's Edge**

Having opened the road of return, the verse now displays its alternative door with candor: *wa in ʿazamū al-ṭalāqa fa-inna Allāha samīʿun ʿalīm* — "and if they resolve upon divorce — truly God is Hearing, Knowing." *ʿAzamū* — *they resolved, determined, decided* — is a verb of *finality*: the commentators note its deliberate weight: forswearing husbands, at the expiry of the four-month horn, must *either* return *or* make the final resolve: no more half-light, no more racking: the woman stands at one of two statuses — wife restored, or woman released: and the second *is lawful*: the Book, after all its teaching of patience, never equates patience with perpetual incarceration: divorce is hated among lawful things (most certainly: the Prophet's memorable word upon this file: *"of all the lawful things, the most detestable to God is divorce"* — Abū Dāwūd 2178; Ibn Mājah 2018 — the Prophet himself, giving the sense of God's disposition upon the finalizing of any divorce) — yet *lawful it remains*: God authorizes the doorway, preferring mercy always, but permitting resolution always: *ʿazamū*: let it be a resolve, not a fog.

**Hearing, Knowing — The Watchtower Over the Home**

The verse then says its Names over the entire difficult case: *samīʿ* — Hearing: God hearing every syllable of these household oaths — every midnight contempt, every breathed threat, every sworn abandonment: nothing in the walls of any house escapes; and *ʿalīm* — Knowing: God knowing every heart behind every word — the husband's sincerity, his repentance, his cruelty in-silence, his hidden intent — the whole interior dossier of the household laid bare. The commentators have never failed to dwell upon the deliberate selection of these two divine Names across the whole menses-oaths-intimacy-forbiddance complex (2:222's purification-pair, 2:224's hearing-pair, 2:227's): the domestic-chamber is not beyond the mosque's gaze: the walls that hide a marriage from neighbors hide nothing from the Seeing-Hearing: and the husband who swears away his wife in darkness, or resolves upon divorce believing it a private whim — verse 227 watches him: *you are heard; you are known*: so the verse cements the honesty of every life inside the house of Islam: no private wrong — however dark its doors — can ring beyond God's twofold registry.

**The Function It Serves in the Book of Divorce**

The verse belongs to the first panel of the sūrah's great divorce-code (226–232): it concludes the forswearing subfile with the clean alternative: the resolve of divorce. The next panels — v. 228: the waiting-period and the rights of the womb; v. 229: the twice-and-third tally of ṭalāq and the wife's own compensation-gate (khulʿ); v. 230: the interdiction of remarrying a thrice-divorced wife except after another marriage; v. 231: the prohibition of divorcing-with-harm-intent; v. 232: the prohibition of barring a divorced woman from her new marriage — are all being announced in the present verse's own sobriety: *ʿazamū* — you who are determined: now take God's whole manual with you: divorce is not a sovereign stroke: it is a legal state with rules, counts, limits, restraints, witnesses — and God's Names encamp above it all: *Hearing, Knowing*: *the ummah thereby learning that all the recesses of a life — even the last exhaustion of a marriage — lie within His statute* — no cruelty beyond chart, no divorce beyond limit.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:228

> **Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles ˹before they can remarry˺. It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they ˹truly˺ believe in Allah and the Last Day. And their husbands reserve the right to take them back within that period if they desire reconciliation. Women have rights similar to those of men equitably, although men have a degree ˹of responsibility˺ above them. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Waiting Period — ʿIddah**

The divorce-code now lays out the framework that surrounds each pronouncement with space and discipline: *wa'l-muṭallaqātu yatarabbaṣna bi-anfusihinna thalāthata qurūʾ* — "divorced women shall wait by themselves for three courses." The *ʿiddah* — the legally-counted waiting — is set at three *qurūʾ* (menstrual cycles or purity-periods; the schools differing on which end-mark the word picks out, each counting identically in practical seasons): its purposes are manifold in the commentators' and jurists' lists: to be sure beyond all doubt whether or not the womb carries a child (for the child's lineage and the mother's custody of her position settle differently with established pregnancy); to grant cooling-time where the verdict was issued in fiery haste; and to give the couple the God-set pause in which arbiters and peacemakers may yet reconcile hearts (4:35's own arbiters being called for precisely in this interim): the three-month pause of the Book has for 1400 years placed its quiet wedge between the disasters of quick fury: the tongue may strike once in the tempest — God's counting gives time for reason.

**No Conceiving by Concealment**

The first specific fear of the Book illustrates what the waiting seasons need protect: *wa lā yaḥillu lahunna an yaktumna mā khalaqa Allāhu fī arḥāmihinna in kunna yuʾminna bi-llāhi wa'l-yawmi al-ākhir* — "and it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs — if they believe in God and the Last Day." The wife who discovers the life in her womb may not hide her pregnancy from the husband — his fatherhood-right is inviolable, his capacity to restore the union binding upon him during the waiting: the clause thereby balances the earlier protections: as the husband cannot hold the wife at swordpoint by endless denial, so the wife cannot decamp with the secret of his child: both sides placed before God's own witness — with the clause *if they believe in God and the Last Day* opening in their domestic conduct at the exact moment where their most profound self-interest might tempt a concealment: the verse's religion does not preach in the clouded-abstractions but exactly at the point where the audit is most urgent: *if you believe* — then do not conceal.

**"Husbands Have Better Right to Restore"**

The verse then frames the mechanism of reconciliation: *wa buʿūlatuhunna aḥaqqu bi-raddihinna fī dhālika in arādū iṣlāḥā* — "and their husbands have better right to take them back during that — if they wish reconciliation": the *buʿūlah* — spouses/husbands — receiving the legal prerogative by which the restitution can be declared within the waiting without any further ceremony: any renewal of married life within the three-course span *counts as the union's resumption* — the wife's status lifts back to wife (with its dues and bed) on the spot of taking-back: with the Book's own qualification *in arādū iṣlāḥā* — *if their hearts have moved toward reconciliation* — forbidding the tactical grab-back by which the husband would take the road of *revocation merely to lengthen the waiting* (the cruelty prosecuted by 2:231's 'do not keep them to harm them'): the condition of *reconciliation intent* persisting as the ordinary proviso over all such re-joinings: God opening the door where re-joining is desired, *not where grinding is intended*.

**"The Like of What They Owe — and a Degree Over Them"**

The verse then enters the oft-recited mutual-rights doctrine whose balance the commentators read as the first comprehensive exposition of its kind in the desert-Arab world: *wa lahunna mithlu alladhī ʿalayhinna bi'l-maʿrūf* — "and [the wives] are owed obligations the like of those they owe — honorably" — *wa li'l-rijāli ʿalayhinna darajah* — "and men have a degree over them." Al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, and the whole tradition work the balance with measured clarity: (1) *mithl* — *the like*: the mutuality of the two rights as human-subjects is absolute — the wife's rights stand measured exactly by her duties: companionship answered by companionship, kindness by kindness, loyalty by loyalty, maintenance by grateful service of the household (and the school stores the beloved teaching of Ibn ʿAbbās at the verse's door: "I beautify myself for my wife, just as she beautifies herself for me"); (2) *darajah* — *a degree*: the husband's exceeding share the exegetes fix in the *spheres of responsibility-not-preference*: men carry the financial yoke, the defense of the house, and (by nearly all early views) the head-authority of the homestead: the degree is a *degree of duty-load and leadership*, not of essential worth: the depth of that rank being one of service — as the same Book everywhere describes the domestic headship as a charge to be carried, not a crown to be worn — and the God of the Book closes the entire mutual right-discourse with the dreadful balance-pair: *wa Allāhu ʿazīzun ḥakīm* — *Mighty, Wise*: the verse's entire legal harmony is His own calibrated governance — the balanced household nests not in male self-primacy nor in the denial of difference of office, but in God's own statutes: *and God is Mighty, Wise.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:229

> **Divorce may be retracted twice, then the husband must retain ˹his wife˺ with honour or separate ˹from her˺ with grace. It is not lawful for husbands to take back anything of the dowry given to their wives, unless the couple fears not being able to keep within the limits of Allah. So if you fear they will not be able to keep within the limits of Allah, there is no blame if the wife compensates the husband to obtain divorce. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, they are the ˹true˺ wrongdoers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Twice — and No More**

The verse opens the divorce-code's own life-meter: *al-ṭalāqu marratān* — "divorce is twice" — *fa-imsākun bi-maʿrūfin aw tasrīḥun bi-iḥsān* — "then retention honorably, or gracious release." The commentators understand its exact counting-system at once (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī consistent): the declarative divorce — a husband's spoken ṭalāq — may be *revoked twice*: first pronouncement — the waiting period (*ʿiddah*) begins, during which the husband may restore the marriage fruitfully; once restored, later pronouncement #2 — another ʿiddah — again revocable; but after the *third* time-assembled divorce declaration — it is final beyond revoking: hence *al-ṭalāqu marratān*: *twice* divorce-declarations with their waiting-periods cooled off and stand as recallable; then one of two righteous ways remains: *imsāk bi-maʿrūf* — retaining her *by recognized goodness* — marriage restored to viable tenderness; or *tasrīḥ bi-iḥsān* — releasing her *with gracious treatment* — divorce completed decently, without cruelty. The Book thus designs between the two sides a *built-in braking architecture*: two full scrubbing-cycles in which both have time to cool, weigh, consult, arbitrate (4:35's own arbiters being made available at such moments), repent, restore: the instantaneous fury-divorce given no fertile ground: the tradition reporting its own civilizational leap: jāhilī times knew no finality — a wife could swing forever between possession and abandonment — Islam *finishing* the third with decisive certainty, protecting the wife from such endless swinging back and forth.

**"Not Lawful to Take Back Aught"**

The verse then seals the bridewealth's status: *wa lā yaḥillu lakum an taʾkhudhū mimmā ātaytumūhunna shayʾan* — "it is not lawful for you to take back anything of what you have given them." The equity-explosion embedded in this rule must be felt against its occasion: at marriage, the bridewealth (*mahr*) passes from man to woman — as the woman's own holding: God's divorce-statute proclaims by fiat that a man may not recuperate it by divorce-pressure: the strategic temptation fixed in the school — a husband, weary of his wife, would sometimes resort to cruelty and humiliation — bringing her to such misery by insult or neglect that *she herself begged release* and offered back her mahr: such seizure is thus instantly declared *ḥarām*: the mahr keeps its course in her hand (save the routine bookkeeping exception at 2:237 for unconsummated unions), and a wife can never be *purchased out* of her own marriage by her husband's meanness: the school basing upon this clause its general protection-scrub of women's conjugal wealth across all centuries of Islamic law.

**Khulʿ — The Wife's Own Door**

Then comes the counter-balance clause of the whole Book of divorce: *illā an yakhāfā allā yuqīmā ḥudūda Allāh* — "except that the two should fear that they would not uphold the limits God has set": and thereby unfolds what the jurists know from its occasion of revelation — the *khulʿ* — the divorce at the wife's instance: the commentary recognizing the wife's own road: when *she* finds the marriage insufferable — the dread of adultery-temptation or sheer loathing wilting her duties as wife — she may go before the qāḍī, offer back her mahr (*al-fidyah* — ransom of herself), and be separated by due process: the Book inserting the wife's door *beside* the husband's — the symmetry already in its fibers — with the occasion-epitaph recorded by al-Ṭabarī and the others on nearly the verse's last word: Thābit ibn Qays's wife, in the famous account, coming before the Prophet complaining of her marriage ('I find no fault in Thābit either in character or religion — but I do not fancy him') — the Prophet confirming her: would you return him his garden (the mahr)? she said yes — and the Prophet divorced them (al-Bukhārī 5273 — the first khulʿ recorded in Islam): the wife's volume-agency in the household economy fully chartered in this verse — and its story itself enshrined at the foundation of every school of law in Islam.

**"These Are the Limits of God — So Transgress Them Not"**

The verse's ending repeats the warning-signature of the whole law-book: *tilka ḥudūdu Allāhi fa-lā taʿtadūhā* — "these are the bounds of God — transgress them not" — *wa man yataʿadda ḥudūda Allāhi fa-ulāʾika humu al-ẓālimūn* — "and whoever transgresses the bounds of God — those are the wrongdoers": the *ḥudūd* — literally *frontier-posts* — being the very term for God's perimeter-commands: the marriage crossing into divorce is not negotiable-free — it moves upon statutes: the wife not left among wolves; the husband not driven through live coals of statute-ignoring protest; but two doors, similarly named *retention in honor* or *release with kindness*, fitted to ride: and the warning's force lands on the word *ẓālimūn* — the very last word of the verse's own judgment: whoever crosses these bounds *is* a wrongdoer — not "will have behaved so as to seem" nor "might arguably be considered" but *is* — the present-tense substantive: the men of power and privilege put precisely where God wants them: under His law: not above it: and the wives of faith left safeguarded by rights the very Revelation itself defends.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:230

> **So if a husband divorces his wife ˹three times˺, then it is not lawful for him to remarry her until after she has married another man and then is divorced. Then it is permissible for them to reunite, as long as they feel they are able to maintain the limits of Allah. These are the limits set by Allah, which He makes clear for people of knowledge.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Divorce — Finality Restored**

The tally of verse 229 now completes itself: *fa-in ṭallaqahā fa-lā taḥillu lahu min baʿdu ḥattā tankiḥa zawjan ghayrah* — "and if he divorces her [the third time], she is no longer lawful for him until she has married another husband." The design's purpose dominates the commentators' (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī's) reading entirely: the barrier prevents the ever-cycling divorce of the jāhilī-house — man declares divorce, takes her back at the brink, declares again, takes back again — the entire year swinging between his whim and her despair, waiting-period after waiting-period stretching her youth into the cage of her vow: *al-ṭalāqu marratān* — *twice* — and no more: upon the third strike, the rope breaks once and for all: *he cannot marry her again*: the marriage is over: the woman stands free at last from the shade of his extreme volatility: and, in the Book's grim tenderness, may find the road into a new marriage — in which case, should the later marriage *also* end, the crossing-back road re-opens: *fa-in ṭallaqahā fa-lā junāḥa ʿalayhimā an yatarājaʿā*: *if her second marriage ends in divorce — no blame on both [former spouses] if they return to each other — if they deem they will keep God's limits*: the Book restoring even the most history-laden reunion upon the steady condition of God-consciousness: keeping God's bounds: a husband reconciled after his own folly thereby meeting the second chance of the same woman whom his demand for temperance has lost — with the condition *an yaẓunnā an yuqīmā ḥudūda Allāh*: both appraising seriously: *can we honestly keep God's commands in one another's home this time?* — the truth-sift of remarriage answered not by wish but by self-search within the hearing of God.

**The Ḥalālah Its Dreaded Guard-Rail**

The law that the third divorce's reunification depends upon an intervening marriage generated, in the practical regime of the early household, the infamous *taḥlīl*-business — men contracting another man to marry-and-release their ex-wife so that they could reclaim her — and the tradition records the Prophet's most devastating scorn upon the industry in the terms preserved by every fiqh-book on the subject (al-Bukhārī 5219; Muslim 1406 — the Prophet's declared word: *"the taḥlīl (the remarriage-facilitator) is refused: the temporary husband — al-mustaḥill — and the one for whom it is done are both cursed"*— the law, thus surgically restrained: the intervening marriage must be a real one — consummated in truth, lived in earnest, ended in earnest — never a hired cycle: the whole stratagem of temporary marriage seeking taḥlīl blocked by the Prophet's own voice: with the school thereby holding that the road back from the third divorce is guarded deeply enough that only fools and frauds attempt it: verse 230 making it plain that the barrier is part of God's protection of the wife: *three strikes and out — and a new marriage determines that the wife's youth shall not continue as the plaything of one man's tempers* — even if her heart still leans back toward him.

**Marked-Clear to People of Knowing**

And the verse seals its whole file with its own final signature of wisdom: *tilka ḥudūdu Allāhi yubayyinuhā li-qawmin yaʿlamūn* — "these are the boundaries of God — which He makes clear to a people who know": the seal's graceful twist — *li-qawmin yaʿlamūn*: *for a people WHO KNOW* — gift-wrapping the whole divorce-law as first-class intelligibility for those who know: the law indeed preserves its meaning — but only those who know see it: the man of knowing grasps in one reading the entire gracious architecture of the two divorces, waiting periods, third-time finalities, remarries-from-what-follows: God's statutes are plain enough — only for a people who know. The verse therefore ends its whole pillar of madinah-muslimah family-law upon its own high homily: **God draws the marks with clear hand — and upon you, O people of knowledge, lies both their preservation and their understanding**.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:231

> **When you divorce women and they have ˹almost˺ reached the end of their waiting period, either retain them honourably or let them go honourably. But do not retain them ˹only˺ to harm them ˹or˺ to take advantage ˹of them˺. Whoever does that surely wrongs his own soul. Do not take Allah’s revelations lightly. Remember Allah’s favours upon you as well as the Book and wisdom He has sent down for your guidance. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Do Not Keep Them to Harm Them"**

The code reaches the last screen of its cruelty-controls: divorce in progress is governed by the two clean channels — *keep her with honor, or release her with honor*: a third channel — invented in the jāhilī world as legalized wife-torture — is cut from the Book with its own decree: *wa lā tumsikūhunna ḍirāran li-taʿtadū* — "do not retain them in harmful fashion so as to transgress" — al-Ṭabarī transmitting the specific scheme: a husband divorces, watches her count down to the last day of waiting, declares the revocation — then divorces again — over and over, dragging her year after year through revolving waiting periods, never wife-enjoyed, never free. The verse's verb — *ḍirāran* — *by way of harm* — makes the *purpose* itself unlawful: not the legal act but the *menacing spirit in it*: and God's sentence falls: *wa man yafʿal dhālika fa-qad ẓalama nafsah* — "whoever does that — he has wronged *himself*": the classical commentators point out that God names the wronged victim not the wife but *the doing husband*: the boomerang always lands: the legal-cruelty pattern dissolves the doer: not only his wife's years but his own soul swelling with damn-worthy stripes: the one who plays with divorce-torture has thrown his own engine into the front-batch of his life — God's economy: his *own self* being the first sacrifice of it.

**"Take Not God's Signs in Mockery"**

The verse then steps up onto the heights of this entire divorce corpus: *wa lā tattakhidhū āyāti Allāhi huzuwā* — "and do not take the signs of God in mockery." The Book forbidding the very thing that law-games and word-play were designed for: the husband who declares divorce and then says "I jest"; the lawyer whose entire trade is the circumvention of the law's boundaries by technicalities; the husband who plays *now-you-have-her-now-you-don't* for a show: the commentators read the mockery-phrase with its full gravity at the side of 5:57 — "do not take those who take your religion in mockery and amusement as allies" — and 45:9 — "whatever signs of his Lord he learns of, he takes them in jest": the dragging of God's law into jest is the most dangerous progress of all: God's statutes *are God's signs* — to toy with them is to handle the Book as a plaything: and the verse's antidote sweeps in as always by the road of remembrance: *wa dhkurū niʿmata Allāhi ʿalaykum* — "remember God's blessing upon you" — *wa mā anzala ʿalaykum mina al-kitābi wa'l-ḥikmati yaʿiẓukum bih* — "and what He sent down upon you of the Book and Wisdom, exhorting you by it": gratitude (blessing) and mentoring (exhortation) the two-handled instrument for uprooting mockery: a man with the memory of God's blessings seared within him cannot transform those statutes into sport: the law's benevolent-author — God — being the same who *exhorts you thereby*.

**Remember, Fear, Know — The Triune Seal**

And the verse's signature closes upon the oldest teaching-triad of this sūrah: *wa-ttaqu Allāha* — *Reverence God* — *wa-ʿlamū anna Allāha bi-kulli shayʾin ʿalīm* — "and know that God of every thing is Knower": 2:231 thereby matching its seal's cadence to the very blanket-seal of the entire Book (2:282's own conclusion: *wa-ttaqu Allāha wa-yuʿallimukumu Allāh wa-Allāhu bi-kulli shayʾin ʿalīm*): every ḥadd-posting of God's family-boundaries built upon the double-pillar: reverence and knowledge: *fear Him* — and know He *knows everything*: including the inscription of every finding decision. The legal tradition's commentators have long dwelt upon the verse's final wisdom: God's *knowing everything* wins over each possible legal sport for every mockery stands already exposed before its Auditor, and every jest at God's signs stands known to God: the statute-book is closed with a bell that rings far into eternity: the Prophet's own most feared warning ever at cheating God's regulations —

> *"Whoever deceives is not of us"* — *man ghashshana fa-laysa minnā* (Muslim 101 — the Prophet's axiom of faith-full directness cited everywhere upon the divine prohibitions on law-gaming — cast over the whole catalogue of 2:226-232's household-boundaries)

And the verse departs having placed the three ancient rules of piety at the very pivot of its own displacement: *no harm-retention; no mockery of God's signs; remember God's blessings*: three columns upon the household-altar of God's people, raised forever.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:232

> **When you have divorced women and they have reached the end of their waiting period, do not prevent them from re-marrying their exhusbands if they come to an honourable agreement. This is enjoined on whoever has faith in Allah and the Last Day. This is purer and more dignifying for you. Allah knows and you do not know.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Do Not Hinder Them" — The Right Renewed**

The legal-table now goes to the divorced woman *after* her waiting period — the state of full release — and cuts the last shackle arising from outside the couple's own consent: *wa idhā ṭallaqtumu al-nisāʾa fa-balaghna ajalahunna fa-lā taʿḍulūhunna an yankiḥna azwājahunna idhā tarāḍaw baynahum bi'l-maʿrūf* — "and when you have divorced women and they have reached their term — do not hinder them from marrying their [former] husbands when they have consented with each other honorably." The commentators (al-Ṭabarī leading) explain the background-case: Maʿqil ibn Yasār's sister (named, in some versions of the report, Khāliṣah) was divorced by her husband; she waited out her ʿiddah; her former husband wished to take her back; and her brother — her legal guardian — refused consent, injured in pride as Muslim families' elders occasionally were: the verse descended upon that very situation: *do not prevent her*: after the waiting-period expires, the marriage-file belongs again to the couple themselves — subject, as the verse notes, *only to their free choice together* — *idhā tarāḍaw baynahum bi'l-maʿrūf*: *when they have mutually consented, in recognized rightness*: the twin foundations of every remarrying thereafter: *consent* — no forcing by either family; and *maʿrūf* — the honorable way: no secret reunion, no revenge-remarriage, no pretense of holiness: two hearts agreeing honorably before God: and the school thereby begins its timeless doctrine of the guardians' *non-veto by grudge*: the wālī (guardian) must not be a *ʿāḍil* — a hinderer of licit unions from personal spite or pride: the Prophet's own judicial practice codifying it:

> *"No marriage without a guardian" — whose counter-rule the jurists have anchored in verse 232's doctrine: guardianship exists to guard, not to bar: the Prophet's courts and the caliphs' having overruled spiteful guardians and given the ward into lawful marriage whence the grudge-hinderer blocked her* (Abū Dāwūd 2085 — with the school on the counter-side: al-Qurṭubī, al-Māwardī, and the fiqh manuals all drawing the exact rule of guardianship's non-obstruction from this very verse, for all the centuries of Islamic family law)

**"More Virtuous and Purer for You"**

The verse then closes with the whole legal-file's own direct appeal to God's intelligence *within* the believers: *dhālikum yūʿaẓu bihi man kāna minkum yuʾminu bi-llāhi wa'l-yawmi al-ākhir dhālikum azkā lakum wa aṭhar* — "this is what those of you are exhorted by — those who believe in God and the Last Day: that is *purer and more virtuous for you*" — *wa Allāhu yaʿlamu wa antum lā taʿlamūn* — "and God knows, and you do not know": the precise epistemic formula returning a third time in the sūrah (earlier at 2:216 and at 2:232 now) as the Book's great doctrinal bell: God knows what is best for His human creatures before their own intelligence arrives: the permission to remarry-to-the-ex is thereby justified as *azkā* — *more growth-nourishing* (from *zakā* — the same root as the purification-words of the sūrah) — and *aṭhar* — *purer* — both for the spouses' souls and for society's altar: the forbidden alternative — barring two consenting hearts — amounts to the householder's tyranny: the permission *it* is virtue/purity alike: since a loving reunion at the aftermath of a failed union is the very proof of a mercy-restoring kindliness between God-Fearing persons: and the Book seals the verse with the same twin-pillar of divine law that ended 2:216: *God knows — and you know not*: the statute is wisdom itself, and what men call a closed gate, God's wisdom proves an open gate.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:233

> **˹Divorced˺ mothers will breastfeed their offspring for two whole years, for those who wish to complete the nursing ˹of their child˺. The child’s father will provide reasonable maintenance and clothing for the mother ˹during that period˺. No one will be charged with more than they can bear. No mother or father should be made to suffer for their child. The ˹father’s˺ heirs are under the same obligation. But if both sides decide—after mutual consultation and consent—to wean a child, then there is no blame on them. And if you decide to have your children nursed by a wet-nurse, it is permissible as long as you pay fairly. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Full Years — The Nursing Statute**

The family-code turns now from the ex-spouses to their children — and the Book enshrines, at the heart of its longest sūrah, a law of the nursery itself: *wa'l-wālidātu yurḍiʿna awlādahunna ḥawlayni kāmilayni li-man arāda an yutimma al-raḍāʿah* — "and let mothers nurse their children — two full years — for whoever desires to complete the suckling." The commentators capture the verse's dual architecture immediately: the *ḥawlayn al-kāmilayn* — the two complete years — is both the *recommended fullness* of nursing and the *legal maximum of the nursing obligation* (the Shāfiʿīs and Ḥanafīs reading the two years as the legitimate interval; the Mālikīs' generalization to full-lactation being held at its broader margin): the two-year clause thereby protects the infant's full season of milk-dependence without abolishing the mother's ease at the border of weaning: and the clause *li-man arāda an yutimma al-raḍāʿah* — *for whoever wishes to complete* — sets the verse into its voluntariness-register instantly: the two years are the *completion*, not a forced imposition: mothers are not coerced into nursing against every circumstance (chronic illness, birth-proximity, or infant-dislike requiring wet-nursing all being provided for): but the *commendation* is final: two complete years if achievable: and the tradition of the Prophet's family-legacy passed on the preferred nursing practices of his own house-hold among the fathers of the sunnah (with the general lore of nursing-virtue expanding gently thereafter out of the communities of godly mothers).

**The Father's Full Charge**

The familial verse then branches into one of its most consequential provisions — the economic rule vaulted into the middle-verse of the ṭalāq-family-code: *wa ʿalā al-mawlūdi lahu rizquhunna wa kiswatuhunna bi'l-maʿrūf* — "and upon the father — his child's [parents' mothers] provision and clothing, in recognition." The Book's grammar is tenderest here: *mawlūd lahu* — *the one to whom the child is born* — the father: the nursing mother's entire provision and clothing being wholly the father's duty — *including in the period after divorce*: as 65:6-7 will later raise the same principle in its own chapter: "house them where you house, in means you can: do not suffer them through the child": the household therefore never ties the wife's nursing to her abandoned survival: while the marriage stands (or its after-divorce ʿiddah owns), her maintenance simply is: from God's law — and then the general-principle sails off the verse into all law: *lā tukallafu nafsun illā wusʿahā* — **"no soul is tasked beyond its capability"** — the verse's own general-word harbored by the schools into the universal legal rule of *fiqh*: no legal command may bear so heavily that its bearer's capability is extraordinary to it: the Book's Old Testament's similar-feeling grace granted the believers at 2:286 ("God charges no soul except to its ability") — and the family-code is already shaping it into settled juristic philosophy: *mutual*: no mother burdened beyond her capacity — no father beyond his: the very weight of the household's duties borne *both sides of its roof*.

**No Harm's Two Sides**

The verse then erects its protection-clause over both parents' and children's whole interplay — *lā tuḍārra wālidatun bi-waladihā wa lā mawlūdun lahu bi-waladihi* — "no mother is to be harmed on account of her child — nor father on account of his child": the critics' acute perception-speaking: the mother unable to be threatened "because of the child": neither by the husband's temper ("give up my son or starve"), nor by the household's pressures ("stop nursing this intrusive infant or depart"), nor by leverage over custody; and precisely determined upon the other side: the husband unable to stand grounds of lifting the mother's baby off her breast to hurt her: *the child's welfare is sacred against BOTH parents' hostage-tactics*: and the *wa ʿalā al-wārithi mithlu dhālik* — *and so equally for the heir* — extending the instruction immediately: if the father dies while the child keeps living, the father's heirs (the father's own father in the first instance — thenceforward his brother on duty) take up the same self-same provision: *the whole legal communion of the child*: her milk-payment, maintenance, needs all descending in inherited line upon whomsoever the father leaves behind in God's providence.

**Weaning by Consent and Consultation**

The verse's final clauses then descend to the domestic sphere of joint decision: *fa-in arādā fiṣālan ʿan tarāḍin minhumā wa tashāwurin fa-lā junāḥa ʿalayhimā* — "if the couple desire the weaning — by mutual consent and consultation — then no blame is upon them": the two rankest verbal-columns of the Holy Law of Muslim household: *tarāḍ* — *mutual consent*: not the husband's unilateral fiat and not the wife's: and *tashāwur* — *mutual consultation*: counseling together: this is the same consultative formula God plants at the root of the Muslim *shūrā*-tradition of public affairs at 42:38 — carrying the foundational ethic of governance into ordinary family-life as well: and the scholars also memorize the verse as Islam's founding legal text for the permissibility of *compensated wet-nursing*: *wa in aradtum an tastarḍiʿū awlādakum fa-lā junāḥa ʿalaykum idhā sallamtum mā ātaytum bi'l-maʿrūf* — "if you wish to have your children wet-nursed — no blame upon you — if you pay honorably what you give": the wet-nurse's wage — her milk's wage — declared lawful and made ordinary — and the whole vast institution of wet-nursing with its later extended-fiṭr lines of milk-kinship (the rules of *raḍāʿah*-suckling relations producing what the jurists call milk-maḥrams out of the wet-nurse's kinship-lines — the fiqh of suckling-relations, detailed in the substantial hadith-collections from the Prophet's own household practices (al-Bukhārī; Muslim's Book of Suckling) — all of this flowing out from the very last clause of verse 233: and the seal unleashes the benign formula of the prior verses: *wa-ttaqu Allāha wa-ʿlamū anna Allāha bi-mā taʿmalūna baṣīr* — *Reverence God — and know that of what you do, God is Seeing* — the sealing vision once more placing each household and each family — even the smallest, even the fatherless — beneath God's own unblinking regard, before the final counting of what you did.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:234

> **As for those of you who die and leave widows behind, let them observe a waiting period of four months and ten days. When they have reached the end of this period, then you are not accountable for what they decide for themselves in a reasonable manner. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Four Months and Ten Days — the Widow's Clock**

The family-law now turns to the hour every earthly marriage ends: not by oath or pronouncement, but by death: *wa-lladhīna yutawaffawna minkum wa yadharūna azwājan yatarabbaṣna bi-anfusihinna arbaʿata ashhurin wa ʿashrā* — "and those of you taken by death, leaving wives behind: let them wait by themselves four months and ten [days]." The commentaries mark this as the *ʿiddat al-wafāh* — the waiting period of widowhood: fundamentally longer than the divorce-ʿiddah of verse 228 (three courses); and the reason the school gives is of deep double-import: first, to establish with final certainty whether the widow carries his child — the pregnancy becoming by law the whole justice of the house — and if she is found pregnant, her waiting goes until the delivery itself (65:4's own rule: "those with child: their appointed time is when they lay down their burden"); and second — and the schools always note this with gravity — *the mourning is not merely a counting, it is a right of sanctity upon the deceased*: the woman's house quietly closes upon the incomparable station of the year of shared life, the months of the intimate body now lowering into the graveside, so that she spends those solemn months in prayer, in sorrow, in the honored laying-to-rest of what remains of the man she shared her years with. The custom of pre-Islamic Arabia, as the commentators record (Ibn Kathīr's account among them), required a widow to mourn *a full year* — living in the worst of her clothes, neither oiling her hair nor exposing herself to anything of adornment, confined in a hut of separation until the year ran out — its end marked by peculiar rites (flinging a piece of dung behind her, rubbing herself with an animal) whose twisted significance even the commentators cannot explain — an inhuman corset upon a woman already dealt more losses than one: God had removed both the year and its superstitious deformities: *four months and ten days* — then the mourning is done and the woman is free — free to do with the remainder of her life whatever honoring companionship God's law affords: the period measured out in God's own justice, with God's own mercy toward the woman.

**"No Blame Upon You in What They Do Themselves"**

The verse then returns with the same formula as upon the ordinary divorced women's *waiting* of 2:228 and the paupers' marriage releases: *fa-idhā balaghna ajalahunna fa-lā junāḥa ʿalaykum fīmā faʿalna fī anfusihinna bi'l-maʿrūf* — "and when they have reached their term — there is no blame upon you in what they do concerning themselves, in recognized rightness": the *junāḥ* — blame — now lifted from the male guardians in the household as well as from her: after the awaited *four months and ten days*, the widowed woman is *free*: free to choose for herself, free to grieve less and rebuild more, free to choose marriages and destinations without the council-of-elders' patience-limit: the schools of law debate the wait's fine-print — some elaborating *yatarabbaṣna bi-anfusihinna* into a fuller self-cloistering (staying home, laying aside perfume and ornament, as the hadith-reports depict her seclusion; al-Qurṭubī carrying this reading); others, with Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's measured plain sense, reading the phrase simply as *abstention from remarriage* until the term expires — but the consensus-light is plainest of all: *the widowed woman is subject to God's statute alone*: her household for these months is God's own guarded house — solitude-filled and mercy-covered — until the lawful term has run its quiet days; and after it, the Book plants its emancipation-clause: *no blame upon you in what they do concerning themselves — in the honorable way* — God's own seal upon the widow's newly-opened future.

**Truly Aware — the Sūrah's Pillar-Sign**

And 2:234 seals with its pillar-signature: *wa Allāhu bi-mā taʿmalūna khabīr* — "and God of what you do is Aware" — the same backward-star among all the seals in the whole chapter (2:234, 2:237, 2:242, 2:265, 2:271, 2:283's own self-same sigil) — reminding guardians and widows alike that while ballots of months count visibly upon the calendar, there is no shadow by which the house's inner doings are hidden from *khabīr* — the very knowledge of things hidden to each other: Allah aware of what the guardians counsel her, aware of what she entreats for herself, aware of both of their inner dispositions at her loss's very edge: the *Aware* — the same Name that ends verse 237 and returns as the pillar-signature of the whole sūrah's law-chapters, rolling onward as the Book nears its spending-laws below (261–274).

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:235

> **There is no blame on you for subtly showing interest in ˹divorced or widowed˺ women or for hiding ˹the intention˺ in your hearts. Allah knows that you are considering them ˹for marriage˺. But do not make a secret commitment with them—you can only show interest in them appropriately. Do not commit to the bond of marriage until the waiting period expires. Know that Allah is aware of what is in your hearts, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Intimating, Not Plighting**

The household's law of the waiting-wives is followed now by the law of the waiting-time suitors: *wa lā junāḥa ʿalaykum fīmā ʿarraḍtum bihi min khiṭbati al-nisāʾi aw akhnaytum fī anfusikum* — "and there is no blame upon you in *intimating* a proposal to these women — or keeping it within yourselves." *Taʿrīḍ* — *intimation, allusion* — is the word the commentators keep rendering with exactness: openness by way of *hint*, not of covenant: the suitor of a waiting wife may let his interest be known — and so perhaps *she* knows, and the whole house knows, that a door of the future stands ajar — but he may not yet go down to the marriage contract itself: the poets of classical Arabic furnished the jurists with the examples of the lawful mode: 'I hope to find a righteous woman,' 'I do not wish to marry any other woman,' 'when the term is fulfilled I shall knock upon a door I have in mind' — all of them licit intimation — while "promise me you shall marry me," "plight me thy troth now" — that is the step the verse comes to fence: *al-ʿaqd* — *the plighting — must wait until the term is fulfilled*: *lā tuʿāhidūhunna sirran illā an taqūlū qawlan maʿrūfan* — "plight not your troth with them secretly — save that you speak a recognizable honorable word": the ḥadīth of the suitor's own cautions the school holds by heart from the Prophet:

> *"Announce the marriage."* (Musnad Aḥmad — from ʿĀʾishah, graded ḥasan by the tradition's authorities — the Prophet's standing rule that the marriage-knot is proclaimed, not hidden: and the school voices its companion-rule from the most frequently quoted marriage-hadith of the books: *"there is no marriage except with a guardian"* — Abū Dāwūd 2085; al-Tirmidhī 1101: the whole sunnah's architecture of public knotting standing guard over verse 235's own teaching: intimation honorable, contract public, timing God's)

The verse then legislates the secret-pledge down as well: whispered agreements of later-marriage made within the ʿiddah are invalid to bind — both parties must await the completion of the appointed time — and the root-sense of the *ʿaqd al-nikāḥ* — the knotting of the marriage-tie — is expressly drawn out: *wa lā taʿzimū ʿuqdata al-nikāḥi ḥattā yablugha al-kitābu ajalah* — "and resolve not upon the marriage-knot until the term prescribed has been fulfilled": the *ajal* — the waiting-end — being in this law the Book's own erected fence: the passion of a longing suitor must open no door before God opens it: God alone closes the wait.

**"God Knows What Is Within Your Souls"**

The verse's deepest language then turns to the watcher within: *wa-ʿlamū anna Allāha yaʿlamu mā fī anfusikum fa-ḥdharūhu* — "and know that God knows what is within your souls — so beware of Him." The torchlight of the innermost human heart is here dedicated over the whole intimate-world of proposals and courtship: the Book has just spoken of intimations outwardly honorable; it now *locks the inner door*: *He knows what is within your souls*: every secret scheme the suitor nurses toward the waiting women of the house, every longing plot of waiting-term evasion, every whisper-plight of the hidden bed — God knows them: *so beware of Him*: the word *ḥdhar* — *take heed, beware* — standing placed just before the final seal: *wa-ʿlamū anna Allāha ghafūrun ḥalīm* — *know that God is Forgiving, Clement*: the darkness-seed within men's souls may twist around the whole wing of the marriage-gate — yet even such sins live within reach of pardon: He forgives them at knock: and His own long patience is placed — *ḥalīm* — that of repentance's hope never drying: so the sūrah of statute closes this household-register on the two sounds of God's own tolerance: *Forgiving, Clement*: *intimate longing — but the Book holds the longing within God's fence: so wait the appointed term; then marry whom you seek — sinlessly.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:236

> **There is no blame if you divorce women before the marriage is consummated or the dowry is settled. But give them a ˹suitable˺ compensation—the rich according to his means and the poor according to his. A reasonable compensation is an obligation on the good-doers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Dissolving the Unconsummated Marriage**

After the widow's passages, the code returns to the earlier edges of the marriage-bond — to the woman whom life had been promised but whose wedding was never consummated: *lā junāḥa ʿalaykum in ṭallaqtumu al-nisāʾa mā lam tamassūhunna aw tafriḍū lahunna farīḍah* — "there is no blame upon you if you divorce women — not having touched them, nor designated a bridewealth for them." The commentators are meticulous over the verse's exact juridical reach (compared at 33:49's own ruling of "O believers!
