When you marry believing women and then divorce them before touching them, you have no ʿiddah to reckon for them first — provide for them and release them with a fair releasing"): the verse opens the simplest track of legal release — the dissolution with the fewest complicating days: (1) when the marriage has been contracted — the woman now bearing her husband's covenant-name — but the union has not yet been consummated; and (2) when the bridewealth itself has never been designated — the marriage-contract-bearing any of its middle numbers for her yet unfixed: then the dissolution is *grace-shut*: she returns to her father's house as she left it: no ʿiddah to serve, no bridewealth's balance to settle — the mourning of separation ended upon her own front door's step. And the clauses favor the wife's own most forceful protection yet at every closed scene — the husband must not send her out with sign of being wronged: God commands: *wa mattiʿūhunna* — *provide for them* — a going-away provision that God made into *obligation upon the virtuous* — *ḥaqqan ʿalā al-muḥsinīn*: not a bare cleanliness but a *virtuous* departure: the divorced wife receives a parting-provision that matches the purpose: something with which to begin anew: some furniture still in her kit, some cloth upon her back, some provision in her purse — so that her word — *he parted with me decently* — survives within the household's memory, and not the contrary.

**Rich One's Riches, Poor One's Pence**

The clause — *ʿalā al-mūsiʿi qadaruhu wa ʿalā al-muqtiri qadaruhu* — "the well-off his capacity — and the straitened his capacity" — is the Book's own position-statement upon the economics of divorce-obligations which commentators (including al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī at this same verse) apply to the whole broad-knee of religious expenditure: God does not necessitate His law for all persons to equal amount: He sets the spendings free upon each person's scale: the wealthy man gives what befits his wealth; the scooped-poor man gives what suits his paucity: neither bankrupts the other: the Law measures effort, not inventory: what God's books thereafter bill is whether the rich man *acted richly* and the poor man *acted honorably*: a rich man's tack of half-hearted smallness upon the scale of his own treasury is a debit against him, while a poor man's scant portion given upon the scale of his own poverty is the greater glory: the Law's real traffic is in *scales-between-hearts*, not in dirhams-between-sacks: where the schooling detains each just: all men equal before God's large-hand, un-equal one to another in his inventory only.

**A Duty Upon the Muḥsinīn**

The seal-pair rings: *mutāʿan bi'l-maʿrūfi ḥaqqan ʿalā al-muḥsinīn* — "an honorable provision — an obligation upon the doers-of-good": *muḥsinīn* — the word the whole sūrah might be said to hinge upon at its far end (2:195's own pericope: *wa aḥsinū inna Allāha yuḥibbu al-muḥsinīn*: God's love being exclusively for the *virtuous* — as and its echo at 2:241's own *obligation upon the reverent*) — the whole school lands its doctrine upon this verse's splendid signature: the divorce-constitution of Islam was *not* a cold-facts register: the Book is everywhere accompanying the legal rule with the call to *taqwā*: *the legally-due is only the floor; upon the God-fearing falls the ceiling*: the statutes' floor being *no must* — the ceiling's flourish being *excellence*: and the sermon-education at this passage has long gone all the way with the Prophet's own etching upon the epochs of the ummah's divorces:

> *"The best of you* — *is he who is best to his family, and I am the best of you to my families"* (al-Tirmidhī 3895; Ibn Mājah 1977 — the Prophet's own standard for the whole household economy: the best in Islam is the best-mannered at the women-quarter, always cited beside verse 236's upon-the-good instruction)

And the Book's marriage's other-page (4:19's: *live with them honorably*) is the next-cage pair beside this one: if the marriages falter before consummation — then too, *your kindness*: the Qur'an's own gracious inheritance is what the Muslims call the family's *law-and-mercy*: *let your goodness outlast the marriage itself — even as she leaves the house*: and the whole way of the Book's law of goodness is summed here: virtue is measured not by the largest remedies but by the finest dispositions.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:237

> **And if you divorce them before consummating the marriage but after deciding on a dowry, pay half of the dowry, unless the wife graciously waives it or the husband graciously pays in full. Graciousness is closer to righteousness. And do not forget kindness among yourselves. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Consummation Half Measure**

The verse now takes up the middle-case verse 236 had not raised — the case when the bridewealth *had* been fixed at the contract, but the marriage was dissolved *before* consummation: *wa in ṭallaqtumūhunna min qabli an tamassūhunna wa qad faraḍtum lahunna farīḍatan fa-niṣfu mā faraḍtum* — "and if you divorce them before touching them — with a bridewealth already set — then half of what you designated": the exact doctrine-ledger of the school inscribed at this very verse (it also is restated at 33:49's own: "you have no ʿiddah to count": but the mahr-rule belongs at the half of this verse): since the covenant was not yet consummated, the schedule of entitlements reduces by half — one-half settling upon the wife — half returning to the husband: the rule of the Book running equally over all the schools of Sunni fiqh across all epochs *in this one specific case*: *half of the fixed bridewealth due, neither full zero nor full whole*: and the women and men of the entire ummah's thirteen centuries have stood under this named rule at every wedding-covenant, its calm equity a defense of the sūrah's own Great Legislation: God *divides* — the covenant contracted legitimately, then dissolved before the marriage-bed: *the bond's dissolver bears its cost — half — and the bond's bereaved keeps her half intact*: better-luck justice with God's own ledger: the binding firm yet merciful: then God immediately softens the whole file with the following clause of gratuitous release: *illā an yaʿfūna aw yaʿfuwa alladhī bi-yadihi ʿuqdatu al-nikāḥ* — "unless they forgo it — or whoever holds the marriage-knot in his hand forgoes": the verse's gallant permission of *waiving*: the one who holds the marriage-knot in hand — read by the earliest commentators as the husband himself, who may forgo the half he could lawfully reclaim, and by others as the wife's guardian acting with her consent — may *forgo*: the wife may waive her half entirely, or the husband waive his reclaim, so that one side releases what the letter of the law would have divided.

**"To Forgo Is Nearer to Reverence"**

The verse then threads the crown of ethics into its next clause — *wa an taʿfū aqrabu li'l-taqwā* — "and to forgo is nearer to reverence": *taqwā* — this sūrah's master-word from its opening page — receives here its most domestic application: reverence is realized in the willingness to let one's own *right* be waived: the one whom taqwā has trained oversteps justice toward forgiveness; he who may claim the half releases it; she who may claim the whole contents herself with grace — and every family files its hardest evenings under this one clause: *to forgo is nearer to reverence* — the verse's own testimony that the path of pardon is the shorter road to God.

**"Forget Not Bounteousness Among Yourselves"**

The verse's closing maxim the Muslim tradition has always treasured among its own family laws' blooming farewell: *wa lā tansawu al-faḍla baynakum* — "forget not bounteousness among yourselves": the Book hastening its pronoun-plural: *baynakum* — *among yourselves* — between men and women, husbands and ex-wives, kinsmen and kinswomen jointly: the command's own remembered-form duplicates at 2:282's own debt-writing clause — "let him not withhold what God has given him" — and 5:2's own charge of *helping one another to goodness and reverence*: the ethic of *faḍl* — *surpassing generosity* — that does the real long day's work beneath the letter of every law: God's statutes determine *the minimum*: God's Prophet teaches *the way: which is to outstep the minimum with good*: so the marriage's true instruction never ends in its statutes but in its generosity: *not to let yourself forget the bounteousness between you*: the verb *tansawu* — *forget* — is the lapse-word the tradition makes sure everyone who has sat in a torn-away household knows by heart: *forgetting* is precisely what happens between feuding families at the courtroom's edge: and God commands the believers here to ***not*** do precisely that: *do not forget the generosity among yourselves* — even while the divorce papers are signed — for the kinship-fabric woven by marriage is not dissolved with the knot's release. The very final clause seals: *inna Allāha bi-mā taʿmalūna baṣīr*: *God of what you do is Seeing*: The verse's entire family-history of lovers' quarrels and divorce-mutinies has proceeded under the eyes of the One Who Sees all you do: the *baṣīr* — *All-Seeing* — the darkness-visible name of God to whom every covenant-cruelty, every bountifulness between families, reveals itself — with the sūrah of statutes resting at the end upon the same humble, God-watching Witness-signature that closes many of its law-verses: *God sees whatsoever you do.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:238

> **Observe the ˹five obligatory˺ prayers—especially the middle prayer—and stand in true devotion to Allah.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Amid Divorce — Prayers**

The household's long legal chapter closes not with statutes' signatures but with the nation's own comfort-cluster — a sudden, astonishing shift the tradition marks as the sūrah's own heart-movement: after the thorniest files of marriage, divorce, widows, nursing-mothers, and bridewealth — God calls: *ḥāfiẓū ʿalā al-ṣalawāti* — "be mindful of your prayers" — *wa'l-ṣalāti al-wusṭā* — "and the middle prayer" — *wa qūmū li-llāhi qānitīn* — "and stand before God, devout." The masters of the tafsīr have always noted the astonishing placement: *why does the verse of prayer come here — after the law of women and divorce, perhaps the most painful chapter of all family law?* — the spiritual commentators give the answer the old masters preserved (al-Rāzī's dimension, al-Qurṭubī's own): the heart that has just trafficked in household-rifles and matrimonial-angst needs now its strongest mooring: the *ṣalāh* — the prayer — which is the pivot-pin of every Muslim life: the believer's daily appointment with God himself: God places it now amidst His most difficult law-verses as if to whisper to the followed: *do not swallow too much of this legal world: your salvation is standing before Me, not the intricacies of retained mahr and wait-moons*: and the injunction *ḥāfiẓū* — *be mindful, guard, sustain* — covers the attendee's entire fiduciary-leash: hold your prayers not merely in time but in heart, in standing, in their purpose: and with the recitation of devout obedience *wa qūmū li-llāhi qānitīn* — the well-known invocation for the verse within its many century-reading of 2:116's own recitants ("to Him is devout whatsoever is in the heavens and the earth") and 4:34's obedience: *qānitīn* — *obedient, striving in prolonged standing before God*: — *Here is the verse of the whole Book for all households where the Beholder of family-dramas is already known — the God whose own summons at the middle prayer ends all arguments and decides all arbiters.*

**The Middle Prayer — Its Endless Veneration**

At the heart of the verse stands one of the Book's most debate-inspiring appurtenances: *al-ṣalāt al-wusṭā* — *the middle prayer*: and the commentators' dossier of its alternate identifications has become a small classical discipline of its own: (1) it is the ʿaṣr — the middling of the five daily prayers in standing-order, and the one whose lightness is most steadfastly touted in the sunnah as the prayer the hypocrites find most painfully heavy (Muslim 622 reporting the Prophet's famous phrase: "if they knew what [rewards] are in the night and midday [Ṣalāt al-fajr wa al-ʿaṣr] they would come even crawling"); (2) the maghrib — the spiritual middle of the whole prayer-cycle dividing day from night — with the 5-prayer total (its tripod-argument: Fajr, Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, Maghrib, ʿIshāʾ: the third sits exact-center); (3) the fajr — the prayer which in the darkness stands as threshold: but the whole tradition turns in its majority to the first reading (Bukhārī 2728 from ʿAlī: "on the Day of the Trench [al-Aḥzāb, A.H. 5] the Prophet kept telling them: *they kept us busy from our middle prayer — may God fill their homes and graves with fire!*" — the Prophet's own verse-usage pinning the middle prayer to al-ʿaṣr's mantle-creed); (4) and the council-others named it the company's Friday-ṣalāh etc. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr give their own carefully-measured verdicts the school ever since sustains: *the identity is an invitation to watchfulness, not to uniform conviction: the prayer of the middle is singled out among the five and wherever* — *the verse thereby accomplishes its widest end: all five prayers are appointed to be guarded, and the one most at risk — the one most quietly forfeited in excuse-laden souls — is singled out for double-vigilance*: and the tradition's own administration brings the whole economy into present-mandate for every Muslim heart, then and now:

The elders' wisdom beside this verse has always been of one tenor: the prayer most easily lost in the day's crush is the one the Day of Judgment will weigh most visibly — and the slippage of a single day's prayers loosens the stitches of whole weeks.

**Standing Devout — Qānitīn**

And the third command lands the vote over the whole: *wa qūmū li-llāhi qānitīn* — "and stand before God as devout ones." *Qunūt* — the standing-devotion whose name also ends at verse 238's own root — is carried glossed-with-hāmilī within: standing upright in God-ness for whatever the flesh attempts: quietness of the limbs, lowering-of-the-gaze, still-hushed intentness before your Lord — the Prophet's own standing example, documented in the books of sunnah that prayer short of this is not prayer but empty form: and with that word the sūrah's household chapter closes upon its remedy for every burdened soul: stand before God — *qānitīn*: the very opening-phrasing of the Fātiḥah's own prayer-petition-forecourt: *while divorce's file and widow's clock rent their nights, the Five Standing-Crowns stand constant before the smitten household* — and the well-known hadith of the Prophet upon the middle prayer's special burden rolls through the floor of hell severest fate:

> *"On the day of the Trench the Prophet kept saying: they kept us busy from the middle prayer — may God fill their bellies and their graves with fire."* (al-Bukhārī 2931; Muslim 627 — of the Prophet, at the encampment of the Trench against the besieging foot and horse of Quraysh — the situation where the middle prayer was suppressed by enemy-press and the Prophet's own exasperated sentence upon them inscribed in sacred emphasis)

— and thereby the most ancient, ever-living warning of the whole Middle-Prayer-Revelation: *the middle prayer sees fit to march before the legions at prayer themselves*: no victory-maneuvre, no mahr-argument, no inheritance gate, no household-quarrel, no work-deadline, no marriage-bed blocks the prayer's own settled morning and middle-duty: *guard the prayers — and the middle prayer — and stand devout before God.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:239

> **If you are in danger, pray on foot or while riding. But when you are safe, ˹take time to˺ remember Allah for teaching you what you did not know.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Prayer Under Fire**

The very next verse after the guarding-command now flexes its strength over the battlefield: *fa-in khiftum fa-rijālan aw rukbānan* — "and if you are in fear — then afoot or mounted" — *fa-idhā amintum fa-dhkurū Allāha kamā ʿallamakum mā lam takūnū taʿlamūn* — "then when you are secure, remember God — as He taught you what you did not know." The commentators read it as the exemption for the terrorized: in danger — war's approach, ambush, persecutions from which flight is forced — the formal prayer need not halt you in full prostrations: *rijālan* — *afoot*: pray while walking; *rukbānan* — *mounted*: pray still sitting astride your horse or camel; the heart's direction mattering and not the body's compass — the jurists unfolding the complete fear-prayer methods (4:101-102 gives the full battlefield ordinance, detailing alternate ranks, arms kept, cycles shortened, sentinels of God literally broken into pairs around the praying community — the martial-ṣalāh even in formal assemblies where the imam becomes also watch-post): prayer under God is never to be shed: even the fighter's modest ride rides his ṣalāh with him: the verse building the spiritual principle that never abandons the servitor at any suffering cost: *the ṣalāh waits for the flight to stop — the ṣalāh never stops first*: and the panic of plausible fear soothes into the limiting rule: on foot or upon horse: pray nonetheless *however short, however angled toward the qiblah or away* — even escape cannot excuse the man's interior voyage from surrender to God almighty.

**"When You Are Secure, Remember God"**

Then the returning-covenant clause pulls to mind exactly what fear had negotiated through its short-suspension: *fa-idhā amintum fa-dhkurū Allāh* — "but when you are safe — *then* remember God": once the danger is past the prayer of quiet-heart re-emerges — no more the battlefield's truncated nod-and-bow but the complete standing, prostrating, long-term praise of the true man of God: the verse's grammar building the precise legislative ethic of the sūrah: danger's exemption is *temporary sacrifice-school*: security resumes *full obligation*: and the remembrance function folds: *kamā ʿallamakum mā lam takūnū taʿlamūn* — "as He taught you what you did not know": the *kamā* of the same form as 2:151's verbatim-answer and 2:198's *kamā hadākum* response: the divinely-born schooling in which the Prophet's mode of prayer — *ṣallū kamā raʾaytumūnī uṣallī* — *"pray as you have seen me pray"* (al-Bukhārī 631 — the yardstick-hadith the school always cites in the registers of fear-ruled practice: the Prophet's own context being that his verbal phrasing here taught them prayer's crib like every other block of ummah's use) — is the whole teaching-bond: *pray as He taught you — what you never knew — so the danger-pause that constrained it shows God's mercy; and the safety-erection that returns it shows God's constancy*: and the whole field of combat fades back beneath its background: prayer stands as a solitary lamp before the face of the Victorious God.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:240

> **Those of you who die leaving widows should bequeath for them a year’s maintenance without forcing them out. But if they choose to leave, you are not accountable for what they reasonably decide for themselves. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Widow's Year — Deathbed Testament**

The Book now supplements the widow's statute with a second rule — this one laid upon the dying husband himself, not only upon the widow: *wa-lladhīna yutawaffawna minkum wa yadharūna azwājan waṣiyyatan li-azwājihim matāʿan ilā al-ḥawli ghayra ikhrāj* — "those of you taken by death, leaving wives — let them bequeath for their wives a provision for the year — without expulsion": the dying husband is thus planted with a deathbed-obligation: by his last will (*waṣiyyah*) he must grant the wife he leaves behind a whole year's maintenance within his home — *without being turned out* — no heirs may push her from his walls empty the hour his soul ceases; and the Book disposes at once of the *if they leave* clause: *fa-in kharajna fa-lā junāḥa ʿalaykum fīmā faʿalna fī anfusihinna bi'l-maʿrūf* — "if they [the widows themselves] depart — no blame upon you in what they do concerning themselves honorably": the widow who declares *herself* fit to exit the late husband's roof before the year's own end releases the heirs from further claims: her autonomy is immediately restored: one may thus see in the verse a second cushion — the protecting year — placed behind the four-months-and-ten ʿiddah of verse 234: even after the mourning-term ends, her housing is guaranteed through the whole year: and the year stands — mercy upon mercy — between the waiting of 2:234 and the utterly-different community-power of the property tests in this one.

**Abrogated or Standing?**

The commentators have much debated whether verse 240's year-bequest was abrogated by 2:234's four-month-ten or by 4:12's inheritance-shares (the widow receiving her fixed portion from the estate) — and al-Qurṭubī together with the majority's own peace-keeping reading finds no need to sever the verse from speaking efficacy: the two rules work along two axes and not upon the same one: (1) 2:234 fixes the *waiting* term after death in which she may not remarry; (2) 2:240 fixes the *dwelling-and-sustenance* term guarding her house-occupation through a whole year even beyond the short ʿiddah when the four months are done — the widowed woman spending her first two-and-a-half months in ʿiddah within the house — and the remaining months under the same sat of the house by bequest — the two statutes stepped-following into the same decree: and even the hadith's own teaching of "no bequest for an heir" (already established at 2:180) leaves room here since the widow's year of shelter is often spoken of as a *right* more than a *portion* of the inheriting: the juridical manuals state the balance plainly: *the year's shelter comes by testament — and beyond it, the widow may also claim her inheritance-share wherever one falls due*: and many schools read the verse as still-standing legislation — and the Book seals the matter with *wa Allāhu ʿazīzun ḥakīm*: *and God is Mighty, Wise*: the mighty God who knows the narrow window of the first year of widowhood — whose wisdom makes room for women in the darkness of bereavement without abandoning their house.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:241

> **Reasonable provisions must be made for divorced women—a duty on those mindful ˹of Allah˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Divorce-Gift — Matāʿ**

In a single sentence-unit of seven Arabic words, the sūrah seals its divorce-cycle with the capstone of departure: *wa li'l-muṭallaqāti matāʿun bi'l-maʿrūfi ḥaqqan ʿalā al-muttaqīn* — "and for divorced women: an honorable provision — an obligation upon the reverent." The commentators observe the verse's own precision: the *matāʿ* — *provision, consolatory-gift* — is God's farewell-bestowal upon a woman whose marriage is severing: she may not be divorced empty-handed: the farewell-settlement itself may consist of clothing, furniture, provisions for her road upon the households' scale-inhabitants: its value calibrated to the man's means (v. 236's own standard: wealthy-by-means, straitened-by-means): and the verse names the obligation the *upon the God-conscious*: *ḥaqqan ʿalā al-muttaqīn*: the very domain this sūrah hewed its whole covenant upon: *taqwā* — the men of reverence fulfill it from the inside out: the dissenting commentators do differ upon whether the clause widens to *every* divorced woman, or takes on its face only the wives *divorced before consummation* — the verse-236 file — but the most carefully-weighted reading (al-Ṭabarī's own) is to read it in its broad sweep: every divorced one: for whom the dissolved bond was never sated fully: which Islam thereafter recognized as the standing legal claim whenever the exits open — the rule its blessing upon the broken household: *farewell with kindness, covenant with integrity — and a parcel of provision at the threshold*.

**Honorably — Within the Language of Goodness**

The verse's middle-adverb is the now-customary *bi'l-maʿrūf* — *in recognized honorableness* — the same common-standard the whole sūrah has now deployed at every corner of its divorce and its marriage-legislation: no bitter release: no revenge-questions: no flinging the woman toward indigence nor toward beggary: God's whole manual of marital separations runs upon the twin floorboards: *what the school calls *justice* — and the *maʿrūf* — *the decency the Arabs' neighborhoods would recognize*: the law binds where ethics bind: the believer handling the largest domestic failure of all — the broken marriage-covenant — is to handle it *honorably*: *with dignity for the woman, with decency toward the children, and with peace toward God above*: and the verse's end-point *ḥaqqan ʿalā al-muttaqīn* — an obligation upon the God-fearing — places the entire statute within the ancient taqwā-deed family of the whole sūrah: the openness-promise inscribed at verse 2 (a guidance for the reverent) returns at the day's closing here: the manual of family laws and the ordnance of divorce are intrinsically measured in every corner and hilltop *by taqwā*: the fear of God lift-caring them all: *and that obligation — upon the reverent — settles the whole revolving door of the Book's longest sūrah's domestic-legislation:* God's sealed statutes between His servants and His own door-post: *a gift of honor to the departing wife — owed by every divorcing husband among the believers*.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:242

> **This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so perhaps you will understand.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Thus" — The Book's Hermeneutic Key**

One sentence of five Arabic words seals the thirty-five-verse treasury of the sūrah's legislation: *kadhālika yubayyinu Allāhu lakum āyātihi laʿallakum taʿqilūn* — "thus does God make His signs clear for you — that you may understand." The commentators attend to the *kadhālika* — *thus* — with exact discipline (as all the āyāt-thematic group closings require): its demonstrative diction points back to the whole preceding corpus — the fast, the ḥajj, the rites of war, of marriage, oaths, divorce, nursing, widowhood, bridewealth, and prayer — and declares that *all of it*, command by command, has served the one agency of *tabyīn*: *making clear*: God has not hidden His purposes in riddles; He has *laid His signs out before the reflecting mind*, specifying *ḥudūd* (limits) precisely so that no man pleads confusion at the Court of His reckoning: and this refrain — planted here after the family-laws, again after the Hagar-and-garden parables at 2:266, again at 3:103 (the covenant-rope), 5:89 (the oaths), and through the rest of the Book — is the Qur'an's own standing disclosure-statement: *I give you not merely rulings but readable signs*: the Law itself is sacred pedagogy, and every statute a text for study.

**Signs of Law, Signs of Mind**

The deeper value of the verse rests in what it discloses of how the believing mind is to read legislation: each rule was a *sign* — not arbitrary fiat but disclosed wisdom. Consider the family-laws just traversed: oaths could not be made shields against goodness; widows could not be imprisoned in year-long superstitions; a mother's two years of milk carried mutual consent at its heart; neither mother nor father was to be harmed through the child; forbidden things pointed always to greater things (*the sin is greater than the benefit*); and every statute terminated with Names — Hearing, Knowing, Forgiving, Clement, Mighty, Wise — each Name an earmark of the rationale under the letter: the Book has been *teaching the understanding*, verse by verse, by the placement of its Seals: and 2:242 gathers all of these signatures into a programmatic statement for everything yet to come: *the laws of God are not mere fences, they are lamps: a fence to keep you in, a lamp to show you why* — the two being one and the same *āyah*.

**"That You May Understand" — The Opening of Reason**

The fruit-word of the refrain — *taʿqilūn* — *that you may understand/comprehend* — belongs to the sūrah's own ordered series of heart-mind terms: remember (*tadhakkarūn*, 2:221), reflect (*tatafakkarūn*, 2:219, 2:266), perceive with the kernel-mind (*ulī'l-albāb*, 2:179, 2:197), and now *taʿqilūn* — the plain, strong verb of intellectual comprehension. The tradition has never missed what the sequence preaches: the Book will not have a community of *hearers who do not think* — the worst indictment of the whole sūrah (2:171: deaf, dumb, blind — they do not understand, *lā yaʿqilūn*) belongs to those who received signs without understanding; and the very phrases God multiplies for its believing hearers are the phrases of mind: *so that you may understand* — that Judaism's own sort of frightful hearing-without-comprehending be cut at its roots among the believers. And it is precisely — as thousands of commentators, preachers, and Sufis have paused to note — at the *lawbook's* densest point that God issues the understanding-rubric: not in a sermon about nature's wonders, but after statutes about mahr-halves and ʿiddah-days: because it is *there*, in the minutiae, that the misconception threatens the community — that someone may treat their Lord as a tax-collector of arbitrary codes rather than a Teacher of luminous signs; and because there, in the micro-statute, the great patterns of the whole Divine Law are most visible: proportionality, mercy, limits, consent, forgiveness: so that the believers *may understand* — understanding being built, clause by clause, by statute upon statute, until the whole vision of God's Law stands before them, complete, in the full noon of its wisdom.

The verse therefore functions as both close and portal: closing the family-law book — and opening the great parable-history of Tālūt and Jālūt (2:246–251), the Ark, the Ark's appointment, the river of drinking, Goliath's fall — whose lessons are *the same understanding now carried through narrative*: God never ceases manifesting His signs: He clarifies them by statute (vv. 163–242) and by saga (vv. 243–251), until, at the End of the End, the man of the transformed heart quite simply *understands*.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:243

> **Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who fled their homes in the thousands for fear of death? Allah said to them, “Die!” then He gave them life. Surely Allah is ever Bountiful to humanity, but most people are ungrateful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Thousands Who Fled Death**

The sūrah now passes from courtroom and prayer-niche (vv. 234–242) to the great transition-parable of mortality: *a lam tara ilā alladhīna kharajū min diyārihim wa hum ulūfun ḥadhara al-mawt* — "have you not seen those who departed their homes by the thousands, fearing death?" The commentators explain the ancient incident (al-Ṭabarī and the classical accounts from the People of the Book, with the cautiousness proper to such transmissions): a community of the Children of Israel — some say of the city of Dawardān, others of the tribes more generally — fled an outbreak (plague or war, the reports differing) in order to escape death, moving by the thousands out of their own quarters into God's broader plains: and the Book depicts their flight's grim irony with its customary terseness: *fear of death* never protects against death: *their fleeing was the very road to their death*: for God said to them *mūtū* — **"Die!"** — and they died: the Book compressing the whole mass-annihilation into one word of one syllable: no battle recorded, no plague named, no protracted hospital of days — the divine order's abrupt sovereignty over everything called alive: *He said: die — and they died*: and then the almost-immediately-following astonishment: *thumma aḥyāhum* — **"then He revived them."** The majority of the commentators (with al-Qurṭubī's report recounting the fuller detail) tell of a prophet sent to them thereafter — often named in the transmitted material — who prayed over their strewn bodies, and God quickened them: thousands resurrected upon a single call: a second entire nation drawn from death to life in the eyes of their contemporaries — a standing proof for any age that God's government holds both death's dispensation and resurrection's in the same hand.

**Two Doctrines Most Pressed Upon the Madinese**

The commentators (al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr) unfailingly set out the doctrines the parable was sent into Madinah bearing: (1) *death is not escaped by flight* — the age-old lie of every coward — and the fleeing of the thousands brought them precisely to their fore-appointed meeting: God said *die*: the deliverance of the city and its sin-glutted shelters could not shelter the ones addressed; and the Prophet's own plague-counsel in the collections preserves the same principle in its Islamic administration:

> *"If you hear of a plague in a land, do not go into it; and if it breaks out in a land where you are, do not leave fleeing from it."* (al-Bukhārī 5729; Muslim 2219 — the Prophet's established quarantine-rule before any medical discovery — its theological root-thesis being the same: deadline and date are God's: man does not escape the decree by geography)

and (2) *resurrection is shown at arm's length to every doubter*: the Book closes the sūrah's precedents already with the valley-of-dry-bones whispers (2:243; many mufassirūn here connect the account to Ezekiel 37's image of God reviving a valley of dry bones while the commentaries note care-taking that the biblical account does not explain how the bones came there — the Qur'anic account's own center being upon God's command above all chronology): the revival of thousands in one instant isforeshadowing-piece for your own age: the God who decreed *mūtū* can equally decree *ḥyā*: He who caused them to die revived them: and behind the revived nation stands the revived world: the Day of Resurrection itself foreseen by sign in this earlier moment: *wa inna Allāha la-dhū faḍlin ʿalā al-nās* — "truly God is Possessed of Bounty for mankind": even the ones who fled were brought back: the whole episode limned to make men *thankful* — *wa lākinna akthara al-nāsi lā yashkurūn* — "but most of mankind do not give thanks": God's benefit pushed between their own institutions of protection-and-escape: the very breaths that men use to flee death are loaned to them by the God they ought to thank: and they still do not thank Him: the verse book-ending the truth all men in their two stances: *God gives — God raises — and they do not give thanks* — the whole seedbed of gratitude and in gratitude etched over one two-word sentence of God: *die* — and *rise again*.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:244

> **Fight in the cause of Allah, and know that Allah is AllHearing, All-Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Command After the Resurrection-Lesson**

Set hard against the dry-bones tableau of death's flight and divine revival, the Book converts its parable into an imperative: *wa qātilū fī sabīli Allāhi wa-ʿlamū anna Allāha samīʿun ʿalīm* — "so fight in God's way — and know that God is Hearing, Knowing." The *wa-qātilū* with its fastened *wa* — *and/so* — clinches the parable's transition: having seen that neither the fleeing thousands nor the stricken nor the revived lie beyond His disposal, the community is told to place its own peril where it belongs: *fight*: since death is not theirs to prevent, fear of death is not theirs to obey. The commentators handle the command's scope with their care-faced discipline (al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī): part of the early teachers hear it specifically as addressed to the revived of verse 243 — *they* were told to fight, having just died and returned; but the majority read the direct-address shape of the sentence as a standing ordinance upon the believers: *and fight in God's way* — the *jihād* clause transported beyond any battle of that day into the requirement of the whole future ummah: and the second clause *in the way of God* holds the whole ethical bracket already laid down at 2:190 in place: fight where God's road directs — and *not* where revenge and lust pitch their battle-icons.

**Hearing and Knowing — Under God's Guarantee**

The seal-pair, third-planting of these two names in the chapter already (v. 181, v. 227, here), arrives precisely in the fighter's hour: *samīʿ* — Hearing: the vows made beside the standard, the cry of the injured, the prayer against the siege — all heard; *ʿalīm* — Knowing: the motive trembling beside the lance — all known: the battle-field is not a place outside the two Names' jurisdiction: and the warrior thereby stands doubly armed: he obeys God's command in the field, and he stands under God's audition in the field. The spiritual commentator tradition (al-Qushayrī's, Abū Ḥayyān's own field-journals of any spiritual reading) already generalizes the command further along: since the *qitāl* of God includes the *jihad al-nafs* — the war upon the lower self — its readers of every age hear the verse's summons in the battlefield of their own striving: *fight your own appetites in God's way — and know He hears what you whisper when you resist them, and knows what slips past your defenses even *you* do not name* — the Names reverberating in either case: the mortal fight of the body and the mortal fight of the soul, both being lodged under the same Watchtower.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:245

> **Who will lend to Allah a good loan which Allah will multiply many times over? It is Allah ˹alone˺ who decreases and increases ˹wealth˺. And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Who Shall Lend God?" — The Astonishing Question**

The Book now casts its begging-question in an utterly unparalleled figure — *man dhā alladhī yuqriḍu Allāha qarḍan ḥasanan* — "who is the one who will lend God a goodly loan?" — *fa-yuḍāʿifahu lahu aḍʿāfan kathīrah* — "and He will multiply it for him many times over." *Qarḍ ḥasan* — *a goodly loan, a beautiful lending*: God — the Self-Sufficient — receives: His servants become the creditors: the theologians throughout tafsīr chronicle this as part of what later anthroposophy named the Book's *humanizing* of the relationship to drive zeal: since no philosophy's God can borrow, the metaphor's own audacity is itself a teaching: God stands behind every good deed as its surest deposit-bank: the giver gives — God takes into custody — God *multiplies*: returns with vast recovery: *yuḍāʿif*: as the Hadith-qudsī's own God of pledge: *"O son of Adam! Spend, and I shall spend upon you"* (al-Bukhārī 5352; Muslim 993) — and as in 6:160: "whoever brings a good deed shall have ten times its like" — the multiplied returns fully guarded: and between 2:41 ('do not sell My signs at a trifling price') and here — *lend*: the Book holding out at this third stage of its little sūrah's *charity* — the most majestic assurance of the whole canvas of donative deeds: *spend — be cheerful — give into God's Own Custody*: the formula ringing the sum while receiving no payback date-save requests.

**Withholds and Outstretches**

The verse finishes its petition with the rhythmic cadence of all heaven's two-terms of provision: *wa Allāhu yaqbiḍu wa yabsuṭu* — "and God *withholds* and *outspreads*" — the verbal-polarity of the two equal-sized divine hands, building several threads of the chronicle at once. In the plain seeing of the school: He tightens *rizq* — sustenance — and He enlarges it, keeping kings and beggars on the same leash of providence — the period your purse had money does not prognosticate the period your purse will have money: hand over — hand withheld — no possession resides permanently in its owner's bank; nothing created endures unless the Giver sustains it: and in the marvelous development the Sufi tradition always carries, *qabḍ* and *basṭ* become the pair of the dread-and-delight of the mystics' states: the constriction of the heart by fear and the expansion by hope: both are His measure: as al-Qushayri’s salaf-register had it, "these two states alternate in the heart like the night follows the day": God's mercy is measured *between* the two — for people of the purified heart, His majesty comes in withholding, His beauty in outspreading (Abū Ḥayyān's recording of the readings at this verse). And the last clause — *wa ilayhi turjaʿūn* — "and unto Him you shall be returned" — repaints the whole thought of the verses just past: the life-lender returns to his true Creditor: every rizq owed; every deposit repaid; the Day of the solemn resurrection itself is the day when these loans are redeemed — all will find their Hand-Givers at God's own gate.

**The Verse the Whole Sūrah Rises From**

The tradition has always preserved verse 245 as its own hub among the talking-pairs of the sūrah — a direct sister to 2:261's manifold-multiplication of the grain-seed (seven hundred for one), and to the charity-parables that follow it — readying the whole sūrah's astonishing sequence of progressive charity-verses, and to His own calling at 64:17: "if you lend God a goodly loan, He will multiply it for you and forgive you." And the Prophet of Allah's own ḥadīth applies the register at its charter-layer:

> *"Charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire"* (al-Tirmidhī 614 — in the long series of the Prophet's own charity-verses of blessing — the dousing-flame analogy standing forever behind the sūrah's devoted charity-explosion of verses 261-274: charity not only *multiplies,* it *extinguishes*)

— so the verse stands eternally calling: *who shall lend to God? Release your purse-string: though all abides in His custody forever — no other bank's interest is worth one touch of His when the Great Returning strikes — and upon Him your eyes will rest* — with the returning alive to the very God's gate.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:246

> **Have you not seen those chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses? They said to one of their prophets, “Appoint for us a king, ˹and˺ we will fight in the cause of Allah.” He said, “Are you not going to cower if ordered to fight?” They replied, “How could we refuse to fight in the cause of Allah, while we were driven out of our homes and ˹separated from˺ our children?” But when they were ordered to fight, they fled, except for a few of them. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Elders' Demand for a King**

The sūrah now mounts the greatest war-and-state parable carried over to the Madinese from the annals of the earlier prophets — recited, as the commentators note, with its strong converse-reflection upon Madinah's own new congregation (the same Prophet being asked, in another context, for authority to enlist; the same belatedness of faith upon the muster-roll): *a lam tara ilā al-malaʾi min banī isrāʾīla min baʿdi mūsā* — "have you not seen the assembly of the Children of Israel, after Moses?" — *idh qālū li-nabiyyin lahumu ibʿath lanā malikan nuqātil fī sabīli Allāh* — "when they said to a prophet of theirs: raise up for us a king — that we may fight in the way of God." Al-Ṭabarī and the tradition's classical transmitters identify the prophet as Samuel — *nabiyy* unnamed in the Book but comfortably read into his history from the mourners' corresponding reports of the tribe of Israel's own Bible (1 Samuel 8:19-20 once matching it phrase by phrase in the whole thrust: "we too will have a king over us, that our king may govern us and go out before us and fight our battles") — the request coming at a crux of national decline: after Moses's and Joshua's centuries, a dozen high-handed regimes shaping into an intermittently tribal malaise without unified command: they ask for *malik* — a crowned king: the one *institution* that would organize the whole host under command's singularity: the era of judges seeming to have proved itself unequal to the nation's new wars: *ibʿath lanā malikan nuqātil fī sabīli Allāh* — *raise us a king, that we may fight*: and the commentators dwell upon the clause's very own theology: fighting is God's (*fī sabīli Allāh*): but the choice of instrument belongs to God's plan: *the community must fight — but by the means He chooses, through the man He sets, not of their own self-willing*.

**The Prophet's Foreboding**

The prophet's rejoinder comes with divine prescience of the tribe's own cherished capacity for hollow clamor: *qāla hal ʿasaytum in kutiba ʿalaykumu al-qitālu allā tuqātilū* — "he said: might it be — if fighting were prescribed for you — that you would not fight?" *ʿasā* — *perhaps* — cast in the Arabic form of *ultra-likely skepticism* upon this very tribe: they who so loudly demand a king are notoriously-refractory upon every external command bearing hardship, their whole history consisting of fronts with scorching-clout and rear with timid-eluding: and their protestation-answer: *wa mā lanā allā nuqātila fī sabīli Allāhi wa qad ukhrijnā min diyārinā wa abnāʾinā* — "and why should we not fight in God's way — when we have been expelled from our homes and our children?" — their argument drawn from the deepest animal-status: exile from the homestead and child-abduction: no cause more just in the sight of man: and the school reads attached to it the plainest lesson the Book wants carved into its whole phraseology of demand-and-response: *in speech fighting seems a simple crown to claim* — *but under arms, it shudders like a grass-stalk* — and the fulfilling-revelation of verse 249-251's whole army-back-to-few follows the same hard decline-curve: *fa-lammā kutiba ʿalayhimu al-qitālu tawallaw illā qalīlan minhum* — **"then when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned back — save a few among them"** — *illā qalīlan minhum* — *save a few among them*: the verse's eternal refrain for every ever-questered ummah: many talked bold, few stood fast: everyone has a hypothesis of heroism; only a few own the practice: and the last seal: *wa Allāhu ʿalīmun bi'l-ẓālimīn* — "and God knows well the wrongdoers": *ẓulm* — *wrongdoing* — attached here not to the front-office of the tyrants but to the back-office of the turners-back: *the real ẓālim is he whose mouth rode to the battle before his feet did*: and the school's classical commentators have dwelt upon this verse for a thousand years as the finest of all warnings against mouth-boldness: *beware of clamoring for the battle before battle is prescribed: for the lip often mounts where the heel cannot follow* — as the verdict now stands written over every generation: *and God knows well the wrongdoers* — the wrong being amongst their own interior accounts, registered before God from the first speech to the last step.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:247

> **Their prophet told them, “Allah has appointed Saul to be your king.” They protested, “How can he be our king when some of us are more deserving of kingship than he, and he has not been blessed with vast riches?” He replied, “Allah has chosen him over you and blessed him with knowledge and stature. Allah grants kingship to whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Tālūt — Raised Out of Nowhere**

Now comes the shock sentence: *wa qāla lahum nabiyyuhum inna Allāha qad baʿatha lakum ṭālūta malikā* — "and their prophet said to them: God has raised up for you Tālūt (Saul) as a king." The commentators recount his profile: Ṭālūt — from the tribe of Benjamin: of neither royal nor priestly extraction — the smallest clans of Israel: of little wealth: utterly outside the lineages in which prestige ran: and God's gesture is pointed throughout the whole chain: **the King is raised by God's own choice — not by the vote of the tribes**. The people had asked for a king to fight their battles; God gave them, through His prophet's mouth, a threshing-floor leader: *the class-pieties of the tribes receive their own lesson at once*: the school retells Saul's own bewilderment from the Bible's records (1 Samuel 9:21 — "I am only a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel, and my family the humblest of all" — and 1 Samuel 10:27, where some "worthless fellows" scoffed, "How can this man save us?") The Qur'anic account fits precisely: shame before the not-kingly appointee: and from the seams of this tiny anecdote the tradition unfurls its whole doctrine of **rule by divine election**: *God exalts whom He wishes*: the thrones of the world are not heritable entitlements passable through laundered rankings of tribes — not by Moses's or Levi's linchpin-blood — but God raises the one He sees fit with the most unlikely launch-pads: and the Madinan Muslims themselves are already reading themselves into these lines: they have just been told that a man of Khuzaʿah-band, orphaned, formerly-poors may be raised to lordship of the ummah: the Prophet himself — not an old-estate Qurashi lord — is God's own appointed guide: and his enemies raised the same objections: "why him?" — the Quraysh asking "why was this Quran not sent down upon a great man from one of the two towns?" (43:31) — and the Book answering them in the same register: "God knows best where to place His message" (6:124).

**"He Has Not Been Given Abundance of Wealth"**

The objections come — as always — upon the points men prize most in their rulers: the gathered elders are scornful of this newly-appointed king *because he has no wealth*: *wa lam yuʾta saʿatan mina al-māl* — "and he is not given abundance of wealth": the same class-arithmetic that the sūrah has never ceased to undress: Abū Dharr had already heard its demolition (2:212); the people of the sūrah's internal reading of the *ṣiḥāb* of God's morning are reminded: God has ever worked contrarily to the estate' b measurements: the old doubt comes from the same ancient heart of men: their confidence follows the counting-purse, although God's own record of their covenant spans their centuries of shifting sand: "how shall he rule who has no treasury?" — man's eternal formula for why a Moses, an Abraham, a Joseph, a Bethlehem-carpenter should not rule: and *the prophet's answer*: *inna Allāha istaṭafāhu ʿalaykum wa zādahu basṭatan fī al-ʿilmi wa'l-jism* — "God has chosen him over you — and increased him amply in knowledge and in body": the Book immediately re-parametrizes what counts in leadership: not the laden-money-box nor the hereditary standing but the actual essentials: *ʿilm* — knowledge: the man's judgment illuminated by wisdom of God's sort; and *jism* — corporeal strength and presence: the verse-style: records the eternal two: knowledge + strength: intelligence for deliberation + capacity for execution: the Book thereby establishing the two-old-leadership criteria it will reiterate throughout its history: and what God enlarged in Tālūt — knowledge and bodily strength — are, as al-Rāzī frames the classic distinction, the **essential** gifts, while wealth and birth are *accidental* endowments, additions from outside: the substance of a king is made of the former, not the latter.

**"God Gives His Sovereignty to Whom He Wills"**

The close is the sūrah's governing axiom declared again in its own section of sovereignty-assignment: *wa Allāhu yuʾtī mulkahu man yashāʾ* — "and God gives His sovereignty to whomsoever He wills" — *wa Allāhu wāsiʿun ʿalīm* — "and God is All-Encompassing, Knowing": the formula of 3:26 ("Say: O God! Possessor of sovereignty! You grant sovereignty to whom You will, and You strip it from whom You will...") declares the same standing doctrine: sovereignty is perpetually transferred by God's own hand: the authority of kings, the crown of prophets, the throne of Saul — *each and all lands where God wills it*: the same words will prove pivotal once again at 2:251's fall of Jālūt under Dāwūd: throne-critical turning of God's hand: and the Names attach: *wāsiʿ* — All-Encompassing: His sovereignty reaches every territory, no limit pins in His allotting; *ʿalīm* — Knowing: His assignment is not random: the encompassing-Grantor hands the kingdom to the one with all the discernment of God on the matter — All-Encompassing in what He can give, All-Knowing in whom He gives it to: never does the trust fall upon a man unworthy of it. And so the verse stands as among the most eloquent defenses the Book has planted everywhere against the ruling-class-accidents: the throne rests upon God's own weighting: Saul rises because *God* raised him: the tribes obey because God has commanded it: *and God is All-Embracing, Knowing* — the doctrine that the school has kept through every rising and slipping of every dynasty of the earth thereafter: God gives His kingdom to whom He wills — and *willingly He raises the great from the dusts of men*.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:248

> **Their prophet further told them, “The sign of Saul’s kingship is that the Ark will come to you—containing reassurance from your Lord and relics of the family of Moses and the family of Aaron, which will be carried by the angels. Surely in this is a sign for you, if you ˹truly˺ believe.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Ark as Credential**

The prophet's answer to the people's incredulous question (*how can this poor Benjaminite rule us — he is not wealthy!*) is God's answer in thing: *inna āyata mulkihi an yaʾtiyakumu al-tābūtu fīhi sakīnatun min rabbikum wa baqiyyatun mimmā taraka ālu mūsā wa ālu hārūna taḥmiluhu al-malāʾikah* — "truly the sign of his kingship is that the Ark shall come to you — in it a *sakīnah* — tranquility — from your Lord — and a remnant of what the house of Moses and the house of Aaron left — angels bearing it." The commentators relate the situation (relying with due restraint upon the accounts of the Israelite histories): the Ark of the Covenant — the greatest sacred relic of the tribes of Israel — had been lost to them: the Philistines had captured it in battle (as all the Bible's own first-book annals tell, or as some Muslim commentaries recount on their own), and during its absence the peoples' heart-clouds hung the heavier: *the command's own origin* — the sign — was not in any self-proclamation Saul could make in his own name: the sign was *God's going out to meet the tribe's doubt*: the Ark returned. God restored to Israel its lost sacred thing — while the Ark's own inner contents had a double-character: a *sakīnah* — a *tranquility-of-presence* — from their Lord, whose very coming down was accompanied by the comfort that at last the heart felt the presence: *and a remnant* — *baqiyyah*: something left from the households of Moses and Aaron: the commentators furnishing all the lore-choices of what may have lain within: the broken Tablets of the Ten Words (7:150's own fragments at the moment of Moses's own cast-down); the staff of Moses with which the sea had been pierced (2:60's own moment); the manna-jar saved as recollection of the wilderness (2:57's own wording of its gift); and, more recent accounts report, the sandals of the Prophet (20:12's own instruction) — the relic of relics: *borne back by angels*: *taḥmiluhu al-malāʾikah* — conveyed by God-guided hands: *and the angelic convoy* was wholly attendable by proof to any doubter: *how does a king secure that the Ark of his people's holiness return of itself, in angel escort, unless God Himself has signed the king with His finger?* The scoffers' own mouths turn: one day Saul's election is on the tribe's lips as an absurdity, the next day the angels carry the ark at his command.

**Sakīnah — The Tranquility Word's Winged History**

The Book's word *sakīnah* is the precious one — the commentators and the scholars of Ṣūfi literature both eager beyond measure at its appearance: *sakīnah* — the deep tranquility that descends upon the hearts of believers at God's charge: *God's in-dwelling peace*: the term returning again in the Book at nine stations (2:248's ark, and notably at 9:26, 40 where it descends upon the Prophet and his army; and 48:4, 18, 26 where it is "sent down upon the believers" at the great crisis-oaths): — the precious pillar-idea standing in one kinship-clan with the whole revelation's teaching of God-Presence: God gives *sakīnah* not to shrines alone but to souls: it accompanies whoever carries God's charge with confidence: as it accompanied Moses and Aaron's house through the wilderness, as it accompanied the Ark through the tribal fields of Canaan, as it accompanies the Messenger's heart through his years of Makkan rejection and his Madinan years of war and danger: and nowhere more memorably than in the cave of Thawr, when the Prophet spoke to his companion at the moment of greatest peril: "fear not! surely God is with us" (9:40) - so the Ark's mere arrival brings the whole *sakīnah* into the villages of Israel. And the tradition has always coupled the Ark's returning to the modern struggles of the ummah: in the shadows of its own the community simply asks: *who have found God's sakīnah — the men who carry His signs, never them; the men of vain boast?* — the men who carry the ark upon whose frame God once wrote "from your Lord": from this verse also flows the balanced doctrine of sacred remnants upon which the commentators reflect with caution: relics may carry *baqiyyah*: remnants of blessing; but only God *gives* tranquility: and the sakīnah cannot be bought by human prestige nor inherited by human genealogy: it is *sent down from your Lord*.

**A Sign — If They Be Believers**

And the verse folds the whole narrative onto the Book's anticipation of the near-future's millenary: *inna fī dhālika la-āyatan lakum in kuntum muʾminīn* — "truly in that is a sign for you — if you are believers": the commentators read the grand second-order lesson: the sakīnah is the sign — but it disperses upon the non-believer's heart as the rain-drops upon the rock: God only gives the true witness *to the believers*: and so the whole gate to the *sakīnah* is faith: *in kuntum muʾminīn*: the story of 2:248 speaking at once to every man who reads the whole sequence (verse 246 standing at its entrance) — the tribes' demand for battle-armed king was authentic, God's choice of Saul was God-like, the tribe's objection was instinctive class-dread — but the sign was *for them — if they are believers*: so the verse closes this file of Saul's designation with the very message the Book had been carrying all along: the best king's kingship comes not with self-aggrandizing gold but with the angel-borne ark: God's own sign of the Prophet's authenticity — carried into the camp by angels — settles nothing *except for the faithful — and the faithful knew, the minute it arrived, that God had matched His prophet's word with His own hand.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:249

> **When Saul marched forth with his army, he cautioned: “Allah will test you with a river. So whoever drinks ˹his fill˺ from it is not with me, and whoever does not taste it—except a sip from the hollow of his hands—is definitely with me.” They all drank ˹their fill˺ except for a few! When he and the ˹remaining˺ faithful with him crossed the river, they said, “Now we are no match for Goliath and his warriors.” But those ˹believers˺ who were certain they would meet Allah reasoned, “How many times has a small force vanquished a mighty army by the Will of Allah! And Allah is ˹always˺ with the steadfast.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A River as a Sieve**

Saul's march begins, and God's test of the host starts at the most mundane checkpoint: a stream: *fa-lammā faṣala ṭālūtu bi'l-junūdi qāla inna Allāha mubtalīkum bi-naharin fa-man shariba minhu fa-laysa minnī* — "and when Saul set out with the hosts, he said: God is testing you with a stream: whoever drinks of it is not of me, and whoever does not taste of it is of me — save one who scoops out a handful." The commentators note the formidable exactingness of the test (al-Rāzī's observation among them): God puts the whole army to the scrutiny of one act of obedience *amid thirst*: the desert-hour had heated the whole column: marching men, sun-scorched, in desperate want of water, reaching the bank: the school recites the commentary's weighing that the test's subtlety was dawning on the narrator even from afar: *most armies cannot be won at the battle-field: they are lost at the stream-bed*: the soldiers who had earlier clamored for a king to lead them into God's fight (v. 246) now stood before their Verdict-gate within a single palmful of water: *he who shall drink is not of me — he who does not taste is of me — save one who scoops a handful*: the concession — *a handful* — set the exact balance: thirst was not to be quenched, only borne with God's allowance: the single scoop marked the border between absolute abstention and absolute indulgence: the commentators noting how immediately the sieve worked: the one who drank satisfied himself — and by that one act showed his impotence of obedience: the one who allowed the water to pass by showed his proficiency of reigning over his thirst: an exercise in self-mastery: an exam in obedience: and the whole army plunged down their thirsty snouts — *save a few among them*: *illā qalīlan minhum*: the Book again punctuating itself with the same refrain as its own ancient principal-lamps: many professed — few persevered — so is the Election of God *by test upon test*.

**Goliath's Host and Small Companies**

The passage proceeds to its second letting-the-spirit-out instalment: upon crossing the stream — *fa-lammā jāwazahu huwa wa-lladhīna āmanū maʿahu* — "and when he crossed it, he and those who believed with him" — they looked ahead unto their enemies: Jālūt and his hosts: their own terrible stature-army crushing the hill-side: and the men who have come so far are overwhelmed: *lā ṭāqata lanā al-yawma bi-jālūta wa junūdih* — "we have no power today against Goliath and his hosts": the verse carrying into its gesture the oldest teaching of the spirituality of numbers: men are crushed not by arms but by *estimation*: the sight of the enemy's sharpening sheen undoes the believers in the flash of the eye: the shop-lists of odds drawn up by natural judgment so stands written the whole cohort of the speechless: and immediately the mighty reply — *qāla alladhīna yaẓunnūna annahum mulāqū Allāh* — *said those who believed that they would meet their Lord*: the Book renaming the full-hearted warriors: *those counted the meeting* — with God — the instrument of their generations's truth-keeping (the glossers explain either that they certified of Resurrection-morning — *knowing the meeting surely* — or that they are prepared to die) — the men of meeting, who had already lost sight of this world to a clearer one, exactly measure the odds contrary-ways: *kam min fiʾatin qalīlatin ghalabat fiʾatan kathīratan bi-idhni Allāh* — **"how many a small company has overcome a large company — by God's leave!"** — the motto the schools of Islam have never ceased passing down its generations of follow-warriors as its supreme counsel: the probability-by-arithmetic is bankrupt: by God's leave the small can conquer the great: and the school documents with unwavering pleasure the direct application of the verse in the Badr narratives: at Badr the Companions themselves stood three hundred and thirteen against a thousand of the idolaters' ranks — and the tafsīr-tradition records that the Companions themselves encouraged one another with *this very verse*: "They consoled each other with it: 'How many a small company has overcome a large company, by God's leave!'" — and the verdict of the sūrah repeats the eternal summary: *wa Allāhu maʿa al-ṣābirīn* — **"and God is with the patient."** The world's whole war-calculus hangs upon the three clauses of the verse: God chooses His kings by His choice (248); God tries His soldiers by His stream (249); God rewrites the odds by His leave (249): *small becomes great — through God's own mechanics — at His own appointed field*: and the believers' own echo is the battle-psychology the schools still practice in the night before struggle: count not the enemies' spear-points; count God's leave.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:250

> **When they advanced to face Goliath and his warriors, they prayed, “Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance, make our steps firm, and give us victory over the disbelieving people.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prayer of the Few**

At the threshold of the battle the Book sets down the oldest duʿāʾ of outnumbered armies: *wa lammā barazū li-jālūta wa junūdihi qālū rabbanā afrigh ʿalaynā ṣabran wa thabbit aqdāmanā wa nṣurnā ʿalā al-qawmi al-kāfirīn* — "and when they went forward against Goliath and his hosts, they said: Our Lord — pour patience upon us — make firm our feet — and help us against the disbelieving people." The commentators attend each petition's imagery with the finest grain of the language's treasury: *afrigh ʿalaynā ṣabran* — *pour out patience upon us*: the verb faragha — to empty, to pour forth: patience envisaged as a liquid blessing poured down upon the faith-heart: not the thin patience of stoicism, not the rebellious fortitude of sheer shame, but *endurance saturated between shoulders and arms, poured from above*: *make firm our steps* — *thabbit aqdāmanā*: hold our feet fast in the moment of advance, when the first clash comes: and *help us against the disbelieving people* — *nṣurnā*: the prayer for victory asked from His hand alone: and the Book names the foe only as *the disbelieving people* — the relationship to God stands first in every battle-line of Islam: and this same liturgy of the few against the many the tradition heard again on the Prophet's own lips at Badr — as the oldest hadith-accounts have it:

> *"The Prophet ﷺ, at Badr, turning his face to the qibla: O God — fulfil Your promise to me. O God — grant us what You have promised us. O God — if You destroy this company of Muslims, You will not be worshipped on earth."* — and Abū Bakr then answering: 'Enough of pleading with your Lord — for He will fulfill His promise to you.'" (Muslim 1763 — the Prophet's own battle-pleading at Badr — reported by ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb — always cited alongside the verse's same liturgy of *rabbānā* from the few against the many at Jālūt's camp-field)

**A Duʿāʾ to Keep in Every Throat**

The verse thereby builds within the tradition its template for *every* outnumbered lawful cause ever since: pray *for Patience* — the pouring *upon you* — *after* requesting God's victory *at His*: and the school applies the three-fold petition in the same triple-array of every spiritual fighting-line as well: (1) patience first — for patience is the host and shelter of every other virtue; (2) firm feet second — for steadfast standing carries the whole cause through the contested hour; (3) help against the foe last — for the petition for victory properly comes after the petitions for endurance and steadiness. The commentary tradition extols the everlasting imagery of verse 250 — *to pour out upon us* — as though patience descended from a pitcher — among the highest fountains of scriptural prayer-language: *God holds a pitcher above the hearts of His servants, and pours of it upon whom He wills* — and the prayer's simple triple-structure has taken its permanent place in the supplication-books of the scholars, from al-Nawawī's to Ibn al-Qayyim's adhkār — the prayer the whole heart may settle into, whenever any army of believers stands before its Goliath.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:251

> **So they defeated them by Allah’s Will, and David killed Goliath. And Allah blessed David with kingship and wisdom and taught him what He willed. Had Allah not repelled a group of people by ˹the might of˺ another, corruption would have dominated the earth, but Allah is Gracious to all.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**By God's Leave — David and the Giant**

The duel of the whole ages concludes with the astonishing brevity God reserves for such moments: *fa-hazamūhum bi-idhni Allāh* — "and they routed them — by God's leave" — *wa qatala dāwūdu jālūt* — "and David slew Goliath." The commentators explain the sentence-order: the whole battle's outcome attributed not to the soldiers' arms nor David's sling-stone — *bi-idhni Allāh* — *by God's leave* — the leave that had already tested them at the river, decreed the victory, sifted their ranks, strengthened their hearts: the famous tradition-about David carried down the Qur'an's narration remains the story the whole world remembers: the young shepherd (not among the armored veterans of Saul's retinue — a boy from Bethlehem tending sheep, sent with provisions, in the accounts) who, hearing Goliath's open morning-and-evening challenges, volunteered — the pagan giant standing with a spear like a weaver's beam, and the youth armed only with sling and stones — and the smooth brook-stone flying from David's sling — and Goliath fell (1 Samuel 17's account holding in the school the same rendering, with his five brook-stones and shepherd's whole kit — the Muslim tradition concurring that David's victory over Goliath brought him simultaneously *mulk* — *kingdom* — and *ḥikmah* — *wisdom* — the twin blessings the rest of verse 251 records: *wa ātāhu Allāhu al-mulka wa'l-ḥikmata wa ʿallamahu mimmā yashāʾ* — "and God gave him the kingdom and wisdom — and taught him what He willed." The school of the commentators pin-points wisdom's use: *ḥikmah* glossed through Prophethood — the station carried into David by his perception of the divine Word that subsequently gives us the Zabūr (the Psalms of David — the sacred book shared in God's designation at 17:55: "and to David We gave the Zabūr") — and *mulk* as the kingship he inherited from Saul's line: so the boy-shepherd became both the people's king and the prophets' heir — kingdom and knowledge fused in one life-story of the shepherd of the flock, the two stations joined in him as the Book joins them in this one sentence.

**"Were It Not for God's Repelling People"**

The verse then reads the larger moral from its own battle-ground into the global architecture of who holds the cosmos on: *wa law lā dafʿu Allāhi al-nāsa baʿḍahum bi-baʿḍin la-fasadati al-arḍ* — "and were it not for God's repelling people — some by means of others — the earth would have been corrupted": the great metaphysical principle: *God maintains the world through repulsion*: evil men driven back by good men; avarice by magnanimity; sacrilege by piety: were it not so — *la-fasadat al-arḍ*: the *earth would corrupt*: with different readings the school maintains: some (al-Qurṭubī's report recording the grant) say by *the Substitutes* (*abdāl*: those devout-world-saints who sustain creation by their very prayers — the name of the writer of history at every turn; the commentators debate their famous numbers, "forty" being the most-loved); others (al-Ṭabarī's view) read into it God's maintaining the balance plainly: the prayer-people *repress* the effects of the sinners; the believers keep earth's moral order from crumbling; and a sound hadith marked by Musnad Aḥmad speaks the fullest version of it:

> *"God drives away the punishment of the one who does not pray — by the one who prays; and of the one who does not give alms — by the one who gives alms; and of the one who does not fast — by the one who fasts; and of the one who does not make ḥajj — by the one who makes ḥajj; and of the one who does not struggle — by the one who struggles."* (the traditionary registers cited at this verse — recorded in the compilations of the salaf and cited throughout al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī — sustaining the verse's great repulsion-theology by the Prophet's own word: *the world's welfare depends upon the continued practice of the devout*)

and the assurance pairing: *wa lākinna Allāha dhū faḍlin ʿalā al-ʿālamīn* — "but God is Possessed of Bounty upon the worlds": all the repelling, all the balancing, all the victories of saints moments before and moments foreseen: *all of it stands by the sustaining favour of God*: for *there is no repulsion without the Repeller, no balance without the King of kingdoms: God is Possessed of Bounty upon the world* — in the plainest of declarations: He is simply Bountiful — and bounty is the very cause for which the world itself continues at all.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:252

> **These are Allah’s revelations which We recite to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth. And you are truly one of the messengers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Recited Signs, Confirmed Messenger**

With the duel entombed and the fells flat, the Book turns its lamp at last upon the one who has been reading it aloud: *tilka āyātu Allāhi natlūhā ʿalayka bi'l-ḥaqqi wa innaka la-mina al-mursalīn* — "these are God's signs — We recite them to you in truth — and truly you are among the messengers." The commentators note the function of the consummating sentence (al-Rāzī's reading of the tonal sequence at the head of the line of liturgical seals: *tilka* — *those* — sweeping the whole narrative-complex into one category: *it was all recitation*: the flight of the hundreds from pestilence, the stream of Saul, the boy with the sling, the Ark returned by angels, all of it — carried in *recitation* from God's word-corpus into the Prophet's mouth — already corporeal event and already God's own proof-material: and the almost tender second clause — *wa innaka la-mina al-mursalīn* — *and truly you are among the messengers*: God Himself adds His own second attestation to the Prophet's ministry: after a whole file of historical precedents showing how God's messengers' churches refused the poor, trusted the river, subdued the giant — God looks to His Prophet and erects the same protected canopy: *you also are among them*: no competitor with Moses, Saul nor David, but their come-up honors' very inheritor: your struggles are the same struggles; your opponent-giants of Quraysh, of Banū Naḍīr's abandonments, of the pagans' massed cavalries — are old foes wearing new eye-patches: and the narration is *truth* — *bi'l-ḥaqq* — matched one to the next *in truth* — not gossip of poets but divinely spun pageantry history: and the sentence's own residual purpose with the length of all its narrative-processes (al-Qurṭubī's summing, Ibn Kathīr's own) is the tender comfort for the beleaguered Messenger: every fearsome account that the Book has just uttered upon the messengers' own fields of fight — rejection, remnant-reductions down to a palmful of waters, spoils of wars, implausible victories — reaches now to his own door: *they all stood where you now stand, and God led them through it all*: *and truly you are among the messengers*: God's own inclusion of the Prophet ﷺ within the unbroken chain of prophets from Adam down: for this is the recurring promise the Book pronounces at the close of all such narratives: they suffered your struggles before you — they triumphed your triumphs — and you are seated now among that company forever.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:253

> **We have chosen some of those messengers above others. Allah spoke directly to some, and raised some high in rank. To Jesus, son of Mary, We gave clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. If Allah had willed, succeeding generations would not have fought ˹among themselves˺ after receiving the clear proofs. But they differed—some believed while others disbelieved. Yet if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another. But Allah does what He wills.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Ranks Among the Messengers**

The whole cavalcade of prophets just narrated — Moses, Saul, David, Goliath-faller — gathers into one summarizing sentence of divine pedagogy: *tilka al-rusulu faḍḍalnā baʿḍahum ʿalā baʿḍ* — "those are the messengers — We have favored some above others." The commentators are fastidious over the reconciliation-word with verse 285's own settled creed ("we make no distinction among any of His messengers"): Muslims are commanded not to *distinguish* in their belief — believing all the prophets — yet God *has* ranked them, in His own judgment of their missions: their missions vary, and their registers vary with them: and still no prophet's servant-hood is greater or less than another's (all equally God's prophets, all equally protected in their faithful being): the variation concerns *missions and signs*. The verse itself catalogues its own differential: *minhum man kallama Allāh* — "among them are those to whom God spoke" — the commentators' designation attaching to Moses especially ("God spoke to Moses directly" — 4:164), some adding Adam's own converse in the Garden and Muḥammad's night-journey dialogues; *wa rafaʿa baʿḍahum darajāt* — "and some He raised up in ranks" — the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ honored by the tradition with the highest of the degrees, sent with the Book for *all of mankind* and not for one tribeic — the master's hadith bestowing his own particular elevation in both khabar-forms:

> *"I have been given five things which no prophet was given before me: I was supported with terror in my enemies' hearts for a month's journey; the earth has been made for me a mosque and a means of purification; the spoils of war have been made lawful for me and were not made lawful for anyone before me; I was given intercession; and prophets used to be sent to their own people, and I was sent to all mankind."* (al-Bukhari 335/438; Muslim 521 — among the most-quoted hadiths of the Prophet's own distinctness — his five-privileges listing standing as the fullest tradition-register upon this verse's *faḍḍalnā* clause)

**Jesus and the Holy Spirit**

Then the naming of Jesus (Eisa ibn Maryam) in particular: *wa ātaynā ʿīsā ibna maryama al-bayyināti wa ayyadnāhu bi-rūḥi al-qudus* — "and We gave Jesus son of Mary the clear proofs, and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit." The conscious reprise of the identical phrase already dispatched at 2:87 — the commentators unfolding the reasons of the repetition: Jesus is the immediately recent one among the messengers of the Israelites' own fold, he before the Prophet's own proximity in the chain: the Book thus honors him with distinctive placement at the head of the ranks just listed — God's grant of *bayyināt* — *evidencing signs* — to him: from the coming-out-of-the-cradle's address (19:30-33) to the healing of the blind and the leper, to the quickening of the dead (3:49; 5:110): every one of them *by God's leave* — and the support of the *rūḥ al-qudus* — *the Holy Spirit*: the Spirit named with the three accepted interpretations the commentators have ever managed: Gabriel the archangel who was with him from conception, through ministry, to ascension; or the very spirit breathed of God's primordial breath (15:29); or the Gospel itself as God's spirit of guidance (all three folded into one term by al-Rāzī's school of readings): the sentence's own measure of reverence already sufficient: God has supported Jesus with the Holy Spirit — no demi-god but *His servant*, dignified by God's selfsame strengthening.

**Had God Willed — The Difference Theodicy**
