And the verse unveils one of the Book of God's most searching gates: *wa law shāʾa Allāhu mā iqtatala alladhīna min baʿdihim min baʿdi mā jāʾathumu al-bayyināt* — "and had God willed — those who came after them would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come": followed by the Book's own answering antithesis: *wa lākini ikhtalafū* — "but they differed": — the great doctrine of religious schism named after itself: they differed: some believers, some disbelievers: — and the answering reduplication: *wa law shāʾa Allāhu mā iqtatalū* — *had God willed they would not have fought*: but *wa Allāhu yafʿalu mā yurīd* — "God does what He wills": the Book now showing the ummah's own theology of the Divine Will in its most scalpel-by-message: God had power to compel them to unity; He chose not to: the door was left open to human divergence: *and God does what He wills*: what He willed was the freedom of religiotheoretical contest within each community of every prophet: not all His people were to be shepherded to one agenda: He permits even the descendants of the prophets to fail, even those who were *given the clear proofs* to fall among themselves: the finite-subjugations the community of the fathers bore — envy, grudge, greed — were not removed by the prophet's miraculous edicts: *God does what He wills*: the verse closes upon the Book's grand balance: man is free to schism; God is free to ordain the stage; both are certain; and the composition of the two gates into one knot is the very religion of submission: *the mind bows: and God does what He wills* — and this knot, when it is untied by submission itself, becomes the believer's soul's first entered arabesque to its All-Knowing King — *He does what He wills* — forever, from the river of Ṭālūt to the Day of Judgment.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:254

> **O believers! Donate from what We have provided for you before the arrival of a Day when there will be no bargaining, friendship, or intercession. Those who disbelieve are ˹truly˺ the wrongdoers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Spending Guard Against the Closed Day**

From the loft of prophet-ranks and divine-will the sūrah returns to its early leitmotif — the spending of what God apportioned (2:3, 2:177) — now with a terrible alert-shout written into the same wall: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū anfiqū mimmā razaqnākum min qabli an yaʾtiya yawmun lā bayʿun fīhi wa lā khullatun wa lā shafāʿah* — "O you who believe — SPEND from what We have provided you — before a day arrives in which there is no sale, no friendship, no intercession": *wa'l-kāfirūna humu al-ẓālimūn* — "and the disbelievers — they are the wrongdoers." The Book is cataloguing the three cisterns of worldly help whose well will dry at that Day: (1) *bayʿ*: commerce — the trading-and-ransoming-economy by which a man may, in this world, recover from almost any debt by payment: there is no buyer then, no seller: no bribe: no restitution by money: as the tradition reads the companion-warnings on the closing of this cistern by still another verse of God's same Book: "on the day when neither wealth nor children shall avail — save him who comes to God with a sound heart" (26:88-89): (2) *khullah*: friendship — the secure circle of powerful protectors: *no friend shall help friend*; for friends that day are enemies one to another (43:67); and all the struts of lineage and patronage collapse there, (3) *shafāʿah*: intercession — one taking another's side for a hand-up in the Judgment: as 2:48 already warned, "no soul shall avail another": intercession will save none of the condemners: and the commentators are careful here (as at 2:48) about the necessary interpunction: the plain sense denies all three to *disbelievers* — while the mercy of prophetic intercession for Muslims by God's own leave remains, God's own great gate of access mentioned elsewhere (2:255's own "who shall intercede with Him save by His leave?"; the tradition's great hadith of shafāʿah: "My intercession is for the people of major sins of my community" — Abū Dāwūd 4739; al-Tirmidhī 2435 — the Prophet's great pledge of mediality for those who clung of the ummah — always mentioned in the mufassirūn's balancing of verses 2:48 and 2:254 upon God's own permission-hold).

**Before the Day Comes — The Word of Urgency**

The urgency-word *min qabli an yaʾtiya yawmun* — *before the day comes* — jams the whole labor into one imperative of *preparation*: the verb *yaʾtiya* — *that comes* — cast in the future: no procrastination is mere man's gift: the Day itself is *already arriving*: the commentators stress the word-times: God uses the participle as if to say to every believer: *prepare now*: and the tradition remembers precisely at the verse the Prophet's own last-warning of the rush of the Day upon little improv:

> *"Be quick in doing good deeds before there come seven things* that no man of you should wait for anything except *poverty that makes one forgetful, or riches that makes one rebellious, or sickness that ruins, or old age that blemishes, or death that hastens, or the Antichrist — the worst of invisible expected — or the Hour — and the Hour is the most grievous and bitter* (al-Tirmidhī 2306 — the Prophet's dreaded record of the Seven Closings: the Day itself sentence-by-delay after delay's weighted-sealed: every one of the forgetting-things one of the *yaʾtiya* of the world's annihilating elegies toward us: *spend before all seven*, the school ever after teaches)

**The Signal of the Fuser**

And the closing word — *wa'l-kāfirūna humu al-ẓālimūn* — "and the disbelievers — they are the wrongdoers" — seals the whole address in the sūrah's own already-aged phrasing-system: the phrase *humu al-ẓālimūn* (they are the wrongdoers) has by now become the sūrah's own great stamp of dis-salvage: from 2:35's Adam-block through 2:51's calf-fabrication through 2:229's ḥudūd-transgressors-down and v. 246's injured-mothers — the emphatic *they* — *they are the wrongdoers* — now collecting the whole refrain into one sealed verdict: God *is* on the side of the givers; the disbelievers who had never given are the ones breaking the covenant of God: *they are the wrongdoers* — and it was the gift of their Islam from God of which they made mock, as if its proffered treasury were nothing. And the school audits at this last word of the sūrah that God's transcription of *justice* (*ʿadl*) into *wrongdoing* (*ẓulm*) inverts precisely where the believers are told to spend: the disbelievers' wrongdoing is not merely their unbelief but their *hoarding, their keeping, their clutching of their gold when God was asking for their dispersing* — the same indictment the Book deploys at the far end of the sūrah's own charity-sequence (2:270–274): the days are running out — *spend* — before there is *no buying* — before *no friendship* — before *no intercession*: and *the disbelievers — they are the wrongdoers* — and God alone is the wrongdoer's Last Master.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:255

> **Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him, the EverLiving, All-Sustaining. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who could possibly intercede with Him without His permission? He ˹fully˺ knows what is ahead of them and what is behind them, but no one can grasp any of His knowledge—except what He wills ˹to reveal˺. His Seat encompasses the heavens and the earth, and the preservation of both does not tire Him. For He is the Most High, the Greatest.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Greatest Verse**

The two hundred and fifty-fifth verse of the Sūrah of the Cow is the crown of the whole Qur'an — as the Prophet ﷺ himself named it when he asked Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, "which verse with you among God's Book is the greatest?" and Ubayy recited this one, and the Prophet struck his breast and said: *"Rejoice in the knowledge, O Abū al-Mundhir!"* — the hadith's own sublime register, at Muslim 810, confirming what the whole tradition enshrines: **Āyat al-Kursī**, the Verse of the Pedestal. The reserves of the Hadith honor it with superlatives unparalleled for any single verse: the Prophet's famous evidence in the Salaf-collection of the greatest verse of God's Book (Bukhari 2311); its instruction for the morning and evening's shield (who recites it after every obligatory prayer, nothing prevents him entering Paradise but death — al-Nasāʾī, among the Adhkār's most-cherished charge; and its safeguard of the sleeper by the teaching that the reciter is guarded through the night — the long tradition of Abu Hurayrah's ghoul-encounter in Bukhari 2311/3275: *"Whoever recites Āyat al-Kursī at night, a guard from God keeps watch over him, and no devil draws near him until morning"*). Its ten short phrases are a complete theology of God in one breath: one God, living, self-sustaining, wakeful, owning all, permitting intercession only by leave, knowing all universally, surrounding all with His Pedestal, unwearied in upholding all — and above all exalted and magnificent: all that any believer ever needs to comprehend — in half a minute's recitation.

**Al-Ḥayy, Al-Qayyūm — The Two Mother-Names**

The verse opens with the most condensed declaration of God's uniqueness and necessary Being in the whole Book: *Allāhu lā ilāha illā huwa* — "God — there is no god but He" — *al-ḥayy* — **the Living**: life par excellence — not created life, not bounded life, not slow-running life winding down toward death — but Life Absolute, the Source of all life, of whom the tradition speaks with the holy names-comprehension the verse itself supplies: — and *al-qayyūm* — **the Self-Subsisting** — the supreme intensive of the verb *qāma*: He *stands* by Himself and *sustains* all that stands: the commentators' classic definition compactly (Ibn Kathīr's, al-Ṭabarī's): *al-qayyūm* — **He who subsists through Himself, by whom all other things subsist**: the two Names together (al-Ḥayy and al-Qayyūm) are cherished by the theologians and spirituals as the "mothers of the Names" — held to the believer as a key for all other names: for only the One whose own Being derives from no one else at all can carry all Beings besides — so the thesis is established: whatever the slave believes, *my Lord needs nothing, stands on nothing; and everything stands on Him.*

**No Slumber, No Sleep**

The third clause slams the entire family of sky-gods and tribal gods with its two-word devastation: *lā taʾkhudhuhu sinatun wa lā nawm* — "slumber overtakes Him not, nor sleep." The commentators gloss the two terms care-takingly: *sinah* — a light drowsing; *nawm* — deep sleep: *neither* so much as brushes God: the verse's implication covers every decay we associate with caregiving — the nurse's two-in-the-morning drooping eyes, the watchman's four-of-night-nod from tedium — *none* of these wearying frames belongs to God: *the heavens and earth are never without His gaze*: when the last lamp of a house drowses out, when the night's last breath of living wits slow down toward exhaustion, **He who *tends* them all is still faithfully at His post**: Al-Rāzī's famous deduction within the theology-schools was already present in the salaf's own longings: *all creation's possible survival from sleep's daily breaks in every sentient being was witnessed to Him as persisting even while everything else runs down*: *no wonder the reciters of every human age have fastened upon the verse as its talisman of insomnias*: the One who never sleeps is standing watch while I finally do. And the sunnah's own bedtime-warrant — the Prophet's advice for night-seekers: recite the verse upon your bedside and *a guard is appointed over you* — becomes at its ultimate depth the waking-one's shielding of the sleeper: *the insomnia of all seekers ends here at the Sureness of the One Who Sleeps Not*.

**"Unto Him Belongs Whatsoever Is"**

Then the verse's own pivot-socket: *lahu mā fī al-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍ* — "unto Him belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth" — the possessive flourish of the sūrah at v. 168's own galaxy-rimming "Unto Him belong the East and the West" now universalized: ownership is total: no square-cubit of universe exists whose dominion is not His: and the two clauses that follow upbuild the tribunal-topography of the entire next world: *man dhā alladhī yashfaʿu ʿindahu illā bi-idhnih* — "who is there who may intercede with Him — save by His leave?" — the Book softening (by the clause "save by His leave") its sternest parallel-phrasing at 2:48 where intercession was refused outright: intercession is hereby opened — but only *by Divine permission*: exegesis: the friends of men like the Prophet and the angels and the martyrs intercede — *as He permits* — the law of leaving abundant grace continued and also every pretension of heaven-vendored sanctity shut off: no saint can pressure God; no harij-crook can buy; but the licensed interceders — Prophet and angels and righteous — plead in the permission-route open to every believer reading aright: and then the last short telescope-iridesence of omniscience: *yaʿlamu mā bayna aydīhim wa mā khalfahum* — "He knows what is before them and what is behind them" — the commentators reading through all registers: the future and the past (the Hereafter and the world); what is ahead in man's tomorrow and what is behind in man's yesterdays — *both of them* are bare before Him: *wa lā yuḥīṭūna bi-shayʾin min ʿilmihi illā bi-mā shāʾ* — "and they encompass nothing of His Knowledge — except what He wills": man's knowing is bucket-scoop of God's Ocean: what He does not disclose, all of his creatures' curiosity is eternally barred from.

**The Pedestal and the Unwearied Sustainer**

The final cadences deliver the verse's iconic image and its great close: *wasiʿa kursiyyuhu al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍ* — "His Pedestal (*kursī*) embraces the heavens and the earth" — the commentators explaining with discipline the sense of *kursī*: either the Pedestal beneath the Throne — the tradition transmitting Ibn ʿAbbās's well-known statement: "what are the heavens and the earth in comparison with the *kursī*, save as a ring cast into the wilderness?" and, in like manner: "what is the *kursī* in comparison with the *ʿarsh*, save as a ring cast into the wilderness?" (Ibn Kathīr recording both versions of the famous saying) — or, by the other commentators' register, God's encompassing Knowledge and Sovereignty named metonymously, as one says "the crown" for the monarch. Either way the sentence stands for direct creed: *wasiʿa*: His sovereignty contains the cosmos; whatever the two expanses unfold, they are enfolded by His Pedestal. *Protecting them tires Him not* — *lā yaʾūduhu ḥifẓuhumā*: His guarding of the whole frame of heaven and earth costs Him nothing: the keeper of all things is not tired, does not sag, has never paused: *He sustains, and He perseveres* — and then the twin Names settle the lock: *wa huwa al-ʿaliyyu al-ʿaẓīm* — "and He is the Exalted, the Magnificent": *al-ʿaliyy* — transcending all things in exaltation; *al-ʿaẓīm* — exceeding all things in magnitudes of greatness: the believer at his prostration praises *subḥāna rabbiya al-aʿlā* — "Glory be to my Lord the Most High" — while his body rests at its lowest point, enacting the creed of the verse in a single posture of flesh: *God is Most High, and I am all-below*: and with this, the whole world stands again huddled in its true footing: creation small, God great; the Pedestal wide, humanity minuscule: and the Prophet's Qur'an plants its observatory here, at the exact midpoint of the long sūrah, for every believer of every age to memorize and recite — the Throne-Verse becoming the believer's daily observance of the High One's own greatness: *Glory be to Him — the Exalted, the Magnificent*.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:256

> **Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood. So whoever renounces false gods and believes in Allah has certainly grasped the firmest, unfailing hand-hold. And Allah is AllHearing, All-Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"No Coercion in Religion" — The Charter Flourish**

From atop the throne-glory of 2:255 — where the ascent toward God's own pedestal has just closed upon the believer's entire faculty — the sūrah opens the plainest religious-freedom charter of all revelation: *lā ikrāha fī al-dīn* — "there is no compulsion in religion" — *qad tabayyana al-rushdu mina al-ghayy* — "sound judgment has been made clear from error": the commentators anchoring the verse's placement among the existing family of Islam's covenant-position (10:99's: "would you then compel men till they become believers?"; 18:29's: "whosoever wills, let him believe, and whosoever wills, let him disbelieve"; and opposed interpreted contexts like 9:5's sword-verses and the apostasy-topics of 2:217): and recording its occasion reports with exact care: the parents of Madinah who in olden days had pledged their surviving children into the Jewish clan (and who, when the Banū al-Naḍīr were exiled, found themselves torn in their hearts over whether to force their grown children out of Judaism into Islam) — with God descending them this very sentence: *no coercion*: *your children's religion is theirs alone: if truth has any handle with them, it shall rise in its own power, not in your compulsion*: — with its sister-accounts the commentators note as well: the two sons of a Muslim of Madinah who went Christian and emigrated with Yemeni caravan-merchants to Syria — and the same Book's *there is no compulsion in religion* as God's own unwonted answer: the religion of the heart cannot be forced from without: *ikrāh* — compulsion, constraint — is not in God's adl (justice) to a free soul, nor in His ḥilm to a seeking soul.

**Truth Clear from Error — Enough**

*Qad tabayyana al-rushdu mina al-ghayy* — the declaration standing now as the rational charter of the very freedom: since truth and falsehood have already been made clear, the need for coercion dissolves: the verse's own reasoning does one simple syllogism: what needs bayonet-force to enter the heart can never truly enter the heart — and what has God's own evidencing proof within it needs no enforcing bayonet: *rushd* — sound directing judgment: from the same root that yields rasā'il and irshād: God has planted His evidences all the way from childhood through the knowing of hearts and of wisdom of life, and the Book contains all the distillations of them — with the outcome: *no forcing required*: so let men come in truth themselves, or remain aside — as the Master's own discipline of religion-absorption *by hearts not by battle* (10:99-100) is God's own instruction: and the whole background of his mission's war-era deals justice to the principle: never in Islamic history did Islam's soldiers take prisoners and line them up for conversion: the Ummah's entire longest-era of proselytism (Abbasid Baghdad being its own fountainhead) imported its millions of missionaries as *science, scholarship, Islamic Arabia* — not by bloodshed but by the free reasoning-in-clarity of the revealed Truth: *rushd from ghayy clear* — enough.

**The Handhold Unbreakable — al-ʿUrwah al-Wuthqā**

Then the creed's own grip-promise is dispensed: *fa-man yakfur bi'l-ṭāghūti wa yuʾmin bi-llāhi fa-qadi istamsaka bi'l-ʿurwati al-wuthqā lā infiṣāma lahā* — "so whoever disavows the false deities (*al-ṭāghūt*) and believes in God — he has grasped the most unfailing handhold — which never breaks." The word *ṭāghūt* — *false-deity tyranny* — the commentators saddle with the broadest possible capacity: Satan himself; idols; sorcerers and soothsayers; demonized rulers; everything unruled that lures human beings out of the domain of God's Own custody: and the scene-image is the one the word wuthqā gives: a *hand-loop, a grasping-hold*: (the Arabic language's classical image of the rope and the knot): the believer's grip upon God's religion compared to a drowning man's grip upon the loop the Rescuer lowers: *lā infiṣāma lahā* — *it shall never break* — with infiṣām glossed by the scholars of language as the shattering that comes after warning (the Book's own register of subtle: no small crack, no whispering split but *snap-sudden-total*): so the bond the believing heart makes toward God cannot part: *God never lets it crack*: and the last seal — *wa Allāhu samīʿun ʿalīm* — "and God is Hearing, Knowing" — revisiting the sealing-pair of vv. 181 and 224 and 227 as the v. 256's own dilatory-witness: God heard what your heart said; God knows whether your hanging-fingers ever truly firmed around the grip: — the qualification of *believes in God* being the Book's own reminder at every sealing: the grip only counts where the belief is real: God hears, and God knows.

**No Compulsion — Because the Handhold Takes Care of Itself**

The tradition always concludes its reading of verse 256 on this two-fold instruction: (1) toward governing: believers are in no department *allowed to force a conversion*: forced faith does not count and no compulsion is allowed; and (2) toward the believer's own spiritual privacy: whoever truly "disavows the ṭāghūt and believes in God" enters into such a union-heaven-cord-clef that *no storm of life* nor storm of heaven can wrench him from it: God's covenant with believers being sealed by the same belt of wuthqā His own verse has just figured — *the most unfailing handhold — never breaking*: and at the heart of the believer's gratitude litany recycles the phrase down every street of Islam since: *alḥamdulillāhi ʿalā naʿmat al-īmān*: praise belongs to God for the goodly-gift of Faith: the covenant's own promise through the grip given in the scripture's grip's own says: *holdfast into the loop*: *it shall never snap*: and God is Hearing, Knowing.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:257

> **Allah is the Guardian of the believers—He brings them out of darkness and into light. As for the disbelievers, their guardians are false gods who lead them out of light and into darkness. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Walī — The Allies in High**

The verse following the freedom-charter now names the necessary symmetry of every believer's own legal custody — and its opposite: *Allāhu waliyyu alladhīna āmanū yukhrijuhum mina al-ẓulumāti ilā al-nūr* — "God is the *Walī* of those who believe — bringing them out from the darknesses into the light" — *wa-lladhīna kafarū awliyāʾuhumu al-ṭāghūtu yukhrijūnahum mina al-nūri ilā al-ẓulumāt* — "and as for those who disbelieve — their protectors are the false idols (*al-ṭāghūt*) — bringing them out from the light into the darknesses." The title *al-walī* is the Book's tender sovereignty-word of tutelage — legal guardian, protector, friend — set over *awliyāʾ* in the plural in the opposite verse-half: *one God* — *many idols*: (1) God is the *single* patron; (2) the false podesta are *legion* — their litany, one following the other as guides in darkness, one multiplying lead after the other: the tradition's own philosophy-of-religion reading the very Arabic plural-structures of it exactly so: religion's route to God is *one*; going astray is always multiple: all roads back lead into the One — but the roads away lead into multitudes.

**Out of Darkness — Into Light; And Back Again**

The commentators (al-Ṭabarī at the head, al-Rāzī following) give the same philosophical contrast-image: ḍulumāt — *darknesses* (the plural) — is glossed as the manifold guises of disbelief — falsehood, terror, doubt, despair, the multiplying non-lights of the soul's own realm; *nūr* — *light* (the singular) — is glossed as the one true faith — the lamp of the believers who say "our own Lord's light" — the writers of tafsir never missing the stroke the Book repeatedly uses for the contrast with the opposite direction recorded: the unbelievers' journey "from the light into the darknesses" re-poses itself as the pluralized darkness: (1) the believer's ending-light *is one*: as at 5:16 and 14:1, 14:5, 57:9 and 65:11 — the entire Qur'an's own account of migration from the many to the One, from plural darkness to singular light: (2) the unbelievers' ending-darknesses *are many* — the whole horror of Ṭāghūt-worship being precisely its plural-proliferating manner of disseminating the leadings: idols following idols, superstitions following superstitions, conquest following conquest unto ruin: and the verse's final sentence *ulāʾika aṣḥābu al-nāri hum fīhā khālidūn* — *those are the dwellers of the Fire, abiding therein* — burning the whole décor of the journey out with a theater-closing pronouncement: *the light-out riders do not discover a bearable country: they discover the Fire*: the journey is terminal, and there is no journey back: the whole judgment-day preaching of Islam's classical sermonists has taken this verse as their own eternal pair-balance for the wandering nations of the strange villages of idols: *God is the walī of the believers — the idols are their awliyāʾ — and He brings them out toward the light — and they bring them out toward the darknesses — and those shall be among the inhabitants of the Fire, abiding forever*.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:258

> **Are you ˹O Prophet˺ not aware of the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord because Allah had granted him kingship? ˹Remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord is the One Who has power to give life and cause death.” He argued, “I too have the power to give life and cause death.” Abraham challenged ˹him˺, “Allah causes the sun to rise from the east. So make it rise from the west.” And so the disbeliever was dumbstruck. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The King Who Disputed Abraham**

The sūrah continues its gallery of lesson-brush portraits mounted after Saul, now drawing the most audacious of all — the crowned man who argued religion with God's Friend: *a lam tara ilā alladhī ḥājja ibrāhīma fī rabbihi an ātāhu Allāhu al-mulk* — "have you not considered him who disputed with Abraham about his Lord — *because God had given him sovereignty*?" The commentators attach the ancient name (wisely withholding its certainty: al-Ṭabarī's reports name Nimrod — the clan-tales' own king of Babel), but the Book does not name him: the Book's interest is the *type*: the king whose crown swelled till it occluded his heavenward sight: the genitive *because* — *an ātāhu Allāhu al-mulk* — being the diagnostic of the debate's psychological root: he argued with Abraham about the Lord *precisely because* God's grant of kingship had intoxicated him: the throne becoming the throne's own argument against the Throne of God. The debate's proceedings stand famous from generation to generation: Abraham began with the creed's plainest summary: *rabbī alladhī yuḥyī wa yumīt* — "My Lord gives life and causes death": and the king, with the improvised theater of tyrant answered, producing two of his prisoners, releasing one, and executing the other, crowed his blasphemous mimicry: *anā uḥyī wa umīt* — "I too give life and cause death": — the same voice Pharaoh will deploy thousands of years later ("I am your lord most high" — 79:24) — always the same stage-play: substitution of judgment-acts for the giving of *life*: presented as substitution itself: the royal delusion that executing or sparing on its grass-throne is equivalent to quickening the dead: the commentators' precision bridles at the absurdity, underlining the verse's own lesson at once: slaying a man who already lives trades in none of the three divine arrests of life (conception, growth, resurrection): one deals only with the removal of what *is*: the other deals with what *wasn't*: and so the prophet's counter-answer arrives in the very warp of nature.

**"Bring the Sun From the West" — The Confounding**

Abraham's riposte, leaving every rehearsal of abstract argument aside, fastens at once upon the one evidence every man sees with his two eyes every morning: *fa-inna Allāha yaʾtī bi'l-shamsi mina al-mashriq* — "truly God brings the sun from the east" — *fa-ʾti bihā mina al-maghrib* — "so bring it from the west": with the final clause breaking in the Book's own taunting after-tune: *fa-buhita alladhī kafar* — "thus was the disbeliever confounded." The verb — *bahata* — *to be dumbfounded, stricken with surprise into silence*: the Book's own eloquence-book severs at once two analyses: the king cannot reverse one degree of sky-work; but more fatally, he cannot *come back* with any logic at all: his pantomime of life-dealing was instantly unmasked by nature's own testimony: every dawn is itself a daily resurrection: the same One who lifts the sun from the east each morning resurrects by the same hand every human body from its after-death: *if your sceptre has no power even over a single morning: how then could you plausibly be the lord of life?* — and the Book's doom-clause seals: *wa Allāhu lā yahdī al-qawma al-ẓālimīn* — "and God does not guide the wrongdoing people": the *lā yahdī* brushed over the whole typologies of the tyrant-evidence: the sun attests; the wrongdoers see nothing: *God guides no wrongdoers*: their perversity is not evidence-lack but stance: the Sufi teachers of the heart have always heard the verse's final sentence as the explanation for the previous two centuries of the whole sūrah's own contentions-with-substitute-intelligence: the mimicker-king's blindness is not an unusual lamp-blindness reserved to Babel; it is the standing plague of every unbelieving argument across the ages: *their reasoning is perversion concluded: God guides not the wrongdoers.*

**Abraham's Two-Lamp Method**

The tradition has ever treasured at the heart of the verse the very two-lamp pattern the Book authored itself: the lamp Abraham lit at 6:75-79 — when he passed night-side gazing upon the ascending star, the waxing moon, the rising sun: "this is my Lord — this is bigger" — the same natural tuition that builds up every man's creed from evidences — and the lamp of 6:78's own subsequent: "this is my Lord" — uttered not in idolatry but in the search of signs -- the Book's two great portraits of its own generations of prophetic natural theologies anchored at *two* Abrahamic occurrences: (a) the sky-gazing: observing the Lord's wisdom in the heavens; (b) the logic defeating: at the artificial-throne's counterfeit of life and light: both confirm that the natural world by which Abraham trained his own eyes is the same natural world the tyrant cannot alter by one measure: *even the sun is Abraham's witness — its eastward rising defies every king's claim*. And the fiqh-school's own tradition-evidence of smallness against every puffed-up king remains as long as these two words the Book's own lyrical mettle: *fa-inna Allāha yaʾtī bi'l-shamsi mina al-mashriq, fa-ʾti bihā mina al-maghrib* — two phrases of not-very-long life-terms of the earth's daily physics dragging down the entire crowned fantasy: and with its fate the tyrant has ever since lain *confounded — fa-buhita alladhī kafar — God guides not wrongdoing people.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:259

> **Or ˹are you not aware of˺ the one who passed by a city which was in ruins. He wondered, “How could Allah bring this back to life after its destruction?” So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years then brought him back to life. Allah asked, “How long have you remained ˹in this state˺?” He replied, “Perhaps a day or part of a day.” Allah said, “No! You have remained here for a hundred years! Just look at your food and drink— they have not spoiled. ˹But now˺ look at ˹the remains of˺ your donkey! And ˹so˺ We have made you into a sign for humanity. And look at the bones ˹of the donkey˺, how We bring them together then clothe them with flesh!” When this was made clear to him, he declared, “˹Now˺ I know that Allah is Most Capable of everything.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Town Upon Its Roofs**

The sūrah's resurrection-cluster proceeds from debate to experience: no argument this time — an object-lesson lived through in the flesh: *aw ka-lladhī marra ʿalā qaryatin wa hiya khāwiyatun ʿalā ʿurūshihā* — "or the like of him who passed by a town as it lay fallen upon its roofs." The commentators set his passing amid the post-exile-deserted land of Palestine — the town thrown down so totally that its roofs were beneath its walls (*khāwiyah ʿalā ʿurūshihā*: the roofs collapsed onto themselves, the phrase also yielding the sense of *empty-hollowed out*): the most-venerable opinion (going back to Ibn ʿAbbās and passed on through al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr) calls the man ʿUzayr — Ezra — though the school carefully registers alternates (Ezekiel, al-Khiḍr, or unnamed others, even irrelevant to the doctrinal heart: al-Rāzī glossing the whole as possible also with an unnamed unbelieving skeptic turned believer). And the man's exclamation, as he viewed the collapsed town, was not in contempt but in width of wonder: *annā yuḥyī hādhihi Allāhu baʿda mawtihā* — "how shall God bring this back to life after its death?" — the phrase *yuḥyī* — *give life* — being the sealed-interrogative of all resurrection-skepticism propounded once the decay has proceeded beyond the archiving human eye: *who* — with what Body-chisel, what monumental re-allocation, what logistics of atom-collecting — would ever rebuild *this*?

**A Hundred Years — As a Day or Part of a Day**

And God answered with the only fitting response to a question of *how*: an embodied demonstration: *fa-amātahu Allāhu miʾata ʿāmin thumma baʿathahu* — "so God caused him to die — one hundred years — then raised him up." The school reports the marvel with its customary awe: he slept; his food was within the city which had been long-framed with desolation; his donkey was beside him: and a hundred years unrolled across the world: empires floated, houses were repopulated, the city's ruins were arranged again into a brightly-inhabited town — while he slept the block-sleep of the dead: until the rousing came: *qāla kam labithta* — "how long have you tarried?" — *qāla labithtu yawman aw baʿḍa yawm* — "a day — or part of a day": — the sleeper's timelessness complete: a century compressed into the senses-scale of a forenoon-nap: — and the responder's disclosure: *bal labithta miʾata ʿāmin* — "no — you have tarried a hundred years" — and then the corroboration wound round by the preservation-miracle itself: *fa-unẓur ilā ṭaʿāmika wa sharābika lam yatasannah* — "look at your food and your drink — they have not spoiled": *a hundred years old, and the bread still unsoured, the drink unspoiled* (God pausing the chemistry of decay over his provisions in proof-sport), *wa unẓur ilā ḥimārik* — "and look at your donkey": — the donkey, dead, dispersed, weathered: characteristic animals' bones strewn, until . . .

**"Look at the Bones, How We Set Them Up"**

The Book crescendos finally to the totem verse of resurrection-experience — *wa li-najʿalaka āyatan li'l-nās* — "and [this was done] that We may make you a sign for mankind" — *wa unẓur ilā al-ʿiẓāmi kayfa nunshizuhā thumma naksūhā laḥmā* — "and look at the bones — how We set them up — then clothe them with flesh": the bones being read both as the dead bones of the donkey (the most acclaimed reading: al-Ṭabarī's and all the classic mufassirūn's — God's prophetic visual-lecture performed upon the animal-carcass in front of the revived man: bones knitting, sinews stretching, hide and flesh clothing the skeleton in sequence) — and equally fitting the man himself (the same physics he had himself just passed through: as al-Rāzī's account allows): and after its completion the words of fresh certitude fall from the believer's own tongue: *aʿlamu anna Allāha ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr* — "I know that God has power over all things": — so the cynic-turned-witness became God's great church-argument: *a sign for mankind*: the tradition's understanding-spelled-out wisdom flowing on with the most-quoted hadith-functional parallel itself, from the description of the sleepers of the cave-cohort (18:19's own similar staging: "so We raised them up that they might question one another... how long have you tarried? They said: a day — or part of a day") — the two sleep-lectures utterly similar in their cropping out the believer's potential answer: he knew — or came to know — *God can indeed* — for He just *did*. The school's own arch-summary of the verse's moral is to the selfsame end as every great tafsīr-school has perpetually authored, passing on down: *whoever asks how resurrection could be — this is the story's own reply: believe first, and you see: not the awaiting: then you know that God can do everything*: and the tradition's own beloved epilogue to it stands in the Prophet's frequent reminders of the same confidence: that resurrection is not the marvel mankind doubts, but the simplest of God's works — as He said: "He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation" (39:6)

**A Sign for Mankind — The Verse's Permanent Window**

The functional effect of verse 259 at all subsequent stages of Islam's creedal canvas is permanent: it is the twin-panel of verse 260's Abraham-vision below us — and both stand for the same great transaction between promise and display: God's resurrection-promises are shown *visible*: granted *as witness*: sign-gifts for mankind to watch-and-hold: beasts demolished re-built; men sent to their death-sleeps and return; cities restored from their own collapsed roofs and floorings: *all of them demonstrations* — that the Grand Resurrection of the World's End is not uncertain: it is *commensurately* — already proven in Adam's own special times: *God can do all things — so believe it* — and with the signing of eyes outside heroes' own silenced witness: Qiyamah is credible, quietening the soul from doubt's dark glaze: and as the tradition repeats for the whole long-needed studies of the rasul-stations: *the same town that stood fallen upon its roofs, stands in the earth's teachings permanently ahead of every believer* — lest he ask again: how — on what handfuls — does God raise the dead — and the Answer comes from the Book: *look then — and be satisfied — and know that God has power over all things.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:260

> **And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord! Show me how you give life to the dead.” Allah responded, “Do you not believe?” Abraham replied, “Yes I do, but just so my heart can be reassured.” Allah said, “Then bring four birds, train them to come to you, ˹then cut them into pieces,˺ and scatter them on different hilltops. Then call them back, they will fly to you in haste. And ˹so you will˺ know that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Show Me How" — The Friend Asks His Friend**

The sūrah's resurrection-cluster closes with the most tender exchange in all of the Abraham-file: *wa idh qāla ibrāhīmu rabbi arinī kayfa tuḥyī al-mawtā* — "and when Abraham said: my Lord — show me how You give life to the dead." The commentators have always been careful to defend the question's honor against every surface-reading of doubt (al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr joining agreement at its iteration): the salaf laid down its interpretive principle in one stroke: Abraham's faith in the *fact* of resurrection was never in question — the question he asks concerns the *mode*: the how, not the whether: the difference between believing in a thing with the heart and seeing it done with the eyes: the request is the petition for *kashf* — unveiling — the same station God Himself describes granting Abraham at 6:75 ("thus We showed Abraham the kingdom of the heavens and the earth — so that he might be of those who certainty"): faith already established, now asking God to *rear it up:* to vision-full assurance: and the tradition's glossers never cease to prize the heavenly rebuke that follows as the Book's most delicate interrogative: *qāla a wa lam tuʾmin* — "He said: do you not believe?" — the very locution aching in its inverse form: He does not say "why do you ask?": He asks, *do you not believe?* — and Abraham answers with every believer's soon-throated answer: *qāla balā* — "yes — indeed!" — *wa lākin li-yaṭmaʾinna qalbī* — "but so that my heart may be at peace": the psalm-phrase has become the ummah's standing dictum of verified belief ever since: faith's verbal confidence seeking its *iṭmiʾnān* — its quieted heart-knowledge: *yes, Lord — but I ask to know more surely*: and the Lord, honoring the petition whose heart it sprang from, grants it.

**Four Birds, Every Mountain**

Then comes God's assignment: *fa-khudh arbaʿatan mina al-ṭayri fa-ṣurhunna ilayka* — "take four birds — and make them be drawn to you" — *thumma ajʿal ʿalā kulli jabalin minhunna juzʾan* — "then place a piece of them on every mountain" — *thumma udʿuhunna yaʾtīnaka saʿyā* — "then call them — they will come to you in haste." The commentators reconstruct the scene with exactness: Abraham takes the four birds; draws them to himself (*ṣur*: inclining, catching, accustomed-tying them); and by God's command dismembers and portions them, setting their parts upon distant hilltops — every mountain beholding one fragment — while retaining in his hand, in the commentators' standard account, their heads; and then calls them — and the dismembered fowl *reassemble and come flying to him,* alive — reconstituted at God's summons just as the verse records it: *they will come to thee in haste*: *saʿy* — *hastening effort*: the birds answered the calling. The school never loses the lesson the Book written into it: the miracle was not chosen at random — it was the perfect miniature of the Resurrection: members scattered, bones dispersed, utterances severed — and at God's call all come back — whole — unlost — *nothing of you shall be lost:* as verse 2:255's own *yaʿlamu mā bayna aydīhim* makes sure: every atom returning to the One who numbered its trajectory: the birds' own reintegration is therefore a standing hadith-image in the medieval-commentary lineage: each generation of believers reads in its own century's ashes and centuries-graves the same thing Abraham saw with his own eyes: *the birds came running back*: *and so we shall come running back at His call*: *and know that God is Mighty, Wise* — as the last words of 2:260 put it.

**Mighty, Wise — The Twin Seals**

The twins of God are the message's last two Names: *ʿazīz* — mighty — whom the resurrecting God binds always to the gravitations of His appointments — and *ḥakīm* — wise: God knows best in whose hands He trusts this great sight: not to idolaters, not to doubters, but to the friend who already believed: the wisdom is doubly manifested: (1) *He grants uncovering to the believing heart, not to the mocking ear*: and (2) *He grants that uncovering in a form that teaches every later believing reader*: Abraham's posture forever the believer's own: *grant me your eyesightu* — *show me how you give life* — *for thou art His friend whose whole belief is already certain* — and the faith-knowers of the Book's own generations reading this verse across the ages have mostly read it in Abraham's own manner: *I believe — but shore me up by this seeing*: *yaṭmaʾinna qalbī* — the very phrase for the heart's quest of equanimity carried forward in the Qur'an's every later usage of the same verb (13:28's own center: "Truly in the remembrance of God do hearts find peace" — always cited at verses 2:260's own shore-lesson: the heart's stillness is God's great sacrament: remembrance being its daily-bread without which no believer can live). And the ends and the lesson of the four-birds-miracle is sealed by their world-warrant: the same reassembly is promised to every believer's own atom-housing one Day of its calling: *that Day their chests shall fly back toward them hasting from every crown-mountain of their scattering*: and the answer God gave Abraham has already answered everything in His servant: *yaṭmaʾinna qalbī* — *my heart is at peace* — and know that God is Mighty, Wise — for all of it is Truth.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:261

> **The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a grain that sprouts into seven ears, each bearing one hundred grains. And Allah multiplies ˹the reward even more˺ to whoever He wills. For Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Seed and the Seven Hundred**

The sūrah now opens its concluding register — the economics of giving — with the most famous agricultural parable of the Book: *mathalu alladhīna yunfiqūna amwālahum fī sabīli Allāhi ka-mathali ḥabbatin anbatat sabʿa sanābila fī kulli sunbulatin miʾatu ḥabbah* — "the parable of those who spend their wealth in God's way is that of a grain that grew seven ears — in every ear a hundred grains." The numbers sit before every hearer, child and scholar alike: one seed → seven ears → seven hundred grains: and the Book deliberately chooses the most humble of images — a single seed — for the most overwhelming of returns: the law of God's giving is *planting*, not subtracting: what goes into the soil does not vanish; it rises in multiples: and the commentators never cease to draw the soul's eye along the parable's full trajectory: the gift, whispered to a poor man's hand on an obscure afternoon, is not *spent*: it is *sown*: the seed sinks into God's field, invisible to the sower, and swells within God's custody until the day it breaks forth as an entire harvest on a Day when every grain shall be needed. The Book elsewhere erects the same multiplication-ladder at other rungs ("whoever brings a good deed shall have ten times its like" — 6:160); here the rungs climb still higher — seven hundredfold — and the Prophet ﷺ drew the ceiling off the whole arithmetic:

> *"Every deed of the son of Adam is multiplied — a good deed between tenfold and seven hundredfold — save fasting: for God says: 'Fasting is Mine, and I Myself reward it.'"* (al-Bukhārī 1904, 5927; Muslim 1151, 1152 — the hadith qudsī on the multiplication of deeds, always quoted beneath this very verse in every tafsīr upon 2:261)

And the tangible camels-and-dinar imagery of these reports — a man gives a camel in God's way; the Prophet tells him: *"on the Day of Judgment you shall have seven hundred camels"* (as Ibn Kathīr's compilation reports of this verse's occasion-family) — shows that the multiplication is meant in the seriousness of actual recompense, not as an allegory of small comfort.

**God Multiplies for Whom He Wills — The Open Multiplier**

The Book does not lock the ratio to *seven hundred* and no more: *wa Allāhu yuḍāʿifu li-man yashāʾ* — "and God multiplies for whomsoever He wills." The commentators perceive in the clause two complementary freedoms: (1) the multiplication can exceed the parable's stated seven hundred — there is no ceiling on God's multiplying: the measure of the increase follows the quality of the giver's heart — the intention, the purity, the follow-through, the gratitude in the begging moment — hence two men may give the same coin and harvest utterly different multiplications, since God multiplies *by His knowledge of hearts*, not by arithmetic of dirhams; and (2) the multiplier attaches equally to the *varieties* of spending: the gold-dinar alms, the cup of water, the carried shoulder of a tired brother, the spoken blessing upon a building — each is a grain; and God multiplies *for whom He wills*: the sower does not appoint his own rates; he simply plants and entrusts. And the ending Names seal the economy: *wa Allāhu wāsiʿun ʿalīm* — "and God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing": *wāsiʿ* — vast of bounty, never exhausted, nowhere pinched; *ʿalīm* — knowing the least seed and the deepest seed-socket of intention: the parable of the grain is therefore a whole doctrine: give without measuring, give without exhausting your Lord's treasury, give perceived that the All-Encompassing already saw.

**The Traditional Harvest**

The earliest teachers of the ummah loved this parable to the ground. The Prophet's community was schooled within it in bodies: Anas ibn Mālik recounts a man singling out his finest camel and saying: "This camel I give in the way of God": and the Prophet's answer sealed its destiny: *"On the Day of Judgment you will have seven hundred camels"* — the *hadith*'s companions' heard in the writing of the primary Anas-adjacent reports (always quoted in the tafsīr classes of this verse); and the Prophet's own fine formulations in the *hadith qudsī* described God's clutch of the morsel:

> *"God takes the good deed from a lawful earning and grows it as one of you grows his foal or his camel, until it becomes like a mountain or greater."* (the paraphrased portion of the Prophet's tradition reported from Abū Hurayrah and others, with its careful — *from a lawful earning* — the very words al-Bukhārī's editors placed in his Book of Zakāh (al-Bukhārī 1410; Muslim 1014 — the Prophet's saying concerning the morsel given in charity that God receives in His right hand and grows like a foal until it is like a mountain, its wording being preserved in its entirety in the two Ṣaḥīḥs)

So the sūrah's seed-and-harvest stands in all the generations of believers: your smallest choice of grace is the farm-field of God's Seven Hundred — and the One who has planted it promises the multiplying of it for whomever He wills: *God is All-Encompassing, Knowing*.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:262

> **Those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah and do not follow their charity with reminders of their generosity or hurtful words—they will get their reward from their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Apostasy-Proverbs of Charity**

The sūrah now attaches to its seed-parable the test of the believing giver: *alladhīna yunfiqūna amwālahum fī sabīli Allāhi thumma lā yutbiʿūna mā anfaqū mannan wa lā adhan* — "those who spend their wealth in God's way, and then follow not what they spent with *mann* — preening — nor *adhā* — injury." The commentators are unanimous in their warnings at the two terms: *mann* — *the reminder* — following a gift with reminders of it: "I clothed you," "I fed you," "remember what I did for you" — the self-congratulation that smothers the reward's flame in its infancy; *adhā* — *injury, hurt* — the gift saddled with worse: humiliation, reproach, slanted comments about the recipient's past and future, or the showcasing of his poverty for public laughter: the gift thus delivered becomes the wound itself, and its recipient wishes he had never accepted. The tradition is unanimous in the severity of these two acts: they nullify the charity — *tabṭal* — as 2:264 will declare: the merely-reminded gift loses its reward in God's books because the giver has already taken his wage in men's compliments: the recompense the beneficiary was meant to owe to God's own treasuries has already been absorbed, so God has no more to pay. And the Book's own opposing-image, at 2:263, completes the portrait: better a kind word than a charity accompanied by injury.

**"Their Reward Is With Their Lord"**

The blessing-stream now turns toward the giving which bears none of these stains: *lahum ajruhum ʿinda rabbihim* — "their reward is with their Lord": the recompense hitched not to the recipient's gratitude, not to public applause, not even to the giver's own memory of it — the wage laid up at God's own treasury where nothing perishes: and then the verse sings the sūrah's own stabilizing anthem — *wa lā khawfun ʿalayhim wa lā hum yaḥzanūn* — "and no fear shall be upon them — nor shall they grieve": the refrain that began its journey through the Book at 2:38 (Adam's own wayward children directed toward Paradise) and moved through 2:62 (the promise for the believing peoples), through 2:112 (whoever submits), and continues through 2:274 and 2:277: the two loudest human anxieties — fear-of-what-lies-ahead (*khawf*) and grief-from-what-has-passed (*ḥuzn*) — both silenced by the giving that never seeks its echo among men: the commentators and the tradition never lose the stillness this sentence delivers: *no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve*: — for the Giver-of-every-harvest comes into their Day.

**The Tradition's Guard**

The Prophet's own teachings anywhere dismissing the exhibitionist-donor anchored themselves in the verse's very two words:

The Prophet's own dread-warning about spiritual adulteration accompanies it:

> *"O people! What I fear most for you is minor shirk." They said: "And what is minor shirk, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Showing off (riyāʾ). God will say on the Day of Judgment, when He requites His servants for their deeds: 'Go to those for whom you showed off in the world, and see whether you find any reward with them.'"* (Musnad Aḥmad — from Maḥmūd ibn Labīd — classed ṣaḥīḥ by the hadith authorities — the famous warning of *al-shirk al-aṣghar*, regularly summoned by the commentators describing *mannan wa adhan* and riyāʾ in the giving)

Rather, the tradition stays steadfast with the ways of the earliest generations: the gift hidden in a blind man's hand at night; the gift tucked beneath the beggar's cloth; the gift slid unseen into the sack between the loaves — and at their head, the Prophet's own testament in the most authenticated of all:

> *"Seven shall God shade on the Day when no shade shadows but His: a just ruler, a youth raised in the worship of God, a man whose heart is bound to the mosques, two men who loved each other for God's sake and gathered and parted in that love, a man who is enticed by a woman of beauty and rank and says: 'I fear God,' a man who gave in charity and concealed it until his left hand knew not what his right hand spent, and a man who remembered God in solitude and his eyes filled with tears."* (al-Bukhārī 660, 1423; Muslim 1031 — the Seven Under Shade: *a man who gave in charity and concealed it until his left hand knew not what his right hand spent* — the very hadith that 2:262 and the concealment-verses of the sūrah have always taught Islam's benefactors to take as their own living rule: the gift taken in God's shade needs no outing show)

Thus the humble gift, sliding into need's direction with no parade before it, takes its motto in the high ends of the sūrah's own column: *their reward is with their Lord* — *no fear shall come upon them — nor shall they grieve* — for the One who shall multiply it knows no equal — and the Day that shall open it is none other than God's own promise.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:263

> **Kind words and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allah is Self-Sufficient, Most Forbearing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Kind Word Outweighs a Wounded Gift**

The charity-code halves its long bloc now to measure the options open to a believer's heart when the beggar's hand extends and his own purse stays shut: *qawlun maʿrūfun wa maghfiratun khayrun min ṣadaqatin yatbaʿuhā adhan* — "an honorable word and forgiveness are better than a charity which injury follows." The commentators draw out the two treasures in full depth (al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī's own diligent registers): *qawl maʿrūf* — *a kindly-honorable word*: the believer's tongue being ever richer than his wallet: when a beggar knocks at a brother's door in the hour of dire need and the brother owns nothing to hand out, the Book instructs him to *speak worthy words* — 'God ease your distress,' 'God is with you, brother,' 'your patience is heard by the Lord' — the poor conscience of the giver not purchased by public fiat of a yawned-shut pocket; and *maghfirah* — *forgiveness*: the poor man's quest and importunity must then be excused at once — his persistence for cash, his brush of rudeness when it comes, all forgiven by the would-be giver: *better to heal-than-hurt*: greater honor to God, greater heart-worth to the giver — than the gift that is wrapped in infection. The verse has ever been read as the supreme Muslim doctrine of poverty-theology: a believer *never fails* the beggar: either with wealth (at the levels already prescribed), or else with dignifying words and the brother's pardon: the tradition recalling at this verse its greatest records of the Prophet's own behavior toward importunate askers — his gentleness-of-refusal recorded in the sunnah as his characteristic attitude (the Ṣaḥīḥ reports carrying scene after scene of the beggar who seized even his cloak, whom he answered without harshness — al-Bukhārī 5368; Muslim 1057) — its standard gloss everywhere: be generous, and be generously silent about it.

**Self-Sufficient, Clement — The Merciful Seals**

The verse's sealing-pair of Names — *wa Allāhu ghaniyyun ḥalīm* — "and God is Self-Sufficient, Clement": — are the two pillars of God's forbearance: *ghani* — *Rich beyond asking*: what any man's hand drops into the beggar's out-turned palm enriches God not one whit — as His own hold of honor-glories from Eternity has it: He needs no charity: the entire give-tribe of the earth's began: *His treasure-house needs no contributions*: and *ḥalīm* — *Clement:* He does not pour down instant putting-out-of-the-fire upon any brash man with a braying tongue — He bears the dickerings, holds off the verdicts, waits for the repentance: the two names now head-projected over the giver-and-beggar marketplace with all of its ancient temptations: the pocket-pinched believer with his head hung at the beggar — God Himself was not dependent on a dinar: speak kindly and forgive the beggar if he is importunate — that *was* the charity; and *God is Self-Sufficient*; and the *brash giver* — donative, yes, but insult-spilling — is not excused from God's account: even *his* beneficence stands nullified (2:264's own next verse says it immediately) — He knows it, and He is *Clement* nonetheless: hence Him dare ask with all the hope of repentance-fire of even the appalling slights the compromised charity: the Ropes of God's mercy are long enough to hold even the poisoned spending-man if he turns: *and God is Self-Sufficient, Clement* — surely Him alone is the infinitely-tolerant One whose account-book of every deed is always running one mercy-reach beyond our worst slump.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:264

> **O believers! Do not waste your charity with reminders ˹of your generosity˺ or hurtful words, like those who donate their wealth just to show off and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. Their example is that of a hard barren rock covered with a thin layer of soil hit by a strong rain— leaving it just a bare stone. Such people are unable to preserve the reward of their charity. Allah does not guide ˹such˺ disbelieving people.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Do Not Annul Your Charities" — The Direct Command**

The sūrah now turns from parable and commendation to legislation proper: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū lā tubṭilū ṣadaqātikum bi'l-manni wa'l-adhā* — "O you who believe — do not annul your acts of charity by preening and by injury." The verb *tubṭilū* — *make void, nullify* — is one of the Book's harshest audit-words (the same family as 2:217's verdict upon apostates: *ḥabiṭat aʿmāluhum* — "their deeds were made void"): the giver who adds *mann* — self-congratulatory reminders — and *adhā* — hurtful treatment — to his gift has *cancelled* the gift: voided it, as one tears up a contract into scraps: the commentators derive the mechanics from the phrase itself: the donation was a seed planted for God's harvest; the reminders and hurts are the salt the sower scatters over his own field; not only does the crop fail, the field itself becomes unworkable: the giving never reaches God's ledger at all. And the Book forthwith attaches the twin sin to its natural parent: *ka-lladhī yunfiqu mālahu riʾāʾa al-nās* — "like one who spends his wealth to be seen by men" — *wa lā yuʾminu bi-llāhi wa'l-yawmi al-ākhir* — "and believes not in God and the Last Day": here the verdict shows its terrible teeth: the *riyāʾ* — the display-heart — is not a peccadillo grown on the charity's edge; it is a flowering planted out of *unbelief*: *he believes not in God and the Last Day*: for the man sincerely reckoning upon God's Day does not perform before men's eyes — he performs before the Eye that will see him then; display is itself a measure of lost faith: the tradition's most sober hadith on exhibitionism stands as verse 264's own extended gloss:

> *"Whoever makes a display of his deeds, God will display him (make his purpose manifest); and whoever acts deceptively before people, God will unmask him."* (al-Bukhārī 6499; Muslim 2987 — the Prophet's saying of *man yurāʾi yurāʾi Allāhu bihi* and *man summaʿa summaʿa Allāhu bihi* — always quoted as the twin-witness with 2:264 in the dossiers of display in every fiqh-and-tazkiyah commentary down the centuries)

**The Smooth Rock and the Sweeping Rain**

Then comes the counter-parable of the grain — the Book deliberately contrasting its two emblematic seeds (the fertile grain of v. 261 against the bare rock of v. 264): *fa-mathaluhu ka-mathali ṣafwānin ʿalayhi turābun fa-aṣābahu wābilun fa-tarakahu ṣaldan* — "his parable is that of a smooth rock: dust upon it — a downpour strikes it — and leaves it barren." The commentators unfold the image's cruel beauty: the *ṣafwān* is a stone slab whose surface is smooth — unable to hold any life — with a mere skin of dust lying over its top: the *wābil* — a heavy, driving downpour — descends: a blessing sent to grow; yet on this surface the blessing achieves the opposite: the rain does not soak in (there is nowhere to soak); it only strips: the dust-jacket is swept clean away, and what remains is *ṣald* — *bare stone, naked and lifeless*: the exhibitionist's charity is thus: he scattered something that bore the *appearance* of generosity, but the soil was stone — intention made of showing — and the Day of Account's first downpour will disclose him utterly denuded: *lā yaqdirūna ʿalā shayʾin mimmā kasabū* — "**they have no power over anything of what they earned**": God's own words passing the sentence on the whole file: not one drachma of all he gave remains to his name at the Reckoning: every coin spent to be seen of men has already drawn its wage in the market of men's gazes — his account stands empty of them all.

**"God Guides Not the Disbelieving People"**

The verse's last signature puts the whole picture under its solemn brand: *wa Allāhu lā yahdī al-qawma al-kāfirīn* — "and God guides not the disbelieving people." The commentators register the shocking appellation without flinching (the brand *kāfirīn* attached to givers whose problem was ostentation): the verse is stern in its doctrine: display-heart is a species of unbelief — for the man who truly believed in God would never trade God's glance for the gazes of the rabble: and guidance is thereby sealed off from the whole class: *God guides not the disbelieving people* — for He guides the sincere, whose pulses beat for an audience of One. And the Tradition's first teachers embedded the lesson so deeply into the believing conscience that the standard prayer of the pious for millennia has feared this exact verdict and begged refuge:

> *"O God, I seek refuge in You from knowingly associating aught with You, and I ask Your forgiveness for what I do unknowingly."* — the refuge-prayer upon *hidden showing-off* from the Prophet's own treasury of supplications (Musnad Aḥmad; al-Ṭabarānī — the Prophet's *duʿāʾ al-shirk al-khafī* — always quoted in the commentators' accounts of 2:264's teachings for asking God's pardon even for veiled ostentation)

And the same tradition passes on what God's own Book itself taught at the foundation: 107:4-6's blistering verse upon those who perform prayers for show with withheld small-kindnesses ("woe to the praying ones — heedless of their prayer — the showmen — who repel even small kindness"): the whole *sūrah* of the almsgiving now passes under God's own scarification: charity, the holiest of externals, is canceled by the least of internals — for God builds His ledger upon sincerity before all sums thereof: *they have no power over anything of what they earned — and God guides not the disbelieving people.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:265

> **And the example of those who donate their wealth, seeking Allah’s pleasure and believing the reward is certain, is that of a garden on a fertile hill: when heavy rain falls, it yields up twice its normal produce. If no heavy rain falls, a drizzle is sufficient. And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Counter-Seed — The Garden on the Hill**

The sūrah's metaphoric gallery of giving now reaches its crowning image — the antitype of the bare rock of the verse preceding: *wa mathalu alladhīna yunfiqūna amwālahumu ibtighāʾa marḍāti Allāhi wa tathbītan min anfusihim ka-mathali jannatin bi-rabwatin* — "and the parable of those who spend their wealth seeking God's Good Pleasure, and out of a confirmation within their souls, is that of a garden upon a hill." The Book is painting the believers' *truest giving*: motivated not by display (*riyāʾ*) but by *ibtighāʾ marḍāti Allāh* — *seeking God's Good Pleasure*: the same phrase that closed 2:207's portrait of the soul-seller — the twin commerce of God's servants: by the same adding-line: *tathbītan min anfusihim* — *out of a confirmation in their souls* — the commentators glossing the beautiful phrase in its accepted registers: an inner firmness, a certainty of soul, a steady dutifulness settled at the center of the heart — not an impulsive, crowd-pleasing splurge, nor tip-collecting of the needy when convenient, but *steady-rooted generosity as a natural flowering of an already-permanent faith*: the heart *confirmed* — established — *tathbīt* — so that the charity appears not as the aberration of an occasionally noble hour but as the natural reflex of a believing soul. This pair — *seeking God's pleasure* (the outward compass) *and out of soul-steadiness* (the inward condition) — titles the verse as the perfect counterweight of 2:264's display-without-faith: one is *pleasure-hunting by God; the other is pleasure-hunting by men*: the two gardens now to bloom in the parables coming after it.

**A Downpour — Or Just a Soft Rain**

The simile's weight and loveliness pass to its apex now: *aṣābahā wābilun fa-ātat ukulahā ḍiʿfayn* — "a downpour strikes it — it brings forth its fruit *twofold*" — *fa-in lam yuṣibhā wābilun fa-ṭall* — "and if a downpour does not strike it — then a soft rain *suffices*." The commentators lose themselves in the parable's two-tier blessing: the same driving downpour that swept 2:264's bare rock barren turns *this* garden's every tree to double-fruitage — the giving done in soul-steadiness produces *twice* the fruit at every turn of history and at every step of God's own nurture — and the miracle of the verse's next clause lies precisely in its counter-sober luxury: *even without the downpour — just a soft drizzle — it yields*: God's own point being: the soul-steady giver's charity *needs no spectacular storms*: the smallest trickle of God's ordinary sustenance suffices for a rich yield of fruit — because the ground itself was true: the garden *upon a hill*: some commentators unfolding the *rabwah* — elevated ground — as signifying the charity-free of stagnant humiliation (raised above petty brook-flooding's dependencies: wholesome soil, not bog; well-drained, not drowned) — al-Rāzī further weighing the hill-site against the hollow-site dialogically: he contends the best garden truly lies *not* at hill-crest (scorched by wind and without streams) nor in bottom-land (drowned by stagnation) but at *level-ease* — *wajd* — but the school holds a broader understanding that *rabwah* bears the sense of *fertile rising soil*: raised above ordinary ground, well-structed for enhancement — as al-Qurṭubī's and Abū Ḥayyān's school both comment with the considered reading favour whenever debate lags: regardless of altitudes: *even the drizzle suffices* — *the soft rain brings it fruit.*

**God Sees What You Do**

The verse closes upon its pillar-signature *wa Allāhu bi-mā taʿmalūna baṣīr* — "and God of whatsoever you do is Seeing": the third planting of *baṣīr* in the sūrah's family-code sequences already (2:233's own sealing at the nursing's end — and again at 2:237's own conclusion of the mahr-clause): with *baṣīr* chosen above every other Name of God as the exact virtue-token for the soul-steady giver: God's seeing is *the audience of the sincere*: where the displayer sought men's eyes, the sincere chooses God's eye — and God's All-Seeing is the price-pays for every unseen doing: let the right hand give without the left's knowledge, let the coin slide into the blind beggar's palm unwitnessed — *Allāhu bi-mā taʿmalūna baṣīr*: He sees both the coin and the intention that moved it. And the tradition's pride in its own concealment-art comes alive at the very place where the school ever since has positioned its charitable-culture-heroine-texts: from Abū Dharr's quiet-shirt of dates-hidden from his own tracing-bearers, to the anonymous giveries at qayrawani and Samarkandi cellars of the poor — whose original source is the same school of *gifts hidden from left hand* — all tracing directly back to the light cast by this very verse and 2:262's own praise of uninjured giving —

> *"On the day when there shall be no shade but God's shade — He shall shade seven: ...a man who gave in charity and concealed it until his left hand knew not what his right hand spent."* (al-Bukhari 660/1423; Muslim 1031 — the standing authentic hadith always cited at this verse's pillar-inscription: *baṣīr*: God sees: you need no audience but His Eye: He is the Shade beneath which the secret-giver walks)

and with their serenest glory the whole concluding tafers of the sūrah now open for us the great gate of *2:266* — the *garden of one vivid hopeless-dream*: the verse of the old man's garden reversed through God's power-hadiths — about which the Book's own final exhortation stands at the school:
> *"Deeds are by their ends"* — and God's whole judgment-eye.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:266

> **Would any of you wish to have a garden with palm trees, grapevines, and all kinds of fruits with rivers flowing underneath and as they grow very old with dependent children, a fiery whirlwind hits the garden, burning it all up? This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so perhaps you will reflect.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Burning Garden — The Parable's Horror**

The sūrah's seed-and-garden gallery ends with its most haunting vision — the parable of the ruined estate: *a yawaddu aḥadukum an takūna lahu jannatun min nakhīlin wa aʿnāb* — "would any one of you be glad to have a garden of date palms and grapevines" — commentators pointing to the two staple-producing trees of the region's agricultural abundance (the date-palm, main food of Arabia; the vineyard, main luxury) — *tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār* — "rivers running beneath it": a garden entirely self-sufficient by the waters that flow beneath it: *lahu fīhā min kulli al-thamarāt* — "possessing therein of every kind of fruit": its inventory dating itself across every variety of harvest; *wa aṣābahu al-kibaru wa lahu dhurriyyatun ḍuʿafāʾ* — "and old age befalls him while he has weak progeny" — *fa-aṣābahā iʿṣārun fīhi nārun fa-iḥtaraqat* — "and then a whirlwind carrying fire strikes it — and it is consumed": — ¡The whole beautiful estate, doubtless maintained across his whole life's wealth, ingathered lore of irrigation and cultivation, the entire sunshine-security for his ancient age — engulfed in one fire-storm!* — his children too young and too weak to rebuild, black ashes lying where orchards were: the verse ending its catastrophe with its account's own horribilis question-form: *would any one of YOU wish this?* — with the answer obvious to everyone hearing it: *never*: the Book's listeners always responding in their hearts with muffled terror at the picture — before the Book drops its verdict into their souls: *such is the estate he leaves behind: a garden consumed before he dies — his long life built on fraud*.

**What the Parable Means — The Parable of the Badly-Lived Wealth**

The commentators unfold the parable in a consistently sacred vocation — with al-Rāzī and the others' most read interpretation: the *garden-owner* matches the man of deeds displayed, deeds annulled, giving emptied by preening and hurt: his good deeds in this world have built him an orchard of immense reward in the next: but through all of it he mixed his display with his sincerity — he was old now, his strength to repair deeds by deeds too dwindling; his own progeny — the fruit to replace the tree — have not gathered strength; and at this very moment — while he awaits the Garden of the Resurrection — the fire-whirlwind of last-tally falls on his account and consumes it: *so no garden*: *reminder + injury* consumed the orchard of alms: *the man enters the next world stripped, without ever standing behind the great garden-owning-wealth he thought he had*. The narration's purpose is to step forward through attack at the walls of our time-bindaged distractability: *you* — every man of you — is *this man*: his age old, his children weak, his wealth devoured: for while one slumbered-playing, years of dispersed lukewarm-warning — mixing of the self-admirable with the God-grade — the whirlwind-fire arrives and burns up what everyone supposed was *his private savings vault* — and the disaster is far greater than its work has ever loss heart to contemplate: this is why the last God-word of the verse drops upon all: *kadhalika yubayyinu Allāhu lakumu al-āyāti laʿallakum tatafakkarūn* — "thus does God make clear for you the signs — that you may reflect": now the sūrah's pillar-seal of this verse-family itself settles down for the third time in the chapter (2:219, 2:242) in this very world.

**Beware the Fire — A Hadith-Matter for Every Age**

The tradition has preserved the verse's doctrine with remarkable fidelity in the schools of the heart: every classical tafsīr of *man and annann*, and every Sufi's hymn of *tawbah*, keeps it close: mixed sincerity — sincerity mingled with display — is the thief of orchards; and the Prophet's own treasury of cautions fits the parable's fire like a glove:

> *"Charity cools the wrath of the Lord and wards off the evil death."* (al-Tirmidhī 664 — classed ḥasan — the most-quoted prophetic word beside the burning-garden: sincere given-ness turns the whirlwind aside)

and the jurists ever after have drawn the parable's whole practical syllogism into the daily piety of believers: *give without reminding; give without injuring; give steadily, as though the garden must outlast winter* — for the watchers are told plainly what the garden's end would be were its soil poisoned: *thus does God make clear unto you the signs, that you may reflect* — and a man may well reflect further: every day on which no sincere seed is sown is a day the fire comes nearer the old man's walls; every day a clean gift goes down into the soil is a day the garden-ingathering spreads — until the Great Audit comes and finds *no fear* upon them *nor shall they grieve*.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:267

> **O believers! Donate from the best of what you have earned and of what We have produced for you from the earth. Do not pick out worthless things for donation, which you yourselves would only accept with closed eyes. And know that Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Give From the Good — Not From the Dregs**

The sūrah's charity-culture now descends to the ethical bottom-line of what is given — with the same intimacy equipped-equivalence 3:92 was given God's selfsame economy ("you will never attain piety until you spend from what you love"): *anfiqū min ṭayyibāti mā kasabtum* — "spend from the good things you have earned" — *wa mimmā akhrajnā lakum min al-arḍ* — "and of that which We have brought forth for you from the earth": *wa lā tayammamū al-khabītha minhu tunfiqūn* — "and do not *intend* the bad — spending of it" — *wa lastum bi-ākhidhīhi illā an tughmiḍū fīh* — "though *you yourselves* would not take it but with closed eyes." The tradition immediately tells the verse's own Sitz-im-Leben: the Companions of Madinah used to bring bunches of dates to the mosque, hanging their garden-offerings by the pillars of the Prophet's mosque for the poorest fasting ones (the *suffah* — the homelessmen's bench at the Mosque's own rear-line): some of the givers brought their *good dates* — the fat and the fresh of the trees — while others, moved by stinginess masquerading as generosity, gathered the *shriveled, bitter, falling dates* — the sweepings the household would not themselves eat — and hung them in offering: and the verses of 2:267 came down for *them*: O you who believe — do not give out the sweepings: God's charter over this is neither the beggar's wormwood measurement, nor the giver's own subjective scale of worthiness: but *the mirror of self-love*: *ask yourself: would you eat this?* — if you would yourself not touch it without opening your eyes and dealing with it — then do not place it in God's treasury: *"do not feed others with what you yourself would not eat"* — the standard citation of the earliest commentators at this very verse: the entire clause *though you yourselves would not take it except with closing your eyes* a permanent charter of golden-rule empathy at the core of Muslim philanthropy: and 3:92's own compact statement of the principle: *no piety until you spend of what you love*.

**Bad Money Not Cleansed by Alms**

The verse's first clause — *good things you have EARNED* — continues with the same aiās-repetition of the charity-tradition's own basic rule: the Book's charity works only upon *good things*: defined — as al-Ṭabarī's and Ibn Kathīr's own glossing — either by *what men find healthful and desirable* (what any honorable man would accept) or by *what is lawful* — *ḥalāl* — not unlawful: the charity from unlawful gain falls into fraud purchase-word of its own: not only does it fail to seed the promised ground, it cannot even enter the Temple-Door: the tradition's most often-quoted hadith upon the same matter (recorded by Muslim 2242 — from Jabir — at the register of this very clause: *"God is pure — He accepts only what is pure"* — the tradition's root-word on the source-purity of every charity ever since: God only accepts cleanliness) — and the Prophet's own long teaching upon ill-gotten (evil-earned) money's having no absolution by throwing-into-charity is preserved down the chain at the verse's own position: *God does not erase evil with evil* — the tradition accounting: *evil does not erase evil — the ill-gotten coin in the poor-box is ill-gotten notwithstanding — and while good finds extra-good by God, the almsgiver's vicious wealth-find does no good at all* — the teaching simply: cleansing the riches *before* the shady-alms: and God's relates-permissibility-becomes-clarity clear and stark: evil has no sanctification by good motives — least of all by charity: and the same Emperor's-Widow-lending tale at 4:29 and other parallel verses of God's whole Book make the same living-wall over the worldly wealth: *clean wealth is the inheritance of piety; and illicit wealth is not erased by alms.*

**God Is Self-Sufficient, Praised**
