And the seal-pair — *wa-ʿlamū anna Allāha ghaniyyun ḥamīd* — "and know that God is Self-Sufficient, Praised" — belongs to the verse's own standards-shattering cadence: ghaniyy — *Self-Sufficient*: God needs no dates anyway, not even dates from you: it is your rectified-by-charity souls at the Day of Reckoning that need them in the scale: so you do Him no favor either by good-giving nor good-omission: nowhere it's about *His* treasury in the alms: *it's your own* — the giving sets your own field; the defective gift burns your own crop; God is blind-to-measure: He seas how you give what you reach (good dates with narrowed eyes included), but stillkeepers the same pure-purity-purity as the seed: praising yourself praiseworthy is *ḥamīd* — *All-Praised*: God has already obtained every praiseworthiness possible from Himself apart from yours: be whatever sacrifices of Rajah-Banquet dates you bring to the mosque's garden-pillars, your chapel's loyal strings do not increase the measure of His glory by a single white-hair: He is already absolutely-praise-earned filled to the crown in Himself: so give the better dates: you only help yourself.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:268

> **The Devil threatens you with ˹the prospect of˺ poverty and bids you to the shameful deed ˹of stinginess˺, while Allah promises you forgiveness and ˹great˺ bounties from Him. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Devil's Threat and the Lord's Promise**

The sūrah now names, with sudden clarity, the invisible actor behind every withheld dinar: *al-shayṭānu yaʿidukumu al-faqra wa yaʾmurukum bi'l-faḥshāʾ* — "Satan threatens you with poverty, and commands you to indecency" — *wa Allāhu yaʿidukum maghfiratan minhu wa faḍlan* — "and God promises you forgiveness from Him — and bounty" — *wa Allāhu wāsiʿun ʿalīm* — "and God is All-Encompassing, Knowing." The commentators (Ibn Kathīr's compendium opening the school-way, al-Rāzī tracing the psychology) unfold Satan's two-pronged operation: first, the dread-whisper of *poverty*: when the believer's hand reaches to give, the whisper comes: *do not open your hand — tomorrow you shall need it — hold fast — save* — a spurious, vivid fear crafted against the whole teaching of verse 261 (sevenfold in every ear, hundredfold in every grain): the devil manufactures *worry over tomorrow* — and then, second, urges *faḥshāʾ* — indecency — for the withholding-man's other movements: miserliness drifts fast into covetous encroachment — the quirks, lies, trespasses of active greed: poverty-fear is the prophet Salmān's and Sufyān's most often-quoted diagnosis of the primary opening in every avaricious soul: the same priming of niggardly withholding runs into all the rest.

**Promise Against Promise**

Against Satan's threat stands God's parallel construction — *yaʿidukum* — He promises: but what God promises differs toto caelo from the devil's: *maghfirah* — forgiveness: the charity spent wipes the slates of sins: and *faḍl* — bounty: God restores and exceeds: the mufassirūn always gloss the structure of this clause as God's own response: while Satan *threatens* at the moment of giving, God *promises* in the very same moment: the one terrifies; the other reassures: the one promises poverty's ghost; the other guarantees bounty and pardon — you need only choose whose promise you believe. The tradition remembers the Prophet's own frequent foretelling at the verse's own purity:

> *"Charity does not decrease wealth"* — *mā naqaṣat ṣadaqatun min māl* — (Muslim 2588 — from Abū Hurayrah — the Prophet's canonical assertion upon which all Muslim charitable-glory is built: no giving ever shrank a believer's wealth — the direct reply against the devil's first whisper)

and the paired hadith already unfolded at 2:61's seed-parable preserving salvation-law of wealth-increase-by-giving in the same exact mode: "every day two angels descend — one says: O God, give the spender recompense; the other says: O God, give the miser destruction" (al-Bukhārī 1442; Muslim 1010 — from Abū Hurayrah — the Prophet's own heraldic duality of bounty and contraction: the verse's God/Devil antithesis vanished into heaven's daily liturgy of aims).

**All-Encompassing, Knowing**

The twin Names that close the verse — *wāsiʿ* — All-Encompassing — *ʿalīm* — All-Knowing — are precisely God's fulfillments to both whispers: His bounty is boundless: He has plenty to recompense every expenditure; and His knowledge misses no whisper, no withheld purse-flap, no reluctance: and the tradition settles the final frequent question of all the verse's mothers: *whose whisper is it — Satan's or the servant's own weakness?* — the commentators reply in the unity of the verse's both parts: when the holding-falter is outward-frightened and then tempted, it is Satan; when the devil is resisted and God is still trusted, it is God's own test: and the tradition's greatest recorded answer for all believers at this spot —

> *"O my servants! All of you are hungry except whom I feed: so ask of Me and I shall feed you; all of you are naked except whom I clothe: so ask of Me and I shall clothe you; all of you are astray except whom I guide: so ask of Me and I shall guide you: all of you are sinners except whom I forgive: so seek My forgiveness and I shall forgive you."* (Muslim 2577 — the great hadith qudsī from Abū Dharr — always read upon God's bounty-side of the verse — the devil's fearmouth of poverty answered with the Lord's own treasury-offering of forgiveness and bounty to the end of the time)

So the antithesis is totally plain: *Satan threatens poverty — God promises forgiveness and bounty* — and the believer's own choice between the two promises is the largest daily election of his morals: *wa Allāhu wāsiʿun ʿalīm* — enough for every giver, morning after morning, both to trust and to be known by.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:269

> **Allah grants wisdom to whoever He wills. And whoever is granted wisdom is certainly blessed with a great privilege. But none will be mindful ˹of this˺ except people of reason.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wisdom Among the World's Many Gifts**

The whole transaction-skyline of the charity-section pivots here upon God's own most precious gardendivision: *yuʾtī al-ḥikmata man yashāʾ* — "He grants wisdom unto whomsoever He wills": — *wa man yūta al-ḥikmata fa-qad ūtiya khayran kathīrā* — "and whosoever is granted wisdom has been granted much good": — *wa mā yadhdhakkaru illā ulū'l-albāb* — "yet none remember save the possessors of intellect." The commentators unfold *ḥikmah* — *wisdom* — through its diverse deep registers: knowledge of the Qur'ān drawn to its depth (including understanding of the abrogating and abrogated, the symbolic and the determined, the chronology of revelation, the ḥalāl from the ḥarām); the fear of God (in keeping with the Book's own ancient principle at 1:7 in the Psalms *fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom* — glossed by the commentators as the seed-registration of all genuinely released wisdom); comprehension (*fahm*), intelligence (*ʿaql*); and, as a few suggested, prophethood (with the majority rejecting this too-narrow identification — for the wisdom described here is clearly shared by all believers who have *ḥilm*, knowledge of the Book and its sciences, *and* the capacity to do right from it — not a mark restricted to the prophets alone): the phrase's built-in parallel — almost a proverb — is read as the Book's own most oft-quoted verse upon knowledge-teaching in the whole corpus: *man yūta al-ḥikmata fa-qad ūtiya khayran kathīrā*: whoever receives wisdom has received *an abundance of the Good* — in the number of the Prophet's own:

> *"There is no envy save in two things*: *a man to whom God has granted wealth and who exhausts it in the way of truth*, and *a man to whom God has granted wisdom and who judges by it and who teaches it*." (al-Bukhari 73 and 7141; Muslim 816 — the only two worth-envying lots: the giver of wealth and the possessor of wisdom: prize-fixing the other three in the one-two of the tradition's own charity/wisdom pairing at this sūrah's whole closing-complex)

**The Book's Old Prayer-Line Resumed**

The closing clause — *wa mā yadhdhakkaru illā ulū'l-albāb* — "only the possessors of intellect remember" — rings the sūrah's oldest bell over the same *ulū'l-albāb* addressed at 2:179 (after retribution) and 2:197 (after the ḥajj-charter): the same perdurable claim: only a certain sort — the men of the inner kernels — can truly *tadhkir* — remember/support-learn — the pages of God: the rest read; they do not grasp; they presume: and the whole charity-order is itself an arena of wisdom: for the wisest give what they can *still own forever* — as the previous verse taught with divine proof: the bad money reaps no benefit (2:267), the displaying one has abnegated his gains (2:264), the injury-and-preening void the whole thing (2:264): the wisdom following the understanding of the ḥalāl and ḥarām of giving — all that *is* the ḥikmah whose possession is the very wealth of wealth: and the school has always managed its most loved-prompting verses at these moments exactly: *whoever has been given wisdom — has been given much good*: total verdict of the ages: wisdom outbids wealth by God's own verdict upon it: and the souls of the knowing still remember it through every veil and crisis of their occasion and age: *He grants wisdom to whomever He wills — who receives it has received much good — but none remember save the men of inner mind.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:270

> **Whatever charities you give or vows you make are surely known to Allah. And the wrongdoers will have no helpers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Not a Grain Without Witness**

The whole charity-sequence now folds under the simplest possible awareness — a ledger whose auditor's powers cannot flatter any occupant of the way it must be told: *wa mā anfaqtum min nafaqatin aw nadhartum min nadhrin fa-inna Allāha yaʿlamuh* — "whatever you spend or vow — truly God knows it": *wa mā li'l-ẓālimīna min anṣār* — "and the wrongdoers shall have no helpers." The commentators unfold the verb *yaʿlamuh* — *knows* — with the whole treasury of Book-awareness (al-Rāzī's register and al-Ṭabarī's audits): God does not merely *record* the gift like some unmoving registry — He knows: the sum, the hand, the intent, the jealousy, the concealed aiming at showing, the unchecked appetite underneath the seemingly noble-same: *all of it is known* — and the clause is unbounded in its two case-configurations: *whatever of moneys you spend* — every dinar here; *whatever of vows you vow* — every pledge uttered at deathbeds and altars, every promised fast, every *if-God-gives-me-meetings* declared under seals: *God knows it*: and the donation-in-vow's all-bestowed verses discover this same admonitory verse everywhere this promissory-wording: by God you shall account: God knows it.

**The Wrongdoers' Choice — No Helpers**

The sentence closes then upon disclosure-driven terror: *wa mā li'l-ẓālimīna min anṣār* — "and the wrongdoers have no helpers": the Book's closing cadence of this whole donation-sealed passage: God knows all — and the men who've set their cells in wrongdoing stand like deer before the lion by the river at the time of count: *anṣār* — *helpers*: the very term whose abolition was sealed at 2:48 ("no soul shall avail another"): and the tradition proclaims all of it minutely now: every pledge shall be weighed; every expenditure shall be answered; and nothing mutters against the *lā anṣār*: thus the verse's own sentence-pairs fall upon the ear of every donor generational: *God alone hears of bounties:* *the mercied ones are the prayers-forgotten*: and the wronged ones *have no helpers*: *but the givers of tides shall have their God as their Reward everlasting*: and the wrongdoers shall have none but its boulders.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:271

> **To give charity publicly is good, but to give to the poor privately is better for you, and will absolve you of your sins. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Charity Shown or Hidden**

The sūrah's most refined charity-perception closes the sequence with a perfectly measured scale between two registers of the same mercy: *in tubdū al-ṣadaqāti fa-niʿimmā hiya* — "if you display your charities — *that is well*": *wa in tukhfūhā wa tuʾtūhā al-fuqarāʾa fa-huwa khayrun lakum* — "but if you conceal them and give them to the poor — it is better for you" — *wa yukaffiru ʿankum min sayyiʾātikum* — "and will acquit you of some of your evil deeds" — *wa Allāhu bi-mā taʿmalūna khabīr* — "and God of whatsoever you do is Aware." The commentators (Ibn Kathīr at the head, al-Rāzī following) survey the verse's disclosure-or-hidden map with enormous care: the disclosure clause — *in tubdū*: *that is well, acceptable* — being God's own charter that the open giver shall not be charged with sin for the openness itself: the man who gives prominently toward public models (encouraged also by the Prophet's own teaching of setting a good example: the man who gives openly, whose example may guide others to do the same): his gift is not tainted by its display: but *the hidden gift is the better:* and the Book-for centuries the tradition-lovers regarding Ibn ʿAbbās's categories (cited by al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr here) distinguish the registers further: voluntary charity — the supererogatory ṣadaqah — is *seventy fold better given privately* than publicly, while the *obligatory alms* (zakāh, the third pillar) is better performed publicly, both because the pillar's community-culture demands is testimony-transparent and because its public performance activates everyone ahead of its administration: thus the Book's own rule illuminates both campfires: *(1) voluntary and free-will charity: hidden is better; (2) the law of zakāh: open is better*: the two guides covering every household's duties in the same manner.

**Acquitting of Evil Deeds — the Erasing Charity**

The second clause establishes theology's own most eagerly grasped miracle for the ummah: *wa yukaffiru ʿankum min sayyiʾātikum* — *and will acquit you of some of your evil deeds*: the verb *kaffara* — *to cover, erase, expunge* — and with it the whole doctrine of good deeds canceling evil — the Book's own strong-for-luck promise registered itself also at 11:114 ("*truly good deeds remove the evil ones*") — as the tradition transits the most frequently-quoted hadith upon the verse's exact word:

> *"Charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire."* (al-Tirmidhī 614 — from Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah — classed ḥasan-ṣaḥīḥ — the most-applied prophetic word of the whole tradition on transgressions-and-charity), and its standing companion in his best-known counsel:

> *"Have piety of God wherever you go — and follow a bad deed with a good deed and it will wipe it — and treat men with goodly character."* (al-Tirmidhī 1987 — the ḥasan-ṣaḥīḥ hadith from Abū Dharr and Muʿādh, the Prophet's own daily-creed for the ummah passed down from his last hospital-meeting — always brought to this very verse by the commentators)

**God Is Aware — khabīr**

And the seal — *wa Allāhu bi-mā taʿmalūna khabīr* — "and God of whatsoever you do is Aware" — closes the whole giving-file in its sealed-witness: the polygraph *khabīr* — *all-aware*, *all-informed-of-the-innermost* — being God's own One-that-sees-between-the-cut-and-the-cash: *the visible charity* you may make and the tiny charity you may keep hidden: He knows — both registers — both their registers and the interiors: and the believers in the whole long file of donations may then be certains of two things: (1) the *seen* charity is acceptable to the faithful, when done spiritually in God's own way; (2) the *hidden* charity remains the best, the purest, the one to shape your charity most into your own invisible-easamen economy: *and God is Aware* — it is enough: God of all-sight: and within the spotlight that is Himself-your-God the two ways have all been seen — and the verified of you stands exactly before His countenance: *hidden or seen — it is not what men see — it is Who sees — that fills the Day of Judgment's books inscribed.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:272

> **You are not responsible for people’s guidance ˹O Prophet˺—it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills. Whatever you ˹believers˺ spend in charity, it is for your own good—as long as you do so seeking the pleasure of Allah. Whatever you donate will be paid back to you in full, and you will not be wronged.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Not Upon Thee Is Their Guidance**

The sūrah's statement upon the bowl-carrying giver of Madinah now enters the charity-polity's own delicate point — whether to give even to the unbelievers, the idolaters, the Jews of the town: *laysa ʿalayka hudāhum* — "not upon you lies their guidance" — *wa lākina Allāha yahdī man yashāʾ* — "but God guides whomsoever He wills": the commentators recounting the exact occasion reports behind the verse: one cluster of accounts tells the Prophet's household-line: some Companions had pagan-grandparents asking them for alms who declined from it until he stood before the Prophet and was answered by His Word; another tells the neighborhood where the Prophet's mansion-neighbors — guided strictly in not being Muslims — set their own calendars of gifts conditioned on their intended receivers' affirming Islam beforehand; and another dwells upon the Jewish-tribe relatives of his own Companions from Banū Qurayẓah: the verse-cover down-clear: *laysa ʿalayka hudāhum*: your duty is always the outgivment; its *alchemy toward conversion* is God's alone: you do not withhold the feeding of a human soul unless your only motive is the conversion-flame of your own tallying: the Book's own (early register's) moments and Arabian at the Jerusalem-bound later also (60:8's: God does not forbid you the righteousness and justice of those who fight you not — always read beside 2:272 in the fiqh-works of the generality) both teaching the same: *guidance is God's parcel — giving is yours*.

**For Yourselves, Seeking the Face**

Then the grand re-orientation of every charity the Book has already taught comes frontward: *wa mā tunfiqūna min khayrin fa-li-anfusikum* — "and whatever good you spend — it is *for yourselves*" — *wa mā tunfiqūna illā ibtighāʾa wajhi Allāh* — "when you spend only in seeking the Face of God": *wa mā tunfiqūna min khayrin yuwaffa ilaykum* — "and whatever good you spend shall be paid to you in full" — *wa antum lā tuẓlamūn* — "and you shall not be wronged." The clauses haul to their own senses in two directions: first, the gift returns unchecked to its own donor's own ledger: *for yourselves*: no beneficence conferred on another is lost into the other's ownership — it is the accumulator-of-the-future-Day's own storebook: so that while worldly accounts report the gift as enriched to the beneficiary, the true enrichment belongs to the giver; second, the motive-meter is planted on the giver's very act itself: *ibtighāʾa wajhi Allāh* — *seeking the Face of God*: the face of God in the giving: not the conversion of the poor, not the spread of Islam's flag, not the applause of the tribes — but simply, purely, *His Face*: *in exchange for Heaven's face* — the most-sublime imagery on verse 76:9 ("we feed you only for the Face of God — we want no thanks from you, nor recompense"): the same vision-plan draws down to the Sufis' very definition of islam: *the gift that asks nothing but the Face* — and the verdict giving it out: *paid to you in full*: with *yuwaffa* — *shall be handed over complete* — the Book spelling the exact ledger-guarantee: no subtraction, no rounding-down, no deduction for alpha-processing: *everything you spent will be returned to you in full*: with *wa antum lā tuẓlamūn*: and you shall NOT be wronged: you shall not be acted-against unjustly: the Book's own most-proffered covenant of total fairness that mankind and its payments all acknowledge by heart-writ: *you shall not be wronged*.

**The Tradition's Seal of Charity-to-Anyone**

The tradition remembered the Prophet's own habitual practice at this verse — his charity flowing to Muslim and non-Muslim neighbor alike — the early accounts in the sīrah and the reports of tafsīr recording his gifts to the Jewish households of Madinah as freely as to the believers (*he gives to all who knock* being the shared register of his household) — and the school drew from it the sunnah-legal rule carried in the schools of law ever since: charitable giving is permissible and meritorious to non-Muslims, subject only to the rules of this verse: the gift's direction is God's — not yours — and the only name written upon it is God's own Face: hence verse 272 stands still wide-open across the centuries as every believer's present warrant for quiet generosity: the Book having closed every excuse for keeping his door locked against any petitioner who knocks in God's own name.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:273

> **˹Charity is˺ for the needy who are too engaged in the cause of Allah to move about in the land ˹for work˺. Those unfamiliar with their situation will think they are not in need ˹of charity˺ because they do not beg. You can recognize them by their appearance. They do not beg people persistently. Whatever you give in charity is certainly well known to Allah.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Poor of the Veranda**

The charity-file names its most honored beneficiaries — the model company the Book holds out to every community of every century as the ugliest-test of every treasury of giving: *li'l-fuqarāʾi alladhīna uḥṣirū fī sabīli Allāh* — "for the poor who are constrained in God's way" — *lā yastaṭiʿūna ḍarban fī al-arḍ*: "who are unable to travel the land": the commentators' favored-name falling almost immediately into the history's lap: the Ahl al-Ṣuffah — *the People of the Veranda* — the most-beloved fraternity of the entire early history of Islam: the poor Madinese countless-migrants who cut themselves loose from homes, wives, lands, travels — lodging in the roofed cloister of the Prophet's mosque — to learn the Qur'an from the Prophet's mouth across the whole span of his Madinan years, having no worldly support except the Prophet's own almsgiving and that of the believers of Madinah: their entire discipline measured not in the smallest-bread ration: these were the *muḥṣarūn* — restrained, pinned-down, bound: a binding portrayed as chosen, not imposed: blocked — fixed in place — *in God's way*: unable to travel the land for trading or for livelihood lest their studious fealty to God's calling and their persistence at the Speaker's side be disrupted: *lā yastaṭīʿūna ḍarban fī al-arḍ*: they could not travel for trade: since *travelling-for-trade is what diners-can: not they*: they had declared their whole lives suspended at one delightful point: to be taught the Book *at* the hand of the Mesenger --- so the compassion of their class touches a donation-seal: *give to these.*

**"You Know Them by Their Mark"**

The verse now turns to the physiognomy the Book provides for telling them apart — for (as commentators of the school ever since), these were not *visible* paupers: they were men of dignity so deep the townfolk mistook them for the moneyed: *yaḥsabuhumu al-jāhilu aghniyāʾa mina al-taʿaffuf* — "the ignorant one supposes them to be wealthy — because of their restraint": *taʿarifuhum bi-sīmāhum* — "you shall know them by their mark": *lā yasʾalūna al-nāsa ilḥāfan* — "they do not ask of people importunately." The tradition supplies the *simā* — the former mark — with two layers-within-layers: (1) at its plainest recognition-frame: the marks that go with genuine poverty worn in bearing: pallor of hunger, weather of exertion, dust of devotion, weight-worn backs: the poor who still declined long begging-work look *weary of worship* but *not of mendicancy*: the listener might observe them *composed* yet *clearly gaunt*: they are *not* burdensome: the mark is not written upon tatter-cloth; it is written upon *grace-within-meagerness*: and (2) more deeply down: the esoteric commentators fasten upon the tradition's long-remembered phrase about true spiritual-spotting: *ittaqi farāsata al-muʾmin fa-innahu yanẓura bi-nūr Allāh* — "Beware the believer's discernment (firāsah) — for he sees by the light of God" (al-Tirmidhī 3127; the tradition's long-cited saying quoted by the compassionate-school at this very verse): the believer sees the dignified poor by God's light: eyes illumined by God perceive dignity even within poverty's plain exterior: this is the Sufi tradition's recurring method of reading the verse across the centuries: *give them, though they never ask*, as they bear their mark written gracious-worn within their faces: *ignorants judge by silks*: *God's-men judge by witness*: it is the going-etched quality of poignant restraint no poor-hands ever wore since: *the best charity is for the ranks that never untie their own mouths to ask.*

**"They Do Not Ask of People Importunately" — the Miskīn's Definition**

The verse's final line-line is the most oft-cited portrait of the poor adjudged, in its own days, as the best of the destitute: and the Prophet himself gave it the final epigraph-translation in his famous hadith upon the very verse:

> *"The destitute (the miskīn) is not the one who turns over their doors and is fed a morsel or two*: *the destitute is the one who keeps his dignity and does not ask of people importunately*" (al-Bukhari 1476, with Muslim 1038 — the Prophet's own verdict over the verse's mirror-text of the honorable poor — quoted on every page of the alms-giving instruction-books of the first six centuries of Islam: the assailant-beggar's mob has never been appointed the depositary of the Book's entire praise; the self-restraining, dignity-preserving poor have been appointed eternally so)

— and the Book resumes its own closing clause with the recurring signature of the section: *wa mā tunfiqūna min khayrin fa-inna Allāha bihi ʿalīm* — "whatever you spend of good — truly God of it is Knowing": the very same clause from every corner of the entire file (236, 215, 270, and now 273 in turn): God's intellect at every tent-flap, over every carried sack, whispered through every private donation-purse — and at every closure: *He knows* — enough.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:274

> **Those who spend their wealth in charity day and night, secretly and openly—their reward is with their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Wageworkers of Both Shifts**

The sūrah's charity-thunder now closes with its most comprehensive personnel-picture of all the giving generations: *alladhīna yunfiqūna amwālahum bi'l-layli wa'l-nahāri sirran wa-ʿalāniyatan* — "those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly": — *fa-lahum ajruhum ʿinda rabbihim* — "so their reward is with their Lord": — *wa lā khawfun ʿalayhim wa lā hum yaḥzanūn* — "**and no fear shall come upon them — nor shall they grieve**." The commentators register the verse's four-part attention with their customary acuteness (Ibn Kathīr's dossier, al-Rāzī's and al-Ṭabarī's dossiers transmitting its early anecdote-times): night-giving — the hadith's own shield-depth languages: the charity at dark to the invisible poor from the moon-lamp's own quietness ("charity in secret cools the wrath of the Lord" — al-Ṭabarānī's hadith already folded in at the head of the section): day-giving — same to be rehearsed in daylight for congregation-classes and the testimony of public beneficence; secret-giving — for the individual's own soul-account between him and God the All-Seeing; open-giving — for the community-model and the inspiration of the like-minded: four covers, four tastes of the same bowl: and the Book names its own list of the liberation-rules at once: *there is no wrong way to give well* — God loves every one of the four, so long as no preening and no injury taint them.

**"Their Reward Is With Their Lord" — The Antipodal Final-refrain**

The verse then delivers the line the whole section (vv. 260–274) has now been carving into the reader's nervous system — *fa-lahum ajruhum ʿinda rabbihim*: the reward *is with their Lord* — and the sūrah's own 2:277's restoration-of-the-exact-same antipsalm ("reward is with their Lord") becomes now the very mouth-door-salt for all the believers of all the generations: it answers, with divine certainty, the devil's whispered poverty-fear of verse 268: *you have not thrown away — you have deposited; you have not dispersed — you have transferred*: every coin whispered into a poor man's hand already lies — inscribed as wage — inside the Treasury of the All-Seeing: the wage *from God* belongs to no other giver: it is *in His Hand*: thus no loss, no lie, no thief, no collapsing marketplace, no aged depression of all the civilized-century's chain-wraps can assay touch the calculation: *their reward is with their Lord* — the very phrase of bone-fortitude the believers shout out of every century's treasure-blocks to come: be their currencies shattered, nations pauperized, estates stolen: God's own Accounts-In-Wage stand un-circulated ever above all distress, and the wage is the wage-saved *already* in God's Own Safe: and the tradition's own records bring-back still more rich illustrations of the verse's occasion:

> *Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib and Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq both gave their riches away by the specific division recorded by the mufassirūn at this very verse: quarter by night — quarter by day — quarter secretly — quarter openly: the whole of the palatable-alms parted-countered-and-spread through the sūrah's great four-quarters charity portrait: so that no quarter of the spiritual discipline of the treasury was left unexplored at their hands.* — the schools' favored accounts of the verse's occasion (Ibn Kathīr's and al-Ṭabarī's, among the salaf-commentary traditions of those who spend both night and day, secretly and openly)

**No Fear, No Grief — The Finale's Cry**

The cry that resolves every verse of the bloc arrives at its station here — *wa lā khawfun ʿalayhim wa lā hum yaḥzanūn*: *no fear — no grief*: the same seal-refrain (2:38, 62, 112, 262 as earlier will-response to the compassionate-pension) repeats at the close of the taw-quarter: the two anxiety-Kings of humans — the fear of what-comes-next and the sorrow for what-is-gone — both driven away by the reward that *in God's pocket already lies*: for grief needs to look down and find that the wealth has shrunk (which auction-counter of God's multiplication has never shrunk the giver's account); and fear needs to look up and find no covering roof (which compensation-accrued in God's own custody can never drop off): *no fear — nor shall they grieve*: the two words closing-off the whole superabundant abundance-giving of the sūrah's own section-file: *ye that spend — upon you no fear — and ye shall not grieve* — the very blessing's cipher the givers down the centuries were always granted to recite at their own golden pavement of God's Unalterable Reward: the verse completing thereby the entire charity-corpus of the sūrah before its own turn into the ribā-forbiddings of 2:275: a grand closing-picture of all the whispers and Count-inner put to the measure of everything that flows from their hand: *spend — be free — no fear, no grief* — and God's own closing-columns of its own glorious register before the passage that follows: *the ribā-devourers — the fire-abiders — except the ones that turn*: ending as always with God's own *All-Knowing*.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:275

> **Those who consume interest will stand ˹on Judgment Day˺ like those driven to madness by Satan’s touch. That is because they say, “Trade is no different than interest.” But Allah has permitted trading and forbidden interest. Whoever refrains—after having received warning from their Lord —may keep their previous gains, and their case is left to Allah. As for those who persist, it is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Rising as Madmen's**

The sūrah's whole progressive ledger of God now clashes into its most catastrophic genre-switch — the *fifty-three-words* that tore into Arabia's longest financial genealogy with an all-shelling verdict: *alladhīna yaʾkulūna al-ribā lā yaqūmūna illā kamā yaqūmu alladhī yatakhabbaṭuhu al-shayṭānu mina al-mass* — "those who devour ribā shall not rise — except as one rises whom Satan's touch has felled": the verbal *yaʾkulūna* — *they devour* — striking first: ribā not merely *taken*, *held*, *collected* — but actually *eaten*: the word carrying the scavenger-stench of organic devouring with it: the usury-silver enters him literally as food — eaten into his own bowels: and rising — as a result, the mufassirūn (Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī leading) unfold the terrible imagery: at the Day of Rising, these ribā-devourers shall rise — with bellies so massive-laden and weighed stuffed with the repelled scent of counterfeit dinar — like men *struck by madness* (*takhabbuṭ* — the satanic jolt-touching): unsure-footed, convulsing, fallen, rising yet unable to stand flat: staggering like men possessed — the very picture their own worldly history knew of demonic seizure: *the practice of swallowing usury* wears in the flesh its own transparency: they rise *as the Devil-touched* — tumbling, stumbling, unable to stand — their physical gait mirroring the spiritual touch long before: *their rising staggers like the devil-touched, whose thought here was devil-touched* — a like-for-like penalty for soul-corrupting sin. — and the commentators attach also the second picture-side of the clause — *mā yaqūmūn illā *: *like the touched-by-satan* — because *Satan's touch is what muddled their minds* in this world's own initial place*: the madmen delivered at the hall of Judgment are the same men who traded with music-of-madness here: *their rising staggers like devil's-touching — whose thought here was devil's-touching* — dua-in-kind penalty for soul-most-corruption sins.

**"Buying and Selling Are Simply Like Usury" — The Justification Stack**

The verse then displays the sinner's entire comprehensive case-law of excuse-by-recapitulation they habitually invented — as cunning-on-evasion-squad at every society in which God has ever set about prohibitions between God's two hands: *dhālika bi-annahum qālū innamā al-bayʿu mithlu al-ribā* — "**Because they say: 'Purchases are simply like usury'**" — *wa aḥalla Allāhu al-bayʿa wa ḥarrama al-ribā* — "**while God has permitted buying-and-selling and has forbidden usury**": the commentators reason the two-classes' stacking fault: (1) in *bayʿ* — buying/selling: the seller holds-physical-risk ownerships-of-commodity: in a sale, goods change hands against price: risk is held by the owner before the sale and by the buyer after it; no one is paid twice for the same thing; (2) in *ribā*: a debt owed — growing merely *with time* — money lending money to money, where the sum itself breeds increase by the passage of days *without any productive exchange*: no risk is shared; only time's ticking enlarges the debt into ever fatter ribs of debt: *forbidden* — God has *ḥarrama* — forbidden-by-holiness-word its whole structure at once — with the *ḥalāl*-aced sale-legitimacy of bayʿ buying: God openly-*aḥalla*: the verse arguing the difference doors-of-taxonomy not of performance-level intentions in their code-law: God allowed the first. forbid the second. And the jailers' codification: *Buy and sell are simply like usury* — the justifying-motto of every ribā-kurd-i-cand after: no, it is not: God has settled it: the first is permitted; the second is forbidden — two different species, not one.

**Desist and It Is Forgiven — Return and It Is Fire**

And the verse gives with good-door doctrine-gate, right at the point when count-effort-clog-guilt could otherwise make despair gulp in the crack of despair: *fa-man jāʾahu mawʿiẓatun min rabbihi fa-intahā fa-lahu mā salaf wa amruhu ilā Allāh* — "but whoever received an admonition from his Lord and desists — shall have what is past; and his affair goes to God" — *wa man ʿāda fa-ulāʾika aṣḥābu al-nāri hum fīhā khālidūn* — "and those who go back — *they are the inhabitants of the Fire, abiding therein*": the Book keeping its whole-domestic classico of granted-restitutions straight and clear: *whoever receives the word-of-admonition-of-God* (the Arabic wording *mawʿiẓah*: admonition, serious counsel) and *desists* — the verb *intahā* — *comes to an end-of: ceases*: then *all that is past is his* — what he collected prior is between him and the Lord of Mercy — with the relation henceforth open to God's own judgment: *his affair is with God* — the clause flying with no emptiness at all also to the men who had profited beforehand on ribā practices before hearing the Book's admonition: but *whoever goes back* — *whoever returns* — *whoever keeps ribā going*: *they are the inhabitants of the Fire, abiding therein* — with the eternity final: *khālidūn*: *abiding*: the ribā-fire lit with no coming-out door ever after: the school recording the exact quotation-touching of the occasion *at which the Prophet ﷺ pronounced his most distinguishing-known verdict upon ribā:* *

> *"The Messenger of God cursed the devourer of ribā, its payer, its writer, and its two witnesses* — *he said* — *they are all alike*" — (Muslim 1598 — from Jābir — the Prophet's own four-wrapped curse: ward-drier for the verse's pointed warning: eating-ribā, feeding-ribā, scribing-ribā, witnessing-ribā — curse-upon-four of them *all* — their whole collusion their own equal-complicity — all of them class-identical in their ribā-calendars)

— the verse's closing verdict standing without a second door: *they are the inhabitants of the Fire, abiding therein forevermore.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:276

> **Allah has made interest fruitless and charity fruitful. And Allah does not like any ungrateful evildoer.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Erasure for the Lender, Growth for the Giver**

One sentence puts the entire economics of the spiritual cosmos upon its two tracks: *yamḥaqu Allāhu al-ribā wa yurbī al-ṣadaqāt* — "God blights usury — and causes acts of charity to grow" — *wa Allāhu lā yuḥibbu kulla kaffārin athīm* — "and God loves not any sinful ingrate." The commentators attend first to the beautiful word-play lodged in the verse's own Arabic incision: *ribā* — usury — is itself the noun of *rabā* — growth: God now chooses the verb *yamḥaq* — *He blots out, He erases, He depletes* — as the true condition of that so-called growth; and opposite it He places the causative *yurbī* — *He causes to grow* — the same *r-b-w* root put to its proper service: **usury, which calls itself growth, God counts as erasure; charity, which looks like diminution, God counts as multiplication**: the entire money-side of the verse therefore undoes man's ledger-dream: you may watch the ribā-holder's account grow — but God is *blotting it out*: its inner blessing is gone already — both its increase out of existence: the debtor from the next-of-kin was sucked not sufficient: and an asset book full of zero-sum gains slowly erodes, shrinks, and stands like bare dust: and meanwhile the charitable purse that appears diminished by every pouring is God's great growing-field — all the more upon the books of Heaven: with the tradition's own report from the Prophet recording throughout the schools of Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī at this verse:

> *"No wealth ever gathered from ribā — but God shall indeed deplete it"* — *mā izdāda mālun min ribā illā ḥaṭṭamahū Allāh*: the most oft-cited verdict of ribā's total bleaching in the force of God's decay-decision, always cited beside this verse in the mufassirūn's ashore-down its own world-historical documentation: the estates of ribā-makers are extinguished over the generations; while the charity-giver's portion stands growing in God's reckoning forever.

**The Ingrate Sinner**

The closing pair — *kull kaffārin athīm* — names the ribā-maker with the Book's most damning joinery: *kaffār* — persistent ingrate: the one who takes God's bountifulness and instantly converts it into greed; and *athīm* — persistent sinner: the one who preys systematically upon the unfortunate: the ribā-seller is truly therefore built of these two: ingratitude for the wealth God vouchsafed him, sin against the unfortunate it swallows: he has God's provision-call but no gratitude, he has his client's misfortune but no mercy: and the verse closes upon the ancient *not-love* formula of the sūrah's charity-file (2:205: God loves not corruption; 2:190: God loves not transgressors) driving home *God loves not the ribā-ingrate*: love having been the Bible-shared resonance of the sūrah's community-actions (2:195: God loves the virtuous; 2:222: God loves the repentants and purifiers) — the file's not-love side is now carried toward its fullest character: every insurrection of soul into ribā is finally indicted by the Lone Verdict: *God does not love the sinful ingrate* — and this is precisely because the man's wretched choice is not *merely* economic: it is his answer of ingratitude to God and its predation to people: the ribā-class, being expelled from the Love of God, remains no longer at home at the Beloved One's own measuring-judge, where the charitable and virtuous dwell eternally: *usury is blotted* — *charity has grown* — and *God loves not the sinful ingrate.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:277

> **Indeed, those who believe, do good, establish prayer, and pay alms-tax will receive their reward from their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Four-Fold Charter**

Between God's erasure of ribā and the sūrah's coming war upon its practitioners, the Book plants once more the community's own positive four-fold: *inna alladhīna āmanū wa ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāti wa aqāmū al-ṣalāta wa ātawu al-zakāta lahum ajruhum ʿinda rabbihim* — "truly those who believe, perform righteous deeds, establish the prayer, and give the alms — theirs is the reward with their Lord" — *wa lā khawfun ʿalayhim wa lā hum yaḥzanūn* — "and no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve." The commentators note with great pleasure how precisely the four pillars belong together, each pillar standing in its own rank within the mercy-structured basis of the sūrah's whole way forward from its opening page at v. 3: belief (*īmān*) — the heart's grounding; righteous deeds (*al-ṣāliḥāt*) — the outward practice; established prayer (*īqām al-ṣalāh*) — the tending and keeping of it (standing crystalline by day and night: the verse's own *aqāmū* — *established, upheld* — not simply performed but *propped up in constancy*); and the alms (*al-zakāh*) — the wealth's regular purification-taxes — each root-word of which derives from *purification* and *growth*: the *zakāh* — the alms under the structure of Islam, precisely where the ribā of verse 275 is torn-out-thrown-down: with their four-fold charter then fitting to the exact same seal-anthem of refuge-completed assurance already laid upon the whole gay, of the sūrah's own history: *no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve* — from the very threshold of v. 38 (for Adam's falling children) to v. 62 (the believing peoples) through v. 262 and v. 274 (the unmoved givers): **the whole sūrah's most-repeated promise** — *fear defused, grief dispersed*

**Preached Now as the Counter-Sign of the Ribā-Field**

The verse arrives at this exact pivot-point — after 2:275–276's whole thunder against ribā — to serve the community as its own counter-sign: *believe — do righteous deeds — establish the prayer — give the alms*: these four are the safe path, just as ribā was the fatal one: the prayer kept, the alms paid in due season, shakes the believer free of the ribā-swamps whose class the last verses drowned and cursed: the commentators' favorite reading at the verse has always been the one addressed to the returning soul: *whatever your past in ribā, here is the abiding home of the believer — and no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve* — for the reward is with their Lord, not in the lost fields of usury.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:278

> **O believers! Fear Allah, and give up outstanding interest if you are ˹true˺ believers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Leave What Remains — The Address to Believer-Bankers**

The Book now puts its own hand right to the moment of the accumulating sails, as a father grabbing his son by the collar of his coat by now. Its own tone now is virtually that of a father past the ages of argument and debate. *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū uttaqu Allāha* — "O you who believe! Reverence God!" — *wa dharū mā baqiya mina al-ribā* — "and leave what remains of usury" — *in kuntum muʾminīn* — "**if you are believers**": the commentators fasten upon the conditional *in kuntum muʾminīn* as the verse's own most pointed bite: this is not a compromise-procedure: the believers are given leave not to quit its ribā en masse through an official licensing-passage or a negotiated pawn-tie covenant of the community: but simply: *leave what remains*: *what remains* — meaning the accumulation still on the books: the outstanding ribā balance still outstanding at the publication of the Book before them (further provisions coming afterward at verse 279): it is to be written off: immediately: no installment glide-path: the bulk of Quraysh-ribā-capital of Arabia is told: drop it now. And the match-comment-part-exact-condition is still pointed: *if you are believers*: so that the ribā-banker hears inside his own ledger the audit-question of the whole Scriptures: *your Islam is presumed upon the ribā-cancellation*: if your faith is genuine, your account-books must change: where faith is not translated into account-books, the whole profession of faith follows into rubble: the commentators always drilling into us the verse's own unmistakable mark: Islam and ribā do not keep company in the heart: and therefore — *if you are believers* — *leave it* — *what remains* — *clean of your earned-Ribā portfolio*: — for every day one delays, the accumulating ribā serves only as further evidence of the rebellion.

**Taqwā — The Creed's Own Name at the Center of Economics**

The imperative *ittaqu Allāha* — *fear God, revere God* — is the sūrah's long-running master-word across the whole law-literature: from v. 2's "guidance for the God-fearing" to v. 179's taqwā at retaliation, v. 183's at fasting, v. 197's at ḥajj, and v. 224's in the covenant of oaths — it is God's own appointed perimeter within which every soul must move. Here it reaches, at last, into the account-books: taqwā is not to be kept *outside* the ledger, isolated in the prayer-niche and the fast; it rules the ledger too. The tradition's never-ceasing reading of the verse in the finance-ethics of later Islam is regrettably simple and forever unanswerable: *the ribā-brotherhood will always present you a hundred reasons why cancellation is impossible — but the word of the Lord offers only one instruction: leave it* — so the separation is made by the believers' own decision — divinely ark'd upon the two pillars: reverence of God — and leaving the ribā: and the end-tag settles its last weight: *if you are believers* — *leave what remains.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:279

> **If you do not, then beware of a war with Allah and His Messenger! But if you repent, you may retain your principal—neither inflicting nor suffering harm.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Take Notice of a War"**

The verse now unrolls the most terrifying sanctions-language the Book has yet placed before any market-practice: *fa-in lam tafʿalū fa-ʾdhanū bi-ḥarbin mina Allāhi wa rasūlihi* — "and if you do not, then *take notice of a war from God and His Messenger*": *wa in tubtum fa-lakum ruʾūsu amwālikum* — "but if you repent, *yours is the principal of your wealth*" — *lā taẓlimūna wa lā tuẓlamūn* — "you shall neither wrong nor be wronged." The legislators attend first to *fa-ʾdhanū bi-ḥarbin* — *take notice, be given fair warning, of a war*: the word root *ʾadhan* — *to announce, proclaim*: the announcement of war itself: and the tradition records the earliest commentators feeling the hair rise upon their own cheeks: the matter of ribā, for every one of the Qur'an's ways, is set among the *flying ranks of Holy War*: God *and* His Messenger declare war upon ribā-practice: the two Names are the same two Names with which the regime of Islam confronts any entity its own rate-making machine has, by war, identified as its sworn enemy — the first time and the only time the entire Book vouchsafes an outright *war-declaration* against a financial-custom: and the register of the whole-fold of wariant commentators at the verse: (1) *by the hand*: Ibn ʿAbbās's report carrying it: *"On the Day of Resurrection it shall be said to the ribā-taker: 'take up your sword* — *war is upon you'* — the sentence of the Resurrection as being delivered physically to the forever-ribā-devourer; (2) *by the tongue and the heart:* the ribā-man's whole gesture being literally war upon God's statute (and its commands to the believers at all times: remodelling the Muse most literally into every one of the community-minds of believers, withdrawing-even-indifferently from everything that is warlike — it's all the same to be hostile: — with the commentators extending the flame further: (3) *by the sword of legitimacy:* as the school's own registration of state-sanctioned jihād upon ribā-entrenched powers: to cultivate ribā formally *can be grounds upon which the lawful authority intervenes* — forcibly — as the divinely-instrumented Islam states religion's execution of its charter on earthly thrones: its own legal machinery being that of the Book's direct promise of a war declared by God and His own Messenger: *so take notice*: the Book's own most dramatic legal-measure taken to protect the wronged of elbow ribā-culture goes-ultimate-further than the league of men whose eyes merely see the market: it is upon God's war — with all the same effects in the whole Islamic Ma consummation of practice's long-sweeping: the ribā-maker is in war with God and His Messenger — *and woe to him*.

**The Principal Yours — No Wrong**

And immediately its mercy-concomitant, toward the repentant's own folding of the boat: *wa in tubtum fa-lakum ruʾūsu amwālikum* — "and if you repent — yours are your **principal-capitals**": the commentators seize at once upon *ruʾūsu amwālikum* — *your capitals*, their heads-sums: what the ribā-lender loses is the *interest-mountain* — but the principal *lent* is left wholly his: God gives him that *as a matter of right* — the repentant lender does not lose his money by repenting — the *original* loan's amount — the exact principal-lent by God-allowed, treble-free Barqa-debt-security of the ribā-calling — is permanently non-wronging: and the verse draws the exact harmonizing-note by which the mathematized-mechanics of the shared economy shall stand at once: *lā taẓlimūna wa lā tuẓlamūn* — **you shall neither wrong nor be wronged**: the perfect balance-slate of God's own ledger — lender's principal secured (he does not lose what he honestly lent) + borrower's interest-erasure freed (he is not milled in by his long-past undoing): both sides saved from ẓulm: God *has not taken any of the principal* — *and the whole ribā is cancelled*: so that the certificates of the solidarity of the world's brokerages may stay always in the steadiness of God's own tending: *you shall neither do wrong nor be wronged.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:280

> **If it is difficult for someone to repay a debt, postpone it until a time of ease. And if you waive it as an act of charity, it will be better for you, if only you knew.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Grace Period — Respite for the Troubled Debtor**

The Book closes its ribā-laws with the tender contour-by-bending that everything the ethics of loaning in Islam has ever been laid upon: *wa in kāna dhū ʿusratin fa-naẓiratun ilā maysarah* — "and if one is in difficult circumstances — *a respite, until there is ease*" — *wa an taṣaddaqū khayrun lakum in kuntum taʿlamūn* — "and that you give it as charity is better for you — if you but knew." The commentators draw the two-step measure with their customary direction-side: (1) *ilā maysarah* — *until ease*: the debtor in genuine straits that day is entitled to lawfully rest his loan until his means are adequate-prepared to repay *not* by compulsion's attendants: no squeezing of the debt out of his throat while his pockets continue vacant: this is not optional for the lender: it is God's own word, written into the same page that should come back to plague some glinting ledger-room of Meccan money-houses as the world of Jewish usury's most maddening mountains were toppling: *a respite* until his own ease restores: and (2) *an taṣaddaqū* — *that you give it as charity*: a second and upper-deal: even beyond the respite — the lender who would take the principal out of his still-struggling debtor's on-payroll wealth at last would better have the principal instead *gifted in charity* — of his own money's vast horde: the Book singing its way around the altruistic-ecstasy always toward the very end: *it is better for you*: with its own twin-refrain of *if you but knew* (*if you only knew* — used twice already in the sūrah's own almsgiving-family, v. 184 and v. 216): *the whole turning of mad-house-bargains into charity is not lost* — it is the preferred gain *if you but knew*.

**Respite's Wage — One Charity-Credit Per Day**

The tradition never tires of adding this verse's own fruit-warp onto every high-heat tajwīd-pronouncing course of Islam in all the alms-wealth-theologies of God's Messenger's followings: the Prophet's exact requital for the grace-giver:

> *"Whoever grants respite to one in difficult circumstances* — *every day of their patience* — *shall be credited a charity* — the Prophet's fixed calculation always tied to the verse's next clause at the school's own always-at-fortitude-depositing morning-portals (cited throughout the school at this verse in both the tafsīr and ḥadīth-commentaries of al-Ṭabarī and afterward)*

— the wage uttered in the world's alms-language beyond all measure of time's ribā-banking: the verse now sends out its two lamps as the last counsel in the matter: *respite until ease* — the debtor given breathing-room before God; *give it as charity* — the lender urged into Heaven's still greater garden: the Book's own *if-only-you-knew* riding the whole sūrah's thrust in every other chapter where the believers' refinement touched one more truth and this one, and now pressing into the deepest encounter of the Book's whole ledger-account — *if you only knew what the accounting-eye of God records at the very moment you choose to write off*: *better for you* — the debtor, absolved before God's measuring, released without recourse — the forgiveness of the debt from his burden — *if you but knew*: the practice is thus the very best of all the ages' own ways: *if only you knew.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:281

> **Be mindful of the Day when you will ˹all˺ be returned to Allah, then every soul will be paid in full for what it has done, and none will be wronged.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Last Word of the Spending Chapter**

The entire charity-and-ribā fabric of the sūrah now turns its twelve-lens toward the unswerving horizon of its conclusion and places its royalties once more upon its most-desired signature-day: *wa-ttaqu yawman turjaʿūna fīhi ilā Allāh* — "and *fear a day — be mindful of a day* — when you shall be returned unto God": *thumma tuwaffā kullu nafsin mā kasabat* — "then every soul shall be paid in full what it has earned" — *wa hum lā yuẓlamūn* — "and they shall not be wronged": the Book's own exact phrase-pair — *tuwaffā* — paid *in full* — the exact designation-word of the uber-track of its long-established treasure of full-shells ("whatever good you spend, it shall be paid to you in full" — 2:272's own pattern refrain): and *lā yuẓlamūn* — *they shall not be wronged* — the precise covenant God declared upon the ribā's own road (2:279's *neither wrong nor be wronged*): the believers' servant-mechanics among the ribā-crisscross of Arabia locking-within once more its last verdict: on that Day *cards are finally shuffled* — nothing of the gift escapes its stored record (2:272); no display-motif flaw escapes registration on the cancellation-file (2:264); no idle class-word marries into the celebration-sermon of a poor man's bread (2:267); no ribā-banker passes through the last door with the *interest-mountain dragged in his own accoutre* (2:279-81): *every soul shall be paid in full what it earned — and they shall not be wronged.*

**"Be Mindful of a Day" — The Exact Closing Formula**

The verse's opening formula — *wa-ttaqu yawman* — *Fear a Day* or, as the Arabic word of boundary claps its shortest phase, *Beware of a Day* — is the exact phrasing the sūrah will apply one final time in its own very-last maslama-verse of its great conclusion (2:281 — and of the Book's of the whole Qur'an on the same tape (3:25's: "beware of a day when you shall be gathered to God — when no soul shall be asked anything of another"): the tradition times and places its favorite recorder-comment to such moments, the verse-memoranda inventorial always of the day of judgment on which *the* every ledger sums, the every transaction closes, the every giver and taker sits across the *unveiled scale*: and the school of the tradition's own high-capacity community-spelling books never stop seizing upon the verse's majestically particular word *tuwaffā* (*shall be paid in full*): paid with full account — nothing held back — no decimal-lamina of the tiniest seed-lend gone: *you shall not be wronged* — even the dust-jewel of a good modest deed-mite here is paid wholeness to you at the Judgment-Round — with the very words making the whole chapter stand as its own deterministic-in-house word: *the believers' whole reservoir* — poured one full-of-full into the Last Day's *payback-full scope*: un-eraseable, uncollapsable, happening-as-promised: in God's Own Account-Book.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:282

> **O believers! When you contract a loan for a fixed period of time, commit it to writing. Let the scribe maintain justice between the parties. The scribe should not refuse to write as Allah has taught them to write. They will write what the debtor dictates, bearing Allah in mind and not defrauding the debt. If the debtor is incompetent, weak, or unable to dictate, let their guardian dictate for them with justice. Call upon two of your men to witness. If two men cannot be found, then one man and two women of your choice will witness—so if one of the women forgets the other may remind her. The witnesses must not refuse when they are summoned. You must not be against writing ˹contracts˺ for a fixed period—whether the sum is small or great. This is more just ˹for you˺ in the sight of Allah, and more convenient to establish evidence and remove doubts. However, if you conduct an immediate transaction among yourselves, then there is no need for you to record it, but call upon witnesses when a deal is finalized. Let no harm come to the scribe or witnesses. If you do, then you have gravely exceeded ˹your limits˺. Be mindful of Allah, for Allah ˹is the One Who˺ teaches you. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Longest Verse of the Qur'an — The Writing of Debts**

This is the longest single verse of the entire Qur'an — and, by the commentators' own serene irony, it concerns neither the Highest Heaven nor the Last Hour but one of the most earthbound materials of social life: the registration of a debt: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū idhā tadāyantum bi-daynin ilā ajalin musamman fa-ktubūhu* — "O you who believe — when you contract a debt with one another for an appointed term — write it down." The tradition identifies its legislative backdrop with the forward-sales of the Madinan date-trade: crops one, two, or three years out could be bought and sold forward — an agricultural economy living and breathing in the dome-set-sands and not in any cash flow — and its own injunction to write it was the very opening cell of the great alms-codes of the Prophet's own community's long financial codification: *write it down*: the four words closing centuries of Arabia's deputies-of-memory: the Book pioneering into a society that trusted spoken promises and blood-money's gallon-backed high honor: into the very first modern civil-religious commandment expressed as *everything on paper — no more oral hand-shake left to sand*.

And every one of the already-familiar juristic forms was plugged into the verse from its first word and neutralized immediately by the authorities across its many centuries: *the writing was intended as a remembrance-aid to the living witness, not as a substitute for oral testimony*: the Islamic courts of subsequent ages continued requiring (as the first centuries of law had built upon the verse of verse 8 (the verse of 281): oral testimony was preeminent, but written recording was *strongly urged*: from voluntary toward encumbrance-instituting (with the commentators reading widely its own two early variants of *farḍ kifāyah* — a communal duty: *let not the scribe refuse to write as God has taught him*: — the duty of teaching-learning the art surface upholding as a social responsibility: everyone should know the writing whereby the writing is taught; if someone amongst us is designed such, let every one of us be more easily able).

**The Debtor Dictates — The Fullest Meaning**

The verse proceeds with its full-share ship-of-justice clauses: the *scribe writes down* (with fairness) — the *debtor dictates* (the Prophet's own hadith of forward-contracts at the school's own standard instruction: *whoever contracts a forward sale, let it be for a set amount, a set weight, and a set time*): the debtor's dictation being exactly the stronger-party instrument: it was the debtor (in all cases, in the commentary tradition's own accountings) who carries the obligation, who is therefore the guarantor of its precise terms: and *let him reverence God, his Lord, and diminish nothing from it*: the *debtor* must not trim his own debt in the dictation; dictate its true amount, dictated *justly*; and wherever the debtor is frail — feeble-minded, minor, sick to incapacity — his guardian dictates for him *justly*: the law first guarding at its low-hanging stage the very weakest in a long-time-constantly-notorious-alley of debt-underpayment and unpayable-in-the-numbers flown-down-again-and-again accrued against the credulous-innocents of the dirt-laden streets of Arabia: and any earthling read the verse in the whole-mission-driven-lengthy law of its holiness: *God stands between every pen and every ledger.*

**"A Man and Two Women" — The Controversial Line**

The verse's most debated clause in fourteen centuries is its testimony-provision: *wa-stashhidū shahīdayni min rijālikum* — "call to witness two witnesses from among your men" — *fa-in lam yakūnā rajulayni fa-rajulun wa-imraʾatāni mimman tarḍawna mina al-shuhadāʾ* — "and if there are not two men — then a man and two women, from among those whom you approve as witnesses" — *an taḍilla iḥdāhumā* — "so that — if one of the two errs" — *fa-tudhakkira iḥdāhumā al-ukhrā* — "the other may remind her." The commentators have circled this clause for centuries with every shading of human thought: (1) the tradition's school of jurists is clear that the context expressly constrains the rule to *forward sales and debt-contracts: a special circumstance* — with debts demanding expert-competence in financial-transaction records — in which men of that society were predominantly involved while women — as a generality — were not (the verse's own *mimman tarḍawna mina al-shuhadāʾ* — *from among those you approve as witnesses*: — the whole selection being based upon *approval and competence in that area*, not upon gender-essence); and (2) the commentators attending to the *protective* translation of the pairing: per Ibn ʿAbbās's brand of reading (Q, Ṭ): a woman alone on a men's-bargaining-terrain would be open to bullying or manipulation at the altar of her testimony: God's rule pairing *two women* thereby honors the very testimony it anticipated would be hard-won amid hard traders, its entire arrangement being *guarding, not debasing* — with 2:282's own great apologist the jurist Abū Bakr ibn ʿArabī of the Mālikīs recording puzzling from the jurists of his own age about exactly why a man cannot simply remind one woman: his wrestle and the often-given reason hanging on the whole problemat of the jurisprudential community ever since: *the rule does not measure women's honesty — it covers the social reality of female exposure in trades whose full disclosure women of that day were not habituated to transact* — compare besides the Book's own equal-standing elsewhere: 24:6–9's own counts in its own counter-religious context (slander-accusation between wife and husband: *his word equal to her word*): the Book *elsewhere* declares plain equivalence; and the sūrah of 2:282 is concerned with something special: a limited evidence-rule for a specific kind of contract in a specific historical society — not with *women's worth*.

**Witnesses Neither Refuse Nor Are Harmed**

And the verse closes with its own three-decree discipled close: (1) *wā-lā yankaru al-shuhadāʾ idhā mā duʿū* — "and let not the witnesses refuse when called": testimony is made a standing-duty for every believer who is called upon to bear it: the public transactions are the public trust: no honest man is excused from this civic duty: (2) *wa lā tudayyartū al-kātiba* — *let no scribe be harmed, nor witness*: — *harm neither the writer nor the witness*: one who coerces them has made their testimony suspect — harm voids its evidentiary flow: (3) *wa in tafʿalū fa-innahu fusūqun bikum* — "if you do that — *it would be iniquitous of you*": — God Himself branding such harm outright *iniquity* — and the verse closes in the sūrah's own signature pattern — *wa-ttaqu Allāha wa-yuʿallimukumu Allāh wa-Allāhu bi-kulli shayʾin ʿalīm* — "**And reverence God — for God teaches you — and God of everything is Knower**": the two solemn calls to reverence and guardianship by God Himself setting the whole verse's whole mission of legal-sag upon God's own teaching: with witnesses unwilling to refuse, scribes unharmed, every debt-instrument written, delivered, signed and witnessed: *God remembers: God teaches: God knows all things*: — the closing beacon of the whole sūrah's longest law.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:283

> **If you are on a journey and a scribe cannot be found, then a security can be taken. If you trust one another, then ˹there is no need for a security, but˺ the debtor should honour this trust ˹by repaying the debt˺—and let them fear Allah, their Lord. And do not conceal the testimony, for whoever conceals it, their hearts are indeed sinful. And Allah ˹fully˺ knows what you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**On a Journey — A Pledge in Hand**

The debt-law closes its door with a humane portal of travel-day-of-the-law: *wa in kuntum ʿalā safarin wa lam tajidū kātiban fa-rihānun maqbūḍah* — "and if you are on a journey and cannot find a scribe — then a pledge in hand": the commentators explaining *rihānun maqbūḍah* — *a pledge taken*: collateral — the debtor (or seller in a forward-sale) handing over some property as deposit-bond into the creditor's trusted keeping: his horse on loan-days of travel, his saddle-bag of goods, whatever moveable both parties agree will stand in its place — making the loan's whole exchange sealed by the thing the one gives the other *without parchment, without scribe, without road-inn witness*: with the tradition pronouncing its most tender rereading of the whole verse upon the Prophet's own use of such a pledge: his celebrated pawn of his shield (an iron-mail cuirass) with a Jewish merchant of Madinah for thirty measures of barley — the account of the pledge standing famously (al-Bukhari 2385 — the *rihān* at its simplest: *the Prophet pawned his shield for the storied barley* — the whole ummah's highest model of the Book's own pledge-putting practice being the Messenger's own own armored pledge in a hand of no one's forgetting); and the verse's last facepardons simplicity without constraint: *and if one of you trusts the other* — trust! — without any collateral at all: let the trust be lived: *let him who is trusted deliver his trust*: the word *addā amānatah* — *deliver his trust* — opening the whole great universe of *amānah* — the-trust-in-inheritance: the debtor who swears, the merchant who promises, the traveler who loans, and the tradition remembering all those who treat their trusts — and its climate-appointment-warms between every soul moving forward in God's name: *amānah* is *the highest private law above every law*: no witness required where God Himself is the Witness: *fear God your Lord*: — the trust sitting comfortably in God's own custody outside the visible world of scribe and seal.

**Conceal Not the Testimony**

The verse now places its final admonition over its whole τradhim-pegs of commerce-witness testimony: *wa lā taktumū al-shahādah* — "and conceal not the testimony" — *wa man yaktumhā fa-innahu āthimun qalbuh* — "and whoever conceals it — truly his *heart* is sinful": the commentators explain the concealment with the vivid ambiguity of its math-of-two-halves: *the witness-holder may forget*, but the concealment-word is reserved-only for him who *knows and suppresses*: not the absently-receiving one — but the wakful silence-maker: the testimony of truth's events deliberately discarded in pockets of unfaithfulness: and it speaks explicitly of the *heart*: not the hand, not the pocket! — the crime is *in the heart*: every lie-stroking dissimulation of evidence, every shrug-off of the witness's duty, every popular concealment of testimony-to-give in court when called: the whole crux of truth's being in God's say-so now planted once again within Heaven's audit-door — *wa Allāhu bi-mā taʿmalūna ʿalīm* — "and God of whatsoever you do is Knowing": the book's own law-of-It-closes now with the Name-choice *Knowing*. And so the chapter of commerce-law of al-Baqarah ends: with pledges in the hand or in the heart, and with witnesses — of the heart or of hearing: with God knowing everything you do.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:284

> **To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Whether you reveal what is in your hearts or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it. He forgives whoever He wills, and punishes whoever He wills. And Allah is Most Capable of everything.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Everything Is His — Everything Is Accountable**

As the longest legislative chapter draws to its very end, the sūrah lifts the whole glory-register of its covenant into its own coronation-ceiling: *li-llāhi mā fī al-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍ* — "unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth": *wa in tubdū mā fī anfusikum aw tukhfūhu yuḥāsibkum bi-hi Allāh* — "and whether you disclose what is in your souls — or hide it — God shall bring you to account for it": *fa-yaghfiru li-man yashāʾu wa yuʿadhdhibu man yashāʾ* — "He forgives whomsoever He wills — and punishes whomsoever He wills": *wa Allāhu ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr* — "and God is Powerful over all things."

The commentators note with reverence that revelation has now ceased legislating — and started unveiling: the verses of the end are not rules — they are unveiling curtains upon the heaven-and-earth of the accounting that stands beyond all rules: the Book is silent no more about the ledger — every clause now *disclosure*, *God Himself in place* — the five clauses being the sūrah's exact five-point creed of God's Own Sovereignty: (1) *li-llāhi mā fī al-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍ*: all is God's: the sūrah's wide-name derived for the last time from the closing name-list of the creation-verse (2:164) and of the ribā (2:275-280's): God's own title of possession closing down, finally, upon every single thought and ledger-entry you have ever carried: (2) *whether you disclose or hide*: God shall *bring you to account for it*: the verb in its God's own verbal form is the Arab verb *ḥāsaba* — *to audit*: the Great Audit: *nothing hidden*: *none of our hearts e'er shone* — not even the buried germs of inmost intention: and the tradition perceives in this closing no wrath-territory but the *very shrug-of-Heaven* — *forgave whomsoever He wills — and punishes whomsoever He wills* — the two wills coming *after* the audit without explanation: *not two tokens of an indifferent God*: the two great rememberings of God's Own Absolute Freedom: the *mashīʾa* — the divine Will — whose beloved servant *either* forgives anyone entirely freely *or* punishes anyone with precisely-matched justice — with no celestial restraint *between* them but the sovereign Choice of God Himself — *and God is Powerful over all things.*

**The Companions' Weeping — and God's Own Lifting-Off**

The tradition preserved the poignant record of how the Companions received this verse (al-Ṭabarī's own reports at the end of the sūrah, widely repeated in the commentary lineage): the verse, descended with its words *whether you disclose what is in your souls or hide it — God will bring you to account for it*, fell upon them like thunderous dread: the Companions sat weeping: *they wept with fear* — swore with amazement: *if we are to be held to account for everything in our souls*, they cried, *who among us can be saved?* — their very distress reaching the borders of despair, and according to the transmitted accounts Gabriel returned from Heaven with the *next two verses* that closes the entire sūrah — verses 285–286. The next two verses answered with the solace of His own words: *lā yukallifu Allāhu nafsan illā wusʿahā* — God tasks no soul beyond its capacity — the load always matched to the shoulders, the account always matched to the soul's actual capacity to carry it: and the tradition ever afterwards taught thereby that the Great Audit weighs deeds and intentions, not the fleeting phantoms of the mind — the Prophet's own report calming every fearful heart: *"God has absolved my community of mistakes, forgetfulness, and what they were compelled to do"* (Ibn Mājah 2043; al-Ḥākim — the Prophet's transmission of God's own answer, always cited beside this verse)

**The Tradition at its End**

With the longest sūrah's final passages now descending as one harmony, the whole chamber of secrets — whatever the Book has recorded of concealments (2:76), hardened hearts (2:74), oaths (2:224–227), testimony suppressed (2:283) — is now called to the Great Court of the Account: *li-llāhi mā fī al-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍ* — all is His: the secrets, the hearts, the oaths, the ledgers: you cannot out-hide the Recorder; you cannot over-rule the Ledger-keeper; you can only reconcile yourself with Him and with His reign. And the tradition preserves as its final counsel the answer of the believers of every age:

> *"Take account of yourselves before you are taken to account."* — the words of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb — the standing counsel carried down the whole caliphal age from this very verse's instruction: the believers' response to 2:284 has always been the same: *we audit ourselves before He audits us; we open the ledger before its final opening* — and then the Last Accounting arrives not as shock but as gratitude: *unto Thee is the journey's end* — the very phrase of the next verse — God bringing all His own accounts to their rendering — with all the heavens and earth being His, forever, *and God is Powerful over all things.*

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:285

> **The Messenger ˹firmly˺ believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. They ˹all˺ believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers. ˹They proclaim,˺ “We make no distinction between any of His messengers.” And they say, “We hear and obey. ˹We seek˺ Your forgiveness, our Lord! And to You ˹alone˺ is the final return.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Creed's Diamond — Two Verses from Beneath the Throne**

The end of the Sūrah of the Cow is its crown: and the tradition records the crown's origin — *given from a storehouse beneath the Throne*: the Prophet himself said: *"I was given the last two verses of 'The Cow' from a treasure beneath the Throne — I have not known anyone before me to have been given them"* (Muslim 807) — the same two verses being among the trove of the gifts brought in the Night-Journey alike: the five prayers, the sealing-verses of the Cow, and forgiveness for his community for everyone from it *who does not associate anything with God — al embracing of the account* (Muslim 807 — the Prophet's heavenly-bringing of cow-seal found also at the end of the sūrah of tradition's own isrāʾ books) — and other authenticated traditions only make the seal more beloved: *"Whoever recites the two verses sealing 'The Cow' at night* — *they will suffice him"* (al-Bukhari 4008, 5009; Muslim 808 — from Abū Masʿūd al-Badrī — *kafātahu*: suffice him: *which the commentators immediately interpret either as sufficient in place of the night's worship* or *sufficient for all the protections he needed*): it carries-out literally every dawn of the Muslim world from that night of the Prophet's own ascension until the trumpet of the Resurrection.

**"We Hear and Obey"**

The creed begins simply — the creed of every believing Muslim until the Day of Judgment: *āmana al-rasūlu bi-mā unzila ilayhi min rabbihi wa'l-muʾminūn* — "The Messenger believes in what was sent down to him from his Lord — as do the believers." — *kullun āmana bi-llāhi wa malāʾikatihi wa kutubihi wa rusulihi* — "each believes in God, His angels, His Books, and His messengers": the five articles of the Islamic creed now crowned in verse-form with the exact same five articled at 2:177 (the piracy-verse of piety where charity, prayer and alms completed them) and spelled out once more at 4:136 (by exact same catalogue as standing creed-essence): belief in God (first), angels (second), Books (third), messengers (fourth), and the Return-to-Him (fifth — *unto Thee is the journey's end* recited by the believers' own velvet-oft-quotation) — with the line's next-particular, *lā nufarriqu bayna aḥadin min rusulihi* — **"we make no distinction among any of His messengers"** — sealing the sūrah's eternal retracing from v. 136's own *la nufarriqu* — the same creed-statement the believers taught to the sūrah's own Abrahamic-creed: lest they fall into the Jews' abandoning of Jesus, or into the Christians' abandoning of the last prophecy: *we accept them all*: the believer's own uniform answer so long as God has set down His prophets — *we pass none — we pass all*: — *heavenly human-rights in the Believers' creed*: and the now-famous response-song already heard and fueled at the end of every calamity-verse of the sūrah's own later-opening to the sūrah's believers' own participial response —

> *samiʿnā wa aṭaʿnā* — **"We hear, and we obey"** —
