> the very words the tafsīr-tradition — in all of Ibn Kathīr's and al-Ṭabarī's recorded reports — says God permitted the Companions *to replace* with their own favored reply to every divine command: for when ordered to repeat their initial ancestors' habit ("samiʿnā" would be transformed into *"samiʿnā wa ʿaṣaynā"* — "*we hear and we disobey*") — as the Child of Israel once replied 2:51's own sullied-countertest at 4:46 — the Lord permits them free-choice instead: *we hear, and we obey* — granting them precisely what the Children had never truly obeyed in — God set in the same mark with His Own "I have heard you" — as the hadith-fixtures report it at every one of this creed's supplications: *I shall surely answer*: *I have done so.*

**Thy Forgiveness, Our Lord — Unto Thee the Journey's End**

And so the creed ends in two magnanimous appeals — *ghufrānaka rabbanā* — **"Thy forgiveness, our Lord!"** — the believers' own last prayers after every of obedience's own trails and errors; with the clause's grammatical stitching * maghfraka* (without a verb) being read as its own abridged entreaty, *grant us Thy forgiveness* — *forgive us* — the actions' unavoidable grind of shortcomings of the ear-and-obey already denoted at the sūrah's *whole*: for the believers' first word was *obey* — yet they knew obedience comes wrapped in failing — so their second word was *forgive* — for forgiveness is what the obedient always need: and its second clause — *wa ilayka al-maṣīr* — "and unto Thee is the journey's end": *maṣīr* — *the point of arrival*: the creed's own eschatological seal set upon the abiding crown: the believer's standing attitude: *we head for God, we go to God — and God meets us when we arrive* — the universal round of birth, life and death closing upon the believer's voyage from dust back to dust: *unto Thee is the journey's end.* — and the tradition also remembers Muʿādh ibn Jabal's own heart-record that upon completing the recitation of al-Baqarah he would say **āmīn** — its own benediction sealed with the last word of the sūrah's very last verse-settling forever — *Āmīn* — God's Acceptable Answer — as it has been said by all the believers in the whole final-corner of the Book itself, ever and ever from the Prophet's death until the end of all community of God's servants from this earth *unto Thee is the journey's end*: and so this creedal word has rung from the believers' response for all the centuries of Islam since the Prophet's own companions — *we hear and we obey* — *Thy forgiveness, our Lord* — *unto Thee is the journey's end* — *Āmīn*.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:286

> **Allah does not require of any soul more than what it can afford. All good will be for its own benefit, and all evil will be to its own loss. ˹The believers pray,˺ “Our Lord! Do not punish us if we forget or make a mistake. Our Lord! Do not place a burden on us like the one you placed on those before us. Our Lord! Do not burden us with what we cannot bear. Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our ˹only˺ Guardian. So grant us victory over the disbelieving people.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**No Soul Tasked Beyond Capacity — God's Last Mercy**

The sūrah closes upon the pillar that calms the storm every believer has singularly found crashing above him: *lā yukallifu Allāhu nafsan illā wusʿahā* — "God tasks no soul beyond its capacity": *lahā mā kasabat wa ʿalayhā mā aktasabat* — "it shall have what it has earned — and be subject to what it has perpetrated": the plainest law of just-sideline-justice of the entire Book with direct siblings throughout the long chain (2:233, 6:152, 7:42, 23:62): with the two verbs mirroring the two sides of the one spiritual ledger: *kasaba* — *earned for herself the good* — *aktasaba* — perpetrated against herself the bad — the two root-forms being the Book's most-careful attribution for all of audit: *each soul carries whatever she has worked for in full and whatever she's worked against in full* — a perfect equation (as already taught at v. 134 twice: *lahā mā kasabat wa lakum mā kasabtum*): — and the Book then closes from high to low with its own perfume of the great six-petition-prayer — the most diligently memorized duʿāʾ of every believer in God upon this earth from its expiry at the Cow-surah's end until this hour of every heavenly ascent into Paradise's own fold thereafter.

**Take Us Not to Task — The Six Petitions of the Ummah**

The prayer begins with its own most universal of the six petitions: *rabbanā lā tuʾākhidhnā in nasīnā aw akhṭaʾanā* — "our Lord, take us not to task if we forget — or err": with the two ruling words being illumined by God's own most divinely-beloved prophetic declaration upon them: the tradition's very very most important hadith-service on the wiping-away of the boundary-keeper of misdeeds: *"Truly God has absolved my community of mistakes, forgetfulness — and that which they were compelled to do"* — the famous absolution of every believer by God's own grant of hope ever since (recorded at Ibn Mājah 2043 and al-Ḥākim, graded ṣaḥīḥ by the tradition's authorities) — the Prophet's own transmission of the divine amnesty standing as the seal of every age's expiation: *no accounting for mistakes* (the law-broke without intent); *no accounting for forgetfulness* (the prayer that slips the memory while fast caught in duty's burdens): *no accounting upon that to which we are coerced* (by sword and by shaft): and the beautiful recorded reply of God at each of the following lines of this last duʿāʾ — with the traditions from Ibn ʿAbbās (and others in the mufassirūn's chain) reporting that after every phrase the Prophet or the believers uttered of these six petitions, the reply came back: **"I have done so"** or **"Yes"** — Gabriel himself vouchsafing in some of the longer accounts: *He has granted it*.

**No Burden Like Those Before Us**

The second petition bows itself toward the long covenant-burden of the earlier Churches, and leaves the believers' own petition-less scholarship out to the reader: *rabbanā wa lā taḥmil ʿalaynā iṣran kamā ḥamaltahu ʿalā alladhīna min qablinā* — "our Lord — lay not upon us a burden like that Thou laid upon those before us": *iṣr* — *a heavy yoke*: the burden of the ancient covenant whose bindings the sūrah's whole Children-of-Israel cycle has been opening to the eye from verse 40 onward: the restrictions of food (4:160), the Sabbaths (4:154), the casuistries of the inherited law — and God lifting that *iṣr* from the new covenant's shoulders, as His own word has it at 7:157: *"He relieves them of their burden and the chains that were upon them"* — the believers pleading thereby to remain forever at that lighter hand: *our Lord, lay not upon us a burden like that Thou laid upon those before us.*

**Nothing We Cannot Bear**

The third petition lifts the last big all-eyes balcony on the suffering of every church from eternity: *rabbanā wa lā tuḥammilnā mā lā ṭāqata lanā bih* — "our Lord — impose not upon us that which we have not the strength to bear": with the invocation-punchword being the sūrah's own long recounting of the times of heavy duty-at-the-point and crying-out at the crossroads of the sūrah's own preceding religion-crises as testimony: *burden us not with that we have not the strength to bear*: and the tradition's own sweetest teaching of relief:

> *"Religion is easy, and no one overburdens himself in religion without being conquered by it."* (al-Bukhārī 39 — the Prophet's canonical maxim of ease, always cited beside this verse: *innā al-dīna yusrun*: the religion is easy — the seal of God's knowing precisely what His servants can bear)=

and the Book's own ever-sounding precept of 22:78: *He has placed no hardship upon you in the religion* — the last recess of v. 2:286's petition *mā lā ṭāqata lanā bih*:

**Pardon, Forgiveness, Mercy — The Triple Headspring**

The fourth triad-petition stands alone in all the ummah's world as the most-comprehensive three-word plea in any possible human speech — the believers' own troika of remission's Names all strung together at once: *wa-ʿfu ʿannā* — **and pardon us** — *wa-ghfir lanā* — **and forgive us** — *wa-rḥamnā* — **and have mercy upon us**: the three petition-terms of God's own three-arrangement-forgiveness-remitting traditions coalesced into one's all-bearing sheltering one: *ʿafw* — *pardon* — the total effacement of the charge from off the tablet itself (along with its effacing-removes even the remembrance-of-the-crime, as the school notes); *maghfirah* — *forgiveness* — the veil-covering of the sin so it will disgrace you nor punish you (as the root *gh-f-r* betokens, as a covering like a helmet over a face); and *raḥmah* — *mercy* — God's own continued-compassion-swing over every rift and breach — from the skies-down over all His creatures ever after: the believers taught to string all three together: *pardon* the erasure; *forgive* the covering; *mercy* the continuing love which sustains over all: the three words thereby coronating the sūrah's own long-chain of Names-pairs ever more precisely (Forbearing-Merciful, Forgiving-Clement, Forgiving-Merciful, Hearing-Knowing etc.) at the very end of their usage: *huwa rabbanā — wa-ʿfu ʿannā wa-ghfir lanā wa-raḥmanā* — *pardon, forgive, mercy*: the triple clause of every Muslim believer's own covenant-word toward his God every morning and every evening: their final blessing-invocation already itself made *the most-believed disciples-chorus prayer in the whole history of piety in God's own book* — with its note * and the same recorded answers coming: "I have pardoned": "I have forgiven": "I have had mercy upon you"*.

**Thou Art Our Master — Upon the Disbelieving People**

The last lines complete the sūrah's own arching back to its own very original battle-cry of 2:142-217's on all its *war-divine* of ribā-the-theft-commission-to-clearings in God's Own transcending-sworn way: *anta mawlānā fa-nṣurnā ʿalā al-qawmi al-kāfirīn* — "Thou art our Master — so help us against the disbelieving people": *(1) *anta mawlānā*: the *mawlā* — *master-guardian-patron* — the *wālī* of all His believing community being the Same who says at 3:150: "God is your Protector (mawlā) — and He is the most excellent of helpers" — the *you are our Master* oral pledge already enshrined in this way: and *(2) *fa-nṣurnā*: *help* — the verb of victory — against the disbelieving people*: the word's own phrasing distinguishing it plainly from all later ages' tribal-contest borrowings, and always seeking *victory* — the disbelieving foil being *the disbelieving people* — not people-everywhere-everything (as numbered by its plural form — whether idolaters of Makkah or the worst betrayal-covenants of the earlier tribes) — and the end of the whole sūrah's own learned long-sobbing chooses its own vanishing-point in full calm-verdict upon all its reciters and their final benedictions: *so help us* — so the whole Nation of God recites its end-soothe as one crowd, per its earliest practice of the congregational finishing in *āmīn* — the same amen already granted to Muʿādh ibn Jabal at the Prophet's own hand-clasped upon the sūrah's final-readings, and the amen to which the believer's own entire ummah has nodded and kneeled upon for the sūrah's very last vows forever since: "Āmīn — O God — amen": with the Book's own long rule now closing and sealing its work from crowned-apex down toward every downward turns of the path of its commentaries-working: *pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy upon us — and help us — and we say — Āmīn*: until the end of days of the awesome sūrah's own final mansion of minorities-committed century: the Cow is complete — and all praise belongs to God, the Exalted and the Magnificent.

---
**[End of the commentary on Sūrah al-Baqarah]**
